/* Caption: Program to build a linked list, print it, and free it. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define Item with a value and a next pointer.
   2. Write push_front() that mallocs a node and links it in front of head.
   3. Write print_list() that follows next until NULL.
   4. Write free_list() that frees every node.
   5. Push 6 values, print the list and free it. */
typedef struct Item {
    int value;
    struct Item *next;
} Item;

/* Allocate a new node and put it in front of the current head. */
Item *push_front(Item *head, int value) {
    Item *node = malloc(sizeof(Item));
    if (node == NULL) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Out of memory\n");
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }
    node->value = value;
    node->next = head;
    return node;
}

void print_list(const Item *head) {
    for (const Item *cur = head; cur != NULL; cur = cur->next) {
        printf("%d -> ", cur->value);
    }
    printf("NULL\n");
}

/* Free every node; save next before freeing the current one. */
void free_list(Item *head) {
    while (head != NULL) {
        Item *next = head->next;
        free(head);
        head = next;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    Item *head = NULL;
    head = push_front(head, 6);
    head = push_front(head, 83);
    head = push_front(head, 13);
    head = push_front(head, 30);
    head = push_front(head, 94);
    head = push_front(head, 48);
    print_list(head);
    free_list(head);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: Each Item holds a value and a pointer to the next node. push_front()
   allocates a node with malloc, puts it in front of head and returns it; print_list()
   follows the next pointers until NULL; free_list() frees every node. main() pushes 6
   values, so they print in reverse order. */

/* Caption: How do I compute the factorial of a number with a loop in C? */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write factorial(num) with result = 1.
   2. Multiply result by every number from 2 to num.
   3. Return result.
   4. Print 4! as an unsigned long long. */
/* Multiply 1 * 2 * ... * n. */
unsigned long long factorial(int num) {
    unsigned long long result = 1;
    for (int i = 2; i <= num; i++) {
        result *= i;
    }
    return result;
}

int main(void) {
    int num = 4;
    printf("%d! = %llu\n", num, factorial(num));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: factorial() multiplies result by every number from 2 up to num. main()
   prints 4! as an unsigned long long, because factorials grow very fast. */
// END

/* Caption: Check whether a year is a leap year. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write is_leap(year).
   2. A year divisible by 4 is a leap year, unless it is divisible by 100.
   3. Years divisible by 400 are leap years again.
   4. Check 2085 and print the result. */
/* Leap years divide by 4, except centuries, which must divide by 400. */
int is_leap(int year) {
    return (year % 4 == 0 && year % 100 != 0) || year % 400 == 0;
}

int main(void) {
    int year = 2085;
    if (is_leap(year)) {
        printf("%d is a leap year\n", year);
    } else {
        printf("%d is not a leap year\n", year);
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: is_leap() returns true for years divisible by 4, except century years,
   which must also be divisible by 400. main() checks 2085 and prints whether it is a leap
   year. */
// END

/* Caption: Reverse the characters of a word. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <string.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write reverse_string() for str.
   2. Set i to the first index and j to the last.
   3. Swap the two characters and move i and j inwards until they meet.
   4. Reverse window and print it. */
/* Swap characters from both ends until they meet in the middle. */
void reverse_string(char *str) {
    int i = 0;
    int j = strlen(str) - 1;
    while (i < j) {
        char tmp = str[i];
        str[i] = str[j];
        str[j] = tmp;
        i++;
        j--;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    char str[] = "window";
    reverse_string(str);
    printf("%s\n", str);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: reverse_string() swaps characters from both ends of str, moving inwards
   until the two indexes meet. main() reverses the word window in place and prints it. */
// END

/* Caption: Compute the mean of a list of numbers. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write average() that takes items and len.
   2. Add the values into the double sum.
   3. Return sum / len.
   4. Print the average with two decimals. */
/* Sum the values, then divide by how many there are. */
double average(const int items[], int len) {
    double sum = 0.0;
    int k = 0;
    while (k < len) {
        sum += items[k];
        k++;
    }
    return sum / len;
}

int main(void) {
    int items[] = {88, 96, 17, 37, 11, 24};
    int len = sizeof(items) / sizeof(items[0]);
    printf("Mean = %.2f\n", average(items, len));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: average() adds the 6 values of items into the double sum and divides by
   len, so the mean keeps its decimal part even when the values are whole numbers. main()
   prints it with two decimals. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to add two 3x2 matrices. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define ROWS as 3 and COLS as 2.
   2. Loop over every row r and column c.
   3. Store a[r][c] + b[r][c] in sum and print it. */
#define ROWS 3
#define COLS 2

int main(void) {
    int a[ROWS][COLS] = {{4, 2}, {6, 1}, {8, 4}};
    int b[ROWS][COLS] = {{6, 4}, {8, 6}, {0, 4}};
    int sum[ROWS][COLS];
    /* Each entry of the result is the sum of the matching entries. */
    for (int r = 0; r < ROWS; r++) {
        for (int c = 0; c < COLS; c++) {
            sum[r][c] = a[r][c] + b[r][c];
            printf("%3d", sum[r][c]);
        }
        printf("\n");
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: Both matrices are 3x2 two-dimensional arrays. Two nested loops visit every
   row r and column c, store a[r][c] + b[r][c] in sum and print each row. */
// END

/* Caption: Multiply two 3x3 matrices. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define N as 3.
   2. For every i and j, add a[i][k] * b[k][j] over k into product[i][j].
   3. Print product row by row. */
#define N 3

int main(void) {
    int a[N][N] = {{3, 9, 3}, {1, 8, 2}, {7, 1, 5}};
    int b[N][N] = {{4, 9, 2}, {6, 3, 7}, {6, 3, 1}};
    int product[N][N] = {0};
    /* product[i][j] is row i of a times column j of b. */
    for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) {
        for (int j = 0; j < N; j++) {
            for (int k = 0; k < N; k++) {
                product[i][j] += a[i][k] * b[k][j];
            }
        }
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) {
        for (int j = 0; j < N; j++) {
            printf("%4d", product[i][j]);
        }
        printf("\n");
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: For each entry product[i][j] the innermost loop adds a[i][k] * b[k][j] over
   k, which is row i of a times column j of b. main() multiplies two 3x3 matrices and
   prints the product. */
// END

/* Caption: Swap two variables using pointers. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write swap() that takes pointers to two int values.
   2. Save *x in tmp, copy *y into *x, then tmp into *y.
   3. In main(), print x and y, call swap(&x, &y) and print them again. */
/* Pass addresses so the function can change the caller's variables. */
void swap(int *x, int *y) {
    int tmp = *x;
    *x = *y;
    *y = tmp;
}

int main(void) {
    int x = 23, y = 56;
    printf("Before: %d %d\n", x, y);
    swap(&x, &y);
    printf("After:  %d %d\n", x, y);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: swap() receives the addresses of x and y, so writing through the pointers
   *x and *y changes the caller's variables. tmp holds one value during the exchange.
   main() declares both variables on one line and prints them before and after the swap. */
// END

/* Caption: Build a FIFO queue using a ring buffer. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define a Queue with room for 16 items, a head and a count.
   2. Write enqueue() that stores at (head + count) % CAPACITY.
   3. Write dequeue() that takes the item at head and moves head on.
   4. Add 4 values, then remove and print them in order. */
#define CAPACITY 16

typedef struct {
    int items[CAPACITY];
    int head;
    int count;
} Queue;

bool enqueue(Queue *q, int value) {
    if (q->count == CAPACITY) {
        return false;
    }
    /* The tail wraps around to the start of the array. */
    q->items[(q->head + q->count) % CAPACITY] = value;
    q->count++;
    return true;
}

bool dequeue(Queue *q, int *value) {
    if (q->count == 0) {
        return false;
    }
    *value = q->items[q->head];
    q->head = (q->head + 1) % CAPACITY;
    q->count--;
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    Queue q = {.head = 0, .count = 0};
    enqueue(&q, 73);
    enqueue(&q, 4);
    enqueue(&q, 48);
    enqueue(&q, 79);
    int value;
    /* Items come out in the order they went in (first in, first out). */
    while (dequeue(&q, &value)) {
        printf("%d ", value);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: The Queue stores up to 16 items in a ring buffer: head is the oldest item
   and % CAPACITY wraps positions back to the start of the array. enqueue() adds at the
   back and dequeue() removes from the front, so main() gets its 4 values back in the same
   order (first in, first out). */
// END

/* Caption: Find the least common multiple of two numbers. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write gcd() with Euclid's algorithm: replace (a, b) by (b, a % b) until b is 0.
   2. Write lcm() as a / gcd(a, b) * b.
   3. Print the LCM of 270 and 56. */
/* Euclid: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a % b) until b becomes zero. */
int gcd(int a, int b) {
    while (b != 0) {
        int r = a % b;
        a = b;
        b = r;
    }
    return a;
}

/* lcm(a, b) = a / gcd(a, b) * b (divide first to avoid overflow). */
long lcm(int a, int b) {
    return (long)a / gcd(a, b) * b;
}

int main(void) {
    printf("lcm(270, 56) = %ld\n", lcm(270, 56));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: gcd() uses Euclid's algorithm: it keeps replacing (a, b) with (b, a % b)
   until b is 0. lcm() divides a by the gcd before multiplying by b, which avoids overflow.
   main() prints the LCM of 270 and 56. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to print the first 20 Fibonacci numbers. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Start with a = 0 and b = 1.
   2. Repeat 20 times and print a each time.
   3. Compute next = a + b, then set a = b and b = next. */
int main(void) {
    long a = 0, b = 1;
    /* Print a term, then slide the pair one step along the sequence. */
    for (int i = 0; i < 20; i++) {
        printf("%ld ", a);
        long next = a + b;
        a = b;
        b = next;
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: The loop keeps the last two numbers in a and b. Each round it prints a,
   then moves the pair forward: a becomes b and b becomes their sum. It prints the first 20
   Fibonacci numbers. */
// END

/* Caption: How do I count how many digits a number has in C? */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Start result at 0.
   2. Divide n by 10 and add one to result.
   3. Repeat until n is 0.
   4. Apply it to 773276 and print the result. */
/* Take the last digit with % 10, then drop it with / 10. */
int count_digits(int n) {
    int result = 0;
    while (n > 0) {
        result++;
        n /= 10;
    }
    return result;
}

int main(void) {
    int number = 773276;
    printf("count of digits of %d: %d\n", number, count_digits(number));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: count_digits() removes the last digit (n / 10) and adds one to result each
   time, until n reaches 0. main() applies it to 773276. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to create a singly linked list by inserting at the head. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define Item with a value and a next pointer.
   2. Write push_front() that mallocs a node and links it in front of head.
   3. Write print_list() that follows next until NULL.
   4. Write free_list() that frees every node.
   5. Push 6 values, print the list and free it. */
typedef struct Item {
    int value;
    struct Item *next;
} Item;

/* Allocate a new node and put it in front of the current head. */
Item *push_front(Item *head, int value) {
    Item *node = malloc(sizeof(Item));
    if (node == NULL) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Out of memory\n");
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }
    node->value = value;
    node->next = head;
    return node;
}

void print_list(const Item *head) {
    for (const Item *cur = head; cur != NULL; cur = cur->next) {
        printf("%d -> ", cur->value);
    }
    printf("NULL\n");
}

/* Free every node; save next before freeing the current one. */
void free_list(Item *head) {
    while (head != NULL) {
        Item *next = head->next;
        free(head);
        head = next;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    Item *head = NULL;
    head = push_front(head, 50);
    head = push_front(head, 37);
    head = push_front(head, 60);
    head = push_front(head, 25);
    head = push_front(head, 91);
    head = push_front(head, 5);
    print_list(head);
    free_list(head);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: Each Item holds a value and a pointer to the next node. push_front()
   allocates a node with malloc, puts it in front of head and returns it; print_list()
   follows the next pointers until NULL; free_list() frees every node. main() pushes 6
   values, so they print in reverse order. */
// END

/* Caption: How do I count the words in a sentence in C? */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <ctype.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write count_words() with words = 0 and an in_word flag.
   2. A space ends a word; a non-space after a space starts a new word and adds one to
      words.
   3. Return words and print it. */
/* A new word starts when a non-space follows a space (or the start). */
int count_words(const char *text) {
    int words = 0;
    int in_word = 0;
    for (int i = 0; text[i] != '\0'; i++) {
        if (isspace((unsigned char)text[i])) {
            in_word = 0;
        } else if (!in_word) {
            in_word = 1;
            words++;
        }
    }
    return words;
}

int main(void) {
    const char *sentence = "good comments explain why the code exists";
    printf("Words: %d\n", count_words(sentence));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: count_words() uses the flag in_word: a new word starts when a non-space
   character follows a space or the start of the text. main() prints the number of words in
   the sentence. */
// END

/* Caption: C program to calculate 7! using iteration. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write factorial(num) with result = 1.
   2. Multiply result by every number from 2 to num.
   3. Return result.
   4. Print 7! as an unsigned long long. */
/* Multiply 1 * 2 * ... * n. */
unsigned long long factorial(int num) {
    unsigned long long result = 1;
    for (int i = 2; i <= num; i++) {
        result *= i;
    }
    return result;
}

int main(void) {
    int num = 7;
    printf("%d! = %llu\n", num, factorial(num));
    return 0;

/* Explanation: factorial() multiplies result by every number from 2 up to num. main()
   prints 7! as an unsigned long long, because factorials grow very fast. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to reverse an array by swapping from both ends. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write reverse_array() for prices.
   2. Set i to the first index and j to the last.
   3. Swap prices[i] and prices[j], then move both inwards.
   4. Stop when i meets j and print the array. */
/* Swap the outer pair, then move both ends toward the middle. */
void reverse_array(int prices[], int length) {
    int i = 0;
    int j = length - 1;
    while (i < j) {
        int tmp = prices[i];
        prices[i] = prices[j];
        prices[j] = tmp;
        i++;
        j--;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    int prices[] = {16, 43, 67, 7, 50, 33, 95};
    const int length = 7;
    reverse_array(prices, length);
    for (int i = 0; i < length; i++) {
        printf("%d ", prices[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: reverse_array() swaps the first and last elements, then moves i forward and
   j backward until they meet, so the array is reversed in place without a second array.
   main() prints the reversed values. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to add 2 integers and print the sum. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Set num1 and num2.

   3. Print the calculation. */

    printf("%ld + %ld = %ld\n", num1, num2, sum);

   sum and prints the whole calculation. */

/* Caption: Use insertion sort to put numbers in descending order. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write insertion_sort() for the int array nums.
   2. Take each element in turn as current.
   3. Shift the smaller values of the sorted part one place right.
   4. Put current into the gap.
   5. Print the sorted values. */
/* Insert each element into the already sorted part on its left. */
void insertion_sort(int nums[], int length) {
    for (int i = 1; i < length; i++) {
        int current = nums[i];
        int j = i - 1;
        while (j >= 0 && nums[j] < current) {
            nums[j + 1] = nums[j];   /* shift bigger values right */
            j--;
        }
        nums[j + 1] = current;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    int nums[] = {43, 75, 84, 36, 43, 23, 62, 23, 33};
    const int length = 9;
    insertion_sort(nums, length);
    for (int i = 0; i < length; i++) {
        printf("%d ", nums[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: insertion_sort() takes each element in turn and shifts the smaller values
   of the sorted part one place right until the element fits. main() then prints the 9
   values in descending order. */
// END

/* Caption: How do I allocate an array with malloc and fill it with multiples in C? */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Use malloc to get room for 7 ints and check for NULL.
   2. Fill list with multiples.
   3. Print the values.
   4. Call free(list) at the end. */
int main(void) {
    int n = 7;
    /* Ask the heap for room for n ints; malloc returns NULL on failure. */
    int *list = malloc(n * sizeof(int));
    if (list == NULL) {
        fprintf(stderr, "malloc failed\n");
        return 1;
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        list[i] = 3 * i;
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        printf("%d ", list[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    free(list);   /* give the memory back */
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: malloc() reserves room for 7 ints on the heap and returns NULL if it fails,
   which the program checks. The first loop fills list with multiples, the second prints
   them, and free() gives the memory back at the end. */
// END

/* Caption: C program to generate the Fibonacci sequence. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Start with a = 0 and b = 1.
   2. Repeat 21 times and print a each time.
   3. Compute next = a + b, then set a = b and b = next. */
int main(void) {
    long a = 0, b = 1;
    /* Print a term, then slide the pair one step along the sequence. */
    for (int i = 0; i < 21; i++) {
        printf("%ld ", a);
        long next = a + b;
        a = b;
        b = next;
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: The loop keeps the last two numbers in a and b. Each round it prints a,
   then moves the pair forward: a becomes b and b becomes their sum. It prints the first 21
   Fibonacci numbers. */
// END

/* Caption: Implement a simple linked list with malloc and free. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define ListNode with a value and a next pointer.
   2. Write push_front() that mallocs a node and links it in front of head.
   3. Write print_list() that follows next until NULL.
   4. Write free_list() that frees every node.
   5. Push 5 values, print the list and free it. */
typedef struct ListNode {
    int value;
    struct ListNode *next;
} ListNode;

/* Allocate a new node and put it in front of the current head. */
ListNode *push_front(ListNode *head, int value) {
    ListNode *node = malloc(sizeof(ListNode));
    if (node == NULL) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Out of memory\n");
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }
    node->value = value;
    node->next = head;
    return node;
}

void print_list(const ListNode *head) {
    for (const ListNode *cur = head; cur != NULL; cur = cur->next) {
        printf("%d -> ", cur->value);
    }
    printf("NULL\n");
}

/* Free every node; save next before freeing the current one. */
void free_list(ListNode *head) {
    while (head != NULL) {
        ListNode *next = head->next;
        free(head);
        head = next;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    ListNode *head = NULL;
    head = push_front(head, 72);
    head = push_front(head, 70);
    head = push_front(head, 20);
    head = push_front(head, 7);
    head = push_front(head, 5);
    print_list(head);
    free_list(head);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: Each ListNode holds a value and a pointer to the next node. push_front()
   allocates a node with malloc, puts it in front of head and returns it; print_list()
   follows the next pointers until NULL; free_list() frees every node. main() pushes 5
   values, so they print in reverse order. */
// END

   1. Define struct Student with a name and a mark.

   3. Print each student and add the marks to total.
   4. Print total divided by the number of students. */
/* A struct groups a student's name and mark together. */

    char name[20];
    int mark;
};

int main(void) {
    struct Student students[] = {
        {"Lena", 50},
        {"Hana", 50},
        {"Chen", 59},
        {"Jia", 73},
        {"Noor", 59}
    };

/* Caption: Find the largest number in an array. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write max_of() that takes ages and length.
   2. Store ages[0] in m.
   3. Loop over the other elements and keep the largest value in m.
   4. Return m and print it. */
/* Start with the first element and keep the largest value seen so far. */
double max_of(const double ages[], int length) {
    double m = ages[0];
    for (int i = 1; i < length; i++) {
        if (ages[i] > m) {
            m = ages[i];
        }
    }
    return m;
}

int main(void) {
    double ages[] = {81.2, 82.5, 74.8, 87.9, 71.1};
    int length = sizeof(ages) / sizeof(ages[0]);
    printf("The largest value is %.2f\n", max_of(ages, length));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: max_of() takes the first element as the largest value so far and stores it
   in m. The loop compares every other element with m using > and keeps the largest one.
   main() prints the largest of the 5 values. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to use a struct to return several results from one function. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define a Stats struct with min, max and average.
   2. Write array_stats() that fills one Stats in a loop.
   3. Return the struct.
   4. Print st.min, st.max and st.average. */
typedef struct {
    int min;
    int max;
    double average;
} Stats;

/* Pack several results into one struct and return it. */
Stats array_stats(const int v[], int n) {
    Stats s = {v[0], v[0], 0.0};
    double total = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        if (v[i] < s.min) {
            s.min = v[i];
        }
        if (v[i] > s.max) {
            s.max = v[i];
        }
        total += v[i];
    }
    s.average = total / n;
    return s;
}

int main(void) {
    int values[] = {22, 59, 73, 4, 19};
    int n = sizeof(values) / sizeof(values[0]);
    Stats st = array_stats(values, n);
    printf("Min %d, Max %d, Average %.2f\n", st.min, st.max, st.average);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: Stats groups three results. array_stats() fills one Stats while it loops
   over the 5 values and returns the whole struct, which is a clean way to return several
   results at once. main() reads them as st.min, st.max and st.average. */
// END

/* Caption: Return a circle's area and circumference through pointers. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write circle_measures() with the pointers area and circumference.
   2. Store PI * r * r and 2 * PI * r through them.
   3. Print both for a radius of 1.0. */
#define PI 3.14159265

void circle_measures(double radius, double *area, double *circumference) {
    *area = PI * radius * radius;
    *circumference = 2 * PI * radius;
}

int main(void) {
    double radius = 1.0;
    double area, circumference;
    circle_measures(radius, &area, &circumference);
    printf("Area: %.2f, Circumference: %.2f\n", area, circumference);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: circle_measures() computes two results from one radius and stores them
   through the pointers area and circumference. main() declares both variables on one line,
   passes their addresses and prints the results for a radius of 1.0. */
// END

/* Caption: Program to find the greatest common divisor of two numbers. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write gcd() with Euclid's algorithm.
   2. Replace (a, b) by (b, a % b) until b is 0.
   3. Return a and print the GCD of 246 and 98. */
/* Euclid: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a % b) until b becomes zero. */
int gcd(int a, int b) {
    while (b != 0) {
        int r = a % b;
        a = b;
        b = r;
    }
    return a;
}

int main(void) {
    int x = 246, y = 98;
    printf("gcd(%d, %d) = %d\n", x, y, gcd(x, y));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: gcd() uses Euclid's algorithm: it keeps replacing (a, b) with (b, a % b)
   until b is 0. The last non-zero value is the greatest common divisor, and main() prints
   the GCD of 246 and 98. */
// END

/* Caption: Calculate 13! using recursion. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write factorial(x) that calls itself.
   2. Return 1 when x is 1 or less.
   3. Otherwise return x * factorial(x - 1).
   4. Print 13! as an unsigned long long. */
/* n! = n * (n - 1)!, and 0! = 1 stops the recursion. */
unsigned long long factorial(int x) {
    if (x <= 1) {
        return 1;
    }
    return x * factorial(x - 1);
}

int main(void) {
    int x = 13;
    printf("%d! = %llu\n", x, factorial(x));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: factorial() calls itself: n! is n * (n - 1)!, and the recursion stops when
   x is 1 or less. main() prints 13! as an unsigned long long, because factorials grow very
   fast. */
// END

/* Caption: How do I count the even values in a list of integers in C? */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write count_even() that takes ages and size.
   2. For each element, test ages[k] % 2 == 0.
   3. Add one to found for every even number.
   4. Return found and print it. */
/* A number is even when the remainder after dividing by 2 is zero. */
int count_even(const int ages[], int size) {
    int found = 0;
    int k = 0;
    while (k < size) {
        if (ages[k] % 2 == 0) {
            found++;
        }
        k++;
    }
    return found;
}

int main(void) {
    int ages[] = {87, 40, 67, 23, 56, 93, 13, 17, 94, 64, 79, 89};
    int size = 12;
    printf("Even numbers: %d\n", count_even(ages, size));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: count_even() tests each element of ages with the % operator: a remainder of
   0 after dividing by 2 means the number is even, so found goes up by one. main() prints
   how many of the 12 values are even. */
// END

/* Caption: How do I write a function that tests if a value is inside a range in C? */

/* Plan:
   1. Write in_range(x, low, high).
   2. Return true when x >= low and x <= high.
   3. Print whether 79 is inside 65 to 69. */
/* true when low <= x <= high */
bool in_range(int x, int low, int high) {
    return x >= low && x <= high;
}

int main(void) {
    int value = 79, low = 65, high = 69;
    printf("%d is %s the range %d to %d\n", value,
           in_range(value, low, high) ? "inside" : "outside", low, high);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: in_range() takes the value and both limits and returns true only when the
   value is at least low and at most high. main() declares value, low and high on one line
   and prints whether 79 is inside 65 to 69. */
// END

/* Caption: Find a number in a sorted array with binary search. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Make sure the array is sorted.
   2. Set lo to 0 and hi to len - 1.
   3. While lo <= hi, compare the middle element mid with the key.
   4. Return the index if it matches; otherwise keep only the half that can hold the
      key.
   5. Return -1 if the range becomes empty, and print the index of 201. */
/* The array must be sorted. Each step halves the range that can still hold the key. */
int binary_search(const int items[], int len, int key) {
    int lo = 0;
    int hi = len - 1;
    while (lo <= hi) {
        int mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;
        if (items[mid] == key) {
            return mid;
        } else if (items[mid] < key) {
            lo = mid + 1;   /* key is in the right half */
        } else {
            hi = mid - 1;   /* key is in the left half */
        }
    }
    return -1;
}

int main(void) {
    int items[] = {29, 57, 69, 74, 82, 94, 102, 154, 156, 169, 171, 196};
    int len = 12;
    int index = binary_search(items, len, 201);
    printf("Index of 201: %d\n", index);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: binary_search() needs a sorted array. It keeps the range from lo to hi,
   compares the middle element mid with the key and throws away the half that cannot
   contain it, so it needs only about log2(n) steps. main() looks for 201 and prints its
   index, or -1 if it is not there. */
// END

/* Caption: Return a Point struct from a function. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define a Point struct with x and y.
   2. Write midpoint() that returns a Point with the averages of x and y.
   3. Print mid.x and mid.y. */
typedef struct {
    double x;
    double y;
} Point;

/* A function can return a whole struct. */
Point midpoint(Point a, Point b) {
    Point m = {(a.x + b.x) / 2, (a.y + b.y) / 2};
    return m;
}

int main(void) {
    Point p = {18, -6}, q = {-11, 10};
    Point mid = midpoint(p, q);
    printf("Midpoint: (%.1f, %.1f)\n", mid.x, mid.y);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: midpoint() takes two Point structs and returns a new Point whose x and y
   are the averages of theirs. main() declares p and q on one line, (18, -6) and (-11, 10),
   and prints the midpoint using mid.x and mid.y. */
// END

/* Caption: Find the arithmetic mean of 3 double values. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write array_average() that takes prices and size.
   2. Add the values into the double total.
   3. Return total / size.
   4. Print the average with two decimals. */
/* Sum the values, then divide by how many there are. */
double array_average(const double prices[], int size) {
    double total = 0.0;
    for (int j = 0; j < size; j++) {
        total += prices[j];
    }
    return total / size;
}

int main(void) {
    double prices[] = {77.3, 62.9, 37.0};
    const int size = 3;
    printf("Mean = %.2f\n", array_average(prices, size));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: array_average() adds the 3 values of prices into the double total and
   divides by size, so the mean keeps its decimal part even when the values are whole
   numbers. main() prints it with two decimals. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to implement a circular queue with an array. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define a Queue with room for 10 items, a head and a count.
   2. Write enqueue() that stores at (head + count) % CAPACITY.
   3. Write dequeue() that takes the item at head and moves head on.
   4. Add 3 values, then remove and print them in order. */
#define CAPACITY 10

typedef struct {
    int items[CAPACITY];
    int head;
    int count;
} Queue;

bool enqueue(Queue *q, int value) {
    if (q->count == CAPACITY) {
        return false;
    }
    /* The tail wraps around to the start of the array. */
    q->items[(q->head + q->count) % CAPACITY] = value;
    q->count++;
    return true;
}

bool dequeue(Queue *q, int *value) {
    if (q->count == 0) {
        return false;
    }
    *value = q->items[q->head];
    q->head = (q->head + 1) % CAPACITY;
    q->count--;
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    Queue q = {.head = 0, .count = 0};
    enqueue(&q, 23);
    enqueue(&q, 9);
    enqueue(&q, 6);
    int value;
    /* Items come out in the order they went in (first in, first out). */
    while (dequeue(&q, &value)) {
        printf("%d ", value);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: The Queue stores up to 10 items in a ring buffer: head is the oldest item
   and % CAPACITY wraps positions back to the start of the array. enqueue() adds at the
   back and dequeue() removes from the front, so main() gets its 3 values back in the same
   order (first in, first out). */
// END

/* Caption: How do I store students in an array of structs and find the class average in C? */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define struct Student with a name and a mark.
   2. Store 3 students in an array.
   3. Print each student and add the marks to total.
   4. Print total divided by the number of students. */
/* A struct groups a student's name and mark together. */
struct Student {
    char name[20];
    int mark;
};

int main(void) {
    struct Student students[] = {
        {"Dara", 45},
        {"Ivan", 100},
        {"Chen", 42}
    };
    int count = sizeof(students) / sizeof(students[0]);
    double total = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < count; i++) {
        printf("%s: %d\n", students[i].name, students[i].mark);
        total += students[i].mark;
    }
    printf("Average mark: %.1f\n", total / count);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: struct Student groups a name and a mark. main() stores 3 students in an
   array of structs, prints each one, adds the marks to total and prints the average. */
// END

/* Caption: Program to sort an array in ascending order using bubble sort. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write bubble_sort() for the int array numbers.
   2. Compare each pair of neighbours.
   3. Swap them when they are in the wrong order for ascending order.
   4. Repeat the passes until the array is sorted.
   5. Print the sorted values. */
/* Repeatedly swap neighbours that are in the wrong order. */
void bubble_sort(int numbers[], int length) {
    for (int i = 0; i < length - 1; i++) {
        for (int j = 0; j < length - 1 - i; j++) {
            if (numbers[j] > numbers[j + 1]) {
                int tmp = numbers[j];
                numbers[j] = numbers[j + 1];
                numbers[j + 1] = tmp;
            }
        }
    }
}

int main(void) {
    int numbers[] = {89, 22, 21, 38, 35, 54};
    const int length = 6;
    bubble_sort(numbers, length);
    for (int i = 0; i < length; i++) {
        printf("%d ", numbers[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: bubble_sort() walks through numbers again and again and swaps neighbours
   that are in the wrong order, so the largest values move to the end first. main() then
   prints the 6 values in ascending order. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to find the minimum and maximum of an array with one function. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write min_max() with the array, its length and the pointers min and max.
   2. Start both at the first element.
   3. Update *min and *max while looping over the rest.
   4. Declare min and max, pass their addresses and print them. */
/* One pass finds both results; they are stored through the pointers. */
void min_max(const int samples[], int len, int *min, int *max) {
    *min = samples[0];
    *max = samples[0];
    for (int i = 1; i < len; i++) {
        if (samples[i] < *min) {
            *min = samples[i];
        }
        if (samples[i] > *max) {
            *max = samples[i];
        }
    }
}

int main(void) {
    int samples[] = {18, 51, 40, 79};
    int len = sizeof(samples) / sizeof(samples[0]);
    int min, max;
    min_max(samples, len, &min, &max);
    printf("Min: %d, Max: %d\n", min, max);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: A C function can return only one value, so min_max() returns void and
   writes its two results through the pointer parameters min and max. main() declares min
   and max on one line and passes their addresses with &, then prints both results for the
   4 values. */
// END

/* Caption: Swap two variables using pointers. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write swap() that takes pointers to two double values.
   2. Save *x in tmp, copy *y into *x, then tmp into *y.
   3. In main(), print x and y, call swap(&x, &y) and print them again. */
/* Pass addresses so the function can change the caller's variables. */
void swap(double *x, double *y) {
    double tmp = *x;
    *x = *y;
    *y = tmp;
}

int main(void) {
    double x = 56.1, y = 11.2;
    printf("Before: %.2f %.2f\n", x, y);
    swap(&x, &y);
    printf("After:  %.2f %.2f\n", x, y);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: swap() receives the addresses of x and y, so writing through the pointers
   *x and *y changes the caller's variables. tmp holds one value during the exchange.
   main() declares both variables on one line and prints them before and after the swap. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to reverse the digits of a number. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Start result at 0.
   2. Multiply result by 10, add n % 10, then divide n by 10.
   3. Repeat until n is 0.
   4. Apply it to 593208 and print the result. */
/* Take the last digit with % 10, then drop it with / 10. */
int reverse_digits(int n) {
    int result = 0;
    while (n > 0) {
        result = result * 10 + n % 10;
        n /= 10;
    }
    return result;
}

int main(void) {
    int number = 593208;
    printf("reverse of digits of %d: %d\n", number, reverse_digits(number));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: reverse_digits() shifts result one place left (result * 10) and adds the
   last digit of n, which reverses the order. main() applies it to 593208. */
// END

/* Caption: Write lines to a text file and read them back. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Open log.txt in write mode and check for NULL.
   2. Write 3 lines with fprintf and close the file.
   3. Open it again in read mode.
   4. Read and print each line with fgets, then close the file. */
int main(void) {
    FILE *file = fopen("log.txt", "w");
    if (file == NULL) {
        perror("fopen");
        return 1;
    }
    fprintf(file, "arrays in c start at index zero\n");
    fprintf(file, "good comments explain why the code exists\n");
    fprintf(file, "keep functions short and focused\n");
    fclose(file);

    /* Reopen the file for reading and print it line by line. */
    file = fopen("log.txt", "r");
    if (file == NULL) {
        perror("fopen");
        return 1;
    }
    char line[128];
    while (fgets(line, sizeof(line), file) != NULL) {
        printf("%s", line);
    }
    fclose(file);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: fopen() in write mode creates log.txt, fprintf() writes 3 lines into it and
   fclose() saves it. The file is then opened again in read mode, and fgets() reads it back
   line by line into the buffer line, which is printed. Every fopen() result is checked for
   NULL. */
// END

/* Caption: Test if 226 is a prime number. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write is_prime(n); numbers below 2 are not prime.
   2. Try every divisor d while d * d <= n.
   3. Return false if one divides n, otherwise true.
   4. Check 226 and print the result. */
/* A prime has no divisor between 2 and its square root. */
bool is_prime(int n) {
    if (n < 2) {
        return false;
    }
    for (int d = 2; d * d <= n; d++) {
        if (n % d == 0) {
            return false;
        }
    }
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    int number = 226;
    printf("%d %s prime\n", number, is_prime(number) ? "is" : "is not");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: is_prime() tries every divisor d from 2 while d * d <= n; if one divides n
   evenly, n is not prime. main() checks 226 and prints whether it is prime. */
// END

/* Caption: C program to list the prime numbers below a limit. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write is_prime(n); numbers below 2 are not prime.
   2. Try every divisor d while d * d <= n.
   3. Return false if one divides n, otherwise true.
   4. Print every prime from 2 to 80. */
/* A prime has no divisor between 2 and its square root. */
bool is_prime(int n) {
    if (n < 2) {
        return false;
    }
    for (int d = 2; d * d <= n; d++) {
        if (n % d == 0) {
            return false;
        }
    }
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    for (int n = 2; n <= 80; n++) {
        if (is_prime(n)) {
            printf("%d ", n);
        }
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: is_prime() tries every divisor d from 2 while d * d <= n; if one divides n
   evenly, n is not prime. main() tests every number from 2 to 80 and prints the primes. */
// END

/* Caption: Use Euclid's algorithm to compute the GCD. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write gcd() with Euclid's algorithm.
   2. Replace (a, b) by (b, a % b) until b is 0.
   3. Return a and print the GCD of 72 and 49. */
/* Euclid: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a % b) until b becomes zero. */
int gcd(int a, int b) {
    while (b != 0) {
        int r = a % b;
        a = b;
        b = r;
    }
    return a;
}

int main(void) {
    int x = 72, y = 49;
    printf("gcd(%d, %d) = %d\n", x, y, gcd(x, y));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: gcd() uses Euclid's algorithm: it keeps replacing (a, b) with (b, a % b)
   until b is 0. The last non-zero value is the greatest common divisor, and main() prints
   the GCD of 72 and 49. */
// END

/* Caption: C program to find the largest of four numbers with a function. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write max2() that returns the larger of two values.
   2. Write max_of_four() as max2(max2(a, b), max2(c, d)).
   3. Print the largest of the four values. */
/* Return the larger of two values. */
int max2(int a, int b) {
    return a > b ? a : b;
}

/* Reuse max2 to compare four values. */
int max_of_four(int a, int b, int c, int d) {
    return max2(max2(a, b), max2(c, d));
}

int main(void) {
    int a = 32, b = 44, c = 88, d = 64;
    printf("Largest: %d\n", max_of_four(a, b, c, d));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: max_of_four() takes four parameters and reuses the helper max2(), which
   returns the larger of two values: it compares a with b, c with d, and then the two
   winners. main() prints the largest of 32, 44, 88 and 64. */
// END

/* Caption: How do I generate the Fibonacci sequence in C? */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write fib(n) that returns n when n < 2.
   2. Otherwise return fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2).
   3. Print fib(i) for i from 0 to 9. */
/* Each Fibonacci number is the sum of the two before it. */
long fib(int n) {
    if (n < 2) {
        return n;
    }
    return fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2);
}

int main(void) {
    for (int i = 0; i < 10; i++) {
        printf("%ld ", fib(i));
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: fib() returns n for 0 and 1 and otherwise adds the two previous Fibonacci
   numbers by calling itself twice, which is simple but slow for large n. main() prints the
   first 10 numbers. */
// END

   2. Pick the bigger of num1 and num2.
   3. Print it. */

    double num1, num2;
    printf("Enter 2 numbers: ");

        printf("Invalid input\n");
        return 1;
    }
    double best = num2;
    if (num1 > num2) {
        best = num1;
    }
    printf("The larger is %.2f\n", best);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: The program reads num1 and num2 from the keyboard with scanf and stops with
   a message if the input is not valid. It starts with best = num2 and replaces it with
   num1 when num1 is bigger, then prints best. */
// END

/* Caption: Calculate 3! using recursion. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write factorial(value) that calls itself.
   2. Return 1 when value is 1 or less.
   3. Otherwise return value * factorial(value - 1).
   4. Print 3! as an unsigned long long. */
/* n! = n * (n - 1)!, and 0! = 1 stops the recursion. */
unsigned long long factorial(int value) {
    if (value <= 1) {
        return 1;
    }
    return value * factorial(value - 1);
}

int main(void) {
    int value = 3;
    printf("%d! = %llu\n", value, factorial(value));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: factorial() calls itself: n! is n * (n - 1)!, and the recursion stops when
   value is 1 or less. main() prints 3! as an unsigned long long, because factorials grow
   very fast. */
// END

/* Caption: Find the maximum of three numbers. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Read a, b and c.
   2. Assume a is the maximum.
   3. Compare it with the other two and keep the bigger value.
   4. Print the result. */
int main(void) {
    int a, b, c;
    printf("Enter three numbers: ");
    if (scanf("%d %d %d", &a, &b, &c) != 3) {
        printf("Invalid input\n");
        return 1;
    }
    int best = a;
    /* Compare with each of the others and keep the bigger one. */
    if (b > best) {
        best = b;
    }
    if (c > best) {
        best = c;
    }
    printf("The maximum is %d\n", best);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: The program reads a, b and c from the keyboard with scanf and stops with a
   message if the input is not valid. It assumes a is the maximum, compares it with the
   other two and keeps the bigger value in best, which it prints. */
// END

/* Caption: Program to compute 3 to the power of 7 without pow(). */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write power(base, exp) with result = 1.
   2. Multiply result by base exp times.
   3. Print 3 to the power 7. */
/* Multiply the base by itself exp times. */
long long power(int base, int exp) {
    long long result = 1;
    for (int i = 0; i < exp; i++) {
        result *= base;
    }
    return result;
}

int main(void) {
    printf("3^7 = %lld\n", power(3, 7));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: power() starts result at 1 and multiplies it by base exp times. It uses
   long long because powers grow quickly. main() prints 3 to the power 7. */
// END

/* Caption: How do I decide if 2037 is a leap year in C? */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write is_leap(year).
   2. A year divisible by 4 is a leap year, unless it is divisible by 100.
   3. Years divisible by 400 are leap years again.
   4. Check 2037 and print the result. */
/* Leap years divide by 4, except centuries, which must divide by 400. */
int is_leap(int year) {
    return (year % 4 == 0 && year % 100 != 0) || year % 400 == 0;
}

int main(void) {
    int year = 2037;
    if (is_leap(year)) {
        printf("%d is a leap year\n", year);
    } else {
        printf("%d is not a leap year\n", year);
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: is_leap() returns true for years divisible by 4, except century years,
   which must also be divisible by 400. main() checks 2037 and prints whether it is a leap
   year. */
// END

/* Caption: Return both the smallest and the largest value of an array through pointers. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write min_max() with the array, its length and the pointers min and max.
   2. Start both at the first element.
   3. Update *min and *max while looping over the rest.
   4. Declare min and max, pass their addresses and print them. */
/* One pass finds both results; they are stored through the pointers. */
void min_max(const int prices[], int size, int *min, int *max) {
    *min = prices[0];
    *max = prices[0];
    for (int i = 1; i < size; i++) {
        if (prices[i] < *min) {
            *min = prices[i];
        }
        if (prices[i] > *max) {
            *max = prices[i];
        }
    }
}

int main(void) {
    int prices[] = {51, 96, 81, 13, 12, 43, 3, 5, 95};
    const int size = 9;
    int min, max;
    min_max(prices, size, &min, &max);
    printf("Min: %d, Max: %d\n", min, max);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: A C function can return only one value, so min_max() returns void and
   writes its two results through the pointer parameters min and max. main() declares min
   and max on one line and passes their addresses with &, then prints both results for the
   9 values. */
// END

/* Caption: C program to return two values from a function using pointer parameters. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write sum_and_average() with the pointers sum and average.
   2. Add the values into *sum.
   3. Store *sum / n in *average.
   4. Declare total and mean, pass their addresses and print them. */
void sum_and_average(const double v[], int n, double *sum, double *average) {
    *sum = 0.0;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        *sum += v[i];
    }
    *average = *sum / n;
}

int main(void) {
    double items[] = {2.5, 9.5, 88.7, 77.0, 26.0};
    int n = sizeof(items) / sizeof(items[0]);
    double total, mean;
    sum_and_average(items, n, &total, &mean);
    printf("Sum: %.2f, Average: %.2f\n", total, mean);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: sum_and_average() takes the array, its length and two pointers. It adds up
   the 5 values through *sum and then stores *sum / n in *average. main() declares total
   and mean on one line and passes their addresses. */
// END

   2. Check whether number % 2 is 0.
   3. Print even or odd. */

    int number;
    printf("Enter a number: ");
    if (scanf("%d", &number) != 1) {
        printf("Invalid input\n");
        return 1;
    }
    /* Even numbers leave no remainder when divided by 2. */

/* Caption: Write a program to print the binary representation of an integer. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write print_binary(n, bits).
   2. Go through the bits from the highest to the lowest.
   3. Print 1 when (n >> b) & 1 is set, otherwise 0.
   4. Print 657 in binary. */
/* Check each bit from the highest to the lowest. */
void print_binary(unsigned int n, int bits) {
    for (int b = bits - 1; b >= 0; b--) {
        putchar((n >> b) & 1 ? '1' : '0');
    }
    putchar('\n');
}

int main(void) {
    unsigned int number = 657;
    printf("%u in binary: ", number);
    print_binary(number, 10);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: print_binary() checks one bit at a time, from the highest to the lowest: (n
   >> b) & 1 is 1 when bit b is set, so it prints the character 1 or 0. main() prints 657
   in binary. */
// END

/* Caption: C program to allocate an array with malloc and fill it with multiples. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Use malloc to get room for 11 ints and check for NULL.
   2. Fill table with multiples.
   3. Print the values.
   4. Call free(table) at the end. */
int main(void) {
    int n = 11;
    /* Ask the heap for room for n ints; malloc returns NULL on failure. */
    int *table = malloc(n * sizeof(int));
    if (table == NULL) {
        fprintf(stderr, "malloc failed\n");
        return 1;
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        table[i] = 5 * i;
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        printf("%d ", table[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    free(table);   /* give the memory back */
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: malloc() reserves room for 11 ints on the heap and returns NULL if it
   fails, which the program checks. The first loop fills table with multiples, the second
   prints them, and free() gives the memory back at the end. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to compute the sum of the digits of an integer. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Start result at 0.
   2. Add n % 10 to result, then divide n by 10.
   3. Repeat until n is 0.
   4. Apply it to 645541 and print the result. */
/* Take the last digit with % 10, then drop it with / 10. */
int sum_digits(int n) {
    int result = 0;
    while (n > 0) {
        result += n % 10;
        n /= 10;
    }
    return result;
}

int main(void) {
    int number = 645541;
    printf("sum of digits of %d: %d\n", number, sum_digits(number));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: sum_digits() adds the last digit (n % 10) to result and then removes it (n
   / 10) until no digits are left. main() applies it to 645541. */
// END

/* Caption: Program to convert seconds into a struct with hours, minutes and seconds. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define a Duration struct with hours, minutes and seconds.
   2. Write from_seconds() that fills it using / and %.
   3. Convert 74008 seconds and print the members. */
typedef struct {
    int hours;
    int minutes;
    int seconds;
} Duration;

Duration from_seconds(int total) {
    Duration d;
    d.hours = total / 3600;
    d.minutes = (total % 3600) / 60;
    d.seconds = total % 60;
    return d;
}

int main(void) {
    Duration d = from_seconds(74008);
    printf("%d h %d min %d s\n", d.hours, d.minutes, d.seconds);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: from_seconds() fills the three members of a Duration struct using / and %,
   then returns the struct. main() converts 74008 seconds and prints the members. */
// END

/* Caption: Reverse an array by swapping from both ends. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write reverse_array() for values.
   2. Set i to the first index and j to the last.
   3. Swap values[i] and values[j], then move both inwards.
   4. Stop when i meets j and print the array. */
/* Swap the outer pair, then move both ends toward the middle. */
void reverse_array(int values[], int length) {
    int i = 0;
    int j = length - 1;
    while (i < j) {
        int tmp = values[i];
        values[i] = values[j];
        values[j] = tmp;
        i++;
        j--;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    int values[] = {74, 53, 82, 34, 89, 20, 91, 75, 57};
    const int length = 9;
    reverse_array(values, length);
    for (int i = 0; i < length; i++) {
        printf("%d ", values[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: reverse_array() swaps the first and last elements, then moves i forward and
   j backward until they meet, so the array is reversed in place without a second array.
   main() prints the reversed values. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to compare two numbers and print the bigger. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Read num1 and num2.
   2. Pick the bigger of num1 and num2.
   3. Print it. */
int main(void) {
    long num1, num2;
    printf("Enter two numbers: ");
    if (scanf("%ld %ld", &num1, &num2) != 2) {
        printf("Invalid input\n");
        return 1;
    }
    long best = (num1 > num2) ? num1 : num2;   /* the ?: operator picks one of two values */
    printf("The bigger is %ld\n", best);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: The program reads num1 and num2 from the keyboard with scanf and stops with
   a message if the input is not valid. The conditional operator (num1 > num2) ? num1 :
   num2 picks the bigger value, which is printed. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to calculate the average of the values in an array. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write average() that takes marks and n.
   2. Add the values into the double sum.
   3. Return sum / n.
   4. Print the average with two decimals. */
/* Sum the values, then divide by how many there are. */
double average(const int marks[], int n) {
    double sum = 0.0;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        sum += marks[i];
    }
    return sum / n;
}

int main(void) {
    int marks[] = {72, 32, 2, 35, 35, 72, 14, 25, 86};
    const int n = 9;
    printf("Mean = %.2f\n", average(marks, n));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: average() adds the 9 values of marks into the double sum and divides by n,
   so the mean keeps its decimal part even when the values are whole numbers. main() prints
   it with two decimals. */
// END

/* Caption: Count how many vowels a string contains. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <string.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write count_vowels() with count = 0.
   2. For each character, check whether strchr finds it in aeiouAEIOU.
   3. Return count and print it. */
/* strchr finds the letter in the list of vowels, or returns NULL. */
int count_vowels(const char *text) {
    int count = 0;
    for (int i = 0; text[i] != '\0'; i++) {
        if (strchr("aeiouAEIOU", text[i]) != NULL) {
            count++;
        }
    }
    return count;
}

int main(void) {
    const char *sentence = "every program starts in main";
    printf("Vowels: %d\n", count_vowels(sentence));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: count_vowels() uses strchr to test whether each character is one of
   aeiouAEIOU and counts the matches. main() prints the number of vowels in the sentence. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to calculate the area and perimeter of a rectangle struct. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define a Rectangle struct with width and height.
   2. Write area() and perimeter().
   3. Make a 8 by 13 rectangle and print both results. */
typedef struct {
    int width;
    int height;
} Rectangle;

int area(Rectangle r) {
    return r.width * r.height;
}

int perimeter(Rectangle r) {
    return 2 * (r.width + r.height);
}

int main(void) {
    Rectangle box = {8, 13};
    printf("Area: %d, Perimeter: %d\n", area(box), perimeter(box));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: Rectangle stores a width and a height. area() returns width * height and
   perimeter() returns 2 * (width + height). main() makes a 8 by 13 rectangle and prints
   both results. */
// END

/* Caption: Copy one string into another by hand. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write copy_string(dest, src).
   2. Copy src into dest one character at a time.
   3. Stop after copying the null character.
   4. Copy noon into text and print it. */
/* Copy each character, including the final '\0'. */
void copy_string(char *dest, const char *src) {
    int i = 0;
    while ((dest[i] = src[i]) != '\0') {
        i++;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    char source[] = "noon";
    char text[32];
    copy_string(text, source);
    printf("Copied: %s\n", text);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: copy_string() copies src into dest one character at a time, including the
   final null character, which is what strcpy does. The array text must be big enough to
   hold the copy. main() copies the word noon and prints it. */
// END

/* Caption: Use Euclid's algorithm to compute the GCD. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write gcd() with Euclid's algorithm.
   2. Replace (a, b) by (b, a % b) until b is 0.
   3. Return a and print the GCD of 211 and 118. */
/* Euclid: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a % b) until b becomes zero. */
int gcd(int a, int b) {
    while (b != 0) {
        int r = a % b;
        a = b;
        b = r;
    }
    return a;
}

int main(void) {
    int x = 211, y = 118;
    printf("gcd(%d, %d) = %d\n", x, y, gcd(x, y));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: gcd() uses Euclid's algorithm: it keeps replacing (a, b) with (b, a % b)
   until b is 0. The last non-zero value is the greatest common divisor, and main() prints
   the GCD of 211 and 118. */
// END

/* Caption: Program to show the Fibonacci series with a loop. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Start with a = 0 and b = 1.
   2. Repeat 23 times and print a each time.
   3. Compute next = a + b, then set a = b and b = next. */
int main(void) {
    long a = 0, b = 1;
    /* Print a term, then slide the pair one step along the sequence. */
    for (int i = 0; i < 23; i++) {
        printf("%ld ", a);
        long next = a + b;
        a = b;
        b = next;
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: The loop keeps the last two numbers in a and b. Each round it prints a,
   then moves the pair forward: a becomes b and b becomes their sum. It prints the first 23
   Fibonacci numbers. */
// END

/* Caption: How do I build a FIFO queue using a ring buffer in C? */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define a Queue with room for 8 items, a head and a count.
   2. Write enqueue() that stores at (head + count) % CAPACITY.
   3. Write dequeue() that takes the item at head and moves head on.
   4. Add 6 values, then remove and print them in order. */
#define CAPACITY 8

typedef struct {
    int items[CAPACITY];
    int head;
    int count;
} Queue;

bool enqueue(Queue *q, int value) {
    if (q->count == CAPACITY) {
        return false;
    }
    /* The tail wraps around to the start of the array. */
    q->items[(q->head + q->count) % CAPACITY] = value;
    q->count++;
    return true;
}

bool dequeue(Queue *q, int *value) {
    if (q->count == 0) {
        return false;
    }
    *value = q->items[q->head];
    q->head = (q->head + 1) % CAPACITY;
    q->count--;
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    Queue q = {.head = 0, .count = 0};
    enqueue(&q, 22);
    enqueue(&q, 3);
    enqueue(&q, 34);
    enqueue(&q, 58);
    enqueue(&q, 7);
    enqueue(&q, 98);
    int value;
    /* Items come out in the order they went in (first in, first out). */
    while (dequeue(&q, &value)) {
        printf("%d ", value);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: The Queue stores up to 8 items in a ring buffer: head is the oldest item
   and % CAPACITY wraps positions back to the start of the array. enqueue() adds at the
   back and dequeue() removes from the front, so main() gets its 6 values back in the same
   order (first in, first out). */
// END

int main(void) {

    };

/* Caption: Write a C program to print the binary representation of an integer. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write print_binary(n, bits).
   2. Go through the bits from the highest to the lowest.
   3. Print 1 when (n >> b) & 1 is set, otherwise 0.
   4. Print 241 in binary. */
/* Check each bit from the highest to the lowest. */
void print_binary(unsigned int n, int bits) {
    for (int b = bits - 1; b >= 0; b--) {
        putchar((n >> b) & 1 ? '1' : '0');
    }
    putchar('\n');
}

int main(void) {
    unsigned int number = 241;
    printf("%u in binary: ", number);
    print_binary(number, 16);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: print_binary() checks one bit at a time, from the highest to the lowest: (n
   >> b) & 1 is 1 when bit b is set, so it prints the character 1 or 0. main() prints 241
   in binary. */
// END

/* Caption: C program to multiply two 2x2 matrices. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define N as 2.
   2. For every i and j, add a[i][k] * b[k][j] over k into product[i][j].
   3. Print product row by row. */
#define N 2

int main(void) {
    int a[N][N] = {{2, 5}, {4, 1}};
    int b[N][N] = {{5, 5}, {6, 3}};
    int product[N][N] = {0};
    /* product[i][j] is row i of a times column j of b. */
    for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) {
        for (int j = 0; j < N; j++) {
            for (int k = 0; k < N; k++) {
                product[i][j] += a[i][k] * b[k][j];
            }
        }
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) {
        for (int j = 0; j < N; j++) {
            printf("%4d", product[i][j]);
        }
        printf("\n");
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: For each entry product[i][j] the innermost loop adds a[i][k] * b[k][j] over
   k, which is row i of a times column j of b. main() multiplies two 2x2 matrices and
   prints the product. */
// END

   3. Print both for a radius of 1.6. */
#define PI 3.14159265

void circle_measures(double radius, double *area, double *circumference) {
    *area = PI * radius * radius;
    *circumference = 2 * PI * radius;
}

int main(void) {

    double area, circumference;

/* Explanation: circle_measures() computes two results from one radius and stores them
   through the pointers area and circumference. main() declares both variables on one line,
   passes their addresses and prints the results for a radius of 1.6. */
// END

/* Caption: Reverse an array by swapping from both ends. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write reverse_array() for numbers.
   2. Set start to the first index and end to the last.
   3. Swap numbers[start] and numbers[end], then move both inwards.
   4. Stop when start meets end and print the array. */
/* Swap the outer pair, then move both ends toward the middle. */
void reverse_array(int numbers[], int length) {
    int start = 0;
    int end = length - 1;
    while (start < end) {
        int tmp = numbers[start];
        numbers[start] = numbers[end];
        numbers[end] = tmp;
        start++;
        end--;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    int numbers[] = {99, 63, 88, 36, 49, 96, 50};
    int length = 7;
    reverse_array(numbers, length);
    for (int i = 0; i < length; i++) {
        printf("%d ", numbers[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: reverse_array() swaps the first and last elements, then moves start forward
   and end backward until they meet, so the array is reversed in place without a second
   array. main() prints the reversed values. */
// END

/* Caption: Build a FIFO queue using a ring buffer. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define a Queue with room for 8 items, a head and a count.
   2. Write enqueue() that stores at (head + count) % CAPACITY.
   3. Write dequeue() that takes the item at head and moves head on.
   4. Add 3 values, then remove and print them in order. */
#define CAPACITY 8

typedef struct {
    int items[CAPACITY];
    int head;
    int count;
} Queue;

bool enqueue(Queue *q, int value) {
    if (q->count == CAPACITY) {
        return false;
    }
    /* The tail wraps around to the start of the array. */
    q->items[(q->head + q->count) % CAPACITY] = value;
    q->count++;
    return true;
}

bool dequeue(Queue *q, int *value) {
    if (q->count == 0) {
        return false;
    }
    *value = q->items[q->head];
    q->head = (q->head + 1) % CAPACITY;
    q->count--;
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    Queue q = {.head = 0, .count = 0};
    enqueue(&q, 52);
    enqueue(&q, 38);
    enqueue(&q, 13);
    int value;
    /* Items come out in the order they went in (first in, first out). */
    while (dequeue(&q, &value)) {
        printf("%d ", value);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: The Queue stores up to 8 items in a ring buffer: head is the oldest item
   and % CAPACITY wraps positions back to the start of the array. enqueue() adds at the
   back and dequeue() removes from the front, so main() gets its 3 values back in the same
   order (first in, first out). */
// END

/* Caption: Program to count the characters in a string. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write string_length() with a counter len = 0.
   2. Move through the string until the null character.
   3. Return len and print the length of stats. */
/* Count characters until the terminating '\0'. */
int string_length(const char *buffer) {
    int len = 0;
    while (buffer[len] != '\0') {
        len++;
    }
    return len;
}

int main(void) {
    const char *buffer = "stats";
    printf("Length of \"%s\" is %d\n", buffer, string_length(buffer));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: string_length() counts characters until it reaches the null character that
   ends every C string. main() prints the length of the word stats. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to count the even values in a list of integers. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write count_even() that takes marks and len.
   2. For each element, test marks[i] % 2 == 0.
   3. Add one to count for every even number.
   4. Return count and print it. */
/* A number is even when the remainder after dividing by 2 is zero. */
int count_even(const int marks[], int len) {
    int count = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < len; i++) {
        if (marks[i] % 2 == 0) {
            count++;
        }
    }
    return count;
}

int main(void) {
    int marks[] = {95, 17, 40, 86, 89};
    const int len = 5;
    printf("Even numbers: %d\n", count_even(marks, len));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: count_even() tests each element of marks with the % operator: a remainder
   of 0 after dividing by 2 means the number is even, so count goes up by one. main()
   prints how many of the 5 values are even. */
// END

/* Caption: Define a Point struct and measure the distance between two points. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <math.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define a Point struct with x and y.
   2. Write distance() using sqrt(dx * dx + dy * dy).
   3. Print the distance between p and q. */
typedef struct {
    double x;
    double y;
} Point;

/* Pythagoras: sqrt(dx * dx + dy * dy). */
double distance(Point a, Point b) {
    double dx = b.x - a.x;
    double dy = b.y - a.y;
    return sqrt(dx * dx + dy * dy);
}

int main(void) {
    Point p = {-7, -9};
    Point q = {5, 1};
    printf("Distance: %.3f\n", distance(p, q));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: Point is a typedef struct with x and y. distance() uses Pythagoras, sqrt(dx
   * dx + dy * dy), to measure the gap between the two points, and main() prints it. */
// END

   3. Return result.

/* Walk through the array and accumulate each value. */
int array_sum(const int marks[], int n) {
    int result = 0;

}

   0, adds every element to it in a for loop and returns the total. main() fills marks with
   9 int values and prints their sum. */
// END

/* Caption: Compute the factorial of a number recursively. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write factorial(x) that calls itself.
   2. Return 1 when x is 1 or less.
   3. Otherwise return x * factorial(x - 1).
   4. Print 4! as an unsigned long long. */
/* n! = n * (n - 1)!, and 0! = 1 stops the recursion. */
unsigned long long factorial(int x) {
    if (x <= 1) {
        return 1;
    }
    return x * factorial(x - 1);
}

int main(void) {
    int x = 4;
    printf("%d! = %llu\n", x, factorial(x));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: factorial() calls itself: n! is n * (n - 1)!, and the recursion stops when
   x is 1 or less. main() prints 4! as an unsigned long long, because factorials grow very
   fast. */
// END

/* Caption: Check whether a year is a leap year. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write is_leap(year).
   2. A year divisible by 4 is a leap year, unless it is divisible by 100.
   3. Years divisible by 400 are leap years again.
   4. Check 1953 and print the result. */
/* Leap years divide by 4, except centuries, which must divide by 400. */
int is_leap(int year) {
    return (year % 4 == 0 && year % 100 != 0) || year % 400 == 0;
}

int main(void) {
    int year = 1953;
    if (is_leap(year)) {
        printf("%d is a leap year\n", year);
    } else {
        printf("%d is not a leap year\n", year);
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: is_leap() returns true for years divisible by 4, except century years,
   which must also be divisible by 400. main() checks 1953 and prints whether it is a leap
   year. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to change every letter in a sentence to a capital letter. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <ctype.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write to_upper() for word.
   2. Replace every character with toupper() until the null character.
   3. Print the sentence. */
/* toupper changes lowercase letters and leaves other characters alone. */
void to_upper(char *word) {
    for (int i = 0; word[i] != '\0'; i++) {
        word[i] = toupper((unsigned char)word[i]);
    }
}

int main(void) {
    char word[] = "good comments explain why the code exists";
    to_upper(word);
    printf("%s\n", word);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: to_upper() walks through word until the null character and replaces each
   character with toupper(), which only changes lowercase letters. main() prints the
   sentence in capitals. */
// END

#include <stdio.h>
#include <string.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write count_vowels() with count = 0.
   2. For each character, check whether strchr finds it in aeiouAEIOU.
   3. Return count and print it. */
/* strchr finds the letter in the list of vowels, or returns NULL. */
int count_vowels(const char *text) {
    int count = 0;
    for (int i = 0; text[i] != '\0'; i++) {
        if (strchr("aeiouAEIOU", text[i]) != NULL) {
            count++;
        }
    }
    return count;
}

int main(void) {
    const char *sentence = "c gives you direct control over memory";
    printf("Vowels: %d\n", count_vowels(sentence));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: count_vowels() uses strchr to test whether each character is one of
   aeiouAEIOU and counts the matches. main() prints the number of vowels in the sentence. */
// END

/* Caption: C program to show the right way to declare several pointers on one line. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Declare x and y on one line.
   2. Declare the pointers px and py on one line, each with its own *.
   3. Add 2 to x through px and print the values. */
int main(void) {
    int x = 13, y = 24;
    /* Each pointer needs its own '*': in "int *p, q;" only p is a pointer. */
    int *px = &x, *py = &y;
    *px += 2;
    printf("x = %d, y = %d\n", x, y);
    printf("*px = %d, *py = %d\n", *px, *py);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: int *px = &x, *py = &y; declares two pointers in one statement; each name
   needs its own *. *px += 2 changes x through the pointer, so x becomes 15 while y stays
   24. */
// END

/* Caption: How do I sum a long array with a helper function in C? */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write add_all() that takes the array samples and its length count.
   2. Start sum at 0 and add every element in a for loop.
   3. Return sum.
   4. In main(), fill samples with 8 values and print the sum. */
/* Add every element to a running total. */
long add_all(const long samples[], int count) {
    long sum = 0;
    for (int j = 0; j < count; j++) {
        sum += samples[j];
    }
    return sum;
}

int main(void) {
    long samples[] = {34L, 22L, 43L, 46L, 2L, 20L, 27L, 75L};
    int count = 8;
    printf("The sum is %ld\n", add_all(samples, count));
    return 0;
}

   0, adds every element to it in a for loop and returns the total. main() fills samples
   with 8 long values and prints their sum. */
// END

/* Caption: How do I compute 2 to the power of 2 without pow() in C? */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write power(base, exp) with result = 1.
   2. Multiply result by base exp times.
   3. Print 2 to the power 2. */
/* Multiply the base by itself exp times. */
long long power(int base, int exp) {
    long long result = 1;
    for (int i = 0; i < exp; i++) {
        result *= base;
    }
    return result;
}

int main(void) {
    printf("2^2 = %lld\n", power(2, 2));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: power() starts result at 1 and multiplies it by base exp times. It uses
   long long because powers grow quickly. main() prints 2 to the power 2. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to convert seconds into a struct with hours, minutes and seconds. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define a Duration struct with hours, minutes and seconds.
   2. Write from_seconds() that fills it using / and %.
   3. Convert 76281 seconds and print the members. */
typedef struct {
    int hours;
    int minutes;
    int seconds;
} Duration;

Duration from_seconds(int total) {
    Duration d;
    d.hours = total / 3600;
    d.minutes = (total % 3600) / 60;
    d.seconds = total % 60;
    return d;
}

int main(void) {
    Duration d = from_seconds(76281);
    printf("%d h %d min %d s\n", d.hours, d.minutes, d.seconds);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: from_seconds() fills the three members of a Duration struct using / and %,
   then returns the struct. main() converts 76281 seconds and prints the members. */
// END

/* Caption: Build a fixed-size integer stack in C. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define a Stack with room for 10 items and a top counter.
   2. Write push() and pop(), returning false when the stack is full or empty.
   3. Push 4 values.
   4. Pop and print until the stack is empty. */
#define CAPACITY 10

typedef struct {
    int items[CAPACITY];
    int top;   /* number of items on the stack */
} Stack;

bool push(Stack *s, int value) {
    if (s->top == CAPACITY) {
        return false;   /* stack is full */
    }
    s->items[s->top++] = value;
    return true;
}

bool pop(Stack *s, int *value) {
    if (s->top == 0) {
        return false;   /* stack is empty */
    }
    *value = s->items[--s->top];
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    Stack s = {.top = 0};
    push(&s, 34);
    push(&s, 80);
    push(&s, 77);
    push(&s, 99);
    int value;
    /* Items come back out in reverse order (last in, first out). */
    while (pop(&s, &value)) {
        printf("%d ", value);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: The Stack keeps up to 10 items in an array, and top counts how many are
   stored. push() adds at the top and pop() removes from the top; both return false when
   they cannot. main() pushes 4 values and pops them all, so they come out in reverse order
   (last in, first out). */
// END

   3. Return len and print the length of matrix. */
/* Count characters until the terminating '\0'. */
int string_length(const char *word) {

    }

}

int main(void) {

    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: string_length() counts characters until it reaches the null character that
   ends every C string. main() prints the length of the word matrix. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to use binary search to locate a value in a sorted list. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Make sure the array is sorted.
   2. Set lo to 0 and hi to size - 1.
   3. While lo <= hi, compare the middle element mid with the key.
   4. Return the index if it matches; otherwise keep only the half that can hold the
      key.
   5. Return -1 if the range becomes empty, and print the index of 35. */
/* The array must be sorted. Each step halves the range that can still hold the key. */
int binary_search(const int values[], int size, int key) {
    int lo = 0;
    int hi = size - 1;
    while (lo <= hi) {
        int mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;
        if (values[mid] == key) {
            return mid;
        } else if (values[mid] < key) {
            lo = mid + 1;   /* key is in the right half */
        } else {
            hi = mid - 1;   /* key is in the left half */
        }
    }
    return -1;
}

int main(void) {
    int values[] = {24, 35, 61, 73, 89, 95, 145, 185};
    int size = 8;
    int index = binary_search(values, size, 35);
    printf("Index of 35: %d\n", index);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: binary_search() needs a sorted array. It keeps the range from lo to hi,
   compares the middle element mid with the key and throws away the half that cannot
   contain it, so it needs only about log2(n) steps. main() looks for 35 and prints its
   index, or -1 if it is not there. */
// END

/* Caption: Check every element of an array to find a target value. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write linear_search() with the array, its length and key.
   2. Compare each element with key.
   3. Return the index of the first match, or -1.
   4. In main(), search for 101 and print the result. */
/* Return the index of key, or -1 when it is not in the array. */
int linear_search(const int prices[], int size, int key) {
    for (int i = 0; i < size; i++) {
        if (prices[i] == key) {
            return i;
        }
    }
    return -1;
}

int main(void) {
    int prices[] = {26, 41, 84, 25, 58, 25, 42, 11, 95};
    int size = sizeof(prices) / sizeof(prices[0]);
    int key = 101;
    int pos = linear_search(prices, size, key);
    if (pos >= 0) {
        printf("Found %d at index %d\n", key, pos);
    } else {
        printf("%d is not in the array\n", key);
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: linear_search() checks the elements of prices one by one and returns the
   index of the first one equal to key, or -1 when it reaches the end without a match.
   main() searches for 101 and prints where it is, or that it is missing. */
// END

/* Caption: Search an array for its largest value. */

/* Plan:

   3. Print mid.x and mid.y. */

    double x;
    double y;

/* A function can return a whole struct. */
Point midpoint(Point a, Point b) {

}

    printf("Midpoint: (%.1f, %.1f)\n", mid.x, mid.y);
    return 0;
}

   are the averages of theirs. main() declares p and q on one line, (-12, -20) and (0, 4),
   and prints the midpoint using mid.x and mid.y. */
// END
