/* Caption: Create a singly linked list by inserting at the head. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define ListNode with a value and a next pointer.
   2. Write push_front() that mallocs a node and links it in front of head.
   3. Write print_list() that follows next until NULL.
   4. Write free_list() that frees every node.
   5. Push 4 values, print the list and free it. */
typedef struct ListNode {
    int value;
    struct ListNode *next;
} ListNode;

/* Allocate a new node and put it in front of the current head. */
ListNode *push_front(ListNode *head, int value) {
    ListNode *node = malloc(sizeof(ListNode));
    if (node == NULL) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Out of memory\n");
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }
    node->value = value;
    node->next = head;
    return node;
}

void print_list(const ListNode *head) {
    for (const ListNode *cur = head; cur != NULL; cur = cur->next) {
        printf("%d -> ", cur->value);
    }
    printf("NULL\n");
}

/* Free every node; save next before freeing the current one. */
void free_list(ListNode *head) {
    while (head != NULL) {
        ListNode *next = head->next;
        free(head);
        head = next;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    ListNode *head = NULL;
    head = push_front(head, 15);
    head = push_front(head, 30);
    head = push_front(head, 4);
    head = push_front(head, 98);
    print_list(head);
    free_list(head);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: Each ListNode holds a value and a pointer to the next node. push_front()
   allocates a node with malloc, puts it in front of head and returns it; print_list()
   follows the next pointers until NULL; free_list() frees every node. main() pushes 4
   values, so they print in reverse order. */
// END

/* Caption: Return two values from a function using pointer parameters. */

/* Plan:
   1. Write circle_measures() with the pointers area and circumference.
   2. Store PI * r * r and 2 * PI * r through them.
   3. Print both for a radius of 10.7. */
#define PI 3.14159265

void circle_measures(double radius, double *area, double *circumference) {
    *area = PI * radius * radius;
    *circumference = 2 * PI * radius;
}

int main(void) {
    double radius = 10.7;
    double area, circumference;
    circle_measures(radius, &area, &circumference);
    printf("Area: %.2f, Circumference: %.2f\n", area, circumference);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: circle_measures() computes two results from one radius and stores them
   through the pointers area and circumference. main() declares both variables on one line,
   passes their addresses and prints the results for a radius of 10.7. */
// END

/* Caption: Find the arithmetic mean of 7 long values. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write compute_mean() that takes data and size.
   2. Add the values into the double sum.
   3. Return sum / size.
   4. Print the average with two decimals. */
/* Sum the values, then divide by how many there are. */
double compute_mean(const long data[], int size) {
    double sum = 0.0;
    for (int idx = 0; idx < size; idx++) {
        sum += data[idx];
    }
    return sum / size;
}

int main(void) {
    long data[] = {19L, 8L, 14L, 60L, 84L, 4L, 19L};
    int size = 7;
    printf("The average is %.2f\n", compute_mean(data, size));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: compute_mean() adds the 7 values of data into the double sum and divides by
   size, so the mean keeps its decimal part even when the values are whole numbers. main()
   prints it with two decimals. */

/* Caption: How do I compute the LCM of two integers using the GCD in C? */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write gcd() with Euclid's algorithm: replace (a, b) by (b, a % b) until b is 0.
   2. Write lcm() as a / gcd(a, b) * b.
   3. Print the LCM of 267 and 48. */
/* Euclid: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a % b) until b becomes zero. */
int gcd(int a, int b) {
    while (b != 0) {
        int r = a % b;
        a = b;
        b = r;
    }
    return a;
}

/* lcm(a, b) = a / gcd(a, b) * b (divide first to avoid overflow). */
long lcm(int a, int b) {
    return (long)a / gcd(a, b) * b;
}

int main(void) {
    printf("lcm(267, 48) = %ld\n", lcm(267, 48));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: gcd() uses Euclid's algorithm: it keeps replacing (a, b) with (b, a % b)
   until b is 0. lcm() divides a by the gcd before multiplying by b, which avoids overflow.
   main() prints the LCM of 267 and 48. */
// END

int count_char(const char *text, char target) {

    /* Compare every character with the target. */
    for (int i = 0; text[i] != '\0'; i++) {

}

}

   and counts the matches. main() prints how many times r appears in the sentence. */
// END

/* Caption: C program to generate the Fibonacci sequence. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Start with prev = 0 and curr = 1.
   2. Repeat 8 times and print prev each time.
   3. Compute next = prev + curr, then set prev = curr and curr = next. */
int main(void) {
    long prev = 0, curr = 1;
    /* Print a term, then slide the pair one step along the sequence. */
    for (int i = 0; i < 8; i++) {
        printf("%ld ", prev);
        long next = prev + curr;
        prev = curr;
        curr = next;
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: The loop keeps the last two numbers in prev and curr. Each round it prints
   prev, then moves the pair forward: prev becomes curr and curr becomes their sum. It
   prints the first 8 Fibonacci numbers. */
// END

/* Caption: Implement a simple linked list with malloc and free. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define Node with a value and a next pointer.
   2. Write push_front() that mallocs a node and links it in front of head.
   3. Write print_list() that follows next until NULL.
   4. Write free_list() that frees every node.
   5. Push 5 values, print the list and free it. */
typedef struct Node {
    int value;
    struct Node *next;
} Node;

/* Allocate a new node and put it in front of the current head. */
Node *push_front(Node *head, int value) {
    Node *node = malloc(sizeof(Node));
    if (node == NULL) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Out of memory\n");
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }
    node->value = value;
    node->next = head;
    return node;
}

void print_list(const Node *head) {
    for (const Node *cur = head; cur != NULL; cur = cur->next) {
        printf("%d -> ", cur->value);
    }
    printf("NULL\n");
}

/* Free every node; save next before freeing the current one. */
void free_list(Node *head) {
    while (head != NULL) {
        Node *next = head->next;
        free(head);
        head = next;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    Node *head = NULL;
    head = push_front(head, 99);
    head = push_front(head, 40);
    head = push_front(head, 29);
    head = push_front(head, 27);
    head = push_front(head, 70);
    print_list(head);
    free_list(head);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: Each Node holds a value and a pointer to the next node. push_front()
   allocates a node with malloc, puts it in front of head and returns it; print_list()
   follows the next pointers until NULL; free_list() frees every node. main() pushes 5
   values, so they print in reverse order. */
// END

/* Caption: Convert 853 to binary. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write print_binary(n, bits).
   2. Go through the bits from the highest to the lowest.
   3. Print 1 when (n >> b) & 1 is set, otherwise 0.
   4. Print 853 in binary. */
/* Check each bit from the highest to the lowest. */
void print_binary(unsigned int n, int bits) {
    for (int b = bits - 1; b >= 0; b--) {
        putchar((n >> b) & 1 ? '1' : '0');
    }
    putchar('\n');
}

int main(void) {
    unsigned int number = 853;
    printf("%u in binary: ", number);
    print_binary(number, 10);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: print_binary() checks one bit at a time, from the highest to the lowest: (n
   >> b) & 1 is 1 when bit b is set, so it prints the character 1 or 0. main() prints 853
   in binary. */
// END

/* Caption: Program to search an array for a value and print its position. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write linear_search() with the array, its length and target.
   2. Compare each element with target.
   3. Return the index of the first match, or -1.
   4. In main(), search for 55 and print the result. */
/* Return the index of target, or -1 when it is not in the array. */
int linear_search(const int samples[], int count, int target) {
    for (int i = 0; i < count; i++) {
        if (samples[i] == target) {
            return i;
        }
    }
    return -1;
}

int main(void) {
    int samples[] = {13, 96, 15, 67, 20, 81, 55, 48, 55};
    int count = 9;
    int target = 55;
    int pos = linear_search(samples, count, target);
    if (pos >= 0) {
        printf("Found %d at index %d\n", target, pos);
    } else {
        printf("%d is not in the array\n", target);
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: linear_search() checks the elements of samples one by one and returns the
   index of the first one equal to target, or -1 when it reaches the end without a match.
   main() searches for 55 and prints where it is, or that it is missing. */
// END

/* Caption: Calculate 9! using recursion. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write factorial(value) that calls itself.
   2. Return 1 when value is 1 or less.
   3. Otherwise return value * factorial(value - 1).
   4. Print 9! as an unsigned long long. */
/* n! = n * (n - 1)!, and 0! = 1 stops the recursion. */
unsigned long long factorial(int value) {
    if (value <= 1) {
        return 1;
    }
    return value * factorial(value - 1);
}

int main(void) {
    int value = 9;
    printf("%d! = %llu\n", value, factorial(value));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: factorial() calls itself: n! is n * (n - 1)!, and the recursion stops when
   value is 1 or less. main() prints 9! as an unsigned long long, because factorials grow
   very fast. */
// END

/* Caption: Search an array for its smallest value. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write smallest_value() that takes scores and len.
   2. Store scores[0] in smallest.
   3. Loop over the other elements and keep the smallest value in smallest.
   4. Return smallest and print it. */
/* Start with the first element and keep the smallest value seen so far. */
int smallest_value(const int scores[], int len) {
    int smallest = scores[0];
    for (int j = 1; j < len; j++) {
        if (scores[j] < smallest) {
            smallest = scores[j];
        }
    }
    return smallest;
}

int main(void) {
    int scores[] = {98, 49, 50, 73, 75, 33, 7};
    int len = sizeof(scores) / sizeof(scores[0]);
    printf("Smallest: %d\n", smallest_value(scores, len));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: smallest_value() takes the first element as the smallest value so far and
   stores it in smallest. The loop compares every other element with smallest using < and
   keeps the smallest one. main() prints the smallest of the 7 values. */
// END

/* Caption: Program to search an array for its largest value. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write find_max() that takes numbers and n.
   2. Store numbers[0] in largest.
   3. Loop over the other elements and keep the largest value in largest.
   4. Return largest and print it. */
/* Start with the first element and keep the largest value seen so far. */
double find_max(const double numbers[], int n) {
    double largest = numbers[0];
    for (int k = 1; k < n; k++) {
        if (numbers[k] > largest) {
            largest = numbers[k];
        }
    }
    return largest;
}

int main(void) {
    double numbers[] = {55.6, 24.6, 97.0, 66.2};
    int n = 4;
    printf("Largest: %.2f\n", find_max(numbers, n));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: find_max() takes the first element as the largest value so far and stores
   it in largest. The loop compares every other element with largest using > and keeps the
   largest one. main() prints the largest of the 4 values. */
// END

/* Caption: Implement a stack with an array (push and pop). */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define a Stack with room for 8 items and a top counter.
   2. Write push() and pop(), returning false when the stack is full or empty.
   3. Push 5 values.
   4. Pop and print until the stack is empty. */
#define CAPACITY 8

typedef struct {
    int items[CAPACITY];
    int top;   /* number of items on the stack */
} Stack;

bool push(Stack *s, int value) {
    if (s->top == CAPACITY) {
        return false;   /* stack is full */
    }
    s->items[s->top++] = value;
    return true;
}

bool pop(Stack *s, int *value) {
    if (s->top == 0) {
        return false;   /* stack is empty */
    }
    *value = s->items[--s->top];
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    Stack s = {.top = 0};
    push(&s, 82);
    push(&s, 51);
    push(&s, 20);
    push(&s, 15);
    push(&s, 4);
    int value;
    /* Items come back out in reverse order (last in, first out). */
    while (pop(&s, &value)) {
        printf("%d ", value);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: The Stack keeps up to 8 items in an array, and top counts how many are
   stored. push() adds at the top and pop() removes from the top; both return false when
   they cannot. main() pushes 5 values and pops them all, so they come out in reverse order
   (last in, first out). */
// END

/* Caption: Compute the mean of a list of numbers. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write average() that takes data and len.
   2. Add the values into the double result.
   3. Return result / len.
   4. Print the average with two decimals. */
/* The mean is the total divided by the count. */
double average(const int data[], int len) {
    double result = 0.0;
    for (int k = 0; k < len; k++) {
        result += data[k];
    }
    return result / len;
}

int main(void) {
    int data[] = {61, 7, 46, 35, 34, 32, 23, 17};
    int len = sizeof(data) / sizeof(data[0]);
    printf("Mean = %.2f\n", average(data, len));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: average() adds the 8 values of data into the double result and divides by
   len, so the mean keeps its decimal part even when the values are whole numbers. main()
   prints it with two decimals. */
// END

/* Caption: How do I use a struct to return several results from one function in C? */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define a Stats struct with min, max and average.
   2. Write array_stats() that fills one Stats in a loop.
   3. Return the struct.
   4. Print st.min, st.max and st.average. */
typedef struct {
    int min;
    int max;
    double average;
} Stats;

/* Pack several results into one struct and return it. */
Stats array_stats(const int v[], int n) {
    Stats s = {v[0], v[0], 0.0};
    double total = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        if (v[i] < s.min) {
            s.min = v[i];
        }
        if (v[i] > s.max) {
            s.max = v[i];
        }
        total += v[i];
    }
    s.average = total / n;
    return s;
}

int main(void) {
    int values[] = {27, 41, 80, 88, 61};
    int n = sizeof(values) / sizeof(values[0]);
    Stats st = array_stats(values, n);
    printf("Min %d, Max %d, Average %.2f\n", st.min, st.max, st.average);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: Stats groups three results. array_stats() fills one Stats while it loops
   over the 5 values and returns the whole struct, which is a clean way to return several
   results at once. main() reads them as st.min, st.max and st.average. */
// END

/* Caption: How do I return two values from a function using pointer parameters in C? */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write sum_and_average() with the pointers sum and average.
   2. Add the values into *sum.
   3. Store *sum / n in *average.
   4. Declare total and mean, pass their addresses and print them. */
void sum_and_average(const double v[], int n, double *sum, double *average) {
    *sum = 0.0;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        *sum += v[i];
    }
    *average = *sum / n;
}

int main(void) {
    double nums[] = {96.7, 29.1, 15.7, 11.9, 62.2, 73.7, 17.2, 72.0};
    int n = sizeof(nums) / sizeof(nums[0]);
    double total, mean;
    sum_and_average(nums, n, &total, &mean);
    printf("Sum: %.2f, Average: %.2f\n", total, mean);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: sum_and_average() takes the array, its length and two pointers. It adds up
   the 8 values through *sum and then stores *sum / n in *average. main() declares total
   and mean on one line and passes their addresses. */
// END

   4. Print the average with two decimals. */

double compute_mean(const int nums[], int count) {

    return total / count;

   by count, so the mean keeps its decimal part even when the values are whole numbers.
   main() prints it with two decimals. */

/* Caption: Compare 2 numbers and print the bigger. */

/* Plan:
   1. Set x and y.
   2. Pick the bigger of x and y.

int main(void) {
    int x = 20, y = 54;

/* Caption: C program to compute the factorial of a number with a loop. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write factorial(value) with result = 1.
   2. Multiply result by every number from 2 to value.
   3. Return result.
   4. Print 14! as an unsigned long long. */
/* Multiply 1 * 2 * ... * n. */
unsigned long long factorial(int value) {
    unsigned long long result = 1;
    for (int i = 2; i <= value; i++) {
        result *= i;
    }
    return result;
}

int main(void) {
    int value = 14;
    printf("%d! = %llu\n", value, factorial(value));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: factorial() multiplies result by every number from 2 up to value. main()
   prints 14! as an unsigned long long, because factorials grow very fast. */
// END

/* Caption: Find the index of a number using linear search. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write linear_search() with the array, its length and wanted.
   2. Compare each element with wanted.
   3. Return the index of the first match, or -1.
   4. In main(), search for 51 and print the result. */
/* Return the index of wanted, or -1 when it is not in the array. */
int linear_search(const int scores[], int size, int wanted) {
    for (int i = 0; i < size; i++) {
        if (scores[i] == wanted) {
            return i;
        }
    }
    return -1;
}

int main(void) {
    int scores[] = {51, 3, 45, 83, 13};
    int size = 5;
    int wanted = 51;
    int pos = linear_search(scores, size, wanted);
    if (pos >= 0) {
        printf("Found %d at index %d\n", wanted, pos);
    } else {
        printf("%d is not in the array\n", wanted);
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: linear_search() checks the elements of scores one by one and returns the
   index of the first one equal to wanted, or -1 when it reaches the end without a match.
   main() searches for 51 and prints where it is, or that it is missing. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to write a function that swaps two long values through pointers. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write swap() that takes pointers to two long values.
   2. Save *x in tmp, copy *y into *x, then tmp into *y.
   3. In main(), print x and y, call swap(&x, &y) and print them again. */
/* Pass addresses so the function can change the caller's variables. */
void swap(long *x, long *y) {
    long tmp = *x;
    *x = *y;
    *y = tmp;
}

int main(void) {
    long x = 15L, y = 87L;
    printf("Before: %ld %ld\n", x, y);
    swap(&x, &y);
    printf("After:  %ld %ld\n", x, y);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: swap() receives the addresses of x and y, so writing through the pointers
   *x and *y changes the caller's variables. tmp holds one value during the exchange.
   main() declares both variables on one line and prints them before and after the swap. */
// END

/* Caption: Copy one string into another by hand. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write copy_string(dest, src).
   2. Copy src into dest one character at a time.
   3. Stop after copying the null character.
   4. Copy kernel into buffer and print it. */
/* Copy each character, including the final '\0'. */
void copy_string(char *dest, const char *src) {
    int i = 0;
    while ((dest[i] = src[i]) != '\0') {
        i++;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    char source[] = "kernel";
    char buffer[64];
    copy_string(buffer, source);
    printf("Copied: %s\n", buffer);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: copy_string() copies src into dest one character at a time, including the
   final null character, which is what strcpy does. The array buffer must be big enough to
   hold the copy. main() copies the word kernel and prints it. */
// END

/* Caption: Reverse an array by swapping from both ends. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write reverse_array() for data.
   2. Set i to the first index and j to the last.
   3. Swap data[i] and data[j], then move both inwards.
   4. Stop when i meets j and print the array. */
/* Swap the outer pair, then move both ends toward the middle. */
void reverse_array(long data[], int count) {
    int i = 0;
    int j = count - 1;
    while (i < j) {
        long tmp = data[i];
        data[i] = data[j];
        data[j] = tmp;
        i++;
        j--;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    long data[] = {65L, 16L, 10L, 99L, 56L, 63L};
    const int count = 6;
    reverse_array(data, count);
    for (int i = 0; i < count; i++) {
        printf("%ld ", data[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: reverse_array() swaps the first and last elements, then moves i forward and
   j backward until they meet, so the array is reversed in place without a second array.
   main() prints the reversed values. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to implement bubble sort for an array of double values. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write bubble_sort() for the double array data.
   2. Compare each pair of neighbours.
   3. Swap them when they are in the wrong order for descending order.
   4. Repeat the passes until the array is sorted.
   5. Print the sorted values. */
/* Repeatedly swap neighbours that are in the wrong order. */
void bubble_sort(double data[], int n) {
    for (int i = 0; i < n - 1; i++) {
        for (int j = 0; j < n - 1 - i; j++) {
            if (data[j] < data[j + 1]) {
                double tmp = data[j];
                data[j] = data[j + 1];
                data[j + 1] = tmp;
            }
        }
    }
}

int main(void) {
    double data[] = {91.6, 51.3, 53.6, 59.3, 67.4};
    const int n = 5;
    bubble_sort(data, n);
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        printf("%.2f ", data[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: bubble_sort() walks through data again and again and swaps neighbours that
   are in the wrong order, so the smallest values move to the end first. main() then prints
   the 5 values in descending order. */
// END

/* Caption: Program to compute the sum of the digits of an integer. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Start result at 0.
   2. Add n % 10 to result, then divide n by 10.
   3. Repeat until n is 0.
   4. Apply it to 365734 and print the result. */
/* Take the last digit with % 10, then drop it with / 10. */
int sum_digits(int n) {
    int result = 0;
    while (n > 0) {
        result += n % 10;
        n /= 10;
    }
    return result;
}

int main(void) {
    int number = 365734;
    printf("sum of digits of %d: %d\n", number, sum_digits(number));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: sum_digits() adds the last digit (n % 10) to result and then removes it (n
   / 10) until no digits are left. main() applies it to 365734. */
// END

/* Caption: Check whether a word is a palindrome. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <string.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write is_palindrome() for line.
   2. Compare the first and last characters, moving inwards.
   3. Return false at the first mismatch, otherwise true.
   4. Check keyboard and print the result. */
/* Compare characters from the front and back, moving inwards. */
bool is_palindrome(const char *line) {
    int i = 0;
    int j = strlen(line) - 1;
    while (i < j) {
        if (line[i] != line[j]) {
            return false;
        }
        i++;
        j--;
    }
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    const char *line = "keyboard";
    printf("%s %s a palindrome\n", line, is_palindrome(line) ? "is" : "is not");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: is_palindrome() compares the first and last characters and moves inwards;
   any mismatch means the word is not a palindrome. main() checks the word keyboard and
   prints the result. */
// END

/* Caption: Find a number in a sorted array with binary search. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Make sure the array is sorted.
   2. Set lo to 0 and hi to length - 1.
   3. While lo <= hi, compare the middle element mid with the key.
   4. Return the index if it matches; otherwise keep only the half that can hold the
      key.
   5. Return -1 if the range becomes empty, and print the index of 201. */
/* The array must be sorted. Each step halves the range that can still hold the key. */
int binary_search(const int prices[], int length, int key) {
    int lo = 0;
    int hi = length - 1;
    while (lo <= hi) {
        int mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;
        if (prices[mid] == key) {
            return mid;
        } else if (prices[mid] < key) {
            lo = mid + 1;   /* key is in the right half */
        } else {
            hi = mid - 1;   /* key is in the left half */
        }
    }
    return -1;
}

int main(void) {
    int prices[] = {34, 44, 52, 80, 116, 140, 166};
    int length = 7;
    int index = binary_search(prices, length, 201);
    printf("Index of 201: %d\n", index);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: binary_search() needs a sorted array. It keeps the range from lo to hi,
   compares the middle element mid with the key and throws away the half that cannot
   contain it, so it needs only about log2(n) steps. main() looks for 201 and prints its
   index, or -1 if it is not there. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to compute the product of two square matrices. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define N as 2.
   2. For every i and j, add a[i][k] * b[k][j] over k into product[i][j].
   3. Print product row by row. */
#define N 2

int main(void) {
    int a[N][N] = {{8, 7}, {1, 9}};
    int b[N][N] = {{8, 3}, {8, 6}};
    int product[N][N] = {0};
    /* product[i][j] is row i of a times column j of b. */
    for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) {
        for (int j = 0; j < N; j++) {
            for (int k = 0; k < N; k++) {
                product[i][j] += a[i][k] * b[k][j];
            }
        }
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) {
        for (int j = 0; j < N; j++) {
            printf("%4d", product[i][j]);
        }
        printf("\n");
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: For each entry product[i][j] the innermost loop adds a[i][k] * b[k][j] over
   k, which is row i of a times column j of b. main() multiplies two 2x2 matrices and
   prints the product. */
// END

/* Caption: C program to compute 4 to the power of 10 without pow(). */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write power(base, exp) with result = 1.
   2. Multiply result by base exp times.
   3. Print 4 to the power 10. */
/* Multiply the base by itself exp times. */
long long power(int base, int exp) {
    long long result = 1;
    for (int i = 0; i < exp; i++) {
        result *= base;
    }
    return result;
}

int main(void) {
    printf("4^10 = %lld\n", power(4, 10));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: power() starts result at 1 and multiplies it by base exp times. It uses
   long long because powers grow quickly. main() prints 4 to the power 10. */
// END

/* Caption: Compute the product of two square matrices. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define N as 3.
   2. For every i and j, add a[i][k] * b[k][j] over k into product[i][j].

#define N 3

int main(void) {
    int a[N][N] = {{0, 5, 2}, {8, 9, 5}, {6, 0, 6}};
    int b[N][N] = {{7, 4, 4}, {4, 1, 4}, {8, 6, 4}};
    int product[N][N] = {0};
    /* product[i][j] is row i of a times column j of b. */
    for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) {
        for (int j = 0; j < N; j++) {
            for (int k = 0; k < N; k++) {
                product[i][j] += a[i][k] * b[k][j];
            }
        }
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) {
        for (int j = 0; j < N; j++) {
            printf("%4d", product[i][j]);
        }
        printf("\n");
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: For each entry product[i][j] the innermost loop adds a[i][k] * b[k][j] over
   k, which is row i of a times column j of b. main() multiplies two 3x3 matrices and
   prints the product. */
// END

/* Caption: Use selection sort to put numbers in descending order. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write selection_sort() for the long array marks.
   2. For each position, find the largest remaining element.
   3. Swap it into that position.
   4. Print the sorted values. */
/* Select the right element for each position and swap it into place. */
void selection_sort(long marks[], int n) {
    for (int i = 0; i < n - 1; i++) {
        int chosen = i;
        for (int j = i + 1; j < n; j++) {
            if (marks[chosen] < marks[j]) {
                chosen = j;
            }
        }
        long tmp = marks[i];
        marks[i] = marks[chosen];
        marks[chosen] = tmp;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    long marks[] = {49L, 8L, 20L, 80L, 99L, 73L};
    int n = sizeof(marks) / sizeof(marks[0]);
    selection_sort(marks, n);
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        printf("%ld ", marks[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: selection_sort() finds the largest remaining element for each position and
   swaps it into place. main() then prints the 6 values in descending order. */
// END

/* Caption: Find the greatest common divisor of two numbers. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write gcd() with Euclid's algorithm.
   2. Replace (a, b) by (b, a % b) until b is 0.
   3. Return a and print the GCD of 247 and 237. */
/* Euclid: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a % b) until b becomes zero. */
int gcd(int a, int b) {
    while (b != 0) {
        int r = a % b;
        a = b;
        b = r;
    }
    return a;
}

int main(void) {
    int x = 247, y = 237;
    printf("gcd(%d, %d) = %d\n", x, y, gcd(x, y));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: gcd() uses Euclid's algorithm: it keeps replacing (a, b) with (b, a % b)
   until b is 0. The last non-zero value is the greatest common divisor, and main() prints
   the GCD of 247 and 237. */
// END

        best = b;

/* Caption: Reverse the elements of an array in place. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write reverse_array() for samples.
   2. Set i to the first index and j to the last.
   3. Swap samples[i] and samples[j], then move both inwards.
   4. Stop when i meets j and print the array. */
/* Swap the outer pair, then move both ends toward the middle. */
void reverse_array(int samples[], int size) {
    int i = 0;
    int j = size - 1;
    while (i < j) {
        int tmp = samples[i];
        samples[i] = samples[j];
        samples[j] = tmp;
        i++;
        j--;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    int samples[] = {62, 22, 65, 74, 62};
    int size = sizeof(samples) / sizeof(samples[0]);
    reverse_array(samples, size);
    for (int i = 0; i < size; i++) {
        printf("%d ", samples[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: reverse_array() swaps the first and last elements, then moves i forward and
   j backward until they meet, so the array is reversed in place without a second array.
   main() prints the reversed values. */
// END

/* Caption: Implement a simple linked list with malloc and free. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define ListNode with a value and a next pointer.
   2. Write push_front() that mallocs a node and links it in front of head.
   3. Write print_list() that follows next until NULL.
   4. Write free_list() that frees every node.
   5. Push 4 values, print the list and free it. */
typedef struct ListNode {
    int value;
    struct ListNode *next;
} ListNode;

/* Allocate a new node and put it in front of the current head. */
ListNode *push_front(ListNode *head, int value) {
    ListNode *node = malloc(sizeof(ListNode));
    if (node == NULL) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Out of memory\n");
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }
    node->value = value;
    node->next = head;
    return node;
}

void print_list(const ListNode *head) {
    for (const ListNode *cur = head; cur != NULL; cur = cur->next) {
        printf("%d -> ", cur->value);
    }
    printf("NULL\n");
}

/* Free every node; save next before freeing the current one. */
void free_list(ListNode *head) {
    while (head != NULL) {
        ListNode *next = head->next;
        free(head);
        head = next;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    ListNode *head = NULL;
    head = push_front(head, 68);
    head = push_front(head, 58);
    head = push_front(head, 80);
    head = push_front(head, 65);
    print_list(head);
    free_list(head);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: Each ListNode holds a value and a pointer to the next node. push_front()
   allocates a node with malloc, puts it in front of head and returns it; print_list()
   follows the next pointers until NULL; free_list() frees every node. main() pushes 4
   values, so they print in reverse order. */
// END

/* Caption: Limit a number to a range with a three-parameter function. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write clamp(value, low, high).
   2. Return low if the value is too small and high if it is too big.
   3. Otherwise return the value.
   4. Set low = 16 and high = 32 and print clamp() for 62, 109 and 71. */
/* Return value, but never less than low or more than high. */
int clamp(int value, int low, int high) {
    if (value < low) {
        return low;
    }
    if (value > high) {
        return high;
    }
    return value;
}

int main(void) {
    int low = 16, high = 32;
    printf("clamp(%d) = %d\n", 62, clamp(62, low, high));
    printf("clamp(%d) = %d\n", 109, clamp(109, low, high));
    printf("clamp(%d) = %d\n", 71, clamp(71, low, high));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: clamp() takes three parameters: the value and the two limits. It returns
   low when the value is too small, high when it is too big and the value itself otherwise.
   main() declares low = 16 and high = 32 on one line and clamps 62, 109 and 71. */
// END

/* Caption: Compute the sum of the digits of an integer. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Start result at 0.
   2. Add n % 10 to result, then divide n by 10.
   3. Repeat until n is 0.
   4. Apply it to 873344 and print the result. */
/* Take the last digit with % 10, then drop it with / 10. */
int sum_digits(int n) {
    int result = 0;
    while (n > 0) {
        result += n % 10;
        n /= 10;
    }
    return result;
}

int main(void) {
    int number = 873344;
    printf("sum of digits of %d: %d\n", number, sum_digits(number));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: sum_digits() adds the last digit (n % 10) to result and then removes it (n
   / 10) until no digits are left. main() applies it to 873344. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to test if 71 is a prime number. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write is_prime(n); numbers below 2 are not prime.
   2. Try every divisor d while d * d <= n.
   3. Return false if one divides n, otherwise true.
   4. Check 71 and print the result. */
/* A prime has no divisor between 2 and its square root. */
bool is_prime(int n) {
    if (n < 2) {
        return false;
    }
    for (int d = 2; d * d <= n; d++) {
        if (n % d == 0) {
            return false;
        }
    }
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    int number = 71;
    printf("%d %s prime\n", number, is_prime(number) ? "is" : "is not");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: is_prime() tries every divisor d from 2 while d * d <= n; if one divides n
   evenly, n is not prime. main() checks 71 and prints whether it is prime. */
// END

/* Caption: How do I use binary search to locate a value in a sorted list in C? */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Make sure the array is sorted.
   2. Set low to 0 and high to length - 1.
   3. While low <= high, compare the middle element mid with the key.
   4. Return the index if it matches; otherwise keep only the half that can hold the
      key.
   5. Return -1 if the range becomes empty, and print the index of 201. */
/* The array must be sorted. Each step halves the range that can still hold the key. */
int binary_search(const int nums[], int length, int key) {
    int low = 0;
    int high = length - 1;
    while (low <= high) {
        int mid = low + (high - low) / 2;
        if (nums[mid] == key) {
            return mid;
        } else if (nums[mid] < key) {
            low = mid + 1;   /* key is in the right half */
        } else {
            high = mid - 1;   /* key is in the left half */
        }
    }
    return -1;
}

int main(void) {
    int nums[] = {9, 33, 38, 52, 79, 105, 119, 133, 166, 184, 199};
    int length = 11;
    int index = binary_search(nums, length, 201);
    printf("Index of 201: %d\n", index);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: binary_search() needs a sorted array. It keeps the range from low to high,
   compares the middle element mid with the key and throws away the half that cannot
   contain it, so it needs only about log2(n) steps. main() looks for 201 and prints its
   index, or -1 if it is not there. */
// END

/* Caption: Use dynamic memory to store the first 5 squares. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Use malloc to get room for 5 ints and check for NULL.
   2. Fill table with squares.
   3. Print the values.
   4. Call free(table) at the end. */
int main(void) {
    int n = 5;
    /* Ask the heap for room for n ints; malloc returns NULL on failure. */
    int *table = malloc(n * sizeof(int));
    if (table == NULL) {
        fprintf(stderr, "malloc failed\n");
        return 1;
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        table[i] = i * i;
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        printf("%d ", table[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    free(table);   /* give the memory back */
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: malloc() reserves room for 5 ints on the heap and returns NULL if it fails,
   which the program checks. The first loop fills table with squares, the second prints
   them, and free() gives the memory back at the end. */
// END

/* Caption: C program to sum a int array with a helper function. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write array_sum() that takes the array ages and its length size.
   2. Start result at 0 and add every element in a while loop.
   3. Return result.
   4. In main(), fill ages with 4 values and print the sum. */
/* Add every element to a running total. */
int array_sum(const int ages[], int size) {
    int result = 0;
    int k = 0;
    while (k < size) {
        result += ages[k];
        k++;
    }
    return result;
}

int main(void) {
    int ages[] = {11, 86, 31, 81};
    int size = 4;
    printf("Sum: %d\n", array_sum(ages, size));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: array_sum() receives the array ages and its length size. It starts result
   at 0, adds every element to it in a while loop and returns the total. main() fills ages
   with 4 int values and prints their sum. */
// END

/* Caption: Transpose a matrix. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define ROWS as 4 and COLS as 4.
   2. Copy m[r][c] into t[c][r] for every element.
   3. Print t row by row. */
#define ROWS 4
#define COLS 4

int main(void) {
    int m[ROWS][COLS] = {{3, 7, 1, 8}, {3, 9, 2, 6}, {4, 3, 7, 2}, {5, 9, 1, 5}};
    int t[COLS][ROWS];
    /* Element (r, c) moves to (c, r). */
    for (int r = 0; r < ROWS; r++) {
        for (int c = 0; c < COLS; c++) {
            t[c][r] = m[r][c];
        }
    }
    for (int r = 0; r < COLS; r++) {
        for (int c = 0; c < ROWS; c++) {
            printf("%3d", t[r][c]);
        }
        printf("\n");
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: The nested loops copy m[r][c] into t[c][r], so the 4x4 matrix becomes 4x4.
   A second pair of loops prints the result. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to convert 420 to binary. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write print_binary(n, bits).
   2. Go through the bits from the highest to the lowest.
   3. Print 1 when (n >> b) & 1 is set, otherwise 0.
   4. Print 420 in binary. */
/* Check each bit from the highest to the lowest. */
void print_binary(unsigned int n, int bits) {
    for (int b = bits - 1; b >= 0; b--) {
        putchar((n >> b) & 1 ? '1' : '0');
    }
    putchar('\n');
}

int main(void) {
    unsigned int number = 420;
    printf("%u in binary: ", number);
    print_binary(number, 16);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: print_binary() checks one bit at a time, from the highest to the lowest: (n
   >> b) & 1 is 1 when bit b is set, so it prints the character 1 or 0. main() prints 420
   in binary. */
// END

/* Caption: Program to count how many times 'l' appears in a string. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write count_char() with count = 0.
   2. Compare each character with the target l.
   3. Return count and print it. */
int count_char(const char *text, char target) {
    int count = 0;
    /* Compare every character with the target. */
    for (int i = 0; text[i] != '\0'; i++) {
        if (text[i] == target) {
            count++;
        }
    }
    return count;
}

int main(void) {
    const char *sentence = "strings end with a null character";
    printf("'l' appears %d times\n", count_char(sentence, 'l'));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: count_char() compares every character of the text with the target character
   and counts the matches. main() prints how many times l appears in the sentence. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a function that returns the quotient and remainder through pointers. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write divide(a, b, &quotient, &remainder) that returns a bool.
   2. Return false if b is 0.
   3. Store a / b and a % b through the pointers and return true.
   4. Divide 323 by 8 and print the results or the error. */
/* Returns false for division by zero; otherwise stores both results. */
bool divide(int a, int b, int *quotient, int *remainder) {
    if (b == 0) {
        return false;
    }
    *quotient = a / b;
    *remainder = a % b;
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    int a = 323, b = 8;
    int q, r;
    if (divide(a, b, &q, &r)) {
        printf("%d / %d = %d remainder %d\n", a, b, q, r);
    } else {
        printf("Cannot divide by zero\n");
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: divide() has four parameters: two inputs and two pointers for the results.
   Its bool return value reports success, while the quotient and remainder are written
   through the pointers. main() divides 323 by 8 and prints both results. */
// END

/* Caption: C program to sort an array in ascending order using insertion sort. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write insertion_sort() for the int array marks.
   2. Take each element in turn as current.
   3. Shift the larger values of the sorted part one place right.
   4. Put current into the gap.
   5. Print the sorted values. */
/* Insert each element into the already sorted part on its left. */
void insertion_sort(int marks[], int len) {
    for (int i = 1; i < len; i++) {
        int current = marks[i];
        int j = i - 1;
        while (j >= 0 && marks[j] > current) {
            marks[j + 1] = marks[j];   /* shift bigger values right */
            j--;
        }
        marks[j + 1] = current;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    int marks[] = {28, 50, 55, 72, 97, 64, 50, 72};
    int len = 8;
    insertion_sort(marks, len);
    for (int i = 0; i < len; i++) {
        printf("%d ", marks[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: insertion_sort() takes each element in turn and shifts the larger values of
   the sorted part one place right until the element fits. main() then prints the 8 values
   in ascending order. */
// END

/* Caption: Print the first 25 Fibonacci numbers. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Start with a = 0 and b = 1.
   2. Repeat 25 times and print a each time.
   3. Compute next = a + b, then set a = b and b = next. */
int main(void) {
    long a = 0, b = 1;
    /* Print a term, then slide the pair one step along the sequence. */
    for (int i = 0; i < 25; i++) {
        printf("%ld ", a);
        long next = a + b;
        a = b;
        b = next;
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: The loop keeps the last two numbers in a and b. Each round it prints a,
   then moves the pair forward: a becomes b and b becomes their sum. It prints the first 25
   Fibonacci numbers. */
// END

/* Caption: Calculate the average of the values in an array. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write compute_mean() that takes numbers and count.
   2. Add the values into the double result.
   3. Return result / count.
   4. Print the average with two decimals. */
/* The mean is the total divided by the count. */
double compute_mean(const int numbers[], int count) {
    double result = 0.0;
    for (int j = 0; j < count; j++) {
        result += numbers[j];
    }
    return result / count;
}

int main(void) {
    int numbers[] = {29, 14, 11};
    const int count = 3;
    printf("The average is %.2f\n", compute_mean(numbers, count));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: compute_mean() adds the 3 values of numbers into the double result and
   divides by count, so the mean keeps its decimal part even when the values are whole
   numbers. main() prints it with two decimals. */
// END

/* Caption: Search an array for its smallest value. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write smallest_value() that takes samples and n.
   2. Store samples[0] in m.
   3. Loop over the other elements and keep the smallest value in m.
   4. Return m and print it. */
/* Start with the first element and keep the smallest value seen so far. */
double smallest_value(const double samples[], int n) {
    double m = samples[0];
    for (int k = 1; k < n; k++) {
        if (samples[k] < m) {
            m = samples[k];
        }
    }
    return m;
}

int main(void) {
    double samples[] = {56.9, 30.5, 30.9, 83.7, 58.2, 76.8, 42.5, 86.7, 56.9};
    int n = 9;
    printf("Smallest: %.2f\n", smallest_value(samples, n));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: smallest_value() takes the first element as the smallest value so far and
   stores it in m. The loop compares every other element with m using < and keeps the
   smallest one. main() prints the smallest of the 9 values. */
// END

#include <ctype.h>

/* Plan:

   2. Replace every character with toupper() until the null character.
   3. Print the sentence. */
/* toupper changes lowercase letters and leaves other characters alone. */
void to_upper(char *word) {
    for (int i = 0; word[i] != '\0'; i++) {

    }
}

int main(void) {

    to_upper(word);
    printf("%s\n", word);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: to_upper() walks through word until the null character and replaces each
   character with toupper(), which only changes lowercase letters. main() prints the
   sentence in capitals. */
// END

/* Caption: Find the greatest common divisor of two numbers. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write gcd() with Euclid's algorithm.
   2. Replace (a, b) by (b, a % b) until b is 0.
   3. Return a and print the GCD of 243 and 7. */
/* Euclid: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a % b) until b becomes zero. */
int gcd(int a, int b) {
    while (b != 0) {
        int r = a % b;
        a = b;
        b = r;
    }
    return a;
}

int main(void) {
    int x = 243, y = 7;
    printf("gcd(%d, %d) = %d\n", x, y, gcd(x, y));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: gcd() uses Euclid's algorithm: it keeps replacing (a, b) with (b, a % b)
   until b is 0. The last non-zero value is the greatest common divisor, and main() prints
   the GCD of 243 and 7. */
// END

/* Caption: How do I implement a stack with an array (push and pop) in C? */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define a Stack with room for 16 items and a top counter.
   2. Write push() and pop(), returning false when the stack is full or empty.
   3. Push 5 values.
   4. Pop and print until the stack is empty. */
#define CAPACITY 16

typedef struct {
    int items[CAPACITY];
    int top;   /* number of items on the stack */
} Stack;

bool push(Stack *s, int value) {
    if (s->top == CAPACITY) {
        return false;   /* stack is full */
    }
    s->items[s->top++] = value;
    return true;
}

bool pop(Stack *s, int *value) {
    if (s->top == 0) {
        return false;   /* stack is empty */
    }
    *value = s->items[--s->top];
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    Stack s = {.top = 0};
    push(&s, 85);
    push(&s, 80);
    push(&s, 18);
    push(&s, 61);
    push(&s, 94);
    int value;
    /* Items come back out in reverse order (last in, first out). */
    while (pop(&s, &value)) {
        printf("%d ", value);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: The Stack keeps up to 16 items in an array, and top counts how many are
   stored. push() adds at the top and pop() removes from the top; both return false when
   they cannot. main() pushes 5 values and pops them all, so they come out in reverse order
   (last in, first out). */
// END

#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:

   2. Declare the pointers px and py on one line, each with its own *.
   3. Add 12 to x through px and print the values. */
int main(void) {
    int x = 9, y = 36;
    /* Each pointer needs its own '*': in "int *p, q;" only p is a pointer. */
    int *px = &x, *py = &y;
    *px += 12;
    printf("x = %d, y = %d\n", x, y);
    printf("*px = %d, *py = %d\n", *px, *py);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: int *px = &x, *py = &y; declares two pointers in one statement; each name
   needs its own *. *px += 12 changes x through the pointer, so x becomes 21 while y stays
   36. */
// END

/* Caption: Program to allocate an array with malloc and fill it with cubes. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Use malloc to get room for 7 ints and check for NULL.
   2. Fill buffer with cubes.
   3. Print the values.
   4. Call free(buffer) at the end. */
int main(void) {
    int n = 7;
    /* Ask the heap for room for n ints; malloc returns NULL on failure. */
    int *buffer = malloc(n * sizeof(int));
    if (buffer == NULL) {
        fprintf(stderr, "malloc failed\n");
        return 1;
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        buffer[i] = i * i * i;
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        printf("%d ", buffer[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    free(buffer);   /* give the memory back */
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: malloc() reserves room for 7 ints on the heap and returns NULL if it fails,
   which the program checks. The first loop fills buffer with cubes, the second prints
   them, and free() gives the memory back at the end. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to write lines to a text file and read them back. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Open log.txt in write mode and check for NULL.
   2. Write 3 lines with fprintf and close the file.
   3. Open it again in read mode.
   4. Read and print each line with fgets, then close the file. */
int main(void) {
    FILE *file = fopen("log.txt", "w");
    if (file == NULL) {
        perror("fopen");
        return 1;
    }
    fprintf(file, "good comments explain why the code exists\n");
    fprintf(file, "the quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog\n");
    fprintf(file, "loops repeat a block of code\n");
    fclose(file);

    /* Reopen the file for reading and print it line by line. */
    file = fopen("log.txt", "r");
    if (file == NULL) {
        perror("fopen");
        return 1;
    }
    char line[128];
    while (fgets(line, sizeof(line), file) != NULL) {
        printf("%s", line);
    }
    fclose(file);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: fopen() in write mode creates log.txt, fprintf() writes 3 lines into it and
   fclose() saves it. The file is then opened again in read mode, and fgets() reads it back
   line by line into the buffer line, which is printed. Every fopen() result is checked for
   NULL. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to write a function that swaps two int values through pointers. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write swap() that takes pointers to two int values.
   2. Save *a in tmp, copy *b into *a, then tmp into *b.
   3. In main(), print a and b, call swap(&a, &b) and print them again. */
/* Pass addresses so the function can change the caller's variables. */
void swap(int *a, int *b) {
    int tmp = *a;
    *a = *b;
    *b = tmp;
}

int main(void) {
    int a = 62, b = 52;
    printf("Before: %d %d\n", a, b);
    swap(&a, &b);
    printf("After:  %d %d\n", a, b);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: swap() receives the addresses of a and b, so writing through the pointers
   *a and *b changes the caller's variables. tmp holds one value during the exchange.
   main() declares both variables on one line and prints them before and after the swap. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to compute 7 to the power of 2 without pow(). */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write power(base, exp) with result = 1.
   2. Multiply result by base exp times.
   3. Print 7 to the power 2. */
/* Multiply the base by itself exp times. */
long long power(int base, int exp) {
    long long result = 1;
    for (int i = 0; i < exp; i++) {
        result *= base;
    }
    return result;
}

int main(void) {
    printf("7^2 = %lld\n", power(7, 2));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: power() starts result at 1 and multiplies it by base exp times. It uses
   long long because powers grow quickly. main() prints 7 to the power 2. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to implement a stack with an array (push and pop). */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define a Stack with room for 10 items and a top counter.
   2. Write push() and pop(), returning false when the stack is full or empty.
   3. Push 4 values.
   4. Pop and print until the stack is empty. */
#define CAPACITY 10

typedef struct {
    int items[CAPACITY];
    int top;   /* number of items on the stack */
} Stack;

bool push(Stack *s, int value) {
    if (s->top == CAPACITY) {
        return false;   /* stack is full */
    }
    s->items[s->top++] = value;
    return true;
}

bool pop(Stack *s, int *value) {
    if (s->top == 0) {
        return false;   /* stack is empty */
    }
    *value = s->items[--s->top];
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    Stack s = {.top = 0};
    push(&s, 4);
    push(&s, 10);
    push(&s, 44);
    push(&s, 53);
    int value;
    /* Items come back out in reverse order (last in, first out). */
    while (pop(&s, &value)) {
        printf("%d ", value);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: The Stack keeps up to 10 items in an array, and top counts how many are
   stored. push() adds at the top and pop() removes from the top; both return false when
   they cannot. main() pushes 4 values and pops them all, so they come out in reverse order
   (last in, first out). */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to count the words in a sentence. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <ctype.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write count_words() with words = 0 and an in_word flag.
   2. A space ends a word; a non-space after a space starts a new word and adds one to
      words.
   3. Return words and print it. */
/* A new word starts when a non-space follows a space (or the start). */
int count_words(const char *text) {
    int words = 0;
    int in_word = 0;
    for (int i = 0; text[i] != '\0'; i++) {
        if (isspace((unsigned char)text[i])) {
            in_word = 0;
        } else if (!in_word) {
            in_word = 1;
            words++;
        }
    }
    return words;
}

int main(void) {
    const char *sentence = "arrays in c start at index zero";
    printf("Words: %d\n", count_words(sentence));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: count_words() uses the flag in_word: a new word starts when a non-space
   character follows a space or the start of the text. main() prints the number of words in
   the sentence. */
// END

/* Caption: Return both the smallest and the largest value of an array through pointers. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write min_max() with the array, its length and the pointers min and max.
   2. Start both at the first element.
   3. Update *min and *max while looping over the rest.
   4. Declare low and high, pass their addresses and print them. */
/* One pass finds both results; they are stored through the pointers. */
void min_max(const int items[], int length, int *min, int *max) {
    *min = items[0];
    *max = items[0];
    for (int i = 1; i < length; i++) {
        if (items[i] < *min) {
            *min = items[i];
        }
        if (items[i] > *max) {
            *max = items[i];
        }
    }
}

int main(void) {
    int items[] = {84, 8, 25, 54, 48, 47, 26, 66, 65};
    int length = 9;
    int low, high;
    min_max(items, length, &low, &high);
    printf("Min: %d, Max: %d\n", low, high);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: A C function can return only one value, so min_max() returns void and
   writes its two results through the pointer parameters min and max. main() declares low
   and high on one line and passes their addresses with &, then prints both results for the
   9 values. */
// END

/* Caption: Use Euclid's algorithm to compute the GCD. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write gcd() with Euclid's algorithm.
   2. Replace (a, b) by (b, a % b) until b is 0.
   3. Return a and print the GCD of 215 and 168. */
/* Euclid: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a % b) until b becomes zero. */
int gcd(int a, int b) {
    while (b != 0) {
        int r = a % b;
        a = b;
        b = r;
    }
    return a;
}

int main(void) {

    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: gcd() uses Euclid's algorithm: it keeps replacing (a, b) with (b, a % b)
   until b is 0. The last non-zero value is the greatest common divisor, and main() prints
   the GCD of 215 and 168. */
// END

/* Caption: C program to test if 232 is a prime number. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write is_prime(n); numbers below 2 are not prime.
   2. Try every divisor d while d * d <= n.
   3. Return false if one divides n, otherwise true.
   4. Check 232 and print the result. */
/* A prime has no divisor between 2 and its square root. */
bool is_prime(int n) {
    if (n < 2) {
        return false;
    }
    for (int d = 2; d * d <= n; d++) {
        if (n % d == 0) {
            return false;
        }
    }
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    int number = 232;
    printf("%d %s prime\n", number, is_prime(number) ? "is" : "is not");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: is_prime() tries every divisor d from 2 while d * d <= n; if one divides n
   evenly, n is not prime. main() checks 232 and prints whether it is prime. */
// END

/* Caption: Find the area and circumference of a circle from its radius. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Read the radius.
   2. Compute the area PI * r * r.
   3. Compute the circumference 2 * PI * r.
   4. Print both. */
#define PI 3.14159265

int main(void) {
    double radius;
    printf("Enter the radius: ");
    if (scanf("%lf", &radius) != 1) {
        printf("Invalid input\n");
        return 1;
    }
    /* area = PI * r * r, circumference = 2 * PI * r */
    printf("Area: %.2f\n", PI * radius * radius);
    printf("Circumference: %.2f\n", 2 * PI * radius);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: The program reads radius from the keyboard with scanf and stops with a
   message if the input is not valid. It uses PI, defined with #define, to print the area
   (PI * r * r) and the circumference (2 * PI * r). */
// END

/* Caption: C program to write lines to a text file and read them back. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Open data.txt in write mode and check for NULL.
   2. Write 3 lines with fprintf and close the file.
   3. Open it again in read mode.
   4. Read and print each line with fgets, then close the file. */
int main(void) {
    FILE *file = fopen("data.txt", "w");
    if (file == NULL) {
        perror("fopen");
        return 1;
    }
    fprintf(file, "a function can call itself recursively\n");
    fprintf(file, "good comments explain why the code exists\n");
    fprintf(file, "the quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog\n");
    fclose(file);

    /* Reopen the file for reading and print it line by line. */
    file = fopen("data.txt", "r");
    if (file == NULL) {
        perror("fopen");
        return 1;
    }
    char line[128];
    while (fgets(line, sizeof(line), file) != NULL) {
        printf("%s", line);
    }
    fclose(file);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: fopen() in write mode creates data.txt, fprintf() writes 3 lines into it
   and fclose() saves it. The file is then opened again in read mode, and fgets() reads it
   back line by line into the buffer line, which is printed. Every fopen() result is
   checked for NULL. */
// END

/* Caption: Test if "program" reads the same backwards. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <string.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write is_palindrome() for line.
   2. Compare the first and last characters, moving inwards.
   3. Return false at the first mismatch, otherwise true.
   4. Check program and print the result. */
/* Compare characters from the front and back, moving inwards. */
bool is_palindrome(const char *line) {
    int i = 0;
    int j = strlen(line) - 1;
    while (i < j) {
        if (line[i] != line[j]) {
            return false;
        }
        i++;
        j--;
    }
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    const char *line = "program";
    printf("%s %s a palindrome\n", line, is_palindrome(line) ? "is" : "is not");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: is_palindrome() compares the first and last characters and moves inwards;
   any mismatch means the word is not a palindrome. main() checks the word program and
   prints the result. */
// END

/* Caption: Use binary search to locate a value in a sorted list. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Make sure the array is sorted.
   2. Set left to 0 and right to count - 1.
   3. While left <= right, compare the middle element middle with the key.
   4. Return the index if it matches; otherwise keep only the half that can hold the
      key.
   5. Return -1 if the range becomes empty, and print the index of 175. */
/* The array must be sorted. Each step halves the range that can still hold the key. */
int binary_search(const int ages[], int count, int key) {
    int left = 0;
    int right = count - 1;
    while (left <= right) {
        int middle = left + (right - left) / 2;
        if (ages[middle] == key) {
            return middle;
        } else if (ages[middle] < key) {
            left = middle + 1;   /* key is in the right half */
        } else {
            right = middle - 1;   /* key is in the left half */
        }
    }
    return -1;
}

int main(void) {
    int ages[] = {1, 24, 38, 51, 116, 175, 181};
    int count = 7;
    int index = binary_search(ages, count, 175);
    printf("Index of 175: %d\n", index);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: binary_search() needs a sorted array. It keeps the range from left to
   right, compares the middle element middle with the key and throws away the half that
   cannot contain it, so it needs only about log2(n) steps. main() looks for 175 and prints
   its index, or -1 if it is not there. */
// END

/* Caption: C program to compute 6 to the power of 8 without pow(). */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write power(base, exp) with result = 1.
   2. Multiply result by base exp times.
   3. Print 6 to the power 8. */
/* Multiply the base by itself exp times. */
long long power(int base, int exp) {
    long long result = 1;
    for (int i = 0; i < exp; i++) {
        result *= base;
    }
    return result;
}

int main(void) {
    printf("6^8 = %lld\n", power(6, 8));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: power() starts result at 1 and multiplies it by base exp times. It uses
   long long because powers grow quickly. main() prints 6 to the power 8. */
// END

/* Caption: Program to find the quotient of 2 numbers. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Read first and second.
   2. If second is 0, print an error and stop.
   3. Print first / second and the remainder first % second. */
int main(void) {
    int first, second;
    printf("Enter 2 numbers: ");
    if (scanf("%d %d", &first, &second) != 2) {
        printf("Invalid input\n");
        return 1;
    }
    /* Dividing by zero is not allowed, so check first. */
    if (second == 0) {
        printf("Cannot divide by zero\n");
        return 1;
    }
    /* Integer division drops the fraction; % gives the remainder. */
    printf("Quotient: %d, remainder: %d\n", first / second, first % second);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: The program reads first and second from the keyboard with scanf and stops
   with a message if the input is not valid. It checks that second is not zero, then prints
   first / second, where integer division drops the fraction, and the remainder first %
   second. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to change every letter in a sentence to a capital letter. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <ctype.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write to_upper() for line.
   2. Replace every character with toupper() until the null character.
   3. Print the sentence. */
/* toupper changes lowercase letters and leaves other characters alone. */
void to_upper(char *line) {
    for (int i = 0; line[i] != '\0'; i++) {
        line[i] = toupper((unsigned char)line[i]);
    }
}

int main(void) {
    char line[] = "always free the memory you allocate";
    to_upper(line);
    printf("%s\n", line);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: to_upper() walks through line until the null character and replaces each
   character with toupper(), which only changes lowercase letters. main() prints the
   sentence in capitals. */
// END

/* Caption: Program to compute the distance between two points with a four-parameter function. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <math.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write distance(x1, y1, x2, y2).
   2. Compute dx and dy, then return sqrt(dx * dx + dy * dy).
   3. Print the distance between (2, -8) and (10, -4). */
/* Pythagoras: the distance is sqrt(dx * dx + dy * dy). */
double distance(double x1, double y1, double x2, double y2) {
    double dx = x2 - x1, dy = y2 - y1;
    return sqrt(dx * dx + dy * dy);
}

int main(void) {
    printf("Distance: %.3f\n", distance(2, -8, 10, -4));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: distance() takes the coordinates of both points as four parameters. It
   declares dx and dy on one line and uses Pythagoras with sqrt() from math.h. main()
   prints the distance between (2, -8) and (10, -4). */
// END

/* Caption: Multiply two 2x2 matrices. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define N as 2.
   2. For every i and j, add a[i][k] * b[k][j] over k into product[i][j].
   3. Print product row by row. */
#define N 2

int main(void) {
    int a[N][N] = {{9, 0}, {6, 4}};
    int b[N][N] = {{4, 1}, {1, 4}};
    int product[N][N] = {0};
    /* product[i][j] is row i of a times column j of b. */
    for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) {
        for (int j = 0; j < N; j++) {
            for (int k = 0; k < N; k++) {
                product[i][j] += a[i][k] * b[k][j];
            }
        }
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) {
        for (int j = 0; j < N; j++) {
            printf("%4d", product[i][j]);
        }
        printf("\n");
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: For each entry product[i][j] the innermost loop adds a[i][k] * b[k][j] over
   k, which is row i of a times column j of b. main() multiplies two 2x2 matrices and
   prints the product. */
// END

/* Caption: Compute the LCM of two integers using the GCD. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write gcd() with Euclid's algorithm: replace (a, b) by (b, a % b) until b is 0.
   2. Write lcm() as a / gcd(a, b) * b.
   3. Print the LCM of 55 and 280. */
/* Euclid: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a % b) until b becomes zero. */
int gcd(int a, int b) {
    while (b != 0) {
        int r = a % b;
        a = b;
        b = r;
    }
    return a;
}

/* lcm(a, b) = a / gcd(a, b) * b (divide first to avoid overflow). */
long lcm(int a, int b) {
    return (long)a / gcd(a, b) * b;
}

int main(void) {
    printf("lcm(55, 280) = %ld\n", lcm(55, 280));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: gcd() uses Euclid's algorithm: it keeps replacing (a, b) with (b, a % b)
   until b is 0. lcm() divides a by the gcd before multiplying by b, which avoids overflow.
   main() prints the LCM of 55 and 280. */
// END

/* Caption: Reverse the elements of an array in place. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write reverse_array() for data.
   2. Set i to the first index and j to the last.
   3. Swap data[i] and data[j], then move both inwards.
   4. Stop when i meets j and print the array. */
/* Swap the outer pair, then move both ends toward the middle. */
void reverse_array(int data[], int n) {
    int i = 0;
    int j = n - 1;
    while (i < j) {
        int tmp = data[i];
        data[i] = data[j];
        data[j] = tmp;
        i++;
        j--;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    int data[] = {10, 11, 48, 98, 56};
    int n = sizeof(data) / sizeof(data[0]);
    reverse_array(data, n);
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        printf("%d ", data[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: reverse_array() swaps the first and last elements, then moves i forward and
   j backward until they meet, so the array is reversed in place without a second array.
   main() prints the reversed values. */
// END

/* Caption: Calculate 13! using recursion. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write factorial(n) that calls itself.
   2. Return 1 when n is 1 or less.
   3. Otherwise return n * factorial(n - 1).
   4. Print 13! as an unsigned long long. */
/* n! = n * (n - 1)!, and 0! = 1 stops the recursion. */
unsigned long long factorial(int n) {
    if (n <= 1) {
        return 1;
    }
    return n * factorial(n - 1);
}

int main(void) {
    int n = 13;
    printf("%d! = %llu\n", n, factorial(n));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: factorial() calls itself: n! is n * (n - 1)!, and the recursion stops when
   n is 1 or less. main() prints 13! as an unsigned long long, because factorials grow very
   fast. */
// END

/* Caption: Count the even values in a list of integers. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write count_even() that takes items and length.
   2. For each element, test items[idx] % 2 == 0.
   3. Add one to count for every even number.
   4. Return count and print it. */
/* A number is even when the remainder after dividing by 2 is zero. */
int count_even(const int items[], int length) {
    int count = 0;
    for (int idx = 0; idx < length; idx++) {
        if (items[idx] % 2 == 0) {
            count++;
        }
    }
    return count;
}

int main(void) {
    int items[] = {41, 41, 89, 28, 18, 19, 76, 10, 7};
    int length = sizeof(items) / sizeof(items[0]);
    printf("Even numbers: %d\n", count_even(items, length));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: count_even() tests each element of items with the % operator: a remainder
   of 0 after dividing by 2 means the number is even, so count goes up by one. main()
   prints how many of the 9 values are even. */
// END

/* Caption: Use binary search to locate a value in a sorted list. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Make sure the array is sorted.
   2. Set low to 0 and high to len - 1.
   3. While low <= high, compare the middle element mid with the key.
   4. Return the index if it matches; otherwise keep only the half that can hold the
      key.
   5. Return -1 if the range becomes empty, and print the index of 190. */
/* The array must be sorted. Each step halves the range that can still hold the key. */
int binary_search(const int numbers[], int len, int key) {

    int high = len - 1;

            low = mid + 1;   /* key is in the right half */
        } else {
            high = mid - 1;   /* key is in the left half */
        }
    }
    return -1;
}

int main(void) {

    const int len = 6;
    int index = binary_search(numbers, len, 190);
    printf("Index of 190: %d\n", index);

/* Caption: Reverse the characters of a word. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <string.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write reverse_string() for buffer.
   2. Set i to the first index and j to the last.
   3. Swap the two characters and move i and j inwards until they meet.
   4. Reverse program and print it. */
/* Swap characters from both ends until they meet in the middle. */
void reverse_string(char *buffer) {
    int i = 0;
    int j = strlen(buffer) - 1;
    while (i < j) {
        char tmp = buffer[i];
        buffer[i] = buffer[j];
        buffer[j] = tmp;
        i++;
        j--;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    char buffer[] = "program";
    reverse_string(buffer);
    printf("%s\n", buffer);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: reverse_string() swaps characters from both ends of buffer, moving inwards
   until the two indexes meet. main() reverses the word program in place and prints it. */
// END

/* Caption: Convert 951 to binary. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write print_binary(n, bits).
   2. Go through the bits from the highest to the lowest.
   3. Print 1 when (n >> b) & 1 is set, otherwise 0.
   4. Print 951 in binary. */
/* Check each bit from the highest to the lowest. */
void print_binary(unsigned int n, int bits) {
    for (int b = bits - 1; b >= 0; b--) {
        putchar((n >> b) & 1 ? '1' : '0');
    }
    putchar('\n');
}

int main(void) {
    unsigned int number = 951;
    printf("%u in binary: ", number);
    print_binary(number, 10);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: print_binary() checks one bit at a time, from the highest to the lowest: (n
   >> b) & 1 is 1 when bit b is set, so it prints the character 1 or 0. main() prints 951
   in binary. */
// END

/* Caption: Limit a number to a range with a three-parameter function. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write clamp(value, low, high).
   2. Return low if the value is too small and high if it is too big.
   3. Otherwise return the value.
   4. Set low = 35 and high = 43 and print clamp() for -10, 103 and 67. */
/* Return value, but never less than low or more than high. */
int clamp(int value, int low, int high) {
    if (value < low) {
        return low;
    }
    if (value > high) {
        return high;
    }
    return value;
}

int main(void) {
    int low = 35, high = 43;
    printf("clamp(%d) = %d\n", -10, clamp(-10, low, high));
    printf("clamp(%d) = %d\n", 103, clamp(103, low, high));
    printf("clamp(%d) = %d\n", 67, clamp(67, low, high));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: clamp() takes three parameters: the value and the two limits. It returns
   low when the value is too small, high when it is too big and the value itself otherwise.
   main() declares low = 35 and high = 43 on one line and clamps -10, 103 and 67. */
// END

/* Caption: Program to sum a int array with a helper function. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write sum_array() that takes the array scores and its length size.
   2. Start acc at 0 and add every element in a for loop.
   3. Return acc.
   4. In main(), fill scores with 9 values and print the sum. */
/* Add every element to a running total. */
int sum_array(const int scores[], int size) {
    int acc = 0;
    for (int idx = 0; idx < size; idx++) {
        acc += scores[idx];
    }
    return acc;
}

int main(void) {
    int scores[] = {37, 11, 32, 91, 21, 74, 12, 26, 60};
    int size = 9;
    printf("The sum is %d\n", sum_array(scores, size));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: sum_array() receives the array scores and its length size. It starts acc at
   0, adds every element to it in a for loop and returns the total. main() fills scores
   with 9 int values and prints their sum. */
// END

/* Caption: How do I use Euclid's algorithm to compute the GCD in C? */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write gcd() with Euclid's algorithm.
   2. Replace (a, b) by (b, a % b) until b is 0.
   3. Return a and print the GCD of 297 and 78. */
/* Euclid: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a % b) until b becomes zero. */
int gcd(int a, int b) {
    while (b != 0) {
        int r = a % b;
        a = b;
        b = r;
    }
    return a;
}

int main(void) {
    int x = 297, y = 78;
    printf("gcd(%d, %d) = %d\n", x, y, gcd(x, y));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: gcd() uses Euclid's algorithm: it keeps replacing (a, b) with (b, a % b)
   until b is 0. The last non-zero value is the greatest common divisor, and main() prints
   the GCD of 297 and 78. */
// END

   4. Return the index if it matches; otherwise keep only the half that can hold the

}

/* Caption: How do I calculate the average of the values in an array in C? */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write array_average() that takes prices and n.
   2. Add the values into the double sum.
   3. Return sum / n.
   4. Print the average with two decimals. */
/* Sum the values, then divide by how many there are. */
double array_average(const int prices[], int n) {
    double sum = 0.0;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        sum += prices[i];
    }
    return sum / n;
}

int main(void) {
    int prices[] = {29, 34, 5};
    const int n = 3;
    printf("The average is %.2f\n", array_average(prices, n));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: array_average() adds the 3 values of prices into the double sum and divides
   by n, so the mean keeps its decimal part even when the values are whole numbers. main()
   prints it with two decimals. */
// END
