/* Caption: Use binary search to locate a value in a sorted list. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Make sure the array is sorted.
   2. Set lo to 0 and hi to size - 1.
   3. While lo <= hi, compare the middle element mid with the key.
   4. Return the index if it matches; otherwise keep only the half that can hold the
      key.
   5. Return -1 if the range becomes empty, and print the index of 43. */
/* The array must be sorted. Each step halves the range that can still hold the key. */
int binary_search(const int scores[], int size, int key) {
    int lo = 0;
    int hi = size - 1;
    while (lo <= hi) {
        int mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;
        if (scores[mid] == key) {
            return mid;
        } else if (scores[mid] < key) {
            lo = mid + 1;   /* key is in the right half */
        } else {
            hi = mid - 1;   /* key is in the left half */
        }
    }
    return -1;
}

int main(void) {
    int scores[] = {2, 10, 21, 38, 43, 58, 75, 128, 166, 178, 183, 186};
    const int size = 12;
    int index = binary_search(scores, size, 43);
    printf("Index of 43: %d\n", index);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: binary_search() needs a sorted array. It keeps the range from lo to hi,
   compares the middle element mid with the key and throws away the half that cannot
   contain it, so it needs only about log2(n) steps. main() looks for 43 and prints its
   index, or -1 if it is not there. */
// END

/* Caption: How do I search an array for a value and print its position in C? */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write linear_search() with the array, its length and wanted.
   2. Compare each element with wanted.
   3. Return the index of the first match, or -1.
   4. In main(), search for 49 and print the result. */
/* Return the index of wanted, or -1 when it is not in the array. */
int linear_search(const int values[], int size, int wanted) {
    for (int i = 0; i < size; i++) {
        if (values[i] == wanted) {
            return i;
        }
    }
    return -1;
}

int main(void) {
    int values[] = {74, 88, 49, 29, 19, 45, 82, 49, 57};
    const int size = 9;
    int wanted = 49;
    int pos = linear_search(values, size, wanted);
    if (pos >= 0) {
        printf("Found %d at index %d\n", wanted, pos);
    } else {
        printf("%d is not in the array\n", wanted);
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: linear_search() checks the elements of values one by one and returns the
   index of the first one equal to wanted, or -1 when it reaches the end without a match.
   main() searches for 49 and prints where it is, or that it is missing. */
// END

/* Caption: How do I calculate the average of the values in an array in C? */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write array_average() that takes prices and length.
   2. Add the values into the double result.
   3. Return result / length.
   4. Print the average with two decimals. */
/* Sum the values, then divide by how many there are. */
double array_average(const int prices[], int length) {
    double result = 0.0;
    for (int k = 0; k < length; k++) {
        result += prices[k];
    }
    return result / length;
}

int main(void) {
    int prices[] = {57, 97, 86, 62, 51, 48};
    int length = 6;
    printf("Mean = %.2f\n", array_average(prices, length));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: array_average() adds the 6 values of prices into the double result and
   divides by length, so the mean keeps its decimal part even when the values are whole
   numbers. main() prints it with two decimals. */
// END

/* Caption: Program to reverse the elements of an array in place. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write reverse_array() for scores.
   2. Set start to the first index and end to the last.
   3. Swap scores[start] and scores[end], then move both inwards.
   4. Stop when start meets end and print the array. */
/* Swap the outer pair, then move both ends toward the middle. */
void reverse_array(int scores[], int count) {
    int start = 0;
    int end = count - 1;
    while (start < end) {
        int tmp = scores[start];
        scores[start] = scores[end];
        scores[end] = tmp;
        start++;
        end--;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    int scores[] = {14, 38, 48, 84, 65, 75};
    int count = sizeof(scores) / sizeof(scores[0]);
    reverse_array(scores, count);
    for (int i = 0; i < count; i++) {
        printf("%d ", scores[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: reverse_array() swaps the first and last elements, then moves start forward
   and end backward until they meet, so the array is reversed in place without a second
   array. main() prints the reversed values. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to print the larger of two long values. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Set num1 and num2.
   2. Pick the bigger of num1 and num2.
   3. Print it. */
int main(void) {
    long num1 = 6L, num2 = 36L;
    long best = (num1 > num2) ? num1 : num2;   /* the ?: operator picks one of two values */
    printf("The larger is %ld\n", best);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: The program uses fixed values for num1 and num2. The conditional operator
   (num1 > num2) ? num1 : num2 picks the bigger value, which is printed. */
// END

/* Caption: Decide if 1990 is a leap year. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write is_leap(year).
   2. A year divisible by 4 is a leap year, unless it is divisible by 100.
   3. Years divisible by 400 are leap years again.
   4. Check 1990 and print the result. */
/* Leap years divide by 4, except centuries, which must divide by 400. */
int is_leap(int year) {
    return (year % 4 == 0 && year % 100 != 0) || year % 400 == 0;
}

int main(void) {
    int year = 1990;
    if (is_leap(year)) {
        printf("%d is a leap year\n", year);
    } else {
        printf("%d is not a leap year\n", year);
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: is_leap() returns true for years divisible by 4, except century years,
   which must also be divisible by 400. main() checks 1990 and prints whether it is a leap
   year. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to check whether a word is a palindrome. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <string.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write is_palindrome() for buffer.
   2. Compare the first and last characters, moving inwards.
   3. Return false at the first mismatch, otherwise true.
   4. Check bridge and print the result. */
/* Compare characters from the front and back, moving inwards. */
bool is_palindrome(const char *buffer) {
    int i = 0;
    int j = strlen(buffer) - 1;
    while (i < j) {
        if (buffer[i] != buffer[j]) {
            return false;
        }
        i++;
        j--;
    }
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    const char *buffer = "bridge";
    printf("%s %s a palindrome\n", buffer, is_palindrome(buffer) ? "is" : "is not");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: is_palindrome() compares the first and last characters and moves inwards;
   any mismatch means the word is not a palindrome. main() checks the word bridge and
   prints the result. */
// END

/* Plan:
   1. Write reverse_string() for buffer.
   2. Set i to the first index and j to the last.
   3. Swap the two characters and move i and j inwards until they meet.
   4. Reverse garden and print it. */
/* Swap characters from both ends until they meet in the middle. */
void reverse_string(char *buffer) {
    int i = 0;

    while (i < j) {
        char tmp = buffer[i];
        buffer[i] = buffer[j];
        buffer[j] = tmp;
        i++;

    }
}

int main(void) {

    reverse_string(buffer);
    printf("%s\n", buffer);
    return 0;
}

   until the two indexes meet. main() reverses the word garden in place and prints it. */

/* Caption: Program to find the largest of four numbers with a function. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write max2() that returns the larger of two values.
   2. Write max_of_four() as max2(max2(a, b), max2(c, d)).
   3. Print the largest of the four values. */
/* Return the larger of two values. */
int max2(int a, int b) {
    return a > b ? a : b;
}

/* Reuse max2 to compare four values. */
int max_of_four(int a, int b, int c, int d) {
    return max2(max2(a, b), max2(c, d));
}

int main(void) {
    int a = 57, b = 14, c = 39, d = 48;
    printf("Largest: %d\n", max_of_four(a, b, c, d));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: max_of_four() takes four parameters and reuses the helper max2(), which
   returns the larger of two values: it compares a with b, c with d, and then the two
   winners. main() prints the largest of 57, 14, 39 and 48. */
// END

/* Caption: How do I calculate the area and perimeter of a rectangle struct in C? */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define a Rectangle struct with width and height.
   2. Write area() and perimeter().
   3. Make a 27 by 5 rectangle and print both results. */
typedef struct {
    int width;
    int height;
} Rectangle;

int area(Rectangle r) {
    return r.width * r.height;
}

int perimeter(Rectangle r) {
    return 2 * (r.width + r.height);
}

int main(void) {
    Rectangle box = {27, 5};
    printf("Area: %d, Perimeter: %d\n", area(box), perimeter(box));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: Rectangle stores a width and a height. area() returns width * height and
   perimeter() returns 2 * (width + height). main() makes a 27 by 5 rectangle and prints
   both results. */
// END

/* Caption: Calculate 5! using recursion. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write factorial(num) that calls itself.
   2. Return 1 when num is 1 or less.
   3. Otherwise return num * factorial(num - 1).
   4. Print 5! as an unsigned long long. */
/* n! = n * (n - 1)!, and 0! = 1 stops the recursion. */
unsigned long long factorial(int num) {
    if (num <= 1) {
        return 1;
    }
    return num * factorial(num - 1);
}

int main(void) {
    int num = 5;
    printf("%d! = %llu\n", num, factorial(num));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: factorial() calls itself: n! is n * (n - 1)!, and the recursion stops when
   num is 1 or less. main() prints 5! as an unsigned long long, because factorials grow
   very fast. */
// END

/* Caption: Swap two variables using pointers. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write swap() that takes pointers to two long values.
   2. Save *a in tmp, copy *b into *a, then tmp into *b.
   3. In main(), print a and b, call swap(&a, &b) and print them again. */
/* Pass addresses so the function can change the caller's variables. */
void swap(long *a, long *b) {
    long tmp = *a;
    *a = *b;
    *b = tmp;
}

int main(void) {
    long a = 94L, b = 29L;
    printf("Before: %ld %ld\n", a, b);
    swap(&a, &b);
    printf("After:  %ld %ld\n", a, b);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: swap() receives the addresses of a and b, so writing through the pointers
   *a and *b changes the caller's variables. tmp holds one value during the exchange.
   main() declares both variables on one line and prints them before and after the swap. */
// END

/* Caption: Program to find the greatest common divisor of two numbers. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write gcd() with Euclid's algorithm.
   2. Replace (a, b) by (b, a % b) until b is 0.
   3. Return a and print the GCD of 34 and 163. */
/* Euclid: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a % b) until b becomes zero. */
int gcd(int a, int b) {
    while (b != 0) {
        int r = a % b;
        a = b;
        b = r;
    }
    return a;
}

int main(void) {
    int x = 34, y = 163;
    printf("gcd(%d, %d) = %d\n", x, y, gcd(x, y));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: gcd() uses Euclid's algorithm: it keeps replacing (a, b) with (b, a % b)
   until b is 0. The last non-zero value is the greatest common divisor, and main() prints
   the GCD of 34 and 163. */
// END

/* Caption: Calculate the average of the values in an array. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write average() that takes values and count.
   2. Add the values into the double total.
   3. Return total / count.
   4. Print the average with two decimals. */
/* Sum the values, then divide by how many there are. */
double average(const double values[], int count) {
    double total = 0.0;
    int i = 0;
    while (i < count) {
        total += values[i];
        i++;
    }
    return total / count;
}

int main(void) {
    double values[] = {15.3, 81.9, 74.3};
    int count = sizeof(values) / sizeof(values[0]);
    printf("Mean = %.2f\n", average(values, count));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: average() adds the 3 values of values into the double total and divides by
   count, so the mean keeps its decimal part even when the values are whole numbers. main()
   prints it with two decimals. */
// END

/* Caption: Sort an array in ascending order using insertion sort. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write insertion_sort() for the double array readings.
   2. Take each element in turn as current.
   3. Shift the larger values of the sorted part one place right.
   4. Put current into the gap.
   5. Print the sorted values. */
/* Insert each element into the already sorted part on its left. */
void insertion_sort(double readings[], int length) {
    for (int i = 1; i < length; i++) {
        double current = readings[i];
        int j = i - 1;
        while (j >= 0 && readings[j] > current) {
            readings[j + 1] = readings[j];   /* shift bigger values right */
            j--;
        }
        readings[j + 1] = current;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    double readings[] = {66.6, 7.9, 52.6, 87.6, 27.3, 5.5, 97.1, 15.4, 25.2, 68.8};
    int length = sizeof(readings) / sizeof(readings[0]);
    insertion_sort(readings, length);
    for (int i = 0; i < length; i++) {
        printf("%.2f ", readings[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: insertion_sort() takes each element in turn and shifts the larger values of
   the sorted part one place right until the element fits. main() then prints the 10 values
   in ascending order. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to add up the digits of a number. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Start result at 0.
   2. Add n % 10 to result, then divide n by 10.
   3. Repeat until n is 0.
   4. Apply it to 794967 and print the result. */
/* Take the last digit with % 10, then drop it with / 10. */
int sum_digits(int n) {
    int result = 0;
    while (n > 0) {
        result += n % 10;
        n /= 10;
    }
    return result;
}

int main(void) {
    int number = 794967;
    printf("sum of digits of %d: %d\n", number, sum_digits(number));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: sum_digits() adds the last digit (n % 10) to result and then removes it (n
   / 10) until no digits are left. main() applies it to 794967. */
// END

/* Caption: Find the smallest number in an array. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write find_min() that takes values and n.
   2. Store values[0] in m.
   3. Loop over the other elements and keep the smallest value in m.
   4. Return m and print it. */
/* Start with the first element and keep the smallest value seen so far. */
double find_min(const double values[], int n) {
    double m = values[0];
    for (int idx = 1; idx < n; idx++) {
        if (values[idx] < m) {
            m = values[idx];
        }
    }
    return m;
}

int main(void) {
    double values[] = {67.5, 27.7, 73.5, 78.9, 67.4, 29.0, 57.3, 27.4, 31.3};
    int n = sizeof(values) / sizeof(values[0]);
    printf("Smallest: %.2f\n", find_min(values, n));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: find_min() takes the first element as the smallest value so far and stores
   it in m. The loop compares every other element with m using < and keeps the smallest
   one. main() prints the smallest of the 9 values. */
// END

/* Caption: Program to generate the Fibonacci sequence. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Start with a = 0 and b = 1.
   2. Repeat 23 times and print a each time.
   3. Compute next = a + b, then set a = b and b = next. */
int main(void) {
    long a = 0, b = 1;
    /* Print a term, then slide the pair one step along the sequence. */
    for (int i = 0; i < 23; i++) {
        printf("%ld ", a);
        long next = a + b;
        a = b;
        b = next;
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: The loop keeps the last two numbers in a and b. Each round it prints a,
   then moves the pair forward: a becomes b and b becomes their sum. It prints the first 23
   Fibonacci numbers. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to write a function that swaps two int values through pointers. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write swap() that takes pointers to two int values.
   2. Save *first in tmp, copy *second into *first, then tmp into *second.
   3. In main(), print first and second, call swap(&first, &second) and print them
      again. */
/* Pass addresses so the function can change the caller's variables. */
void swap(int *first, int *second) {
    int tmp = *first;
    *first = *second;
    *second = tmp;
}

int main(void) {
    int first = 76, second = 52;
    printf("Before: %d %d\n", first, second);
    swap(&first, &second);
    printf("After:  %d %d\n", first, second);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: swap() receives the addresses of first and second, so writing through the
   pointers *first and *second changes the caller's variables. tmp holds one value during
   the exchange. main() declares both variables on one line and prints them before and
   after the swap. */
// END

/* Caption: Use dynamic memory to store the first 7 multiples. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Use malloc to get room for 7 ints and check for NULL.
   2. Fill arr with multiples.
   3. Print the values.
   4. Call free(arr) at the end. */
int main(void) {
    int n = 7;
    /* Ask the heap for room for n ints; malloc returns NULL on failure. */
    int *arr = malloc(n * sizeof(int));
    if (arr == NULL) {
        fprintf(stderr, "malloc failed\n");
        return 1;
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        arr[i] = 8 * i;
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        printf("%d ", arr[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    free(arr);   /* give the memory back */
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: malloc() reserves room for 7 ints on the heap and returns NULL if it fails,
   which the program checks. The first loop fills arr with multiples, the second prints
   them, and free() gives the memory back at the end. */
// END

/* Caption: Program to convert 567 to binary. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write print_binary(n, bits).
   2. Go through the bits from the highest to the lowest.
   3. Print 1 when (n >> b) & 1 is set, otherwise 0.
   4. Print 567 in binary. */
/* Check each bit from the highest to the lowest. */
void print_binary(unsigned int n, int bits) {
    for (int b = bits - 1; b >= 0; b--) {
        putchar((n >> b) & 1 ? '1' : '0');
    }
    putchar('\n');
}

int main(void) {
    unsigned int number = 567;
    printf("%u in binary: ", number);
    print_binary(number, 12);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: print_binary() checks one bit at a time, from the highest to the lowest: (n
   >> b) & 1 is 1 when bit b is set, so it prints the character 1 or 0. main() prints 567
   in binary. */
// END

/* Caption: C program to sort an array in ascending order using insertion sort. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write insertion_sort() for the double array samples.
   2. Take each element in turn as current.
   3. Shift the larger values of the sorted part one place right.
   4. Put current into the gap.
   5. Print the sorted values. */
/* Insert each element into the already sorted part on its left. */
void insertion_sort(double samples[], int length) {
    for (int i = 1; i < length; i++) {
        double current = samples[i];
        int j = i - 1;
        while (j >= 0 && samples[j] > current) {
            samples[j + 1] = samples[j];   /* shift bigger values right */
            j--;
        }
        samples[j + 1] = current;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    double samples[] = {14.9, 79.3, 81.0, 71.1, 83.8, 74.9, 82.1, 21.0};
    int length = 8;
    insertion_sort(samples, length);
    for (int i = 0; i < length; i++) {
        printf("%.2f ", samples[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: insertion_sort() takes each element in turn and shifts the larger values of
   the sorted part one place right until the element fits. main() then prints the 8 values
   in ascending order. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to reverse the digits of a number. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Start result at 0.
   2. Multiply result by 10, add n % 10, then divide n by 10.
   3. Repeat until n is 0.
   4. Apply it to 744109 and print the result. */
/* Take the last digit with % 10, then drop it with / 10. */
int reverse_digits(int n) {
    int result = 0;
    while (n > 0) {
        result = result * 10 + n % 10;
        n /= 10;
    }
    return result;
}

int main(void) {
    int number = 744109;
    printf("reverse of digits of %d: %d\n", number, reverse_digits(number));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: reverse_digits() shifts result one place left (result * 10) and adds the
   last digit of n, which reverses the order. main() applies it to 744109. */
// END

/* Caption: C program to build a fixed-size integer stack in C. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define a Stack with room for 32 items and a top counter.
   2. Write push() and pop(), returning false when the stack is full or empty.
   3. Push 4 values.
   4. Pop and print until the stack is empty. */
#define CAPACITY 32

typedef struct {
    int items[CAPACITY];
    int top;   /* number of items on the stack */
} Stack;

bool push(Stack *s, int value) {
    if (s->top == CAPACITY) {
        return false;   /* stack is full */
    }
    s->items[s->top++] = value;
    return true;
}

bool pop(Stack *s, int *value) {
    if (s->top == 0) {
        return false;   /* stack is empty */
    }
    *value = s->items[--s->top];
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    Stack s = {.top = 0};
    push(&s, 76);
    push(&s, 60);
    push(&s, 36);
    push(&s, 77);
    int value;
    /* Items come back out in reverse order (last in, first out). */
    while (pop(&s, &value)) {
        printf("%d ", value);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: The Stack keeps up to 32 items in an array, and top counts how many are
   stored. push() adds at the top and pop() removes from the top; both return false when
   they cannot. main() pushes 4 values and pops them all, so they come out in reverse order
   (last in, first out). */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to decide if 1969 is a leap year. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write is_leap(year).
   2. A year divisible by 4 is a leap year, unless it is divisible by 100.
   3. Years divisible by 400 are leap years again.
   4. Check 1969 and print the result. */
/* Leap years divide by 4, except centuries, which must divide by 400. */
int is_leap(int year) {
    return (year % 4 == 0 && year % 100 != 0) || year % 400 == 0;
}

int main(void) {
    int year = 1969;
    if (is_leap(year)) {
        printf("%d is a leap year\n", year);
    } else {
        printf("%d is not a leap year\n", year);
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: is_leap() returns true for years divisible by 4, except century years,
   which must also be divisible by 400. main() checks 1969 and prints whether it is a leap
   year. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to find the arithmetic mean of 5 double values. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write mean() that takes nums and size.
   2. Add the values into the double sum.
   3. Return sum / size.
   4. Print the average with two decimals. */
/* Sum the values, then divide by how many there are. */
double mean(const double nums[], int size) {
    double sum = 0.0;
    for (int j = 0; j < size; j++) {
        sum += nums[j];
    }
    return sum / size;
}

int main(void) {
    double nums[] = {80.0, 73.1, 43.6, 42.9, 47.7};
    int size = sizeof(nums) / sizeof(nums[0]);
    printf("The average is %.2f\n", mean(nums, size));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: mean() adds the 5 values of nums into the double sum and divides by size,
   so the mean keeps its decimal part even when the values are whole numbers. main() prints
   it with two decimals. */
// END

/* Caption: Search a sorted array by halving the search range each step. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Make sure the array is sorted.
   2. Set lo to 0 and hi to size - 1.
   3. While lo <= hi, compare the middle element mid with the key.
   4. Return the index if it matches; otherwise keep only the half that can hold the
      key.
   5. Return -1 if the range becomes empty, and print the index of 30. */
/* The array must be sorted. Each step halves the range that can still hold the key. */
int binary_search(const int samples[], int size, int key) {
    int lo = 0;
    int hi = size - 1;
    while (lo <= hi) {
        int mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;
        if (samples[mid] == key) {
            return mid;
        } else if (samples[mid] < key) {
            lo = mid + 1;   /* key is in the right half */
        } else {
            hi = mid - 1;   /* key is in the left half */
        }
    }
    return -1;
}

int main(void) {
    int samples[] = {23, 30, 36, 55, 83, 160};
    int size = sizeof(samples) / sizeof(samples[0]);
    int index = binary_search(samples, size, 30);
    printf("Index of 30: %d\n", index);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: binary_search() needs a sorted array. It keeps the range from lo to hi,
   compares the middle element mid with the key and throws away the half that cannot
   contain it, so it needs only about log2(n) steps. main() looks for 30 and prints its
   index, or -1 if it is not there. */
// END

/* Caption: Reverse a string in place. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <string.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write reverse_string() for text.
   2. Set i to the first index and j to the last.
   3. Swap the two characters and move i and j inwards until they meet.
   4. Reverse racecar and print it. */
/* Swap characters from both ends until they meet in the middle. */
void reverse_string(char *text) {
    int i = 0;
    int j = strlen(text) - 1;
    while (i < j) {
        char tmp = text[i];
        text[i] = text[j];
        text[j] = tmp;
        i++;
        j--;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    char text[] = "racecar";
    reverse_string(text);
    printf("%s\n", text);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: reverse_string() swaps characters from both ends of text, moving inwards
   until the two indexes meet. main() reverses the word racecar in place and prints it. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a function that swaps two long values through pointers. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write swap() that takes pointers to two long values.
   2. Save *x in tmp, copy *y into *x, then tmp into *y.
   3. In main(), print x and y, call swap(&x, &y) and print them again. */
/* Pass addresses so the function can change the caller's variables. */
void swap(long *x, long *y) {
    long tmp = *x;
    *x = *y;
    *y = tmp;
}

int main(void) {
    long x = 13L, y = 11L;
    printf("Before: %ld %ld\n", x, y);
    swap(&x, &y);
    printf("After:  %ld %ld\n", x, y);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: swap() receives the addresses of x and y, so writing through the pointers
   *x and *y changes the caller's variables. tmp holds one value during the exchange.
   main() declares both variables on one line and prints them before and after the swap. */
// END

   of 0 after dividing by 2 means the number is even, so found goes up by one. main()
   prints how many of the 10 values are even. */
// END

/* Caption: Find a number in a sorted array with binary search. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Make sure the array is sorted.
   2. Set left to 0 and right to n - 1.
   3. While left <= right, compare the middle element middle with the key.
   4. Return the index if it matches; otherwise keep only the half that can hold the
      key.
   5. Return -1 if the range becomes empty, and print the index of 165. */
/* The array must be sorted. Each step halves the range that can still hold the key. */
int binary_search(const int nums[], int n, int key) {
    int left = 0;
    int right = n - 1;
    while (left <= right) {
        int middle = left + (right - left) / 2;
        if (nums[middle] == key) {
            return middle;
        } else if (nums[middle] < key) {
            left = middle + 1;   /* key is in the right half */
        } else {
            right = middle - 1;   /* key is in the left half */
        }
    }
    return -1;
}

int main(void) {
    int nums[] = {20, 36, 86, 94, 104, 128, 150, 165, 168};
    const int n = 9;
    int index = binary_search(nums, n, 165);
    printf("Index of 165: %d\n", index);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: binary_search() needs a sorted array. It keeps the range from left to
   right, compares the middle element middle with the key and throws away the half that
   cannot contain it, so it needs only about log2(n) steps. main() looks for 165 and prints
   its index, or -1 if it is not there. */
// END

/* The array must be sorted. Each step halves the range that can still hold the key. */

        if (items[mid] == key) {

            lo = mid + 1;   /* key is in the right half */
        } else {
            hi = mid - 1;   /* key is in the left half */
        }
    }
    return -1;
}

int main(void) {

/* Explanation: binary_search() needs a sorted array. It keeps the range from lo to hi,
   compares the middle element mid with the key and throws away the half that cannot
   contain it, so it needs only about log2(n) steps. main() looks for 149 and prints its

/* A number is odd when the remainder after dividing by 2 is one. */

    int matches = 0;
    int idx = 0;

        if (values[idx] % 2 != 0) {
            matches++;

        idx++;

    return matches;
}

int main(void) {

    const int size = 12;
    printf("Odd numbers: %d\n", count_odd(values, size));
    return 0;
}

   of 1 after dividing by 2 means the number is odd, so matches goes up by one. main()
   prints how many of the 12 values are odd. */
// END

/* Caption: Program to build a FIFO queue using a ring buffer. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define a Queue with room for 16 items, a head and a count.
   2. Write enqueue() that stores at (head + count) % CAPACITY.
   3. Write dequeue() that takes the item at head and moves head on.
   4. Add 6 values, then remove and print them in order. */
#define CAPACITY 16

typedef struct {
    int items[CAPACITY];
    int head;
    int count;
} Queue;

bool enqueue(Queue *q, int value) {
    if (q->count == CAPACITY) {
        return false;
    }
    /* The tail wraps around to the start of the array. */
    q->items[(q->head + q->count) % CAPACITY] = value;
    q->count++;
    return true;
}

bool dequeue(Queue *q, int *value) {
    if (q->count == 0) {
        return false;
    }
    *value = q->items[q->head];
    q->head = (q->head + 1) % CAPACITY;
    q->count--;
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    Queue q = {.head = 0, .count = 0};
    enqueue(&q, 26);
    enqueue(&q, 63);
    enqueue(&q, 90);
    enqueue(&q, 21);
    enqueue(&q, 67);
    enqueue(&q, 81);
    int value;
    /* Items come out in the order they went in (first in, first out). */
    while (dequeue(&q, &value)) {
        printf("%d ", value);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: The Queue stores up to 16 items in a ring buffer: head is the oldest item
   and % CAPACITY wraps positions back to the start of the array. enqueue() adds at the
   back and dequeue() removes from the front, so main() gets its 6 values back in the same
   order (first in, first out). */
// END

/* Caption: C program to reverse the elements of an array in place. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write reverse_array() for prices.
   2. Set left to the first index and right to the last.
   3. Swap prices[left] and prices[right], then move both inwards.
   4. Stop when left meets right and print the array. */
/* Swap the outer pair, then move both ends toward the middle. */
void reverse_array(int prices[], int size) {
    int left = 0;
    int right = size - 1;
    while (left < right) {
        int tmp = prices[left];
        prices[left] = prices[right];
        prices[right] = tmp;
        left++;
        right--;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    int prices[] = {96, 55, 10, 12, 39, 9};
    int size = 6;
    reverse_array(prices, size);
    for (int i = 0; i < size; i++) {
        printf("%d ", prices[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: reverse_array() swaps the first and last elements, then moves left forward
   and right backward until they meet, so the array is reversed in place without a second
   array. main() prints the reversed values. */
// END

/* Caption: Program to write a function with four parameters that returns the maximum. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write max2() that returns the larger of two values.
   2. Write max_of_four() as max2(max2(a, b), max2(c, d)).
   3. Print the largest of the four values. */
/* Return the larger of two values. */
int max2(int a, int b) {
    return a > b ? a : b;
}

/* Reuse max2 to compare four values. */
int max_of_four(int a, int b, int c, int d) {
    return max2(max2(a, b), max2(c, d));
}

int main(void) {
    int a = 65, b = 96, c = 43, d = 66;
    printf("Largest: %d\n", max_of_four(a, b, c, d));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: max_of_four() takes four parameters and reuses the helper max2(), which
   returns the larger of two values: it compares a with b, c with d, and then the two
   winners. main() prints the largest of 65, 96, 43 and 66. */
// END

/* Caption: Write your own version of strcpy. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write copy_string(dest, src).
   2. Copy src into dest one character at a time.
   3. Stop after copying the null character.
   4. Copy noon into buffer and print it. */
/* Copy each character, including the final '\0'. */
void copy_string(char *dest, const char *src) {
    int i = 0;
    while ((dest[i] = src[i]) != '\0') {
        i++;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    char source[] = "noon";
    char buffer[32];
    copy_string(buffer, source);
    printf("Copied: %s\n", buffer);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: copy_string() copies src into dest one character at a time, including the
   final null character, which is what strcpy does. The array buffer must be big enough to
   hold the copy. main() copies the word noon and prints it. */
// END

/* Caption: Program to check every element of an array to find a target value. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write linear_search() with the array, its length and needle.
   2. Compare each element with needle.
   3. Return the index of the first match, or -1.
   4. In main(), search for 191 and print the result. */
/* Return the index of needle, or -1 when it is not in the array. */
int linear_search(const int numbers[], int count, int needle) {
    for (int i = 0; i < count; i++) {
        if (numbers[i] == needle) {
            return i;
        }
    }
    return -1;
}

int main(void) {
    int numbers[] = {66, 34, 73, 75, 42};
    const int count = 5;
    int needle = 191;
    int pos = linear_search(numbers, count, needle);
    if (pos >= 0) {
        printf("Found %d at index %d\n", needle, pos);
    } else {
        printf("%d is not in the array\n", needle);
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: linear_search() checks the elements of numbers one by one and returns the
   index of the first one equal to needle, or -1 when it reaches the end without a match.
   main() searches for 191 and prints where it is, or that it is missing. */
// END

/* Caption: Reverse an array by swapping from both ends. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write reverse_array() for readings.
   2. Set i to the first index and j to the last.
   3. Swap readings[i] and readings[j], then move both inwards.
   4. Stop when i meets j and print the array. */
/* Swap the outer pair, then move both ends toward the middle. */
void reverse_array(int readings[], int size) {
    int i = 0;
    int j = size - 1;
    while (i < j) {
        int tmp = readings[i];
        readings[i] = readings[j];
        readings[j] = tmp;
        i++;
        j--;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    int readings[] = {64, 11, 58, 34, 12, 2, 30, 67};
    int size = sizeof(readings) / sizeof(readings[0]);
    reverse_array(readings, size);
    for (int i = 0; i < size; i++) {
        printf("%d ", readings[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: reverse_array() swaps the first and last elements, then moves i forward and
   j backward until they meet, so the array is reversed in place without a second array.
   main() prints the reversed values. */
// END

/* Caption: C program to check whether a year is a leap year. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write is_leap(year).
   2. A year divisible by 4 is a leap year, unless it is divisible by 100.
   3. Years divisible by 400 are leap years again.
   4. Check 1976 and print the result. */
/* Leap years divide by 4, except centuries, which must divide by 400. */
int is_leap(int year) {
    return (year % 4 == 0 && year % 100 != 0) || year % 400 == 0;
}

int main(void) {
    int year = 1976;
    if (is_leap(year)) {
        printf("%d is a leap year\n", year);
    } else {
        printf("%d is not a leap year\n", year);
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: is_leap() returns true for years divisible by 4, except century years,
   which must also be divisible by 400. main() checks 1976 and prints whether it is a leap
   year. */
// END

/* Caption: Find the total of all elements in an array using a loop. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write total_of() that takes the array nums and its length length.
   2. Start total at 0 and add every element in a for loop.
   3. Return total.
   4. In main(), fill nums with 5 values and print the sum. */
/* Add every element to a running total. */
double total_of(const double nums[], int length) {
    double total = 0;
    for (int idx = 0; idx < length; idx++) {
        total += nums[idx];
    }
    return total;
}

int main(void) {
    double nums[] = {20.2, 71.9, 49.5, 7.7, 47.2};
    int length = sizeof(nums) / sizeof(nums[0]);
    printf("Total = %.2f\n", total_of(nums, length));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: total_of() receives the array nums and its length length. It starts total
   at 0, adds every element to it in a for loop and returns the total. main() fills nums
   with 5 double values and prints their sum. */
// END

/* Caption: C program to create a singly linked list by inserting at the head. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define Node with a value and a next pointer.
   2. Write push_front() that mallocs a node and links it in front of head.
   3. Write print_list() that follows next until NULL.
   4. Write free_list() that frees every node.
   5. Push 4 values, print the list and free it. */
typedef struct Node {
    int value;
    struct Node *next;
} Node;

/* Allocate a new node and put it in front of the current head. */
Node *push_front(Node *head, int value) {
    Node *node = malloc(sizeof(Node));
    if (node == NULL) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Out of memory\n");
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }
    node->value = value;
    node->next = head;
    return node;
}

void print_list(const Node *head) {
    for (const Node *cur = head; cur != NULL; cur = cur->next) {
        printf("%d -> ", cur->value);
    }
    printf("NULL\n");
}

/* Free every node; save next before freeing the current one. */
void free_list(Node *head) {
    while (head != NULL) {
        Node *next = head->next;
        free(head);
        head = next;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    Node *head = NULL;
    head = push_front(head, 91);
    head = push_front(head, 32);
    head = push_front(head, 74);
    head = push_front(head, 33);
    print_list(head);
    free_list(head);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: Each Node holds a value and a pointer to the next node. push_front()
   allocates a node with malloc, puts it in front of head and returns it; print_list()
   follows the next pointers until NULL; free_list() frees every node. main() pushes 4
   values, so they print in reverse order. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a function that returns a Fraction struct. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define a Fraction struct with num and den.
   2. Write multiply() that returns num = a.num * b.num and den = a.den * b.den.
   3. Print 2/6 times 7/7. */
typedef struct {
    int num;
    int den;
} Fraction;

/* Multiply the numerators and the denominators. */
Fraction multiply(Fraction a, Fraction b) {
    Fraction r = {a.num * b.num, a.den * b.den};
    return r;
}

int main(void) {
    Fraction x = {2, 6}, y = {7, 7};
    Fraction p = multiply(x, y);
    printf("%d/%d * %d/%d = %d/%d\n", x.num, x.den, y.num, y.den, p.num, p.den);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: Fraction stores a numerator and a denominator. multiply() takes two
   Fractions and returns a new one with num = a.num * b.num and den = a.den * b.den. main()
   multiplies 2/6 by 7/7 (without reducing the result). */
// END

/* Caption: How do I write a function that swaps two long values through pointers in C? */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write swap() that takes pointers to two long values.
   2. Save *a in tmp, copy *b into *a, then tmp into *b.
   3. In main(), print a and b, call swap(&a, &b) and print them again. */
/* Pass addresses so the function can change the caller's variables. */
void swap(long *a, long *b) {
    long tmp = *a;
    *a = *b;
    *b = tmp;
}

int main(void) {
    long a = 52L, b = 6L;
    printf("Before: %ld %ld\n", a, b);
    swap(&a, &b);
    printf("After:  %ld %ld\n", a, b);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: swap() receives the addresses of a and b, so writing through the pointers
   *a and *b changes the caller's variables. tmp holds one value during the exchange.
   main() declares both variables on one line and prints them before and after the swap. */
// END

/* Caption: Return two values from a function using pointer parameters. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write divide(a, b, &quotient, &remainder) that returns a bool.
   2. Return false if b is 0.
   3. Store a / b and a % b through the pointers and return true.
   4. Divide 255 by 0 and print the results or the error. */
/* Returns false for division by zero; otherwise stores both results. */
bool divide(int a, int b, int *quotient, int *remainder) {
    if (b == 0) {
        return false;
    }
    *quotient = a / b;
    *remainder = a % b;
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    int a = 255, b = 0;
    int q, r;
    if (divide(a, b, &q, &r)) {
        printf("%d / %d = %d remainder %d\n", a, b, q, r);
    } else {
        printf("Cannot divide by zero\n");
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: divide() has four parameters: two inputs and two pointers for the results.
   Its bool return value reports success, while the quotient and remainder are written
   through the pointers. main() divides 255 by 0, which fails because the divisor is zero. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to add two matrices element by element. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define ROWS as 3 and COLS as 2.
   2. Loop over every row r and column c.
   3. Store a[r][c] + b[r][c] in sum and print it. */
#define ROWS 3
#define COLS 2

int main(void) {
    int a[ROWS][COLS] = {{0, 4}, {0, 4}, {5, 2}};
    int b[ROWS][COLS] = {{1, 3}, {2, 5}, {2, 0}};
    int sum[ROWS][COLS];
    /* Each entry of the result is the sum of the matching entries. */
    for (int r = 0; r < ROWS; r++) {
        for (int c = 0; c < COLS; c++) {
            sum[r][c] = a[r][c] + b[r][c];
            printf("%3d", sum[r][c]);
        }
        printf("\n");
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: Both matrices are 3x2 two-dimensional arrays. Two nested loops visit every
   row r and column c, store a[r][c] + b[r][c] in sum and print each row. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to build a linked list, print it, and free it. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define Item with a value and a next pointer.
   2. Write push_front() that mallocs a node and links it in front of head.
   3. Write print_list() that follows next until NULL.
   4. Write free_list() that frees every node.
   5. Push 5 values, print the list and free it. */
typedef struct Item {
    int value;
    struct Item *next;
} Item;

/* Allocate a new node and put it in front of the current head. */
Item *push_front(Item *head, int value) {
    Item *node = malloc(sizeof(Item));
    if (node == NULL) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Out of memory\n");
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }
    node->value = value;
    node->next = head;
    return node;
}

void print_list(const Item *head) {
    for (const Item *cur = head; cur != NULL; cur = cur->next) {
        printf("%d -> ", cur->value);
    }
    printf("NULL\n");
}

/* Free every node; save next before freeing the current one. */
void free_list(Item *head) {
    while (head != NULL) {
        Item *next = head->next;
        free(head);
        head = next;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    Item *head = NULL;
    head = push_front(head, 68);
    head = push_front(head, 40);
    head = push_front(head, 69);
    head = push_front(head, 34);
    head = push_front(head, 60);
    print_list(head);
    free_list(head);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: Each Item holds a value and a pointer to the next node. push_front()
   allocates a node with malloc, puts it in front of head and returns it; print_list()
   follows the next pointers until NULL; free_list() frees every node. main() pushes 5
   values, so they print in reverse order. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to count how many even numbers are in an array. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write count_even() that takes samples and count.
   2. For each element, test samples[i] % 2 == 0.
   3. Add one to matches for every even number.
   4. Return matches and print it. */
/* A number is even when the remainder after dividing by 2 is zero. */
int count_even(const int samples[], int count) {
    int matches = 0;
    int i = 0;
    while (i < count) {
        if (samples[i] % 2 == 0) {
            matches++;
        }
        i++;
    }
    return matches;
}

int main(void) {
    int samples[] = {1, 90, 78, 1, 72, 93, 71};
    int count = 7;
    printf("Count of even values = %d\n", count_even(samples, count));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: count_even() tests each element of samples with the % operator: a remainder
   of 0 after dividing by 2 means the number is even, so matches goes up by one. main()
   prints how many of the 7 values are even. */
// END

/* Caption: Program to return a sum and an average together using pointer parameters. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write sum_and_average() with the pointers sum and average.
   2. Add the values into *sum.
   3. Store *sum / n in *average.
   4. Declare total and mean, pass their addresses and print them. */
void sum_and_average(const double v[], int n, double *sum, double *average) {
    *sum = 0.0;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        *sum += v[i];
    }
    *average = *sum / n;
}

int main(void) {
    double marks[] = {59.8, 31.0, 43.6, 46.9};
    int n = sizeof(marks) / sizeof(marks[0]);
    double total, mean;
    sum_and_average(marks, n, &total, &mean);
    printf("Sum: %.2f, Average: %.2f\n", total, mean);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: sum_and_average() takes the array, its length and two pointers. It adds up
   the 4 values through *sum and then stores *sum / n in *average. main() declares total
   and mean on one line and passes their addresses. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to turn the rows of a 2x3 matrix into columns. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define ROWS as 2 and COLS as 3.
   2. Copy m[r][c] into t[c][r] for every element.
   3. Print t row by row. */
#define ROWS 2
#define COLS 3

int main(void) {
    int m[ROWS][COLS] = {{1, 5, 6}, {8, 9, 4}};
    int t[COLS][ROWS];
    /* Element (r, c) moves to (c, r). */
    for (int r = 0; r < ROWS; r++) {
        for (int c = 0; c < COLS; c++) {
            t[c][r] = m[r][c];
        }
    }
    for (int r = 0; r < COLS; r++) {
        for (int c = 0; c < ROWS; c++) {
            printf("%3d", t[r][c]);
        }
        printf("\n");
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: The nested loops copy m[r][c] into t[c][r], so the 2x3 matrix becomes 3x2.
   A second pair of loops prints the result. */
// END

/* Caption: Show the Fibonacci series using recursion. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write fib(n) that returns n when n < 2.
   2. Otherwise return fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2).
   3. Print fib(i) for i from 0 to 17. */
/* Each Fibonacci number is the sum of the two before it. */
long fib(int n) {
    if (n < 2) {
        return n;
    }
    return fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2);
}

int main(void) {
    for (int i = 0; i < 18; i++) {
        printf("%ld ", fib(i));
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: fib() returns n for 0 and 1 and otherwise adds the two previous Fibonacci
   numbers by calling itself twice, which is simple but slow for large n. main() prints the
   first 18 numbers. */
// END

#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Open data.txt in write mode and check for NULL.
   2. Write 2 lines with fprintf and close the file.
   3. Open it again in read mode.
   4. Read and print each line with fgets, then close the file. */

    FILE *file = fopen("data.txt", "w");
    if (file == NULL) {
        perror("fopen");
        return 1;
    }
    fprintf(file, "a function can call itself recursively\n");
    fprintf(file, "loops repeat a block of code\n");
    fclose(file);

    /* Reopen the file for reading and print it line by line. */
    file = fopen("data.txt", "r");
    if (file == NULL) {
        perror("fopen");
        return 1;
    }
    char line[128];
    while (fgets(line, sizeof(line), file) != NULL) {
        printf("%s", line);
    }
    fclose(file);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: fopen() in write mode creates data.txt, fprintf() writes 2 lines into it
   and fclose() saves it. The file is then opened again in read mode, and fgets() reads it
   back line by line into the buffer line, which is printed. Every fopen() result is
   checked for NULL. */
// END

/* Caption: Calculate 3! using iteration. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write factorial(num) with result = 1.
   2. Multiply result by every number from 2 to num.
   3. Return result.
   4. Print 3! as an unsigned long long. */
/* Multiply 1 * 2 * ... * n. */
unsigned long long factorial(int num) {
    unsigned long long result = 1;
    for (int i = 2; i <= num; i++) {
        result *= i;
    }
    return result;
}

int main(void) {
    int num = 3;
    printf("%d! = %llu\n", num, factorial(num));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: factorial() multiplies result by every number from 2 up to num. main()
   prints 3! as an unsigned long long, because factorials grow very fast. */
// END

/* Caption: Print the first 24 Fibonacci numbers. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Start with prev = 0 and curr = 1.
   2. Repeat 24 times and print prev each time.
   3. Compute next = prev + curr, then set prev = curr and curr = next. */
int main(void) {
    long prev = 0, curr = 1;
    /* Print a term, then slide the pair one step along the sequence. */
    for (int i = 0; i < 24; i++) {
        printf("%ld ", prev);
        long next = prev + curr;
        prev = curr;
        curr = next;
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: The loop keeps the last two numbers in prev and curr. Each round it prints
   prev, then moves the pair forward: prev becomes curr and curr becomes their sum. It
   prints the first 24 Fibonacci numbers. */
// END

/* Caption: Program to use insertion sort to put numbers in ascending order. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write insertion_sort() for the double array scores.
   2. Take each element in turn as current.
   3. Shift the larger values of the sorted part one place right.
   4. Put current into the gap.
   5. Print the sorted values. */
/* Insert each element into the already sorted part on its left. */
void insertion_sort(double scores[], int len) {
    for (int i = 1; i < len; i++) {
        double current = scores[i];
        int j = i - 1;
        while (j >= 0 && scores[j] > current) {
            scores[j + 1] = scores[j];   /* shift bigger values right */
            j--;
        }
        scores[j + 1] = current;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    double scores[] = {46.2, 65.6, 48.5, 17.4, 52.9, 21.9, 36.3, 40.2, 74.6};
    int len = sizeof(scores) / sizeof(scores[0]);
    insertion_sort(scores, len);
    for (int i = 0; i < len; i++) {
        printf("%.2f ", scores[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: insertion_sort() takes each element in turn and shifts the larger values of
   the sorted part one place right until the element fits. main() then prints the 9 values
   in ascending order. */
// END

/* Caption: Find the difference of two integers. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Set num1 and num2.
   2. Store num1 - num2 in result.
   3. Print the calculation. */

/* Caption: Count the occurrences of a character in a sentence. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write count_char() with count = 0.
   2. Compare each character with the target a.
   3. Return count and print it. */
int count_char(const char *text, char target) {
    int count = 0;
    /* Compare every character with the target. */
    for (int i = 0; text[i] != '\0'; i++) {
        if (text[i] == target) {
            count++;
        }
    }
    return count;
}

int main(void) {
    const char *sentence = "strings end with a null character";
    printf("'a' appears %d times\n", count_char(sentence, 'a'));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: count_char() compares every character of the text with the target character
   and counts the matches. main() prints how many times a appears in the sentence. */
// END

/* Walk through the array and accumulate each value. */
int add_all(const int prices[], int size) {
    int sum = 0;

/* Caption: Reverse an array by swapping from both ends. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write reverse_array() for ages.
   2. Set i to the first index and j to the last.
   3. Swap ages[i] and ages[j], then move both inwards.
   4. Stop when i meets j and print the array. */
/* Swap the outer pair, then move both ends toward the middle. */
void reverse_array(long ages[], int len) {
    int i = 0;
    int j = len - 1;
    while (i < j) {
        long tmp = ages[i];
        ages[i] = ages[j];
        ages[j] = tmp;
        i++;
        j--;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    long ages[] = {28L, 40L, 73L, 13L, 4L, 92L};
    const int len = 6;
    reverse_array(ages, len);
    for (int i = 0; i < len; i++) {
        printf("%ld ", ages[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: reverse_array() swaps the first and last elements, then moves i forward and
   j backward until they meet, so the array is reversed in place without a second array.
   main() prints the reversed values. */
// END

/* Caption: Find a number in a sorted array with binary search. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Make sure the array is sorted.
   2. Set lo to 0 and hi to count - 1.
   3. While lo <= hi, compare the middle element mid with the key.
   4. Return the index if it matches; otherwise keep only the half that can hold the
      key.
   5. Return -1 if the range becomes empty, and print the index of 173. */
/* The array must be sorted. Each step halves the range that can still hold the key. */
int binary_search(const int items[], int count, int key) {
    int lo = 0;
    int hi = count - 1;
    while (lo <= hi) {
        int mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;
        if (items[mid] == key) {
            return mid;
        } else if (items[mid] < key) {
            lo = mid + 1;   /* key is in the right half */
        } else {
            hi = mid - 1;   /* key is in the left half */
        }
    }
    return -1;
}

int main(void) {
    int items[] = {61, 86, 109, 118, 166, 173, 194};
    int count = sizeof(items) / sizeof(items[0]);
    int index = binary_search(items, count, 173);
    printf("Index of 173: %d\n", index);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: binary_search() needs a sorted array. It keeps the range from lo to hi,
   compares the middle element mid with the key and throws away the half that cannot
   contain it, so it needs only about log2(n) steps. main() looks for 173 and prints its
   index, or -1 if it is not there. */
// END

/* Caption: Find the index of a number using linear search. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write linear_search() with the array, its length and wanted.
   2. Compare each element with wanted.
   3. Return the index of the first match, or -1.
   4. In main(), search for 117 and print the result. */
/* Return the index of wanted, or -1 when it is not in the array. */
int linear_search(const int samples[], int n, int wanted) {
    for (int idx = 0; idx < n; idx++) {
        if (samples[idx] == wanted) {
            return idx;
        }
    }
    return -1;
}

int main(void) {
    int samples[] = {27, 34, 27, 70, 75};
    const int n = 5;
    int wanted = 117;
    int pos = linear_search(samples, n, wanted);
    if (pos >= 0) {
        printf("Found %d at index %d\n", wanted, pos);
    } else {
        printf("%d is not in the array\n", wanted);
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: linear_search() checks the elements of samples one by one and returns the
   index of the first one equal to wanted, or -1 when it reaches the end without a match.
   main() searches for 117 and prints where it is, or that it is missing. */
// END

/* Caption: Use selection sort to put numbers in ascending order. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write selection_sort() for the int array numbers.
   2. For each position, find the smallest remaining element.
   3. Swap it into that position.
   4. Print the sorted values. */
/* Select the right element for each position and swap it into place. */
void selection_sort(int numbers[], int len) {
    for (int i = 0; i < len - 1; i++) {
        int chosen = i;
        for (int j = i + 1; j < len; j++) {
            if (numbers[chosen] > numbers[j]) {
                chosen = j;
            }
        }
        int tmp = numbers[i];
        numbers[i] = numbers[chosen];
        numbers[chosen] = tmp;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    int numbers[] = {74, 7, 93, 38, 13};
    const int len = 5;
    selection_sort(numbers, len);
    for (int i = 0; i < len; i++) {
        printf("%d ", numbers[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: selection_sort() finds the smallest remaining element for each position and
   swaps it into place. main() then prints the 5 values in ascending order. */
// END

/* Caption: Compute the sum and the average of an array in one function. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write sum_and_average() with the pointers sum and average.
   2. Add the values into *sum.
   3. Store *sum / n in *average.
   4. Declare total and mean, pass their addresses and print them. */
void sum_and_average(const double v[], int n, double *sum, double *average) {
    *sum = 0.0;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        *sum += v[i];
    }
    *average = *sum / n;
}

int main(void) {
    double marks[] = {56.1, 29.8, 74.6};
    int n = sizeof(marks) / sizeof(marks[0]);
    double total, mean;
    sum_and_average(marks, n, &total, &mean);
    printf("Sum: %.2f, Average: %.2f\n", total, mean);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: sum_and_average() takes the array, its length and two pointers. It adds up
   the 3 values through *sum and then stores *sum / n in *average. main() declares total
   and mean on one line and passes their addresses. */
// END

/* Caption: Search an array for its largest value. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write find_max() that takes nums and n.
   2. Store nums[0] in largest.
   3. Loop over the other elements and keep the largest value in largest.
   4. Return largest and print it. */
/* Start with the first element and keep the largest value seen so far. */
double find_max(const double nums[], int n) {
    double largest = nums[0];
    for (int k = 1; k < n; k++) {
        if (nums[k] > largest) {
            largest = nums[k];
        }
    }
    return largest;
}

int main(void) {
    double nums[] = {95.1, 10.5, 73.4, 15.9, 28.9, 87.3, 93.0, 82.8, 3.6, 92.4};
    int n = sizeof(nums) / sizeof(nums[0]);
    printf("Largest: %.2f\n", find_max(nums, n));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: find_max() takes the first element as the largest value so far and stores
   it in largest. The loop compares every other element with largest using > and keeps the
   largest one. main() prints the largest of the 10 values. */
// END

/* Caption: Create a singly linked list by inserting at the head. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define Item with a value and a next pointer.
   2. Write push_front() that mallocs a node and links it in front of head.
   3. Write print_list() that follows next until NULL.
   4. Write free_list() that frees every node.
   5. Push 3 values, print the list and free it. */
typedef struct Item {
    int value;
    struct Item *next;
} Item;

/* Allocate a new node and put it in front of the current head. */
Item *push_front(Item *head, int value) {
    Item *node = malloc(sizeof(Item));
    if (node == NULL) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Out of memory\n");
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }
    node->value = value;
    node->next = head;
    return node;
}

void print_list(const Item *head) {
    for (const Item *cur = head; cur != NULL; cur = cur->next) {
        printf("%d -> ", cur->value);
    }
    printf("NULL\n");
}

/* Free every node; save next before freeing the current one. */
void free_list(Item *head) {
    while (head != NULL) {
        Item *next = head->next;
        free(head);
        head = next;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    Item *head = NULL;
    head = push_front(head, 26);
    head = push_front(head, 23);
    head = push_front(head, 22);
    print_list(head);
    free_list(head);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: Each Item holds a value and a pointer to the next node. push_front()
   allocates a node with malloc, puts it in front of head and returns it; print_list()
   follows the next pointers until NULL; free_list() frees every node. main() pushes 3
   values, so they print in reverse order. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to compute the distance between two points with a four-parameter function. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <math.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write distance(x1, y1, x2, y2).
   2. Compute dx and dy, then return sqrt(dx * dx + dy * dy).
   3. Print the distance between (7, 9) and (-1, 0). */
/* Pythagoras: the distance is sqrt(dx * dx + dy * dy). */
double distance(double x1, double y1, double x2, double y2) {
    double dx = x2 - x1, dy = y2 - y1;

    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: distance() takes the coordinates of both points as four parameters. It
   declares dx and dy on one line and uses Pythagoras with sqrt() from math.h. main()
   prints the distance between (7, 9) and (-1, 0). */
// END

   of 1 after dividing by 2 means the number is odd, so tally goes up by one. main() prints
   how many of the 7 values are odd. */

/* Caption: List the prime numbers below a limit. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write is_prime(n); numbers below 2 are not prime.
   2. Try every divisor d while d * d <= n.
   3. Return false if one divides n, otherwise true.
   4. Print every prime from 2 to 94. */
/* A prime has no divisor between 2 and its square root. */
bool is_prime(int n) {
    if (n < 2) {
        return false;
    }
    for (int d = 2; d * d <= n; d++) {
        if (n % d == 0) {
            return false;
        }
    }
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    for (int n = 2; n <= 94; n++) {
        if (is_prime(n)) {
            printf("%d ", n);
        }
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: is_prime() tries every divisor d from 2 while d * d <= n; if one divides n
   evenly, n is not prime. main() tests every number from 2 to 94 and prints the primes. */
// END

/* Caption: Find a number in a sorted array with binary search. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Make sure the array is sorted.
   2. Set left to 0 and right to count - 1.
   3. While left <= right, compare the middle element middle with the key.
   4. Return the index if it matches; otherwise keep only the half that can hold the
      key.
   5. Return -1 if the range becomes empty, and print the index of 107. */
/* The array must be sorted. Each step halves the range that can still hold the key. */
int binary_search(const int samples[], int count, int key) {
    int left = 0;
    int right = count - 1;
    while (left <= right) {
        int middle = left + (right - left) / 2;
        if (samples[middle] == key) {
            return middle;
        } else if (samples[middle] < key) {
            left = middle + 1;   /* key is in the right half */
        } else {
            right = middle - 1;   /* key is in the left half */
        }
    }
    return -1;
}

int main(void) {
    int samples[] = {50, 53, 107, 141, 166, 172};
    int count = sizeof(samples) / sizeof(samples[0]);
    int index = binary_search(samples, count, 107);
    printf("Index of 107: %d\n", index);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: binary_search() needs a sorted array. It keeps the range from left to
   right, compares the middle element middle with the key and throws away the half that
   cannot contain it, so it needs only about log2(n) steps. main() looks for 107 and prints
   its index, or -1 if it is not there. */
// END

/* Caption: Print the factorial of an integer. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write factorial(value) that calls itself.
   2. Return 1 when value is 1 or less.
   3. Otherwise return value * factorial(value - 1).
   4. Print 8! as an unsigned long long. */
/* n! = n * (n - 1)!, and 0! = 1 stops the recursion. */
unsigned long long factorial(int value) {
    if (value <= 1) {
        return 1;
    }
    return value * factorial(value - 1);
}

int main(void) {
    int value = 8;
    printf("%d! = %llu\n", value, factorial(value));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: factorial() calls itself: n! is n * (n - 1)!, and the recursion stops when
   value is 1 or less. main() prints 8! as an unsigned long long, because factorials grow
   very fast. */
// END

/* Caption: Reverse a string in place. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <string.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write reverse_string() for buffer.
   2. Set i to the first index and j to the last.
   3. Swap the two characters and move i and j inwards until they meet.
   4. Reverse stats and print it. */
/* Swap characters from both ends until they meet in the middle. */
void reverse_string(char *buffer) {
    int i = 0;
    int j = strlen(buffer) - 1;
    while (i < j) {
        char tmp = buffer[i];
        buffer[i] = buffer[j];
        buffer[j] = tmp;
        i++;
        j--;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    char buffer[] = "stats";
    reverse_string(buffer);
    printf("%s\n", buffer);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: reverse_string() swaps characters from both ends of buffer, moving inwards
   until the two indexes meet. main() reverses the word stats in place and prints it. */
// END

/* Caption: How do I search a sorted array by halving the search range each step in C? */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Make sure the array is sorted.
   2. Set low to 0 and high to size - 1.
   3. While low <= high, compare the middle element mid with the key.
   4. Return the index if it matches; otherwise keep only the half that can hold the
      key.
   5. Return -1 if the range becomes empty, and print the index of 45. */
/* The array must be sorted. Each step halves the range that can still hold the key. */
int binary_search(const int marks[], int size, int key) {
    int low = 0;
    int high = size - 1;
    while (low <= high) {
        int mid = low + (high - low) / 2;
        if (marks[mid] == key) {
            return mid;
        } else if (marks[mid] < key) {
            low = mid + 1;   /* key is in the right half */
        } else {
            high = mid - 1;   /* key is in the left half */
        }
    }
    return -1;
}

int main(void) {
    int marks[] = {39, 45, 60, 86, 96, 145, 148, 155, 160, 191};
    const int size = 10;
    int index = binary_search(marks, size, 45);
    printf("Index of 45: %d\n", index);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: binary_search() needs a sorted array. It keeps the range from low to high,
   compares the middle element mid with the key and throws away the half that cannot
   contain it, so it needs only about log2(n) steps. main() looks for 45 and prints its
   index, or -1 if it is not there. */
// END

/* Caption: C program to use insertion sort to put numbers in ascending order. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write insertion_sort() for the int array readings.
   2. Take each element in turn as current.
   3. Shift the larger values of the sorted part one place right.
   4. Put current into the gap.
   5. Print the sorted values. */
/* Insert each element into the already sorted part on its left. */
void insertion_sort(int readings[], int size) {
    for (int i = 1; i < size; i++) {
        int current = readings[i];
        int j = i - 1;
        while (j >= 0 && readings[j] > current) {
            readings[j + 1] = readings[j];   /* shift bigger values right */
            j--;
        }
        readings[j + 1] = current;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    int readings[] = {52, 42, 82, 44, 6, 48, 76, 45, 26};
    const int size = 9;
    insertion_sort(readings, size);
    for (int i = 0; i < size; i++) {
        printf("%d ", readings[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: insertion_sort() takes each element in turn and shifts the larger values of
   the sorted part one place right until the element fits. main() then prints the 9 values
   in ascending order. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to print an integer with its digits reversed. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Start result at 0.
   2. Multiply result by 10, add n % 10, then divide n by 10.
   3. Repeat until n is 0.
   4. Apply it to 300196 and print the result. */
/* Take the last digit with % 10, then drop it with / 10. */
int reverse_digits(int n) {
    int result = 0;
    while (n > 0) {
        result = result * 10 + n % 10;
        n /= 10;
    }
    return result;
}

int main(void) {
    int number = 300196;
    printf("reverse of digits of %d: %d\n", number, reverse_digits(number));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: reverse_digits() shifts result one place left (result * 10) and adds the
   last digit of n, which reverses the order. main() applies it to 300196. */
// END

/* Caption: Compute the distance between two points with a four-parameter function. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <math.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write distance(x1, y1, x2, y2).
   2. Compute dx and dy, then return sqrt(dx * dx + dy * dy).
   3. Print the distance between (4, -1) and (-1, 3). */
/* Pythagoras: the distance is sqrt(dx * dx + dy * dy). */
double distance(double x1, double y1, double x2, double y2) {
    double dx = x2 - x1, dy = y2 - y1;
    return sqrt(dx * dx + dy * dy);
}

int main(void) {
    printf("Distance: %.3f\n", distance(4, -1, -1, 3));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: distance() takes the coordinates of both points as four parameters. It
   declares dx and dy on one line and uses Pythagoras with sqrt() from math.h. main()
   prints the distance between (4, -1) and (-1, 3). */
// END

/* Caption: C program to list the prime numbers below a limit. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write is_prime(n); numbers below 2 are not prime.
   2. Try every divisor d while d * d <= n.
   3. Return false if one divides n, otherwise true.
   4. Print every prime from 2 to 114. */
/* A prime has no divisor between 2 and its square root. */
bool is_prime(int n) {
    if (n < 2) {
        return false;
    }
    for (int d = 2; d * d <= n; d++) {
        if (n % d == 0) {
            return false;
        }
    }
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    for (int n = 2; n <= 114; n++) {
        if (is_prime(n)) {
            printf("%d ", n);
        }
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: is_prime() tries every divisor d from 2 while d * d <= n; if one divides n
   evenly, n is not prime. main() tests every number from 2 to 114 and prints the primes. */
// END

/* Caption: Search an array for its smallest value. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write smallest_value() that takes scores and size.
   2. Store scores[0] in m.
   3. Loop over the other elements and keep the smallest value in m.
   4. Return m and print it. */
/* Start with the first element and keep the smallest value seen so far. */
double smallest_value(const double scores[], int size) {
    double m = scores[0];
    for (int idx = 1; idx < size; idx++) {
        if (scores[idx] < m) {
            m = scores[idx];

}

    int size = 6;

}
/* Explanation: smallest_value() takes the first element as the smallest value so far and
   stores it in m. The loop compares every other element with m using < and keeps the
   smallest one. main() prints the smallest of the 6 values. */
// END

    int n = 7;

    int *buffer = malloc(n * sizeof(int));
    if (buffer == NULL) {
        fprintf(stderr, "malloc failed\n");
        return 1;
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        buffer[i] = 9 * i;
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {

    return 0;

/* Caption: Implement bubble sort for an array of int values. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write bubble_sort() for the int array values.
   2. Compare each pair of neighbours.
   3. Swap them when they are in the wrong order for ascending order.
   4. Repeat the passes until the array is sorted.
   5. Print the sorted values. */
/* Repeatedly swap neighbours that are in the wrong order. */
void bubble_sort(int values[], int n) {
    for (int i = 0; i < n - 1; i++) {
        for (int j = 0; j < n - 1 - i; j++) {
            if (values[j] > values[j + 1]) {
                int tmp = values[j];
                values[j] = values[j + 1];
                values[j + 1] = tmp;
            }
        }
    }
}

int main(void) {
    int values[] = {39, 14, 92, 22, 34, 3, 44, 80, 13, 66};
    int n = sizeof(values) / sizeof(values[0]);
    bubble_sort(values, n);
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        printf("%d ", values[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: bubble_sort() walks through values again and again and swaps neighbours
   that are in the wrong order, so the largest values move to the end first. main() then
   prints the 10 values in ascending order. */
// END

   100 degrees Celsius in steps of 20. */
// END

/* Caption: Program to count how many odd numbers are in an array. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write count_odd() that takes ages and length.
   2. For each element, test ages[i] % 2 != 0.
   3. Add one to tally for every odd number.
   4. Return tally and print it. */
/* A number is odd when the remainder after dividing by 2 is one. */
int count_odd(const int ages[], int length) {
    int tally = 0;
    int i = 0;
    while (i < length) {
        if (ages[i] % 2 != 0) {
            tally++;
        }
        i++;
    }
    return tally;
}

int main(void) {
    int ages[] = {61, 69, 93, 57, 78, 10, 45, 71, 93};
    int length = sizeof(ages) / sizeof(ages[0]);
    printf("Odd numbers: %d\n", count_odd(ages, length));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: count_odd() tests each element of ages with the % operator: a remainder of
   1 after dividing by 2 means the number is odd, so tally goes up by one. main() prints
   how many of the 9 values are odd. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to find the greatest common divisor of two numbers. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write gcd() with Euclid's algorithm.
   2. Replace (a, b) by (b, a % b) until b is 0.
   3. Return a and print the GCD of 149 and 143. */
/* Euclid: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a % b) until b becomes zero. */
int gcd(int a, int b) {
    while (b != 0) {
        int r = a % b;
        a = b;
        b = r;
    }
    return a;
}

int main(void) {
    int x = 149, y = 143;
    printf("gcd(%d, %d) = %d\n", x, y, gcd(x, y));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: gcd() uses Euclid's algorithm: it keeps replacing (a, b) with (b, a % b)
   until b is 0. The last non-zero value is the greatest common divisor, and main() prints
   the GCD of 149 and 143. */
// END

/* Caption: Calculate the average of the values in an array. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write array_average() that takes values and n.
   2. Add the values into the double result.
   3. Return result / n.
   4. Print the average with two decimals. */
/* The mean is the total divided by the count. */
double array_average(const long values[], int n) {
    double result = 0.0;
    int i = 0;
    while (i < n) {
        result += values[i];
        i++;
    }
    return result / n;
}

int main(void) {
    long values[] = {81L, 96L, 14L, 49L, 94L};
    int n = 5;
    printf("Mean = %.2f\n", array_average(values, n));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: array_average() adds the 5 values of values into the double result and
   divides by n, so the mean keeps its decimal part even when the values are whole numbers.
   main() prints it with two decimals. */
// END

/* Caption: Convert 487 to binary. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write print_binary(n, bits).
   2. Go through the bits from the highest to the lowest.
   3. Print 1 when (n >> b) & 1 is set, otherwise 0.
   4. Print 487 in binary. */
/* Check each bit from the highest to the lowest. */
void print_binary(unsigned int n, int bits) {
    for (int b = bits - 1; b >= 0; b--) {
        putchar((n >> b) & 1 ? '1' : '0');
    }
    putchar('\n');
}

int main(void) {
    unsigned int number = 487;
    printf("%u in binary: ", number);
    print_binary(number, 10);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: print_binary() checks one bit at a time, from the highest to the lowest: (n
   >> b) & 1 is 1 when bit b is set, so it prints the character 1 or 0. main() prints 487
   in binary. */
// END
