/* Caption: Build a fixed-size integer stack in C. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define a Stack with room for 32 items and a top counter.
   2. Write push() and pop(), returning false when the stack is full or empty.
   3. Push 6 values.
   4. Pop and print until the stack is empty. */
#define CAPACITY 32

typedef struct {
    int items[CAPACITY];
    int top;   /* number of items on the stack */
} Stack;

bool push(Stack *s, int value) {
    if (s->top == CAPACITY) {
        return false;   /* stack is full */
    }
    s->items[s->top++] = value;
    return true;
}

bool pop(Stack *s, int *value) {
    if (s->top == 0) {
        return false;   /* stack is empty */
    }
    *value = s->items[--s->top];
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    Stack s = {.top = 0};
    push(&s, 51);
    push(&s, 53);
    push(&s, 82);
    push(&s, 82);
    push(&s, 67);
    push(&s, 41);
    int value;
    /* Items come back out in reverse order (last in, first out). */
    while (pop(&s, &value)) {
        printf("%d ", value);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: The Stack keeps up to 32 items in an array, and top counts how many are
   stored. push() adds at the top and pop() removes from the top; both return false when
   they cannot. main() pushes 6 values and pops them all, so they come out in reverse order
   (last in, first out). */
// END

/* Caption: Search an array for its largest value. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write max_of() that takes readings and len.
   2. Store readings[0] in current.
   3. Loop over the other elements and keep the largest value in current.
   4. Return current and print it. */
/* Start with the first element and keep the largest value seen so far. */
double max_of(const double readings[], int len) {
    double current = readings[0];
    for (int idx = 1; idx < len; idx++) {
        if (readings[idx] > current) {
            current = readings[idx];
        }
    }
    return current;
}

int main(void) {
    double readings[] = {73.4, 23.3, 78.4, 29.6, 20.3, 8.5, 76.2, 51.2, 40.5, 28.1};
    int len = 10;
    printf("Largest: %.2f\n", max_of(readings, len));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: max_of() takes the first element as the largest value so far and stores it
   in current. The loop compares every other element with current using > and keeps the
   largest one. main() prints the largest of the 10 values. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to sort an array in ascending order using selection sort. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write selection_sort() for the int array samples.
   2. For each position, find the smallest remaining element.
   3. Swap it into that position.
   4. Print the sorted values. */
/* Select the right element for each position and swap it into place. */
void selection_sort(int samples[], int size) {
    for (int i = 0; i < size - 1; i++) {
        int chosen = i;
        for (int j = i + 1; j < size; j++) {
            if (samples[chosen] > samples[j]) {
                chosen = j;
            }
        }
        int tmp = samples[i];
        samples[i] = samples[chosen];
        samples[chosen] = tmp;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    int samples[] = {34, 54, 89, 13, 49, 7};
    int size = 6;
    selection_sort(samples, size);
    for (int i = 0; i < size; i++) {
        printf("%d ", samples[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: selection_sort() finds the smallest remaining element for each position and
   swaps it into place. main() then prints the 6 values in ascending order. */
// END

/* Caption: Count the words in a sentence. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <ctype.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write count_words() with words = 0 and an in_word flag.
   2. A space ends a word; a non-space after a space starts a new word and adds one to
      words.
   3. Return words and print it. */
/* A new word starts when a non-space follows a space (or the start). */
int count_words(const char *text) {
    int words = 0;
    int in_word = 0;
    for (int i = 0; text[i] != '\0'; i++) {
        if (isspace((unsigned char)text[i])) {
            in_word = 0;
        } else if (!in_word) {
            in_word = 1;
            words++;
        }
    }
    return words;
}

int main(void) {
    const char *sentence = "the quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog";
    printf("Words: %d\n", count_words(sentence));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: count_words() uses the flag in_word: a new word starts when a non-space
   character follows a space or the start of the text. main() prints the number of words in
   the sentence. */
// END

#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write power(base, exp) with result = 1.
   2. Multiply result by base exp times.
   3. Print 2 to the power 8. */
/* Multiply the base by itself exp times. */
long long power(int base, int exp) {
    long long result = 1;
    for (int i = 0; i < exp; i++) {
        result *= base;
    }
    return result;
}

int main(void) {
    printf("2^8 = %lld\n", power(2, 8));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: power() starts result at 1 and multiplies it by base exp times. It uses
   long long because powers grow quickly. main() prints 2 to the power 8. */
// END

/* Caption: How do I print the binary representation of an integer in C? */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write print_binary(n, bits).
   2. Go through the bits from the highest to the lowest.
   3. Print 1 when (n >> b) & 1 is set, otherwise 0.
   4. Print 639 in binary. */
/* Check each bit from the highest to the lowest. */
void print_binary(unsigned int n, int bits) {
    for (int b = bits - 1; b >= 0; b--) {
        putchar((n >> b) & 1 ? '1' : '0');
    }
    putchar('\n');
}

int main(void) {
    unsigned int number = 639;
    printf("%u in binary: ", number);
    print_binary(number, 12);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: print_binary() checks one bit at a time, from the highest to the lowest: (n
   >> b) & 1 is 1 when bit b is set, so it prints the character 1 or 0. main() prints 639
   in binary. */
// END

/* Caption: Program to print an integer with its digits reversed. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Start result at 0.
   2. Multiply result by 10, add n % 10, then divide n by 10.
   3. Repeat until n is 0.
   4. Apply it to 701024 and print the result. */
/* Take the last digit with % 10, then drop it with / 10. */
int reverse_digits(int n) {
    int result = 0;
    while (n > 0) {
        result = result * 10 + n % 10;
        n /= 10;
    }
    return result;
}

int main(void) {
    int number = 701024;
    printf("reverse of digits of %d: %d\n", number, reverse_digits(number));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: reverse_digits() shifts result one place left (result * 10) and adds the
   last digit of n, which reverses the order. main() applies it to 701024. */
// END

/* Caption: Sum a double array with a helper function. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write total_of() that takes the array prices and its length size.
   2. Start acc at 0 and add every element in a while loop.
   3. Return acc.
   4. In main(), fill prices with 5 values and print the sum. */
/* Add every element to a running total. */
double total_of(const double prices[], int size) {
    double acc = 0;
    int idx = 0;
    while (idx < size) {
        acc += prices[idx];
        idx++;
    }
    return acc;
}

int main(void) {
    double prices[] = {73.5, 73.6, 40.2, 13.9, 82.7};
    const int size = 5;
    printf("Sum: %.2f\n", total_of(prices, size));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: total_of() receives the array prices and its length size. It starts acc at
   0, adds every element to it in a while loop and returns the total. main() fills prices
   with 5 double values and prints their sum. */
// END

/* Caption: C program to use insertion sort to put numbers in ascending order. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write insertion_sort() for the double array numbers.
   2. Take each element in turn as current.
   3. Shift the larger values of the sorted part one place right.
   4. Put current into the gap.
   5. Print the sorted values. */
/* Insert each element into the already sorted part on its left. */
void insertion_sort(double numbers[], int count) {
    for (int i = 1; i < count; i++) {
        double current = numbers[i];
        int j = i - 1;
        while (j >= 0 && numbers[j] > current) {
            numbers[j + 1] = numbers[j];   /* shift bigger values right */
            j--;
        }
        numbers[j + 1] = current;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    double numbers[] = {61.9, 11.2, 34.7, 94.3, 25.3};
    const int count = 5;
    insertion_sort(numbers, count);
    for (int i = 0; i < count; i++) {
        printf("%.2f ", numbers[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: insertion_sort() takes each element in turn and shifts the larger values of
   the sorted part one place right until the element fits. main() then prints the 5 values
   in ascending order. */
// END

/* Caption: How do I add two 4x4 matrices in C? */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define ROWS as 4 and COLS as 4.
   2. Loop over every row r and column c.
   3. Store a[r][c] + b[r][c] in sum and print it. */
#define ROWS 4
#define COLS 4

int main(void) {
    int a[ROWS][COLS] = {{1, 4, 2, 6}, {4, 1, 3, 6}, {6, 0, 4, 6}, {7, 4, 3, 4}};
    int b[ROWS][COLS] = {{6, 0, 7, 3}, {4, 7, 9, 9}, {3, 9, 4, 7}, {4, 8, 3, 9}};
    int sum[ROWS][COLS];
    /* Each entry of the result is the sum of the matching entries. */
    for (int r = 0; r < ROWS; r++) {
        for (int c = 0; c < COLS; c++) {
            sum[r][c] = a[r][c] + b[r][c];
            printf("%3d", sum[r][c]);
        }
        printf("\n");
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: Both matrices are 4x4 two-dimensional arrays. Two nested loops visit every
   row r and column c, store a[r][c] + b[r][c] in sum and print each row. */
// END

/* Caption: Compute the distance between two points with a four-parameter function. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <math.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write distance(x1, y1, x2, y2).
   2. Compute dx and dy, then return sqrt(dx * dx + dy * dy).
   3. Print the distance between (4, 8) and (-10, -8). */
/* Pythagoras: the distance is sqrt(dx * dx + dy * dy). */
double distance(double x1, double y1, double x2, double y2) {
    double dx = x2 - x1, dy = y2 - y1;
    return sqrt(dx * dx + dy * dy);
}

int main(void) {
    printf("Distance: %.3f\n", distance(4, 8, -10, -8));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: distance() takes the coordinates of both points as four parameters. It
   declares dx and dy on one line and uses Pythagoras with sqrt() from math.h. main()
   prints the distance between (4, 8) and (-10, -8). */
// END

/* Caption: Check whether a number is prime. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write is_prime(n); numbers below 2 are not prime.
   2. Try every divisor d while d * d <= n.
   3. Return false if one divides n, otherwise true.
   4. Check 293 and print the result. */
/* A prime has no divisor between 2 and its square root. */
bool is_prime(int n) {
    if (n < 2) {
        return false;
    }
    for (int d = 2; d * d <= n; d++) {
        if (n % d == 0) {
            return false;
        }
    }
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    int number = 293;
    printf("%d %s prime\n", number, is_prime(number) ? "is" : "is not");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: is_prime() tries every divisor d from 2 while d * d <= n; if one divides n
   evenly, n is not prime. main() checks 293 and prints whether it is prime. */
// END

/* Caption: Sort an array in ascending order using selection sort. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write selection_sort() for the double array nums.
   2. For each position, find the smallest remaining element.
   3. Swap it into that position.
   4. Print the sorted values. */
/* Select the right element for each position and swap it into place. */
void selection_sort(double nums[], int size) {
    for (int i = 0; i < size - 1; i++) {
        int chosen = i;
        for (int j = i + 1; j < size; j++) {
            if (nums[chosen] > nums[j]) {
                chosen = j;
            }
        }
        double tmp = nums[i];
        nums[i] = nums[chosen];
        nums[chosen] = tmp;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    double nums[] = {55.7, 46.5, 70.2, 55.8, 72.9, 58.6, 89.7, 56.4, 77.4};
    int size = sizeof(nums) / sizeof(nums[0]);
    selection_sort(nums, size);
    for (int i = 0; i < size; i++) {
        printf("%.2f ", nums[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: selection_sort() finds the smallest remaining element for each position and
   swaps it into place. main() then prints the 9 values in ascending order. */
// END

/* Caption: Calculate the sum of the first n natural numbers. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Set n = 43.
   2. Compute n * (n + 1) / 2.
   3. Print the result. */
int main(void) {
    int n = 43;
    /* Gauss's formula: 1 + 2 + ... + n = n * (n + 1) / 2 */
    int sum = n * (n + 1) / 2;
    printf("Sum of 1 to %d = %d\n", n, sum);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: Instead of a loop it uses Gauss's formula n * (n + 1) / 2, which gives the
   sum of 1 to 43 in one step. */
// END

/* Caption: Declare several variables on one line without initial values. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Declare count, total and i on one line without values.
   2. Set count = 6 and total = 0.
   3. Add the squares of 1 to count to total and print it. */
int main(void) {
    int count, total, i;   /* declared now, given values below */
    count = 6;
    total = 0;
    for (i = 1; i <= count; i++) {
        total += i * i;
    }
    printf("Sum of the first %d squares: %d\n", count, total);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: count, total and i are declared together on one line without values, then
   assigned before they are used, because an uninitialised local variable holds garbage.
   The loop adds the squares of 1 to 6 to total. */
// END

/* Caption: Show how to declare variables of different types on one line each. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Declare three ints on one line.
   2. Declare two doubles and two chars the same way.
   3. Print each group and the sum of the ints. */
int main(void) {
    /* Variables of the same type can share one declaration, separated by commas. */
    int a = 94, b = 45, c = 51;
    double x = 54.8, y = 17.9;
    char first = 'T', last = 'V';
    printf("a = %d, b = %d, c = %d\n", a, b, c);
    printf("x = %.2f, y = %.2f\n", x, y);
    printf("first = %c, last = %c\n", first, last);
    printf("a + b + c = %d\n", a + b + c);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: Each line declares several variables of one type, separated by commas, and
   gives each its own starting value: three ints, two doubles and two chars. printf()
   prints them with %d, %.2f and %c, and the last line prints the sum of a, b and c. */
// END

#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write is_prime(n); numbers below 2 are not prime.
   2. Try every divisor d while d * d <= n.

/* A prime has no divisor between 2 and its square root. */

/* Caption: Find the index of a number using linear search. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write linear_search() with the array, its length and key.
   2. Compare each element with key.
   3. Return the index of the first match, or -1.
   4. In main(), search for 13 and print the result. */
/* Return the index of key, or -1 when it is not in the array. */
int linear_search(const int data[], int size, int key) {
    for (int j = 0; j < size; j++) {
        if (data[j] == key) {
            return j;
        }
    }
    return -1;
}

int main(void) {
    int data[] = {24, 62, 81, 63, 99, 92, 30, 13, 90};
    int size = sizeof(data) / sizeof(data[0]);
    int key = 13;
    int pos = linear_search(data, size, key);
    if (pos >= 0) {
        printf("Found %d at index %d\n", key, pos);
    } else {
        printf("%d is not in the array\n", key);
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: linear_search() checks the elements of data one by one and returns the
   index of the first one equal to key, or -1 when it reaches the end without a match.
   main() searches for 13 and prints where it is, or that it is missing. */
// END

/* Caption: Return a Duration struct built from a number of seconds. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define a Duration struct with hours, minutes and seconds.
   2. Write from_seconds() that fills it using / and %.
   3. Convert 25803 seconds and print the members. */
typedef struct {
    int hours;
    int minutes;
    int seconds;
} Duration;

Duration from_seconds(int total) {
    Duration d;
    d.hours = total / 3600;
    d.minutes = (total % 3600) / 60;
    d.seconds = total % 60;
    return d;
}

int main(void) {
    Duration d = from_seconds(25803);
    printf("%d h %d min %d s\n", d.hours, d.minutes, d.seconds);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: from_seconds() fills the three members of a Duration struct using / and %,
   then returns the struct. main() converts 25803 seconds and prints the members. */
// END

/* Caption: Check whether a number lies between two limits. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write in_range(x, low, high).
   2. Return true when x >= low and x <= high.
   3. Print whether 9 is inside 24 to 72. */
/* true when low <= x <= high */
bool in_range(int x, int low, int high) {
    return x >= low && x <= high;
}

int main(void) {
    int value = 9, low = 24, high = 72;
    printf("%d is %s the range %d to %d\n", value,
           in_range(value, low, high) ? "inside" : "outside", low, high);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: in_range() takes the value and both limits and returns true only when the
   value is at least low and at most high. main() declares value, low and high on one line
   and prints whether 9 is inside 24 to 72. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to calculate the average of the values in an array. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write average() that takes values and n.
   2. Add the values into the double total.
   3. Return total / n.
   4. Print the average with two decimals. */
/* Sum the values, then divide by how many there are. */
double average(const int values[], int n) {
    double total = 0.0;
    int i = 0;
    while (i < n) {
        total += values[i];
        i++;
    }
    return total / n;
}

int main(void) {
    int values[] = {45, 23, 77};
    const int n = 3;
    printf("The average is %.2f\n", average(values, n));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: average() adds the 3 values of values into the double total and divides by
   n, so the mean keeps its decimal part even when the values are whole numbers. main()
   prints it with two decimals. */
// END

/* Caption: Add up the digits of a number. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Start result at 0.
   2. Add n % 10 to result, then divide n by 10.
   3. Repeat until n is 0.
   4. Apply it to 315769 and print the result. */
/* Take the last digit with % 10, then drop it with / 10. */
int sum_digits(int n) {
    int result = 0;
    while (n > 0) {
        result += n % 10;
        n /= 10;
    }
    return result;
}

int main(void) {
    int number = 315769;
    printf("sum of digits of %d: %d\n", number, sum_digits(number));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: sum_digits() adds the last digit (n % 10) to result and then removes it (n
   / 10) until no digits are left. main() applies it to 315769. */
// END

/* Caption: Swap two variables using pointers. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write swap() that takes pointers to two int values.
   2. Save *x in tmp, copy *y into *x, then tmp into *y.
   3. In main(), print x and y, call swap(&x, &y) and print them again. */
/* Pass addresses so the function can change the caller's variables. */
void swap(int *x, int *y) {
    int tmp = *x;
    *x = *y;
    *y = tmp;
}

int main(void) {
    int x = 8, y = 27;
    printf("Before: %d %d\n", x, y);
    swap(&x, &y);
    printf("After:  %d %d\n", x, y);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: swap() receives the addresses of x and y, so writing through the pointers
   *x and *y changes the caller's variables. tmp holds one value during the exchange.
   main() declares both variables on one line and prints them before and after the swap. */
// END

/* Caption: C program to find the arithmetic mean of 6 int values. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write average() that takes scores and size.
   2. Add the values into the double sum.
   3. Return sum / size.
   4. Print the average with two decimals. */
/* The mean is the total divided by the count. */
double average(const int scores[], int size) {
    double sum = 0.0;
    for (int k = 0; k < size; k++) {
        sum += scores[k];
    }
    return sum / size;
}

int main(void) {
    int scores[] = {47, 66, 52, 58, 41, 54};
    int size = sizeof(scores) / sizeof(scores[0]);
    printf("Average: %.2f\n", average(scores, size));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: average() adds the 6 values of scores into the double sum and divides by
   size, so the mean keeps its decimal part even when the values are whole numbers. main()
   prints it with two decimals. */
// END

/* Caption: How do I store students in an array of structs and find the class average in C? */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define struct Student with a name and a mark.
   2. Store 5 students in an array.
   3. Print each student and add the marks to total.
   4. Print total divided by the number of students. */
/* A struct groups a student's name and mark together. */
struct Student {
    char name[20];
    int mark;
};

int main(void) {
    struct Student students[] = {
        {"Asha", 78},
        {"Ben", 87},
        {"Kofi", 61},
        {"Fatima", 56},
        {"Jia", 66}
    };
    int count = sizeof(students) / sizeof(students[0]);
    double total = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < count; i++) {
        printf("%s: %d\n", students[i].name, students[i].mark);
        total += students[i].mark;
    }
    printf("Average mark: %.1f\n", total / count);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: struct Student groups a name and a mark. main() stores 5 students in an
   array of structs, prints each one, adds the marks to total and prints the average. */

/* Caption: How do I show the right way to declare several pointers on one line in C? */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Declare x and y on one line.
   2. Declare the pointers px and py on one line, each with its own *.
   3. Add 14 to x through px and print the values. */
int main(void) {
    int x = 20, y = 36;
    /* Each pointer needs its own '*': in "int *p, q;" only p is a pointer. */
    int *px = &x, *py = &y;
    *px += 14;
    printf("x = %d, y = %d\n", x, y);
    printf("*px = %d, *py = %d\n", *px, *py);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: int *px = &x, *py = &y; declares two pointers in one statement; each name
   needs its own *. *px += 14 changes x through the pointer, so x becomes 34 while y stays
   36. */
// END

/* Caption: Program to return two values from a function using pointer parameters. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write circle_measures() with the pointers area and circumference.
   2. Store PI * r * r and 2 * PI * r through them.
   3. Print both for a radius of 10.6. */
#define PI 3.14159265

void circle_measures(double radius, double *area, double *circumference) {
    *area = PI * radius * radius;
    *circumference = 2 * PI * radius;
}

int main(void) {

/* Caption: Compute the sum of the elements of an array. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write array_sum() that takes the array values and its length size.
   2. Start sum at 0 and add every element in a while loop.
   3. Return sum.
   4. In main(), fill values with 4 values and print the sum. */
/* Walk through the array and accumulate each value. */
long array_sum(const long values[], int size) {
    long sum = 0;
    int i = 0;
    while (i < size) {
        sum += values[i];
        i++;
    }
    return sum;
}

int main(void) {
    long values[] = {67L, 79L, 90L, 21L};
    int size = sizeof(values) / sizeof(values[0]);
    printf("The sum is %ld\n", array_sum(values, size));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: array_sum() receives the array values and its length size. It starts sum at
   0, adds every element to it in a while loop and returns the total. main() fills values
   with 4 long values and prints their sum. */
// END

/* Caption: Use insertion sort to put numbers in descending order. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write insertion_sort() for the double array data.
   2. Take each element in turn as current.
   3. Shift the smaller values of the sorted part one place right.
   4. Put current into the gap.
   5. Print the sorted values. */
/* Insert each element into the already sorted part on its left. */
void insertion_sort(double data[], int len) {
    for (int i = 1; i < len; i++) {
        double current = data[i];
        int j = i - 1;
        while (j >= 0 && data[j] < current) {
            data[j + 1] = data[j];   /* shift bigger values right */
            j--;
        }
        data[j + 1] = current;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    double data[] = {63.2, 81.3, 7.3, 86.4, 46.3};
    int len = 5;
    insertion_sort(data, len);
    for (int i = 0; i < len; i++) {
        printf("%.2f ", data[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: insertion_sort() takes each element in turn and shifts the smaller values
   of the sorted part one place right until the element fits. main() then prints the 5
   values in descending order. */
// END

/* Caption: Find the minimum and maximum of an array with one function. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write min_max() with the array, its length and the pointers min and max.
   2. Start both at the first element.
   3. Update *min and *max while looping over the rest.
   4. Declare lowest and highest, pass their addresses and print them. */
/* One pass finds both results; they are stored through the pointers. */
void min_max(const int prices[], int n, int *min, int *max) {

    *max = prices[0];
    for (int i = 1; i < n; i++) {
        if (prices[i] < *min) {
            *min = prices[i];

        if (prices[i] > *max) {
            *max = prices[i];
        }
    }
}

int main(void) {

    int n = 9;
    int lowest, highest;
    min_max(prices, n, &lowest, &highest);
    printf("Min: %d, Max: %d\n", lowest, highest);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: A C function can return only one value, so min_max() returns void and
   writes its two results through the pointer parameters min and max. main() declares
   lowest and highest on one line and passes their addresses with &, then prints both
   results for the 9 values. */
// END

/* Caption: Check whether a year is a leap year. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write is_leap(year).
   2. A year divisible by 4 is a leap year, unless it is divisible by 100.
   3. Years divisible by 400 are leap years again.
   4. Check 1950 and print the result. */
/* Leap years divide by 4, except centuries, which must divide by 400. */
int is_leap(int year) {
    return (year % 4 == 0 && year % 100 != 0) || year % 400 == 0;
}

int main(void) {
    int year = 1950;
    if (is_leap(year)) {
        printf("%d is a leap year\n", year);
    } else {
        printf("%d is not a leap year\n", year);
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: is_leap() returns true for years divisible by 4, except century years,
   which must also be divisible by 400. main() checks 1950 and prints whether it is a leap
   year. */
// END

/* Caption: Calculate 6! using recursion. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write factorial(n) that calls itself.
   2. Return 1 when n is 1 or less.
   3. Otherwise return n * factorial(n - 1).
   4. Print 6! as an unsigned long long. */
/* n! = n * (n - 1)!, and 0! = 1 stops the recursion. */
unsigned long long factorial(int n) {
    if (n <= 1) {
        return 1;
    }
    return n * factorial(n - 1);
}

int main(void) {
    int n = 6;
    printf("%d! = %llu\n", n, factorial(n));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: factorial() calls itself: n! is n * (n - 1)!, and the recursion stops when
   n is 1 or less. main() prints 6! as an unsigned long long, because factorials grow very
   fast. */
// END

/* Caption: Multiply two 2x2 matrices. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define N as 2.
   2. For every i and j, add a[i][k] * b[k][j] over k into product[i][j].
   3. Print product row by row. */
#define N 2

int main(void) {
    int a[N][N] = {{3, 5}, {9, 3}};
    int b[N][N] = {{5, 3}, {7, 5}};
    int product[N][N] = {0};
    /* product[i][j] is row i of a times column j of b. */
    for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) {
        for (int j = 0; j < N; j++) {
            for (int k = 0; k < N; k++) {
                product[i][j] += a[i][k] * b[k][j];
            }
        }
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) {
        for (int j = 0; j < N; j++) {
            printf("%4d", product[i][j]);
        }
        printf("\n");
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: For each entry product[i][j] the innermost loop adds a[i][k] * b[k][j] over
   k, which is row i of a times column j of b. main() multiplies two 2x2 matrices and
   prints the product. */
// END

/* Caption: How do I reverse an array by swapping from both ends in C? */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write reverse_array() for marks.
   2. Set start to the first index and end to the last.
   3. Swap marks[start] and marks[end], then move both inwards.
   4. Stop when start meets end and print the array. */
/* Swap the outer pair, then move both ends toward the middle. */
void reverse_array(int marks[], int count) {
    int start = 0;
    int end = count - 1;
    while (start < end) {
        int tmp = marks[start];
        marks[start] = marks[end];
        marks[end] = tmp;
        start++;
        end--;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    int marks[] = {30, 71, 66, 40, 19, 60};
    const int count = 6;
    reverse_array(marks, count);
    for (int i = 0; i < count; i++) {
        printf("%d ", marks[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: reverse_array() swaps the first and last elements, then moves start forward
   and end backward until they meet, so the array is reversed in place without a second
   array. main() prints the reversed values. */
// END

/* Caption: Print the first 8 Fibonacci numbers. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Start with prev = 0 and curr = 1.
   2. Repeat 8 times and print prev each time.
   3. Compute next = prev + curr, then set prev = curr and curr = next. */
int main(void) {
    long prev = 0, curr = 1;
    /* Print a term, then slide the pair one step along the sequence. */
    for (int i = 0; i < 8; i++) {
        printf("%ld ", prev);
        long next = prev + curr;
        prev = curr;
        curr = next;
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: The loop keeps the last two numbers in prev and curr. Each round it prints
   prev, then moves the pair forward: prev becomes curr and curr becomes their sum. It
   prints the first 8 Fibonacci numbers. */
// END

/* Caption: Implement bubble sort for an array of int values. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write bubble_sort() for the int array data.
   2. Compare each pair of neighbours.
   3. Swap them when they are in the wrong order for ascending order.
   4. Repeat the passes until the array is sorted.
   5. Print the sorted values. */
/* Repeatedly swap neighbours that are in the wrong order. */
void bubble_sort(int data[], int length) {
    for (int i = 0; i < length - 1; i++) {
        for (int j = 0; j < length - 1 - i; j++) {
            if (data[j] > data[j + 1]) {
                int tmp = data[j];
                data[j] = data[j + 1];
                data[j + 1] = tmp;
            }
        }
    }
}

int main(void) {
    int data[] = {79, 26, 32, 63, 74, 89, 37};
    int length = sizeof(data) / sizeof(data[0]);
    bubble_sort(data, length);
    for (int i = 0; i < length; i++) {
        printf("%d ", data[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: bubble_sort() walks through data again and again and swaps neighbours that
   are in the wrong order, so the largest values move to the end first. main() then prints
   the 7 values in ascending order. */
// END

   1. Write find_max() that takes marks and n.

   3. Loop over the other elements and keep the largest value in largest.
   4. Return largest and print it. */

}

   it in largest. The loop compares every other element with largest using > and keeps the
   largest one. main() prints the largest of the 9 values. */
// END

/* Caption: C program to build a FIFO queue using a ring buffer. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define a Queue with room for 8 items, a head and a count.
   2. Write enqueue() that stores at (head + count) % CAPACITY.
   3. Write dequeue() that takes the item at head and moves head on.
   4. Add 6 values, then remove and print them in order. */
#define CAPACITY 8

typedef struct {
    int items[CAPACITY];
    int head;
    int count;
} Queue;

bool enqueue(Queue *q, int value) {
    if (q->count == CAPACITY) {
        return false;
    }
    /* The tail wraps around to the start of the array. */
    q->items[(q->head + q->count) % CAPACITY] = value;
    q->count++;
    return true;
}

bool dequeue(Queue *q, int *value) {
    if (q->count == 0) {
        return false;
    }
    *value = q->items[q->head];
    q->head = (q->head + 1) % CAPACITY;
    q->count--;
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    Queue q = {.head = 0, .count = 0};
    enqueue(&q, 45);
    enqueue(&q, 95);
    enqueue(&q, 74);
    enqueue(&q, 90);
    enqueue(&q, 8);
    enqueue(&q, 37);
    int value;
    /* Items come out in the order they went in (first in, first out). */
    while (dequeue(&q, &value)) {
        printf("%d ", value);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: The Queue stores up to 8 items in a ring buffer: head is the oldest item
   and % CAPACITY wraps positions back to the start of the array. enqueue() adds at the
   back and dequeue() removes from the front, so main() gets its 6 values back in the same
   order (first in, first out). */
// END

/* Caption: Use insertion sort to put numbers in ascending order. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write insertion_sort() for the long array ages.
   2. Take each element in turn as current.
   3. Shift the larger values of the sorted part one place right.
   4. Put current into the gap.
   5. Print the sorted values. */
/* Insert each element into the already sorted part on its left. */
void insertion_sort(long ages[], int length) {
    for (int i = 1; i < length; i++) {
        long current = ages[i];
        int j = i - 1;
        while (j >= 0 && ages[j] > current) {
            ages[j + 1] = ages[j];   /* shift bigger values right */
            j--;
        }
        ages[j + 1] = current;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    long ages[] = {37L, 93L, 35L, 75L, 24L, 80L, 13L};
    const int length = 7;
    insertion_sort(ages, length);
    for (int i = 0; i < length; i++) {
        printf("%ld ", ages[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: insertion_sort() takes each element in turn and shifts the larger values of
   the sorted part one place right until the element fits. main() then prints the 7 values
   in ascending order. */
// END

/* Plan:
   1. Define ListNode with a value and a next pointer.
   2. Write push_front() that mallocs a node and links it in front of head.
   3. Write print_list() that follows next until NULL.
   4. Write free_list() that frees every node.
   5. Push 5 values, print the list and free it. */
typedef struct ListNode {
    int value;
    struct ListNode *next;
} ListNode;

/* Allocate a new node and put it in front of the current head. */
ListNode *push_front(ListNode *head, int value) {
    ListNode *node = malloc(sizeof(ListNode));
    if (node == NULL) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Out of memory\n");
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }
    node->value = value;
    node->next = head;
    return node;
}

void print_list(const ListNode *head) {
    for (const ListNode *cur = head; cur != NULL; cur = cur->next) {
        printf("%d -> ", cur->value);
    }
    printf("NULL\n");
}

/* Free every node; save next before freeing the current one. */
void free_list(ListNode *head) {
    while (head != NULL) {
        ListNode *next = head->next;
        free(head);
        head = next;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    ListNode *head = NULL;
    head = push_front(head, 56);
    head = push_front(head, 69);
    head = push_front(head, 56);
    head = push_front(head, 38);
    head = push_front(head, 26);
    print_list(head);
    free_list(head);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: Each ListNode holds a value and a pointer to the next node. push_front()
   allocates a node with malloc, puts it in front of head and returns it; print_list()
   follows the next pointers until NULL; free_list() frees every node. main() pushes 5
   values, so they print in reverse order. */
// END

/* Caption: How do I use bubble sort to put numbers in ascending order in C? */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write bubble_sort() for the int array scores.
   2. Compare each pair of neighbours.
   3. Swap them when they are in the wrong order for ascending order.
   4. Repeat the passes until the array is sorted.
   5. Print the sorted values. */
/* Repeatedly swap neighbours that are in the wrong order. */
void bubble_sort(int scores[], int length) {
    for (int i = 0; i < length - 1; i++) {
        for (int j = 0; j < length - 1 - i; j++) {
            if (scores[j] > scores[j + 1]) {
                int tmp = scores[j];
                scores[j] = scores[j + 1];
                scores[j + 1] = tmp;
            }
        }
    }
}

int main(void) {
    int scores[] = {2, 62, 22, 2, 42, 20, 63};
    int length = sizeof(scores) / sizeof(scores[0]);
    bubble_sort(scores, length);
    for (int i = 0; i < length; i++) {
        printf("%d ", scores[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: bubble_sort() walks through scores again and again and swaps neighbours
   that are in the wrong order, so the largest values move to the end first. main() then
   prints the 7 values in ascending order. */
// END

/* Caption: Define a Point struct and measure the distance between two points. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <math.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define a Point struct with x and y.
   2. Write distance() using sqrt(dx * dx + dy * dy).
   3. Print the distance between p and q. */
typedef struct {
    double x;
    double y;
} Point;

/* Pythagoras: sqrt(dx * dx + dy * dy). */
double distance(Point a, Point b) {
    double dx = b.x - a.x;
    double dy = b.y - a.y;
    return sqrt(dx * dx + dy * dy);
}

int main(void) {
    Point p = {-9, -4};
    Point q = {5, -5};
    printf("Distance: %.3f\n", distance(p, q));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: Point is a typedef struct with x and y. distance() uses Pythagoras, sqrt(dx
   * dx + dy * dy), to measure the gap between the two points, and main() prints it. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to sort an array in descending order using selection sort. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write selection_sort() for the int array samples.
   2. For each position, find the largest remaining element.
   3. Swap it into that position.
   4. Print the sorted values. */
/* Select the right element for each position and swap it into place. */
void selection_sort(int samples[], int len) {
    for (int i = 0; i < len - 1; i++) {
        int chosen = i;
        for (int j = i + 1; j < len; j++) {
            if (samples[chosen] < samples[j]) {
                chosen = j;
            }
        }
        int tmp = samples[i];
        samples[i] = samples[chosen];
        samples[chosen] = tmp;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    int samples[] = {65, 51, 21, 59, 56};
    const int len = 5;
    selection_sort(samples, len);
    for (int i = 0; i < len; i++) {
        printf("%d ", samples[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: selection_sort() finds the largest remaining element for each position and
   swaps it into place. main() then prints the 5 values in descending order. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a function that returns a Fraction struct. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define a Fraction struct with num and den.
   2. Write multiply() that returns num = a.num * b.num and den = a.den * b.den.
   3. Print 2/7 times 9/5. */
typedef struct {
    int num;
    int den;
} Fraction;

/* Multiply the numerators and the denominators. */
Fraction multiply(Fraction a, Fraction b) {
    Fraction r = {a.num * b.num, a.den * b.den};
    return r;
}

int main(void) {
    Fraction x = {2, 7}, y = {9, 5};
    Fraction p = multiply(x, y);
    printf("%d/%d * %d/%d = %d/%d\n", x.num, x.den, y.num, y.den, p.num, p.den);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: Fraction stores a numerator and a denominator. multiply() takes two
   Fractions and returns a new one with num = a.num * b.num and den = a.den * b.den. main()
   multiplies 2/7 by 9/5 (without reducing the result). */
// END

/* Caption: Write a function that swaps two int values through pointers. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write swap() that takes pointers to two int values.
   2. Save *first in tmp, copy *second into *first, then tmp into *second.
   3. In main(), print first and second, call swap(&first, &second) and print them
      again. */
/* Pass addresses so the function can change the caller's variables. */
void swap(int *first, int *second) {
    int tmp = *first;
    *first = *second;
    *second = tmp;
}

int main(void) {
    int first = 44, second = 36;
    printf("Before: %d %d\n", first, second);
    swap(&first, &second);
    printf("After:  %d %d\n", first, second);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: swap() receives the addresses of first and second, so writing through the
   pointers *first and *second changes the caller's variables. tmp holds one value during
   the exchange. main() declares both variables on one line and prints them before and
   after the swap. */
// END

   3. Print it. */
int main(void) {
    int num1 = 26, num2 = 74;

/* Explanation: The program uses fixed values for num1 and num2. The conditional operator
   (num1 > num2) ? num1 : num2 picks the bigger value, which is printed. */

/* Caption: Find the least common multiple of two numbers. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write gcd() with Euclid's algorithm: replace (a, b) by (b, a % b) until b is 0.
   2. Write lcm() as a / gcd(a, b) * b.
   3. Print the LCM of 40 and 233. */
/* Euclid: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a % b) until b becomes zero. */
int gcd(int a, int b) {
    while (b != 0) {
        int r = a % b;
        a = b;
        b = r;
    }
    return a;
}

/* lcm(a, b) = a / gcd(a, b) * b (divide first to avoid overflow). */
long lcm(int a, int b) {
    return (long)a / gcd(a, b) * b;
}

int main(void) {
    printf("lcm(40, 233) = %ld\n", lcm(40, 233));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: gcd() uses Euclid's algorithm: it keeps replacing (a, b) with (b, a % b)
   until b is 0. lcm() divides a by the gcd before multiplying by b, which avoids overflow.
   main() prints the LCM of 40 and 233. */
// END

#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write in_range(x, low, high).
   2. Return true when x >= low and x <= high.
   3. Print whether 22 is inside 63 to 68. */
/* true when low <= x <= high */
bool in_range(int x, int low, int high) {
    return x >= low && x <= high;

int main(void) {
    int value = 22, low = 63, high = 68;
    printf("%d is %s the range %d to %d\n", value,
           in_range(value, low, high) ? "inside" : "outside", low, high);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: in_range() takes the value and both limits and returns true only when the
   value is at least low and at most high. main() declares value, low and high on one line
   and prints whether 22 is inside 63 to 68. */
// END

/* Caption: Program to allocate an array with malloc and fill it with evens. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Use malloc to get room for 8 ints and check for NULL.
   2. Fill arr with evens.
   3. Print the values.
   4. Call free(arr) at the end. */
int main(void) {
    int n = 8;
    /* Ask the heap for room for n ints; malloc returns NULL on failure. */
    int *arr = malloc(n * sizeof(int));
    if (arr == NULL) {
        fprintf(stderr, "malloc failed\n");
        return 1;
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        arr[i] = 2 * i;
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        printf("%d ", arr[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    free(arr);   /* give the memory back */
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: malloc() reserves room for 8 ints on the heap and returns NULL if it fails,
   which the program checks. The first loop fills arr with evens, the second prints them,
   and free() gives the memory back at the end. */
// END

/* Caption: Count the characters in a string. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write string_length() with a counter len = 0.
   2. Move through the string until the null character.
   3. Return len and print the length of level. */
/* Count characters until the terminating '\0'. */
int string_length(const char *word) {
    int len = 0;
    while (word[len] != '\0') {
        len++;
    }
    return len;
}

int main(void) {
    const char *word = "level";
    printf("Length of \"%s\" is %d\n", word, string_length(word));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: string_length() counts characters until it reaches the null character that
   ends every C string. main() prints the length of the word level. */
// END

   passes their addresses and prints the results for a radius of 25.9. */

/* Caption: Add two 2x4 matrices. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define ROWS as 2 and COLS as 4.
   2. Loop over every row r and column c.
   3. Store a[r][c] + b[r][c] in sum and print it. */
#define ROWS 2
#define COLS 4

int main(void) {
    int a[ROWS][COLS] = {{9, 1, 5, 5}, {7, 1, 2, 9}};
    int b[ROWS][COLS] = {{5, 5, 7, 2}, {3, 9, 7, 4}};
    int sum[ROWS][COLS];
    /* Each entry of the result is the sum of the matching entries. */
    for (int r = 0; r < ROWS; r++) {
        for (int c = 0; c < COLS; c++) {
            sum[r][c] = a[r][c] + b[r][c];
            printf("%3d", sum[r][c]);
        }
        printf("\n");
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: Both matrices are 2x4 two-dimensional arrays. Two nested loops visit every
   row r and column c, store a[r][c] + b[r][c] in sum and print each row. */
// END

/* Caption: Print the factorial of an integer. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write factorial(value) that calls itself.
   2. Return 1 when value is 1 or less.
   3. Otherwise return value * factorial(value - 1).
   4. Print 4! as an unsigned long long. */
/* n! = n * (n - 1)!, and 0! = 1 stops the recursion. */
unsigned long long factorial(int value) {
    if (value <= 1) {
        return 1;
    }
    return value * factorial(value - 1);
}

int main(void) {
    int value = 4;
    printf("%d! = %llu\n", value, factorial(value));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: factorial() calls itself: n! is n * (n - 1)!, and the recursion stops when
   value is 1 or less. main() prints 4! as an unsigned long long, because factorials grow
   very fast. */
// END

/* Caption: Implement a stack with an array (push and pop). */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define a Stack with room for 16 items and a top counter.
   2. Write push() and pop(), returning false when the stack is full or empty.
   3. Push 6 values.
   4. Pop and print until the stack is empty. */
#define CAPACITY 16

typedef struct {
    int items[CAPACITY];
    int top;   /* number of items on the stack */
} Stack;

bool push(Stack *s, int value) {
    if (s->top == CAPACITY) {
        return false;   /* stack is full */
    }
    s->items[s->top++] = value;
    return true;
}

bool pop(Stack *s, int *value) {
    if (s->top == 0) {
        return false;   /* stack is empty */
    }
    *value = s->items[--s->top];
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    Stack s = {.top = 0};
    push(&s, 36);
    push(&s, 49);
    push(&s, 3);
    push(&s, 89);
    push(&s, 92);
    push(&s, 28);
    int value;
    /* Items come back out in reverse order (last in, first out). */
    while (pop(&s, &value)) {
        printf("%d ", value);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: The Stack keeps up to 16 items in an array, and top counts how many are
   stored. push() adds at the top and pop() removes from the top; both return false when
   they cannot. main() pushes 6 values and pops them all, so they come out in reverse order
   (last in, first out). */
// END

/* Plan:
   1. Set n = 8.
   2. Compute n * (n + 1) / 2.
   3. Print the result. */

    int n = 8;

    int sum = n * (n + 1) / 2;

/* Caption: Implement selection sort for an array of int values. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write selection_sort() for the int array numbers.
   2. For each position, find the smallest remaining element.
   3. Swap it into that position.
   4. Print the sorted values. */
/* Select the right element for each position and swap it into place. */
void selection_sort(int numbers[], int count) {
    for (int i = 0; i < count - 1; i++) {
        int chosen = i;
        for (int j = i + 1; j < count; j++) {
            if (numbers[chosen] > numbers[j]) {
                chosen = j;
            }
        }
        int tmp = numbers[i];
        numbers[i] = numbers[chosen];
        numbers[chosen] = tmp;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    int numbers[] = {39, 19, 50, 51, 95, 28};
    int count = 6;
    selection_sort(numbers, count);
    for (int i = 0; i < count; i++) {
        printf("%d ", numbers[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: selection_sort() finds the smallest remaining element for each position and
   swaps it into place. main() then prints the 6 values in ascending order. */
// END

/* Caption: C program to write your own version of strcpy. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write copy_string(dest, src).
   2. Copy src into dest one character at a time.
   3. Stop after copying the null character.
   4. Copy noon into text and print it. */
/* Copy each character, including the final '\0'. */
void copy_string(char *dest, const char *src) {
    int i = 0;
    while ((dest[i] = src[i]) != '\0') {
        i++;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    char source[] = "noon";
    char text[100];
    copy_string(text, source);
    printf("Copied: %s\n", text);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: copy_string() copies src into dest one character at a time, including the
   final null character, which is what strcpy does. The array text must be big enough to
   hold the copy. main() copies the word noon and prints it. */
// END

/* Caption: Use binary search to locate a value in a sorted list. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Make sure the array is sorted.
   2. Set low to 0 and high to n - 1.
   3. While low <= high, compare the middle element mid with the key.
   4. Return the index if it matches; otherwise keep only the half that can hold the
      key.
   5. Return -1 if the range becomes empty, and print the index of 201. */
/* The array must be sorted. Each step halves the range that can still hold the key. */
int binary_search(const int scores[], int n, int key) {
    int low = 0;
    int high = n - 1;
    while (low <= high) {
        int mid = low + (high - low) / 2;
        if (scores[mid] == key) {
            return mid;
        } else if (scores[mid] < key) {
            low = mid + 1;   /* key is in the right half */
        } else {
            high = mid - 1;   /* key is in the left half */
        }
    }
    return -1;
}

int main(void) {
    int scores[] = {16, 17, 33, 53, 66, 85, 154, 180, 188, 195};
    int n = sizeof(scores) / sizeof(scores[0]);
    int index = binary_search(scores, n, 201);
    printf("Index of 201: %d\n", index);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: binary_search() needs a sorted array. It keeps the range from low to high,
   compares the middle element mid with the key and throws away the half that cannot
   contain it, so it needs only about log2(n) steps. main() looks for 201 and prints its
   index, or -1 if it is not there. */
// END

/* Caption: Add up all the numbers in an array of double values. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write array_sum() that takes the array samples and its length count.
   2. Start sum at 0 and add every element in a for loop.
   3. Return sum.
   4. In main(), fill samples with 5 values and print the sum. */
/* Walk through the array and accumulate each value. */
double array_sum(const double samples[], int count) {
    double sum = 0;
    for (int k = 0; k < count; k++) {
        sum += samples[k];
    }
    return sum;
}

int main(void) {
    double samples[] = {23.2, 44.2, 42.0, 65.5, 70.5};
    int count = sizeof(samples) / sizeof(samples[0]);
    printf("The sum is %.2f\n", array_sum(samples, count));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: array_sum() receives the array samples and its length count. It starts sum
   at 0, adds every element to it in a for loop and returns the total. main() fills samples
   with 5 double values and prints their sum. */
// END

/* Caption: How do I sort an array in ascending order using bubble sort in C? */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write bubble_sort() for the double array scores.
   2. Compare each pair of neighbours.
   3. Swap them when they are in the wrong order for ascending order.
   4. Repeat the passes until the array is sorted.
   5. Print the sorted values. */
/* Repeatedly swap neighbours that are in the wrong order. */
void bubble_sort(double scores[], int count) {
    for (int i = 0; i < count - 1; i++) {
        for (int j = 0; j < count - 1 - i; j++) {
            if (scores[j] > scores[j + 1]) {
                double tmp = scores[j];
                scores[j] = scores[j + 1];
                scores[j + 1] = tmp;
            }
        }
    }
}

int main(void) {
    double scores[] = {92.3, 63.3, 53.6, 87.3, 20.6, 96.1, 26.8, 30.9, 2.0};
    int count = 9;
    bubble_sort(scores, count);
    for (int i = 0; i < count; i++) {
        printf("%.2f ", scores[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: bubble_sort() walks through scores again and again and swaps neighbours
   that are in the wrong order, so the largest values move to the end first. main() then
   prints the 9 values in ascending order. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to use dynamic memory to store the first 13 evens. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Use malloc to get room for 13 ints and check for NULL.
   2. Fill table with evens.
   3. Print the values.
   4. Call free(table) at the end. */
int main(void) {
    int n = 13;
    /* Ask the heap for room for n ints; malloc returns NULL on failure. */
    int *table = malloc(n * sizeof(int));
    if (table == NULL) {
        fprintf(stderr, "malloc failed\n");
        return 1;
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        table[i] = 2 * i;
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        printf("%d ", table[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    free(table);   /* give the memory back */
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: malloc() reserves room for 13 ints on the heap and returns NULL if it
   fails, which the program checks. The first loop fills table with evens, the second
   prints them, and free() gives the memory back at the end. */
// END

/* Caption: Count how many words are separated by spaces in a string. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <ctype.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write count_words() with words = 0 and an in_word flag.
   2. A space ends a word; a non-space after a space starts a new word and adds one to
      words.
   3. Return words and print it. */
/* A new word starts when a non-space follows a space (or the start). */
int count_words(const char *text) {
    int words = 0;
    int in_word = 0;
    for (int i = 0; text[i] != '\0'; i++) {
        if (isspace((unsigned char)text[i])) {
            in_word = 0;
        } else if (!in_word) {
            in_word = 1;
            words++;
        }
    }
    return words;
}

int main(void) {
    const char *sentence = "pointers store the address of another variable";
    printf("Words: %d\n", count_words(sentence));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: count_words() uses the flag in_word: a new word starts when a non-space
   character follows a space or the start of the text. main() prints the number of words in
   the sentence. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to test if "banana" reads the same backwards. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <string.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write is_palindrome() for buffer.
   2. Compare the first and last characters, moving inwards.
   3. Return false at the first mismatch, otherwise true.
   4. Check banana and print the result. */
/* Compare characters from the front and back, moving inwards. */
bool is_palindrome(const char *buffer) {
    int i = 0;
    int j = strlen(buffer) - 1;
    while (i < j) {
        if (buffer[i] != buffer[j]) {
            return false;
        }
        i++;
        j--;
    }
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    const char *buffer = "banana";
    printf("%s %s a palindrome\n", buffer, is_palindrome(buffer) ? "is" : "is not");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: is_palindrome() compares the first and last characters and moves inwards;
   any mismatch means the word is not a palindrome. main() checks the word banana and
   prints the result. */
// END

/* Caption: Implement a simple linked list with malloc and free. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define ListNode with a value and a next pointer.
   2. Write push_front() that mallocs a node and links it in front of head.
   3. Write print_list() that follows next until NULL.
   4. Write free_list() that frees every node.
   5. Push 5 values, print the list and free it. */
typedef struct ListNode {
    int value;
    struct ListNode *next;
} ListNode;

/* Allocate a new node and put it in front of the current head. */
ListNode *push_front(ListNode *head, int value) {
    ListNode *node = malloc(sizeof(ListNode));
    if (node == NULL) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Out of memory\n");
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }
    node->value = value;
    node->next = head;
    return node;
}

void print_list(const ListNode *head) {
    for (const ListNode *cur = head; cur != NULL; cur = cur->next) {
        printf("%d -> ", cur->value);
    }
    printf("NULL\n");
}

/* Free every node; save next before freeing the current one. */
void free_list(ListNode *head) {
    while (head != NULL) {
        ListNode *next = head->next;
        free(head);
        head = next;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    ListNode *head = NULL;
    head = push_front(head, 34);
    head = push_front(head, 26);
    head = push_front(head, 6);
    head = push_front(head, 95);
    head = push_front(head, 21);
    print_list(head);
    free_list(head);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: Each ListNode holds a value and a pointer to the next node. push_front()
   allocates a node with malloc, puts it in front of head and returns it; print_list()
   follows the next pointers until NULL; free_list() frees every node. main() pushes 5
   values, so they print in reverse order. */
// END

/* Caption: C program to compute 3 to the power of 12 without pow(). */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write power(base, exp) with result = 1.
   2. Multiply result by base exp times.
   3. Print 3 to the power 12. */
/* Multiply the base by itself exp times. */
long long power(int base, int exp) {
    long long result = 1;
    for (int i = 0; i < exp; i++) {
        result *= base;
    }
    return result;
}

int main(void) {
    printf("3^12 = %lld\n", power(3, 12));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: power() starts result at 1 and multiplies it by base exp times. It uses
   long long because powers grow quickly. main() prints 3 to the power 12. */
// END

/* Caption: Reverse an array by swapping from both ends. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write reverse_array() for samples.
   2. Set i to the first index and j to the last.
   3. Swap samples[i] and samples[j], then move both inwards.
   4. Stop when i meets j and print the array. */
/* Swap the outer pair, then move both ends toward the middle. */
void reverse_array(long samples[], int length) {
    int i = 0;
    int j = length - 1;
    while (i < j) {
        long tmp = samples[i];
        samples[i] = samples[j];
        samples[j] = tmp;
        i++;
        j--;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    long samples[] = {62L, 22L, 43L, 90L, 16L};
    int length = sizeof(samples) / sizeof(samples[0]);
    reverse_array(samples, length);
    for (int i = 0; i < length; i++) {
        printf("%ld ", samples[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: reverse_array() swaps the first and last elements, then moves i forward and
   j backward until they meet, so the array is reversed in place without a second array.
   main() prints the reversed values. */
// END

/* Caption: Program to compute the factorial of a number with a loop. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write factorial(x) with result = 1.
   2. Multiply result by every number from 2 to x.
   3. Return result.
   4. Print 12! as an unsigned long long. */
/* Multiply 1 * 2 * ... * n. */
unsigned long long factorial(int x) {
    unsigned long long result = 1;
    for (int i = 2; i <= x; i++) {
        result *= i;
    }
    return result;
}

int main(void) {
    int x = 12;
    printf("%d! = %llu\n", x, factorial(x));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: factorial() multiplies result by every number from 2 up to x. main() prints
   12! as an unsigned long long, because factorials grow very fast. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to test if 8 is a prime number. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write is_prime(n); numbers below 2 are not prime.
   2. Try every divisor d while d * d <= n.
   3. Return false if one divides n, otherwise true.
   4. Check 8 and print the result. */
/* A prime has no divisor between 2 and its square root. */
bool is_prime(int n) {
    if (n < 2) {
        return false;
    }
    for (int d = 2; d * d <= n; d++) {
        if (n % d == 0) {
            return false;
        }
    }
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    int number = 8;
    printf("%d %s prime\n", number, is_prime(number) ? "is" : "is not");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: is_prime() tries every divisor d from 2 while d * d <= n; if one divides n
   evenly, n is not prime. main() checks 8 and prints whether it is prime. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to search a sorted array by halving the search range each step. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Make sure the array is sorted.
   2. Set left to 0 and right to len - 1.
   3. While left <= right, compare the middle element middle with the key.
   4. Return the index if it matches; otherwise keep only the half that can hold the
      key.
   5. Return -1 if the range becomes empty, and print the index of 130. */
/* The array must be sorted. Each step halves the range that can still hold the key. */
int binary_search(const int scores[], int len, int key) {
    int left = 0;
    int right = len - 1;
    while (left <= right) {
        int middle = left + (right - left) / 2;
        if (scores[middle] == key) {
            return middle;
        } else if (scores[middle] < key) {
            left = middle + 1;   /* key is in the right half */
        } else {
            right = middle - 1;   /* key is in the left half */
        }
    }
    return -1;
}

int main(void) {
    int scores[] = {2, 79, 130, 144, 152, 162, 191};
    int len = 7;
    int index = binary_search(scores, len, 130);
    printf("Index of 130: %d\n", index);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: binary_search() needs a sorted array. It keeps the range from left to
   right, compares the middle element middle with the key and throws away the half that
   cannot contain it, so it needs only about log2(n) steps. main() looks for 130 and prints
   its index, or -1 if it is not there. */
// END

/* Caption: C program to save text to a file with fprintf and print it with fgets. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Open output.txt in write mode and check for NULL.
   2. Write 2 lines with fprintf and close the file.
   3. Open it again in read mode.
   4. Read and print each line with fgets, then close the file. */
int main(void) {

        perror("fopen");
        return 1;

    fprintf(file, "loops repeat a block of code\n");

    fclose(file);

    /* Reopen the file for reading and print it line by line. */

    if (file == NULL) {
        perror("fopen");
        return 1;
    }
    char line[128];
    while (fgets(line, sizeof(line), file) != NULL) {
        printf("%s", line);
    }
    fclose(file);
    return 0;

/* Explanation: fopen() in write mode creates output.txt, fprintf() writes 2 lines into it

/* Caption: Write a C program to turn the rows of a 3x3 matrix into columns. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define ROWS as 3 and COLS as 3.
   2. Copy m[r][c] into t[c][r] for every element.
   3. Print t row by row. */
#define ROWS 3
#define COLS 3

int main(void) {
    int m[ROWS][COLS] = {{1, 9, 7}, {0, 0, 2}, {6, 0, 5}};
    int t[COLS][ROWS];
    /* Element (r, c) moves to (c, r). */
    for (int r = 0; r < ROWS; r++) {
        for (int c = 0; c < COLS; c++) {
            t[c][r] = m[r][c];
        }
    }
    for (int r = 0; r < COLS; r++) {
        for (int c = 0; c < ROWS; c++) {
            printf("%3d", t[r][c]);
        }
        printf("\n");
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: The nested loops copy m[r][c] into t[c][r], so the 3x3 matrix becomes 3x3.
   A second pair of loops prints the result. */
// END

/* Caption: C program to return both the smallest and the largest value of an array through pointers. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write min_max() with the array, its length and the pointers min and max.
   2. Start both at the first element.
   3. Update *min and *max while looping over the rest.
   4. Declare smallest and largest, pass their addresses and print them. */
/* One pass finds both results; they are stored through the pointers. */
void min_max(const int items[], int length, int *min, int *max) {
    *min = items[0];
    *max = items[0];
    for (int i = 1; i < length; i++) {
        if (items[i] < *min) {
            *min = items[i];
        }
        if (items[i] > *max) {
            *max = items[i];
        }
    }
}

int main(void) {
    int items[] = {61, 38, 79, 73, 39, 94};
    int length = sizeof(items) / sizeof(items[0]);
    int smallest, largest;
    min_max(items, length, &smallest, &largest);
    printf("Min: %d, Max: %d\n", smallest, largest);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: A C function can return only one value, so min_max() returns void and
   writes its two results through the pointer parameters min and max. main() declares
   smallest and largest on one line and passes their addresses with &, then prints both
   results for the 6 values. */
// END

/* Caption: Calculate 11! using iteration. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write factorial(num) with result = 1.
   2. Multiply result by every number from 2 to num.
   3. Return result.
   4. Print 11! as an unsigned long long. */
/* Multiply 1 * 2 * ... * n. */
unsigned long long factorial(int num) {
    unsigned long long result = 1;
    for (int i = 2; i <= num; i++) {
        result *= i;
    }
    return result;
}

int main(void) {
    int num = 11;
    printf("%d! = %llu\n", num, factorial(num));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: factorial() multiplies result by every number from 2 up to num. main()
   prints 11! as an unsigned long long, because factorials grow very fast. */
// END

/* Caption: Count the words in a sentence. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <ctype.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write count_words() with words = 0 and an in_word flag.
   2. A space ends a word; a non-space after a space starts a new word and adds one to
      words.
   3. Return words and print it. */
/* A new word starts when a non-space follows a space (or the start). */
int count_words(const char *text) {
    int words = 0;
    int in_word = 0;
    for (int i = 0; text[i] != '\0'; i++) {
        if (isspace((unsigned char)text[i])) {
            in_word = 0;
        } else if (!in_word) {
            in_word = 1;
            words++;
        }
    }
    return words;
}

int main(void) {
    const char *sentence = "good comments explain why the code exists";
    printf("Words: %d\n", count_words(sentence));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: count_words() uses the flag in_word: a new word starts when a non-space
   character follows a space or the start of the text. main() prints the number of words in
   the sentence. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to test if 178 is a prime number. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write is_prime(n); numbers below 2 are not prime.
   2. Try every divisor d while d * d <= n.
   3. Return false if one divides n, otherwise true.
   4. Check 178 and print the result. */
/* A prime has no divisor between 2 and its square root. */
bool is_prime(int n) {
    if (n < 2) {
        return false;
    }
    for (int d = 2; d * d <= n; d++) {
        if (n % d == 0) {
            return false;
        }
    }
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    int number = 178;
    printf("%d %s prime\n", number, is_prime(number) ? "is" : "is not");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: is_prime() tries every divisor d from 2 while d * d <= n; if one divides n
   evenly, n is not prime. main() checks 178 and prints whether it is prime. */
// END

/* Caption: Compute the mean of a list of numbers. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write array_average() that takes scores and length.
   2. Add the values into the double total.
   3. Return total / length.
   4. Print the average with two decimals. */
/* The mean is the total divided by the count. */
double array_average(const double scores[], int length) {
    double total = 0.0;
    for (int k = 0; k < length; k++) {
        total += scores[k];
    }
    return total / length;
}

int main(void) {
    double scores[] = {13.8, 11.1, 73.0, 92.1};
    int length = 4;
    printf("The average is %.2f\n", array_average(scores, length));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: array_average() adds the 4 values of scores into the double total and
   divides by length, so the mean keeps its decimal part even when the values are whole
   numbers. main() prints it with two decimals. */
// END

/* Caption: C program to use insertion sort to put numbers in descending order. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write insertion_sort() for the double array prices.
   2. Take each element in turn as current.
   3. Shift the smaller values of the sorted part one place right.
   4. Put current into the gap.
   5. Print the sorted values. */
/* Insert each element into the already sorted part on its left. */
void insertion_sort(double prices[], int len) {
    for (int i = 1; i < len; i++) {
        double current = prices[i];
        int j = i - 1;
        while (j >= 0 && prices[j] < current) {
            prices[j + 1] = prices[j];   /* shift bigger values right */
            j--;
        }
        prices[j + 1] = current;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    double prices[] = {44.8, 19.3, 23.8, 35.2, 63.8, 30.1};
    const int len = 6;
    insertion_sort(prices, len);
    for (int i = 0; i < len; i++) {
        printf("%.2f ", prices[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: insertion_sort() takes each element in turn and shifts the smaller values
   of the sorted part one place right until the element fits. main() then prints the 6
   values in descending order. */
// END

/* Caption: Use Euclid's algorithm to compute the GCD. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write gcd() with Euclid's algorithm.
   2. Replace (a, b) by (b, a % b) until b is 0.
   3. Return a and print the GCD of 200 and 110. */
/* Euclid: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a % b) until b becomes zero. */
int gcd(int a, int b) {
    while (b != 0) {
        int r = a % b;
        a = b;
        b = r;
    }
    return a;
}

int main(void) {
    int x = 200, y = 110;
    printf("gcd(%d, %d) = %d\n", x, y, gcd(x, y));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: gcd() uses Euclid's algorithm: it keeps replacing (a, b) with (b, a % b)
   until b is 0. The last non-zero value is the greatest common divisor, and main() prints
   the GCD of 200 and 110. */
// END

/* Plan:

    for (int i = 0; i < len; i++) {
        printf("%d ", data[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: insertion_sort() takes each element in turn and shifts the larger values of
   the sorted part one place right until the element fits. main() then prints the 9 values
   in ascending order. */

/* Caption: Program to decide if 2022 is a leap year. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write is_leap(year).
   2. A year divisible by 4 is a leap year, unless it is divisible by 100.
   3. Years divisible by 400 are leap years again.
   4. Check 2022 and print the result. */
/* Leap years divide by 4, except centuries, which must divide by 400. */
int is_leap(int year) {
    return (year % 4 == 0 && year % 100 != 0) || year % 400 == 0;
}

int main(void) {
    int year = 2022;
    if (is_leap(year)) {
        printf("%d is a leap year\n", year);
    } else {
        printf("%d is not a leap year\n", year);
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: is_leap() returns true for years divisible by 4, except century years,
   which must also be divisible by 400. main() checks 2022 and prints whether it is a leap
   year. */
// END

/* Caption: C program to find the arithmetic mean of 8 int values. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write compute_mean() that takes marks and count.
   2. Add the values into the double sum.
   3. Return sum / count.
   4. Print the average with two decimals. */
/* Sum the values, then divide by how many there are. */
double compute_mean(const int marks[], int count) {
    double sum = 0.0;
    int j = 0;
    while (j < count) {
        sum += marks[j];
        j++;
    }
    return sum / count;
}

int main(void) {
    int marks[] = {9, 55, 10, 23, 47, 82, 7, 75};
    int count = 8;
    printf("The average is %.2f\n", compute_mean(marks, count));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: compute_mean() adds the 8 values of marks into the double sum and divides
   by count, so the mean keeps its decimal part even when the values are whole numbers.
   main() prints it with two decimals. */
// END

/* Caption: C program to use binary search to locate a value in a sorted list. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Make sure the array is sorted.
   2. Set left to 0 and right to len - 1.
   3. While left <= right, compare the middle element middle with the key.
   4. Return the index if it matches; otherwise keep only the half that can hold the
      key.
   5. Return -1 if the range becomes empty, and print the index of 201. */
/* The array must be sorted. Each step halves the range that can still hold the key. */
int binary_search(const int readings[], int len, int key) {
    int left = 0;
    int right = len - 1;
    while (left <= right) {
        int middle = left + (right - left) / 2;
        if (readings[middle] == key) {
            return middle;
        } else if (readings[middle] < key) {
            left = middle + 1;   /* key is in the right half */
        } else {
            right = middle - 1;   /* key is in the left half */
        }
    }
    return -1;
}

int main(void) {
    int readings[] = {2, 38, 104, 123, 124, 138};
    int len = 6;
    int index = binary_search(readings, len, 201);
    printf("Index of 201: %d\n", index);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: binary_search() needs a sorted array. It keeps the range from left to
   right, compares the middle element middle with the key and throws away the half that
   cannot contain it, so it needs only about log2(n) steps. main() looks for 201 and prints
   its index, or -1 if it is not there. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to write a function that swaps two int values through pointers. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write swap() that takes pointers to two int values.
   2. Save *x in tmp, copy *y into *x, then tmp into *y.
   3. In main(), print x and y, call swap(&x, &y) and print them again. */
/* Pass addresses so the function can change the caller's variables. */
void swap(int *x, int *y) {
    int tmp = *x;
    *x = *y;
    *y = tmp;
}

int main(void) {
    int x = 21, y = 51;
    printf("Before: %d %d\n", x, y);
    swap(&x, &y);
    printf("After:  %d %d\n", x, y);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: swap() receives the addresses of x and y, so writing through the pointers
   *x and *y changes the caller's variables. tmp holds one value during the exchange.
   main() declares both variables on one line and prints them before and after the swap. */
// END

/* Explanation: line_y() takes the slope m, the position x and the offset c and returns m *

/* Caption: Program to use a struct to hold names and marks, then print the average mark. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define struct Student with a name and a mark.
   2. Store 3 students in an array.
   3. Print each student and add the marks to total.
   4. Print total divided by the number of students. */
/* A struct groups a student's name and mark together. */
struct Student {
    char name[20];
    int mark;
};

int main(void) {
    struct Student students[] = {
        {"Eli", 78},
        {"Kofi", 76},
        {"Ivan", 50}
    };
    int count = sizeof(students) / sizeof(students[0]);
    double total = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < count; i++) {
        printf("%s: %d\n", students[i].name, students[i].mark);
        total += students[i].mark;
    }
    printf("Average mark: %.1f\n", total / count);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: struct Student groups a name and a mark. main() stores 3 students in an
   array of structs, prints each one, adds the marks to total and prints the average. */
// END

/* Plan:
   1. Open output.txt in write mode and check for NULL.
   2. Write 2 lines with fprintf and close the file.
   3. Open it again in read mode.
   4. Read and print each line with fgets, then close the file. */
int main(void) {
    FILE *file = fopen("output.txt", "w");
    if (file == NULL) {
        perror("fopen");
        return 1;
    }
    fprintf(file, "the compiler turns source code into machine code\n");
    fprintf(file, "pointers store the address of another variable\n");
    fclose(file);

    /* Reopen the file for reading and print it line by line. */
    file = fopen("output.txt", "r");
    if (file == NULL) {
        perror("fopen");
        return 1;
    }
    char line[128];
    while (fgets(line, sizeof(line), file) != NULL) {
        printf("%s", line);
    }
    fclose(file);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: fopen() in write mode creates output.txt, fprintf() writes 2 lines into it
   and fclose() saves it. The file is then opened again in read mode, and fgets() reads it
   back line by line into the buffer line, which is printed. Every fopen() result is
   checked for NULL. */
// END
