/* Caption: Write a program to divide two integers and get both the quotient and the remainder. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write divide(a, b, &quotient, &remainder) that returns a bool.
   2. Return false if b is 0.
   3. Store a / b and a % b through the pointers and return true.
   4. Divide 18 by 15 and print the results or the error. */
/* Returns false for division by zero; otherwise stores both results. */
bool divide(int a, int b, int *quotient, int *remainder) {
    if (b == 0) {
        return false;
    }
    *quotient = a / b;
    *remainder = a % b;
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    int a = 18, b = 15;
    int q, r;
    if (divide(a, b, &q, &r)) {
        printf("%d / %d = %d remainder %d\n", a, b, q, r);
    } else {
        printf("Cannot divide by zero\n");
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: divide() has four parameters: two inputs and two pointers for the results.
   Its bool return value reports success, while the quotient and remainder are written
   through the pointers. main() divides 18 by 15 and prints both results. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to convert a string to uppercase. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <ctype.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write to_upper() for word.
   2. Replace every character with toupper() until the null character.
   3. Print the sentence. */
/* toupper changes lowercase letters and leaves other characters alone. */
void to_upper(char *word) {
    for (int i = 0; word[i] != '\0'; i++) {
        word[i] = toupper((unsigned char)word[i]);
    }
}

int main(void) {
    char word[] = "pointers store the address of another variable";
    to_upper(word);
    printf("%s\n", word);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: to_upper() walks through word until the null character and replaces each
   character with toupper(), which only changes lowercase letters. main() prints the
   sentence in capitals. */
// END

/* Caption: Swap two variables using pointers. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write swap() that takes pointers to two int values.
   2. Save *a in tmp, copy *b into *a, then tmp into *b.
   3. In main(), print a and b, call swap(&a, &b) and print them again. */
/* Pass addresses so the function can change the caller's variables. */
void swap(int *a, int *b) {
    int tmp = *a;
    *a = *b;
    *b = tmp;
}

int main(void) {
    int a = 73, b = 64;
    printf("Before: %d %d\n", a, b);
    swap(&a, &b);
    printf("After:  %d %d\n", a, b);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: swap() receives the addresses of a and b, so writing through the pointers
   *a and *b changes the caller's variables. tmp holds one value during the exchange.
   main() declares both variables on one line and prints them before and after the swap. */
// END

/* Caption: How do I decide if 1991 is a leap year in C? */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write is_leap(year).
   2. A year divisible by 4 is a leap year, unless it is divisible by 100.
   3. Years divisible by 400 are leap years again.
   4. Check 1991 and print the result. */
/* Leap years divide by 4, except centuries, which must divide by 400. */
int is_leap(int year) {
    return (year % 4 == 0 && year % 100 != 0) || year % 400 == 0;
}

int main(void) {
    int year = 1991;
    if (is_leap(year)) {
        printf("%d is a leap year\n", year);
    } else {
        printf("%d is not a leap year\n", year);
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: is_leap() returns true for years divisible by 4, except century years,
   which must also be divisible by 400. main() checks 1991 and prints whether it is a leap
   year. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to reverse the elements of an array in place. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write reverse_array() for ages.
   2. Set start to the first index and end to the last.
   3. Swap ages[start] and ages[end], then move both inwards.
   4. Stop when start meets end and print the array. */
/* Swap the outer pair, then move both ends toward the middle. */
void reverse_array(double ages[], int n) {
    int start = 0;
    int end = n - 1;
    while (start < end) {
        double tmp = ages[start];
        ages[start] = ages[end];
        ages[end] = tmp;
        start++;
        end--;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    double ages[] = {19.7, 44.5, 66.4, 1.4, 16.1, 58.6, 18.0, 71.0, 32.3};
    int n = 9;
    reverse_array(ages, n);
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        printf("%.2f ", ages[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: reverse_array() swaps the first and last elements, then moves start forward
   and end backward until they meet, so the array is reversed in place without a second
   array. main() prints the reversed values. */
// END

/* Caption: Program to compute the distance between two points with a four-parameter function. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <math.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write distance(x1, y1, x2, y2).
   2. Compute dx and dy, then return sqrt(dx * dx + dy * dy).
   3. Print the distance between (7, 8) and (-9, 5). */
/* Pythagoras: the distance is sqrt(dx * dx + dy * dy). */
double distance(double x1, double y1, double x2, double y2) {
    double dx = x2 - x1, dy = y2 - y1;
    return sqrt(dx * dx + dy * dy);
}

int main(void) {
    printf("Distance: %.3f\n", distance(7, 8, -9, 5));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: distance() takes the coordinates of both points as four parameters. It
   declares dx and dy on one line and uses Pythagoras with sqrt() from math.h. main()
   prints the distance between (7, 8) and (-9, 5). */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to add two matrices element by element. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define ROWS as 4 and COLS as 4.
   2. Loop over every row r and column c.
   3. Store a[r][c] + b[r][c] in sum and print it. */
#define ROWS 4
#define COLS 4

int main(void) {
    int a[ROWS][COLS] = {{2, 1, 8, 5}, {3, 3, 0, 4}, {4, 9, 4, 2}, {8, 2, 8, 4}};
    int b[ROWS][COLS] = {{1, 3, 0, 9}, {3, 1, 6, 4}, {1, 7, 9, 0}, {4, 6, 0, 6}};
    int sum[ROWS][COLS];
    /* Each entry of the result is the sum of the matching entries. */
    for (int r = 0; r < ROWS; r++) {
        for (int c = 0; c < COLS; c++) {
            sum[r][c] = a[r][c] + b[r][c];
            printf("%3d", sum[r][c]);
        }
        printf("\n");
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: Both matrices are 4x4 two-dimensional arrays. Two nested loops visit every
   row r and column c, store a[r][c] + b[r][c] in sum and print each row. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a function with four parameters that returns the maximum. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write max2() that returns the larger of two values.
   2. Write max_of_four() as max2(max2(a, b), max2(c, d)).
   3. Print the largest of the four values. */
/* Return the larger of two values. */
int max2(int a, int b) {
    return a > b ? a : b;
}

/* Reuse max2 to compare four values. */
int max_of_four(int a, int b, int c, int d) {
    return max2(max2(a, b), max2(c, d));
}

int main(void) {
    int a = 63, b = 50, c = 43, d = 11;
    printf("Largest: %d\n", max_of_four(a, b, c, d));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: max_of_four() takes four parameters and reuses the helper max2(), which
   returns the larger of two values: it compares a with b, c with d, and then the two
   winners. main() prints the largest of 63, 50, 43 and 11. */
// END

/* Caption: Compute the product of two square matrices. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define N as 2.
   2. For every i and j, add a[i][k] * b[k][j] over k into product[i][j].
   3. Print product row by row. */
#define N 2

int main(void) {
    int a[N][N] = {{9, 7}, {0, 8}};
    int b[N][N] = {{4, 1}, {1, 4}};
    int product[N][N] = {0};
    /* product[i][j] is row i of a times column j of b. */
    for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) {
        for (int j = 0; j < N; j++) {
            for (int k = 0; k < N; k++) {
                product[i][j] += a[i][k] * b[k][j];
            }
        }
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) {
        for (int j = 0; j < N; j++) {
            printf("%4d", product[i][j]);
        }
        printf("\n");
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: For each entry product[i][j] the innermost loop adds a[i][k] * b[k][j] over
   k, which is row i of a times column j of b. main() multiplies two 2x2 matrices and
   prints the product. */
// END

/* Caption: Implement selection sort for an array of int values. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write selection_sort() for the int array data.
   2. For each position, find the smallest remaining element.
   3. Swap it into that position.
   4. Print the sorted values. */
/* Select the right element for each position and swap it into place. */
void selection_sort(int data[], int len) {
    for (int i = 0; i < len - 1; i++) {
        int chosen = i;
        for (int j = i + 1; j < len; j++) {
            if (data[chosen] > data[j]) {
                chosen = j;
            }
        }
        int tmp = data[i];
        data[i] = data[chosen];
        data[chosen] = tmp;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    int data[] = {38, 62, 22, 2, 97};
    int len = sizeof(data) / sizeof(data[0]);
    selection_sort(data, len);
    for (int i = 0; i < len; i++) {
        printf("%d ", data[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: selection_sort() finds the smallest remaining element for each position and
   swaps it into place. main() then prints the 5 values in ascending order. */
// END

/* Caption: Program to implement a circular queue with an array. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define a Queue with room for 32 items, a head and a count.
   2. Write enqueue() that stores at (head + count) % CAPACITY.
   3. Write dequeue() that takes the item at head and moves head on.
   4. Add 3 values, then remove and print them in order. */
#define CAPACITY 32

typedef struct {
    int items[CAPACITY];
    int head;
    int count;
} Queue;

bool enqueue(Queue *q, int value) {
    if (q->count == CAPACITY) {
        return false;
    }
    /* The tail wraps around to the start of the array. */
    q->items[(q->head + q->count) % CAPACITY] = value;
    q->count++;
    return true;
}

bool dequeue(Queue *q, int *value) {
    if (q->count == 0) {
        return false;
    }
    *value = q->items[q->head];
    q->head = (q->head + 1) % CAPACITY;
    q->count--;
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    Queue q = {.head = 0, .count = 0};
    enqueue(&q, 81);
    enqueue(&q, 1);
    enqueue(&q, 60);
    int value;
    /* Items come out in the order they went in (first in, first out). */
    while (dequeue(&q, &value)) {
        printf("%d ", value);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: The Queue stores up to 32 items in a ring buffer: head is the oldest item
   and % CAPACITY wraps positions back to the start of the array. enqueue() adds at the
   back and dequeue() removes from the front, so main() gets its 3 values back in the same
   order (first in, first out). */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to use a struct to return several results from one function. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define a Stats struct with min, max and average.
   2. Write array_stats() that fills one Stats in a loop.
   3. Return the struct.
   4. Print st.min, st.max and st.average. */
typedef struct {
    int min;
    int max;
    double average;
} Stats;

/* Pack several results into one struct and return it. */
Stats array_stats(const int v[], int n) {
    Stats s = {v[0], v[0], 0.0};
    double total = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        if (v[i] < s.min) {
            s.min = v[i];
        }
        if (v[i] > s.max) {
            s.max = v[i];
        }
        total += v[i];
    }
    s.average = total / n;
    return s;
}

int main(void) {
    int prices[] = {24, 53, 44, 10, 54, 69, 53};
    int n = sizeof(prices) / sizeof(prices[0]);
    Stats st = array_stats(prices, n);
    printf("Min %d, Max %d, Average %.2f\n", st.min, st.max, st.average);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: Stats groups three results. array_stats() fills one Stats while it loops
   over the 7 values and returns the whole struct, which is a clean way to return several
   results at once. main() reads them as st.min, st.max and st.average. */
// END

/* Caption: How do I show the right way to declare several pointers on one line in C? */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Declare x and y on one line.
   2. Declare the pointers px and py on one line, each with its own *.
   3. Add 15 to x through px and print the values. */
int main(void) {
    int x = 3, y = 26;
    /* Each pointer needs its own '*': in "int *p, q;" only p is a pointer. */
    int *px = &x, *py = &y;
    *px += 15;
    printf("x = %d, y = %d\n", x, y);
    printf("*px = %d, *py = %d\n", *px, *py);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: int *px = &x, *py = &y; declares two pointers in one statement; each name
   needs its own *. *px += 15 changes x through the pointer, so x becomes 18 while y stays
   26. */
// END

/* Caption: Use Euclid's algorithm to compute the GCD. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write gcd() with Euclid's algorithm.
   2. Replace (a, b) by (b, a % b) until b is 0.
   3. Return a and print the GCD of 297 and 131. */
/* Euclid: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a % b) until b becomes zero. */
int gcd(int a, int b) {
    while (b != 0) {
        int r = a % b;
        a = b;
        b = r;
    }
    return a;
}

int main(void) {
    int x = 297, y = 131;
    printf("gcd(%d, %d) = %d\n", x, y, gcd(x, y));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: gcd() uses Euclid's algorithm: it keeps replacing (a, b) with (b, a % b)
   until b is 0. The last non-zero value is the greatest common divisor, and main() prints
   the GCD of 297 and 131. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to print the factorial of an integer. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write factorial(num) with result = 1.
   2. Multiply result by every number from 2 to num.
   3. Return result.
   4. Print 12! as an unsigned long long. */
/* Multiply 1 * 2 * ... * n. */
unsigned long long factorial(int num) {
    unsigned long long result = 1;
    for (int i = 2; i <= num; i++) {
        result *= i;
    }
    return result;
}

int main(void) {
    int num = 12;
    printf("%d! = %llu\n", num, factorial(num));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: factorial() multiplies result by every number from 2 up to num. main()
   prints 12! as an unsigned long long, because factorials grow very fast. */
// END

/* Caption: Find a number in a sorted array with binary search. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Make sure the array is sorted.
   2. Set lo to 0 and hi to size - 1.
   3. While lo <= hi, compare the middle element mid with the key.
   4. Return the index if it matches; otherwise keep only the half that can hold the
      key.
   5. Return -1 if the range becomes empty, and print the index of 201. */
/* The array must be sorted. Each step halves the range that can still hold the key. */
int binary_search(const int scores[], int size, int key) {
    int lo = 0;
    int hi = size - 1;
    while (lo <= hi) {
        int mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;
        if (scores[mid] == key) {
            return mid;
        } else if (scores[mid] < key) {
            lo = mid + 1;   /* key is in the right half */
        } else {
            hi = mid - 1;   /* key is in the left half */
        }
    }
    return -1;
}

int main(void) {
    int scores[] = {7, 39, 57, 64, 105, 110, 119, 120, 148, 151, 168, 172};
    int size = sizeof(scores) / sizeof(scores[0]);
    int index = binary_search(scores, size, 201);
    printf("Index of 201: %d\n", index);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: binary_search() needs a sorted array. It keeps the range from lo to hi,
   compares the middle element mid with the key and throws away the half that cannot
   contain it, so it needs only about log2(n) steps. main() looks for 201 and prints its
   index, or -1 if it is not there. */
// END

int gcd(int a, int b) {

/* Caption: Find the minimum and maximum of an array with one function. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write min_max() with the array, its length and the pointers min and max.
   2. Start both at the first element.
   3. Update *min and *max while looping over the rest.
   4. Declare low and high, pass their addresses and print them. */
/* One pass finds both results; they are stored through the pointers. */
void min_max(const int items[], int len, int *min, int *max) {
    *min = items[0];
    *max = items[0];
    for (int i = 1; i < len; i++) {
        if (items[i] < *min) {
            *min = items[i];
        }
        if (items[i] > *max) {
            *max = items[i];
        }
    }
}

int main(void) {
    int items[] = {25, 34, 28, 97, 41};
    int len = 5;
    int low, high;
    min_max(items, len, &low, &high);
    printf("Min: %d, Max: %d\n", low, high);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: A C function can return only one value, so min_max() returns void and
   writes its two results through the pointer parameters min and max. main() declares low
   and high on one line and passes their addresses with &, then prints both results for the
   5 values. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to compute the factorial of a number with a loop. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write factorial(x) with result = 1.
   2. Multiply result by every number from 2 to x.
   3. Return result.
   4. Print 3! as an unsigned long long. */
/* Multiply 1 * 2 * ... * n. */
unsigned long long factorial(int x) {
    unsigned long long result = 1;
    for (int i = 2; i <= x; i++) {
        result *= i;
    }
    return result;
}

int main(void) {
    int x = 3;
    printf("%d! = %llu\n", x, factorial(x));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: factorial() multiplies result by every number from 2 up to x. main() prints
   3! as an unsigned long long, because factorials grow very fast. */
// END

/* Caption: Check whether a year is a leap year. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write is_leap(year).
   2. A year divisible by 4 is a leap year, unless it is divisible by 100.
   3. Years divisible by 400 are leap years again.
   4. Check 1994 and print the result. */
/* Leap years divide by 4, except centuries, which must divide by 400. */
int is_leap(int year) {
    return (year % 4 == 0 && year % 100 != 0) || year % 400 == 0;
}

int main(void) {
    int year = 1994;
    if (is_leap(year)) {
        printf("%d is a leap year\n", year);
    } else {
        printf("%d is not a leap year\n", year);
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: is_leap() returns true for years divisible by 4, except century years,
   which must also be divisible by 400. main() checks 1994 and prints whether it is a leap
   year. */
// END

/* Caption: C program to use dynamic memory to store the first 8 squares. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Use malloc to get room for 8 ints and check for NULL.
   2. Fill list with squares.
   3. Print the values.
   4. Call free(list) at the end. */
int main(void) {
    int n = 8;
    /* Ask the heap for room for n ints; malloc returns NULL on failure. */
    int *list = malloc(n * sizeof(int));
    if (list == NULL) {
        fprintf(stderr, "malloc failed\n");
        return 1;
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        list[i] = i * i;
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        printf("%d ", list[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    free(list);   /* give the memory back */
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: malloc() reserves room for 8 ints on the heap and returns NULL if it fails,
   which the program checks. The first loop fills list with squares, the second prints
   them, and free() gives the memory back at the end. */
// END

   2. Write area() and perimeter().

    int width;
    int height;

    return r.width * r.height;

int perimeter(Rectangle r) {
    return 2 * (r.width + r.height);
}

int main(void) {
    Rectangle box = {21, 2};
    printf("Area: %d, Perimeter: %d\n", area(box), perimeter(box));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: Rectangle stores a width and a height. area() returns width * height and
   perimeter() returns 2 * (width + height). main() makes a 21 by 2 rectangle and prints
   both results. */
// END

/* Caption: Use selection sort to put numbers in descending order. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write selection_sort() for the int array numbers.
   2. For each position, find the largest remaining element.
   3. Swap it into that position.
   4. Print the sorted values. */
/* Select the right element for each position and swap it into place. */
void selection_sort(int numbers[], int length) {
    for (int i = 0; i < length - 1; i++) {
        int chosen = i;
        for (int j = i + 1; j < length; j++) {
            if (numbers[chosen] < numbers[j]) {
                chosen = j;
            }
        }
        int tmp = numbers[i];
        numbers[i] = numbers[chosen];
        numbers[chosen] = tmp;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    int numbers[] = {24, 26, 68, 32, 45, 6, 52, 65, 98};
    int length = sizeof(numbers) / sizeof(numbers[0]);
    selection_sort(numbers, length);
    for (int i = 0; i < length; i++) {
        printf("%d ", numbers[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: selection_sort() finds the largest remaining element for each position and
   swaps it into place. main() then prints the 9 values in descending order. */
// END

/* Caption: Write your own version of strcpy. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write copy_string(dest, src).
   2. Copy src into dest one character at a time.
   3. Stop after copying the null character.
   4. Copy planet into buffer and print it. */
/* Copy each character, including the final '\0'. */
void copy_string(char *dest, const char *src) {
    int i = 0;
    while ((dest[i] = src[i]) != '\0') {
        i++;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    char source[] = "planet";
    char buffer[32];
    copy_string(buffer, source);
    printf("Copied: %s\n", buffer);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: copy_string() copies src into dest one character at a time, including the
   final null character, which is what strcpy does. The array buffer must be big enough to
   hold the copy. main() copies the word planet and prints it. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to count how many words are separated by spaces in a string. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <ctype.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write count_words() with words = 0 and an in_word flag.
   2. A space ends a word; a non-space after a space starts a new word and adds one to
      words.
   3. Return words and print it. */
/* A new word starts when a non-space follows a space (or the start). */
int count_words(const char *text) {
    int words = 0;
    int in_word = 0;
    for (int i = 0; text[i] != '\0'; i++) {
        if (isspace((unsigned char)text[i])) {
            in_word = 0;
        } else if (!in_word) {
            in_word = 1;
            words++;
        }
    }
    return words;
}

int main(void) {
    const char *sentence = "the quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog";
    printf("Words: %d\n", count_words(sentence));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: count_words() uses the flag in_word: a new word starts when a non-space
   character follows a space or the start of the text. main() prints the number of words in
   the sentence. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to compute the sum of the digits of an integer. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Start result at 0.
   2. Add n % 10 to result, then divide n by 10.
   3. Repeat until n is 0.
   4. Apply it to 777990 and print the result. */
/* Take the last digit with % 10, then drop it with / 10. */
int sum_digits(int n) {
    int result = 0;
    while (n > 0) {
        result += n % 10;
        n /= 10;
    }
    return result;
}

int main(void) {
    int number = 777990;
    printf("sum of digits of %d: %d\n", number, sum_digits(number));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: sum_digits() adds the last digit (n % 10) to result and then removes it (n
   / 10) until no digits are left. main() applies it to 777990. */
// END

/* Caption: How do I use binary search to locate a value in a sorted list in C? */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Make sure the array is sorted.
   2. Set left to 0 and right to size - 1.
   3. While left <= right, compare the middle element middle with the key.
   4. Return the index if it matches; otherwise keep only the half that can hold the
      key.
   5. Return -1 if the range becomes empty, and print the index of 67. */
/* The array must be sorted. Each step halves the range that can still hold the key. */
int binary_search(const int readings[], int size, int key) {
    int left = 0;
    int right = size - 1;
    while (left <= right) {
        int middle = left + (right - left) / 2;
        if (readings[middle] == key) {
            return middle;
        } else if (readings[middle] < key) {
            left = middle + 1;   /* key is in the right half */
        } else {
            right = middle - 1;   /* key is in the left half */
        }
    }
    return -1;
}

int main(void) {
    int readings[] = {6, 36, 42, 67, 79, 93, 117, 121, 144, 160, 179};
    int size = 11;
    int index = binary_search(readings, size, 67);
    printf("Index of 67: %d\n", index);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: binary_search() needs a sorted array. It keeps the range from left to
   right, compares the middle element middle with the key and throws away the half that
   cannot contain it, so it needs only about log2(n) steps. main() looks for 67 and prints
   its index, or -1 if it is not there. */
// END

/* Caption: Compute the sum and the average of an array in one function. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write sum_and_average() with the pointers sum and average.
   2. Add the values into *sum.
   3. Store *sum / n in *average.
   4. Declare total and mean, pass their addresses and print them. */
void sum_and_average(const double v[], int n, double *sum, double *average) {
    *sum = 0.0;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        *sum += v[i];
    }
    *average = *sum / n;
}

int main(void) {
    double scores[] = {63.8, 19.4, 34.6, 42.0, 93.5, 86.0, 5.3, 20.6};
    int n = sizeof(scores) / sizeof(scores[0]);
    double total, mean;
    sum_and_average(scores, n, &total, &mean);
    printf("Sum: %.2f, Average: %.2f\n", total, mean);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: sum_and_average() takes the array, its length and two pointers. It adds up
   the 8 values through *sum and then stores *sum / n in *average. main() declares total
   and mean on one line and passes their addresses. */
// END

/* Caption: Check whether a number is prime. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write is_prime(n); numbers below 2 are not prime.
   2. Try every divisor d while d * d <= n.
   3. Return false if one divides n, otherwise true.
   4. Check 304 and print the result. */
/* A prime has no divisor between 2 and its square root. */
bool is_prime(int n) {
    if (n < 2) {
        return false;
    }
    for (int d = 2; d * d <= n; d++) {
        if (n % d == 0) {
            return false;
        }
    }
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    int number = 304;
    printf("%d %s prime\n", number, is_prime(number) ? "is" : "is not");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: is_prime() tries every divisor d from 2 while d * d <= n; if one divides n
   evenly, n is not prime. main() checks 304 and prints whether it is prime. */
// END

/* Caption: Program to return the smallest element of an array of double values. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write find_min() that takes values and count.
   2. Store values[0] in current.
   3. Loop over the other elements and keep the smallest value in current.
   4. Return current and print it. */
/* Start with the first element and keep the smallest value seen so far. */
double find_min(const double values[], int count) {
    double current = values[0];
    for (int i = 1; i < count; i++) {
        if (values[i] < current) {
            current = values[i];
        }
    }
    return current;
}

int main(void) {
    double values[] = {56.6, 16.5, 37.7, 10.6, 38.1, 9.4, 91.6, 71.5, 14.2};
    int count = 9;
    printf("The smallest value is %.2f\n", find_min(values, count));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: find_min() takes the first element as the smallest value so far and stores
   it in current. The loop compares every other element with current using < and keeps the
   smallest one. main() prints the smallest of the 9 values. */
// END

/* Caption: Compute 7 to the power of 8 without pow(). */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write power(base, exp) with result = 1.
   2. Multiply result by base exp times.
   3. Print 7 to the power 8. */
/* Multiply the base by itself exp times. */
long long power(int base, int exp) {
    long long result = 1;
    for (int i = 0; i < exp; i++) {
        result *= base;
    }
    return result;
}

int main(void) {
    printf("7^8 = %lld\n", power(7, 8));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: power() starts result at 1 and multiplies it by base exp times. It uses
   long long because powers grow quickly. main() prints 7 to the power 8. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to find the greatest common divisor of two numbers. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write gcd() with Euclid's algorithm.
   2. Replace (a, b) by (b, a % b) until b is 0.
   3. Return a and print the GCD of 18 and 9. */
/* Euclid: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a % b) until b becomes zero. */
int gcd(int a, int b) {
    while (b != 0) {
        int r = a % b;
        a = b;
        b = r;
    }
    return a;
}

int main(void) {
    int x = 18, y = 9;
    printf("gcd(%d, %d) = %d\n", x, y, gcd(x, y));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: gcd() uses Euclid's algorithm: it keeps replacing (a, b) with (b, a % b)
   until b is 0. The last non-zero value is the greatest common divisor, and main() prints
   the GCD of 18 and 9. */
// END

/* Caption: Calculate the average of the values in an array. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write compute_mean() that takes numbers and n.
   2. Add the values into the double result.
   3. Return result / n.
   4. Print the average with two decimals. */
/* Sum the values, then divide by how many there are. */
double compute_mean(const int numbers[], int n) {
    double result = 0.0;
    int idx = 0;
    while (idx < n) {
        result += numbers[idx];
        idx++;
    }
    return result / n;
}

int main(void) {
    int numbers[] = {41, 41, 46, 1};
    int n = 4;
    printf("Average: %.2f\n", compute_mean(numbers, n));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: compute_mean() adds the 4 values of numbers into the double result and
   divides by n, so the mean keeps its decimal part even when the values are whole numbers.
   main() prints it with two decimals. */
// END

/* Caption: C program to convert 847 to binary. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write print_binary(n, bits).
   2. Go through the bits from the highest to the lowest.
   3. Print 1 when (n >> b) & 1 is set, otherwise 0.
   4. Print 847 in binary. */
/* Check each bit from the highest to the lowest. */
void print_binary(unsigned int n, int bits) {
    for (int b = bits - 1; b >= 0; b--) {
        putchar((n >> b) & 1 ? '1' : '0');
    }
    putchar('\n');
}

int main(void) {
    unsigned int number = 847;
    printf("%u in binary: ", number);
    print_binary(number, 8);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: print_binary() checks one bit at a time, from the highest to the lowest: (n
   >> b) & 1 is 1 when bit b is set, so it prints the character 1 or 0. main() prints 847
   in binary. */
// END

/* Caption: Search an array for a value and print its position. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write linear_search() with the array, its length and key.
   2. Compare each element with key.
   3. Return the index of the first match, or -1.
   4. In main(), search for 120 and print the result. */
/* Return the index of key, or -1 when it is not in the array. */
int linear_search(const int numbers[], int n, int key) {
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        if (numbers[i] == key) {
            return i;
        }
    }
    return -1;
}

int main(void) {
    int numbers[] = {92, 80, 83, 73, 33, 56, 13, 60, 57, 96};
    int n = 10;
    int key = 120;
    int pos = linear_search(numbers, n, key);
    if (pos >= 0) {
        printf("Found %d at index %d\n", key, pos);
    } else {
        printf("%d is not in the array\n", key);
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: linear_search() checks the elements of numbers one by one and returns the
   index of the first one equal to key, or -1 when it reaches the end without a match.
   main() searches for 120 and prints where it is, or that it is missing. */
// END

/* Caption: How do I compute the sum of the digits of an integer in C? */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Start result at 0.
   2. Add n % 10 to result, then divide n by 10.
   3. Repeat until n is 0.
   4. Apply it to 300021 and print the result. */
/* Take the last digit with % 10, then drop it with / 10. */
int sum_digits(int n) {
    int result = 0;
    while (n > 0) {
        result += n % 10;
        n /= 10;
    }
    return result;
}

int main(void) {
    int number = 300021;
    printf("sum of digits of %d: %d\n", number, sum_digits(number));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: sum_digits() adds the last digit (n % 10) to result and then removes it (n
   / 10) until no digits are left. main() applies it to 300021. */
// END

/* Caption: Count how many even numbers are in an array. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write count_even() that takes readings and count.
   2. For each element, test readings[i] % 2 == 0.
   3. Add one to found for every even number.
   4. Return found and print it. */
/* A number is even when the remainder after dividing by 2 is zero. */
int count_even(const int readings[], int count) {
    int found = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < count; i++) {
        if (readings[i] % 2 == 0) {
            found++;
        }
    }
    return found;
}

int main(void) {
    int readings[] = {89, 52, 93, 80, 25, 53, 33, 8, 62, 96, 50, 7};
    const int count = 12;
    printf("Count of even values = %d\n", count_even(readings, count));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: count_even() tests each element of readings with the % operator: a
   remainder of 0 after dividing by 2 means the number is even, so found goes up by one.
   main() prints how many of the 12 values are even. */
// END

/* Caption: Compute the factorial of a number recursively. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write factorial(num) that calls itself.
   2. Return 1 when num is 1 or less.
   3. Otherwise return num * factorial(num - 1).
   4. Print 13! as an unsigned long long. */
/* n! = n * (n - 1)!, and 0! = 1 stops the recursion. */
unsigned long long factorial(int num) {
    if (num <= 1) {
        return 1;
    }
    return num * factorial(num - 1);
}

int main(void) {
    int num = 13;
    printf("%d! = %llu\n", num, factorial(num));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: factorial() calls itself: n! is n * (n - 1)!, and the recursion stops when
   num is 1 or less. main() prints 13! as an unsigned long long, because factorials grow
   very fast. */
// END

/* Caption: Program to calculate the average of the values in an array. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write mean() that takes numbers and len.
   2. Add the values into the double acc.
   3. Return acc / len.
   4. Print the average with two decimals. */
/* Sum the values, then divide by how many there are. */
double mean(const double numbers[], int len) {
    double acc = 0.0;
    for (int k = 0; k < len; k++) {
        acc += numbers[k];
    }
    return acc / len;
}

int main(void) {
    double numbers[] = {36.3, 76.4, 40.6, 93.5, 16.2, 5.2, 57.4};
    int len = sizeof(numbers) / sizeof(numbers[0]);
    printf("The average is %.2f\n", mean(numbers, len));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: mean() adds the 7 values of numbers into the double acc and divides by len,
   so the mean keeps its decimal part even when the values are whole numbers. main() prints
   it with two decimals. */
// END

/* Plan:
   1. Define a Rectangle struct with width and height.
   2. Write area() and perimeter().
   3. Make a 27 by 27 rectangle and print both results. */
typedef struct {
    int width;
    int height;
} Rectangle;

int area(Rectangle r) {
    return r.width * r.height;
}

int perimeter(Rectangle r) {
    return 2 * (r.width + r.height);
}

int main(void) {
    Rectangle box = {27, 27};
    printf("Area: %d, Perimeter: %d\n", area(box), perimeter(box));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: Rectangle stores a width and a height. area() returns width * height and
   perimeter() returns 2 * (width + height). main() makes a 27 by 27 rectangle and prints
   both results. */
// END

/* Caption: Convert 434 to binary. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write print_binary(n, bits).
   2. Go through the bits from the highest to the lowest.
   3. Print 1 when (n >> b) & 1 is set, otherwise 0.
   4. Print 434 in binary. */
/* Check each bit from the highest to the lowest. */
void print_binary(unsigned int n, int bits) {
    for (int b = bits - 1; b >= 0; b--) {
        putchar((n >> b) & 1 ? '1' : '0');
    }
    putchar('\n');
}

int main(void) {
    unsigned int number = 434;
    printf("%u in binary: ", number);
    print_binary(number, 16);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: print_binary() checks one bit at a time, from the highest to the lowest: (n
   >> b) & 1 is 1 when bit b is set, so it prints the character 1 or 0. main() prints 434
   in binary. */
// END

/* Caption: How do I find the arithmetic mean of 4 int values in C? */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write average() that takes ages and count.
   2. Add the values into the double acc.
   3. Return acc / count.
   4. Print the average with two decimals. */
/* The mean is the total divided by the count. */
double average(const int ages[], int count) {
    double acc = 0.0;
    int i = 0;
    while (i < count) {
        acc += ages[i];
        i++;
    }
    return acc / count;
}

int main(void) {
    int ages[] = {80, 14, 1, 38};
    int count = sizeof(ages) / sizeof(ages[0]);
    printf("The average is %.2f\n", average(ages, count));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: average() adds the 4 values of ages into the double acc and divides by
   count, so the mean keeps its decimal part even when the values are whole numbers. main()
   prints it with two decimals. */
// END

/* Caption: Find the greatest common divisor of two numbers. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write gcd() with Euclid's algorithm.
   2. Replace (a, b) by (b, a % b) until b is 0.
   3. Return a and print the GCD of 237 and 195. */
/* Euclid: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a % b) until b becomes zero. */
int gcd(int a, int b) {
    while (b != 0) {
        int r = a % b;
        a = b;
        b = r;
    }
    return a;
}

int main(void) {
    int x = 237, y = 195;
    printf("gcd(%d, %d) = %d\n", x, y, gcd(x, y));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: gcd() uses Euclid's algorithm: it keeps replacing (a, b) with (b, a % b)
   until b is 0. The last non-zero value is the greatest common divisor, and main() prints
   the GCD of 237 and 195. */
// END

/* Caption: Use dynamic memory to store the first 7 cubes. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Use malloc to get room for 7 ints and check for NULL.
   2. Fill arr with cubes.
   3. Print the values.
   4. Call free(arr) at the end. */
int main(void) {
    int n = 7;
    /* Ask the heap for room for n ints; malloc returns NULL on failure. */
    int *arr = malloc(n * sizeof(int));
    if (arr == NULL) {
        fprintf(stderr, "malloc failed\n");
        return 1;
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        arr[i] = i * i * i;
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        printf("%d ", arr[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    free(arr);   /* give the memory back */
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: malloc() reserves room for 7 ints on the heap and returns NULL if it fails,
   which the program checks. The first loop fills arr with cubes, the second prints them,
   and free() gives the memory back at the end. */
// END

/* Caption: Check whether a number is prime. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write is_prime(n); numbers below 2 are not prime.
   2. Try every divisor d while d * d <= n.
   3. Return false if one divides n, otherwise true.
   4. Check 227 and print the result. */
/* A prime has no divisor between 2 and its square root. */
bool is_prime(int n) {
    if (n < 2) {
        return false;
    }
    for (int d = 2; d * d <= n; d++) {
        if (n % d == 0) {
            return false;
        }
    }
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    int number = 227;
    printf("%d %s prime\n", number, is_prime(number) ? "is" : "is not");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: is_prime() tries every divisor d from 2 while d * d <= n; if one divides n
   evenly, n is not prime. main() checks 227 and prints whether it is prime. */
// END

/* Caption: Copy one string into another by hand. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write copy_string(dest, src).
   2. Copy src into dest one character at a time.
   3. Stop after copying the null character.
   4. Copy racecar into buffer and print it. */
/* Copy each character, including the final '\0'. */
void copy_string(char *dest, const char *src) {
    int i = 0;
    while ((dest[i] = src[i]) != '\0') {
        i++;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    char source[] = "racecar";
    char buffer[100];
    copy_string(buffer, source);
    printf("Copied: %s\n", buffer);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: copy_string() copies src into dest one character at a time, including the
   final null character, which is what strcpy does. The array buffer must be big enough to
   hold the copy. main() copies the word racecar and prints it. */
// END

/* Caption: Check whether a year is a leap year. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write is_leap(year).
   2. A year divisible by 4 is a leap year, unless it is divisible by 100.
   3. Years divisible by 400 are leap years again.
   4. Check 1972 and print the result. */
/* Leap years divide by 4, except centuries, which must divide by 400. */
int is_leap(int year) {
    return (year % 4 == 0 && year % 100 != 0) || year % 400 == 0;
}

int main(void) {
    int year = 1972;
    if (is_leap(year)) {
        printf("%d is a leap year\n", year);
    } else {
        printf("%d is not a leap year\n", year);
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: is_leap() returns true for years divisible by 4, except century years,
   which must also be divisible by 400. main() checks 1972 and prints whether it is a leap
   year. */
// END

/* Caption: How do I save text to a file with fprintf and print it with fgets in C? */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Open notes.txt in write mode and check for NULL.
   2. Write 2 lines with fprintf and close the file.
   3. Open it again in read mode.
   4. Read and print each line with fgets, then close the file. */
int main(void) {
    FILE *file = fopen("notes.txt", "w");
    if (file == NULL) {
        perror("fopen");
        return 1;
    }
    fprintf(file, "arrays in c start at index zero\n");
    fprintf(file, "loops repeat a block of code\n");
    fclose(file);

    /* Reopen the file for reading and print it line by line. */
    file = fopen("notes.txt", "r");
    if (file == NULL) {
        perror("fopen");
        return 1;
    }
    char line[128];
    while (fgets(line, sizeof(line), file) != NULL) {
        printf("%s", line);
    }
    fclose(file);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: fopen() in write mode creates notes.txt, fprintf() writes 2 lines into it
   and fclose() saves it. The file is then opened again in read mode, and fgets() reads it
   back line by line into the buffer line, which is printed. Every fopen() result is
   checked for NULL. */
// END

/* Caption: Program to find the greatest common divisor of two numbers. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write gcd() with Euclid's algorithm.
   2. Replace (a, b) by (b, a % b) until b is 0.
   3. Return a and print the GCD of 244 and 195. */
/* Euclid: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a % b) until b becomes zero. */
int gcd(int a, int b) {
    while (b != 0) {
        int r = a % b;
        a = b;
        b = r;
    }
    return a;
}

int main(void) {
    int x = 244, y = 195;
    printf("gcd(%d, %d) = %d\n", x, y, gcd(x, y));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: gcd() uses Euclid's algorithm: it keeps replacing (a, b) with (b, a % b)
   until b is 0. The last non-zero value is the greatest common divisor, and main() prints
   the GCD of 244 and 195. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to count how many vowels a string contains. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <string.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write count_vowels() with count = 0.
   2. For each character, check whether strchr finds it in aeiouAEIOU.
   3. Return count and print it. */
/* strchr finds the letter in the list of vowels, or returns NULL. */
int count_vowels(const char *text) {
    int count = 0;
    for (int i = 0; text[i] != '\0'; i++) {
        if (strchr("aeiouAEIOU", text[i]) != NULL) {
            count++;
        }
    }
    return count;
}

int main(void) {
    const char *sentence = "good comments explain why the code exists";
    printf("Vowels: %d\n", count_vowels(sentence));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: count_vowels() uses strchr to test whether each character is one of
   aeiouAEIOU and counts the matches. main() prints the number of vowels in the sentence. */
// END

/* Caption: C program to use insertion sort to put numbers in descending order. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write insertion_sort() for the int array values.
   2. Take each element in turn as current.
   3. Shift the smaller values of the sorted part one place right.
   4. Put current into the gap.
   5. Print the sorted values. */
/* Insert each element into the already sorted part on its left. */
void insertion_sort(int values[], int size) {
    for (int i = 1; i < size; i++) {
        int current = values[i];
        int j = i - 1;
        while (j >= 0 && values[j] < current) {
            values[j + 1] = values[j];   /* shift bigger values right */
            j--;
        }
        values[j + 1] = current;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    int values[] = {59, 45, 14, 64, 70, 1, 77, 6, 63};
    int size = sizeof(values) / sizeof(values[0]);
    insertion_sort(values, size);
    for (int i = 0; i < size; i++) {
        printf("%d ", values[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: insertion_sort() takes each element in turn and shifts the smaller values
   of the sorted part one place right until the element fits. main() then prints the 9
   values in descending order. */
// END

#include <stdio.h>
#include <ctype.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write count_words() with words = 0 and an in_word flag.
   2. A space ends a word; a non-space after a space starts a new word and adds one to
      words.
   3. Return words and print it. */
/* A new word starts when a non-space follows a space (or the start). */
int count_words(const char *text) {
    int words = 0;
    int in_word = 0;
    for (int i = 0; text[i] != '\0'; i++) {
        if (isspace((unsigned char)text[i])) {
            in_word = 0;
        } else if (!in_word) {
            in_word = 1;
            words++;
        }
    }
    return words;
}

int main(void) {
    const char *sentence = "loops repeat a block of code";
    printf("Words: %d\n", count_words(sentence));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: count_words() uses the flag in_word: a new word starts when a non-space
   character follows a space or the start of the text. main() prints the number of words in
   the sentence. */
// END

/* Caption: Print all prime numbers up to 27. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write is_prime(n); numbers below 2 are not prime.
   2. Try every divisor d while d * d <= n.
   3. Return false if one divides n, otherwise true.
   4. Print every prime from 2 to 27. */
/* A prime has no divisor between 2 and its square root. */
bool is_prime(int n) {
    if (n < 2) {
        return false;
    }
    for (int d = 2; d * d <= n; d++) {
        if (n % d == 0) {
            return false;
        }
    }
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    for (int n = 2; n <= 27; n++) {
        if (is_prime(n)) {
            printf("%d ", n);
        }
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: is_prime() tries every divisor d from 2 while d * d <= n; if one divides n
   evenly, n is not prime. main() tests every number from 2 to 27 and prints the primes. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a function with four parameters that returns the maximum. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write max2() that returns the larger of two values.
   2. Write max_of_four() as max2(max2(a, b), max2(c, d)).
   3. Print the largest of the four values. */
/* Return the larger of two values. */
int max2(int a, int b) {
    return a > b ? a : b;
}

/* Reuse max2 to compare four values. */
int max_of_four(int a, int b, int c, int d) {
    return max2(max2(a, b), max2(c, d));
}

int main(void) {
    int a = 64, b = 60, c = 48, d = 60;
    printf("Largest: %d\n", max_of_four(a, b, c, d));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: max_of_four() takes four parameters and reuses the helper max2(), which
   returns the larger of two values: it compares a with b, c with d, and then the two
   winners. main() prints the largest of 64, 60, 48 and 60. */
// END

/* Caption: Build a linked list, print it, and free it. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define Node with a value and a next pointer.
   2. Write push_front() that mallocs a node and links it in front of head.
   3. Write print_list() that follows next until NULL.
   4. Write free_list() that frees every node.
   5. Push 6 values, print the list and free it. */
typedef struct Node {
    int value;
    struct Node *next;
} Node;

/* Allocate a new node and put it in front of the current head. */
Node *push_front(Node *head, int value) {
    Node *node = malloc(sizeof(Node));
    if (node == NULL) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Out of memory\n");
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }
    node->value = value;
    node->next = head;
    return node;
}

void print_list(const Node *head) {
    for (const Node *cur = head; cur != NULL; cur = cur->next) {
        printf("%d -> ", cur->value);
    }
    printf("NULL\n");
}

/* Free every node; save next before freeing the current one. */
void free_list(Node *head) {
    while (head != NULL) {
        Node *next = head->next;
        free(head);
        head = next;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    Node *head = NULL;
    head = push_front(head, 57);
    head = push_front(head, 90);
    head = push_front(head, 8);
    head = push_front(head, 15);
    head = push_front(head, 24);
    head = push_front(head, 26);
    print_list(head);
    free_list(head);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: Each Node holds a value and a pointer to the next node. push_front()
   allocates a node with malloc, puts it in front of head and returns it; print_list()
   follows the next pointers until NULL; free_list() frees every node. main() pushes 6
   values, so they print in reverse order. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to implement a stack with an array (push and pop). */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define a Stack with room for 32 items and a top counter.
   2. Write push() and pop(), returning false when the stack is full or empty.
   3. Push 4 values.
   4. Pop and print until the stack is empty. */
#define CAPACITY 32

typedef struct {
    int items[CAPACITY];
    int top;   /* number of items on the stack */
} Stack;

bool push(Stack *s, int value) {
    if (s->top == CAPACITY) {
        return false;   /* stack is full */
    }
    s->items[s->top++] = value;
    return true;
}

bool pop(Stack *s, int *value) {
    if (s->top == 0) {
        return false;   /* stack is empty */
    }
    *value = s->items[--s->top];
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    Stack s = {.top = 0};
    push(&s, 99);
    push(&s, 45);
    push(&s, 92);
    push(&s, 26);
    int value;
    /* Items come back out in reverse order (last in, first out). */
    while (pop(&s, &value)) {
        printf("%d ", value);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: The Stack keeps up to 32 items in an array, and top counts how many are
   stored. push() adds at the top and pop() removes from the top; both return false when
   they cannot. main() pushes 4 values and pops them all, so they come out in reverse order
   (last in, first out). */
// END

/* Caption: Allocate an array with malloc and fill it with multiples. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Use malloc to get room for 7 ints and check for NULL.
   2. Fill table with multiples.
   3. Print the values.
   4. Call free(table) at the end. */
int main(void) {
    int n = 7;
    /* Ask the heap for room for n ints; malloc returns NULL on failure. */
    int *table = malloc(n * sizeof(int));
    if (table == NULL) {
        fprintf(stderr, "malloc failed\n");
        return 1;
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        table[i] = 5 * i;
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        printf("%d ", table[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    free(table);   /* give the memory back */
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: malloc() reserves room for 7 ints on the heap and returns NULL if it fails,
   which the program checks. The first loop fills table with multiples, the second prints
   them, and free() gives the memory back at the end. */
// END

/* Caption: Reverse an array by swapping from both ends. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write reverse_array() for samples.
   2. Set left to the first index and right to the last.
   3. Swap samples[left] and samples[right], then move both inwards.
   4. Stop when left meets right and print the array. */
/* Swap the outer pair, then move both ends toward the middle. */
void reverse_array(double samples[], int length) {
    int left = 0;
    int right = length - 1;
    while (left < right) {
        double tmp = samples[left];
        samples[left] = samples[right];
        samples[right] = tmp;
        left++;
        right--;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    double samples[] = {43.7, 21.4, 28.1, 76.9};
    int length = sizeof(samples) / sizeof(samples[0]);
    reverse_array(samples, length);
    for (int i = 0; i < length; i++) {
        printf("%.2f ", samples[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: reverse_array() swaps the first and last elements, then moves left forward
   and right backward until they meet, so the array is reversed in place without a second
   array. main() prints the reversed values. */
// END

/* Caption: Add two matrices element by element. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define ROWS as 2 and COLS as 2.
   2. Loop over every row r and column c.
   3. Store a[r][c] + b[r][c] in sum and print it. */
#define ROWS 2
#define COLS 2

int main(void) {
    int a[ROWS][COLS] = {{1, 8}, {1, 6}};
    int b[ROWS][COLS] = {{5, 7}, {7, 2}};
    int sum[ROWS][COLS];
    /* Each entry of the result is the sum of the matching entries. */
    for (int r = 0; r < ROWS; r++) {
        for (int c = 0; c < COLS; c++) {
            sum[r][c] = a[r][c] + b[r][c];
            printf("%3d", sum[r][c]);
        }
        printf("\n");
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: Both matrices are 2x2 two-dimensional arrays. Two nested loops visit every
   row r and column c, store a[r][c] + b[r][c] in sum and print each row. */
// END

/* Caption: Compute the distance between two points using a struct. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <math.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define a Point struct with x and y.
   2. Write distance() using sqrt(dx * dx + dy * dy).
   3. Print the distance between p and q. */
typedef struct {
    double x;
    double y;
} Point;

/* Pythagoras: sqrt(dx * dx + dy * dy). */
double distance(Point a, Point b) {
    double dx = b.x - a.x;
    double dy = b.y - a.y;
    return sqrt(dx * dx + dy * dy);
}

int main(void) {
    Point p = {-4, 0};
    Point q = {7, 5};
    printf("Distance: %.3f\n", distance(p, q));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: Point is a typedef struct with x and y. distance() uses Pythagoras, sqrt(dx
   * dx + dy * dy), to measure the gap between the two points, and main() prints it. */
// END

/* Caption: Program to write a function that swaps two double values through pointers. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write swap() that takes pointers to two double values.
   2. Save *first in tmp, copy *second into *first, then tmp into *second.
   3. In main(), print first and second, call swap(&first, &second) and print them
      again. */
/* Pass addresses so the function can change the caller's variables. */
void swap(double *first, double *second) {
    double tmp = *first;
    *first = *second;
    *second = tmp;
}

int main(void) {
    double first = 71.3, second = 9.6;
    printf("Before: %.2f %.2f\n", first, second);
    swap(&first, &second);
    printf("After:  %.2f %.2f\n", first, second);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: swap() receives the addresses of first and second, so writing through the
   pointers *first and *second changes the caller's variables. tmp holds one value during
   the exchange. main() declares both variables on one line and prints them before and
   after the swap. */
// END

/* Caption: Print the binary representation of an integer. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write print_binary(n, bits).
   2. Go through the bits from the highest to the lowest.
   3. Print 1 when (n >> b) & 1 is set, otherwise 0.
   4. Print 132 in binary. */
/* Check each bit from the highest to the lowest. */
void print_binary(unsigned int n, int bits) {
    for (int b = bits - 1; b >= 0; b--) {
        putchar((n >> b) & 1 ? '1' : '0');
    }
    putchar('\n');
}

int main(void) {
    unsigned int number = 132;
    printf("%u in binary: ", number);
    print_binary(number, 16);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: print_binary() checks one bit at a time, from the highest to the lowest: (n
   >> b) & 1 is 1 when bit b is set, so it prints the character 1 or 0. main() prints 132
   in binary. */
// END

/* Caption: Compute the mean of a list of numbers. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write array_average() that takes numbers and length.
   2. Add the values into the double total.
   3. Return total / length.
   4. Print the average with two decimals. */
/* Sum the values, then divide by how many there are. */
double array_average(const int numbers[], int length) {
    double total = 0.0;
    for (int i = 0; i < length; i++) {
        total += numbers[i];
    }
    return total / length;
}

int main(void) {
    int numbers[] = {92, 10, 15, 58, 43, 53, 57};
    const int length = 7;
    printf("Average: %.2f\n", array_average(numbers, length));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: array_average() adds the 7 values of numbers into the double total and
   divides by length, so the mean keeps its decimal part even when the values are whole
   numbers. main() prints it with two decimals. */
// END

/* Swap the outer pair, then move both ends toward the middle. */

        printf("%ld ", marks[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;

   array. main() prints the reversed values. */

/* Caption: How do I show the right way to declare several pointers on one line in C? */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Declare x and y on one line.
   2. Declare the pointers px and py on one line, each with its own *.
   3. Add 15 to x through px and print the values. */
int main(void) {
    int x = 49, y = 47;
    /* Each pointer needs its own '*': in "int *p, q;" only p is a pointer. */
    int *px = &x, *py = &y;
    *px += 15;
    printf("x = %d, y = %d\n", x, y);
    printf("*px = %d, *py = %d\n", *px, *py);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: int *px = &x, *py = &y; declares two pointers in one statement; each name
   needs its own *. *px += 15 changes x through the pointer, so x becomes 64 while y stays
   47. */
// END

/* Caption: Convert temperatures from Celsius to Fahrenheit. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write to_fahrenheit() with F = C * 9 / 5 + 32.
   2. Loop c from -20 to 60 in steps of 20.
   3. Print each Celsius value with its Fahrenheit value. */
/* F = C * 9 / 5 + 32 */
double to_fahrenheit(double celsius) {
    return celsius * 9.0 / 5.0 + 32.0;
}

int main(void) {
    printf("Celsius  Fahrenheit\n");
    for (int c = -20; c <= 60; c += 20) {
        printf("%7d  %10.1f\n", c, to_fahrenheit(c));
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: to_fahrenheit() applies F = C * 9 / 5 + 32. main() prints a table from -20
   to 60 degrees Celsius in steps of 20. */
// END

/* Caption: Use Euclid's algorithm to compute the GCD. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write gcd() with Euclid's algorithm.
   2. Replace (a, b) by (b, a % b) until b is 0.
   3. Return a and print the GCD of 293 and 291. */
/* Euclid: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a % b) until b becomes zero. */
int gcd(int a, int b) {
    while (b != 0) {
        int r = a % b;
        a = b;
        b = r;
    }
    return a;
}

int main(void) {
    int x = 293, y = 291;
    printf("gcd(%d, %d) = %d\n", x, y, gcd(x, y));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: gcd() uses Euclid's algorithm: it keeps replacing (a, b) with (b, a % b)
   until b is 0. The last non-zero value is the greatest common divisor, and main() prints
   the GCD of 293 and 291. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to check every element of an array to find a target value. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write linear_search() with the array, its length and key.
   2. Compare each element with key.
   3. Return the index of the first match, or -1.
   4. In main(), search for 21 and print the result. */
/* Return the index of key, or -1 when it is not in the array. */
int linear_search(const int readings[], int n, int key) {
    for (int idx = 0; idx < n; idx++) {
        if (readings[idx] == key) {
            return idx;
        }
    }
    return -1;
}

int main(void) {
    int readings[] = {36, 40, 70, 21, 93, 35, 6, 72, 65};
    int n = sizeof(readings) / sizeof(readings[0]);
    int key = 21;
    int pos = linear_search(readings, n, key);
    if (pos >= 0) {
        printf("Found %d at index %d\n", key, pos);
    } else {
        printf("%d is not in the array\n", key);
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: linear_search() checks the elements of readings one by one and returns the
   index of the first one equal to key, or -1 when it reaches the end without a match.
   main() searches for 21 and prints where it is, or that it is missing. */
// END

/* Caption: Turn the rows of a 4x3 matrix into columns. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define ROWS as 4 and COLS as 3.
   2. Copy m[r][c] into t[c][r] for every element.
   3. Print t row by row. */
#define ROWS 4
#define COLS 3

int main(void) {
    int m[ROWS][COLS] = {{4, 6, 0}, {5, 9, 8}, {4, 8, 8}, {9, 1, 4}};
    int t[COLS][ROWS];
    /* Element (r, c) moves to (c, r). */
    for (int r = 0; r < ROWS; r++) {
        for (int c = 0; c < COLS; c++) {
            t[c][r] = m[r][c];
        }
    }
    for (int r = 0; r < COLS; r++) {
        for (int c = 0; c < ROWS; c++) {
            printf("%3d", t[r][c]);
        }
        printf("\n");
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: The nested loops copy m[r][c] into t[c][r], so the 4x3 matrix becomes 3x4.
   A second pair of loops prints the result. */
// END

/* Caption: C program to implement a simple linked list with malloc and free. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define ListNode with a value and a next pointer.
   2. Write push_front() that mallocs a node and links it in front of head.
   3. Write print_list() that follows next until NULL.
   4. Write free_list() that frees every node.
   5. Push 4 values, print the list and free it. */
typedef struct ListNode {
    int value;
    struct ListNode *next;
} ListNode;

/* Allocate a new node and put it in front of the current head. */
ListNode *push_front(ListNode *head, int value) {
    ListNode *node = malloc(sizeof(ListNode));
    if (node == NULL) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Out of memory\n");
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }
    node->value = value;
    node->next = head;
    return node;
}

void print_list(const ListNode *head) {
    for (const ListNode *cur = head; cur != NULL; cur = cur->next) {
        printf("%d -> ", cur->value);
    }
    printf("NULL\n");
}

/* Free every node; save next before freeing the current one. */
void free_list(ListNode *head) {
    while (head != NULL) {
        ListNode *next = head->next;
        free(head);
        head = next;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    ListNode *head = NULL;
    head = push_front(head, 14);
    head = push_front(head, 99);
    head = push_front(head, 92);
    head = push_front(head, 31);
    print_list(head);
    free_list(head);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: Each ListNode holds a value and a pointer to the next node. push_front()
   allocates a node with malloc, puts it in front of head and returns it; print_list()
   follows the next pointers until NULL; free_list() frees every node. main() pushes 4
   values, so they print in reverse order. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to find the arithmetic mean of 9 int values. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write array_average() that takes nums and n.
   2. Add the values into the double result.
   3. Return result / n.
   4. Print the average with two decimals. */
/* The mean is the total divided by the count. */
double array_average(const int nums[], int n) {
    double result = 0.0;
    int i = 0;
    while (i < n) {
        result += nums[i];
        i++;
    }
    return result / n;
}

int main(void) {
    int nums[] = {79, 66, 47, 13, 93, 74, 75, 95, 54};
    int n = 9;
    printf("The average is %.2f\n", array_average(nums, n));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: array_average() adds the 9 values of nums into the double result and
   divides by n, so the mean keeps its decimal part even when the values are whole numbers.
   main() prints it with two decimals. */
// END

/* Caption: Compute the sum and the average of an array in one function. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write sum_and_average() with the pointers sum and average.
   2. Add the values into *sum.
   3. Store *sum / n in *average.
   4. Declare total and mean, pass their addresses and print them. */
void sum_and_average(const double v[], int n, double *sum, double *average) {
    *sum = 0.0;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        *sum += v[i];
    }
    *average = *sum / n;
}

int main(void) {
    double samples[] = {26.4, 86.2, 52.6};
    int n = sizeof(samples) / sizeof(samples[0]);
    double total, mean;
    sum_and_average(samples, n, &total, &mean);
    printf("Sum: %.2f, Average: %.2f\n", total, mean);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: sum_and_average() takes the array, its length and two pointers. It adds up
   the 3 values through *sum and then stores *sum / n in *average. main() declares total
   and mean on one line and passes their addresses. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to use dynamic memory to store the first 10 evens. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Use malloc to get room for 10 ints and check for NULL.
   2. Fill list with evens.
   3. Print the values.
   4. Call free(list) at the end. */
int main(void) {
    int n = 10;
    /* Ask the heap for room for n ints; malloc returns NULL on failure. */
    int *list = malloc(n * sizeof(int));
    if (list == NULL) {
        fprintf(stderr, "malloc failed\n");
        return 1;
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        list[i] = 2 * i;
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        printf("%d ", list[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    free(list);   /* give the memory back */
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: malloc() reserves room for 10 ints on the heap and returns NULL if it
   fails, which the program checks. The first loop fills list with evens, the second prints
   them, and free() gives the memory back at the end. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to write lines to a text file and read them back. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Open notes.txt in write mode and check for NULL.
   2. Write 4 lines with fprintf and close the file.
   3. Open it again in read mode.
   4. Read and print each line with fgets, then close the file. */
int main(void) {
    FILE *file = fopen("notes.txt", "w");
    if (file == NULL) {
        perror("fopen");
        return 1;
    }
    fprintf(file, "c gives you direct control over memory\n");
    fprintf(file, "pointers store the address of another variable\n");
    fprintf(file, "the quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog\n");
    fprintf(file, "arrays in c start at index zero\n");
    fclose(file);

    /* Reopen the file for reading and print it line by line. */
    file = fopen("notes.txt", "r");
    if (file == NULL) {
        perror("fopen");
        return 1;
    }
    char line[128];
    while (fgets(line, sizeof(line), file) != NULL) {
        printf("%s", line);
    }
    fclose(file);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: fopen() in write mode creates notes.txt, fprintf() writes 4 lines into it
   and fclose() saves it. The file is then opened again in read mode, and fgets() reads it
   back line by line into the buffer line, which is printed. Every fopen() result is
   checked for NULL. */
// END

/* Caption: Program to raise a number to an integer power with a loop. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write power(base, exp) with result = 1.
   2. Multiply result by base exp times.
   3. Print 8 to the power 10. */
/* Multiply the base by itself exp times. */
long long power(int base, int exp) {
    long long result = 1;
    for (int i = 0; i < exp; i++) {
        result *= base;
    }
    return result;
}

int main(void) {
    printf("8^10 = %lld\n", power(8, 10));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: power() starts result at 1 and multiplies it by base exp times. It uses
   long long because powers grow quickly. main() prints 8 to the power 10. */
// END

/* Caption: C program to write a function that returns a Fraction struct. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define a Fraction struct with num and den.
   2. Write multiply() that returns num = a.num * b.num and den = a.den * b.den.
   3. Print 6/7 times 1/9. */
typedef struct {
    int num;
    int den;
} Fraction;

/* Multiply the numerators and the denominators. */
Fraction multiply(Fraction a, Fraction b) {
    Fraction r = {a.num * b.num, a.den * b.den};
    return r;
}

int main(void) {
    Fraction x = {6, 7}, y = {1, 9};
    Fraction p = multiply(x, y);
    printf("%d/%d * %d/%d = %d/%d\n", x.num, x.den, y.num, y.den, p.num, p.den);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: Fraction stores a numerator and a denominator. multiply() takes two
   Fractions and returns a new one with num = a.num * b.num and den = a.den * b.den. main()
   multiplies 6/7 by 1/9 (without reducing the result). */
// END

/* Caption: Sort an array in ascending order using insertion sort. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write insertion_sort() for the int array scores.
   2. Take each element in turn as current.
   3. Shift the larger values of the sorted part one place right.
   4. Put current into the gap.
   5. Print the sorted values. */
/* Insert each element into the already sorted part on its left. */
void insertion_sort(int scores[], int length) {
    for (int i = 1; i < length; i++) {
        int current = scores[i];
        int j = i - 1;
        while (j >= 0 && scores[j] > current) {
            scores[j + 1] = scores[j];   /* shift bigger values right */
            j--;
        }
        scores[j + 1] = current;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    int scores[] = {40, 97, 60, 37, 72, 62};
    const int length = 6;
    insertion_sort(scores, length);
    for (int i = 0; i < length; i++) {
        printf("%d ", scores[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: insertion_sort() takes each element in turn and shifts the larger values of
   the sorted part one place right until the element fits. main() then prints the 6 values
   in ascending order. */
// END

/* Caption: Reverse the digits of a number. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Start result at 0.
   2. Multiply result by 10, add n % 10, then divide n by 10.
   3. Repeat until n is 0.
   4. Apply it to 461662 and print the result. */
/* Take the last digit with % 10, then drop it with / 10. */
int reverse_digits(int n) {
    int result = 0;
    while (n > 0) {
        result = result * 10 + n % 10;
        n /= 10;
    }
    return result;
}

int main(void) {
    int number = 461662;
    printf("reverse of digits of %d: %d\n", number, reverse_digits(number));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: reverse_digits() shifts result one place left (result * 10) and adds the
   last digit of n, which reverses the order. main() applies it to 461662. */
// END

/* Caption: Compute the distance between two points with a four-parameter function. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <math.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write distance(x1, y1, x2, y2).
   2. Compute dx and dy, then return sqrt(dx * dx + dy * dy).
   3. Print the distance between (-8, -7) and (8, 6). */
/* Pythagoras: the distance is sqrt(dx * dx + dy * dy). */
double distance(double x1, double y1, double x2, double y2) {
    double dx = x2 - x1, dy = y2 - y1;
    return sqrt(dx * dx + dy * dy);
}

int main(void) {
    printf("Distance: %.3f\n", distance(-8, -7, 8, 6));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: distance() takes the coordinates of both points as four parameters. It
   declares dx and dy on one line and uses Pythagoras with sqrt() from math.h. main()
   prints the distance between (-8, -7) and (8, 6). */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to write a function that returns the midpoint of two points as a struct. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define a Point struct with x and y.
   2. Write midpoint() that returns a Point with the averages of x and y.
   3. Print mid.x and mid.y. */
typedef struct {
    double x;
    double y;
} Point;

/* A function can return a whole struct. */
Point midpoint(Point a, Point b) {
    Point m = {(a.x + b.x) / 2, (a.y + b.y) / 2};
    return m;
}

int main(void) {
    Point p = {18, 16}, q = {2, 9};
    Point mid = midpoint(p, q);
    printf("Midpoint: (%.1f, %.1f)\n", mid.x, mid.y);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: midpoint() takes two Point structs and returns a new Point whose x and y
   are the averages of theirs. main() declares p and q on one line, (18, 16) and (2, 9),
   and prints the midpoint using mid.x and mid.y. */
// END

/* Caption: Check whether a word is a palindrome. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <string.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write is_palindrome() for word.
   2. Compare the first and last characters, moving inwards.
   3. Return false at the first mismatch, otherwise true.
   4. Check rotor and print the result. */
/* Compare characters from the front and back, moving inwards. */
bool is_palindrome(const char *word) {
    int i = 0;
    int j = strlen(word) - 1;
    while (i < j) {
        if (word[i] != word[j]) {
            return false;
        }
        i++;
        j--;
    }
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    const char *word = "rotor";
    printf("%s %s a palindrome\n", word, is_palindrome(word) ? "is" : "is not");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: is_palindrome() compares the first and last characters and moves inwards;
   any mismatch means the word is not a palindrome. main() checks the word rotor and prints
   the result. */
// END

   5 int values and prints their sum. */

/* Caption: Program to reverse the elements of an array in place. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write reverse_array() for items.
   2. Set i to the first index and j to the last.
   3. Swap items[i] and items[j], then move both inwards.
   4. Stop when i meets j and print the array. */
/* Swap the outer pair, then move both ends toward the middle. */
void reverse_array(double items[], int len) {
    int i = 0;
    int j = len - 1;
    while (i < j) {
        double tmp = items[i];
        items[i] = items[j];
        items[j] = tmp;
        i++;
        j--;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    double items[] = {58.0, 24.5, 50.2, 81.8, 11.7, 68.2};
    const int len = 6;
    reverse_array(items, len);
    for (int i = 0; i < len; i++) {
        printf("%.2f ", items[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: reverse_array() swaps the first and last elements, then moves i forward and
   j backward until they meet, so the array is reversed in place without a second array.
   main() prints the reversed values. */
// END
