#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Set n = 85 and sum = 0.
   2. Add every number from 1 to n to sum.
   3. Print sum. */
int main(void) {
    int n = 85;
    int sum = 0;
    for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++) {
        sum += i;
    }
    printf("Sum of 1 to %d = %d\n", n, sum);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: The for loop adds every number from 1 to 85 to sum and prints the result. */
// END

/* Caption: How do I reverse the elements of an array in place in C? */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write reverse_array() for samples.
   2. Set start to the first index and end to the last.
   3. Swap samples[start] and samples[end], then move both inwards.
   4. Stop when start meets end and print the array. */
/* Swap the outer pair, then move both ends toward the middle. */
void reverse_array(int samples[], int size) {
    int start = 0;
    int end = size - 1;
    while (start < end) {
        int tmp = samples[start];
        samples[start] = samples[end];
        samples[end] = tmp;
        start++;
        end--;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    int samples[] = {88, 33, 32, 77, 83, 9, 1, 77, 81};
    int size = sizeof(samples) / sizeof(samples[0]);
    reverse_array(samples, size);
    for (int i = 0; i < size; i++) {
        printf("%d ", samples[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: reverse_array() swaps the first and last elements, then moves start forward
   and end backward until they meet, so the array is reversed in place without a second
   array. main() prints the reversed values. */
// END

/* Caption: Build a linked list, print it, and free it. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define ListNode with a value and a next pointer.
   2. Write push_front() that mallocs a node and links it in front of head.
   3. Write print_list() that follows next until NULL.
   4. Write free_list() that frees every node.
   5. Push 4 values, print the list and free it. */
typedef struct ListNode {
    int value;
    struct ListNode *next;
} ListNode;

/* Allocate a new node and put it in front of the current head. */
ListNode *push_front(ListNode *head, int value) {
    ListNode *node = malloc(sizeof(ListNode));
    if (node == NULL) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Out of memory\n");
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }
    node->value = value;
    node->next = head;
    return node;
}

void print_list(const ListNode *head) {
    for (const ListNode *cur = head; cur != NULL; cur = cur->next) {
        printf("%d -> ", cur->value);
    }
    printf("NULL\n");
}

/* Free every node; save next before freeing the current one. */
void free_list(ListNode *head) {
    while (head != NULL) {
        ListNode *next = head->next;
        free(head);
        head = next;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    ListNode *head = NULL;
    head = push_front(head, 27);
    head = push_front(head, 7);
    head = push_front(head, 67);
    head = push_front(head, 99);
    print_list(head);
    free_list(head);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: Each ListNode holds a value and a pointer to the next node. push_front()
   allocates a node with malloc, puts it in front of head and returns it; print_list()
   follows the next pointers until NULL; free_list() frees every node. main() pushes 4
   values, so they print in reverse order. */
// END

   3. Print both for a radius of 0.6. */

/* Caption: Calculate the average of the values in an array. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write compute_mean() that takes items and size.
   2. Add the values into the double acc.
   3. Return acc / size.
   4. Print the average with two decimals. */
/* Sum the values, then divide by how many there are. */
double compute_mean(const int items[], int size) {
    double acc = 0.0;
    int i = 0;
    while (i < size) {
        acc += items[i];

    }

   main() prints it with two decimals. */

/* Caption: Use Euclid's algorithm to compute the GCD. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write gcd() with Euclid's algorithm.
   2. Replace (a, b) by (b, a % b) until b is 0.
   3. Return a and print the GCD of 281 and 90. */
/* Euclid: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a % b) until b becomes zero. */
int gcd(int a, int b) {
    while (b != 0) {
        int r = a % b;
        a = b;
        b = r;
    }
    return a;
}

int main(void) {
    int x = 281, y = 90;
    printf("gcd(%d, %d) = %d\n", x, y, gcd(x, y));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: gcd() uses Euclid's algorithm: it keeps replacing (a, b) with (b, a % b)
   until b is 0. The last non-zero value is the greatest common divisor, and main() prints
   the GCD of 281 and 90. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to compute 4 to the power of 3 without pow(). */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write power(base, exp) with result = 1.
   2. Multiply result by base exp times.
   3. Print 4 to the power 3. */
/* Multiply the base by itself exp times. */
long long power(int base, int exp) {
    long long result = 1;
    for (int i = 0; i < exp; i++) {
        result *= base;
    }
    return result;
}

int main(void) {
    printf("4^3 = %lld\n", power(4, 3));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: power() starts result at 1 and multiplies it by base exp times. It uses
   long long because powers grow quickly. main() prints 4 to the power 3. */
// END

/* Caption: How do I sort an array in ascending order using insertion sort in C? */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write insertion_sort() for the double array samples.
   2. Take each element in turn as current.
   3. Shift the larger values of the sorted part one place right.
   4. Put current into the gap.
   5. Print the sorted values. */
/* Insert each element into the already sorted part on its left. */
void insertion_sort(double samples[], int length) {
    for (int i = 1; i < length; i++) {
        double current = samples[i];
        int j = i - 1;
        while (j >= 0 && samples[j] > current) {
            samples[j + 1] = samples[j];   /* shift bigger values right */
            j--;
        }
        samples[j + 1] = current;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    double samples[] = {9.1, 90.6, 94.7, 98.6, 84.8, 39.1};
    int length = 6;
    insertion_sort(samples, length);
    for (int i = 0; i < length; i++) {
        printf("%.2f ", samples[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: insertion_sort() takes each element in turn and shifts the larger values of
   the sorted part one place right until the element fits. main() then prints the 6 values
   in ascending order. */
// END

   of 1 after dividing by 2 means the number is odd, so matches goes up by one. main()
   prints how many of the 12 values are odd. */

/* Plan:

   2. Return false if b is 0.
   3. Store a / b and a % b through the pointers and return true.
   4. Divide 396 by 0 and print the results or the error. */
/* Returns false for division by zero; otherwise stores both results. */
bool divide(int a, int b, int *quotient, int *remainder) {
    if (b == 0) {
        return false;

    *quotient = a / b;
    *remainder = a % b;

    int q, r;
    if (divide(a, b, &q, &r)) {
        printf("%d / %d = %d remainder %d\n", a, b, q, r);
    } else {
        printf("Cannot divide by zero\n");
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: divide() has four parameters: two inputs and two pointers for the results.
   Its bool return value reports success, while the quotient and remainder are written
   through the pointers. main() divides 396 by 0, which fails because the divisor is zero. */
// END

   array. main() prints the reversed values. */

/* Caption: Write a C program to create a singly linked list by inserting at the head. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define Node with a value and a next pointer.
   2. Write push_front() that mallocs a node and links it in front of head.
   3. Write print_list() that follows next until NULL.
   4. Write free_list() that frees every node.
   5. Push 3 values, print the list and free it. */
typedef struct Node {
    int value;
    struct Node *next;
} Node;

/* Allocate a new node and put it in front of the current head. */
Node *push_front(Node *head, int value) {
    Node *node = malloc(sizeof(Node));
    if (node == NULL) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Out of memory\n");
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }
    node->value = value;
    node->next = head;
    return node;
}

void print_list(const Node *head) {
    for (const Node *cur = head; cur != NULL; cur = cur->next) {
        printf("%d -> ", cur->value);
    }
    printf("NULL\n");
}

/* Free every node; save next before freeing the current one. */
void free_list(Node *head) {
    while (head != NULL) {
        Node *next = head->next;
        free(head);
        head = next;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    Node *head = NULL;
    head = push_front(head, 33);
    head = push_front(head, 62);
    head = push_front(head, 48);
    print_list(head);
    free_list(head);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: Each Node holds a value and a pointer to the next node. push_front()
   allocates a node with malloc, puts it in front of head and returns it; print_list()
   follows the next pointers until NULL; free_list() frees every node. main() pushes 3
   values, so they print in reverse order. */
// END

/* Caption: Write lines to a text file and read them back. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Open log.txt in write mode and check for NULL.
   2. Write 3 lines with fprintf and close the file.
   3. Open it again in read mode.
   4. Read and print each line with fgets, then close the file. */
int main(void) {
    FILE *file = fopen("log.txt", "w");
    if (file == NULL) {
        perror("fopen");
        return 1;
    }
    fprintf(file, "the compiler turns source code into machine code\n");
    fprintf(file, "learning c teaches how computers work\n");
    fprintf(file, "always free the memory you allocate\n");
    fclose(file);

    /* Reopen the file for reading and print it line by line. */
    file = fopen("log.txt", "r");
    if (file == NULL) {
        perror("fopen");
        return 1;
    }
    char line[128];
    while (fgets(line, sizeof(line), file) != NULL) {
        printf("%s", line);
    }
    fclose(file);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: fopen() in write mode creates log.txt, fprintf() writes 3 lines into it and
   fclose() saves it. The file is then opened again in read mode, and fgets() reads it back
   line by line into the buffer line, which is printed. Every fopen() result is checked for
   NULL. */
// END

/* Caption: Use bubble sort to put numbers in descending order. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write bubble_sort() for the int array items.
   2. Compare each pair of neighbours.
   3. Swap them when they are in the wrong order for descending order.
   4. Repeat the passes until the array is sorted.
   5. Print the sorted values. */
/* Repeatedly swap neighbours that are in the wrong order. */
void bubble_sort(int items[], int count) {
    for (int i = 0; i < count - 1; i++) {
        for (int j = 0; j < count - 1 - i; j++) {
            if (items[j] < items[j + 1]) {
                int tmp = items[j];
                items[j] = items[j + 1];
                items[j + 1] = tmp;
            }
        }
    }
}

int main(void) {
    int items[] = {7, 92, 13, 24, 27, 51, 88, 14};
    const int count = 8;
    bubble_sort(items, count);
    for (int i = 0; i < count; i++) {
        printf("%d ", items[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: bubble_sort() walks through items again and again and swaps neighbours that
   are in the wrong order, so the smallest values move to the end first. main() then prints
   the 8 values in descending order. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to allocate an array with malloc and fill it with multiples. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Use malloc to get room for 12 ints and check for NULL.
   2. Fill list with multiples.
   3. Print the values.
   4. Call free(list) at the end. */
int main(void) {
    int n = 12;
    /* Ask the heap for room for n ints; malloc returns NULL on failure. */
    int *list = malloc(n * sizeof(int));
    if (list == NULL) {
        fprintf(stderr, "malloc failed\n");
        return 1;
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        list[i] = 9 * i;
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        printf("%d ", list[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    free(list);   /* give the memory back */
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: malloc() reserves room for 12 ints on the heap and returns NULL if it
   fails, which the program checks. The first loop fills list with multiples, the second
   prints them, and free() gives the memory back at the end. */
// END

/* Caption: Search an array for its largest value. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write max_of() that takes values and count.
   2. Store values[0] in m.
   3. Loop over the other elements and keep the largest value in m.
   4. Return m and print it. */
/* Start with the first element and keep the largest value seen so far. */
long max_of(const long values[], int count) {
    long m = values[0];
    for (int i = 1; i < count; i++) {
        if (values[i] > m) {
            m = values[i];
        }
    }
    return m;
}

int main(void) {
    long values[] = {8L, 90L, 69L, 99L, 60L, 27L, 63L, 30L};
    int count = sizeof(values) / sizeof(values[0]);
    printf("The largest value is %ld\n", max_of(values, count));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: max_of() takes the first element as the largest value so far and stores it
   in m. The loop compares every other element with m using > and keeps the largest one.
   main() prints the largest of the 8 values. */
// END

/* Caption: Compute the product of two square matrices. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define N as 3.
   2. For every i and j, add a[i][k] * b[k][j] over k into product[i][j].
   3. Print product row by row. */
#define N 3

int main(void) {
    int a[N][N] = {{9, 7, 1}, {9, 3, 2}, {9, 9, 7}};
    int b[N][N] = {{0, 3, 5}, {7, 2, 3}, {1, 7, 0}};
    int product[N][N] = {0};
    /* product[i][j] is row i of a times column j of b. */
    for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) {
        for (int j = 0; j < N; j++) {
            for (int k = 0; k < N; k++) {
                product[i][j] += a[i][k] * b[k][j];
            }
        }
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) {
        for (int j = 0; j < N; j++) {
            printf("%4d", product[i][j]);
        }
        printf("\n");
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: For each entry product[i][j] the innermost loop adds a[i][k] * b[k][j] over
   k, which is row i of a times column j of b. main() multiplies two 3x3 matrices and
   prints the product. */
// END

/* Caption: C program to calculate the area and perimeter of a rectangle struct. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define a Rectangle struct with width and height.
   2. Write area() and perimeter().
   3. Make a 1 by 2 rectangle and print both results. */
typedef struct {
    int width;
    int height;
} Rectangle;

int area(Rectangle r) {
    return r.width * r.height;
}

int perimeter(Rectangle r) {
    return 2 * (r.width + r.height);
}

int main(void) {
    Rectangle box = {1, 2};
    printf("Area: %d, Perimeter: %d\n", area(box), perimeter(box));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: Rectangle stores a width and a height. area() returns width * height and
   perimeter() returns 2 * (width + height). main() makes a 1 by 2 rectangle and prints
   both results. */
// END

/* Caption: Build a FIFO queue using a ring buffer. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define a Queue with room for 8 items, a head and a count.
   2. Write enqueue() that stores at (head + count) % CAPACITY.
   3. Write dequeue() that takes the item at head and moves head on.
   4. Add 6 values, then remove and print them in order. */
#define CAPACITY 8

typedef struct {
    int items[CAPACITY];
    int head;
    int count;
} Queue;

bool enqueue(Queue *q, int value) {
    if (q->count == CAPACITY) {
        return false;
    }
    /* The tail wraps around to the start of the array. */
    q->items[(q->head + q->count) % CAPACITY] = value;
    q->count++;
    return true;
}

bool dequeue(Queue *q, int *value) {
    if (q->count == 0) {
        return false;
    }
    *value = q->items[q->head];
    q->head = (q->head + 1) % CAPACITY;
    q->count--;
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    Queue q = {.head = 0, .count = 0};
    enqueue(&q, 69);
    enqueue(&q, 28);
    enqueue(&q, 94);
    enqueue(&q, 34);
    enqueue(&q, 44);
    enqueue(&q, 17);
    int value;
    /* Items come out in the order they went in (first in, first out). */
    while (dequeue(&q, &value)) {
        printf("%d ", value);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: The Queue stores up to 8 items in a ring buffer: head is the oldest item
   and % CAPACITY wraps positions back to the start of the array. enqueue() adds at the
   back and dequeue() removes from the front, so main() gets its 6 values back in the same
   order (first in, first out). */
// END

/* Caption: Check whether a word is a palindrome. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <string.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write is_palindrome() for str.
   2. Compare the first and last characters, moving inwards.
   3. Return false at the first mismatch, otherwise true.
   4. Check stack and print the result. */
/* Compare characters from the front and back, moving inwards. */
bool is_palindrome(const char *str) {
    int i = 0;
    int j = strlen(str) - 1;
    while (i < j) {
        if (str[i] != str[j]) {
            return false;
        }
        i++;
        j--;
    }
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    const char *str = "stack";
    printf("%s %s a palindrome\n", str, is_palindrome(str) ? "is" : "is not");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: is_palindrome() compares the first and last characters and moves inwards;
   any mismatch means the word is not a palindrome. main() checks the word stack and prints
   the result. */
// END

/* Caption: Compute the sum of the elements of an array. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write total_of() that takes the array readings and its length n.
   2. Start acc at 0 and add every element in a for loop.
   3. Return acc.
   4. In main(), fill readings with 4 values and print the sum. */
/* Walk through the array and accumulate each value. */
long total_of(const long readings[], int n) {
    long acc = 0;
    for (int k = 0; k < n; k++) {
        acc += readings[k];
    }
    return acc;
}

int main(void) {
    long readings[] = {10L, 72L, 84L, 31L};
    int n = 4;
    printf("Sum: %ld\n", total_of(readings, n));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: total_of() receives the array readings and its length n. It starts acc at
   0, adds every element to it in a for loop and returns the total. main() fills readings
   with 4 long values and prints their sum. */
// END

/* Caption: How do I search a sorted array by halving the search range each step in C? */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Make sure the array is sorted.
   2. Set low to 0 and high to n - 1.
   3. While low <= high, compare the middle element mid with the key.
   4. Return the index if it matches; otherwise keep only the half that can hold the
      key.
   5. Return -1 if the range becomes empty, and print the index of 201. */
/* The array must be sorted. Each step halves the range that can still hold the key. */
int binary_search(const int scores[], int n, int key) {
    int low = 0;
    int high = n - 1;
    while (low <= high) {
        int mid = low + (high - low) / 2;
        if (scores[mid] == key) {
            return mid;
        } else if (scores[mid] < key) {
            low = mid + 1;   /* key is in the right half */
        } else {
            high = mid - 1;   /* key is in the left half */
        }
    }
    return -1;
}

int main(void) {
    int scores[] = {5, 37, 38, 46, 68, 101, 109, 149, 162, 182};
    int n = 10;
    int index = binary_search(scores, n, 201);
    printf("Index of 201: %d\n", index);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: binary_search() needs a sorted array. It keeps the range from low to high,
   compares the middle element mid with the key and throws away the half that cannot
   contain it, so it needs only about log2(n) steps. main() looks for 201 and prints its
   index, or -1 if it is not there. */
// END

/* Caption: Return both the smallest and the largest value of an array through pointers. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write min_max() with the array, its length and the pointers min and max.
   2. Start both at the first element.
   3. Update *min and *max while looping over the rest.
   4. Declare low and high, pass their addresses and print them. */
/* One pass finds both results; they are stored through the pointers. */
void min_max(const int samples[], int count, int *min, int *max) {
    *min = samples[0];
    *max = samples[0];
    for (int i = 1; i < count; i++) {
        if (samples[i] < *min) {
            *min = samples[i];
        }
        if (samples[i] > *max) {
            *max = samples[i];
        }
    }
}

int main(void) {
    int samples[] = {16, 24, 32, 42, 48, 91, 58, 8};
    const int count = 8;
    int low, high;
    min_max(samples, count, &low, &high);
    printf("Min: %d, Max: %d\n", low, high);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: A C function can return only one value, so min_max() returns void and
   writes its two results through the pointer parameters min and max. main() declares low
   and high on one line and passes their addresses with &, then prints both results for the
   8 values. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to list the prime numbers below a limit. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write is_prime(n); numbers below 2 are not prime.
   2. Try every divisor d while d * d <= n.
   3. Return false if one divides n, otherwise true.
   4. Print every prime from 2 to 58. */
/* A prime has no divisor between 2 and its square root. */
bool is_prime(int n) {
    if (n < 2) {
        return false;
    }
    for (int d = 2; d * d <= n; d++) {
        if (n % d == 0) {
            return false;
        }
    }
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    for (int n = 2; n <= 58; n++) {
        if (is_prime(n)) {
            printf("%d ", n);
        }
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: is_prime() tries every divisor d from 2 while d * d <= n; if one divides n
   evenly, n is not prime. main() tests every number from 2 to 58 and prints the primes. */
// END

/* Caption: Divide 2 numbers. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Read a and b.
   2. If b is 0, print an error and stop.
   3. Print a / b and the remainder a % b. */
int main(void) {
    int a, b;
    printf("Enter 2 numbers: ");
    if (scanf("%d %d", &a, &b) != 2) {
        printf("Invalid input\n");
        return 1;
    }
    /* Dividing by zero is not allowed, so check first. */
    if (b == 0) {
        printf("Cannot divide by zero\n");
        return 1;
    }
    /* Integer division drops the fraction; % gives the remainder. */
    printf("Quotient: %d, remainder: %d\n", a / b, a % b);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: The program reads a and b from the keyboard with scanf and stops with a
   message if the input is not valid. It checks that b is not zero, then prints a / b,
   where integer division drops the fraction, and the remainder a % b. */
// END

/* Caption: How do I compute the mean of a list of numbers in C? */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write array_average() that takes marks and count.
   2. Add the values into the double sum.
   3. Return sum / count.
   4. Print the average with two decimals. */
/* The mean is the total divided by the count. */
double array_average(const int marks[], int count) {
    double sum = 0.0;
    for (int i = 0; i < count; i++) {
        sum += marks[i];
    }
    return sum / count;
}

int main(void) {
    int marks[] = {40, 25, 93, 11, 47, 19};
    int count = sizeof(marks) / sizeof(marks[0]);
    printf("Average: %.2f\n", array_average(marks, count));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: array_average() adds the 6 values of marks into the double sum and divides
   by count, so the mean keeps its decimal part even when the values are whole numbers.
   main() prints it with two decimals. */
// END

/* Caption: C program to count the odd values in a list of integers. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write count_odd() that takes ages and length.
   2. For each element, test ages[j] % 2 != 0.
   3. Add one to count for every odd number.
   4. Return count and print it. */
/* A number is odd when the remainder after dividing by 2 is one. */
int count_odd(const int ages[], int length) {
    int count = 0;
    for (int j = 0; j < length; j++) {
        if (ages[j] % 2 != 0) {
            count++;
        }
    }
    return count;
}

int main(void) {
    int ages[] = {82, 16, 29, 87, 19, 40, 61, 54, 17};
    int length = sizeof(ages) / sizeof(ages[0]);
    printf("Odd numbers: %d\n", count_odd(ages, length));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: count_odd() tests each element of ages with the % operator: a remainder of
   1 after dividing by 2 means the number is odd, so count goes up by one. main() prints
   how many of the 9 values are odd. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to swap two variables using pointers. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write swap() that takes pointers to two int values.
   2. Save *a in tmp, copy *b into *a, then tmp into *b.
   3. In main(), print a and b, call swap(&a, &b) and print them again. */
/* Pass addresses so the function can change the caller's variables. */
void swap(int *a, int *b) {
    int tmp = *a;
    *a = *b;
    *b = tmp;
}

int main(void) {
    int a = 47, b = 32;
    printf("Before: %d %d\n", a, b);
    swap(&a, &b);
    printf("After:  %d %d\n", a, b);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: swap() receives the addresses of a and b, so writing through the pointers
   *a and *b changes the caller's variables. tmp holds one value during the exchange.
   main() declares both variables on one line and prints them before and after the swap. */
// END

/* Plan:
   1. Define struct Student with a name and a mark.
   2. Store 2 students in an array.
   3. Print each student and add the marks to total.
   4. Print total divided by the number of students. */
/* A struct groups a student's name and mark together. */
struct Student {
    char name[20];
    int mark;
};

int main(void) {
    struct Student students[] = {
        {"Eli", 52},
        {"Ben", 60}
    };
    int count = sizeof(students) / sizeof(students[0]);
    double total = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < count; i++) {
        printf("%s: %d\n", students[i].name, students[i].mark);
        total += students[i].mark;
    }
    printf("Average mark: %.1f\n", total / count);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: struct Student groups a name and a mark. main() stores 2 students in an
   array of structs, prints each one, adds the marks to total and prints the average. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a function that returns a Fraction struct. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define a Fraction struct with num and den.
   2. Write multiply() that returns num = a.num * b.num and den = a.den * b.den.
   3. Print 8/5 times 6/4. */
typedef struct {
    int num;
    int den;
} Fraction;

/* Multiply the numerators and the denominators. */
Fraction multiply(Fraction a, Fraction b) {
    Fraction r = {a.num * b.num, a.den * b.den};
    return r;
}

int main(void) {
    Fraction x = {8, 5}, y = {6, 4};
    Fraction p = multiply(x, y);
    printf("%d/%d * %d/%d = %d/%d\n", x.num, x.den, y.num, y.den, p.num, p.den);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: Fraction stores a numerator and a denominator. multiply() takes two
   Fractions and returns a new one with num = a.num * b.num and den = a.den * b.den. main()
   multiplies 8/5 by 6/4 (without reducing the result). */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to build a fixed-size integer stack in C. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define a Stack with room for 16 items and a top counter.
   2. Write push() and pop(), returning false when the stack is full or empty.
   3. Push 6 values.
   4. Pop and print until the stack is empty. */
#define CAPACITY 16

typedef struct {
    int items[CAPACITY];
    int top;   /* number of items on the stack */
} Stack;

bool push(Stack *s, int value) {
    if (s->top == CAPACITY) {
        return false;   /* stack is full */
    }
    s->items[s->top++] = value;
    return true;
}

bool pop(Stack *s, int *value) {
    if (s->top == 0) {
        return false;   /* stack is empty */
    }
    *value = s->items[--s->top];
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    Stack s = {.top = 0};
    push(&s, 38);
    push(&s, 84);
    push(&s, 83);
    push(&s, 55);
    push(&s, 85);
    push(&s, 69);
    int value;
    /* Items come back out in reverse order (last in, first out). */
    while (pop(&s, &value)) {
        printf("%d ", value);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: The Stack keeps up to 16 items in an array, and top counts how many are
   stored. push() adds at the top and pop() removes from the top; both return false when
   they cannot. main() pushes 6 values and pops them all, so they come out in reverse order
   (last in, first out). */
// END

/* Caption: Check every element of an array to find a target value. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write linear_search() with the array, its length and wanted.
   2. Compare each element with wanted.
   3. Return the index of the first match, or -1.
   4. In main(), search for 51 and print the result. */
/* Return the index of wanted, or -1 when it is not in the array. */
int linear_search(const int readings[], int count, int wanted) {
    for (int j = 0; j < count; j++) {
        if (readings[j] == wanted) {
            return j;
        }
    }
    return -1;
}

int main(void) {
    int readings[] = {7, 25, 51, 71, 53, 94};
    int count = 6;
    int wanted = 51;
    int pos = linear_search(readings, count, wanted);
    if (pos >= 0) {
        printf("Found %d at index %d\n", wanted, pos);
    } else {
        printf("%d is not in the array\n", wanted);
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: linear_search() checks the elements of readings one by one and returns the
   index of the first one equal to wanted, or -1 when it reaches the end without a match.
   main() searches for 51 and prints where it is, or that it is missing. */
// END

/* Caption: Program to compute the distance between two points using a struct. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <math.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define a Point struct with x and y.
   2. Write distance() using sqrt(dx * dx + dy * dy).
   3. Print the distance between p and q. */
typedef struct {
    double x;
    double y;
} Point;

/* Pythagoras: sqrt(dx * dx + dy * dy). */
double distance(Point a, Point b) {
    double dx = b.x - a.x;
    double dy = b.y - a.y;
    return sqrt(dx * dx + dy * dy);
}

int main(void) {
    Point p = {2, 3};
    Point q = {6, -3};
    printf("Distance: %.3f\n", distance(p, q));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: Point is a typedef struct with x and y. distance() uses Pythagoras, sqrt(dx
   * dx + dy * dy), to measure the gap between the two points, and main() prints it. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to turn the rows of a 4x3 matrix into columns. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define ROWS as 4 and COLS as 3.
   2. Copy m[r][c] into t[c][r] for every element.
   3. Print t row by row. */
#define ROWS 4
#define COLS 3

int main(void) {
    int m[ROWS][COLS] = {{6, 4, 7}, {5, 5, 7}, {7, 9, 2}, {9, 6, 0}};
    int t[COLS][ROWS];
    /* Element (r, c) moves to (c, r). */
    for (int r = 0; r < ROWS; r++) {
        for (int c = 0; c < COLS; c++) {
            t[c][r] = m[r][c];
        }
    }
    for (int r = 0; r < COLS; r++) {
        for (int c = 0; c < ROWS; c++) {
            printf("%3d", t[r][c]);
        }
        printf("\n");
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: The nested loops copy m[r][c] into t[c][r], so the 4x3 matrix becomes 3x4.
   A second pair of loops prints the result. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to print the first 15 Fibonacci numbers. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write fib(n) that returns n when n < 2.
   2. Otherwise return fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2).
   3. Print fib(i) for i from 0 to 14. */
/* Each Fibonacci number is the sum of the two before it. */
long fib(int n) {
    if (n < 2) {
        return n;
    }
    return fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2);
}

int main(void) {
    for (int i = 0; i < 15; i++) {
        printf("%ld ", fib(i));
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: fib() returns n for 0 and 1 and otherwise adds the two previous Fibonacci
   numbers by calling itself twice, which is simple but slow for large n. main() prints the
   first 15 numbers. */
// END

/* Caption: How do I write a function that returns a Fraction struct in C? */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define a Fraction struct with num and den.
   2. Write multiply() that returns num = a.num * b.num and den = a.den * b.den.
   3. Print 8/2 times 8/9. */
typedef struct {
    int num;
    int den;
} Fraction;

/* Multiply the numerators and the denominators. */
Fraction multiply(Fraction a, Fraction b) {
    Fraction r = {a.num * b.num, a.den * b.den};
    return r;
}

int main(void) {
    Fraction x = {8, 2}, y = {8, 9};
    Fraction p = multiply(x, y);
    printf("%d/%d * %d/%d = %d/%d\n", x.num, x.den, y.num, y.den, p.num, p.den);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: Fraction stores a numerator and a denominator. multiply() takes two
   Fractions and returns a new one with num = a.num * b.num and den = a.den * b.den. main()
   multiplies 8/2 by 8/9 (without reducing the result). */
// END

/* Caption: Reverse the digits of a number. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Start result at 0.
   2. Multiply result by 10, add n % 10, then divide n by 10.
   3. Repeat until n is 0.
   4. Apply it to 389807 and print the result. */
/* Take the last digit with % 10, then drop it with / 10. */
int reverse_digits(int n) {
    int result = 0;
    while (n > 0) {
        result = result * 10 + n % 10;
        n /= 10;
    }
    return result;
}

int main(void) {
    int number = 389807;
    printf("reverse of digits of %d: %d\n", number, reverse_digits(number));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: reverse_digits() shifts result one place left (result * 10) and adds the
   last digit of n, which reverses the order. main() applies it to 389807. */
// END

/* Caption: C program to find the least common multiple of two numbers. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write gcd() with Euclid's algorithm: replace (a, b) by (b, a % b) until b is 0.
   2. Write lcm() as a / gcd(a, b) * b.
   3. Print the LCM of 73 and 108. */
/* Euclid: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a % b) until b becomes zero. */
int gcd(int a, int b) {
    while (b != 0) {
        int r = a % b;
        a = b;
        b = r;
    }
    return a;
}

/* lcm(a, b) = a / gcd(a, b) * b (divide first to avoid overflow). */
long lcm(int a, int b) {
    return (long)a / gcd(a, b) * b;
}

int main(void) {
    printf("lcm(73, 108) = %ld\n", lcm(73, 108));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: gcd() uses Euclid's algorithm: it keeps replacing (a, b) with (b, a % b)
   until b is 0. lcm() divides a by the gcd before multiplying by b, which avoids overflow.
   main() prints the LCM of 73 and 108. */
// END

/* Caption: Search a sorted array by halving the search range each step. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Make sure the array is sorted.
   2. Set left to 0 and right to count - 1.
   3. While left <= right, compare the middle element middle with the key.
   4. Return the index if it matches; otherwise keep only the half that can hold the
      key.
   5. Return -1 if the range becomes empty, and print the index of 58. */
/* The array must be sorted. Each step halves the range that can still hold the key. */
int binary_search(const int samples[], int count, int key) {
    int left = 0;
    int right = count - 1;
    while (left <= right) {
        int middle = left + (right - left) / 2;
        if (samples[middle] == key) {
            return middle;
        } else if (samples[middle] < key) {
            left = middle + 1;   /* key is in the right half */
        } else {
            right = middle - 1;   /* key is in the left half */
        }
    }
    return -1;
}

int main(void) {
    int samples[] = {1, 10, 12, 37, 49, 58, 59, 64, 80, 132, 144, 165};
    int count = sizeof(samples) / sizeof(samples[0]);
    int index = binary_search(samples, count, 58);
    printf("Index of 58: %d\n", index);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: binary_search() needs a sorted array. It keeps the range from left to
   right, compares the middle element middle with the key and throws away the half that
   cannot contain it, so it needs only about log2(n) steps. main() looks for 58 and prints
   its index, or -1 if it is not there. */
// END

/* Explanation: The for loop starts at 27 and subtracts one each round (i--) until it
   reaches 1. */
// END

/* Caption: How do I use binary search to locate a value in a sorted list in C? */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Make sure the array is sorted.
   2. Set low to 0 and high to len - 1.
   3. While low <= high, compare the middle element mid with the key.
   4. Return the index if it matches; otherwise keep only the half that can hold the
      key.
   5. Return -1 if the range becomes empty, and print the index of 178. */
/* The array must be sorted. Each step halves the range that can still hold the key. */
int binary_search(const int items[], int len, int key) {
    int low = 0;
    int high = len - 1;
    while (low <= high) {
        int mid = low + (high - low) / 2;
        if (items[mid] == key) {
            return mid;
        } else if (items[mid] < key) {
            low = mid + 1;   /* key is in the right half */
        } else {
            high = mid - 1;   /* key is in the left half */
        }
    }
    return -1;
}

int main(void) {
    int items[] = {24, 62, 75, 96, 121, 141, 167, 176, 178, 198};
    const int len = 10;
    int index = binary_search(items, len, 178);
    printf("Index of 178: %d\n", index);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: binary_search() needs a sorted array. It keeps the range from low to high,
   compares the middle element mid with the key and throws away the half that cannot
   contain it, so it needs only about log2(n) steps. main() looks for 178 and prints its
   index, or -1 if it is not there. */
// END

/* Caption: Print the first 15 Fibonacci numbers. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Start with first = 0 and second = 1.
   2. Repeat 15 times and print first each time.
   3. Compute next = first + second, then set first = second and second = next. */
int main(void) {
    long first = 0, second = 1;
    /* Print a term, then slide the pair one step along the sequence. */
    for (int i = 0; i < 15; i++) {
        printf("%ld ", first);
        long next = first + second;
        first = second;
        second = next;
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: The loop keeps the last two numbers in first and second. Each round it
   prints first, then moves the pair forward: first becomes second and second becomes their
   sum. It prints the first 15 Fibonacci numbers. */
// END

/* Caption: Compute the sum of the elements of an array. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write array_sum() that takes the array data and its length n.
   2. Start acc at 0 and add every element in a for loop.
   3. Return acc.
   4. In main(), fill data with 8 values and print the sum. */
/* Walk through the array and accumulate each value. */
int array_sum(const int data[], int n) {
    int acc = 0;
    for (int j = 0; j < n; j++) {
        acc += data[j];
    }
    return acc;
}

int main(void) {
    int data[] = {26, 43, 94, 69, 44, 98, 49, 29};
    int n = sizeof(data) / sizeof(data[0]);
    printf("Total = %d\n", array_sum(data, n));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: array_sum() receives the array data and its length n. It starts acc at 0,
   adds every element to it in a for loop and returns the total. main() fills data with 8
   int values and prints their sum. */
// END

/* Caption: Create a singly linked list by inserting at the head. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define Item with a value and a next pointer.
   2. Write push_front() that mallocs a node and links it in front of head.
   3. Write print_list() that follows next until NULL.
   4. Write free_list() that frees every node.
   5. Push 3 values, print the list and free it. */
typedef struct Item {
    int value;
    struct Item *next;
} Item;

/* Allocate a new node and put it in front of the current head. */
Item *push_front(Item *head, int value) {
    Item *node = malloc(sizeof(Item));
    if (node == NULL) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Out of memory\n");
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }
    node->value = value;
    node->next = head;
    return node;
}

void print_list(const Item *head) {
    for (const Item *cur = head; cur != NULL; cur = cur->next) {
        printf("%d -> ", cur->value);
    }
    printf("NULL\n");
}

/* Free every node; save next before freeing the current one. */
void free_list(Item *head) {
    while (head != NULL) {
        Item *next = head->next;
        free(head);
        head = next;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    Item *head = NULL;
    head = push_front(head, 22);
    head = push_front(head, 37);
    head = push_front(head, 43);
    print_list(head);
    free_list(head);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: Each Item holds a value and a pointer to the next node. push_front()
   allocates a node with malloc, puts it in front of head and returns it; print_list()
   follows the next pointers until NULL; free_list() frees every node. main() pushes 3
   values, so they print in reverse order. */
// END

/* Caption: Check whether a word is a palindrome. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <string.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write is_palindrome() for word.
   2. Compare the first and last characters, moving inwards.
   3. Return false at the first mismatch, otherwise true.
   4. Check network and print the result. */
/* Compare characters from the front and back, moving inwards. */
bool is_palindrome(const char *word) {
    int i = 0;
    int j = strlen(word) - 1;
    while (i < j) {
        if (word[i] != word[j]) {
            return false;
        }
        i++;
        j--;
    }
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    const char *word = "network";
    printf("%s %s a palindrome\n", word, is_palindrome(word) ? "is" : "is not");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: is_palindrome() compares the first and last characters and moves inwards;
   any mismatch means the word is not a palindrome. main() checks the word network and
   prints the result. */
// END

/* Caption: How do I declare two pointers in one statement and use them in C? */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Declare x and y on one line.
   2. Declare the pointers px and py on one line, each with its own *.
   3. Add 3 to x through px and print the values. */
int main(void) {
    int x = 45, y = 43;
    /* Each pointer needs its own '*': in "int *p, q;" only p is a pointer. */
    int *px = &x, *py = &y;
    *px += 3;
    printf("x = %d, y = %d\n", x, y);
    printf("*px = %d, *py = %d\n", *px, *py);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: int *px = &x, *py = &y; declares two pointers in one statement; each name
   needs its own *. *px += 3 changes x through the pointer, so x becomes 48 while y stays
   43. */
// END

/* Caption: C program to compute the mean of a list of numbers. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write array_average() that takes items and size.
   2. Add the values into the double total.
   3. Return total / size.
   4. Print the average with two decimals. */
/* Sum the values, then divide by how many there are. */
double array_average(const double items[], int size) {
    double total = 0.0;
    for (int i = 0; i < size; i++) {
        total += items[i];
    }
    return total / size;
}

int main(void) {
    double items[] = {36.8, 34.3, 73.7, 11.4};
    const int size = 4;
    printf("Mean = %.2f\n", array_average(items, size));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: array_average() adds the 4 values of items into the double total and
   divides by size, so the mean keeps its decimal part even when the values are whole
   numbers. main() prints it with two decimals. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to use dynamic memory to store the first 13 multiples. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Use malloc to get room for 13 ints and check for NULL.
   2. Fill list with multiples.
   3. Print the values.
   4. Call free(list) at the end. */
int main(void) {
    int n = 13;
    /* Ask the heap for room for n ints; malloc returns NULL on failure. */
    int *list = malloc(n * sizeof(int));
    if (list == NULL) {
        fprintf(stderr, "malloc failed\n");
        return 1;
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        list[i] = 8 * i;
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        printf("%d ", list[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    free(list);   /* give the memory back */
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: malloc() reserves room for 13 ints on the heap and returns NULL if it
   fails, which the program checks. The first loop fills list with multiples, the second
   prints them, and free() gives the memory back at the end. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to count the vowels in a sentence. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <string.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write count_vowels() with count = 0.
   2. For each character, check whether strchr finds it in aeiouAEIOU.
   3. Return count and print it. */
/* strchr finds the letter in the list of vowels, or returns NULL. */
int count_vowels(const char *text) {
    int count = 0;
    for (int i = 0; text[i] != '\0'; i++) {
        if (strchr("aeiouAEIOU", text[i]) != NULL) {
            count++;
        }
    }
    return count;
}

int main(void) {
    const char *sentence = "every program starts in main";
    printf("Vowels: %d\n", count_vowels(sentence));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: count_vowels() uses strchr to test whether each character is one of
   aeiouAEIOU and counts the matches. main() prints the number of vowels in the sentence. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to count the occurrences of a character in a sentence. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write count_char() with count = 0.
   2. Compare each character with the target d.
   3. Return count and print it. */
int count_char(const char *text, char target) {
    int count = 0;
    /* Compare every character with the target. */
    for (int i = 0; text[i] != '\0'; i++) {
        if (text[i] == target) {
            count++;
        }
    }
    return count;
}

int main(void) {
    const char *sentence = "structs group related data together";
    printf("'d' appears %d times\n", count_char(sentence, 'd'));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: count_char() compares every character of the text with the target character
   and counts the matches. main() prints how many times d appears in the sentence. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to add up the digits of a number. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Start result at 0.
   2. Add n % 10 to result, then divide n by 10.
   3. Repeat until n is 0.
   4. Apply it to 366220 and print the result. */
/* Take the last digit with % 10, then drop it with / 10. */
int sum_digits(int n) {
    int result = 0;
    while (n > 0) {
        result += n % 10;
        n /= 10;
    }
    return result;
}

int main(void) {
    int number = 366220;
    printf("sum of digits of %d: %d\n", number, sum_digits(number));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: sum_digits() adds the last digit (n % 10) to result and then removes it (n
   / 10) until no digits are left. main() applies it to 366220. */
// END

/* Caption: Save text to a file with fprintf and print it with fgets. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Open data.txt in write mode and check for NULL.
   2. Write 4 lines with fprintf and close the file.
   3. Open it again in read mode.
   4. Read and print each line with fgets, then close the file. */
int main(void) {
    FILE *file = fopen("data.txt", "w");
    if (file == NULL) {
        perror("fopen");
        return 1;
    }
    fprintf(file, "loops repeat a block of code\n");
    fprintf(file, "every program starts in main\n");
    fprintf(file, "structs group related data together\n");
    fprintf(file, "keep functions short and focused\n");
    fclose(file);

    /* Reopen the file for reading and print it line by line. */
    file = fopen("data.txt", "r");
    if (file == NULL) {
        perror("fopen");
        return 1;
    }
    char line[128];
    while (fgets(line, sizeof(line), file) != NULL) {
        printf("%s", line);
    }
    fclose(file);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: fopen() in write mode creates data.txt, fprintf() writes 4 lines into it
   and fclose() saves it. The file is then opened again in read mode, and fgets() reads it
   back line by line into the buffer line, which is printed. Every fopen() result is
   checked for NULL. */
// END

/* Caption: How do I print a Celsius to Fahrenheit conversion table in C? */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write to_fahrenheit() with F = C * 9 / 5 + 32.
   2. Loop c from 0 to 100 in steps of 20.
   3. Print each Celsius value with its Fahrenheit value. */
/* F = C * 9 / 5 + 32 */
double to_fahrenheit(double celsius) {
    return celsius * 9.0 / 5.0 + 32.0;
}

int main(void) {
    printf("Celsius  Fahrenheit\n");
    for (int c = 0; c <= 100; c += 20) {
        printf("%7d  %10.1f\n", c, to_fahrenheit(c));
    }
    return 0;
}

   100 degrees Celsius in steps of 20. */
// END

/* Caption: Test if 295 is a prime number. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write is_prime(n); numbers below 2 are not prime.
   2. Try every divisor d while d * d <= n.
   3. Return false if one divides n, otherwise true.
   4. Check 295 and print the result. */
/* A prime has no divisor between 2 and its square root. */
bool is_prime(int n) {
    if (n < 2) {
        return false;
    }
    for (int d = 2; d * d <= n; d++) {
        if (n % d == 0) {
            return false;
        }
    }
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    int number = 295;
    printf("%d %s prime\n", number, is_prime(number) ? "is" : "is not");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: is_prime() tries every divisor d from 2 while d * d <= n; if one divides n
   evenly, n is not prime. main() checks 295 and prints whether it is prime. */
// END

/* Caption: Build a FIFO queue using a ring buffer. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define a Queue with room for 10 items, a head and a count.
   2. Write enqueue() that stores at (head + count) % CAPACITY.
   3. Write dequeue() that takes the item at head and moves head on.
   4. Add 3 values, then remove and print them in order. */
#define CAPACITY 10

typedef struct {
    int items[CAPACITY];
    int head;
    int count;
} Queue;

bool enqueue(Queue *q, int value) {
    if (q->count == CAPACITY) {
        return false;
    }
    /* The tail wraps around to the start of the array. */
    q->items[(q->head + q->count) % CAPACITY] = value;
    q->count++;
    return true;
}

bool dequeue(Queue *q, int *value) {
    if (q->count == 0) {
        return false;
    }
    *value = q->items[q->head];
    q->head = (q->head + 1) % CAPACITY;
    q->count--;
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    Queue q = {.head = 0, .count = 0};
    enqueue(&q, 9);
    enqueue(&q, 34);
    enqueue(&q, 20);
    int value;
    /* Items come out in the order they went in (first in, first out). */
    while (dequeue(&q, &value)) {
        printf("%d ", value);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: The Queue stores up to 10 items in a ring buffer: head is the oldest item
   and % CAPACITY wraps positions back to the start of the array. enqueue() adds at the
   back and dequeue() removes from the front, so main() gets its 3 values back in the same
   order (first in, first out). */
// END

/* Caption: Use dynamic memory to store the first 13 multiples. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Use malloc to get room for 13 ints and check for NULL.
   2. Fill buffer with multiples.
   3. Print the values.
   4. Call free(buffer) at the end. */
int main(void) {
    int n = 13;
    /* Ask the heap for room for n ints; malloc returns NULL on failure. */
    int *buffer = malloc(n * sizeof(int));
    if (buffer == NULL) {
        fprintf(stderr, "malloc failed\n");
        return 1;
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        buffer[i] = 3 * i;
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        printf("%d ", buffer[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    free(buffer);   /* give the memory back */
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: malloc() reserves room for 13 ints on the heap and returns NULL if it
   fails, which the program checks. The first loop fills buffer with multiples, the second
   prints them, and free() gives the memory back at the end. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to find the index of a number using linear search. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write linear_search() with the array, its length and wanted.
   2. Compare each element with wanted.
   3. Return the index of the first match, or -1.
   4. In main(), search for 72 and print the result. */
/* Return the index of wanted, or -1 when it is not in the array. */
int linear_search(const int prices[], int count, int wanted) {
    for (int idx = 0; idx < count; idx++) {
        if (prices[idx] == wanted) {
            return idx;
        }
    }
    return -1;
}

int main(void) {
    int prices[] = {14, 96, 99, 74, 72, 90, 33};
    int count = sizeof(prices) / sizeof(prices[0]);
    int wanted = 72;
    int pos = linear_search(prices, count, wanted);
    if (pos >= 0) {
        printf("Found %d at index %d\n", wanted, pos);
    } else {
        printf("%d is not in the array\n", wanted);
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: linear_search() checks the elements of prices one by one and returns the
   index of the first one equal to wanted, or -1 when it reaches the end without a match.
   main() searches for 72 and prints where it is, or that it is missing. */
// END

/* Caption: Add two 4x2 matrices. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define ROWS as 4 and COLS as 2.
   2. Loop over every row r and column c.
   3. Store a[r][c] + b[r][c] in sum and print it. */
#define ROWS 4
#define COLS 2

int main(void) {
    int a[ROWS][COLS] = {{3, 3}, {3, 7}, {1, 0}, {7, 8}};
    int b[ROWS][COLS] = {{4, 0}, {0, 6}, {5, 5}, {9, 9}};
    int sum[ROWS][COLS];
    /* Each entry of the result is the sum of the matching entries. */
    for (int r = 0; r < ROWS; r++) {
        for (int c = 0; c < COLS; c++) {
            sum[r][c] = a[r][c] + b[r][c];
            printf("%3d", sum[r][c]);
        }
        printf("\n");
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: Both matrices are 4x2 two-dimensional arrays. Two nested loops visit every
   row r and column c, store a[r][c] + b[r][c] in sum and print each row. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a function that returns the distance between two points given x1, y1, x2 and y2. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <math.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write distance(x1, y1, x2, y2).
   2. Compute dx and dy, then return sqrt(dx * dx + dy * dy).
   3. Print the distance between (-1, -5) and (3, 1). */
/* Pythagoras: the distance is sqrt(dx * dx + dy * dy). */
double distance(double x1, double y1, double x2, double y2) {
    double dx = x2 - x1, dy = y2 - y1;
    return sqrt(dx * dx + dy * dy);
}

int main(void) {
    printf("Distance: %.3f\n", distance(-1, -5, 3, 1));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: distance() takes the coordinates of both points as four parameters. It
   declares dx and dy on one line and uses Pythagoras with sqrt() from math.h. main()
   prints the distance between (-1, -5) and (3, 1). */
// END

/* Caption: Find the greatest common divisor of two numbers. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write gcd() with Euclid's algorithm.
   2. Replace (a, b) by (b, a % b) until b is 0.
   3. Return a and print the GCD of 160 and 294. */
/* Euclid: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a % b) until b becomes zero. */
int gcd(int a, int b) {
    while (b != 0) {
        int r = a % b;
        a = b;
        b = r;
    }
    return a;
}

int main(void) {
    int x = 160, y = 294;
    printf("gcd(%d, %d) = %d\n", x, y, gcd(x, y));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: gcd() uses Euclid's algorithm: it keeps replacing (a, b) with (b, a % b)
   until b is 0. The last non-zero value is the greatest common divisor, and main() prints
   the GCD of 160 and 294. */
// END

#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:

bool dequeue(Queue *q, int *value) {

/* Caption: Program to build a fixed-size integer stack in C. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define a Stack with room for 10 items and a top counter.
   2. Write push() and pop(), returning false when the stack is full or empty.
   3. Push 4 values.
   4. Pop and print until the stack is empty. */
#define CAPACITY 10

typedef struct {
    int items[CAPACITY];
    int top;   /* number of items on the stack */
} Stack;

bool push(Stack *s, int value) {
    if (s->top == CAPACITY) {
        return false;   /* stack is full */
    }
    s->items[s->top++] = value;
    return true;
}

bool pop(Stack *s, int *value) {
    if (s->top == 0) {
        return false;   /* stack is empty */
    }
    *value = s->items[--s->top];
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    Stack s = {.top = 0};
    push(&s, 85);
    push(&s, 23);
    push(&s, 53);
    push(&s, 18);
    int value;
    /* Items come back out in reverse order (last in, first out). */
    while (pop(&s, &value)) {
        printf("%d ", value);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: The Stack keeps up to 10 items in an array, and top counts how many are
   stored. push() adds at the top and pop() removes from the top; both return false when
   they cannot. main() pushes 4 values and pops them all, so they come out in reverse order
   (last in, first out). */
// END

/* Caption: Write a function that swaps two int values through pointers. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write swap() that takes pointers to two int values.
   2. Save *first in tmp, copy *second into *first, then tmp into *second.
   3. In main(), print first and second, call swap(&first, &second) and print them
      again. */
/* Pass addresses so the function can change the caller's variables. */
void swap(int *first, int *second) {
    int tmp = *first;
    *first = *second;
    *second = tmp;
}

int main(void) {
    int first = 30, second = 87;
    printf("Before: %d %d\n", first, second);
    swap(&first, &second);
    printf("After:  %d %d\n", first, second);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: swap() receives the addresses of first and second, so writing through the
   pointers *first and *second changes the caller's variables. tmp holds one value during
   the exchange. main() declares both variables on one line and prints them before and
   after the swap. */
// END

/* Caption: Create a singly linked list by inserting at the head. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define Node with a value and a next pointer.
   2. Write push_front() that mallocs a node and links it in front of head.
   3. Write print_list() that follows next until NULL.
   4. Write free_list() that frees every node.
   5. Push 3 values, print the list and free it. */
typedef struct Node {
    int value;
    struct Node *next;
} Node;

/* Allocate a new node and put it in front of the current head. */
Node *push_front(Node *head, int value) {
    Node *node = malloc(sizeof(Node));
    if (node == NULL) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Out of memory\n");
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }
    node->value = value;
    node->next = head;
    return node;
}

void print_list(const Node *head) {
    for (const Node *cur = head; cur != NULL; cur = cur->next) {
        printf("%d -> ", cur->value);
    }
    printf("NULL\n");
}

/* Free every node; save next before freeing the current one. */
void free_list(Node *head) {
    while (head != NULL) {
        Node *next = head->next;
        free(head);
        head = next;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    Node *head = NULL;
    head = push_front(head, 90);
    head = push_front(head, 95);
    head = push_front(head, 70);
    print_list(head);
    free_list(head);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: Each Node holds a value and a pointer to the next node. push_front()
   allocates a node with malloc, puts it in front of head and returns it; print_list()
   follows the next pointers until NULL; free_list() frees every node. main() pushes 3
   values, so they print in reverse order. */
// END

/* Caption: C program to convert 1012 to binary. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write print_binary(n, bits).
   2. Go through the bits from the highest to the lowest.
   3. Print 1 when (n >> b) & 1 is set, otherwise 0.
   4. Print 1012 in binary. */
/* Check each bit from the highest to the lowest. */
void print_binary(unsigned int n, int bits) {
    for (int b = bits - 1; b >= 0; b--) {
        putchar((n >> b) & 1 ? '1' : '0');
    }
    putchar('\n');
}

int main(void) {
    unsigned int number = 1012;
    printf("%u in binary: ", number);
    print_binary(number, 8);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: print_binary() checks one bit at a time, from the highest to the lowest: (n
   >> b) & 1 is 1 when bit b is set, so it prints the character 1 or 0. main() prints 1012
   in binary. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to sort an array in descending order using bubble sort. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write bubble_sort() for the int array scores.
   2. Compare each pair of neighbours.
   3. Swap them when they are in the wrong order for descending order.
   4. Repeat the passes until the array is sorted.
   5. Print the sorted values. */
/* Repeatedly swap neighbours that are in the wrong order. */
void bubble_sort(int scores[], int length) {
    for (int i = 0; i < length - 1; i++) {
        for (int j = 0; j < length - 1 - i; j++) {
            if (scores[j] < scores[j + 1]) {
                int tmp = scores[j];
                scores[j] = scores[j + 1];
                scores[j + 1] = tmp;
            }
        }
    }
}

int main(void) {
    int scores[] = {90, 85, 49, 21, 84, 41, 42, 76};
    int length = 8;
    bubble_sort(scores, length);
    for (int i = 0; i < length; i++) {
        printf("%d ", scores[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: bubble_sort() walks through scores again and again and swaps neighbours
   that are in the wrong order, so the smallest values move to the end first. main() then
   prints the 8 values in descending order. */
// END

}
/* Explanation: The program reads a and b from the keyboard with scanf and stops with a
   message if the input is not valid. The conditional operator (a > b) ? a : b picks the

// END

/* Caption: Program to count how many times 's' appears in a string. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write count_char() with count = 0.
   2. Compare each character with the target s.
   3. Return count and print it. */
int count_char(const char *text, char target) {
    int count = 0;
    /* Compare every character with the target. */
    for (int i = 0; text[i] != '\0'; i++) {
        if (text[i] == target) {
            count++;

    return count;

    printf("'s' appears %d times\n", count_char(sentence, 's'));
    return 0;

   and counts the matches. main() prints how many times s appears in the sentence. */

/* Caption: How do I implement a simple linked list with malloc and free in C? */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define Node with a value and a next pointer.
   2. Write push_front() that mallocs a node and links it in front of head.
   3. Write print_list() that follows next until NULL.
   4. Write free_list() that frees every node.
   5. Push 5 values, print the list and free it. */
typedef struct Node {
    int value;
    struct Node *next;
} Node;

/* Allocate a new node and put it in front of the current head. */
Node *push_front(Node *head, int value) {
    Node *node = malloc(sizeof(Node));
    if (node == NULL) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Out of memory\n");
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }
    node->value = value;
    node->next = head;
    return node;
}

void print_list(const Node *head) {
    for (const Node *cur = head; cur != NULL; cur = cur->next) {
        printf("%d -> ", cur->value);
    }
    printf("NULL\n");
}

/* Free every node; save next before freeing the current one. */
void free_list(Node *head) {
    while (head != NULL) {
        Node *next = head->next;
        free(head);
        head = next;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    Node *head = NULL;

/* Caption: Write a program to compute the factorial of a number recursively. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write factorial(value) that calls itself.
   2. Return 1 when value is 1 or less.
   3. Otherwise return value * factorial(value - 1).
   4. Print 3! as an unsigned long long. */
/* n! = n * (n - 1)!, and 0! = 1 stops the recursion. */
unsigned long long factorial(int value) {
    if (value <= 1) {
        return 1;
    }
    return value * factorial(value - 1);
}

int main(void) {
    int value = 3;
    printf("%d! = %llu\n", value, factorial(value));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: factorial() calls itself: n! is n * (n - 1)!, and the recursion stops when
   value is 1 or less. main() prints 3! as an unsigned long long, because factorials grow
   very fast. */
// END

/* Caption: How do I compute the mean of a list of numbers in C? */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write array_average() that takes values and count.
   2. Add the values into the double total.
   3. Return total / count.
   4. Print the average with two decimals. */
/* The mean is the total divided by the count. */
double array_average(const int values[], int count) {
    double total = 0.0;
    for (int i = 0; i < count; i++) {
        total += values[i];
    }
    return total / count;
}

int main(void) {
    int values[] = {10, 19, 21, 67, 15, 92, 76, 28};
    const int count = 8;
    printf("Mean = %.2f\n", array_average(values, count));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: array_average() adds the 8 values of values into the double total and
   divides by count, so the mean keeps its decimal part even when the values are whole
   numbers. main() prints it with two decimals. */
// END

/* Plan:
   1. Start result at 0.
   2. Divide n by 10 and add one to result.
   3. Repeat until n is 0.
   4. Apply it to 58272 and print the result. */
/* Take the last digit with % 10, then drop it with / 10. */
int count_digits(int n) {
    int result = 0;
    while (n > 0) {
        result++;
        n /= 10;
    }
    return result;
}

int main(void) {

/* Caption: Implement selection sort for an array of int values. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write selection_sort() for the int array values.
   2. For each position, find the smallest remaining element.
   3. Swap it into that position.
   4. Print the sorted values. */
/* Select the right element for each position and swap it into place. */
void selection_sort(int values[], int size) {
    for (int i = 0; i < size - 1; i++) {
        int chosen = i;
        for (int j = i + 1; j < size; j++) {
            if (values[chosen] > values[j]) {
                chosen = j;
            }
        }
        int tmp = values[i];
        values[i] = values[chosen];
        values[chosen] = tmp;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    int values[] = {93, 86, 49, 36, 34, 48};
    int size = 6;
    selection_sort(values, size);
    for (int i = 0; i < size; i++) {
        printf("%d ", values[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: selection_sort() finds the smallest remaining element for each position and
   swaps it into place. main() then prints the 6 values in ascending order. */
// END

/* Caption: Check every element of an array to find a target value. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write linear_search() with the array, its length and wanted.
   2. Compare each element with wanted.
   3. Return the index of the first match, or -1.
   4. In main(), search for 2 and print the result. */
/* Return the index of wanted, or -1 when it is not in the array. */
int linear_search(const int numbers[], int len, int wanted) {
    for (int i = 0; i < len; i++) {
        if (numbers[i] == wanted) {
            return i;
        }
    }
    return -1;
}

int main(void) {
    int numbers[] = {77, 91, 48, 59, 2};
    int len = 5;
    int wanted = 2;
    int pos = linear_search(numbers, len, wanted);
    if (pos >= 0) {
        printf("Found %d at index %d\n", wanted, pos);
    } else {
        printf("%d is not in the array\n", wanted);
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: linear_search() checks the elements of numbers one by one and returns the
   index of the first one equal to wanted, or -1 when it reaches the end without a match.
   main() searches for 2 and prints where it is, or that it is missing. */
// END

/* Caption: How do I find the arithmetic mean of 9 double values in C? */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write mean() that takes prices and n.
   2. Add the values into the double result.
   3. Return result / n.
   4. Print the average with two decimals. */
/* Sum the values, then divide by how many there are. */
double mean(const double prices[], int n) {
    double result = 0.0;
    int j = 0;
    while (j < n) {
        result += prices[j];
        j++;
    }
    return result / n;
}

int main(void) {
    double prices[] = {80.2, 58.3, 42.1, 90.8, 48.6, 10.5, 44.0, 8.6, 11.6};
    int n = sizeof(prices) / sizeof(prices[0]);
    printf("Mean = %.2f\n", mean(prices, n));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: mean() adds the 9 values of prices into the double result and divides by n,
   so the mean keeps its decimal part even when the values are whole numbers. main() prints
   it with two decimals. */
// END

/* Caption: Turn the rows of a 2x2 matrix into columns. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define ROWS as 2 and COLS as 2.
   2. Copy m[r][c] into t[c][r] for every element.
   3. Print t row by row. */
#define ROWS 2
#define COLS 2

int main(void) {
    int m[ROWS][COLS] = {{8, 6}, {1, 1}};
    int t[COLS][ROWS];
    /* Element (r, c) moves to (c, r). */
    for (int r = 0; r < ROWS; r++) {
        for (int c = 0; c < COLS; c++) {
            t[c][r] = m[r][c];
        }
    }
    for (int r = 0; r < COLS; r++) {
        for (int c = 0; c < ROWS; c++) {
            printf("%3d", t[r][c]);
        }
        printf("\n");
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: The nested loops copy m[r][c] into t[c][r], so the 2x2 matrix becomes 2x2.
   A second pair of loops prints the result. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a function that swaps two long values through pointers. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write swap() that takes pointers to two long values.
   2. Save *x in tmp, copy *y into *x, then tmp into *y.
   3. In main(), print x and y, call swap(&x, &y) and print them again. */
/* Pass addresses so the function can change the caller's variables. */
void swap(long *x, long *y) {
    long tmp = *x;
    *x = *y;
    *y = tmp;
}

int main(void) {
    long x = 39L, y = 94L;
    printf("Before: %ld %ld\n", x, y);
    swap(&x, &y);
    printf("After:  %ld %ld\n", x, y);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: swap() receives the addresses of x and y, so writing through the pointers
   *x and *y changes the caller's variables. tmp holds one value during the exchange.
   main() declares both variables on one line and prints them before and after the swap. */
// END

/* Caption: Print an integer with its digits reversed. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Start result at 0.
   2. Multiply result by 10, add n % 10, then divide n by 10.
   3. Repeat until n is 0.
   4. Apply it to 98729 and print the result. */
/* Take the last digit with % 10, then drop it with / 10. */
int reverse_digits(int n) {
    int result = 0;
    while (n > 0) {
        result = result * 10 + n % 10;
        n /= 10;
    }
    return result;
}

int main(void) {
    int number = 98729;
    printf("reverse of digits of %d: %d\n", number, reverse_digits(number));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: reverse_digits() shifts result one place left (result * 10) and adds the
   last digit of n, which reverses the order. main() applies it to 98729. */
// END

/* Caption: Program to create a singly linked list by inserting at the head. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define Node with a value and a next pointer.
   2. Write push_front() that mallocs a node and links it in front of head.
   3. Write print_list() that follows next until NULL.
   4. Write free_list() that frees every node.
   5. Push 5 values, print the list and free it. */
typedef struct Node {
    int value;
    struct Node *next;
} Node;

/* Allocate a new node and put it in front of the current head. */
Node *push_front(Node *head, int value) {
    Node *node = malloc(sizeof(Node));
    if (node == NULL) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Out of memory\n");
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }
    node->value = value;
    node->next = head;
    return node;
}

void print_list(const Node *head) {
    for (const Node *cur = head; cur != NULL; cur = cur->next) {
        printf("%d -> ", cur->value);
    }
    printf("NULL\n");
}

/* Free every node; save next before freeing the current one. */
void free_list(Node *head) {
    while (head != NULL) {
        Node *next = head->next;
        free(head);
        head = next;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    Node *head = NULL;
    head = push_front(head, 77);
    head = push_front(head, 78);
    head = push_front(head, 57);
    head = push_front(head, 7);
    head = push_front(head, 18);
    print_list(head);
    free_list(head);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: Each Node holds a value and a pointer to the next node. push_front()
   allocates a node with malloc, puts it in front of head and returns it; print_list()
   follows the next pointers until NULL; free_list() frees every node. main() pushes 5
   values, so they print in reverse order. */
// END

/* Caption: How do I compute 4 to the power of 3 without pow() in C? */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write power(base, exp) with result = 1.
   2. Multiply result by base exp times.
   3. Print 4 to the power 3. */
/* Multiply the base by itself exp times. */
long long power(int base, int exp) {
    long long result = 1;
    for (int i = 0; i < exp; i++) {
        result *= base;
    }
    return result;
}

int main(void) {
    printf("4^3 = %lld\n", power(4, 3));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: power() starts result at 1 and multiplies it by base exp times. It uses
   long long because powers grow quickly. main() prints 4 to the power 3. */
// END

/* Caption: Program to allocate an array with malloc and fill it with squares. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Use malloc to get room for 7 ints and check for NULL.
   2. Fill table with squares.
   3. Print the values.
   4. Call free(table) at the end. */
int main(void) {
    int n = 7;
    /* Ask the heap for room for n ints; malloc returns NULL on failure. */
    int *table = malloc(n * sizeof(int));
    if (table == NULL) {
        fprintf(stderr, "malloc failed\n");
        return 1;
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        table[i] = i * i;
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        printf("%d ", table[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    free(table);   /* give the memory back */
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: malloc() reserves room for 7 ints on the heap and returns NULL if it fails,
   which the program checks. The first loop fills table with squares, the second prints
   them, and free() gives the memory back at the end. */
// END

/* Caption: Show the Fibonacci series with a loop. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Start with first = 0 and second = 1.
   2. Repeat 21 times and print first each time.
   3. Compute next = first + second, then set first = second and second = next. */
int main(void) {
    long first = 0, second = 1;
    /* Print a term, then slide the pair one step along the sequence. */
    for (int i = 0; i < 21; i++) {
        printf("%ld ", first);
        long next = first + second;
        first = second;
        second = next;
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: The loop keeps the last two numbers in first and second. Each round it
   prints first, then moves the pair forward: first becomes second and second becomes their
   sum. It prints the first 21 Fibonacci numbers. */
// END

/* Caption: Use insertion sort to put numbers in ascending order. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write insertion_sort() for the double array data.
   2. Take each element in turn as current.
   3. Shift the larger values of the sorted part one place right.
   4. Put current into the gap.
   5. Print the sorted values. */
/* Insert each element into the already sorted part on its left. */
void insertion_sort(double data[], int count) {
    for (int i = 1; i < count; i++) {
        double current = data[i];
        int j = i - 1;
        while (j >= 0 && data[j] > current) {
            data[j + 1] = data[j];   /* shift bigger values right */
            j--;
        }
        data[j + 1] = current;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    double data[] = {15.2, 95.8, 47.7, 78.1, 60.7};
    int count = 5;
    insertion_sort(data, count);
    for (int i = 0; i < count; i++) {
        printf("%.2f ", data[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: insertion_sort() takes each element in turn and shifts the larger values of
   the sorted part one place right until the element fits. main() then prints the 5 values
   in ascending order. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to use a struct to store a rectangle and print its area and perimeter. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define a Rectangle struct with width and height.
   2. Write area() and perimeter().
   3. Make a 16 by 18 rectangle and print both results. */
typedef struct {
    int width;
    int height;
} Rectangle;

int area(Rectangle r) {
    return r.width * r.height;
}

int perimeter(Rectangle r) {
    return 2 * (r.width + r.height);
}

int main(void) {
    Rectangle box = {16, 18};
    printf("Area: %d, Perimeter: %d\n", area(box), perimeter(box));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: Rectangle stores a width and a height. area() returns width * height and
   perimeter() returns 2 * (width + height). main() makes a 16 by 18 rectangle and prints
   both results. */
// END

/* Caption: C program to use insertion sort to put numbers in ascending order. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write insertion_sort() for the int array prices.
   2. Take each element in turn as current.
   3. Shift the larger values of the sorted part one place right.
   4. Put current into the gap.
   5. Print the sorted values. */
/* Insert each element into the already sorted part on its left. */
void insertion_sort(int prices[], int length) {
    for (int i = 1; i < length; i++) {
        int current = prices[i];
        int j = i - 1;
        while (j >= 0 && prices[j] > current) {
            prices[j + 1] = prices[j];   /* shift bigger values right */
