/* Caption: Count how many times 'n' appears in a string. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write count_char() with count = 0.
   2. Compare each character with the target n.
   3. Return count and print it. */
int count_char(const char *text, char target) {
    int count = 0;
    /* Compare every character with the target. */
    for (int i = 0; text[i] != '\0'; i++) {
        if (text[i] == target) {
            count++;
        }
    }
    return count;
}

int main(void) {
    const char *sentence = "keep functions short and focused";
    printf("'n' appears %d times\n", count_char(sentence, 'n'));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: count_char() compares every character of the text with the target character
   and counts the matches. main() prints how many times n appears in the sentence. */
// END

/* Caption: Add two 3x2 matrices. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define ROWS as 3 and COLS as 2.
   2. Loop over every row r and column c.
   3. Store a[r][c] + b[r][c] in sum and print it. */
#define ROWS 3
#define COLS 2

int main(void) {
    int a[ROWS][COLS] = {{4, 2}, {9, 3}, {5, 8}};
    int b[ROWS][COLS] = {{5, 9}, {0, 2}, {5, 7}};
    int sum[ROWS][COLS];
    /* Each entry of the result is the sum of the matching entries. */
    for (int r = 0; r < ROWS; r++) {
        for (int c = 0; c < COLS; c++) {
            sum[r][c] = a[r][c] + b[r][c];
            printf("%3d", sum[r][c]);
        }
        printf("\n");
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: Both matrices are 3x2 two-dimensional arrays. Two nested loops visit every
   row r and column c, store a[r][c] + b[r][c] in sum and print each row. */
// END

/* Caption: Search an array for a value and print its position. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write linear_search() with the array, its length and needle.
   2. Compare each element with needle.
   3. Return the index of the first match, or -1.
   4. In main(), search for 67 and print the result. */
/* Return the index of needle, or -1 when it is not in the array. */
int linear_search(const int ages[], int count, int needle) {
    for (int i = 0; i < count; i++) {
        if (ages[i] == needle) {
            return i;
        }
    }
    return -1;
}

int main(void) {
    int ages[] = {67, 91, 36, 24, 32, 70, 72};
    int count = sizeof(ages) / sizeof(ages[0]);
    int needle = 67;
    int pos = linear_search(ages, count, needle);
    if (pos >= 0) {
        printf("Found %d at index %d\n", needle, pos);
    } else {
        printf("%d is not in the array\n", needle);
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: linear_search() checks the elements of ages one by one and returns the
   index of the first one equal to needle, or -1 when it reaches the end without a match.
   main() searches for 67 and prints where it is, or that it is missing. */
// END

/* Caption: Convert seconds into a struct with hours, minutes and seconds. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define a Duration struct with hours, minutes and seconds.
   2. Write from_seconds() that fills it using / and %.
   3. Convert 54508 seconds and print the members. */
typedef struct {
    int hours;
    int minutes;
    int seconds;
} Duration;

Duration from_seconds(int total) {
    Duration d;
    d.hours = total / 3600;
    d.minutes = (total % 3600) / 60;
    d.seconds = total % 60;
    return d;
}

int main(void) {
    Duration d = from_seconds(54508);
    printf("%d h %d min %d s\n", d.hours, d.minutes, d.seconds);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: from_seconds() fills the three members of a Duration struct using / and %,
   then returns the struct. main() converts 54508 seconds and prints the members. */
// END

/* Caption: How do I build a linked list, print it, and free it in C? */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define Item with a value and a next pointer.
   2. Write push_front() that mallocs a node and links it in front of head.
   3. Write print_list() that follows next until NULL.
   4. Write free_list() that frees every node.
   5. Push 4 values, print the list and free it. */
typedef struct Item {
    int value;
    struct Item *next;
} Item;

/* Allocate a new node and put it in front of the current head. */
Item *push_front(Item *head, int value) {
    Item *node = malloc(sizeof(Item));
    if (node == NULL) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Out of memory\n");
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }
    node->value = value;
    node->next = head;
    return node;
}

void print_list(const Item *head) {
    for (const Item *cur = head; cur != NULL; cur = cur->next) {
        printf("%d -> ", cur->value);
    }
    printf("NULL\n");
}

/* Free every node; save next before freeing the current one. */
void free_list(Item *head) {
    while (head != NULL) {
        Item *next = head->next;
        free(head);
        head = next;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    Item *head = NULL;
    head = push_front(head, 62);
    head = push_front(head, 36);
    head = push_front(head, 38);
    head = push_front(head, 5);
    print_list(head);
    free_list(head);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: Each Item holds a value and a pointer to the next node. push_front()
   allocates a node with malloc, puts it in front of head and returns it; print_list()
   follows the next pointers until NULL; free_list() frees every node. main() pushes 4
   values, so they print in reverse order. */
// END

/* Caption: Divide two integers and get both the quotient and the remainder. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write divide(a, b, &quotient, &remainder) that returns a bool.
   2. Return false if b is 0.
   3. Store a / b and a % b through the pointers and return true.
   4. Divide 245 by 14 and print the results or the error. */
/* Returns false for division by zero; otherwise stores both results. */
bool divide(int a, int b, int *quotient, int *remainder) {
    if (b == 0) {
        return false;
    }
    *quotient = a / b;
    *remainder = a % b;
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    int a = 245, b = 14;
    int q, r;
    if (divide(a, b, &q, &r)) {
        printf("%d / %d = %d remainder %d\n", a, b, q, r);
    } else {
        printf("Cannot divide by zero\n");
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: divide() has four parameters: two inputs and two pointers for the results.
   Its bool return value reports success, while the quotient and remainder are written
   through the pointers. main() divides 245 by 14 and prints both results. */
// END

/* Caption: Program to swap two variables using pointers. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write swap() that takes pointers to two int values.
   2. Save *a in tmp, copy *b into *a, then tmp into *b.
   3. In main(), print a and b, call swap(&a, &b) and print them again. */
/* Pass addresses so the function can change the caller's variables. */
void swap(int *a, int *b) {
    int tmp = *a;
    *a = *b;
    *b = tmp;
}

int main(void) {
    int a = 43, b = 54;
    printf("Before: %d %d\n", a, b);
    swap(&a, &b);
    printf("After:  %d %d\n", a, b);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: swap() receives the addresses of a and b, so writing through the pointers
   *a and *b changes the caller's variables. tmp holds one value during the exchange.
   main() declares both variables on one line and prints them before and after the swap. */
// END

/* Caption: Keep a value inside the limits low and high. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write clamp(value, low, high).
   2. Return low if the value is too small and high if it is too big.
   3. Otherwise return the value.
   4. Set low = 54 and high = 98 and print clamp() for 0, 8 and 113. */
/* Return value, but never less than low or more than high. */
int clamp(int value, int low, int high) {
    if (value < low) {
        return low;
    }
    if (value > high) {
        return high;
    }
    return value;
}

int main(void) {
    int low = 54, high = 98;
    printf("clamp(%d) = %d\n", 0, clamp(0, low, high));
    printf("clamp(%d) = %d\n", 8, clamp(8, low, high));
    printf("clamp(%d) = %d\n", 113, clamp(113, low, high));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: clamp() takes three parameters: the value and the two limits. It returns
   low when the value is too small, high when it is too big and the value itself otherwise.
   main() declares low = 54 and high = 98 on one line and clamps 0, 8 and 113. */
// END

/* Caption: Compare 2 numbers and print the larger. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Read a and b.
   2. Pick the bigger of a and b.
   3. Print it. */
int main(void) {
    double a, b;
    printf("Enter 2 numbers: ");
    if (scanf("%lf %lf", &a, &b) != 2) {
        printf("Invalid input\n");
        return 1;
    }
    double best = (a > b) ? a : b;   /* the ?: operator picks one of two values */
    printf("The larger is %.2f\n", best);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: The program reads a and b from the keyboard with scanf and stops with a
   message if the input is not valid. The conditional operator (a > b) ? a : b picks the
   bigger value, which is printed. */
// END

/* Caption: Generate the Fibonacci sequence. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Start with a = 0 and b = 1.
   2. Repeat 18 times and print a each time.
   3. Compute next = a + b, then set a = b and b = next. */
int main(void) {
    long a = 0, b = 1;
    /* Print a term, then slide the pair one step along the sequence. */
    for (int i = 0; i < 18; i++) {
        printf("%ld ", a);
        long next = a + b;
        a = b;
        b = next;
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: The loop keeps the last two numbers in a and b. Each round it prints a,
   then moves the pair forward: a becomes b and b becomes their sum. It prints the first 18
   Fibonacci numbers. */
// END

/* Caption: Program to return two values from a function using pointer parameters. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write min_max() with the array, its length and the pointers min and max.
   2. Start both at the first element.
   3. Update *min and *max while looping over the rest.
   4. Declare smallest and largest, pass their addresses and print them. */
/* One pass finds both results; they are stored through the pointers. */
void min_max(const int ages[], int n, int *min, int *max) {
    *min = ages[0];
    *max = ages[0];
    for (int i = 1; i < n; i++) {
        if (ages[i] < *min) {
            *min = ages[i];
        }
        if (ages[i] > *max) {
            *max = ages[i];
        }
    }
}

int main(void) {
    int ages[] = {6, 81, 62, 41, 51};
    const int n = 5;
    int smallest, largest;
    min_max(ages, n, &smallest, &largest);
    printf("Min: %d, Max: %d\n", smallest, largest);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: A C function can return only one value, so min_max() returns void and
   writes its two results through the pointer parameters min and max. main() declares
   smallest and largest on one line and passes their addresses with &, then prints both
   results for the 5 values. */
// END

/* Caption: Count how many odd numbers are in an array. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write count_odd() that takes readings and n.
   2. For each element, test readings[j] % 2 != 0.
   3. Add one to tally for every odd number.
   4. Return tally and print it. */
/* A number is odd when the remainder after dividing by 2 is one. */
int count_odd(const int readings[], int n) {
    int tally = 0;
    for (int j = 0; j < n; j++) {
        if (readings[j] % 2 != 0) {
            tally++;
        }
    }
    return tally;
}

int main(void) {
    int readings[] = {77, 70, 97, 55, 24, 44, 86, 82};
    int n = sizeof(readings) / sizeof(readings[0]);
    printf("Count of odd values = %d\n", count_odd(readings, n));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: count_odd() tests each element of readings with the % operator: a remainder
   of 1 after dividing by 2 means the number is odd, so tally goes up by one. main() prints
   how many of the 8 values are odd. */
// END

/* Caption: How do I find the smallest number in an array in C? */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write find_min() that takes samples and len.
   2. Store samples[0] in m.
   3. Loop over the other elements and keep the smallest value in m.
   4. Return m and print it. */
/* Start with the first element and keep the smallest value seen so far. */
double find_min(const double samples[], int len) {
    double m = samples[0];
    for (int i = 1; i < len; i++) {
        if (samples[i] < m) {
            m = samples[i];
        }
    }
    return m;
}

int main(void) {
    double samples[] = {46.7, 42.1, 70.5, 71.3, 53.9, 46.6, 65.8, 37.5};
    int len = 8;
    printf("Smallest: %.2f\n", find_min(samples, len));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: find_min() takes the first element as the smallest value so far and stores
   it in m. The loop compares every other element with m using < and keeps the smallest
   one. main() prints the smallest of the 8 values. */
// END

/* Caption: Declare several variables on one line without initial values. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Declare count, total and i on one line without values.
   2. Set count = 5 and total = 0.
   3. Add the squares of 1 to count to total and print it. */
int main(void) {
    int count, total, i;   /* declared now, given values below */
    count = 5;
    total = 0;
    for (i = 1; i <= count; i++) {
        total += i * i;
    }
    printf("Sum of the first %d squares: %d\n", count, total);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: count, total and i are declared together on one line without values, then
   assigned before they are used, because an uninitialised local variable holds garbage.
   The loop adds the squares of 1 to 5 to total. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to compute the mean of a list of numbers. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write mean() that takes scores and n.
   2. Add the values into the double result.
   3. Return result / n.
   4. Print the average with two decimals. */
/* Sum the values, then divide by how many there are. */
double mean(const double scores[], int n) {
    double result = 0.0;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        result += scores[i];
    }
    return result / n;
}

int main(void) {
    double scores[] = {74.3, 1.4, 8.9, 34.5, 49.7};
    int n = sizeof(scores) / sizeof(scores[0]);
    printf("The average is %.2f\n", mean(scores, n));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: mean() adds the 5 values of scores into the double result and divides by n,
   so the mean keeps its decimal part even when the values are whole numbers. main() prints
   it with two decimals. */
// END

/* Caption: Implement a simple linked list with malloc and free. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define Item with a value and a next pointer.
   2. Write push_front() that mallocs a node and links it in front of head.
   3. Write print_list() that follows next until NULL.
   4. Write free_list() that frees every node.
   5. Push 5 values, print the list and free it. */
typedef struct Item {
    int value;
    struct Item *next;
} Item;

/* Allocate a new node and put it in front of the current head. */
Item *push_front(Item *head, int value) {
    Item *node = malloc(sizeof(Item));
    if (node == NULL) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Out of memory\n");
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }
    node->value = value;
    node->next = head;
    return node;
}

void print_list(const Item *head) {
    for (const Item *cur = head; cur != NULL; cur = cur->next) {
        printf("%d -> ", cur->value);
    }
    printf("NULL\n");
}

/* Free every node; save next before freeing the current one. */
void free_list(Item *head) {
    while (head != NULL) {
        Item *next = head->next;
        free(head);
        head = next;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    Item *head = NULL;
    head = push_front(head, 50);
    head = push_front(head, 10);
    head = push_front(head, 29);
    head = push_front(head, 42);
    head = push_front(head, 84);
    print_list(head);
    free_list(head);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: Each Item holds a value and a pointer to the next node. push_front()
   allocates a node with malloc, puts it in front of head and returns it; print_list()
   follows the next pointers until NULL; free_list() frees every node. main() pushes 5
   values, so they print in reverse order. */
// END

/* Explanation: The program uses fixed values for a and b. It checks that b is not zero,

// END

/* Caption: Sort an array in ascending order using bubble sort. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write bubble_sort() for the int array items.
   2. Compare each pair of neighbours.
   3. Swap them when they are in the wrong order for ascending order.
   4. Repeat the passes until the array is sorted.
   5. Print the sorted values. */
/* Repeatedly swap neighbours that are in the wrong order. */
void bubble_sort(int items[], int length) {
    for (int i = 0; i < length - 1; i++) {
        for (int j = 0; j < length - 1 - i; j++) {
            if (items[j] > items[j + 1]) {
                int tmp = items[j];
                items[j] = items[j + 1];
                items[j + 1] = tmp;
            }
        }
    }
}

int main(void) {
    int items[] = {36, 82, 62, 32, 63, 15};
    int length = 6;
    bubble_sort(items, length);
    for (int i = 0; i < length; i++) {
        printf("%d ", items[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: bubble_sort() walks through items again and again and swaps neighbours that
   are in the wrong order, so the largest values move to the end first. main() then prints
   the 6 values in ascending order. */
// END

/* Caption: Print all prime numbers up to 103. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write is_prime(n); numbers below 2 are not prime.
   2. Try every divisor d while d * d <= n.
   3. Return false if one divides n, otherwise true.
   4. Print every prime from 2 to 103. */
/* A prime has no divisor between 2 and its square root. */
bool is_prime(int n) {
    if (n < 2) {
        return false;
    }
    for (int d = 2; d * d <= n; d++) {
        if (n % d == 0) {
            return false;
        }
    }
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    for (int n = 2; n <= 103; n++) {
        if (is_prime(n)) {
            printf("%d ", n);
        }
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: is_prime() tries every divisor d from 2 while d * d <= n; if one divides n
   evenly, n is not prime. main() tests every number from 2 to 103 and prints the primes. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to declare two pointers in one statement and use them. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Declare x and y on one line.
   2. Declare the pointers px and py on one line, each with its own *.
   3. Add 17 to x through px and print the values. */
int main(void) {
    int x = 11, y = 25;
    /* Each pointer needs its own '*': in "int *p, q;" only p is a pointer. */
    int *px = &x, *py = &y;
    *px += 17;
    printf("x = %d, y = %d\n", x, y);
    printf("*px = %d, *py = %d\n", *px, *py);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: int *px = &x, *py = &y; declares two pointers in one statement; each name
   needs its own *. *px += 17 changes x through the pointer, so x becomes 28 while y stays
   25. */
// END

/* Caption: Test if 50 is a prime number. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write is_prime(n); numbers below 2 are not prime.
   2. Try every divisor d while d * d <= n.
   3. Return false if one divides n, otherwise true.
   4. Check 50 and print the result. */
/* A prime has no divisor between 2 and its square root. */
bool is_prime(int n) {
    if (n < 2) {
        return false;
    }
    for (int d = 2; d * d <= n; d++) {
        if (n % d == 0) {
            return false;
        }
    }
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    int number = 50;
    printf("%d %s prime\n", number, is_prime(number) ? "is" : "is not");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: is_prime() tries every divisor d from 2 while d * d <= n; if one divides n
   evenly, n is not prime. main() checks 50 and prints whether it is prime. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to build a linked list, print it, and free it. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define Node with a value and a next pointer.
   2. Write push_front() that mallocs a node and links it in front of head.
   3. Write print_list() that follows next until NULL.
   4. Write free_list() that frees every node.
   5. Push 6 values, print the list and free it. */
typedef struct Node {
    int value;
    struct Node *next;
} Node;

/* Allocate a new node and put it in front of the current head. */
Node *push_front(Node *head, int value) {
    Node *node = malloc(sizeof(Node));
    if (node == NULL) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Out of memory\n");
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }
    node->value = value;
    node->next = head;
    return node;
}

void print_list(const Node *head) {
    for (const Node *cur = head; cur != NULL; cur = cur->next) {
        printf("%d -> ", cur->value);
    }
    printf("NULL\n");
}

/* Free every node; save next before freeing the current one. */
void free_list(Node *head) {
    while (head != NULL) {
        Node *next = head->next;
        free(head);
        head = next;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    Node *head = NULL;
    head = push_front(head, 16);
    head = push_front(head, 21);
    head = push_front(head, 44);
    head = push_front(head, 41);
    head = push_front(head, 61);
    head = push_front(head, 4);
    print_list(head);
    free_list(head);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: Each Node holds a value and a pointer to the next node. push_front()
   allocates a node with malloc, puts it in front of head and returns it; print_list()
   follows the next pointers until NULL; free_list() frees every node. main() pushes 6
   values, so they print in reverse order. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to add two matrices element by element. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define ROWS as 3 and COLS as 2.
   2. Loop over every row r and column c.
   3. Store a[r][c] + b[r][c] in sum and print it. */
#define ROWS 3
#define COLS 2

int main(void) {
    int a[ROWS][COLS] = {{9, 5}, {2, 1}, {6, 8}};
    int b[ROWS][COLS] = {{2, 6}, {9, 1}, {1, 2}};
    int sum[ROWS][COLS];
    /* Each entry of the result is the sum of the matching entries. */
    for (int r = 0; r < ROWS; r++) {
        for (int c = 0; c < COLS; c++) {
            sum[r][c] = a[r][c] + b[r][c];
            printf("%3d", sum[r][c]);
        }
        printf("\n");
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: Both matrices are 3x2 two-dimensional arrays. Two nested loops visit every
   row r and column c, store a[r][c] + b[r][c] in sum and print each row. */
// END

   3. Print the result. */
int main(void) {

    int sum = n * (n + 1) / 2;
    printf("Sum of 1 to %d = %d\n", n, sum);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: Instead of a loop it uses Gauss's formula n * (n + 1) / 2, which gives the
   sum of 1 to 71 in one step. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to count the occurrences of a character in a sentence. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write count_char() with count = 0.
   2. Compare each character with the target a.
   3. Return count and print it. */
int count_char(const char *text, char target) {
    int count = 0;
    /* Compare every character with the target. */
    for (int i = 0; text[i] != '\0'; i++) {
        if (text[i] == target) {
            count++;
        }
    }
    return count;
}

int main(void) {
    const char *sentence = "arrays in c start at index zero";
    printf("'a' appears %d times\n", count_char(sentence, 'a'));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: count_char() compares every character of the text with the target character
   and counts the matches. main() prints how many times a appears in the sentence. */
// END

/* Caption: How do I compute 8 to the power of 8 without pow() in C? */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write power(base, exp) with result = 1.
   2. Multiply result by base exp times.
   3. Print 8 to the power 8. */
/* Multiply the base by itself exp times. */
long long power(int base, int exp) {
    long long result = 1;
    for (int i = 0; i < exp; i++) {
        result *= base;
    }
    return result;
}

int main(void) {
    printf("8^8 = %lld\n", power(8, 8));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: power() starts result at 1 and multiplies it by base exp times. It uses
   long long because powers grow quickly. main() prints 8 to the power 8. */
// END

/* Caption: Implement insertion sort for an array of long values. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write insertion_sort() for the long array prices.
   2. Take each element in turn as current.
   3. Shift the larger values of the sorted part one place right.
   4. Put current into the gap.
   5. Print the sorted values. */
/* Insert each element into the already sorted part on its left. */
void insertion_sort(long prices[], int size) {
    for (int i = 1; i < size; i++) {
        long current = prices[i];
        int j = i - 1;
        while (j >= 0 && prices[j] > current) {
            prices[j + 1] = prices[j];   /* shift bigger values right */
            j--;
        }
        prices[j + 1] = current;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    long prices[] = {7L, 71L, 7L, 98L, 40L, 47L, 72L, 84L, 65L, 21L};
    const int size = 10;
    insertion_sort(prices, size);
    for (int i = 0; i < size; i++) {
        printf("%ld ", prices[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}

/* Caption: Write a C program to reverse the characters of a word. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <string.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write reverse_string() for word.
   2. Set i to the first index and j to the last.
   3. Swap the two characters and move i and j inwards until they meet.
   4. Reverse window and print it. */
/* Swap characters from both ends until they meet in the middle. */
void reverse_string(char *word) {
    int i = 0;
    int j = strlen(word) - 1;
    while (i < j) {
        char tmp = word[i];
        word[i] = word[j];
        word[j] = tmp;
        i++;
        j--;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    char word[] = "window";
    reverse_string(word);
    printf("%s\n", word);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: reverse_string() swaps characters from both ends of word, moving inwards
   until the two indexes meet. main() reverses the word window in place and prints it. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to create a singly linked list by inserting at the head. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define Item with a value and a next pointer.
   2. Write push_front() that mallocs a node and links it in front of head.
   3. Write print_list() that follows next until NULL.
   4. Write free_list() that frees every node.
   5. Push 3 values, print the list and free it. */
typedef struct Item {
    int value;
    struct Item *next;
} Item;

/* Allocate a new node and put it in front of the current head. */
Item *push_front(Item *head, int value) {
    Item *node = malloc(sizeof(Item));
    if (node == NULL) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Out of memory\n");
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }
    node->value = value;
    node->next = head;
    return node;
}

void print_list(const Item *head) {
    for (const Item *cur = head; cur != NULL; cur = cur->next) {
        printf("%d -> ", cur->value);
    }
    printf("NULL\n");
}

/* Free every node; save next before freeing the current one. */
void free_list(Item *head) {
    while (head != NULL) {
        Item *next = head->next;
        free(head);
        head = next;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    Item *head = NULL;
    head = push_front(head, 59);
    head = push_front(head, 99);
    head = push_front(head, 23);
    print_list(head);
    free_list(head);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: Each Item holds a value and a pointer to the next node. push_front()
   allocates a node with malloc, puts it in front of head and returns it; print_list()
   follows the next pointers until NULL; free_list() frees every node. main() pushes 3
   values, so they print in reverse order. */
// END

/* Caption: How do I copy one string into another by hand in C? */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write copy_string(dest, src).
   2. Copy src into dest one character at a time.
   3. Stop after copying the null character.
   4. Copy refer into text and print it. */
/* Copy each character, including the final '\0'. */
void copy_string(char *dest, const char *src) {
    int i = 0;
    while ((dest[i] = src[i]) != '\0') {
        i++;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    char source[] = "refer";
    char text[64];
    copy_string(text, source);
    printf("Copied: %s\n", text);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: copy_string() copies src into dest one character at a time, including the
   final null character, which is what strcpy does. The array text must be big enough to
   hold the copy. main() copies the word refer and prints it. */
// END

/* Caption: How do I build a FIFO queue using a ring buffer in C? */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define a Queue with room for 16 items, a head and a count.
   2. Write enqueue() that stores at (head + count) % CAPACITY.
   3. Write dequeue() that takes the item at head and moves head on.
   4. Add 3 values, then remove and print them in order. */
#define CAPACITY 16

typedef struct {
    int items[CAPACITY];
    int head;
    int count;
} Queue;

bool enqueue(Queue *q, int value) {
    if (q->count == CAPACITY) {
        return false;
    }
    /* The tail wraps around to the start of the array. */
    q->items[(q->head + q->count) % CAPACITY] = value;
    q->count++;
    return true;
}

bool dequeue(Queue *q, int *value) {
    if (q->count == 0) {
        return false;
    }
    *value = q->items[q->head];
    q->head = (q->head + 1) % CAPACITY;
    q->count--;
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    Queue q = {.head = 0, .count = 0};
    enqueue(&q, 68);
    enqueue(&q, 40);
    enqueue(&q, 21);
    int value;
    /* Items come out in the order they went in (first in, first out). */
    while (dequeue(&q, &value)) {
        printf("%d ", value);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: The Queue stores up to 16 items in a ring buffer: head is the oldest item
   and % CAPACITY wraps positions back to the start of the array. enqueue() adds at the
   back and dequeue() removes from the front, so main() gets its 3 values back in the same
   order (first in, first out). */
// END

/* Caption: C program to count how many even numbers are in an array. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write count_even() that takes marks and n.
   2. For each element, test marks[j] % 2 == 0.
   3. Add one to tally for every even number.

/* A number is even when the remainder after dividing by 2 is zero. */
int count_even(const int marks[], int n) {
    int tally = 0;
    int j = 0;

}
/* Explanation: count_even() tests each element of marks with the % operator: a remainder
   of 0 after dividing by 2 means the number is even, so tally goes up by one. main()
   prints how many of the 5 values are even. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to sort an array in descending order using insertion sort. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write insertion_sort() for the int array data.
   2. Take each element in turn as current.
   3. Shift the smaller values of the sorted part one place right.
   4. Put current into the gap.
   5. Print the sorted values. */
/* Insert each element into the already sorted part on its left. */
void insertion_sort(int data[], int count) {
    for (int i = 1; i < count; i++) {
        int current = data[i];
        int j = i - 1;
        while (j >= 0 && data[j] < current) {
            data[j + 1] = data[j];   /* shift bigger values right */
            j--;
        }
        data[j + 1] = current;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    int data[] = {86, 99, 8, 96, 13, 28, 20};
    const int count = 7;
    insertion_sort(data, count);
    for (int i = 0; i < count; i++) {
        printf("%d ", data[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: insertion_sort() takes each element in turn and shifts the smaller values
   of the sorted part one place right until the element fits. main() then prints the 7
   values in descending order. */
// END

/* Caption: How do I reverse an array by swapping from both ends in C? */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write reverse_array() for ages.
   2. Set left to the first index and right to the last.
   3. Swap ages[left] and ages[right], then move both inwards.
   4. Stop when left meets right and print the array. */
/* Swap the outer pair, then move both ends toward the middle. */
void reverse_array(long ages[], int size) {
    int left = 0;
    int right = size - 1;
    while (left < right) {
        long tmp = ages[left];
        ages[left] = ages[right];
        ages[right] = tmp;
        left++;
        right--;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    long ages[] = {77L, 80L, 59L, 29L, 63L, 36L, 75L, 71L};
    int size = 8;
    reverse_array(ages, size);
    for (int i = 0; i < size; i++) {
        printf("%ld ", ages[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: reverse_array() swaps the first and last elements, then moves left forward
   and right backward until they meet, so the array is reversed in place without a second
   array. main() prints the reversed values. */
// END

/* Caption: C program to implement selection sort for an array of long values. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write selection_sort() for the long array prices.
   2. For each position, find the smallest remaining element.
   3. Swap it into that position.
   4. Print the sorted values. */
/* Select the right element for each position and swap it into place. */
void selection_sort(long prices[], int len) {
    for (int i = 0; i < len - 1; i++) {
        int chosen = i;
        for (int j = i + 1; j < len; j++) {
            if (prices[chosen] > prices[j]) {
                chosen = j;
            }
        }
        long tmp = prices[i];
        prices[i] = prices[chosen];
        prices[chosen] = tmp;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    long prices[] = {55L, 69L, 15L, 83L, 47L, 10L, 73L};
    int len = 7;
    selection_sort(prices, len);
    for (int i = 0; i < len; i++) {
        printf("%ld ", prices[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: selection_sort() finds the smallest remaining element for each position and
   swaps it into place. main() then prints the 7 values in ascending order. */
// END

/* Caption: C program to compute the mean of a list of numbers. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write mean() that takes marks and length.
   2. Add the values into the double acc.
   3. Return acc / length.
   4. Print the average with two decimals. */
/* Sum the values, then divide by how many there are. */
double mean(const long marks[], int length) {
    double acc = 0.0;
    int k = 0;
    while (k < length) {
        acc += marks[k];
        k++;
    }
    return acc / length;
}

int main(void) {
    long marks[] = {21L, 92L, 86L, 44L};
    int length = sizeof(marks) / sizeof(marks[0]);
    printf("Mean = %.2f\n", mean(marks, length));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: mean() adds the 4 values of marks into the double acc and divides by
   length, so the mean keeps its decimal part even when the values are whole numbers.
   main() prints it with two decimals. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to convert 2 to binary. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write print_binary(n, bits).
   2. Go through the bits from the highest to the lowest.
   3. Print 1 when (n >> b) & 1 is set, otherwise 0.
   4. Print 2 in binary. */
/* Check each bit from the highest to the lowest. */
void print_binary(unsigned int n, int bits) {
    for (int b = bits - 1; b >= 0; b--) {
        putchar((n >> b) & 1 ? '1' : '0');
    }
    putchar('\n');
}

int main(void) {
    unsigned int number = 2;
    printf("%u in binary: ", number);
    print_binary(number, 10);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: print_binary() checks one bit at a time, from the highest to the lowest: (n
   >> b) & 1 is 1 when bit b is set, so it prints the character 1 or 0. main() prints 2 in
   binary. */
// END

/* Caption: Reverse a string in place. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <string.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write reverse_string() for text.
   2. Set i to the first index and j to the last.
   3. Swap the two characters and move i and j inwards until they meet.
   4. Reverse matrix and print it. */
/* Swap characters from both ends until they meet in the middle. */
void reverse_string(char *text) {
    int i = 0;
    int j = strlen(text) - 1;
    while (i < j) {
        char tmp = text[i];
        text[i] = text[j];
        text[j] = tmp;
        i++;
        j--;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    char text[] = "matrix";
    reverse_string(text);
    printf("%s\n", text);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: reverse_string() swaps characters from both ends of text, moving inwards
   until the two indexes meet. main() reverses the word matrix in place and prints it. */
// END

/* Caption: How do I find the greatest common divisor of two numbers in C? */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write gcd() with Euclid's algorithm.
   2. Replace (a, b) by (b, a % b) until b is 0.
   3. Return a and print the GCD of 230 and 208. */
/* Euclid: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a % b) until b becomes zero. */
int gcd(int a, int b) {
    while (b != 0) {
        int r = a % b;
        a = b;
        b = r;
    }
    return a;
}

int main(void) {
    int x = 230, y = 208;
    printf("gcd(%d, %d) = %d\n", x, y, gcd(x, y));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: gcd() uses Euclid's algorithm: it keeps replacing (a, b) with (b, a % b)
   until b is 0. The last non-zero value is the greatest common divisor, and main() prints
   the GCD of 230 and 208. */
// END

/* Caption: Declare two pointers in one statement and use them. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Declare x and y on one line.
   2. Declare the pointers px and py on one line, each with its own *.
   3. Add 14 to x through px and print the values. */
int main(void) {
    int x = 42, y = 18;
    /* Each pointer needs its own '*': in "int *p, q;" only p is a pointer. */
    int *px = &x, *py = &y;
    *px += 14;
    printf("x = %d, y = %d\n", x, y);
    printf("*px = %d, *py = %d\n", *px, *py);
    return 0;

/* Caption: Write a program to reverse the characters of a word. */

#include <string.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write reverse_string() for str.
   2. Set i to the first index and j to the last.
   3. Swap the two characters and move i and j inwards until they meet.
   4. Reverse stats and print it. */
/* Swap characters from both ends until they meet in the middle. */
void reverse_string(char *str) {
    int i = 0;
    int j = strlen(str) - 1;

/* Caption: Reverse the elements of an array in place. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write reverse_array() for samples.
   2. Set i to the first index and j to the last.
   3. Swap samples[i] and samples[j], then move both inwards.
   4. Stop when i meets j and print the array. */
/* Swap the outer pair, then move both ends toward the middle. */
void reverse_array(long samples[], int count) {
    int i = 0;
    int j = count - 1;
    while (i < j) {
        long tmp = samples[i];
        samples[i] = samples[j];
        samples[j] = tmp;
        i++;
        j--;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    long samples[] = {12L, 75L, 21L, 49L, 44L, 5L, 65L};
    int count = sizeof(samples) / sizeof(samples[0]);
    reverse_array(samples, count);
    for (int i = 0; i < count; i++) {
        printf("%ld ", samples[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: reverse_array() swaps the first and last elements, then moves i forward and
   j backward until they meet, so the array is reversed in place without a second array.
   main() prints the reversed values. */
// END

/* Caption: Change every letter in a sentence to a capital letter. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <ctype.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write to_upper() for word.
   2. Replace every character with toupper() until the null character.
   3. Print the sentence. */
/* toupper changes lowercase letters and leaves other characters alone. */
void to_upper(char *word) {
    for (int i = 0; word[i] != '\0'; i++) {
        word[i] = toupper((unsigned char)word[i]);
    }
}

int main(void) {
    char word[] = "every program starts in main";
    to_upper(word);
    printf("%s\n", word);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: to_upper() walks through word until the null character and replaces each
   character with toupper(), which only changes lowercase letters. main() prints the
   sentence in capitals. */
// END

/* Caption: Test if "planet" reads the same backwards. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <string.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write is_palindrome() for line.
   2. Compare the first and last characters, moving inwards.
   3. Return false at the first mismatch, otherwise true.
   4. Check planet and print the result. */
/* Compare characters from the front and back, moving inwards. */
bool is_palindrome(const char *line) {
    int i = 0;
    int j = strlen(line) - 1;
    while (i < j) {
        if (line[i] != line[j]) {
            return false;
        }
        i++;
        j--;
    }
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    const char *line = "planet";
    printf("%s %s a palindrome\n", line, is_palindrome(line) ? "is" : "is not");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: is_palindrome() compares the first and last characters and moves inwards;
   any mismatch means the word is not a palindrome. main() checks the word planet and
   prints the result. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a function that swaps two int values through pointers. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write swap() that takes pointers to two int values.
   2. Save *x in tmp, copy *y into *x, then tmp into *y.
   3. In main(), print x and y, call swap(&x, &y) and print them again. */
/* Pass addresses so the function can change the caller's variables. */
void swap(int *x, int *y) {
    int tmp = *x;
    *x = *y;
    *y = tmp;
}

int main(void) {
    int x = 23, y = 76;
    printf("Before: %d %d\n", x, y);
    swap(&x, &y);
    printf("After:  %d %d\n", x, y);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: swap() receives the addresses of x and y, so writing through the pointers
   *x and *y changes the caller's variables. tmp holds one value during the exchange.
   main() declares both variables on one line and prints them before and after the swap. */
// END

void split_seconds(int total, int *hours, int *minutes, int *seconds) {
    *hours = total / 3600;

    *seconds = total % 60;

    return 0;
}

   3600, minutes is what is left divided by 60, and seconds is total % 60. main() declares
   h, m and s on one line and converts 67650 seconds. */
// END

/* Caption: C program to allocate an array with malloc and fill it with evens. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Use malloc to get room for 7 ints and check for NULL.
   2. Fill table with evens.
   3. Print the values.
   4. Call free(table) at the end. */
int main(void) {
    int n = 7;
    /* Ask the heap for room for n ints; malloc returns NULL on failure. */
    int *table = malloc(n * sizeof(int));
    if (table == NULL) {
        fprintf(stderr, "malloc failed\n");
        return 1;
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        table[i] = 2 * i;
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        printf("%d ", table[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    free(table);   /* give the memory back */
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: malloc() reserves room for 7 ints on the heap and returns NULL if it fails,
   which the program checks. The first loop fills table with evens, the second prints them,
   and free() gives the memory back at the end. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to use selection sort to put numbers in descending order. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write selection_sort() for the int array scores.
   2. For each position, find the largest remaining element.
   3. Swap it into that position.
   4. Print the sorted values. */
/* Select the right element for each position and swap it into place. */
void selection_sort(int scores[], int count) {
    for (int i = 0; i < count - 1; i++) {
        int chosen = i;
        for (int j = i + 1; j < count; j++) {
            if (scores[chosen] < scores[j]) {
                chosen = j;
            }
        }
        int tmp = scores[i];
        scores[i] = scores[chosen];
        scores[chosen] = tmp;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    int scores[] = {68, 93, 32, 46, 41, 82, 95, 26, 61, 34};
    int count = 10;
    selection_sort(scores, count);
    for (int i = 0; i < count; i++) {
        printf("%d ", scores[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: selection_sort() finds the largest remaining element for each position and
   swaps it into place. main() then prints the 10 values in descending order. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to show the right way to declare several pointers on one line. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Declare x and y on one line.
   2. Declare the pointers px and py on one line, each with its own *.
   3. Add 19 to x through px and print the values. */
int main(void) {
    int x = 46, y = 16;
    /* Each pointer needs its own '*': in "int *p, q;" only p is a pointer. */
    int *px = &x, *py = &y;
    *px += 19;
    printf("x = %d, y = %d\n", x, y);
    printf("*px = %d, *py = %d\n", *px, *py);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: int *px = &x, *py = &y; declares two pointers in one statement; each name
   needs its own *. *px += 19 changes x through the pointer, so x becomes 65 while y stays
   16. */
// END

   3. Print the result. */

    int n = 5;

/* Caption: Write a C program to save text to a file with fprintf and print it with fgets. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Open output.txt in write mode and check for NULL.
   2. Write 4 lines with fprintf and close the file.
   3. Open it again in read mode.
   4. Read and print each line with fgets, then close the file. */
int main(void) {
    FILE *file = fopen("output.txt", "w");
    if (file == NULL) {
        perror("fopen");
        return 1;
    }
    fprintf(file, "c gives you direct control over memory\n");
    fprintf(file, "the quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog\n");
    fprintf(file, "strings end with a null character\n");
    fprintf(file, "keep functions short and focused\n");
    fclose(file);

    /* Reopen the file for reading and print it line by line. */
    file = fopen("output.txt", "r");
    if (file == NULL) {
        perror("fopen");
        return 1;
    }
    char line[128];
    while (fgets(line, sizeof(line), file) != NULL) {
        printf("%s", line);
    }
    fclose(file);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: fopen() in write mode creates output.txt, fprintf() writes 4 lines into it
   and fclose() saves it. The file is then opened again in read mode, and fgets() reads it
   back line by line into the buffer line, which is printed. Every fopen() result is
   checked for NULL. */
// END

/* Caption: Return two values from a function using pointer parameters. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write divide(a, b, &quotient, &remainder) that returns a bool.
   2. Return false if b is 0.
   3. Store a / b and a % b through the pointers and return true.
   4. Divide 289 by 21 and print the results or the error. */
/* Returns false for division by zero; otherwise stores both results. */
bool divide(int a, int b, int *quotient, int *remainder) {
    if (b == 0) {
        return false;
    }
    *quotient = a / b;
    *remainder = a % b;
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    int a = 289, b = 21;
    int q, r;
    if (divide(a, b, &q, &r)) {
        printf("%d / %d = %d remainder %d\n", a, b, q, r);
    } else {
        printf("Cannot divide by zero\n");
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: divide() has four parameters: two inputs and two pointers for the results.
   Its bool return value reports success, while the quotient and remainder are written
   through the pointers. main() divides 289 by 21 and prints both results. */
// END

/* Caption: Program to reverse the elements of an array in place. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write reverse_array() for samples.
   2. Set start to the first index and end to the last.
   3. Swap samples[start] and samples[end], then move both inwards.
   4. Stop when start meets end and print the array. */
/* Swap the outer pair, then move both ends toward the middle. */
void reverse_array(int samples[], int size) {
    int start = 0;
    int end = size - 1;
    while (start < end) {
        int tmp = samples[start];
        samples[start] = samples[end];
        samples[end] = tmp;
        start++;
        end--;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    int samples[] = {99, 96, 96, 52, 83, 64, 94, 49};
    int size = sizeof(samples) / sizeof(samples[0]);
    reverse_array(samples, size);
    for (int i = 0; i < size; i++) {
        printf("%d ", samples[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: reverse_array() swaps the first and last elements, then moves start forward
   and end backward until they meet, so the array is reversed in place without a second
   array. main() prints the reversed values. */
// END

/* Caption: Count the characters in a string. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write string_length() with a counter len = 0.
   2. Move through the string until the null character.
   3. Return len and print the length of binary. */
/* Count characters until the terminating '\0'. */
int string_length(const char *word) {
    int len = 0;
    while (word[len] != '\0') {
        len++;
    }
    return len;
}

int main(void) {
    const char *word = "binary";
    printf("Length of \"%s\" is %d\n", word, string_length(word));
    return 0;
}

   ends every C string. main() prints the length of the word binary. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to return both the smallest and the largest value of an array through pointers. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write min_max() with the array, its length and the pointers min and max.
   2. Start both at the first element.
   3. Update *min and *max while looping over the rest.
   4. Declare lowest and highest, pass their addresses and print them. */
/* One pass finds both results; they are stored through the pointers. */
void min_max(const int readings[], int len, int *min, int *max) {
    *min = readings[0];
    *max = readings[0];
    for (int i = 1; i < len; i++) {
        if (readings[i] < *min) {
            *min = readings[i];
        }
        if (readings[i] > *max) {
            *max = readings[i];
        }
    }
}

int main(void) {
    int readings[] = {87, 8, 14, 98, 10, 32, 18, 76};
    int len = sizeof(readings) / sizeof(readings[0]);
    int lowest, highest;
    min_max(readings, len, &lowest, &highest);
    printf("Min: %d, Max: %d\n", lowest, highest);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: A C function can return only one value, so min_max() returns void and
   writes its two results through the pointer parameters min and max. main() declares
   lowest and highest on one line and passes their addresses with &, then prints both
   results for the 8 values. */
// END

/* Caption: Program to keep a value inside the limits low and high. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write clamp(value, low, high).
   2. Return low if the value is too small and high if it is too big.
   3. Otherwise return the value.
   4. Set low = 38 and high = 69 and print clamp() for 90, 44 and 2. */
/* Return value, but never less than low or more than high. */
int clamp(int value, int low, int high) {
    if (value < low) {
        return low;
    }
    if (value > high) {
        return high;
    }
    return value;
}

int main(void) {
    int low = 38, high = 69;
    printf("clamp(%d) = %d\n", 90, clamp(90, low, high));
    printf("clamp(%d) = %d\n", 44, clamp(44, low, high));
    printf("clamp(%d) = %d\n", 2, clamp(2, low, high));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: clamp() takes three parameters: the value and the two limits. It returns
   low when the value is too small, high when it is too big and the value itself otherwise.
   main() declares low = 38 and high = 69 on one line and clamps 90, 44 and 2. */
// END

   how many of the 5 values are odd. */

/* Caption: Use dynamic memory to store the first 15 cubes. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Use malloc to get room for 15 ints and check for NULL.
   2. Fill buffer with cubes.
   3. Print the values.
   4. Call free(buffer) at the end. */
int main(void) {
    int n = 15;
    /* Ask the heap for room for n ints; malloc returns NULL on failure. */
    int *buffer = malloc(n * sizeof(int));
    if (buffer == NULL) {
        fprintf(stderr, "malloc failed\n");
        return 1;
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        buffer[i] = i * i * i;
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        printf("%d ", buffer[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    free(buffer);   /* give the memory back */
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: malloc() reserves room for 15 ints on the heap and returns NULL if it
   fails, which the program checks. The first loop fills buffer with cubes, the second
   prints them, and free() gives the memory back at the end. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to use Euclid's algorithm to compute the GCD. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write gcd() with Euclid's algorithm.
   2. Replace (a, b) by (b, a % b) until b is 0.
   3. Return a and print the GCD of 260 and 291. */
/* Euclid: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a % b) until b becomes zero. */
int gcd(int a, int b) {
    while (b != 0) {
        int r = a % b;
        a = b;
        b = r;
    }
    return a;
}

int main(void) {
    int x = 260, y = 291;
    printf("gcd(%d, %d) = %d\n", x, y, gcd(x, y));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: gcd() uses Euclid's algorithm: it keeps replacing (a, b) with (b, a % b)
   until b is 0. The last non-zero value is the greatest common divisor, and main() prints
   the GCD of 260 and 291. */
// END

/* Caption: List the prime numbers below a limit. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write is_prime(n); numbers below 2 are not prime.
   2. Try every divisor d while d * d <= n.
   3. Return false if one divides n, otherwise true.
   4. Print every prime from 2 to 82. */
/* A prime has no divisor between 2 and its square root. */
bool is_prime(int n) {
    if (n < 2) {
        return false;
    }
    for (int d = 2; d * d <= n; d++) {
        if (n % d == 0) {
            return false;
        }
    }
    return true;
}

    for (int n = 2; n <= 82; n++) {
        if (is_prime(n)) {
            printf("%d ", n);
        }
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: is_prime() tries every divisor d from 2 while d * d <= n; if one divides n
   evenly, n is not prime. main() tests every number from 2 to 82 and prints the primes. */
// END

/* Caption: Find the arithmetic mean of 5 double values. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write average() that takes items and n.
   2. Add the values into the double result.
   3. Return result / n.
   4. Print the average with two decimals. */
/* The mean is the total divided by the count. */
double average(const double items[], int n) {
    double result = 0.0;
    int idx = 0;
    while (idx < n) {
        result += items[idx];
        idx++;
    }
    return result / n;
}

int main(void) {
    double items[] = {90.9, 87.3, 66.7, 48.5, 13.6};
    int n = 5;
    printf("Mean = %.2f\n", average(items, n));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: average() adds the 5 values of items into the double result and divides by
   n, so the mean keeps its decimal part even when the values are whole numbers. main()
   prints it with two decimals. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a function that swaps two long values through pointers. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write swap() that takes pointers to two long values.
   2. Save *x in tmp, copy *y into *x, then tmp into *y.
   3. In main(), print x and y, call swap(&x, &y) and print them again. */
/* Pass addresses so the function can change the caller's variables. */
void swap(long *x, long *y) {
    long tmp = *x;
    *x = *y;
    *y = tmp;
}

int main(void) {
    long x = 26L, y = 81L;
    printf("Before: %ld %ld\n", x, y);
    swap(&x, &y);
    printf("After:  %ld %ld\n", x, y);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: swap() receives the addresses of x and y, so writing through the pointers
   *x and *y changes the caller's variables. tmp holds one value during the exchange.
   main() declares both variables on one line and prints them before and after the swap. */
// END

   and prints whether 60 is inside 41 to 81. */

/* Caption: Write a program to use binary search to locate a value in a sorted list. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Make sure the array is sorted.
   2. Set lo to 0 and hi to n - 1.
   3. While lo <= hi, compare the middle element mid with the key.
   4. Return the index if it matches; otherwise keep only the half that can hold the
      key.
   5. Return -1 if the range becomes empty, and print the index of 201. */
/* The array must be sorted. Each step halves the range that can still hold the key. */
int binary_search(const int marks[], int n, int key) {
    int lo = 0;
    int hi = n - 1;
    while (lo <= hi) {
        int mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;
        if (marks[mid] == key) {
            return mid;
        } else if (marks[mid] < key) {
            lo = mid + 1;   /* key is in the right half */
        } else {
            hi = mid - 1;   /* key is in the left half */
        }
    }
    return -1;
}

int main(void) {
    int marks[] = {14, 31, 46, 92, 104, 120, 135, 139, 143, 161, 174, 193};
    int n = sizeof(marks) / sizeof(marks[0]);
    int index = binary_search(marks, n, 201);
    printf("Index of 201: %d\n", index);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: binary_search() needs a sorted array. It keeps the range from lo to hi,
   compares the middle element mid with the key and throws away the half that cannot
   contain it, so it needs only about log2(n) steps. main() looks for 201 and prints its
   index, or -1 if it is not there. */
// END

/* Caption: Compute the length of a string without strlen. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write string_length() with a counter len = 0.
   2. Move through the string until the null character.
   3. Return len and print the length of rocket. */
/* Count characters until the terminating '\0'. */
int string_length(const char *line) {
    int len = 0;
    while (line[len] != '\0') {
        len++;
    }
    return len;
}

int main(void) {

    printf("Length of \"%s\" is %d\n", line, string_length(line));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: string_length() counts characters until it reaches the null character that
   ends every C string. main() prints the length of the word rocket. */
// END

/* Caption: Convert seconds into a struct with hours, minutes and seconds. */

/* Plan:

/* Caption: Check whether a year is a leap year. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write is_leap(year).
   2. A year divisible by 4 is a leap year, unless it is divisible by 100.
   3. Years divisible by 400 are leap years again.
   4. Check 2024 and print the result. */
/* Leap years divide by 4, except centuries, which must divide by 400. */
int is_leap(int year) {
    return (year % 4 == 0 && year % 100 != 0) || year % 400 == 0;
}

int main(void) {
    int year = 2024;
    if (is_leap(year)) {
        printf("%d is a leap year\n", year);
    } else {
        printf("%d is not a leap year\n", year);
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: is_leap() returns true for years divisible by 4, except century years,
   which must also be divisible by 400. main() checks 2024 and prints whether it is a leap
   year. */
// END

/* Caption: C program to implement bubble sort for an array of double values. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write bubble_sort() for the double array values.
   2. Compare each pair of neighbours.
   3. Swap them when they are in the wrong order for ascending order.
   4. Repeat the passes until the array is sorted.
   5. Print the sorted values. */
/* Repeatedly swap neighbours that are in the wrong order. */
void bubble_sort(double values[], int len) {
    for (int i = 0; i < len - 1; i++) {
        for (int j = 0; j < len - 1 - i; j++) {
            if (values[j] > values[j + 1]) {
                double tmp = values[j];
                values[j] = values[j + 1];
                values[j + 1] = tmp;
            }
        }
    }
}

int main(void) {
    double values[] = {26.8, 1.5, 41.2, 23.0, 22.0, 3.3, 92.5, 51.2};
    int len = 8;
    bubble_sort(values, len);
    for (int i = 0; i < len; i++) {
        printf("%.2f ", values[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: bubble_sort() walks through values again and again and swaps neighbours
   that are in the wrong order, so the largest values move to the end first. main() then
   prints the 8 values in ascending order. */
// END

/* Caption: Reverse an array by swapping from both ends. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write reverse_array() for samples.
   2. Set start to the first index and end to the last.
   3. Swap samples[start] and samples[end], then move both inwards.
   4. Stop when start meets end and print the array. */
/* Swap the outer pair, then move both ends toward the middle. */
void reverse_array(int samples[], int count) {
    int start = 0;
    int end = count - 1;
    while (start < end) {
        int tmp = samples[start];
        samples[start] = samples[end];
        samples[end] = tmp;
        start++;
        end--;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    int samples[] = {96, 46, 77, 84, 83, 3, 75};
    int count = 7;
    reverse_array(samples, count);
    for (int i = 0; i < count; i++) {
        printf("%d ", samples[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: reverse_array() swaps the first and last elements, then moves start forward
   and end backward until they meet, so the array is reversed in place without a second
   array. main() prints the reversed values. */
// END

/* Caption: Compute the sum and the average of an array in one function. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write sum_and_average() with the pointers sum and average.
   2. Add the values into *sum.
   3. Store *sum / n in *average.
   4. Declare total and mean, pass their addresses and print them. */
void sum_and_average(const double v[], int n, double *sum, double *average) {
    *sum = 0.0;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        *sum += v[i];
    }
    *average = *sum / n;
}

int main(void) {
    double scores[] = {7.5, 51.0, 42.0, 44.3, 84.7};
    int n = sizeof(scores) / sizeof(scores[0]);
    double total, mean;
    sum_and_average(scores, n, &total, &mean);
    printf("Sum: %.2f, Average: %.2f\n", total, mean);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: sum_and_average() takes the array, its length and two pointers. It adds up
   the 5 values through *sum and then stores *sum / n in *average. main() declares total
   and mean on one line and passes their addresses. */
// END

/* Caption: Show the Fibonacci series using recursion. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write fib(n) that returns n when n < 2.
   2. Otherwise return fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2).
   3. Print fib(i) for i from 0 to 20. */
/* Each Fibonacci number is the sum of the two before it. */
long fib(int n) {
    if (n < 2) {
        return n;
    }
    return fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2);
}

int main(void) {
    for (int i = 0; i < 21; i++) {
        printf("%ld ", fib(i));
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: fib() returns n for 0 and 1 and otherwise adds the two previous Fibonacci
   numbers by calling itself twice, which is simple but slow for large n. main() prints the
   first 21 numbers. */
// END

/* Return value, but never less than low or more than high. */
int clamp(int value, int low, int high) {

/* Caption: How do I write a function with four parameters that returns the maximum in C? */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write max2() that returns the larger of two values.
   2. Write max_of_four() as max2(max2(a, b), max2(c, d)).
   3. Print the largest of the four values. */
/* Return the larger of two values. */
int max2(int a, int b) {
    return a > b ? a : b;
}

/* Reuse max2 to compare four values. */
int max_of_four(int a, int b, int c, int d) {
    return max2(max2(a, b), max2(c, d));
}

int main(void) {
    int a = 62, b = 67, c = 66, d = 4;
    printf("Largest: %d\n", max_of_four(a, b, c, d));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: max_of_four() takes four parameters and reuses the helper max2(), which
   returns the larger of two values: it compares a with b, c with d, and then the two
   winners. main() prints the largest of 62, 67, 66 and 4. */
// END

/* Caption: C program to search an array for its smallest value. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write min_of() that takes values and length.
   2. Store values[0] in best.
   3. Loop over the other elements and keep the smallest value in best.
   4. Return best and print it. */
/* Start with the first element and keep the smallest value seen so far. */
int min_of(const int values[], int length) {
    int best = values[0];
    for (int j = 1; j < length; j++) {
        if (values[j] < best) {
            best = values[j];
        }
    }
    return best;
}

int main(void) {
    int values[] = {32, 2, 75, 37, 8, 56, 39, 46, 3};
    int length = sizeof(values) / sizeof(values[0]);
    printf("The smallest value is %d\n", min_of(values, length));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: min_of() takes the first element as the smallest value so far and stores it
   in best. The loop compares every other element with best using < and keeps the smallest
   one. main() prints the smallest of the 9 values. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to implement insertion sort for an array of int values. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write insertion_sort() for the int array marks.
   2. Take each element in turn as current.
   3. Shift the larger values of the sorted part one place right.
   4. Put current into the gap.
   5. Print the sorted values. */
/* Insert each element into the already sorted part on its left. */
void insertion_sort(int marks[], int count) {
    for (int i = 1; i < count; i++) {
        int current = marks[i];
        int j = i - 1;
        while (j >= 0 && marks[j] > current) {
            marks[j + 1] = marks[j];   /* shift bigger values right */
            j--;
        }
        marks[j + 1] = current;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    int marks[] = {95, 71, 93, 24, 56, 31, 81, 47, 39, 96};
    int count = sizeof(marks) / sizeof(marks[0]);
    insertion_sort(marks, count);
    for (int i = 0; i < count; i++) {
        printf("%d ", marks[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: insertion_sort() takes each element in turn and shifts the larger values of
   the sorted part one place right until the element fits. main() then prints the 10 values
   in ascending order. */
// END

/* Caption: Implement a simple linked list with malloc and free. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define Item with a value and a next pointer.
   2. Write push_front() that mallocs a node and links it in front of head.
   3. Write print_list() that follows next until NULL.
   4. Write free_list() that frees every node.
   5. Push 6 values, print the list and free it. */
typedef struct Item {
    int value;
    struct Item *next;
} Item;

/* Allocate a new node and put it in front of the current head. */
Item *push_front(Item *head, int value) {
    Item *node = malloc(sizeof(Item));
    if (node == NULL) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Out of memory\n");
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }
    node->value = value;
    node->next = head;
    return node;
}

void print_list(const Item *head) {
    for (const Item *cur = head; cur != NULL; cur = cur->next) {
        printf("%d -> ", cur->value);
    }
    printf("NULL\n");
}

/* Free every node; save next before freeing the current one. */
void free_list(Item *head) {
    while (head != NULL) {
        Item *next = head->next;
        free(head);
        head = next;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    Item *head = NULL;
    head = push_front(head, 53);
    head = push_front(head, 42);
    head = push_front(head, 49);
    head = push_front(head, 73);
    head = push_front(head, 99);
    head = push_front(head, 37);
    print_list(head);
    free_list(head);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: Each Item holds a value and a pointer to the next node. push_front()
   allocates a node with malloc, puts it in front of head and returns it; print_list()
   follows the next pointers until NULL; free_list() frees every node. main() pushes 6
   values, so they print in reverse order. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to add two matrices element by element. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define ROWS as 2 and COLS as 3.
   2. Loop over every row r and column c.
   3. Store a[r][c] + b[r][c] in sum and print it. */
#define ROWS 2
#define COLS 3

int main(void) {
    int a[ROWS][COLS] = {{5, 8, 4}, {0, 0, 6}};
    int b[ROWS][COLS] = {{4, 9, 2}, {9, 7, 3}};
    int sum[ROWS][COLS];
    /* Each entry of the result is the sum of the matching entries. */
    for (int r = 0; r < ROWS; r++) {
        for (int c = 0; c < COLS; c++) {
            sum[r][c] = a[r][c] + b[r][c];
            printf("%3d", sum[r][c]);
        }
        printf("\n");
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: Both matrices are 2x3 two-dimensional arrays. Two nested loops visit every
   row r and column c, store a[r][c] + b[r][c] in sum and print each row. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to reverse the digits of a number. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Start result at 0.
   2. Multiply result by 10, add n % 10, then divide n by 10.
   3. Repeat until n is 0.
   4. Apply it to 572588 and print the result. */
/* Take the last digit with % 10, then drop it with / 10. */
int reverse_digits(int n) {
    int result = 0;
    while (n > 0) {
        result = result * 10 + n % 10;
        n /= 10;
    }
    return result;
}

int main(void) {
    int number = 572588;
    printf("reverse of digits of %d: %d\n", number, reverse_digits(number));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: reverse_digits() shifts result one place left (result * 10) and adds the
   last digit of n, which reverses the order. main() applies it to 572588. */
// END

/* Caption: Allocate an array with malloc and fill it with multiples. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Use malloc to get room for 8 ints and check for NULL.

   3. Print the values.

/* Caption: C program to swap two variables using pointers. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write swap() that takes pointers to two int values.
   2. Save *x in tmp, copy *y into *x, then tmp into *y.
   3. In main(), print x and y, call swap(&x, &y) and print them again. */
/* Pass addresses so the function can change the caller's variables. */
void swap(int *x, int *y) {
    int tmp = *x;
    *x = *y;
    *y = tmp;
}

int main(void) {
    int x = 63, y = 26;
    printf("Before: %d %d\n", x, y);
    swap(&x, &y);
    printf("After:  %d %d\n", x, y);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: swap() receives the addresses of x and y, so writing through the pointers
   *x and *y changes the caller's variables. tmp holds one value during the exchange.
   main() declares both variables on one line and prints them before and after the swap. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to reverse the elements of an array in place. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write reverse_array() for values.
   2. Set left to the first index and right to the last.
   3. Swap values[left] and values[right], then move both inwards.
   4. Stop when left meets right and print the array. */
/* Swap the outer pair, then move both ends toward the middle. */
void reverse_array(int values[], int size) {
    int left = 0;
    int right = size - 1;
    while (left < right) {
        int tmp = values[left];
        values[left] = values[right];
        values[right] = tmp;
        left++;
        right--;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    int values[] = {64, 63, 74, 70, 68, 88};
    int size = 6;
    reverse_array(values, size);
    for (int i = 0; i < size; i++) {
        printf("%d ", values[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: reverse_array() swaps the first and last elements, then moves left forward
   and right backward until they meet, so the array is reversed in place without a second
   array. main() prints the reversed values. */
// END

/* Caption: Implement a stack with an array (push and pop). */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define a Stack with room for 10 items and a top counter.
   2. Write push() and pop(), returning false when the stack is full or empty.
   3. Push 6 values.
   4. Pop and print until the stack is empty. */
#define CAPACITY 10

typedef struct {
    int items[CAPACITY];
    int top;   /* number of items on the stack */
} Stack;

bool push(Stack *s, int value) {
    if (s->top == CAPACITY) {
        return false;   /* stack is full */
    }
    s->items[s->top++] = value;
    return true;
}

bool pop(Stack *s, int *value) {
    if (s->top == 0) {
        return false;   /* stack is empty */
    }
    *value = s->items[--s->top];
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    Stack s = {.top = 0};
    push(&s, 34);
    push(&s, 40);
    push(&s, 86);
    push(&s, 53);
    push(&s, 45);
    push(&s, 11);
    int value;
    /* Items come back out in reverse order (last in, first out). */
    while (pop(&s, &value)) {
        printf("%d ", value);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: The Stack keeps up to 10 items in an array, and top counts how many are
   stored. push() adds at the top and pop() removes from the top; both return false when
   they cannot. main() pushes 6 values and pops them all, so they come out in reverse order
   (last in, first out). */
// END

/* Caption: Calculate the area and perimeter of a rectangle struct. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define a Rectangle struct with width and height.
   2. Write area() and perimeter().
   3. Make a 29 by 27 rectangle and print both results. */
typedef struct {
    int width;
    int height;
} Rectangle;

int area(Rectangle r) {
    return r.width * r.height;
}

int perimeter(Rectangle r) {
    return 2 * (r.width + r.height);
}

    printf("Area: %d, Perimeter: %d\n", area(box), perimeter(box));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: Rectangle stores a width and a height. area() returns width * height and
   perimeter() returns 2 * (width + height). main() makes a 29 by 27 rectangle and prints
   both results. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to count how many times 'o' appears in a string. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write count_char() with count = 0.
   2. Compare each character with the target o.
   3. Return count and print it. */
int count_char(const char *text, char target) {
    int count = 0;
    /* Compare every character with the target. */
    for (int i = 0; text[i] != '\0'; i++) {
        if (text[i] == target) {
            count++;
        }
    }
    return count;
}

int main(void) {
    const char *sentence = "the quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog";
    printf("'o' appears %d times\n", count_char(sentence, 'o'));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: count_char() compares every character of the text with the target character
   and counts the matches. main() prints how many times o appears in the sentence. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to compute the sum and the average of an array in one function. */

/* Plan:
   1. Write sum_and_average() with the pointers sum and average.
   2. Add the values into *sum.
   3. Store *sum / n in *average.
   4. Declare total and mean, pass their addresses and print them. */
void sum_and_average(const double v[], int n, double *sum, double *average) {

    printf("Sum: %.2f, Average: %.2f\n", total, mean);
    return 0;
}

   and mean on one line and passes their addresses. */

/* Caption: Write lines to a text file and read them back. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Open log.txt in write mode and check for NULL.
   2. Write 3 lines with fprintf and close the file.
   3. Open it again in read mode.
   4. Read and print each line with fgets, then close the file. */
int main(void) {
    FILE *file = fopen("log.txt", "w");
    if (file == NULL) {
        perror("fopen");
        return 1;
    }
    fprintf(file, "structs group related data together\n");
    fprintf(file, "strings end with a null character\n");
    fprintf(file, "the quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog\n");
    fclose(file);

    /* Reopen the file for reading and print it line by line. */
    file = fopen("log.txt", "r");
    if (file == NULL) {
        perror("fopen");
        return 1;
    }
    char line[128];
    while (fgets(line, sizeof(line), file) != NULL) {
        printf("%s", line);
    }
    fclose(file);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: fopen() in write mode creates log.txt, fprintf() writes 3 lines into it and
   fclose() saves it. The file is then opened again in read mode, and fgets() reads it back
   line by line into the buffer line, which is printed. Every fopen() result is checked for
   NULL. */
// END

/* Caption: Define a Point struct and measure the distance between two points. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <math.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define a Point struct with x and y.
   2. Write distance() using sqrt(dx * dx + dy * dy).
   3. Print the distance between p and q. */
typedef struct {
    double x;
    double y;
} Point;

/* Pythagoras: sqrt(dx * dx + dy * dy). */
double distance(Point a, Point b) {
    double dx = b.x - a.x;
    double dy = b.y - a.y;
    return sqrt(dx * dx + dy * dy);
}

int main(void) {
    Point p = {8, 6};
    Point q = {-8, -3};
    printf("Distance: %.3f\n", distance(p, q));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: Point is a typedef struct with x and y. distance() uses Pythagoras, sqrt(dx
   * dx + dy * dy), to measure the gap between the two points, and main() prints it. */
// END

/* Caption: Convert 950 to binary. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write print_binary(n, bits).
   2. Go through the bits from the highest to the lowest.
   3. Print 1 when (n >> b) & 1 is set, otherwise 0.
   4. Print 950 in binary. */
/* Check each bit from the highest to the lowest. */
void print_binary(unsigned int n, int bits) {
    for (int b = bits - 1; b >= 0; b--) {
        putchar((n >> b) & 1 ? '1' : '0');
    }
    putchar('\n');
}

int main(void) {
    unsigned int number = 950;

/* Caption: Swap two variables using pointers. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write swap() that takes pointers to two double values.
   2. Save *x in tmp, copy *y into *x, then tmp into *y.
   3. In main(), print x and y, call swap(&x, &y) and print them again. */
/* Pass addresses so the function can change the caller's variables. */
void swap(double *x, double *y) {
    double tmp = *x;
    *x = *y;
    *y = tmp;
}

int main(void) {
    double x = 51.2, y = 12.2;
    printf("Before: %.2f %.2f\n", x, y);
    swap(&x, &y);
    printf("After:  %.2f %.2f\n", x, y);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: swap() receives the addresses of x and y, so writing through the pointers
   *x and *y changes the caller's variables. tmp holds one value during the exchange.
   main() declares both variables on one line and prints them before and after the swap. */
// END

    }
    int best = (a > b) ? a : b;   /* the ?: operator picks one of two values */
    printf("The bigger is %d\n", best);

}
/* Explanation: The program reads a and b from the keyboard with scanf and stops with a
