/* Caption: Program to use binary search to locate a value in a sorted list. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Make sure the array is sorted.
   2. Set left to 0 and right to len - 1.
   3. While left <= right, compare the middle element middle with the key.
   4. Return the index if it matches; otherwise keep only the half that can hold the
      key.
   5. Return -1 if the range becomes empty, and print the index of 171. */
/* The array must be sorted. Each step halves the range that can still hold the key. */
int binary_search(const int ages[], int len, int key) {
    int left = 0;
    int right = len - 1;
    while (left <= right) {
        int middle = left + (right - left) / 2;
        if (ages[middle] == key) {
            return middle;
        } else if (ages[middle] < key) {
            left = middle + 1;   /* key is in the right half */
        } else {
            right = middle - 1;   /* key is in the left half */
        }
    }
    return -1;
}

int main(void) {
    int ages[] = {63, 92, 96, 110, 121, 171, 186};
    int len = sizeof(ages) / sizeof(ages[0]);
    int index = binary_search(ages, len, 171);
    printf("Index of 171: %d\n", index);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: binary_search() needs a sorted array. It keeps the range from left to
   right, compares the middle element middle with the key and throws away the half that
   cannot contain it, so it needs only about log2(n) steps. main() looks for 171 and prints
   its index, or -1 if it is not there. */
// END

/* Caption: Calculate 8! using iteration. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write factorial(num) with result = 1.
   2. Multiply result by every number from 2 to num.
   3. Return result.
   4. Print 8! as an unsigned long long. */
/* Multiply 1 * 2 * ... * n. */
unsigned long long factorial(int num) {
    unsigned long long result = 1;
    for (int i = 2; i <= num; i++) {
        result *= i;
    }
    return result;
}

int main(void) {
    int num = 8;
    printf("%d! = %llu\n", num, factorial(num));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: factorial() multiplies result by every number from 2 up to num. main()
   prints 8! as an unsigned long long, because factorials grow very fast. */
// END

/* Caption: Check every element of an array to find a target value. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write linear_search() with the array, its length and key.
   2. Compare each element with key.
   3. Return the index of the first match, or -1.
   4. In main(), search for 37 and print the result. */
/* Return the index of key, or -1 when it is not in the array. */
int linear_search(const int samples[], int size, int key) {
    for (int i = 0; i < size; i++) {
        if (samples[i] == key) {
            return i;
        }
    }
    return -1;
}

int main(void) {
    int samples[] = {37, 44, 23, 24, 60, 10, 49, 24};
    int size = 8;
    int key = 37;
    int pos = linear_search(samples, size, key);
    if (pos >= 0) {
        printf("Found %d at index %d\n", key, pos);
    } else {
        printf("%d is not in the array\n", key);
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: linear_search() checks the elements of samples one by one and returns the
   index of the first one equal to key, or -1 when it reaches the end without a match.
   main() searches for 37 and prints where it is, or that it is missing. */
// END

/* Caption: Implement a circular queue with an array. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define a Queue with room for 32 items, a head and a count.
   2. Write enqueue() that stores at (head + count) % CAPACITY.
   3. Write dequeue() that takes the item at head and moves head on.
   4. Add 6 values, then remove and print them in order. */
#define CAPACITY 32

typedef struct {
    int items[CAPACITY];
    int head;
    int count;
} Queue;

bool enqueue(Queue *q, int value) {
    if (q->count == CAPACITY) {
        return false;
    }
    /* The tail wraps around to the start of the array. */
    q->items[(q->head + q->count) % CAPACITY] = value;
    q->count++;
    return true;
}

bool dequeue(Queue *q, int *value) {
    if (q->count == 0) {
        return false;
    }
    *value = q->items[q->head];
    q->head = (q->head + 1) % CAPACITY;
    q->count--;
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    Queue q = {.head = 0, .count = 0};
    enqueue(&q, 39);
    enqueue(&q, 36);
    enqueue(&q, 23);
    enqueue(&q, 54);
    enqueue(&q, 48);
    enqueue(&q, 40);
    int value;
    /* Items come out in the order they went in (first in, first out). */
    while (dequeue(&q, &value)) {
        printf("%d ", value);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: The Queue stores up to 32 items in a ring buffer: head is the oldest item
   and % CAPACITY wraps positions back to the start of the array. enqueue() adds at the
   back and dequeue() removes from the front, so main() gets its 6 values back in the same
   order (first in, first out). */
// END

/* Caption: Test if "integer" reads the same backwards. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <string.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write is_palindrome() for buffer.
   2. Compare the first and last characters, moving inwards.
   3. Return false at the first mismatch, otherwise true.
   4. Check integer and print the result. */
/* Compare characters from the front and back, moving inwards. */
bool is_palindrome(const char *buffer) {
    int i = 0;
    int j = strlen(buffer) - 1;
    while (i < j) {
        if (buffer[i] != buffer[j]) {
            return false;
        }
        i++;
        j--;
    }
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    const char *buffer = "integer";
    printf("%s %s a palindrome\n", buffer, is_palindrome(buffer) ? "is" : "is not");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: is_palindrome() compares the first and last characters and moves inwards;
   any mismatch means the word is not a palindrome. main() checks the word integer and
   prints the result. */
// END

/* Caption: Compute the sum of the elements of an array. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write array_sum() that takes the array items and its length len.
   2. Start total at 0 and add every element in a while loop.
   3. Return total.
   4. In main(), fill items with 4 values and print the sum. */
/* Walk through the array and accumulate each value. */
double array_sum(const double items[], int len) {
    double total = 0;
    int idx = 0;
    while (idx < len) {
        total += items[idx];
        idx++;
    }
    return total;
}

int main(void) {
    double items[] = {72.5, 5.7, 77.2, 22.6};
    int len = sizeof(items) / sizeof(items[0]);
    printf("Sum: %.2f\n", array_sum(items, len));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: array_sum() receives the array items and its length len. It starts total at
   0, adds every element to it in a while loop and returns the total. main() fills items
   with 4 double values and prints their sum. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to change every letter in a sentence to a capital letter. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <ctype.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write to_upper() for str.
   2. Replace every character with toupper() until the null character.
   3. Print the sentence. */
/* toupper changes lowercase letters and leaves other characters alone. */
void to_upper(char *str) {
    for (int i = 0; str[i] != '\0'; i++) {
        str[i] = toupper((unsigned char)str[i]);
    }
}

int main(void) {
    char str[] = "pointers store the address of another variable";
    to_upper(str);
    printf("%s\n", str);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: to_upper() walks through str until the null character and replaces each
   character with toupper(), which only changes lowercase letters. main() prints the
   sentence in capitals. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to write a function that returns the distance between two points given x1, y1, x2 and y2. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <math.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write distance(x1, y1, x2, y2).
   2. Compute dx and dy, then return sqrt(dx * dx + dy * dy).
   3. Print the distance between (-4, 9) and (9, -7). */
/* Pythagoras: the distance is sqrt(dx * dx + dy * dy). */
double distance(double x1, double y1, double x2, double y2) {
    double dx = x2 - x1, dy = y2 - y1;
    return sqrt(dx * dx + dy * dy);
}

int main(void) {
    printf("Distance: %.3f\n", distance(-4, 9, 9, -7));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: distance() takes the coordinates of both points as four parameters. It
   declares dx and dy on one line and uses Pythagoras with sqrt() from math.h. main()
   prints the distance between (-4, 9) and (9, -7). */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to implement a stack with an array (push and pop). */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define a Stack with room for 16 items and a top counter.
   2. Write push() and pop(), returning false when the stack is full or empty.
   3. Push 6 values.
   4. Pop and print until the stack is empty. */
#define CAPACITY 16

typedef struct {
    int items[CAPACITY];
    int top;   /* number of items on the stack */
} Stack;

bool push(Stack *s, int value) {
    if (s->top == CAPACITY) {
        return false;   /* stack is full */
    }
    s->items[s->top++] = value;
    return true;
}

bool pop(Stack *s, int *value) {
    if (s->top == 0) {
        return false;   /* stack is empty */
    }
    *value = s->items[--s->top];
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    Stack s = {.top = 0};
    push(&s, 47);
    push(&s, 78);
    push(&s, 94);
    push(&s, 94);
    push(&s, 15);
    push(&s, 81);
    int value;
    /* Items come back out in reverse order (last in, first out). */
    while (pop(&s, &value)) {
        printf("%d ", value);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: The Stack keeps up to 16 items in an array, and top counts how many are
   stored. push() adds at the top and pop() removes from the top; both return false when
   they cannot. main() pushes 6 values and pops them all, so they come out in reverse order
   (last in, first out). */
// END

/* Caption: Use dynamic memory to store the first 6 cubes. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Use malloc to get room for 6 ints and check for NULL.
   2. Fill arr with cubes.
   3. Print the values.
   4. Call free(arr) at the end. */
int main(void) {
    int n = 6;
    /* Ask the heap for room for n ints; malloc returns NULL on failure. */
    int *arr = malloc(n * sizeof(int));
    if (arr == NULL) {
        fprintf(stderr, "malloc failed\n");
        return 1;
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        arr[i] = i * i * i;
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        printf("%d ", arr[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    free(arr);   /* give the memory back */
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: malloc() reserves room for 6 ints on the heap and returns NULL if it fails,
   which the program checks. The first loop fills arr with cubes, the second prints them,
   and free() gives the memory back at the end. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to count how many even numbers are in an array. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write count_even() that takes readings and len.
   2. For each element, test readings[i] % 2 == 0.
   3. Add one to count for every even number.
   4. Return count and print it. */
/* A number is even when the remainder after dividing by 2 is zero. */
int count_even(const int readings[], int len) {
    int count = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < len; i++) {
        if (readings[i] % 2 == 0) {
            count++;
        }
    }
    return count;
}

int main(void) {
    int readings[] = {53, 32, 45, 23, 12};
    const int len = 5;
    printf("Even numbers: %d\n", count_even(readings, len));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: count_even() tests each element of readings with the % operator: a
   remainder of 0 after dividing by 2 means the number is even, so count goes up by one.
   main() prints how many of the 5 values are even. */
// END

/* Caption: Compute the length of a string without strlen. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write string_length() with a counter len = 0.
   2. Move through the string until the null character.
   3. Return len and print the length of rotor. */
/* Count characters until the terminating '\0'. */
int string_length(const char *word) {
    int len = 0;
    while (word[len] != '\0') {
        len++;
    }
    return len;
}

int main(void) {
    const char *word = "rotor";
    printf("Length of \"%s\" is %d\n", word, string_length(word));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: string_length() counts characters until it reaches the null character that
   ends every C string. main() prints the length of the word rotor. */
// END

/* Caption: C program to print the binary representation of an integer. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write print_binary(n, bits).
   2. Go through the bits from the highest to the lowest.
   3. Print 1 when (n >> b) & 1 is set, otherwise 0.
   4. Print 296 in binary. */
/* Check each bit from the highest to the lowest. */
void print_binary(unsigned int n, int bits) {
    for (int b = bits - 1; b >= 0; b--) {
        putchar((n >> b) & 1 ? '1' : '0');
    }
    putchar('\n');
}

int main(void) {
    unsigned int number = 296;
    printf("%u in binary: ", number);
    print_binary(number, 8);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: print_binary() checks one bit at a time, from the highest to the lowest: (n
   >> b) & 1 is 1 when bit b is set, so it prints the character 1 or 0. main() prints 296
   in binary. */
// END

/* Caption: Sort an array in ascending order using bubble sort. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write bubble_sort() for the double array numbers.
   2. Compare each pair of neighbours.
   3. Swap them when they are in the wrong order for ascending order.
   4. Repeat the passes until the array is sorted.
   5. Print the sorted values. */
/* Repeatedly swap neighbours that are in the wrong order. */
void bubble_sort(double numbers[], int len) {
    for (int i = 0; i < len - 1; i++) {
        for (int j = 0; j < len - 1 - i; j++) {
            if (numbers[j] > numbers[j + 1]) {
                double tmp = numbers[j];
                numbers[j] = numbers[j + 1];
                numbers[j + 1] = tmp;
            }
        }
    }
}

int main(void) {
    double numbers[] = {35.6, 52.0, 90.2, 35.0, 89.5, 83.7, 38.0, 88.7, 13.3, 38.5};
    const int len = 10;
    bubble_sort(numbers, len);
    for (int i = 0; i < len; i++) {
        printf("%.2f ", numbers[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: bubble_sort() walks through numbers again and again and swaps neighbours
   that are in the wrong order, so the largest values move to the end first. main() then
   prints the 10 values in ascending order. */
// END

   1. Write count_vowels() with count = 0.

    for (int i = 0; text[i] != '\0'; i++) {

            count++;

    return count;
}

    const char *sentence = "c gives you direct control over memory";
    printf("Vowels: %d\n", count_vowels(sentence));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: count_vowels() uses strchr to test whether each character is one of
   aeiouAEIOU and counts the matches. main() prints the number of vowels in the sentence. */
// END

/* Caption: C program to declare two pointers in one statement and use them. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Declare x and y on one line.
   2. Declare the pointers px and py on one line, each with its own *.
   3. Add 2 to x through px and print the values. */
int main(void) {
    int x = 28, y = 16;
    /* Each pointer needs its own '*': in "int *p, q;" only p is a pointer. */
    int *px = &x, *py = &y;
    *px += 2;
    printf("x = %d, y = %d\n", x, y);
    printf("*px = %d, *py = %d\n", *px, *py);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: int *px = &x, *py = &y; declares two pointers in one statement; each name
   needs its own *. *px += 2 changes x through the pointer, so x becomes 30 while y stays
   16. */
// END

/* Caption: Program to raise a number to an integer power with a loop. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write power(base, exp) with result = 1.
   2. Multiply result by base exp times.
   3. Print 9 to the power 5. */
/* Multiply the base by itself exp times. */
long long power(int base, int exp) {
    long long result = 1;
    for (int i = 0; i < exp; i++) {
        result *= base;
    }
    return result;
}

int main(void) {
    printf("9^5 = %lld\n", power(9, 5));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: power() starts result at 1 and multiplies it by base exp times. It uses
   long long because powers grow quickly. main() prints 9 to the power 5. */
// END

/* Caption: Build a fixed-size integer stack in C. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define a Stack with room for 32 items and a top counter.
   2. Write push() and pop(), returning false when the stack is full or empty.
   3. Push 5 values.
   4. Pop and print until the stack is empty. */
#define CAPACITY 32

typedef struct {
    int items[CAPACITY];
    int top;   /* number of items on the stack */
} Stack;

bool push(Stack *s, int value) {
    if (s->top == CAPACITY) {
        return false;   /* stack is full */
    }
    s->items[s->top++] = value;
    return true;
}

bool pop(Stack *s, int *value) {
    if (s->top == 0) {
        return false;   /* stack is empty */
    }
    *value = s->items[--s->top];
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    Stack s = {.top = 0};
    push(&s, 71);
    push(&s, 20);
    push(&s, 15);
    push(&s, 9);
    push(&s, 14);
    int value;
    /* Items come back out in reverse order (last in, first out). */
    while (pop(&s, &value)) {
        printf("%d ", value);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: The Stack keeps up to 32 items in an array, and top counts how many are
   stored. push() adds at the top and pop() removes from the top; both return false when
   they cannot. main() pushes 5 values and pops them all, so they come out in reverse order
   (last in, first out). */
// END

/* Caption: Swap two variables using pointers. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write swap() that takes pointers to two double values.
   2. Save *x in tmp, copy *y into *x, then tmp into *y.
   3. In main(), print x and y, call swap(&x, &y) and print them again. */
/* Pass addresses so the function can change the caller's variables. */
void swap(double *x, double *y) {
    double tmp = *x;
    *x = *y;
    *y = tmp;
}

int main(void) {
    double x = 84.4, y = 13.3;
    printf("Before: %.2f %.2f\n", x, y);
    swap(&x, &y);
    printf("After:  %.2f %.2f\n", x, y);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: swap() receives the addresses of x and y, so writing through the pointers
   *x and *y changes the caller's variables. tmp holds one value during the exchange.
   main() declares both variables on one line and prints them before and after the swap. */
// END

/* Caption: C program to use selection sort to put numbers in descending order. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write selection_sort() for the long array prices.
   2. For each position, find the largest remaining element.
   3. Swap it into that position.
   4. Print the sorted values. */
/* Select the right element for each position and swap it into place. */
void selection_sort(long prices[], int size) {
    for (int i = 0; i < size - 1; i++) {
        int chosen = i;
        for (int j = i + 1; j < size; j++) {
            if (prices[chosen] < prices[j]) {
                chosen = j;
            }
        }
        long tmp = prices[i];
        prices[i] = prices[chosen];
        prices[chosen] = tmp;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    long prices[] = {59L, 21L, 98L, 25L, 53L};
    int size = sizeof(prices) / sizeof(prices[0]);
    selection_sort(prices, size);
    for (int i = 0; i < size; i++) {
        printf("%ld ", prices[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: selection_sort() finds the largest remaining element for each position and
   swaps it into place. main() then prints the 5 values in descending order. */
// END

/* Caption: Allocate an array with malloc and fill it with cubes. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Use malloc to get room for 6 ints and check for NULL.
   2. Fill buffer with cubes.
   3. Print the values.
   4. Call free(buffer) at the end. */
int main(void) {
    int n = 6;
    /* Ask the heap for room for n ints; malloc returns NULL on failure. */
    int *buffer = malloc(n * sizeof(int));
    if (buffer == NULL) {
        fprintf(stderr, "malloc failed\n");
        return 1;
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        buffer[i] = i * i * i;
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        printf("%d ", buffer[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    free(buffer);   /* give the memory back */
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: malloc() reserves room for 6 ints on the heap and returns NULL if it fails,
   which the program checks. The first loop fills buffer with cubes, the second prints
   them, and free() gives the memory back at the end. */
// END

/* Caption: Find the largest number in an array. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write find_max() that takes ages and count.
   2. Store ages[0] in largest.
   3. Loop over the other elements and keep the largest value in largest.
   4. Return largest and print it. */
/* Start with the first element and keep the largest value seen so far. */
int find_max(const int ages[], int count) {
    int largest = ages[0];
    for (int j = 1; j < count; j++) {
        if (ages[j] > largest) {
            largest = ages[j];
        }
    }
    return largest;
}

int main(void) {
    int ages[] = {81, 57, 69, 31, 16};
    int count = sizeof(ages) / sizeof(ages[0]);
    printf("The largest value is %d\n", find_max(ages, count));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: find_max() takes the first element as the largest value so far and stores
   it in largest. The loop compares every other element with largest using > and keeps the
   largest one. main() prints the largest of the 5 values. */
// END

/* Caption: Sum a int array with a helper function. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write sum_values() that takes the array values and its length count.
   2. Start sum at 0 and add every element in a for loop.
   3. Return sum.
   4. In main(), fill values with 5 values and print the sum. */
/* Walk through the array and accumulate each value. */
int sum_values(const int values[], int count) {
    int sum = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < count; i++) {
        sum += values[i];
    }
    return sum;
}

int main(void) {
    int values[] = {32, 80, 87, 28, 52};
    int count = 5;
    printf("The sum is %d\n", sum_values(values, count));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: sum_values() receives the array values and its length count. It starts sum
   at 0, adds every element to it in a for loop and returns the total. main() fills values
   with 5 int values and prints their sum. */
// END

/* Caption: How do I print the first 23 Fibonacci numbers in C? */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Start with first = 0 and second = 1.
   2. Repeat 23 times and print first each time.
   3. Compute next = first + second, then set first = second and second = next. */
int main(void) {
    long first = 0, second = 1;
    /* Print a term, then slide the pair one step along the sequence. */
    for (int i = 0; i < 23; i++) {
        printf("%ld ", first);
        long next = first + second;
        first = second;
        second = next;
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: The loop keeps the last two numbers in first and second. Each round it
   prints first, then moves the pair forward: first becomes second and second becomes their
   sum. It prints the first 23 Fibonacci numbers. */
// END

/* Caption: Store a name, age and height in variables and print them. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:

/* Caption: How do I compute the LCM of two integers using the GCD in C? */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write gcd() with Euclid's algorithm: replace (a, b) by (b, a % b) until b is 0.
   2. Write lcm() as a / gcd(a, b) * b.
   3. Print the LCM of 44 and 117. */
/* Euclid: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a % b) until b becomes zero. */
int gcd(int a, int b) {
    while (b != 0) {
        int r = a % b;
        a = b;
        b = r;
    }
    return a;
}

/* lcm(a, b) = a / gcd(a, b) * b (divide first to avoid overflow). */
long lcm(int a, int b) {
    return (long)a / gcd(a, b) * b;
}

int main(void) {
    printf("lcm(44, 117) = %ld\n", lcm(44, 117));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: gcd() uses Euclid's algorithm: it keeps replacing (a, b) with (b, a % b)
   until b is 0. lcm() divides a by the gcd before multiplying by b, which avoids overflow.
   main() prints the LCM of 44 and 117. */
// END

/* Caption: How do I print an integer with its digits reversed in C? */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Start result at 0.
   2. Multiply result by 10, add n % 10, then divide n by 10.
   3. Repeat until n is 0.
   4. Apply it to 184452 and print the result. */
/* Take the last digit with % 10, then drop it with / 10. */
int reverse_digits(int n) {
    int result = 0;
    while (n > 0) {
        result = result * 10 + n % 10;
        n /= 10;
    }
    return result;
}

int main(void) {
    int number = 184452;
    printf("reverse of digits of %d: %d\n", number, reverse_digits(number));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: reverse_digits() shifts result one place left (result * 10) and adds the
   last digit of n, which reverses the order. main() applies it to 184452. */
// END

/* Caption: Keep a value inside the limits low and high. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write clamp(value, low, high).
   2. Return low if the value is too small and high if it is too big.
   3. Otherwise return the value.
   4. Set low = 66 and high = 96 and print clamp() for 69, 28 and 81. */
/* Return value, but never less than low or more than high. */
int clamp(int value, int low, int high) {
    if (value < low) {
        return low;
    }
    if (value > high) {
        return high;
    }
    return value;
}

int main(void) {
    int low = 66, high = 96;
    printf("clamp(%d) = %d\n", 69, clamp(69, low, high));
    printf("clamp(%d) = %d\n", 28, clamp(28, low, high));
    printf("clamp(%d) = %d\n", 81, clamp(81, low, high));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: clamp() takes three parameters: the value and the two limits. It returns
   low when the value is too small, high when it is too big and the value itself otherwise.
   main() declares low = 66 and high = 96 on one line and clamps 69, 28 and 81. */
// END

/* Caption: How do I count how many odd numbers are in an array in C? */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write count_odd() that takes prices and n.
   2. For each element, test prices[i] % 2 != 0.
   3. Add one to tally for every odd number.
   4. Return tally and print it. */
/* A number is odd when the remainder after dividing by 2 is one. */
int count_odd(const int prices[], int n) {
    int tally = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        if (prices[i] % 2 != 0) {
            tally++;
        }
    }
    return tally;
}

int main(void) {
    int prices[] = {22, 59, 28, 82, 53, 24};
    int n = sizeof(prices) / sizeof(prices[0]);
    printf("Count of odd values = %d\n", count_odd(prices, n));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: count_odd() tests each element of prices with the % operator: a remainder
   of 1 after dividing by 2 means the number is odd, so tally goes up by one. main() prints
   how many of the 6 values are odd. */
// END

#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write gcd() with Euclid's algorithm.
   2. Replace (a, b) by (b, a % b) until b is 0.
   3. Return a and print the GCD of 18 and 64. */
/* Euclid: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a % b) until b becomes zero. */
int gcd(int a, int b) {
    while (b != 0) {
        int r = a % b;
        a = b;
        b = r;
    }
    return a;

/* Caption: Compute the distance between two points using a struct. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <math.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define a Point struct with x and y.
   2. Write distance() using sqrt(dx * dx + dy * dy).
   3. Print the distance between p and q. */
typedef struct {
    double x;
    double y;
} Point;

/* Pythagoras: sqrt(dx * dx + dy * dy). */
double distance(Point a, Point b) {
    double dx = b.x - a.x;
    double dy = b.y - a.y;
    return sqrt(dx * dx + dy * dy);
}

int main(void) {
    Point p = {8, -7};
    Point q = {10, 7};
    printf("Distance: %.3f\n", distance(p, q));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: Point is a typedef struct with x and y. distance() uses Pythagoras, sqrt(dx
   * dx + dy * dy), to measure the gap between the two points, and main() prints it. */
// END

/* Caption: C program to use a struct to hold names and marks, then print the average mark. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define struct Student with a name and a mark.
   2. Store 2 students in an array.
   3. Print each student and add the marks to total.
   4. Print total divided by the number of students. */
/* A struct groups a student's name and mark together. */
struct Student {
    char name[20];
    int mark;
};

int main(void) {
    struct Student students[] = {
        {"Ivan", 97},
        {"Dara", 87}
    };
    int count = sizeof(students) / sizeof(students[0]);
    double total = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < count; i++) {
        printf("%s: %d\n", students[i].name, students[i].mark);
        total += students[i].mark;
    }
    printf("Average mark: %.1f\n", total / count);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: struct Student groups a name and a mark. main() stores 2 students in an
   array of structs, prints each one, adds the marks to total and prints the average. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to implement a simple linked list with malloc and free. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define Item with a value and a next pointer.
   2. Write push_front() that mallocs a node and links it in front of head.
   3. Write print_list() that follows next until NULL.
   4. Write free_list() that frees every node.
   5. Push 4 values, print the list and free it. */
typedef struct Item {
    int value;
    struct Item *next;
} Item;

/* Allocate a new node and put it in front of the current head. */
Item *push_front(Item *head, int value) {
    Item *node = malloc(sizeof(Item));
    if (node == NULL) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Out of memory\n");
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }
    node->value = value;
    node->next = head;
    return node;
}

void print_list(const Item *head) {
    for (const Item *cur = head; cur != NULL; cur = cur->next) {
        printf("%d -> ", cur->value);
    }
    printf("NULL\n");
}

/* Free every node; save next before freeing the current one. */
void free_list(Item *head) {
    while (head != NULL) {
        Item *next = head->next;
        free(head);
        head = next;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    Item *head = NULL;
    head = push_front(head, 71);
    head = push_front(head, 90);
    head = push_front(head, 29);
    head = push_front(head, 92);
    print_list(head);
    free_list(head);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: Each Item holds a value and a pointer to the next node. push_front()
   allocates a node with malloc, puts it in front of head and returns it; print_list()
   follows the next pointers until NULL; free_list() frees every node. main() pushes 4
   values, so they print in reverse order. */
// END

/* Caption: C program to check whether a year is a leap year. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write is_leap(year).
   2. A year divisible by 4 is a leap year, unless it is divisible by 100.
   3. Years divisible by 400 are leap years again.
   4. Check 2046 and print the result. */
/* Leap years divide by 4, except centuries, which must divide by 400. */
int is_leap(int year) {
    return (year % 4 == 0 && year % 100 != 0) || year % 400 == 0;
}

int main(void) {
    int year = 2046;
    if (is_leap(year)) {
        printf("%d is a leap year\n", year);
    } else {
        printf("%d is not a leap year\n", year);
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: is_leap() returns true for years divisible by 4, except century years,
   which must also be divisible by 400. main() checks 2046 and prints whether it is a leap
   year. */
// END

/* Caption: Test if "compiler" reads the same backwards. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <string.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write is_palindrome() for str.
   2. Compare the first and last characters, moving inwards.
   3. Return false at the first mismatch, otherwise true.
   4. Check compiler and print the result. */
/* Compare characters from the front and back, moving inwards. */
bool is_palindrome(const char *str) {
    int i = 0;
    int j = strlen(str) - 1;
    while (i < j) {
        if (str[i] != str[j]) {
            return false;
        }
        i++;
        j--;
    }
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    const char *str = "compiler";
    printf("%s %s a palindrome\n", str, is_palindrome(str) ? "is" : "is not");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: is_palindrome() compares the first and last characters and moves inwards;
   any mismatch means the word is not a palindrome. main() checks the word compiler and
   prints the result. */
// END

/* Caption: Compute the area and circumference of a circle with one function. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write circle_measures() with the pointers area and circumference.
   2. Store PI * r * r and 2 * PI * r through them.
   3. Print both for a radius of 1.6. */
#define PI 3.14159265

void circle_measures(double radius, double *area, double *circumference) {
    *area = PI * radius * radius;
    *circumference = 2 * PI * radius;
}

int main(void) {
    double radius = 1.6;
    double area, circumference;
    circle_measures(radius, &area, &circumference);
    printf("Area: %.2f, Circumference: %.2f\n", area, circumference);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: circle_measures() computes two results from one radius and stores them
   through the pointers area and circumference. main() declares both variables on one line,
   passes their addresses and prints the results for a radius of 1.6. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to reverse the characters of a word. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <string.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write reverse_string() for line.
   2. Set i to the first index and j to the last.
   3. Swap the two characters and move i and j inwards until they meet.
   4. Reverse deified and print it. */
/* Swap characters from both ends until they meet in the middle. */
void reverse_string(char *line) {
    int i = 0;
    int j = strlen(line) - 1;
    while (i < j) {
        char tmp = line[i];
        line[i] = line[j];
        line[j] = tmp;
        i++;
        j--;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    char line[] = "deified";
    reverse_string(line);
    printf("%s\n", line);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: reverse_string() swaps characters from both ends of line, moving inwards
   until the two indexes meet. main() reverses the word deified in place and prints it. */
// END

/* Caption: How do I add up all the numbers in an array of int values in C? */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write add_all() that takes the array nums and its length len.
   2. Start result at 0 and add every element in a for loop.
   3. Return result.
   4. In main(), fill nums with 10 values and print the sum. */
/* Return the sum of the first n elements. */
int add_all(const int nums[], int len) {
    int result = 0;
    for (int j = 0; j < len; j++) {
        result += nums[j];
    }
    return result;
}

int main(void) {
    int nums[] = {54, 45, 64, 88, 96, 47, 36, 98, 85, 37};
    const int len = 10;
    printf("The sum is %d\n", add_all(nums, len));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: add_all() receives the array nums and its length len. It starts result at
   0, adds every element to it in a for loop and returns the total. main() fills nums with
   10 int values and prints their sum. */
// END

/* Caption: Turn the rows of a 2x3 matrix into columns. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define ROWS as 2 and COLS as 3.
   2. Copy m[r][c] into t[c][r] for every element.
   3. Print t row by row. */
#define ROWS 2
#define COLS 3

int main(void) {
    int m[ROWS][COLS] = {{7, 9, 2}, {9, 9, 5}};
    int t[COLS][ROWS];
    /* Element (r, c) moves to (c, r). */
    for (int r = 0; r < ROWS; r++) {
        for (int c = 0; c < COLS; c++) {
            t[c][r] = m[r][c];
        }
    }
    for (int r = 0; r < COLS; r++) {
        for (int c = 0; c < ROWS; c++) {
            printf("%3d", t[r][c]);
        }
        printf("\n");
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: The nested loops copy m[r][c] into t[c][r], so the 2x3 matrix becomes 3x2.
   A second pair of loops prints the result. */
// END

/* Caption: Search a sorted array by halving the search range each step. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Make sure the array is sorted.
   2. Set left to 0 and right to size - 1.
   3. While left <= right, compare the middle element middle with the key.
   4. Return the index if it matches; otherwise keep only the half that can hold the
      key.
   5. Return -1 if the range becomes empty, and print the index of 83. */
/* The array must be sorted. Each step halves the range that can still hold the key. */
int binary_search(const int readings[], int size, int key) {
    int left = 0;
    int right = size - 1;
    while (left <= right) {
        int middle = left + (right - left) / 2;
        if (readings[middle] == key) {
            return middle;
        } else if (readings[middle] < key) {
            left = middle + 1;   /* key is in the right half */
        } else {
            right = middle - 1;   /* key is in the left half */
        }
    }
    return -1;
}

int main(void) {
    int readings[] = {47, 58, 71, 83, 124, 140, 181, 193};
    int size = 8;
    int index = binary_search(readings, size, 83);
    printf("Index of 83: %d\n", index);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: binary_search() needs a sorted array. It keeps the range from left to
   right, compares the middle element middle with the key and throws away the half that
   cannot contain it, so it needs only about log2(n) steps. main() looks for 83 and prints
   its index, or -1 if it is not there. */
// END

/* Caption: C program to build a fixed-size integer stack in C. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define a Stack with room for 8 items and a top counter.
   2. Write push() and pop(), returning false when the stack is full or empty.
   3. Push 5 values.
   4. Pop and print until the stack is empty. */
#define CAPACITY 8

typedef struct {
    int items[CAPACITY];
    int top;   /* number of items on the stack */
} Stack;

bool push(Stack *s, int value) {
    if (s->top == CAPACITY) {
        return false;   /* stack is full */
    }
    s->items[s->top++] = value;
    return true;
}

bool pop(Stack *s, int *value) {
    if (s->top == 0) {
        return false;   /* stack is empty */
    }
    *value = s->items[--s->top];
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    Stack s = {.top = 0};
    push(&s, 50);
    push(&s, 96);
    push(&s, 99);
    push(&s, 72);
    push(&s, 62);
    int value;
    /* Items come back out in reverse order (last in, first out). */
    while (pop(&s, &value)) {
        printf("%d ", value);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: The Stack keeps up to 8 items in an array, and top counts how many are
   stored. push() adds at the top and pop() removes from the top; both return false when
   they cannot. main() pushes 5 values and pops them all, so they come out in reverse order
   (last in, first out). */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to search a sorted array by halving the search range each step. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Make sure the array is sorted.
   2. Set lo to 0 and hi to size - 1.
   3. While lo <= hi, compare the middle element mid with the key.
   4. Return the index if it matches; otherwise keep only the half that can hold the
      key.
   5. Return -1 if the range becomes empty, and print the index of 201. */
/* The array must be sorted. Each step halves the range that can still hold the key. */
int binary_search(const int data[], int size, int key) {
    int lo = 0;
    int hi = size - 1;
    while (lo <= hi) {
        int mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;
        if (data[mid] == key) {
            return mid;
        } else if (data[mid] < key) {
            lo = mid + 1;   /* key is in the right half */
        } else {
            hi = mid - 1;   /* key is in the left half */
        }
    }
    return -1;
}

int main(void) {
    int data[] = {39, 116, 124, 130, 138, 163, 170, 178, 191};
    const int size = 9;
    int index = binary_search(data, size, 201);
    printf("Index of 201: %d\n", index);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: binary_search() needs a sorted array. It keeps the range from lo to hi,
   compares the middle element mid with the key and throws away the half that cannot
   contain it, so it needs only about log2(n) steps. main() looks for 201 and prints its
   index, or -1 if it is not there. */
// END

/* Caption: Show the Fibonacci series using recursion. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write fib(n) that returns n when n < 2.
   2. Otherwise return fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2).
   3. Print fib(i) for i from 0 to 16. */
/* Each Fibonacci number is the sum of the two before it. */
long fib(int n) {
    if (n < 2) {
        return n;
    }
    return fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2);
}

int main(void) {
    for (int i = 0; i < 17; i++) {
        printf("%ld ", fib(i));
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: fib() returns n for 0 and 1 and otherwise adds the two previous Fibonacci
   numbers by calling itself twice, which is simple but slow for large n. main() prints the
   first 17 numbers. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to print the binary representation of an integer. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write print_binary(n, bits).
   2. Go through the bits from the highest to the lowest.
   3. Print 1 when (n >> b) & 1 is set, otherwise 0.
   4. Print 487 in binary. */
/* Check each bit from the highest to the lowest. */
void print_binary(unsigned int n, int bits) {
    for (int b = bits - 1; b >= 0; b--) {
        putchar((n >> b) & 1 ? '1' : '0');
    }
    putchar('\n');
}

int main(void) {
    unsigned int number = 487;
    printf("%u in binary: ", number);
    print_binary(number, 16);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: print_binary() checks one bit at a time, from the highest to the lowest: (n
   >> b) & 1 is 1 when bit b is set, so it prints the character 1 or 0. main() prints 487
   in binary. */
// END

/* Plan:
   1. Start result at 0.
   2. Divide n by 10 and add one to result.
   3. Repeat until n is 0.
   4. Apply it to 221078 and print the result. */
/* Take the last digit with % 10, then drop it with / 10. */
int count_digits(int n) {
    int result = 0;
    while (n > 0) {
        result++;
        n /= 10;
    }
    return result;
}

/* Caption: Write a C program to calculate 12! using recursion. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write factorial(value) that calls itself.
   2. Return 1 when value is 1 or less.
   3. Otherwise return value * factorial(value - 1).
   4. Print 12! as an unsigned long long. */
/* n! = n * (n - 1)!, and 0! = 1 stops the recursion. */
unsigned long long factorial(int value) {
    if (value <= 1) {
        return 1;
    }
    return value * factorial(value - 1);
}

int main(void) {
    int value = 12;
    printf("%d! = %llu\n", value, factorial(value));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: factorial() calls itself: n! is n * (n - 1)!, and the recursion stops when
   value is 1 or less. main() prints 12! as an unsigned long long, because factorials grow
   very fast. */
// END

/* Caption: How do I decide if 1965 is a leap year in C? */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write is_leap(year).
   2. A year divisible by 4 is a leap year, unless it is divisible by 100.
   3. Years divisible by 400 are leap years again.
   4. Check 1965 and print the result. */
/* Leap years divide by 4, except centuries, which must divide by 400. */
int is_leap(int year) {
    return (year % 4 == 0 && year % 100 != 0) || year % 400 == 0;
}

int main(void) {
    int year = 1965;
    if (is_leap(year)) {
        printf("%d is a leap year\n", year);
    } else {
        printf("%d is not a leap year\n", year);
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: is_leap() returns true for years divisible by 4, except century years,
   which must also be divisible by 400. main() checks 1965 and prints whether it is a leap
   year. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to check whether a word is a palindrome. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <string.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write is_palindrome() for buffer.
   2. Compare the first and last characters, moving inwards.
   3. Return false at the first mismatch, otherwise true.
   4. Check keyboard and print the result. */
/* Compare characters from the front and back, moving inwards. */
bool is_palindrome(const char *buffer) {
    int i = 0;
    int j = strlen(buffer) - 1;
    while (i < j) {
        if (buffer[i] != buffer[j]) {
            return false;
        }
        i++;
        j--;
    }
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    const char *buffer = "keyboard";
    printf("%s %s a palindrome\n", buffer, is_palindrome(buffer) ? "is" : "is not");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: is_palindrome() compares the first and last characters and moves inwards;
   any mismatch means the word is not a palindrome. main() checks the word keyboard and
   prints the result. */
// END

/* Caption: How do I check every element of an array to find a target value in C? */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write linear_search() with the array, its length and key.
   2. Compare each element with key.
   3. Return the index of the first match, or -1.
   4. In main(), search for 61 and print the result. */
/* Return the index of key, or -1 when it is not in the array. */
int linear_search(const int items[], int n, int key) {
    for (int k = 0; k < n; k++) {
        if (items[k] == key) {
            return k;
        }
    }
    return -1;
}

int main(void) {
    int items[] = {97, 61, 93, 83, 13, 76, 94, 79};
    int n = sizeof(items) / sizeof(items[0]);
    int key = 61;
    int pos = linear_search(items, n, key);
    if (pos >= 0) {
        printf("Found %d at index %d\n", key, pos);
    } else {
        printf("%d is not in the array\n", key);
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: linear_search() checks the elements of items one by one and returns the
   index of the first one equal to key, or -1 when it reaches the end without a match.
   main() searches for 61 and prints where it is, or that it is missing. */
// END

/* Caption: Count how many even numbers are in an array. */

/* Plan:
   1. Write count_even() that takes nums and count.
   2. For each element, test nums[j] % 2 == 0.
   3. Add one to found for every even number.
   4. Return found and print it. */
/* A number is even when the remainder after dividing by 2 is zero. */
int count_even(const int nums[], int count) {
    int found = 0;
    for (int j = 0; j < count; j++) {
        if (nums[j] % 2 == 0) {
            found++;
        }
    }
    return found;
}

int main(void) {

    const int count = 9;
    printf("Even numbers: %d\n", count_even(nums, count));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: count_even() tests each element of nums with the % operator: a remainder of
   0 after dividing by 2 means the number is even, so found goes up by one. main() prints
   how many of the 9 values are even. */
// END

/* Caption: Find the smallest number in an array. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write min_of() that takes ages and length.
   2. Store ages[0] in current.
   3. Loop over the other elements and keep the smallest value in current.
   4. Return current and print it. */
/* Start with the first element and keep the smallest value seen so far. */
int min_of(const int ages[], int length) {
    int current = ages[0];
    for (int idx = 1; idx < length; idx++) {
        if (ages[idx] < current) {
            current = ages[idx];
        }
    }
    return current;
}

int main(void) {
    int ages[] = {6, 13, 30, 65, 28, 23};
    int length = sizeof(ages) / sizeof(ages[0]);
    printf("Smallest: %d\n", min_of(ages, length));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: min_of() takes the first element as the smallest value so far and stores it
   in current. The loop compares every other element with current using < and keeps the
   smallest one. main() prints the smallest of the 6 values. */
// END

/* Caption: Program to return a sum and an average together using pointer parameters. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write sum_and_average() with the pointers sum and average.
   2. Add the values into *sum.
   3. Store *sum / n in *average.
   4. Declare total and mean, pass their addresses and print them. */
void sum_and_average(const double v[], int n, double *sum, double *average) {
    *sum = 0.0;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        *sum += v[i];
    }
    *average = *sum / n;
}

int main(void) {
    double prices[] = {98.2, 84.2, 50.3, 50.5};
    int n = sizeof(prices) / sizeof(prices[0]);
    double total, mean;
    sum_and_average(prices, n, &total, &mean);
    printf("Sum: %.2f, Average: %.2f\n", total, mean);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: sum_and_average() takes the array, its length and two pointers. It adds up
   the 4 values through *sum and then stores *sum / n in *average. main() declares total
   and mean on one line and passes their addresses. */
// END

#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Open notes.txt in write mode and check for NULL.
   2. Write 2 lines with fprintf and close the file.
   3. Open it again in read mode.
   4. Read and print each line with fgets, then close the file. */

    FILE *file = fopen("notes.txt", "w");
    if (file == NULL) {
        perror("fopen");
        return 1;

    fprintf(file, "keep functions short and focused\n");
    fprintf(file, "loops repeat a block of code\n");

    /* Reopen the file for reading and print it line by line. */

    if (file == NULL) {
        perror("fopen");
        return 1;
    }
    char line[128];
    while (fgets(line, sizeof(line), file) != NULL) {
        printf("%s", line);
    }
    fclose(file);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: fopen() in write mode creates notes.txt, fprintf() writes 2 lines into it
   and fclose() saves it. The file is then opened again in read mode, and fgets() reads it
   back line by line into the buffer line, which is printed. Every fopen() result is
   checked for NULL. */

/* Caption: C program to add two matrices element by element. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define ROWS as 2 and COLS as 4.
   2. Loop over every row r and column c.
   3. Store a[r][c] + b[r][c] in sum and print it. */
#define ROWS 2
#define COLS 4

int main(void) {
    int a[ROWS][COLS] = {{1, 9, 5, 1}, {8, 3, 6, 3}};
    int b[ROWS][COLS] = {{1, 4, 3, 5}, {4, 2, 8, 5}};
    int sum[ROWS][COLS];
    /* Each entry of the result is the sum of the matching entries. */
    for (int r = 0; r < ROWS; r++) {
        for (int c = 0; c < COLS; c++) {
            sum[r][c] = a[r][c] + b[r][c];
            printf("%3d", sum[r][c]);
        }
        printf("\n");
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: Both matrices are 2x4 two-dimensional arrays. Two nested loops visit every
   row r and column c, store a[r][c] + b[r][c] in sum and print each row. */
// END

   h, m and s on one line and converts 74151 seconds. */
// END

/* Caption: C program to count the words in a sentence. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <ctype.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write count_words() with words = 0 and an in_word flag.
   2. A space ends a word; a non-space after a space starts a new word and adds one to
      words.
   3. Return words and print it. */
/* A new word starts when a non-space follows a space (or the start). */
int count_words(const char *text) {
    int words = 0;
    int in_word = 0;
    for (int i = 0; text[i] != '\0'; i++) {
        if (isspace((unsigned char)text[i])) {
            in_word = 0;
        } else if (!in_word) {
            in_word = 1;
            words++;
        }
    }
    return words;
}

int main(void) {
    const char *sentence = "structs group related data together";
    printf("Words: %d\n", count_words(sentence));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: count_words() uses the flag in_word: a new word starts when a non-space
   character follows a space or the start of the text. main() prints the number of words in
   the sentence. */
// END

/* Plan:
   1. Start result at 0.
   2. Multiply result by 10, add n % 10, then divide n by 10.
   3. Repeat until n is 0.

/* Take the last digit with % 10, then drop it with / 10. */
int reverse_digits(int n) {

    while (n > 0) {
        result = result * 10 + n % 10;

    }
    return result;
}

int main(void) {

    printf("reverse of digits of %d: %d\n", number, reverse_digits(number));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: reverse_digits() shifts result one place left (result * 10) and adds the
   last digit of n, which reverses the order. main() applies it to 329902. */
// END

/* Caption: Use insertion sort to put numbers in descending order. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write insertion_sort() for the int array readings.
   2. Take each element in turn as current.
   3. Shift the smaller values of the sorted part one place right.
   4. Put current into the gap.
   5. Print the sorted values. */
/* Insert each element into the already sorted part on its left. */
void insertion_sort(int readings[], int len) {
    for (int i = 1; i < len; i++) {
        int current = readings[i];
        int j = i - 1;
        while (j >= 0 && readings[j] < current) {
            readings[j + 1] = readings[j];   /* shift bigger values right */
            j--;
        }
        readings[j + 1] = current;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    int readings[] = {50, 73, 76, 35, 37};
    int len = 5;
    insertion_sort(readings, len);
    for (int i = 0; i < len; i++) {
        printf("%d ", readings[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: insertion_sort() takes each element in turn and shifts the smaller values
   of the sorted part one place right until the element fits. main() then prints the 5
   values in descending order. */
// END

/* Caption: Print the binary representation of an integer. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write print_binary(n, bits).
   2. Go through the bits from the highest to the lowest.
   3. Print 1 when (n >> b) & 1 is set, otherwise 0.
   4. Print 241 in binary. */
/* Check each bit from the highest to the lowest. */
void print_binary(unsigned int n, int bits) {
    for (int b = bits - 1; b >= 0; b--) {
        putchar((n >> b) & 1 ? '1' : '0');
    }
    putchar('\n');
}

int main(void) {
    unsigned int number = 241;
    printf("%u in binary: ", number);
    print_binary(number, 16);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: print_binary() checks one bit at a time, from the highest to the lowest: (n
   >> b) & 1 is 1 when bit b is set, so it prints the character 1 or 0. main() prints 241
   in binary. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to add two integers. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Read first and second.
   2. Write add_numbers() that returns p + q.
   3. Print the sum it returns. */
/* Return the sum of two numbers. */

}

int main(void) {

    if (scanf("%ld %ld", &first, &second) != 2) {

        return 1;
    }
    printf("Sum: %ld\n", add_numbers(first, second));

/* Caption: Compute the mean of a list of numbers. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write compute_mean() that takes marks and len.
   2. Add the values into the double total.
   3. Return total / len.
   4. Print the average with two decimals. */
/* Sum the values, then divide by how many there are. */
double compute_mean(const double marks[], int len) {
    double total = 0.0;
    int i = 0;
    while (i < len) {
        total += marks[i];
        i++;
    }
    return total / len;
}

int main(void) {
    double marks[] = {39.0, 16.0, 14.9, 54.1, 78.7, 70.3, 3.7, 44.2};
    int len = 8;
    printf("The average is %.2f\n", compute_mean(marks, len));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: compute_mean() adds the 8 values of marks into the double total and divides
   by len, so the mean keeps its decimal part even when the values are whole numbers.
   main() prints it with two decimals. */
// END

/* Caption: Implement selection sort for an array of long values. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write selection_sort() for the long array values.
   2. For each position, find the largest remaining element.
   3. Swap it into that position.
   4. Print the sorted values. */
/* Select the right element for each position and swap it into place. */
void selection_sort(long values[], int n) {
    for (int i = 0; i < n - 1; i++) {
        int chosen = i;
        for (int j = i + 1; j < n; j++) {
            if (values[chosen] < values[j]) {
                chosen = j;
            }
        }
        long tmp = values[i];
        values[i] = values[chosen];
        values[chosen] = tmp;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    long values[] = {38L, 95L, 98L, 30L, 14L, 73L, 34L, 59L, 42L, 3L};
    const int n = 10;
    selection_sort(values, n);
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        printf("%ld ", values[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: selection_sort() finds the largest remaining element for each position and
   swaps it into place. main() then prints the 10 values in descending order. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to return two values from a function using pointer parameters. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write sum_and_average() with the pointers sum and average.
   2. Add the values into *sum.
   3. Store *sum / n in *average.
   4. Declare total and mean, pass their addresses and print them. */
void sum_and_average(const double v[], int n, double *sum, double *average) {
    *sum = 0.0;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        *sum += v[i];
    }
    *average = *sum / n;
}

int main(void) {
    double values[] = {79.2, 13.3, 57.5, 76.7, 80.8, 47.6, 71.0, 32.9};
    int n = sizeof(values) / sizeof(values[0]);
    double total, mean;
    sum_and_average(values, n, &total, &mean);
    printf("Sum: %.2f, Average: %.2f\n", total, mean);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: sum_and_average() takes the array, its length and two pointers. It adds up
   the 8 values through *sum and then stores *sum / n in *average. main() declares total
   and mean on one line and passes their addresses. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to build a fixed-size integer stack in C. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define a Stack with room for 8 items and a top counter.
   2. Write push() and pop(), returning false when the stack is full or empty.
   3. Push 3 values.
   4. Pop and print until the stack is empty. */
#define CAPACITY 8

typedef struct {
    int items[CAPACITY];
    int top;   /* number of items on the stack */
} Stack;

bool push(Stack *s, int value) {
    if (s->top == CAPACITY) {
        return false;   /* stack is full */
    }
    s->items[s->top++] = value;
    return true;
}

bool pop(Stack *s, int *value) {
    if (s->top == 0) {
        return false;   /* stack is empty */
    }
    *value = s->items[--s->top];
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    Stack s = {.top = 0};
    push(&s, 54);
    push(&s, 95);
    push(&s, 85);
    int value;
    /* Items come back out in reverse order (last in, first out). */
    while (pop(&s, &value)) {
        printf("%d ", value);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: The Stack keeps up to 8 items in an array, and top counts how many are
   stored. push() adds at the top and pop() removes from the top; both return false when
   they cannot. main() pushes 3 values and pops them all, so they come out in reverse order
   (last in, first out). */
// END

/* Caption: C program to check whether a word is a palindrome. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <string.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write is_palindrome() for buffer.
   2. Compare the first and last characters, moving inwards.
   3. Return false at the first mismatch, otherwise true.
   4. Check pointer and print the result. */
/* Compare characters from the front and back, moving inwards. */
bool is_palindrome(const char *buffer) {
    int i = 0;
    int j = strlen(buffer) - 1;
    while (i < j) {
        if (buffer[i] != buffer[j]) {
            return false;
        }
        i++;
        j--;
    }
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    const char *buffer = "pointer";
    printf("%s %s a palindrome\n", buffer, is_palindrome(buffer) ? "is" : "is not");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: is_palindrome() compares the first and last characters and moves inwards;
   any mismatch means the word is not a palindrome. main() checks the word pointer and
   prints the result. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to use bubble sort to put numbers in ascending order. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write bubble_sort() for the int array values.
   2. Compare each pair of neighbours.
   3. Swap them when they are in the wrong order for ascending order.
   4. Repeat the passes until the array is sorted.
   5. Print the sorted values. */
/* Repeatedly swap neighbours that are in the wrong order. */
void bubble_sort(int values[], int len) {
    for (int i = 0; i < len - 1; i++) {
        for (int j = 0; j < len - 1 - i; j++) {
            if (values[j] > values[j + 1]) {
                int tmp = values[j];
                values[j] = values[j + 1];
                values[j + 1] = tmp;
            }
        }
    }
}

int main(void) {
    int values[] = {85, 71, 56, 17, 75, 7, 2, 79};
    int len = 8;
    bubble_sort(values, len);
    for (int i = 0; i < len; i++) {
        printf("%d ", values[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: bubble_sort() walks through values again and again and swaps neighbours
   that are in the wrong order, so the largest values move to the end first. main() then
   prints the 8 values in ascending order. */
// END

/* Plan:
   1. Write add_all() that takes the array readings and its length n.

/* Return the sum of the first n elements. */
int add_all(const int readings[], int n) {
    int result = 0;
    int k = 0;
    while (k < n) {
        result += readings[k];

}

int main(void) {

    const int n = 4;
    printf("Sum: %d\n", add_all(readings, n));

}
/* Explanation: add_all() receives the array readings and its length n. It starts result at

/* Caption: How do I sort an array in ascending order using insertion sort in C? */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write insertion_sort() for the long array items.
   2. Take each element in turn as current.
   3. Shift the larger values of the sorted part one place right.
   4. Put current into the gap.
   5. Print the sorted values. */
/* Insert each element into the already sorted part on its left. */
void insertion_sort(long items[], int n) {
    for (int i = 1; i < n; i++) {
        long current = items[i];
        int j = i - 1;
        while (j >= 0 && items[j] > current) {
            items[j + 1] = items[j];   /* shift bigger values right */
            j--;
        }
        items[j + 1] = current;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    long items[] = {41L, 10L, 58L, 42L, 44L, 71L, 31L, 1L, 36L, 75L};
    const int n = 10;
    insertion_sort(items, n);
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        printf("%ld ", items[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: insertion_sort() takes each element in turn and shifts the larger values of
   the sorted part one place right until the element fits. main() then prints the 10 values
   in ascending order. */
// END

/* Caption: Compute the sum of the digits of an integer. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Start result at 0.
   2. Add n % 10 to result, then divide n by 10.
   3. Repeat until n is 0.
   4. Apply it to 769619 and print the result. */
/* Take the last digit with % 10, then drop it with / 10. */
int sum_digits(int n) {
    int result = 0;
    while (n > 0) {
        result += n % 10;
        n /= 10;
    }
    return result;
}

int main(void) {
    int number = 769619;
    printf("sum of digits of %d: %d\n", number, sum_digits(number));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: sum_digits() adds the last digit (n % 10) to result and then removes it (n
   / 10) until no digits are left. main() applies it to 769619. */
// END

/* Caption: How do I allocate an array with malloc and fill it with multiples in C? */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Use malloc to get room for 10 ints and check for NULL.
   2. Fill arr with multiples.
   3. Print the values.
   4. Call free(arr) at the end. */
int main(void) {
    int n = 10;
    /* Ask the heap for room for n ints; malloc returns NULL on failure. */
    int *arr = malloc(n * sizeof(int));
    if (arr == NULL) {
        fprintf(stderr, "malloc failed\n");
        return 1;
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        arr[i] = 9 * i;
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        printf("%d ", arr[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    free(arr);   /* give the memory back */
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: malloc() reserves room for 10 ints on the heap and returns NULL if it
   fails, which the program checks. The first loop fills arr with multiples, the second
   prints them, and free() gives the memory back at the end. */
// END

/* Caption: Use binary search to locate a value in a sorted list. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Make sure the array is sorted.
   2. Set lo to 0 and hi to length - 1.
   3. While lo <= hi, compare the middle element mid with the key.
   4. Return the index if it matches; otherwise keep only the half that can hold the
      key.
   5. Return -1 if the range becomes empty, and print the index of 201. */
/* The array must be sorted. Each step halves the range that can still hold the key. */
int binary_search(const int scores[], int length, int key) {
    int lo = 0;
    int hi = length - 1;
    while (lo <= hi) {
        int mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;
        if (scores[mid] == key) {
            return mid;
        } else if (scores[mid] < key) {
            lo = mid + 1;   /* key is in the right half */
        } else {
            hi = mid - 1;   /* key is in the left half */
        }
    }
    return -1;
}

int main(void) {
    int scores[] = {31, 44, 57, 123, 149, 153, 177};
    int length = 7;
    int index = binary_search(scores, length, 201);
    printf("Index of 201: %d\n", index);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: binary_search() needs a sorted array. It keeps the range from lo to hi,
   compares the middle element mid with the key and throws away the half that cannot
   contain it, so it needs only about log2(n) steps. main() looks for 201 and prints its
   index, or -1 if it is not there. */
// END

/* Caption: Check whether a year is a leap year. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write is_leap(year).
   2. A year divisible by 4 is a leap year, unless it is divisible by 100.
   3. Years divisible by 400 are leap years again.
   4. Check 1930 and print the result. */
/* Leap years divide by 4, except centuries, which must divide by 400. */
int is_leap(int year) {
    return (year % 4 == 0 && year % 100 != 0) || year % 400 == 0;
}

int main(void) {
    int year = 1930;
    if (is_leap(year)) {
        printf("%d is a leap year\n", year);
    } else {
        printf("%d is not a leap year\n", year);
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: is_leap() returns true for years divisible by 4, except century years,
   which must also be divisible by 400. main() checks 1930 and prints whether it is a leap
   year. */
// END

/* Caption: Implement a simple linked list with malloc and free. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define ListNode with a value and a next pointer.
   2. Write push_front() that mallocs a node and links it in front of head.
   3. Write print_list() that follows next until NULL.
   4. Write free_list() that frees every node.
   5. Push 6 values, print the list and free it. */
typedef struct ListNode {
    int value;
    struct ListNode *next;
} ListNode;

/* Allocate a new node and put it in front of the current head. */
ListNode *push_front(ListNode *head, int value) {
    ListNode *node = malloc(sizeof(ListNode));
    if (node == NULL) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Out of memory\n");
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }
    node->value = value;
    node->next = head;
    return node;
}

void print_list(const ListNode *head) {
    for (const ListNode *cur = head; cur != NULL; cur = cur->next) {
        printf("%d -> ", cur->value);
    }
    printf("NULL\n");
}

/* Free every node; save next before freeing the current one. */
void free_list(ListNode *head) {
    while (head != NULL) {
        ListNode *next = head->next;
        free(head);
        head = next;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    ListNode *head = NULL;
    head = push_front(head, 9);
    head = push_front(head, 66);
    head = push_front(head, 98);
    head = push_front(head, 13);
    head = push_front(head, 36);
    head = push_front(head, 24);
    print_list(head);
    free_list(head);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: Each ListNode holds a value and a pointer to the next node. push_front()
   allocates a node with malloc, puts it in front of head and returns it; print_list()
   follows the next pointers until NULL; free_list() frees every node. main() pushes 6
   values, so they print in reverse order. */
// END

/* Caption: Program to declare two pointers in one statement and use them. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Declare x and y on one line.
   2. Declare the pointers px and py on one line, each with its own *.
   3. Add 17 to x through px and print the values. */
int main(void) {
    int x = 19, y = 3;
    /* Each pointer needs its own '*': in "int *p, q;" only p is a pointer. */
    int *px = &x, *py = &y;
    *px += 17;
    printf("x = %d, y = %d\n", x, y);
    printf("*px = %d, *py = %d\n", *px, *py);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: int *px = &x, *py = &y; declares two pointers in one statement; each name
   needs its own *. *px += 17 changes x through the pointer, so x becomes 36 while y stays
   3. */
// END

/* Caption: C program to calculate 12! using recursion. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write factorial(num) that calls itself.
   2. Return 1 when num is 1 or less.
   3. Otherwise return num * factorial(num - 1).
   4. Print 12! as an unsigned long long. */
/* n! = n * (n - 1)!, and 0! = 1 stops the recursion. */
unsigned long long factorial(int num) {
    if (num <= 1) {
        return 1;
    }
    return num * factorial(num - 1);
}

int main(void) {
    int num = 12;
    printf("%d! = %llu\n", num, factorial(num));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: factorial() calls itself: n! is n * (n - 1)!, and the recursion stops when
   num is 1 or less. main() prints 12! as an unsigned long long, because factorials grow
   very fast. */
// END

/* Caption: Compute the LCM of two integers using the GCD. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write gcd() with Euclid's algorithm: replace (a, b) by (b, a % b) until b is 0.
   2. Write lcm() as a / gcd(a, b) * b.
   3. Print the LCM of 7 and 143. */
/* Euclid: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a % b) until b becomes zero. */
int gcd(int a, int b) {
    while (b != 0) {
        int r = a % b;
        a = b;
        b = r;
    }
    return a;
}

/* lcm(a, b) = a / gcd(a, b) * b (divide first to avoid overflow). */
long lcm(int a, int b) {
    return (long)a / gcd(a, b) * b;
}

int main(void) {
    printf("lcm(7, 143) = %ld\n", lcm(7, 143));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: gcd() uses Euclid's algorithm: it keeps replacing (a, b) with (b, a % b)
   until b is 0. lcm() divides a by the gcd before multiplying by b, which avoids overflow.
   main() prints the LCM of 7 and 143. */
// END

/* Caption: How do I count how many even numbers are in an array in C? */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write count_even() that takes readings and length.
   2. For each element, test readings[j] % 2 == 0.
   3. Add one to found for every even number.
   4. Return found and print it. */
/* A number is even when the remainder after dividing by 2 is zero. */
int count_even(const int readings[], int length) {
    int found = 0;
    int j = 0;
    while (j < length) {
        if (readings[j] % 2 == 0) {
            found++;
        }
        j++;
    }
    return found;
}

int main(void) {
    int readings[] = {11, 96, 64, 75, 74};
    int length = sizeof(readings) / sizeof(readings[0]);
    printf("Even numbers: %d\n", count_even(readings, length));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: count_even() tests each element of readings with the % operator: a
   remainder of 0 after dividing by 2 means the number is even, so found goes up by one.
   main() prints how many of the 5 values are even. */
// END

/* Caption: Reverse the characters of a word. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <string.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write reverse_string() for word.
   2. Set i to the first index and j to the last.
   3. Swap the two characters and move i and j inwards until they meet.
   4. Reverse bridge and print it. */
/* Swap characters from both ends until they meet in the middle. */
void reverse_string(char *word) {
    int i = 0;
    int j = strlen(word) - 1;
    while (i < j) {
        char tmp = word[i];
        word[i] = word[j];
        word[j] = tmp;
        i++;
        j--;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    char word[] = "bridge";
    reverse_string(word);
    printf("%s\n", word);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: reverse_string() swaps characters from both ends of word, moving inwards
   until the two indexes meet. main() reverses the word bridge in place and prints it. */
// END

/* Caption: Find the number of digits in an integer. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Start result at 0.
   2. Divide n by 10 and add one to result.
   3. Repeat until n is 0.
   4. Apply it to 195584 and print the result. */
/* Take the last digit with % 10, then drop it with / 10. */
int count_digits(int n) {
    int result = 0;
    while (n > 0) {
        result++;
        n /= 10;
    }
    return result;
}

int main(void) {
    int number = 195584;
    printf("count of digits of %d: %d\n", number, count_digits(number));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: count_digits() removes the last digit (n / 10) and adds one to result each
   time, until n reaches 0. main() applies it to 195584. */
// END

/* Caption: How do I add two 3x4 matrices in C? */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define ROWS as 3 and COLS as 4.
   2. Loop over every row r and column c.
   3. Store a[r][c] + b[r][c] in sum and print it. */
#define ROWS 3
#define COLS 4

int main(void) {
    int a[ROWS][COLS] = {{3, 7, 2, 6}, {8, 3, 4, 8}, {7, 8, 6, 6}};
    int b[ROWS][COLS] = {{4, 9, 7, 6}, {0, 3, 9, 8}, {7, 5, 4, 0}};
    int sum[ROWS][COLS];
    /* Each entry of the result is the sum of the matching entries. */
    for (int r = 0; r < ROWS; r++) {
        for (int c = 0; c < COLS; c++) {
            sum[r][c] = a[r][c] + b[r][c];
            printf("%3d", sum[r][c]);
        }
        printf("\n");
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: Both matrices are 3x4 two-dimensional arrays. Two nested loops visit every
   row r and column c, store a[r][c] + b[r][c] in sum and print each row. */
// END

/* Caption: Use a struct to return several results from one function. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define a Stats struct with min, max and average.
   2. Write array_stats() that fills one Stats in a loop.
   3. Return the struct.
   4. Print st.min, st.max and st.average. */
typedef struct {
    int min;
    int max;
    double average;
} Stats;

/* Pack several results into one struct and return it. */
Stats array_stats(const int v[], int n) {
    Stats s = {v[0], v[0], 0.0};
    double total = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        if (v[i] < s.min) {
            s.min = v[i];
        }
        if (v[i] > s.max) {
            s.max = v[i];
        }
        total += v[i];
    }
    s.average = total / n;
    return s;
}

int main(void) {
    int values[] = {50, 72, 16, 67, 65};
    int n = sizeof(values) / sizeof(values[0]);
    Stats st = array_stats(values, n);
    printf("Min %d, Max %d, Average %.2f\n", st.min, st.max, st.average);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: Stats groups three results. array_stats() fills one Stats while it loops
   over the 5 values and returns the whole struct, which is a clean way to return several
   results at once. main() reads them as st.min, st.max and st.average. */
// END

/* Caption: Build a linked list, print it, and free it. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define Item with a value and a next pointer.
   2. Write push_front() that mallocs a node and links it in front of head.
   3. Write print_list() that follows next until NULL.
   4. Write free_list() that frees every node.
   5. Push 6 values, print the list and free it. */
typedef struct Item {
    int value;
    struct Item *next;
} Item;

/* Allocate a new node and put it in front of the current head. */
Item *push_front(Item *head, int value) {
    Item *node = malloc(sizeof(Item));
    if (node == NULL) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Out of memory\n");
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }
    node->value = value;
    node->next = head;
    return node;
}

void print_list(const Item *head) {
    for (const Item *cur = head; cur != NULL; cur = cur->next) {
        printf("%d -> ", cur->value);
    }
    printf("NULL\n");
}

/* Free every node; save next before freeing the current one. */
void free_list(Item *head) {
    while (head != NULL) {
        Item *next = head->next;
        free(head);
        head = next;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    Item *head = NULL;
    head = push_front(head, 81);
    head = push_front(head, 32);
    head = push_front(head, 27);
    head = push_front(head, 48);
    head = push_front(head, 3);
    head = push_front(head, 73);
    print_list(head);
    free_list(head);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: Each Item holds a value and a pointer to the next node. push_front()
   allocates a node with malloc, puts it in front of head and returns it; print_list()
   follows the next pointers until NULL; free_list() frees every node. main() pushes 6
   values, so they print in reverse order. */
// END

/* Caption: Print the binary representation of an integer. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write print_binary(n, bits).
   2. Go through the bits from the highest to the lowest.
   3. Print 1 when (n >> b) & 1 is set, otherwise 0.
   4. Print 23 in binary. */
/* Check each bit from the highest to the lowest. */
void print_binary(unsigned int n, int bits) {
    for (int b = bits - 1; b >= 0; b--) {
        putchar((n >> b) & 1 ? '1' : '0');
    }
    putchar('\n');
}

int main(void) {
    unsigned int number = 23;
    printf("%u in binary: ", number);
    print_binary(number, 12);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: print_binary() checks one bit at a time, from the highest to the lowest: (n
   >> b) & 1 is 1 when bit b is set, so it prints the character 1 or 0. main() prints 23 in
   binary. */
// END
