/* Caption: C program to compute 3 to the power of 7 without pow(). */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write power(base, exp) with result = 1.
   2. Multiply result by base exp times.
   3. Print 3 to the power 7. */
/* Multiply the base by itself exp times. */
long long power(int base, int exp) {
    long long result = 1;
    for (int i = 0; i < exp; i++) {
        result *= base;
    }
    return result;
}

int main(void) {
    printf("3^7 = %lld\n", power(3, 7));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: power() starts result at 1 and multiplies it by base exp times. It uses
   long long because powers grow quickly. main() prints 3 to the power 7. */
// END

/* Caption: Check every element of an array to find a target value. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write linear_search() with the array, its length and key.
   2. Compare each element with key.
   3. Return the index of the first match, or -1.
   4. In main(), search for 170 and print the result. */
/* Return the index of key, or -1 when it is not in the array. */
int linear_search(const int values[], int n, int key) {
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        if (values[i] == key) {
            return i;
        }
    }
    return -1;
}

int main(void) {
    int values[] = {19, 36, 74, 48, 13};
    int n = 5;
    int key = 170;
    int pos = linear_search(values, n, key);
    if (pos >= 0) {
        printf("Found %d at index %d\n", key, pos);
    } else {
        printf("%d is not in the array\n", key);
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: linear_search() checks the elements of values one by one and returns the
   index of the first one equal to key, or -1 when it reaches the end without a match.
   main() searches for 170 and prints where it is, or that it is missing. */
// END

/* Caption: Test if "keyboard" reads the same backwards. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <string.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write is_palindrome() for buffer.
   2. Compare the first and last characters, moving inwards.
   3. Return false at the first mismatch, otherwise true.
   4. Check keyboard and print the result. */
/* Compare characters from the front and back, moving inwards. */
bool is_palindrome(const char *buffer) {
    int i = 0;
    int j = strlen(buffer) - 1;
    while (i < j) {
        if (buffer[i] != buffer[j]) {
            return false;
        }
        i++;
        j--;
    }
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    const char *buffer = "keyboard";
    printf("%s %s a palindrome\n", buffer, is_palindrome(buffer) ? "is" : "is not");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: is_palindrome() compares the first and last characters and moves inwards;
   any mismatch means the word is not a palindrome. main() checks the word keyboard and
   prints the result. */
// END

/* Caption: Use dynamic memory to store the first 9 cubes. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Use malloc to get room for 9 ints and check for NULL.
   2. Fill arr with cubes.
   3. Print the values.
   4. Call free(arr) at the end. */
int main(void) {
    int n = 9;
    /* Ask the heap for room for n ints; malloc returns NULL on failure. */
    int *arr = malloc(n * sizeof(int));
    if (arr == NULL) {
        fprintf(stderr, "malloc failed\n");
        return 1;
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        arr[i] = i * i * i;
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        printf("%d ", arr[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    free(arr);   /* give the memory back */
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: malloc() reserves room for 9 ints on the heap and returns NULL if it fails,
   which the program checks. The first loop fills arr with cubes, the second prints them,
   and free() gives the memory back at the end. */
// END

/* Plan:
   1. Write clamp(value, low, high).
   2. Return low if the value is too small and high if it is too big.
   3. Otherwise return the value.
   4. Set low = 19 and high = 23 and print clamp() for 1, 17 and 69. */
/* Return value, but never less than low or more than high. */
int clamp(int value, int low, int high) {
    if (value < low) {
        return low;
    }
    if (value > high) {
        return high;
    }
    return value;
}

int main(void) {
    int low = 19, high = 23;
    printf("clamp(%d) = %d\n", 1, clamp(1, low, high));
    printf("clamp(%d) = %d\n", 17, clamp(17, low, high));
    printf("clamp(%d) = %d\n", 69, clamp(69, low, high));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: clamp() takes three parameters: the value and the two limits. It returns
   low when the value is too small, high when it is too big and the value itself otherwise.
   main() declares low = 19 and high = 23 on one line and clamps 1, 17 and 69. */
// END

/* Caption: C program to compute the sum of the digits of an integer. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Start result at 0.
   2. Add n % 10 to result, then divide n by 10.
   3. Repeat until n is 0.
   4. Apply it to 83860 and print the result. */
/* Take the last digit with % 10, then drop it with / 10. */
int sum_digits(int n) {
    int result = 0;
    while (n > 0) {
        result += n % 10;
        n /= 10;
    }
    return result;
}

int main(void) {
    int number = 83860;
    printf("sum of digits of %d: %d\n", number, sum_digits(number));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: sum_digits() adds the last digit (n % 10) to result and then removes it (n
   / 10) until no digits are left. main() applies it to 83860. */
// END

#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Read num1, num2 and num3.
   2. Assume num1 is the largest.
   3. Compare it with the other two and keep the bigger value.
   4. Print the result. */
int main(void) {
    int num1, num2, num3;
    printf("Enter 3 numbers: ");
    if (scanf("%d %d %d", &num1, &num2, &num3) != 3) {
        printf("Invalid input\n");
        return 1;
    }
    int best = num1;
    /* Compare with each of the others and keep the bigger one. */
    if (num2 > best) {
        best = num2;
    }
    if (num3 > best) {
        best = num3;
    }
    printf("The largest is %d\n", best);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: The program reads num1, num2 and num3 from the keyboard with scanf and
   stops with a message if the input is not valid. It assumes num1 is the largest, compares
   it with the other two and keeps the bigger value in best, which it prints. */
// END

/* Caption: Compute the distance between two points using a struct. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <math.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define a Point struct with x and y.
   2. Write distance() using sqrt(dx * dx + dy * dy).
   3. Print the distance between p and q. */
typedef struct {
    double x;
    double y;
} Point;

/* Pythagoras: sqrt(dx * dx + dy * dy). */
double distance(Point a, Point b) {
    double dx = b.x - a.x;
    double dy = b.y - a.y;
    return sqrt(dx * dx + dy * dy);
}

int main(void) {
    Point p = {-9, 6};
    Point q = {8, -9};
    printf("Distance: %.3f\n", distance(p, q));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: Point is a typedef struct with x and y. distance() uses Pythagoras, sqrt(dx
   * dx + dy * dy), to measure the gap between the two points, and main() prints it. */
// END

/* Caption: Calculate 4! using recursion. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write factorial(x) that calls itself.
   2. Return 1 when x is 1 or less.
   3. Otherwise return x * factorial(x - 1).
   4. Print 4! as an unsigned long long. */
/* n! = n * (n - 1)!, and 0! = 1 stops the recursion. */
unsigned long long factorial(int x) {
    if (x <= 1) {
        return 1;
    }
    return x * factorial(x - 1);
}

int main(void) {
    int x = 4;
    printf("%d! = %llu\n", x, factorial(x));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: factorial() calls itself: n! is n * (n - 1)!, and the recursion stops when
   x is 1 or less. main() prints 4! as an unsigned long long, because factorials grow very
   fast. */
// END

/* Caption: Compute the factorial of a number with a loop. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write factorial(value) with result = 1.
   2. Multiply result by every number from 2 to value.
   3. Return result.
   4. Print 15! as an unsigned long long. */
/* Multiply 1 * 2 * ... * n. */
unsigned long long factorial(int value) {
    unsigned long long result = 1;
    for (int i = 2; i <= value; i++) {
        result *= i;
    }
    return result;
}

int main(void) {
    int value = 15;
    printf("%d! = %llu\n", value, factorial(value));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: factorial() multiplies result by every number from 2 up to value. main()
   prints 15! as an unsigned long long, because factorials grow very fast. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to allocate an array with malloc and fill it with cubes. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Use malloc to get room for 15 ints and check for NULL.
   2. Fill buffer with cubes.
   3. Print the values.
   4. Call free(buffer) at the end. */
int main(void) {
    int n = 15;
    /* Ask the heap for room for n ints; malloc returns NULL on failure. */
    int *buffer = malloc(n * sizeof(int));
    if (buffer == NULL) {
        fprintf(stderr, "malloc failed\n");
        return 1;
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        buffer[i] = i * i * i;
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        printf("%d ", buffer[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    free(buffer);   /* give the memory back */
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: malloc() reserves room for 15 ints on the heap and returns NULL if it
   fails, which the program checks. The first loop fills buffer with cubes, the second
   prints them, and free() gives the memory back at the end. */
// END

/* Caption: Program to compute 6 to the power of 3 without pow(). */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write power(base, exp) with result = 1.
   2. Multiply result by base exp times.
   3. Print 6 to the power 3. */
/* Multiply the base by itself exp times. */
long long power(int base, int exp) {
    long long result = 1;
    for (int i = 0; i < exp; i++) {
        result *= base;
    }
    return result;
}

int main(void) {
    printf("6^3 = %lld\n", power(6, 3));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: power() starts result at 1 and multiplies it by base exp times. It uses
   long long because powers grow quickly. main() prints 6 to the power 3. */
// END

/* Caption: Program to count how many even numbers are in an array. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write count_even() that takes items and length.
   2. For each element, test items[idx] % 2 == 0.
   3. Add one to found for every even number.
   4. Return found and print it. */
/* A number is even when the remainder after dividing by 2 is zero. */
int count_even(const int items[], int length) {
    int found = 0;
    for (int idx = 0; idx < length; idx++) {
        if (items[idx] % 2 == 0) {
            found++;
        }
    }
    return found;
}

int main(void) {
    int items[] = {46, 82, 66, 72, 98, 62};
    int length = 6;
    printf("Count of even values = %d\n", count_even(items, length));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: count_even() tests each element of items with the % operator: a remainder
   of 0 after dividing by 2 means the number is even, so found goes up by one. main()
   prints how many of the 6 values are even. */
// END

/* Caption: Decide if 2060 is a leap year. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write is_leap(year).
   2. A year divisible by 4 is a leap year, unless it is divisible by 100.
   3. Years divisible by 400 are leap years again.
   4. Check 2060 and print the result. */
/* Leap years divide by 4, except centuries, which must divide by 400. */
int is_leap(int year) {
    return (year % 4 == 0 && year % 100 != 0) || year % 400 == 0;
}

int main(void) {
    int year = 2060;
    if (is_leap(year)) {
        printf("%d is a leap year\n", year);
    } else {
        printf("%d is not a leap year\n", year);
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: is_leap() returns true for years divisible by 4, except century years,
   which must also be divisible by 400. main() checks 2060 and prints whether it is a leap
   year. */
// END

/* Caption: Reverse an array by swapping from both ends. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write reverse_array() for data.
   2. Set i to the first index and j to the last.
   3. Swap data[i] and data[j], then move both inwards.
   4. Stop when i meets j and print the array. */
/* Swap the outer pair, then move both ends toward the middle. */
void reverse_array(int data[], int length) {
    int i = 0;
    int j = length - 1;
    while (i < j) {
        int tmp = data[i];
        data[i] = data[j];
        data[j] = tmp;
        i++;
        j--;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    int data[] = {63, 40, 93, 24, 58, 60, 70};
    int length = 7;
    reverse_array(data, length);
    for (int i = 0; i < length; i++) {
        printf("%d ", data[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: reverse_array() swaps the first and last elements, then moves i forward and
   j backward until they meet, so the array is reversed in place without a second array.
   main() prints the reversed values. */
// END

/* Caption: Find the arithmetic mean of 3 double values. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write compute_mean() that takes prices and length.
   2. Add the values into the double total.
   3. Return total / length.
   4. Print the average with two decimals. */
/* The mean is the total divided by the count. */
double compute_mean(const double prices[], int length) {
    double total = 0.0;
    int j = 0;
    while (j < length) {
        total += prices[j];
        j++;
    }
    return total / length;
}

int main(void) {
    double prices[] = {93.1, 1.3, 87.5};
    int length = sizeof(prices) / sizeof(prices[0]);
    printf("Mean = %.2f\n", compute_mean(prices, length));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: compute_mean() adds the 3 values of prices into the double total and
   divides by length, so the mean keeps its decimal part even when the values are whole
   numbers. main() prints it with two decimals. */
// END

/* Caption: Find the minimum and maximum of an array with one function. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write min_max() with the array, its length and the pointers min and max.
   2. Start both at the first element.
   3. Update *min and *max while looping over the rest.
   4. Declare low and high, pass their addresses and print them. */
/* One pass finds both results; they are stored through the pointers. */
void min_max(const int items[], int size, int *min, int *max) {
    *min = items[0];
    *max = items[0];
    for (int i = 1; i < size; i++) {
        if (items[i] < *min) {
            *min = items[i];
        }
        if (items[i] > *max) {
            *max = items[i];
        }
    }
}

int main(void) {
    int items[] = {56, 85, 18, 8, 97, 88, 10};
    int size = sizeof(items) / sizeof(items[0]);
    int low, high;
    min_max(items, size, &low, &high);
    printf("Min: %d, Max: %d\n", low, high);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: A C function can return only one value, so min_max() returns void and
   writes its two results through the pointer parameters min and max. main() declares low
   and high on one line and passes their addresses with &, then prints both results for the
   7 values. */
// END

/* Caption: Count how many vowels a string contains. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <string.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write count_vowels() with count = 0.
   2. For each character, check whether strchr finds it in aeiouAEIOU.
   3. Return count and print it. */
/* strchr finds the letter in the list of vowels, or returns NULL. */
int count_vowels(const char *text) {
    int count = 0;
    for (int i = 0; text[i] != '\0'; i++) {
        if (strchr("aeiouAEIOU", text[i]) != NULL) {
            count++;
        }
    }
    return count;
}

int main(void) {
    const char *sentence = "keep functions short and focused";
    printf("Vowels: %d\n", count_vowels(sentence));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: count_vowels() uses strchr to test whether each character is one of
   aeiouAEIOU and counts the matches. main() prints the number of vowels in the sentence. */
// END

/* Caption: Search a sorted array by halving the search range each step. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Make sure the array is sorted.
   2. Set lo to 0 and hi to length - 1.
   3. While lo <= hi, compare the middle element mid with the key.
   4. Return the index if it matches; otherwise keep only the half that can hold the
      key.
   5. Return -1 if the range becomes empty, and print the index of 201. */
/* The array must be sorted. Each step halves the range that can still hold the key. */
int binary_search(const int prices[], int length, int key) {
    int lo = 0;
    int hi = length - 1;
    while (lo <= hi) {
        int mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;
        if (prices[mid] == key) {
            return mid;
        } else if (prices[mid] < key) {
            lo = mid + 1;   /* key is in the right half */
        } else {
            hi = mid - 1;   /* key is in the left half */
        }
    }
    return -1;
}

int main(void) {
    int prices[] = {26, 47, 62, 82, 99, 159, 189};
    int length = 7;
    int index = binary_search(prices, length, 201);
    printf("Index of 201: %d\n", index);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: binary_search() needs a sorted array. It keeps the range from lo to hi,
   compares the middle element mid with the key and throws away the half that cannot
   contain it, so it needs only about log2(n) steps. main() looks for 201 and prints its
   index, or -1 if it is not there. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to divide two integers and get both the quotient and the remainder. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write divide(a, b, &quotient, &remainder) that returns a bool.
   2. Return false if b is 0.
   3. Store a / b and a % b through the pointers and return true.
   4. Divide 111 by 7 and print the results or the error. */
/* Returns false for division by zero; otherwise stores both results. */
bool divide(int a, int b, int *quotient, int *remainder) {
    if (b == 0) {
        return false;
    }
    *quotient = a / b;
    *remainder = a % b;
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    int a = 111, b = 7;
    int q, r;
    if (divide(a, b, &q, &r)) {
        printf("%d / %d = %d remainder %d\n", a, b, q, r);
    } else {
        printf("Cannot divide by zero\n");
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: divide() has four parameters: two inputs and two pointers for the results.
   Its bool return value reports success, while the quotient and remainder are written
   through the pointers. main() divides 111 by 7 and prints both results. */
// END

/* Caption: Use Euclid's algorithm to compute the GCD. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write gcd() with Euclid's algorithm.
   2. Replace (a, b) by (b, a % b) until b is 0.
   3. Return a and print the GCD of 249 and 71. */
/* Euclid: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a % b) until b becomes zero. */
int gcd(int a, int b) {
    while (b != 0) {
        int r = a % b;
        a = b;
        b = r;
    }
    return a;
}

int main(void) {
    int x = 249, y = 71;
    printf("gcd(%d, %d) = %d\n", x, y, gcd(x, y));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: gcd() uses Euclid's algorithm: it keeps replacing (a, b) with (b, a % b)
   until b is 0. The last non-zero value is the greatest common divisor, and main() prints
   the GCD of 249 and 71. */
// END

#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define Item with a value and a next pointer.
   2. Write push_front() that mallocs a node and links it in front of head.
   3. Write print_list() that follows next until NULL.
   4. Write free_list() that frees every node.
   5. Push 6 values, print the list and free it. */
typedef struct Item {
    int value;
    struct Item *next;
} Item;

/* Allocate a new node and put it in front of the current head. */
Item *push_front(Item *head, int value) {
    Item *node = malloc(sizeof(Item));
    if (node == NULL) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Out of memory\n");
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }
    node->value = value;
    node->next = head;
    return node;
}

void print_list(const Item *head) {
    for (const Item *cur = head; cur != NULL; cur = cur->next) {
        printf("%d -> ", cur->value);
    }
    printf("NULL\n");
}

/* Free every node; save next before freeing the current one. */
void free_list(Item *head) {
    while (head != NULL) {
        Item *next = head->next;
        free(head);
        head = next;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    Item *head = NULL;
    head = push_front(head, 81);
    head = push_front(head, 62);
    head = push_front(head, 62);
    head = push_front(head, 74);
    head = push_front(head, 45);
    head = push_front(head, 99);
    print_list(head);
    free_list(head);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: Each Item holds a value and a pointer to the next node. push_front()
   allocates a node with malloc, puts it in front of head and returns it; print_list()
   follows the next pointers until NULL; free_list() frees every node. main() pushes 6
   values, so they print in reverse order. */
// END

/* Caption: Compute the mean of a list of numbers. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write compute_mean() that takes prices and size.
   2. Add the values into the double result.
   3. Return result / size.
   4. Print the average with two decimals. */
/* The mean is the total divided by the count. */
double compute_mean(const long prices[], int size) {
    double result = 0.0;
    for (int k = 0; k < size; k++) {
        result += prices[k];
    }
    return result / size;
}

int main(void) {
    long prices[] = {23L, 78L, 95L};
    int size = sizeof(prices) / sizeof(prices[0]);
    printf("Average: %.2f\n", compute_mean(prices, size));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: compute_mean() adds the 3 values of prices into the double result and
   divides by size, so the mean keeps its decimal part even when the values are whole
   numbers. main() prints it with two decimals. */
// END

/* Caption: Implement insertion sort for an array of int values. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write insertion_sort() for the int array data.
   2. Take each element in turn as current.
   3. Shift the smaller values of the sorted part one place right.
   4. Put current into the gap.
   5. Print the sorted values. */
/* Insert each element into the already sorted part on its left. */
void insertion_sort(int data[], int count) {
    for (int i = 1; i < count; i++) {
        int current = data[i];
        int j = i - 1;
        while (j >= 0 && data[j] < current) {
            data[j + 1] = data[j];   /* shift bigger values right */
            j--;
        }
        data[j + 1] = current;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    int data[] = {90, 96, 53, 19, 4, 49};
    int count = 6;
    insertion_sort(data, count);
    for (int i = 0; i < count; i++) {
        printf("%d ", data[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: insertion_sort() takes each element in turn and shifts the smaller values
   of the sorted part one place right until the element fits. main() then prints the 6
   values in descending order. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to search an array for a value and print its position. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write linear_search() with the array, its length and needle.
   2. Compare each element with needle.
   3. Return the index of the first match, or -1.
   4. In main(), search for 93 and print the result. */
/* Return the index of needle, or -1 when it is not in the array. */
int linear_search(const int marks[], int count, int needle) {
    for (int k = 0; k < count; k++) {
        if (marks[k] == needle) {
            return k;
        }
    }
    return -1;
}

int main(void) {
    int marks[] = {91, 93, 20, 77, 93, 5, 43, 78, 1};
    int count = 9;
    int needle = 93;
    int pos = linear_search(marks, count, needle);
    if (pos >= 0) {
        printf("Found %d at index %d\n", needle, pos);
    } else {
        printf("%d is not in the array\n", needle);
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: linear_search() checks the elements of marks one by one and returns the
   index of the first one equal to needle, or -1 when it reaches the end without a match.
   main() searches for 93 and prints where it is, or that it is missing. */
// END

/* Caption: Define a Point struct and measure the distance between two points. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <math.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define a Point struct with x and y.
   2. Write distance() using sqrt(dx * dx + dy * dy).
   3. Print the distance between p and q. */
typedef struct {
    double x;
    double y;
} Point;

/* Pythagoras: sqrt(dx * dx + dy * dy). */
double distance(Point a, Point b) {
    double dx = b.x - a.x;
    double dy = b.y - a.y;
    return sqrt(dx * dx + dy * dy);
}

int main(void) {
    Point p = {-7, 8};
    Point q = {-10, -6};
    printf("Distance: %.3f\n", distance(p, q));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: Point is a typedef struct with x and y. distance() uses Pythagoras, sqrt(dx
   * dx + dy * dy), to measure the gap between the two points, and main() prints it. */
// END

/* Caption: How do I count how many words are separated by spaces in a string in C? */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <ctype.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write count_words() with words = 0 and an in_word flag.
   2. A space ends a word; a non-space after a space starts a new word and adds one to
      words.
   3. Return words and print it. */
/* A new word starts when a non-space follows a space (or the start). */
int count_words(const char *text) {
    int words = 0;
    int in_word = 0;
    for (int i = 0; text[i] != '\0'; i++) {
        if (isspace((unsigned char)text[i])) {
            in_word = 0;
        } else if (!in_word) {
            in_word = 1;
            words++;
        }
    }
    return words;
}

int main(void) {
    const char *sentence = "arrays in c start at index zero";
    printf("Words: %d\n", count_words(sentence));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: count_words() uses the flag in_word: a new word starts when a non-space
   character follows a space or the start of the text. main() prints the number of words in
   the sentence. */
// END

/* Caption: Generate the Fibonacci sequence. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Start with first = 0 and second = 1.
   2. Repeat 24 times and print first each time.
   3. Compute next = first + second, then set first = second and second = next. */
int main(void) {
    long first = 0, second = 1;
    /* Print a term, then slide the pair one step along the sequence. */
    for (int i = 0; i < 24; i++) {
        printf("%ld ", first);
        long next = first + second;
        first = second;
        second = next;
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: The loop keeps the last two numbers in first and second. Each round it
   prints first, then moves the pair forward: first becomes second and second becomes their
   sum. It prints the first 24 Fibonacci numbers. */
// END

/* Caption: How do I find the greatest common divisor of two numbers in C? */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write gcd() with Euclid's algorithm.
   2. Replace (a, b) by (b, a % b) until b is 0.
   3. Return a and print the GCD of 166 and 159. */
/* Euclid: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a % b) until b becomes zero. */
int gcd(int a, int b) {
    while (b != 0) {
        int r = a % b;
        a = b;
        b = r;
    }
    return a;
}

int main(void) {
    int x = 166, y = 159;
    printf("gcd(%d, %d) = %d\n", x, y, gcd(x, y));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: gcd() uses Euclid's algorithm: it keeps replacing (a, b) with (b, a % b)
   until b is 0. The last non-zero value is the greatest common divisor, and main() prints
   the GCD of 166 and 159. */
// END

/* Plan:

   2. Write 3 lines with fprintf and close the file.
   3. Open it again in read mode.
   4. Read and print each line with fgets, then close the file. */
int main(void) {
    FILE *file = fopen("notes.txt", "w");
    if (file == NULL) {
        perror("fopen");
        return 1;
    }
    fprintf(file, "good comments explain why the code exists\n");
    fprintf(file, "the quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog\n");
    fprintf(file, "c gives you direct control over memory\n");
    fclose(file);

    /* Reopen the file for reading and print it line by line. */
    file = fopen("notes.txt", "r");
    if (file == NULL) {
        perror("fopen");
        return 1;
    }
    char line[128];
    while (fgets(line, sizeof(line), file) != NULL) {
        printf("%s", line);
    }
    fclose(file);
    return 0;

   back line by line into the buffer line, which is printed. Every fopen() result is
   checked for NULL. */

/* Caption: Search a sorted array by halving the search range each step. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Make sure the array is sorted.
   2. Set lo to 0 and hi to length - 1.
   3. While lo <= hi, compare the middle element mid with the key.
   4. Return the index if it matches; otherwise keep only the half that can hold the
      key.
   5. Return -1 if the range becomes empty, and print the index of 201. */
/* The array must be sorted. Each step halves the range that can still hold the key. */
int binary_search(const int data[], int length, int key) {
    int lo = 0;
    int hi = length - 1;
    while (lo <= hi) {
        int mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;
        if (data[mid] == key) {
            return mid;
        } else if (data[mid] < key) {
            lo = mid + 1;   /* key is in the right half */
        } else {
            hi = mid - 1;   /* key is in the left half */
        }
    }
    return -1;
}

int main(void) {
    int data[] = {4, 23, 34, 76, 135, 149};
    const int length = 6;
    int index = binary_search(data, length, 201);
    printf("Index of 201: %d\n", index);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: binary_search() needs a sorted array. It keeps the range from lo to hi,
   compares the middle element mid with the key and throws away the half that cannot
   contain it, so it needs only about log2(n) steps. main() looks for 201 and prints its
   index, or -1 if it is not there. */
// END

/* Caption: Search an array for its largest value. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write largest_value() that takes items and size.
   2. Store items[0] in m.
   3. Loop over the other elements and keep the largest value in m.
   4. Return m and print it. */
/* Start with the first element and keep the largest value seen so far. */
int largest_value(const int items[], int size) {
    int m = items[0];
    for (int i = 1; i < size; i++) {
        if (items[i] > m) {
            m = items[i];
        }
    }
    return m;
}

int main(void) {
    int items[] = {85, 14, 25, 57, 9, 38, 10};
    const int size = 7;
    printf("The largest value is %d\n", largest_value(items, size));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: largest_value() takes the first element as the largest value so far and
   stores it in m. The loop compares every other element with m using > and keeps the
   largest one. main() prints the largest of the 7 values. */
// END

   both results. */
// END

/* Caption: Count the even values in a list of integers. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write count_even() that takes numbers and size.
   2. For each element, test numbers[idx] % 2 == 0.
   3. Add one to found for every even number.
   4. Return found and print it. */
/* A number is even when the remainder after dividing by 2 is zero. */
int count_even(const int numbers[], int size) {
    int found = 0;
    for (int idx = 0; idx < size; idx++) {
        if (numbers[idx] % 2 == 0) {
            found++;
        }
    }
    return found;
}

int main(void) {
    int numbers[] = {28, 63, 50, 47, 39, 84, 81, 25, 31};
    int size = sizeof(numbers) / sizeof(numbers[0]);
    printf("Even numbers: %d\n", count_even(numbers, size));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: count_even() tests each element of numbers with the % operator: a remainder
   of 0 after dividing by 2 means the number is even, so found goes up by one. main()
   prints how many of the 9 values are even. */
// END

/* Caption: Swap two variables using pointers. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write swap() that takes pointers to two int values.
   2. Save *a in tmp, copy *b into *a, then tmp into *b.
   3. In main(), print a and b, call swap(&a, &b) and print them again. */
/* Pass addresses so the function can change the caller's variables. */
void swap(int *a, int *b) {
    int tmp = *a;
    *a = *b;
    *b = tmp;
}

int main(void) {
    int a = 2, b = 52;
    printf("Before: %d %d\n", a, b);
    swap(&a, &b);
    printf("After:  %d %d\n", a, b);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: swap() receives the addresses of a and b, so writing through the pointers
   *a and *b changes the caller's variables. tmp holds one value during the exchange.
   main() declares both variables on one line and prints them before and after the swap. */
// END

/* Caption: Check whether a word is a palindrome. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <string.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write is_palindrome() for line.
   2. Compare the first and last characters, moving inwards.
   3. Return false at the first mismatch, otherwise true.
   4. Check matrix and print the result. */
/* Compare characters from the front and back, moving inwards. */
bool is_palindrome(const char *line) {
    int i = 0;
    int j = strlen(line) - 1;
    while (i < j) {
        if (line[i] != line[j]) {
            return false;
        }
        i++;
        j--;
    }
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    const char *line = "matrix";
    printf("%s %s a palindrome\n", line, is_palindrome(line) ? "is" : "is not");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: is_palindrome() compares the first and last characters and moves inwards;
   any mismatch means the word is not a palindrome. main() checks the word matrix and
   prints the result. */
// END

/* Caption: Reverse an array by swapping from both ends. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write reverse_array() for numbers.
   2. Set i to the first index and j to the last.
   3. Swap numbers[i] and numbers[j], then move both inwards.
   4. Stop when i meets j and print the array. */
/* Swap the outer pair, then move both ends toward the middle. */
void reverse_array(int numbers[], int size) {
    int i = 0;
    int j = size - 1;
    while (i < j) {
        int tmp = numbers[i];
        numbers[i] = numbers[j];
        numbers[j] = tmp;
        i++;
        j--;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    int numbers[] = {78, 56, 19, 49, 81};
    int size = sizeof(numbers) / sizeof(numbers[0]);
    reverse_array(numbers, size);
    for (int i = 0; i < size; i++) {
        printf("%d ", numbers[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: reverse_array() swaps the first and last elements, then moves i forward and
   j backward until they meet, so the array is reversed in place without a second array.
   main() prints the reversed values. */
// END

/* Caption: Generate the Fibonacci sequence. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write fib(n) that returns n when n < 2.
   2. Otherwise return fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2).
   3. Print fib(i) for i from 0 to 17. */
/* Each Fibonacci number is the sum of the two before it. */
long fib(int n) {
    if (n < 2) {
        return n;
    }
    return fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2);
}

int main(void) {
    for (int i = 0; i < 18; i++) {
        printf("%ld ", fib(i));
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: fib() returns n for 0 and 1 and otherwise adds the two previous Fibonacci
   numbers by calling itself twice, which is simple but slow for large n. main() prints the
   first 18 numbers. */
// END

/* Caption: Program to write your own version of strcpy. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write copy_string(dest, src).
   2. Copy src into dest one character at a time.
   3. Stop after copying the null character.
   4. Copy library into word and print it. */
/* Copy each character, including the final '\0'. */
void copy_string(char *dest, const char *src) {
    int i = 0;
    while ((dest[i] = src[i]) != '\0') {
        i++;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    char source[] = "library";
    char word[32];
    copy_string(word, source);
    printf("Copied: %s\n", word);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: copy_string() copies src into dest one character at a time, including the
   final null character, which is what strcpy does. The array word must be big enough to
   hold the copy. main() copies the word library and prints it. */
// END

/* Caption: Return both the smallest and the largest value of an array through pointers. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write min_max() with the array, its length and the pointers min and max.
   2. Start both at the first element.
   3. Update *min and *max while looping over the rest.
   4. Declare lowest and highest, pass their addresses and print them. */
/* One pass finds both results; they are stored through the pointers. */
void min_max(const int scores[], int count, int *min, int *max) {
    *min = scores[0];
    *max = scores[0];
    for (int i = 1; i < count; i++) {
        if (scores[i] < *min) {
            *min = scores[i];
        }
        if (scores[i] > *max) {
            *max = scores[i];
        }
    }
}

int main(void) {
    int scores[] = {37, 19, 85, 19};
    const int count = 4;
    int lowest, highest;
    min_max(scores, count, &lowest, &highest);
    printf("Min: %d, Max: %d\n", lowest, highest);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: A C function can return only one value, so min_max() returns void and
   writes its two results through the pointer parameters min and max. main() declares
   lowest and highest on one line and passes their addresses with &, then prints both
   results for the 4 values. */
// END

/* Caption: C program to compute the factorial of a number recursively. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write factorial(n) that calls itself.
   2. Return 1 when n is 1 or less.
   3. Otherwise return n * factorial(n - 1).
   4. Print 6! as an unsigned long long. */
/* n! = n * (n - 1)!, and 0! = 1 stops the recursion. */
unsigned long long factorial(int n) {
    if (n <= 1) {
        return 1;
    }
    return n * factorial(n - 1);
}

int main(void) {
    int n = 6;
    printf("%d! = %llu\n", n, factorial(n));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: factorial() calls itself: n! is n * (n - 1)!, and the recursion stops when
   n is 1 or less. main() prints 6! as an unsigned long long, because factorials grow very
   fast. */
// END

/* Caption: Compute the LCM of two integers using the GCD. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write gcd() with Euclid's algorithm: replace (a, b) by (b, a % b) until b is 0.
   2. Write lcm() as a / gcd(a, b) * b.
   3. Print the LCM of 282 and 77. */
/* Euclid: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a % b) until b becomes zero. */
int gcd(int a, int b) {
    while (b != 0) {
        int r = a % b;
        a = b;
        b = r;
    }
    return a;
}

/* lcm(a, b) = a / gcd(a, b) * b (divide first to avoid overflow). */
long lcm(int a, int b) {
    return (long)a / gcd(a, b) * b;
}

int main(void) {
    printf("lcm(282, 77) = %ld\n", lcm(282, 77));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: gcd() uses Euclid's algorithm: it keeps replacing (a, b) with (b, a % b)
   until b is 0. lcm() divides a by the gcd before multiplying by b, which avoids overflow.
   main() prints the LCM of 282 and 77. */
// END

/* Caption: Find the number of digits in an integer. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Start result at 0.
   2. Divide n by 10 and add one to result.
   3. Repeat until n is 0.
   4. Apply it to 331665 and print the result. */
/* Take the last digit with % 10, then drop it with / 10. */
int count_digits(int n) {
    int result = 0;
    while (n > 0) {
        result++;
        n /= 10;
    }
    return result;
}

int main(void) {
    int number = 331665;
    printf("count of digits of %d: %d\n", number, count_digits(number));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: count_digits() removes the last digit (n / 10) and adds one to result each
   time, until n reaches 0. main() applies it to 331665. */
// END

int string_length(const char *str) {

/* Caption: How do I use binary search to locate a value in a sorted list in C? */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Make sure the array is sorted.
   2. Set left to 0 and right to n - 1.
   3. While left <= right, compare the middle element middle with the key.
   4. Return the index if it matches; otherwise keep only the half that can hold the
      key.
   5. Return -1 if the range becomes empty, and print the index of 201. */
/* The array must be sorted. Each step halves the range that can still hold the key. */
int binary_search(const int prices[], int n, int key) {
    int left = 0;
    int right = n - 1;
    while (left <= right) {
        int middle = left + (right - left) / 2;
        if (prices[middle] == key) {
            return middle;
        } else if (prices[middle] < key) {
            left = middle + 1;   /* key is in the right half */
        } else {
            right = middle - 1;   /* key is in the left half */
        }
    }
    return -1;
}

int main(void) {
    int prices[] = {14, 30, 72, 96, 130, 146, 174, 176, 180, 193};
    const int n = 10;
    int index = binary_search(prices, n, 201);
    printf("Index of 201: %d\n", index);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: binary_search() needs a sorted array. It keeps the range from left to
   right, compares the middle element middle with the key and throws away the half that
   cannot contain it, so it needs only about log2(n) steps. main() looks for 201 and prints
   its index, or -1 if it is not there. */
// END

/* Caption: Program to reverse a string in place. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <string.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write reverse_string() for str.
   2. Set i to the first index and j to the last.
   3. Swap the two characters and move i and j inwards until they meet.
   4. Reverse rocket and print it. */
/* Swap characters from both ends until they meet in the middle. */
void reverse_string(char *str) {
    int i = 0;
    int j = strlen(str) - 1;
    while (i < j) {
        char tmp = str[i];
        str[i] = str[j];
        str[j] = tmp;
        i++;
        j--;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    char str[] = "rocket";
    reverse_string(str);
    printf("%s\n", str);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: reverse_string() swaps characters from both ends of str, moving inwards
   until the two indexes meet. main() reverses the word rocket in place and prints it. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to test if 57 is a prime number. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write is_prime(n); numbers below 2 are not prime.
   2. Try every divisor d while d * d <= n.
   3. Return false if one divides n, otherwise true.
   4. Check 57 and print the result. */
/* A prime has no divisor between 2 and its square root. */
bool is_prime(int n) {
    if (n < 2) {
        return false;
    }
    for (int d = 2; d * d <= n; d++) {
        if (n % d == 0) {
            return false;
        }
    }
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    int number = 57;
    printf("%d %s prime\n", number, is_prime(number) ? "is" : "is not");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: is_prime() tries every divisor d from 2 while d * d <= n; if one divides n
   evenly, n is not prime. main() checks 57 and prints whether it is prime. */
// END

/* Caption: Check whether a word is a palindrome. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <string.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write is_palindrome() for buffer.
   2. Compare the first and last characters, moving inwards.
   3. Return false at the first mismatch, otherwise true.
   4. Check matrix and print the result. */
/* Compare characters from the front and back, moving inwards. */
bool is_palindrome(const char *buffer) {
    int i = 0;
    int j = strlen(buffer) - 1;
    while (i < j) {
        if (buffer[i] != buffer[j]) {
            return false;
        }
        i++;
        j--;
    }
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    const char *buffer = "matrix";
    printf("%s %s a palindrome\n", buffer, is_palindrome(buffer) ? "is" : "is not");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: is_palindrome() compares the first and last characters and moves inwards;
   any mismatch means the word is not a palindrome. main() checks the word matrix and
   prints the result. */
// END

/* Caption: Count how many words are separated by spaces in a string. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <ctype.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write count_words() with words = 0 and an in_word flag.
   2. A space ends a word; a non-space after a space starts a new word and adds one to
      words.
   3. Return words and print it. */
/* A new word starts when a non-space follows a space (or the start). */
int count_words(const char *text) {
    int words = 0;
    int in_word = 0;
    for (int i = 0; text[i] != '\0'; i++) {
        if (isspace((unsigned char)text[i])) {
            in_word = 0;
        } else if (!in_word) {
            in_word = 1;
            words++;
        }
    }
    return words;
}

int main(void) {
    const char *sentence = "strings end with a null character";
    printf("Words: %d\n", count_words(sentence));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: count_words() uses the flag in_word: a new word starts when a non-space
   character follows a space or the start of the text. main() prints the number of words in
   the sentence. */
// END

/* Caption: How do I list the prime numbers below a limit in C? */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write is_prime(n); numbers below 2 are not prime.
   2. Try every divisor d while d * d <= n.
   3. Return false if one divides n, otherwise true.
   4. Print every prime from 2 to 31. */
/* A prime has no divisor between 2 and its square root. */
bool is_prime(int n) {
    if (n < 2) {
        return false;
    }
    for (int d = 2; d * d <= n; d++) {

            return false;

    }
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    for (int n = 2; n <= 31; n++) {
        if (is_prime(n)) {
            printf("%d ", n);
        }
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: is_prime() tries every divisor d from 2 while d * d <= n; if one divides n
   evenly, n is not prime. main() tests every number from 2 to 31 and prints the primes. */
// END

/* Caption: Create a singly linked list by inserting at the head. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define Node with a value and a next pointer.
   2. Write push_front() that mallocs a node and links it in front of head.
   3. Write print_list() that follows next until NULL.
   4. Write free_list() that frees every node.
   5. Push 3 values, print the list and free it. */
typedef struct Node {
    int value;
    struct Node *next;
} Node;

/* Allocate a new node and put it in front of the current head. */
Node *push_front(Node *head, int value) {
    Node *node = malloc(sizeof(Node));
    if (node == NULL) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Out of memory\n");
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }
    node->value = value;
    node->next = head;
    return node;
}

void print_list(const Node *head) {
    for (const Node *cur = head; cur != NULL; cur = cur->next) {
        printf("%d -> ", cur->value);
    }
    printf("NULL\n");
}

/* Free every node; save next before freeing the current one. */
void free_list(Node *head) {
    while (head != NULL) {
        Node *next = head->next;
        free(head);
        head = next;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    Node *head = NULL;
    head = push_front(head, 4);
    head = push_front(head, 82);
    head = push_front(head, 69);
    print_list(head);
    free_list(head);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: Each Node holds a value and a pointer to the next node. push_front()
   allocates a node with malloc, puts it in front of head and returns it; print_list()
   follows the next pointers until NULL; free_list() frees every node. main() pushes 3
   values, so they print in reverse order. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to sum a int array with a helper function. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write sum_values() that takes the array marks and its length size.
   2. Start total at 0 and add every element in a while loop.
   3. Return total.
   4. In main(), fill marks with 10 values and print the sum. */
/* Return the sum of the first n elements. */
int sum_values(const int marks[], int size) {
    int total = 0;
    int j = 0;
    while (j < size) {
        total += marks[j];

    }
    return total;
}

}
/* Explanation: sum_values() receives the array marks and its length size. It starts total
   at 0, adds every element to it in a while loop and returns the total. main() fills marks
   with 10 int values and prints their sum. */
// END

/* Caption: How do I search a sorted array by halving the search range each step in C? */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Make sure the array is sorted.
   2. Set low to 0 and high to count - 1.
   3. While low <= high, compare the middle element mid with the key.
   4. Return the index if it matches; otherwise keep only the half that can hold the
      key.
   5. Return -1 if the range becomes empty, and print the index of 198. */
/* The array must be sorted. Each step halves the range that can still hold the key. */
int binary_search(const int nums[], int count, int key) {
    int low = 0;
    int high = count - 1;
    while (low <= high) {
        int mid = low + (high - low) / 2;
        if (nums[mid] == key) {
            return mid;
        } else if (nums[mid] < key) {
            low = mid + 1;   /* key is in the right half */
        } else {
            high = mid - 1;   /* key is in the left half */
        }
    }
    return -1;
}

int main(void) {
    int nums[] = {40, 56, 59, 91, 128, 151, 152, 154, 166, 192, 198};
    int count = 11;
    int index = binary_search(nums, count, 198);
    printf("Index of 198: %d\n", index);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: binary_search() needs a sorted array. It keeps the range from low to high,
   compares the middle element mid with the key and throws away the half that cannot
   contain it, so it needs only about log2(n) steps. main() looks for 198 and prints its
   index, or -1 if it is not there. */
// END

/* Caption: Calculate the average of the values in an array. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write mean() that takes readings and n.
   2. Add the values into the double sum.
   3. Return sum / n.
   4. Print the average with two decimals. */
/* Sum the values, then divide by how many there are. */
double mean(const int readings[], int n) {
    double sum = 0.0;
    for (int idx = 0; idx < n; idx++) {
        sum += readings[idx];
    }
    return sum / n;
}

int main(void) {
    int readings[] = {92, 52, 67};
    int n = sizeof(readings) / sizeof(readings[0]);
    printf("Mean = %.2f\n", mean(readings, n));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: mean() adds the 3 values of readings into the double sum and divides by n,
   so the mean keeps its decimal part even when the values are whole numbers. main() prints
   it with two decimals. */
// END

/* Caption: Compare three numbers and print the biggest. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Read a, b and c.
   2. Assume a is the biggest.
   3. Compare it with the other two and keep the bigger value.
   4. Print the result. */

    double a, b, c;
    printf("Enter three numbers: ");
    if (scanf("%lf %lf %lf", &a, &b, &c) != 3) {
        printf("Invalid input\n");
        return 1;
    }
    double best = a;
    /* Compare with each of the others and keep the bigger one. */
    if (b > best) {
        best = b;
    }
    if (c > best) {
        best = c;
    }
    printf("The biggest is %.2f\n", best);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: The program reads a, b and c from the keyboard with scanf and stops with a
   message if the input is not valid. It assumes a is the biggest, compares it with the
   other two and keeps the bigger value in best, which it prints. */
// END

/* Caption: C program to find the average of three numbers. */

        printf("Invalid input\n");

/* Caption: Search an array for a value and print its position. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write linear_search() with the array, its length and wanted.
   2. Compare each element with wanted.
   3. Return the index of the first match, or -1.
   4. In main(), search for 156 and print the result. */
/* Return the index of wanted, or -1 when it is not in the array. */
int linear_search(const int ages[], int n, int wanted) {
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        if (ages[i] == wanted) {
            return i;
        }
    }
    return -1;
}

int main(void) {
    int ages[] = {26, 71, 24, 71, 17, 91, 59, 63, 89};
    const int n = 9;
    int wanted = 156;
    int pos = linear_search(ages, n, wanted);
    if (pos >= 0) {
        printf("Found %d at index %d\n", wanted, pos);
    } else {
        printf("%d is not in the array\n", wanted);
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: linear_search() checks the elements of ages one by one and returns the
   index of the first one equal to wanted, or -1 when it reaches the end without a match.
   main() searches for 156 and prints where it is, or that it is missing. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to calculate the average of the values in an array. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write mean() that takes prices and n.
   2. Add the values into the double acc.
   3. Return acc / n.
   4. Print the average with two decimals. */
/* The mean is the total divided by the count. */
double mean(const int prices[], int n) {
    double acc = 0.0;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        acc += prices[i];
    }
    return acc / n;
}

int main(void) {
    int prices[] = {60, 14, 58, 14, 68, 78, 68, 4, 83};
    int n = 9;
    printf("The average is %.2f\n", mean(prices, n));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: mean() adds the 9 values of prices into the double acc and divides by n, so
   the mean keeps its decimal part even when the values are whole numbers. main() prints it
   with two decimals. */
// END

/* Caption: Print the binary representation of an integer. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write print_binary(n, bits).
   2. Go through the bits from the highest to the lowest.
   3. Print 1 when (n >> b) & 1 is set, otherwise 0.
   4. Print 984 in binary. */
/* Check each bit from the highest to the lowest. */
void print_binary(unsigned int n, int bits) {
    for (int b = bits - 1; b >= 0; b--) {
        putchar((n >> b) & 1 ? '1' : '0');
    }
    putchar('\n');
}

int main(void) {
    unsigned int number = 984;
    printf("%u in binary: ", number);
    print_binary(number, 12);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: print_binary() checks one bit at a time, from the highest to the lowest: (n
   >> b) & 1 is 1 when bit b is set, so it prints the character 1 or 0. main() prints 984
   in binary. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to return the smallest element of an array of long values. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write min_of() that takes items and n.
   2. Store items[0] in smallest.
   3. Loop over the other elements and keep the smallest value in smallest.
   4. Return smallest and print it. */
/* Start with the first element and keep the smallest value seen so far. */
long min_of(const long items[], int n) {
    long smallest = items[0];
    for (int i = 1; i < n; i++) {
        if (items[i] < smallest) {
            smallest = items[i];
        }
    }
    return smallest;
}

int main(void) {
    long items[] = {8L, 44L, 18L, 19L, 57L};
    int n = 5;
    printf("Smallest: %ld\n", min_of(items, n));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: min_of() takes the first element as the smallest value so far and stores it
   in smallest. The loop compares every other element with smallest using < and keeps the
   smallest one. main() prints the smallest of the 5 values. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to implement a simple linked list with malloc and free. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define Item with a value and a next pointer.
   2. Write push_front() that mallocs a node and links it in front of head.
   3. Write print_list() that follows next until NULL.
   4. Write free_list() that frees every node.
   5. Push 4 values, print the list and free it. */
typedef struct Item {
    int value;
    struct Item *next;
} Item;

/* Allocate a new node and put it in front of the current head. */
Item *push_front(Item *head, int value) {
    Item *node = malloc(sizeof(Item));
    if (node == NULL) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Out of memory\n");
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }
    node->value = value;
    node->next = head;
    return node;
}

void print_list(const Item *head) {
    for (const Item *cur = head; cur != NULL; cur = cur->next) {
        printf("%d -> ", cur->value);
    }
    printf("NULL\n");
}

/* Free every node; save next before freeing the current one. */
void free_list(Item *head) {
    while (head != NULL) {
        Item *next = head->next;
        free(head);
        head = next;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    Item *head = NULL;
    head = push_front(head, 94);
    head = push_front(head, 80);
    head = push_front(head, 1);
    head = push_front(head, 72);
    print_list(head);
    free_list(head);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: Each Item holds a value and a pointer to the next node. push_front()
   allocates a node with malloc, puts it in front of head and returns it; print_list()
   follows the next pointers until NULL; free_list() frees every node. main() pushes 4
   values, so they print in reverse order. */
// END

/* Caption: C program to add up all the numbers in an array of double values. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write total_of() that takes the array data and its length n.
   2. Start total at 0 and add every element in a while loop.
   3. Return total.
   4. In main(), fill data with 9 values and print the sum. */
/* Add every element to a running total. */
double total_of(const double data[], int n) {
    double total = 0;
    int k = 0;
    while (k < n) {
        total += data[k];
        k++;
    }
    return total;
}

int main(void) {
    double data[] = {47.6, 73.2, 71.2, 84.5, 34.2, 42.3, 39.4, 5.9, 10.2};
    int n = 9;
    printf("Total = %.2f\n", total_of(data, n));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: total_of() receives the array data and its length n. It starts total at 0,
   adds every element to it in a while loop and returns the total. main() fills data with 9
   double values and prints their sum. */
// END

/* Caption: Swap two variables using pointers. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write swap() that takes pointers to two int values.
   2. Save *x in tmp, copy *y into *x, then tmp into *y.
   3. In main(), print x and y, call swap(&x, &y) and print them again. */
/* Pass addresses so the function can change the caller's variables. */
void swap(int *x, int *y) {
    int tmp = *x;
    *x = *y;
    *y = tmp;
}

int main(void) {
    int x = 5, y = 45;
    printf("Before: %d %d\n", x, y);
    swap(&x, &y);
    printf("After:  %d %d\n", x, y);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: swap() receives the addresses of x and y, so writing through the pointers
   *x and *y changes the caller's variables. tmp holds one value during the exchange.
   main() declares both variables on one line and prints them before and after the swap. */
// END

/* Caption: Use bubble sort to put numbers in ascending order. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write bubble_sort() for the int array values.
   2. Compare each pair of neighbours.
   3. Swap them when they are in the wrong order for ascending order.
   4. Repeat the passes until the array is sorted.
   5. Print the sorted values. */
/* Repeatedly swap neighbours that are in the wrong order. */
void bubble_sort(int values[], int size) {
    for (int i = 0; i < size - 1; i++) {
        for (int j = 0; j < size - 1 - i; j++) {
            if (values[j] > values[j + 1]) {
                int tmp = values[j];
                values[j] = values[j + 1];
                values[j + 1] = tmp;
            }
        }
    }
}

int main(void) {
    int values[] = {66, 62, 62, 51, 71};
    int size = 5;
    bubble_sort(values, size);
    for (int i = 0; i < size; i++) {
        printf("%d ", values[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: bubble_sort() walks through values again and again and swaps neighbours
   that are in the wrong order, so the largest values move to the end first. main() then
   prints the 5 values in ascending order. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to divide two integers and get both the quotient and the remainder. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write divide(a, b, &quotient, &remainder) that returns a bool.
   2. Return false if b is 0.
   3. Store a / b and a % b through the pointers and return true.
   4. Divide 185 by 26 and print the results or the error. */
/* Returns false for division by zero; otherwise stores both results. */
bool divide(int a, int b, int *quotient, int *remainder) {
    if (b == 0) {
        return false;
    }
    *quotient = a / b;
    *remainder = a % b;
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    int a = 185, b = 26;
    int q, r;
    if (divide(a, b, &q, &r)) {
        printf("%d / %d = %d remainder %d\n", a, b, q, r);
    } else {
        printf("Cannot divide by zero\n");
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: divide() has four parameters: two inputs and two pointers for the results.
   Its bool return value reports success, while the quotient and remainder are written
   through the pointers. main() divides 185 by 26 and prints both results. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to return both the smallest and the largest value of an array through pointers. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write min_max() with the array, its length and the pointers min and max.
   2. Start both at the first element.
   3. Update *min and *max while looping over the rest.
   4. Declare smallest and largest, pass their addresses and print them. */
/* One pass finds both results; they are stored through the pointers. */
void min_max(const int samples[], int size, int *min, int *max) {
    *min = samples[0];
    *max = samples[0];
    for (int i = 1; i < size; i++) {
        if (samples[i] < *min) {
            *min = samples[i];
        }
        if (samples[i] > *max) {
            *max = samples[i];
        }
    }
}

int main(void) {
    int samples[] = {62, 36, 99, 24};
    int size = sizeof(samples) / sizeof(samples[0]);
    int smallest, largest;
    min_max(samples, size, &smallest, &largest);
    printf("Min: %d, Max: %d\n", smallest, largest);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: A C function can return only one value, so min_max() returns void and
   writes its two results through the pointer parameters min and max. main() declares
   smallest and largest on one line and passes their addresses with &, then prints both
   results for the 4 values. */
// END

/* Caption: Implement a simple linked list with malloc and free. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define Node with a value and a next pointer.
   2. Write push_front() that mallocs a node and links it in front of head.
   3. Write print_list() that follows next until NULL.
   4. Write free_list() that frees every node.
   5. Push 5 values, print the list and free it. */
typedef struct Node {
    int value;
    struct Node *next;
} Node;

/* Allocate a new node and put it in front of the current head. */
Node *push_front(Node *head, int value) {
    Node *node = malloc(sizeof(Node));
    if (node == NULL) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Out of memory\n");
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }
    node->value = value;
    node->next = head;
    return node;
}

void print_list(const Node *head) {
    for (const Node *cur = head; cur != NULL; cur = cur->next) {
        printf("%d -> ", cur->value);
    }
    printf("NULL\n");
}

/* Free every node; save next before freeing the current one. */
void free_list(Node *head) {
    while (head != NULL) {
        Node *next = head->next;
        free(head);
        head = next;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    Node *head = NULL;
    head = push_front(head, 66);
    head = push_front(head, 22);
    head = push_front(head, 33);
    head = push_front(head, 81);
    head = push_front(head, 26);
    print_list(head);
    free_list(head);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: Each Node holds a value and a pointer to the next node. push_front()
   allocates a node with malloc, puts it in front of head and returns it; print_list()
   follows the next pointers until NULL; free_list() frees every node. main() pushes 5
   values, so they print in reverse order. */
// END

/* Caption: Reverse the digits of a number. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Start result at 0.
   2. Multiply result by 10, add n % 10, then divide n by 10.
   3. Repeat until n is 0.
   4. Apply it to 365100 and print the result. */
/* Take the last digit with % 10, then drop it with / 10. */
int reverse_digits(int n) {
    int result = 0;
    while (n > 0) {
        result = result * 10 + n % 10;
        n /= 10;
    }
    return result;
}

int main(void) {
    int number = 365100;
    printf("reverse of digits of %d: %d\n", number, reverse_digits(number));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: reverse_digits() shifts result one place left (result * 10) and adds the
   last digit of n, which reverses the order. main() applies it to 365100. */
// END

/* Caption: Compute the distance between two points using a struct. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <math.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define a Point struct with x and y.
   2. Write distance() using sqrt(dx * dx + dy * dy).
   3. Print the distance between p and q. */
typedef struct {
    double x;
    double y;
} Point;

/* Pythagoras: sqrt(dx * dx + dy * dy). */
double distance(Point a, Point b) {
    double dx = b.x - a.x;
    double dy = b.y - a.y;
    return sqrt(dx * dx + dy * dy);
}

int main(void) {
    Point p = {-3, 1};
    Point q = {3, 1};
    printf("Distance: %.3f\n", distance(p, q));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: Point is a typedef struct with x and y. distance() uses Pythagoras, sqrt(dx
   * dx + dy * dy), to measure the gap between the two points, and main() prints it. */
// END

/* Caption: Use a struct to store a rectangle and print its area and perimeter. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define a Rectangle struct with width and height.
   2. Write area() and perimeter().
   3. Make a 17 by 29 rectangle and print both results. */
typedef struct {
    int width;
    int height;
} Rectangle;

int area(Rectangle r) {
    return r.width * r.height;
}

int perimeter(Rectangle r) {
    return 2 * (r.width + r.height);
}

int main(void) {
    Rectangle box = {17, 29};
    printf("Area: %d, Perimeter: %d\n", area(box), perimeter(box));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: Rectangle stores a width and a height. area() returns width * height and
   perimeter() returns 2 * (width + height). main() makes a 17 by 29 rectangle and prints
   both results. */
// END

/* Caption: Sort an array in descending order using selection sort. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write selection_sort() for the int array marks.
   2. For each position, find the largest remaining element.
   3. Swap it into that position.
   4. Print the sorted values. */
/* Select the right element for each position and swap it into place. */
void selection_sort(int marks[], int count) {
    for (int i = 0; i < count - 1; i++) {
        int chosen = i;
        for (int j = i + 1; j < count; j++) {
            if (marks[chosen] < marks[j]) {
                chosen = j;
            }
        }
        int tmp = marks[i];
        marks[i] = marks[chosen];
        marks[chosen] = tmp;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    int marks[] = {49, 62, 22, 84, 12, 45, 98};
    int count = sizeof(marks) / sizeof(marks[0]);
    selection_sort(marks, count);
    for (int i = 0; i < count; i++) {
        printf("%d ", marks[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: selection_sort() finds the largest remaining element for each position and
   swaps it into place. main() then prints the 7 values in descending order. */
// END

/* Caption: Compute the product of two square matrices. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define N as 3.
   2. For every i and j, add a[i][k] * b[k][j] over k into product[i][j].
   3. Print product row by row. */
#define N 3

int main(void) {
    int a[N][N] = {{4, 2, 1}, {6, 7, 9}, {6, 0, 0}};
    int b[N][N] = {{6, 8, 4}, {9, 0, 5}, {0, 4, 4}};
    int product[N][N] = {0};
    /* product[i][j] is row i of a times column j of b. */
    for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) {
        for (int j = 0; j < N; j++) {
            for (int k = 0; k < N; k++) {
                product[i][j] += a[i][k] * b[k][j];
            }
        }
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) {
        for (int j = 0; j < N; j++) {
            printf("%4d", product[i][j]);
        }
        printf("\n");
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: For each entry product[i][j] the innermost loop adds a[i][k] * b[k][j] over
   k, which is row i of a times column j of b. main() multiplies two 3x3 matrices and
   prints the product. */
// END

/* Caption: C program to compute the LCM of two integers using the GCD. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write gcd() with Euclid's algorithm: replace (a, b) by (b, a % b) until b is 0.
   2. Write lcm() as a / gcd(a, b) * b.
   3. Print the LCM of 258 and 207. */
/* Euclid: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a % b) until b becomes zero. */
int gcd(int a, int b) {
    while (b != 0) {
        int r = a % b;
        a = b;
        b = r;
    }
    return a;
}

/* lcm(a, b) = a / gcd(a, b) * b (divide first to avoid overflow). */
long lcm(int a, int b) {
    return (long)a / gcd(a, b) * b;
}

int main(void) {
    printf("lcm(258, 207) = %ld\n", lcm(258, 207));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: gcd() uses Euclid's algorithm: it keeps replacing (a, b) with (b, a % b)
   until b is 0. lcm() divides a by the gcd before multiplying by b, which avoids overflow.
   main() prints the LCM of 258 and 207. */
// END

/* Caption: Check every element of an array to find a target value. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write linear_search() with the array, its length and target.
   2. Compare each element with target.
   3. Return the index of the first match, or -1.
   4. In main(), search for 76 and print the result. */
/* Return the index of target, or -1 when it is not in the array. */
int linear_search(const int nums[], int count, int target) {
    for (int i = 0; i < count; i++) {
        if (nums[i] == target) {
            return i;
        }
    }
    return -1;
}

int main(void) {
    int nums[] = {50, 42, 40, 76, 38};
    int count = 5;
    int target = 76;
    int pos = linear_search(nums, count, target);
    if (pos >= 0) {
        printf("Found %d at index %d\n", target, pos);
    } else {
        printf("%d is not in the array\n", target);
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: linear_search() checks the elements of nums one by one and returns the
   index of the first one equal to target, or -1 when it reaches the end without a match.
   main() searches for 76 and prints where it is, or that it is missing. */
// END

/* Caption: How do I reverse an array by swapping from both ends in C? */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write reverse_array() for marks.
   2. Set start to the first index and end to the last.
   3. Swap marks[start] and marks[end], then move both inwards.
   4. Stop when start meets end and print the array. */
/* Swap the outer pair, then move both ends toward the middle. */
void reverse_array(long marks[], int count) {
    int start = 0;
    int end = count - 1;
    while (start < end) {
        long tmp = marks[start];
        marks[start] = marks[end];
        marks[end] = tmp;
        start++;
        end--;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    long marks[] = {30L, 26L, 65L, 40L, 13L, 39L};
    int count = 6;
    reverse_array(marks, count);
    for (int i = 0; i < count; i++) {
        printf("%ld ", marks[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: reverse_array() swaps the first and last elements, then moves start forward
   and end backward until they meet, so the array is reversed in place without a second
   array. main() prints the reversed values. */
// END

/* Caption: Implement bubble sort for an array of int values. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write bubble_sort() for the int array data.
   2. Compare each pair of neighbours.
   3. Swap them when they are in the wrong order for ascending order.
   4. Repeat the passes until the array is sorted.
   5. Print the sorted values. */
/* Repeatedly swap neighbours that are in the wrong order. */
void bubble_sort(int data[], int count) {
    for (int i = 0; i < count - 1; i++) {
        for (int j = 0; j < count - 1 - i; j++) {
            if (data[j] > data[j + 1]) {
                int tmp = data[j];
                data[j] = data[j + 1];
                data[j + 1] = tmp;
            }
        }
    }
}

int main(void) {
    int data[] = {66, 70, 59, 96, 41, 13, 93, 16, 50, 99};
    const int count = 10;
    bubble_sort(data, count);
    for (int i = 0; i < count; i++) {
        printf("%d ", data[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: bubble_sort() walks through data again and again and swaps neighbours that
   are in the wrong order, so the largest values move to the end first. main() then prints
   the 10 values in ascending order. */
// END

/* Caption: C program to create a singly linked list by inserting at the head. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define ListNode with a value and a next pointer.
   2. Write push_front() that mallocs a node and links it in front of head.
   3. Write print_list() that follows next until NULL.
   4. Write free_list() that frees every node.
   5. Push 4 values, print the list and free it. */
typedef struct ListNode {
    int value;
    struct ListNode *next;
} ListNode;

/* Allocate a new node and put it in front of the current head. */
ListNode *push_front(ListNode *head, int value) {
    ListNode *node = malloc(sizeof(ListNode));
    if (node == NULL) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Out of memory\n");
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }
    node->value = value;
    node->next = head;
    return node;
}

void print_list(const ListNode *head) {
    for (const ListNode *cur = head; cur != NULL; cur = cur->next) {
        printf("%d -> ", cur->value);
    }
    printf("NULL\n");
}

/* Free every node; save next before freeing the current one. */
void free_list(ListNode *head) {
    while (head != NULL) {
        ListNode *next = head->next;
        free(head);
        head = next;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    ListNode *head = NULL;
    head = push_front(head, 4);
    head = push_front(head, 71);
    head = push_front(head, 86);
    head = push_front(head, 73);
    print_list(head);
    free_list(head);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: Each ListNode holds a value and a pointer to the next node. push_front()
   allocates a node with malloc, puts it in front of head and returns it; print_list()
   follows the next pointers until NULL; free_list() frees every node. main() pushes 4
   values, so they print in reverse order. */
// END

/* Caption: How do I build a fixed-size integer stack in C in C? */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define a Stack with room for 32 items and a top counter.
   2. Write push() and pop(), returning false when the stack is full or empty.
   3. Push 3 values.
   4. Pop and print until the stack is empty. */
#define CAPACITY 32

typedef struct {
    int items[CAPACITY];
    int top;   /* number of items on the stack */
} Stack;

bool push(Stack *s, int value) {
    if (s->top == CAPACITY) {
        return false;   /* stack is full */
    }
    s->items[s->top++] = value;
    return true;
}

bool pop(Stack *s, int *value) {
    if (s->top == 0) {
        return false;   /* stack is empty */
    }
    *value = s->items[--s->top];
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    Stack s = {.top = 0};
    push(&s, 53);
    push(&s, 90);
    push(&s, 52);
    int value;
    /* Items come back out in reverse order (last in, first out). */
    while (pop(&s, &value)) {
        printf("%d ", value);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: The Stack keeps up to 32 items in an array, and top counts how many are
   stored. push() adds at the top and pop() removes from the top; both return false when
   they cannot. main() pushes 3 values and pops them all, so they come out in reverse order
   (last in, first out). */
// END

/* Caption: Return the minimum, maximum and average of an array in a struct. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define a Stats struct with min, max and average.
   2. Write array_stats() that fills one Stats in a loop.
   3. Return the struct.
   4. Print st.min, st.max and st.average. */
typedef struct {
    int min;
    int max;
    double average;
} Stats;

/* Pack several results into one struct and return it. */
Stats array_stats(const int v[], int n) {
    Stats s = {v[0], v[0], 0.0};
    double total = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        if (v[i] < s.min) {
            s.min = v[i];
        }
        if (v[i] > s.max) {
            s.max = v[i];
        }
        total += v[i];
    }
    s.average = total / n;
    return s;
}

int main(void) {
    int marks[] = {76, 23, 68, 76, 78, 11, 60};
    int n = sizeof(marks) / sizeof(marks[0]);
    Stats st = array_stats(marks, n);
    printf("Min %d, Max %d, Average %.2f\n", st.min, st.max, st.average);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: Stats groups three results. array_stats() fills one Stats while it loops
   over the 7 values and returns the whole struct, which is a clean way to return several
   results at once. main() reads them as st.min, st.max and st.average. */
// END

/* Caption: Convert 174 to binary. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write print_binary(n, bits).
   2. Go through the bits from the highest to the lowest.
   3. Print 1 when (n >> b) & 1 is set, otherwise 0.
   4. Print 174 in binary. */
/* Check each bit from the highest to the lowest. */
void print_binary(unsigned int n, int bits) {
    for (int b = bits - 1; b >= 0; b--) {
        putchar((n >> b) & 1 ? '1' : '0');
    }
    putchar('\n');
}

int main(void) {
    unsigned int number = 174;
    printf("%u in binary: ", number);
    print_binary(number, 12);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: print_binary() checks one bit at a time, from the highest to the lowest: (n
   >> b) & 1 is 1 when bit b is set, so it prints the character 1 or 0. main() prints 174
   in binary. */
// END

/* Caption: Find the largest number in an array. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write max_of() that takes prices and count.
   2. Store prices[0] in current.
   3. Loop over the other elements and keep the largest value in current.
   4. Return current and print it. */
/* Start with the first element and keep the largest value seen so far. */
int max_of(const int prices[], int count) {
    int current = prices[0];
    for (int j = 1; j < count; j++) {
        if (prices[j] > current) {
            current = prices[j];
        }
    }
    return current;
}

int main(void) {
    int prices[] = {51, 3, 52, 31, 97, 32, 65};
    const int count = 7;
    printf("The largest value is %d\n", max_of(prices, count));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: max_of() takes the first element as the largest value so far and stores it
   in current. The loop compares every other element with current using > and keeps the
   largest one. main() prints the largest of the 7 values. */
// END
