/* Caption: C program to use binary search to locate a value in a sorted list. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Make sure the array is sorted.
   2. Set left to 0 and right to len - 1.
   3. While left <= right, compare the middle element middle with the key.
   4. Return the index if it matches; otherwise keep only the half that can hold the
      key.
   5. Return -1 if the range becomes empty, and print the index of 128. */
/* The array must be sorted. Each step halves the range that can still hold the key. */
int binary_search(const int values[], int len, int key) {
    int left = 0;
    int right = len - 1;
    while (left <= right) {
        int middle = left + (right - left) / 2;
        if (values[middle] == key) {
            return middle;
        } else if (values[middle] < key) {
            left = middle + 1;   /* key is in the right half */
        } else {
            right = middle - 1;   /* key is in the left half */
        }
    }
    return -1;
}

int main(void) {
    int values[] = {17, 26, 30, 118, 121, 126, 128, 179};
    const int len = 8;
    int index = binary_search(values, len, 128);
    printf("Index of 128: %d\n", index);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: binary_search() needs a sorted array. It keeps the range from left to
   right, compares the middle element middle with the key and throws away the half that
   cannot contain it, so it needs only about log2(n) steps. main() looks for 128 and prints
   its index, or -1 if it is not there. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to write your own version of strcpy. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write copy_string(dest, src).
   2. Copy src into dest one character at a time.
   3. Stop after copying the null character.
   4. Copy matrix into str and print it. */
/* Copy each character, including the final '\0'. */
void copy_string(char *dest, const char *src) {
    int i = 0;
    while ((dest[i] = src[i]) != '\0') {
        i++;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    char source[] = "matrix";
    char str[100];
    copy_string(str, source);
    printf("Copied: %s\n", str);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: copy_string() copies src into dest one character at a time, including the
   final null character, which is what strcpy does. The array str must be big enough to
   hold the copy. main() copies the word matrix and prints it. */
// END

/* Caption: Check whether a year is a leap year. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write is_leap(year).
   2. A year divisible by 4 is a leap year, unless it is divisible by 100.
   3. Years divisible by 400 are leap years again.
   4. Check 2011 and print the result. */
/* Leap years divide by 4, except centuries, which must divide by 400. */
int is_leap(int year) {
    return (year % 4 == 0 && year % 100 != 0) || year % 400 == 0;
}

int main(void) {
    int year = 2011;
    if (is_leap(year)) {
        printf("%d is a leap year\n", year);
    } else {
        printf("%d is not a leap year\n", year);
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: is_leap() returns true for years divisible by 4, except century years,
   which must also be divisible by 400. main() checks 2011 and prints whether it is a leap
   year. */
// END

   4. Print the average with two decimals. */

   count, so the mean keeps its decimal part even when the values are whole numbers. main()
   prints it with two decimals. */

/* Multiply 1 * 2 * ... * n. */

/* Caption: Write a program to build a fixed-size integer stack in C. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define a Stack with room for 8 items and a top counter.
   2. Write push() and pop(), returning false when the stack is full or empty.
   3. Push 6 values.
   4. Pop and print until the stack is empty. */
#define CAPACITY 8

typedef struct {
    int items[CAPACITY];
    int top;   /* number of items on the stack */
} Stack;

bool push(Stack *s, int value) {
    if (s->top == CAPACITY) {
        return false;   /* stack is full */
    }
    s->items[s->top++] = value;
    return true;
}

bool pop(Stack *s, int *value) {
    if (s->top == 0) {
        return false;   /* stack is empty */
    }
    *value = s->items[--s->top];
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    Stack s = {.top = 0};
    push(&s, 81);
    push(&s, 70);
    push(&s, 70);
    push(&s, 71);
    push(&s, 70);
    push(&s, 41);
    int value;
    /* Items come back out in reverse order (last in, first out). */
    while (pop(&s, &value)) {
        printf("%d ", value);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: The Stack keeps up to 8 items in an array, and top counts how many are
   stored. push() adds at the top and pop() removes from the top; both return false when
   they cannot. main() pushes 6 values and pops them all, so they come out in reverse order
   (last in, first out). */
// END

/* Caption: How do I print the binary representation of an integer in C? */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write print_binary(n, bits).
   2. Go through the bits from the highest to the lowest.
   3. Print 1 when (n >> b) & 1 is set, otherwise 0.
   4. Print 957 in binary. */
/* Check each bit from the highest to the lowest. */
void print_binary(unsigned int n, int bits) {
    for (int b = bits - 1; b >= 0; b--) {
        putchar((n >> b) & 1 ? '1' : '0');
    }
    putchar('\n');
}

int main(void) {
    unsigned int number = 957;
    printf("%u in binary: ", number);
    print_binary(number, 8);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: print_binary() checks one bit at a time, from the highest to the lowest: (n
   >> b) & 1 is 1 when bit b is set, so it prints the character 1 or 0. main() prints 957
   in binary. */
// END

/* Caption: Use selection sort to put numbers in ascending order. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write selection_sort() for the double array prices.
   2. For each position, find the smallest remaining element.
   3. Swap it into that position.
   4. Print the sorted values. */
/* Select the right element for each position and swap it into place. */
void selection_sort(double prices[], int size) {
    for (int i = 0; i < size - 1; i++) {
        int chosen = i;
        for (int j = i + 1; j < size; j++) {
            if (prices[chosen] > prices[j]) {
                chosen = j;
            }
        }
        double tmp = prices[i];
        prices[i] = prices[chosen];
        prices[chosen] = tmp;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    double prices[] = {80.3, 60.3, 41.3, 51.1, 71.9, 78.7, 31.6, 97.4, 10.0};
    int size = 9;
    selection_sort(prices, size);
    for (int i = 0; i < size; i++) {
        printf("%.2f ", prices[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: selection_sort() finds the smallest remaining element for each position and
   swaps it into place. main() then prints the 9 values in ascending order. */
// END

/* Caption: How do I print the first 12 Fibonacci numbers in C? */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Start with first = 0 and second = 1.
   2. Repeat 12 times and print first each time.
   3. Compute next = first + second, then set first = second and second = next. */
int main(void) {
    long first = 0, second = 1;
    /* Print a term, then slide the pair one step along the sequence. */
    for (int i = 0; i < 12; i++) {
        printf("%ld ", first);
        long next = first + second;
        first = second;
        second = next;
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: The loop keeps the last two numbers in first and second. Each round it
   prints first, then moves the pair forward: first becomes second and second becomes their
   sum. It prints the first 12 Fibonacci numbers. */
// END

/* Caption: Use binary search to locate a value in a sorted list. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Make sure the array is sorted.
   2. Set lo to 0 and hi to count - 1.
   3. While lo <= hi, compare the middle element mid with the key.
   4. Return the index if it matches; otherwise keep only the half that can hold the
      key.
   5. Return -1 if the range becomes empty, and print the index of 102. */
/* The array must be sorted. Each step halves the range that can still hold the key. */
int binary_search(const int readings[], int count, int key) {
    int lo = 0;
    int hi = count - 1;
    while (lo <= hi) {
        int mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;
        if (readings[mid] == key) {
            return mid;
        } else if (readings[mid] < key) {
            lo = mid + 1;   /* key is in the right half */
        } else {
            hi = mid - 1;   /* key is in the left half */
        }
    }
    return -1;
}

int main(void) {
    int readings[] = {11, 22, 37, 61, 94, 102, 105, 147, 178, 183};
    int count = sizeof(readings) / sizeof(readings[0]);
    int index = binary_search(readings, count, 102);
    printf("Index of 102: %d\n", index);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: binary_search() needs a sorted array. It keeps the range from lo to hi,
   compares the middle element mid with the key and throws away the half that cannot
   contain it, so it needs only about log2(n) steps. main() looks for 102 and prints its
   index, or -1 if it is not there. */
// END

/* Caption: Raise a number to an integer power with a loop. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:

   2. Multiply result by base exp times.
   3. Print 9 to the power 2. */
/* Multiply the base by itself exp times. */
long long power(int base, int exp) {
    long long result = 1;
    for (int i = 0; i < exp; i++) {
        result *= base;
    }
    return result;
}

int main(void) {
    printf("9^2 = %lld\n", power(9, 2));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: power() starts result at 1 and multiplies it by base exp times. It uses
   long long because powers grow quickly. main() prints 9 to the power 2. */
// END

/* Caption: Print an integer with its digits reversed. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Start result at 0.
   2. Multiply result by 10, add n % 10, then divide n by 10.
   3. Repeat until n is 0.
   4. Apply it to 238289 and print the result. */
/* Take the last digit with % 10, then drop it with / 10. */
int reverse_digits(int n) {
    int result = 0;
    while (n > 0) {
        result = result * 10 + n % 10;
        n /= 10;
    }
    return result;
}

int main(void) {
    int number = 238289;
    printf("reverse of digits of %d: %d\n", number, reverse_digits(number));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: reverse_digits() shifts result one place left (result * 10) and adds the
   last digit of n, which reverses the order. main() applies it to 238289. */
// END

/* Caption: Program to use bubble sort to put numbers in ascending order. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write bubble_sort() for the double array readings.
   2. Compare each pair of neighbours.
   3. Swap them when they are in the wrong order for ascending order.
   4. Repeat the passes until the array is sorted.
   5. Print the sorted values. */
/* Repeatedly swap neighbours that are in the wrong order. */
void bubble_sort(double readings[], int size) {
    for (int i = 0; i < size - 1; i++) {
        for (int j = 0; j < size - 1 - i; j++) {
            if (readings[j] > readings[j + 1]) {
                double tmp = readings[j];
                readings[j] = readings[j + 1];
                readings[j + 1] = tmp;
            }
        }
    }
}

int main(void) {
    double readings[] = {95.3, 43.4, 91.0, 67.4, 9.3, 1.0};
    int size = 6;
    bubble_sort(readings, size);
    for (int i = 0; i < size; i++) {
        printf("%.2f ", readings[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: bubble_sort() walks through readings again and again and swaps neighbours
   that are in the wrong order, so the largest values move to the end first. main() then
   prints the 6 values in ascending order. */
// END

/* Caption: How do I swap two variables using pointers in C? */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write swap() that takes pointers to two int values.
   2. Save *first in tmp, copy *second into *first, then tmp into *second.
   3. In main(), print first and second, call swap(&first, &second) and print them
      again. */
/* Pass addresses so the function can change the caller's variables. */
void swap(int *first, int *second) {
    int tmp = *first;
    *first = *second;
    *second = tmp;
}

int main(void) {
    int first = 60, second = 81;
    printf("Before: %d %d\n", first, second);
    swap(&first, &second);
    printf("After:  %d %d\n", first, second);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: swap() receives the addresses of first and second, so writing through the
   pointers *first and *second changes the caller's variables. tmp holds one value during
   the exchange. main() declares both variables on one line and prints them before and
   after the swap. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a function that returns the midpoint of two points as a struct. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define a Point struct with x and y.
   2. Write midpoint() that returns a Point with the averages of x and y.
   3. Print mid.x and mid.y. */
typedef struct {
    double x;
    double y;
} Point;

/* A function can return a whole struct. */
Point midpoint(Point a, Point b) {
    Point m = {(a.x + b.x) / 2, (a.y + b.y) / 2};
    return m;
}

int main(void) {
    Point p = {6, 7}, q = {-12, -18};
    Point mid = midpoint(p, q);
    printf("Midpoint: (%.1f, %.1f)\n", mid.x, mid.y);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: midpoint() takes two Point structs and returns a new Point whose x and y
   are the averages of theirs. main() declares p and q on one line, (6, 7) and (-12, -18),
   and prints the midpoint using mid.x and mid.y. */
// END

/* Caption: Reverse an array by swapping from both ends. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write reverse_array() for prices.
   2. Set left to the first index and right to the last.
   3. Swap prices[left] and prices[right], then move both inwards.
   4. Stop when left meets right and print the array. */
/* Swap the outer pair, then move both ends toward the middle. */
void reverse_array(int prices[], int count) {
    int left = 0;
    int right = count - 1;
    while (left < right) {
        int tmp = prices[left];
        prices[left] = prices[right];
        prices[right] = tmp;
        left++;
        right--;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    int prices[] = {13, 77, 41, 59, 41, 37};
    const int count = 6;
    reverse_array(prices, count);
    for (int i = 0; i < count; i++) {
        printf("%d ", prices[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: reverse_array() swaps the first and last elements, then moves left forward
   and right backward until they meet, so the array is reversed in place without a second
   array. main() prints the reversed values. */
// END

/* Caption: Convert 560 to binary. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write print_binary(n, bits).
   2. Go through the bits from the highest to the lowest.
   3. Print 1 when (n >> b) & 1 is set, otherwise 0.
   4. Print 560 in binary. */
/* Check each bit from the highest to the lowest. */
void print_binary(unsigned int n, int bits) {
    for (int b = bits - 1; b >= 0; b--) {
        putchar((n >> b) & 1 ? '1' : '0');
    }
    putchar('\n');
}

int main(void) {
    unsigned int number = 560;
    printf("%u in binary: ", number);
    print_binary(number, 12);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: print_binary() checks one bit at a time, from the highest to the lowest: (n
   >> b) & 1 is 1 when bit b is set, so it prints the character 1 or 0. main() prints 560
   in binary. */
// END

#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write in_range(x, low, high).
   2. Return true when x >= low and x <= high.
   3. Print whether -1 is inside 63 to 98. */
/* true when low <= x <= high */
bool in_range(int x, int low, int high) {
    return x >= low && x <= high;
}

int main(void) {
    int value = -1, low = 63, high = 98;
    printf("%d is %s the range %d to %d\n", value,
           in_range(value, low, high) ? "inside" : "outside", low, high);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: in_range() takes the value and both limits and returns true only when the
   value is at least low and at most high. main() declares value, low and high on one line
   and prints whether -1 is inside 63 to 98. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to change every letter in a sentence to a capital letter. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <ctype.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write to_upper() for str.
   2. Replace every character with toupper() until the null character.
   3. Print the sentence. */
/* toupper changes lowercase letters and leaves other characters alone. */
void to_upper(char *str) {
    for (int i = 0; str[i] != '\0'; i++) {
        str[i] = toupper((unsigned char)str[i]);
    }

    to_upper(str);
    printf("%s\n", str);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: to_upper() walks through str until the null character and replaces each
   character with toupper(), which only changes lowercase letters. main() prints the
   sentence in capitals. */
// END

/* Caption: Return a Duration struct built from a number of seconds. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define a Duration struct with hours, minutes and seconds.
   2. Write from_seconds() that fills it using / and %.
   3. Convert 78876 seconds and print the members. */
typedef struct {
    int hours;
    int minutes;
    int seconds;
} Duration;

Duration from_seconds(int total) {
    Duration d;
    d.hours = total / 3600;
    d.minutes = (total % 3600) / 60;
    d.seconds = total % 60;
    return d;
}

int main(void) {
    Duration d = from_seconds(78876);
    printf("%d h %d min %d s\n", d.hours, d.minutes, d.seconds);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: from_seconds() fills the three members of a Duration struct using / and %,
   then returns the struct. main() converts 78876 seconds and prints the members. */
// END

/* Caption: Find the quotient of 2 integers. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Read num1 and num2.
   2. If num2 is 0, print an error and stop.
   3. Print num1 / num2 and the remainder num1 % num2. */
int main(void) {
    int num1, num2;
    printf("Enter 2 numbers: ");
    if (scanf("%d %d", &num1, &num2) != 2) {
        printf("Invalid input\n");
        return 1;
    }
    /* Dividing by zero is not allowed, so check first. */
    if (num2 == 0) {
        printf("Cannot divide by zero\n");
        return 1;
    }
    /* Integer division drops the fraction; % gives the remainder. */
    printf("Quotient: %d, remainder: %d\n", num1 / num2, num1 % num2);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: The program reads num1 and num2 from the keyboard with scanf and stops with
   a message if the input is not valid. It checks that num2 is not zero, then prints num1 /
   num2, where integer division drops the fraction, and the remainder num1 % num2. */
// END

/* Caption: Print a Celsius to Fahrenheit conversion table. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write to_fahrenheit() with F = C * 9 / 5 + 32.
   2. Loop c from 0 to 40 in steps of 10.
   3. Print each Celsius value with its Fahrenheit value. */
/* F = C * 9 / 5 + 32 */
double to_fahrenheit(double celsius) {
    return celsius * 9.0 / 5.0 + 32.0;
}

int main(void) {
    printf("Celsius  Fahrenheit\n");
    for (int c = 0; c <= 40; c += 10) {
        printf("%7d  %10.1f\n", c, to_fahrenheit(c));
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: to_fahrenheit() applies F = C * 9 / 5 + 32. main() prints a table from 0 to
   40 degrees Celsius in steps of 10. */
// END

/* Caption: Swap two variables using pointers. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write swap() that takes pointers to two int values.
   2. Save *a in tmp, copy *b into *a, then tmp into *b.
   3. In main(), print a and b, call swap(&a, &b) and print them again. */
/* Pass addresses so the function can change the caller's variables. */
void swap(int *a, int *b) {
    int tmp = *a;
    *a = *b;
    *b = tmp;
}

int main(void) {
    int a = 32, b = 89;
    printf("Before: %d %d\n", a, b);
    swap(&a, &b);
    printf("After:  %d %d\n", a, b);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: swap() receives the addresses of a and b, so writing through the pointers
   *a and *b changes the caller's variables. tmp holds one value during the exchange.
   main() declares both variables on one line and prints them before and after the swap. */
// END

/* Caption: Calculate the average of the values in an array. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write mean() that takes items and count.
   2. Add the values into the double result.
   3. Return result / count.
   4. Print the average with two decimals. */
/* The mean is the total divided by the count. */
double mean(const int items[], int count) {
    double result = 0.0;
    for (int k = 0; k < count; k++) {
        result += items[k];
    }
    return result / count;
}

int main(void) {
    int items[] = {26, 18, 24};
    int count = 3;
    printf("Average: %.2f\n", mean(items, count));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: mean() adds the 3 values of items into the double result and divides by
   count, so the mean keeps its decimal part even when the values are whole numbers. main()
   prints it with two decimals. */
// END

/* Caption: Save text to a file with fprintf and print it with fgets. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Open log.txt in write mode and check for NULL.
   2. Write 2 lines with fprintf and close the file.
   3. Open it again in read mode.
   4. Read and print each line with fgets, then close the file. */
int main(void) {
    FILE *file = fopen("log.txt", "w");
    if (file == NULL) {
        perror("fopen");
        return 1;
    }
    fprintf(file, "arrays in c start at index zero\n");
    fprintf(file, "good comments explain why the code exists\n");
    fclose(file);

    /* Reopen the file for reading and print it line by line. */
    file = fopen("log.txt", "r");
    if (file == NULL) {
        perror("fopen");
        return 1;
    }
    char line[128];
    while (fgets(line, sizeof(line), file) != NULL) {
        printf("%s", line);
    }
    fclose(file);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: fopen() in write mode creates log.txt, fprintf() writes 2 lines into it and
   fclose() saves it. The file is then opened again in read mode, and fgets() reads it back
   line by line into the buffer line, which is printed. Every fopen() result is checked for
   NULL. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to raise a number to an integer power with a loop. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write power(base, exp) with result = 1.
   2. Multiply result by base exp times.
   3. Print 7 to the power 12. */
/* Multiply the base by itself exp times. */
long long power(int base, int exp) {
    long long result = 1;
    for (int i = 0; i < exp; i++) {
        result *= base;
    }
    return result;
}

int main(void) {
    printf("7^12 = %lld\n", power(7, 12));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: power() starts result at 1 and multiplies it by base exp times. It uses
   long long because powers grow quickly. main() prints 7 to the power 12. */
// END

/* Plan:
   1. Write count_even() that takes scores and length.
   2. For each element, test scores[i] % 2 == 0.
   3. Add one to matches for every even number.
   4. Return matches and print it. */
/* A number is even when the remainder after dividing by 2 is zero. */

    int matches = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < length; i++) {

            matches++;
        }
    }
    return matches;
}

    int length = 9;
    printf("Count of even values = %d\n", count_even(scores, length));
    return 0;
}

   of 0 after dividing by 2 means the number is even, so matches goes up by one. main()
   prints how many of the 9 values are even. */
// END

/* Caption: Sort an array in descending order using bubble sort. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write bubble_sort() for the int array data.
   2. Compare each pair of neighbours.
   3. Swap them when they are in the wrong order for descending order.
   4. Repeat the passes until the array is sorted.
   5. Print the sorted values. */
/* Repeatedly swap neighbours that are in the wrong order. */
void bubble_sort(int data[], int length) {
    for (int i = 0; i < length - 1; i++) {
        for (int j = 0; j < length - 1 - i; j++) {
            if (data[j] < data[j + 1]) {
                int tmp = data[j];
                data[j] = data[j + 1];
                data[j + 1] = tmp;
            }
        }
    }
}

int main(void) {
    int data[] = {89, 24, 53, 32, 85, 42, 1, 11, 74, 17};
    const int length = 10;
    bubble_sort(data, length);
    for (int i = 0; i < length; i++) {
        printf("%d ", data[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: bubble_sort() walks through data again and again and swaps neighbours that
   are in the wrong order, so the smallest values move to the end first. main() then prints
   the 10 values in descending order. */
// END

/* Caption: Create a singly linked list by inserting at the head. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define ListNode with a value and a next pointer.
   2. Write push_front() that mallocs a node and links it in front of head.
   3. Write print_list() that follows next until NULL.
   4. Write free_list() that frees every node.
   5. Push 3 values, print the list and free it. */
typedef struct ListNode {
    int value;
    struct ListNode *next;
} ListNode;

/* Allocate a new node and put it in front of the current head. */
ListNode *push_front(ListNode *head, int value) {
    ListNode *node = malloc(sizeof(ListNode));
    if (node == NULL) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Out of memory\n");
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }
    node->value = value;
    node->next = head;
    return node;
}

void print_list(const ListNode *head) {
    for (const ListNode *cur = head; cur != NULL; cur = cur->next) {
        printf("%d -> ", cur->value);
    }
    printf("NULL\n");
}

/* Free every node; save next before freeing the current one. */
void free_list(ListNode *head) {
    while (head != NULL) {
        ListNode *next = head->next;
        free(head);
        head = next;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    ListNode *head = NULL;
    head = push_front(head, 18);
    head = push_front(head, 57);
    head = push_front(head, 38);
    print_list(head);
    free_list(head);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: Each ListNode holds a value and a pointer to the next node. push_front()
   allocates a node with malloc, puts it in front of head and returns it; print_list()
   follows the next pointers until NULL; free_list() frees every node. main() pushes 3
   values, so they print in reverse order. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to compute the factorial of a number recursively. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write factorial(value) that calls itself.
   2. Return 1 when value is 1 or less.
   3. Otherwise return value * factorial(value - 1).
   4. Print 11! as an unsigned long long. */
/* n! = n * (n - 1)!, and 0! = 1 stops the recursion. */
unsigned long long factorial(int value) {
    if (value <= 1) {
        return 1;
    }
    return value * factorial(value - 1);
}

int main(void) {
    int value = 11;
    printf("%d! = %llu\n", value, factorial(value));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: factorial() calls itself: n! is n * (n - 1)!, and the recursion stops when
   value is 1 or less. main() prints 11! as an unsigned long long, because factorials grow
   very fast. */
// END

/* Caption: How do I implement bubble sort for an array of long values in C? */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write bubble_sort() for the long array prices.
   2. Compare each pair of neighbours.
   3. Swap them when they are in the wrong order for ascending order.
   4. Repeat the passes until the array is sorted.
   5. Print the sorted values. */
/* Repeatedly swap neighbours that are in the wrong order. */
void bubble_sort(long prices[], int count) {
    for (int i = 0; i < count - 1; i++) {
        for (int j = 0; j < count - 1 - i; j++) {
            if (prices[j] > prices[j + 1]) {
                long tmp = prices[j];
                prices[j] = prices[j + 1];
                prices[j + 1] = tmp;
            }
        }
    }
}

int main(void) {
    long prices[] = {2L, 54L, 56L, 42L, 17L, 11L};
    int count = sizeof(prices) / sizeof(prices[0]);
    bubble_sort(prices, count);
    for (int i = 0; i < count; i++) {
        printf("%ld ", prices[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: bubble_sort() walks through prices again and again and swaps neighbours
   that are in the wrong order, so the largest values move to the end first. main() then
   prints the 6 values in ascending order. */
// END

/* Caption: Calculate the average of the values in an array. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write mean() that takes data and size.
   2. Add the values into the double total.
   3. Return total / size.
   4. Print the average with two decimals. */
/* Sum the values, then divide by how many there are. */
double mean(const double data[], int size) {
    double total = 0.0;
    for (int k = 0; k < size; k++) {
        total += data[k];
    }
    return total / size;
}

int main(void) {
    double data[] = {5.2, 28.5, 43.9, 3.4};
    int size = sizeof(data) / sizeof(data[0]);
    printf("Mean = %.2f\n", mean(data, size));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: mean() adds the 4 values of data into the double total and divides by size,
   so the mean keeps its decimal part even when the values are whole numbers. main() prints
   it with two decimals. */
// END

   prints it with two decimals. */

/* Caption: Use binary search to locate a value in a sorted list. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Make sure the array is sorted.
   2. Set lo to 0 and hi to size - 1.
   3. While lo <= hi, compare the middle element mid with the key.
   4. Return the index if it matches; otherwise keep only the half that can hold the
      key.
   5. Return -1 if the range becomes empty, and print the index of 177. */
/* The array must be sorted. Each step halves the range that can still hold the key. */
int binary_search(const int samples[], int size, int key) {
    int lo = 0;
    int hi = size - 1;
    while (lo <= hi) {
        int mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;
        if (samples[mid] == key) {
            return mid;
        } else if (samples[mid] < key) {
            lo = mid + 1;   /* key is in the right half */
        } else {
            hi = mid - 1;   /* key is in the left half */
        }
    }
    return -1;
}

int main(void) {
    int samples[] = {23, 60, 62, 76, 138, 177, 185};
    int size = sizeof(samples) / sizeof(samples[0]);
    int index = binary_search(samples, size, 177);
    printf("Index of 177: %d\n", index);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: binary_search() needs a sorted array. It keeps the range from lo to hi,
   compares the middle element mid with the key and throws away the half that cannot
   contain it, so it needs only about log2(n) steps. main() looks for 177 and prints its
   index, or -1 if it is not there. */
// END

/* Caption: Implement insertion sort for an array of int values. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write insertion_sort() for the int array values.
   2. Take each element in turn as current.
   3. Shift the larger values of the sorted part one place right.
   4. Put current into the gap.
   5. Print the sorted values. */
/* Insert each element into the already sorted part on its left. */
void insertion_sort(int values[], int count) {
    for (int i = 1; i < count; i++) {
        int current = values[i];
        int j = i - 1;
        while (j >= 0 && values[j] > current) {
            values[j + 1] = values[j];   /* shift bigger values right */
            j--;
        }
        values[j + 1] = current;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    int values[] = {74, 96, 70, 25, 71, 72, 78, 89, 40};
    int count = 9;
    insertion_sort(values, count);
    for (int i = 0; i < count; i++) {
        printf("%d ", values[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: insertion_sort() takes each element in turn and shifts the larger values of
   the sorted part one place right until the element fits. main() then prints the 9 values
   in ascending order. */
// END

/* Caption: Convert 679 to binary. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write print_binary(n, bits).
   2. Go through the bits from the highest to the lowest.
   3. Print 1 when (n >> b) & 1 is set, otherwise 0.
   4. Print 679 in binary. */
/* Check each bit from the highest to the lowest. */
void print_binary(unsigned int n, int bits) {
    for (int b = bits - 1; b >= 0; b--) {
        putchar((n >> b) & 1 ? '1' : '0');
    }
    putchar('\n');
}

int main(void) {
    unsigned int number = 679;
    printf("%u in binary: ", number);
    print_binary(number, 8);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: print_binary() checks one bit at a time, from the highest to the lowest: (n
   >> b) & 1 is 1 when bit b is set, so it prints the character 1 or 0. main() prints 679
   in binary. */
// END

/* Caption: Reverse an array by swapping from both ends. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write reverse_array() for samples.
   2. Set left to the first index and right to the last.
   3. Swap samples[left] and samples[right], then move both inwards.
   4. Stop when left meets right and print the array. */
/* Swap the outer pair, then move both ends toward the middle. */
void reverse_array(int samples[], int n) {
    int left = 0;
    int right = n - 1;
    while (left < right) {
        int tmp = samples[left];
        samples[left] = samples[right];
        samples[right] = tmp;
        left++;
        right--;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    int samples[] = {12, 83, 84, 33, 32, 64};
    int n = sizeof(samples) / sizeof(samples[0]);
    reverse_array(samples, n);
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        printf("%d ", samples[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: reverse_array() swaps the first and last elements, then moves left forward
   and right backward until they meet, so the array is reversed in place without a second
   array. main() prints the reversed values. */
// END

    }
    return 0;
}

   Its bool return value reports success, while the quotient and remainder are written
   through the pointers. main() divides 226 by 27 and prints both results. */
// END

/* Caption: Find the total of all elements in an array using a loop. */

/* Plan:
   1. Write array_sum() that takes the array items and its length count.
   2. Start result at 0 and add every element in a while loop.
   3. Return result.

/* Walk through the array and accumulate each value. */

/* Caption: How do I implement bubble sort for an array of double values in C? */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write bubble_sort() for the double array prices.
   2. Compare each pair of neighbours.
   3. Swap them when they are in the wrong order for ascending order.
   4. Repeat the passes until the array is sorted.
   5. Print the sorted values. */
/* Repeatedly swap neighbours that are in the wrong order. */
void bubble_sort(double prices[], int length) {
    for (int i = 0; i < length - 1; i++) {
        for (int j = 0; j < length - 1 - i; j++) {
            if (prices[j] > prices[j + 1]) {
                double tmp = prices[j];
                prices[j] = prices[j + 1];
                prices[j + 1] = tmp;
            }
        }
    }
}

int main(void) {
    double prices[] = {33.2, 97.3, 54.5, 27.6, 50.5};
    int length = 5;
    bubble_sort(prices, length);
    for (int i = 0; i < length; i++) {
        printf("%.2f ", prices[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: bubble_sort() walks through prices again and again and swaps neighbours
   that are in the wrong order, so the largest values move to the end first. main() then
   prints the 5 values in ascending order. */
// END

/* Caption: Find the smallest number in an array. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write min_of() that takes data and len.
   2. Store data[0] in current.
   3. Loop over the other elements and keep the smallest value in current.
   4. Return current and print it. */
/* Start with the first element and keep the smallest value seen so far. */
int min_of(const int data[], int len) {
    int current = data[0];
    for (int k = 1; k < len; k++) {
        if (data[k] < current) {
            current = data[k];
        }
    }
    return current;
}

int main(void) {
    int data[] = {27, 13, 54, 25, 62, 64, 14, 35, 12};
    const int len = 9;
    printf("The smallest value is %d\n", min_of(data, len));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: min_of() takes the first element as the smallest value so far and stores it
   in current. The loop compares every other element with current using < and keeps the
   smallest one. main() prints the smallest of the 9 values. */
// END

/* Caption: Build a FIFO queue using a ring buffer. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define a Queue with room for 32 items, a head and a count.
   2. Write enqueue() that stores at (head + count) % CAPACITY.
   3. Write dequeue() that takes the item at head and moves head on.
   4. Add 5 values, then remove and print them in order. */
#define CAPACITY 32

typedef struct {
    int items[CAPACITY];
    int head;
    int count;
} Queue;

bool enqueue(Queue *q, int value) {
    if (q->count == CAPACITY) {
        return false;
    }
    /* The tail wraps around to the start of the array. */
    q->items[(q->head + q->count) % CAPACITY] = value;
    q->count++;
    return true;
}

bool dequeue(Queue *q, int *value) {
    if (q->count == 0) {
        return false;
    }
    *value = q->items[q->head];
    q->head = (q->head + 1) % CAPACITY;
    q->count--;
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    Queue q = {.head = 0, .count = 0};
    enqueue(&q, 21);
    enqueue(&q, 2);
    enqueue(&q, 28);
    enqueue(&q, 7);
    enqueue(&q, 38);
    int value;
    /* Items come out in the order they went in (first in, first out). */
    while (dequeue(&q, &value)) {
        printf("%d ", value);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: The Queue stores up to 32 items in a ring buffer: head is the oldest item
   and % CAPACITY wraps positions back to the start of the array. enqueue() adds at the
   back and dequeue() removes from the front, so main() gets its 5 values back in the same
   order (first in, first out). */
// END

/* Caption: Multiply two 2x2 matrices. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define N as 2.
   2. For every i and j, add a[i][k] * b[k][j] over k into product[i][j].
   3. Print product row by row. */
#define N 2

int main(void) {
    int a[N][N] = {{0, 9}, {2, 3}};
    int b[N][N] = {{9, 9}, {6, 5}};
    int product[N][N] = {0};
    /* product[i][j] is row i of a times column j of b. */
    for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) {
        for (int j = 0; j < N; j++) {
            for (int k = 0; k < N; k++) {
                product[i][j] += a[i][k] * b[k][j];
            }
        }
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) {
        for (int j = 0; j < N; j++) {
            printf("%4d", product[i][j]);
        }
        printf("\n");
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: For each entry product[i][j] the innermost loop adds a[i][k] * b[k][j] over
   k, which is row i of a times column j of b. main() multiplies two 2x2 matrices and
   prints the product. */
// END

/* Caption: Program to print all prime numbers up to 64. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write is_prime(n); numbers below 2 are not prime.
   2. Try every divisor d while d * d <= n.
   3. Return false if one divides n, otherwise true.
   4. Print every prime from 2 to 64. */
/* A prime has no divisor between 2 and its square root. */
bool is_prime(int n) {
    if (n < 2) {
        return false;
    }
    for (int d = 2; d * d <= n; d++) {
        if (n % d == 0) {
            return false;
        }
    }
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    for (int n = 2; n <= 64; n++) {
        if (is_prime(n)) {
            printf("%d ", n);
        }
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: is_prime() tries every divisor d from 2 while d * d <= n; if one divides n
   evenly, n is not prime. main() tests every number from 2 to 64 and prints the primes. */
// END

/* Caption: Reverse an array by swapping from both ends. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write reverse_array() for nums.
   2. Set start to the first index and end to the last.
   3. Swap nums[start] and nums[end], then move both inwards.
   4. Stop when start meets end and print the array. */
/* Swap the outer pair, then move both ends toward the middle. */
void reverse_array(int nums[], int count) {
    int start = 0;
    int end = count - 1;
    while (start < end) {
        int tmp = nums[start];
        nums[start] = nums[end];
        nums[end] = tmp;
        start++;
        end--;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    int nums[] = {95, 58, 89, 17, 37, 88};
    int count = sizeof(nums) / sizeof(nums[0]);
    reverse_array(nums, count);
    for (int i = 0; i < count; i++) {
        printf("%d ", nums[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: reverse_array() swaps the first and last elements, then moves start forward
   and end backward until they meet, so the array is reversed in place without a second
   array. main() prints the reversed values. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to compute the factorial of a number recursively. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write factorial(value) that calls itself.
   2. Return 1 when value is 1 or less.
   3. Otherwise return value * factorial(value - 1).
   4. Print 7! as an unsigned long long. */
/* n! = n * (n - 1)!, and 0! = 1 stops the recursion. */
unsigned long long factorial(int value) {
    if (value <= 1) {
        return 1;
    }
    return value * factorial(value - 1);
}

int main(void) {
    int value = 7;
    printf("%d! = %llu\n", value, factorial(value));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: factorial() calls itself: n! is n * (n - 1)!, and the recursion stops when
   value is 1 or less. main() prints 7! as an unsigned long long, because factorials grow
   very fast. */
// END

/* Caption: Program to test if "banana" reads the same backwards. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <string.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write is_palindrome() for buffer.
   2. Compare the first and last characters, moving inwards.
   3. Return false at the first mismatch, otherwise true.
   4. Check banana and print the result. */
/* Compare characters from the front and back, moving inwards. */
bool is_palindrome(const char *buffer) {
    int i = 0;
    int j = strlen(buffer) - 1;
    while (i < j) {
        if (buffer[i] != buffer[j]) {
            return false;
        }
        i++;
        j--;
    }
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    const char *buffer = "banana";
    printf("%s %s a palindrome\n", buffer, is_palindrome(buffer) ? "is" : "is not");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: is_palindrome() compares the first and last characters and moves inwards;
   any mismatch means the word is not a palindrome. main() checks the word banana and
   prints the result. */
// END

/* Caption: Sort an array in ascending order using bubble sort. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write bubble_sort() for the int array marks.
   2. Compare each pair of neighbours.
   3. Swap them when they are in the wrong order for ascending order.
   4. Repeat the passes until the array is sorted.
   5. Print the sorted values. */
/* Repeatedly swap neighbours that are in the wrong order. */
void bubble_sort(int marks[], int length) {
    for (int i = 0; i < length - 1; i++) {
        for (int j = 0; j < length - 1 - i; j++) {
            if (marks[j] > marks[j + 1]) {
                int tmp = marks[j];
                marks[j] = marks[j + 1];
                marks[j + 1] = tmp;
            }
        }
    }
}

int main(void) {
    int marks[] = {52, 93, 74, 94, 28, 82};
    const int length = 6;
    bubble_sort(marks, length);
    for (int i = 0; i < length; i++) {
        printf("%d ", marks[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: bubble_sort() walks through marks again and again and swaps neighbours that
   are in the wrong order, so the largest values move to the end first. main() then prints
   the 6 values in ascending order. */
// END

/* Caption: Swap two variables using pointers. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write swap() that takes pointers to two int values.
   2. Save *first in tmp, copy *second into *first, then tmp into *second.
   3. In main(), print first and second, call swap(&first, &second) and print them
      again. */
/* Pass addresses so the function can change the caller's variables. */
void swap(int *first, int *second) {
    int tmp = *first;
    *first = *second;
    *second = tmp;
}

int main(void) {
    int first = 98, second = 55;
    printf("Before: %d %d\n", first, second);
    swap(&first, &second);
    printf("After:  %d %d\n", first, second);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: swap() receives the addresses of first and second, so writing through the
   pointers *first and *second changes the caller's variables. tmp holds one value during
   the exchange. main() declares both variables on one line and prints them before and
   after the swap. */
// END

#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write is_prime(n); numbers below 2 are not prime.
   2. Try every divisor d while d * d <= n.
   3. Return false if one divides n, otherwise true.

}

        if (is_prime(n)) {
            printf("%d ", n);
        }
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: is_prime() tries every divisor d from 2 while d * d <= n; if one divides n
   evenly, n is not prime. main() tests every number from 2 to 74 and prints the primes. */
// END

/* Caption: C program to search a sorted array by halving the search range each step. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Make sure the array is sorted.
   2. Set lo to 0 and hi to count - 1.
   3. While lo <= hi, compare the middle element mid with the key.
   4. Return the index if it matches; otherwise keep only the half that can hold the
      key.
   5. Return -1 if the range becomes empty, and print the index of 80. */
/* The array must be sorted. Each step halves the range that can still hold the key. */
int binary_search(const int numbers[], int count, int key) {
    int lo = 0;
    int hi = count - 1;
    while (lo <= hi) {
        int mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;
        if (numbers[mid] == key) {
            return mid;
        } else if (numbers[mid] < key) {
            lo = mid + 1;   /* key is in the right half */
        } else {
            hi = mid - 1;   /* key is in the left half */
        }
    }
    return -1;
}

int main(void) {
    int numbers[] = {80, 92, 145, 146, 153, 184, 193};
    int count = sizeof(numbers) / sizeof(numbers[0]);
    int index = binary_search(numbers, count, 80);
    printf("Index of 80: %d\n", index);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: binary_search() needs a sorted array. It keeps the range from lo to hi,
   compares the middle element mid with the key and throws away the half that cannot
   contain it, so it needs only about log2(n) steps. main() looks for 80 and prints its
   index, or -1 if it is not there. */
// END

   3. Print whether -2 is inside 59 to 85. */
/* true when low <= x <= high */
bool in_range(int x, int low, int high) {
    return x >= low && x <= high;
}

int main(void) {
    int value = -2, low = 59, high = 85;
    printf("%d is %s the range %d to %d\n", value,
           in_range(value, low, high) ? "inside" : "outside", low, high);

/* Explanation: in_range() takes the value and both limits and returns true only when the

   and prints whether -2 is inside 59 to 85. */
// END

/* Caption: Count the words in a sentence. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <ctype.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write count_words() with words = 0 and an in_word flag.
   2. A space ends a word; a non-space after a space starts a new word and adds one to
      words.
   3. Return words and print it. */
/* A new word starts when a non-space follows a space (or the start). */
int count_words(const char *text) {
    int words = 0;
    int in_word = 0;
    for (int i = 0; text[i] != '\0'; i++) {
        if (isspace((unsigned char)text[i])) {
            in_word = 0;
        } else if (!in_word) {
            in_word = 1;
            words++;
        }
    }
    return words;
}

int main(void) {
    const char *sentence = "pointers store the address of another variable";
    printf("Words: %d\n", count_words(sentence));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: count_words() uses the flag in_word: a new word starts when a non-space
   character follows a space or the start of the text. main() prints the number of words in
   the sentence. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to calculate 3! using recursion. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write factorial(x) that calls itself.
   2. Return 1 when x is 1 or less.
   3. Otherwise return x * factorial(x - 1).
   4. Print 3! as an unsigned long long. */
/* n! = n * (n - 1)!, and 0! = 1 stops the recursion. */
unsigned long long factorial(int x) {
    if (x <= 1) {
        return 1;
    }
    return x * factorial(x - 1);
}

int main(void) {
    int x = 3;
    printf("%d! = %llu\n", x, factorial(x));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: factorial() calls itself: n! is n * (n - 1)!, and the recursion stops when
   x is 1 or less. main() prints 3! as an unsigned long long, because factorials grow very
   fast. */
// END

/* Caption: How do I use insertion sort to put numbers in ascending order in C? */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write insertion_sort() for the double array prices.
   2. Take each element in turn as current.
   3. Shift the larger values of the sorted part one place right.
   4. Put current into the gap.
   5. Print the sorted values. */
/* Insert each element into the already sorted part on its left. */
void insertion_sort(double prices[], int size) {
    for (int i = 1; i < size; i++) {
        double current = prices[i];
        int j = i - 1;
        while (j >= 0 && prices[j] > current) {
            prices[j + 1] = prices[j];   /* shift bigger values right */
            j--;
        }
        prices[j + 1] = current;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    double prices[] = {6.1, 61.3, 73.9, 71.6, 34.1, 47.8, 43.5, 12.3, 25.0, 78.9};
    int size = sizeof(prices) / sizeof(prices[0]);
    insertion_sort(prices, size);
    for (int i = 0; i < size; i++) {
        printf("%.2f ", prices[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: insertion_sort() takes each element in turn and shifts the larger values of
   the sorted part one place right until the element fits. main() then prints the 10 values
   in ascending order. */
// END

   h, m and s on one line and converts 37774 seconds. */

/* Caption: Program to reverse the digits of a number. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Start result at 0.
   2. Multiply result by 10, add n % 10, then divide n by 10.
   3. Repeat until n is 0.
   4. Apply it to 120084 and print the result. */
/* Take the last digit with % 10, then drop it with / 10. */
int reverse_digits(int n) {
    int result = 0;
    while (n > 0) {
        result = result * 10 + n % 10;
        n /= 10;
    }
    return result;
}

int main(void) {
    int number = 120084;
    printf("reverse of digits of %d: %d\n", number, reverse_digits(number));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: reverse_digits() shifts result one place left (result * 10) and adds the
   last digit of n, which reverses the order. main() applies it to 120084. */
// END

/* Caption: Program to use Euclid's algorithm to compute the GCD. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write gcd() with Euclid's algorithm.
   2. Replace (a, b) by (b, a % b) until b is 0.
   3. Return a and print the GCD of 150 and 87. */
/* Euclid: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a % b) until b becomes zero. */
int gcd(int a, int b) {
    while (b != 0) {
        int r = a % b;
        a = b;
        b = r;
    }
    return a;
}

int main(void) {
    int x = 150, y = 87;
    printf("gcd(%d, %d) = %d\n", x, y, gcd(x, y));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: gcd() uses Euclid's algorithm: it keeps replacing (a, b) with (b, a % b)
   until b is 0. The last non-zero value is the greatest common divisor, and main() prints
   the GCD of 150 and 87. */
// END

/* Caption: C program to use dynamic memory to store the first 7 squares. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Use malloc to get room for 7 ints and check for NULL.
   2. Fill table with squares.
   3. Print the values.
   4. Call free(table) at the end. */
int main(void) {
    int n = 7;
    /* Ask the heap for room for n ints; malloc returns NULL on failure. */
    int *table = malloc(n * sizeof(int));
    if (table == NULL) {
        fprintf(stderr, "malloc failed\n");
        return 1;
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        table[i] = i * i;
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        printf("%d ", table[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    free(table);   /* give the memory back */
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: malloc() reserves room for 7 ints on the heap and returns NULL if it fails,
   which the program checks. The first loop fills table with squares, the second prints
   them, and free() gives the memory back at the end. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to sort an array in descending order using selection sort. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write selection_sort() for the int array prices.
   2. For each position, find the largest remaining element.
   3. Swap it into that position.
   4. Print the sorted values. */
/* Select the right element for each position and swap it into place. */
void selection_sort(int prices[], int size) {
    for (int i = 0; i < size - 1; i++) {
        int chosen = i;
        for (int j = i + 1; j < size; j++) {
            if (prices[chosen] < prices[j]) {
                chosen = j;
            }
        }
        int tmp = prices[i];
        prices[i] = prices[chosen];
        prices[chosen] = tmp;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    int prices[] = {93, 5, 3, 13, 36};
    const int size = 5;
    selection_sort(prices, size);
    for (int i = 0; i < size; i++) {
        printf("%d ", prices[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: selection_sort() finds the largest remaining element for each position and
   swaps it into place. main() then prints the 5 values in descending order. */
// END

/* Caption: C program to compute the factorial of a number with a loop. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write factorial(n) with result = 1.
   2. Multiply result by every number from 2 to n.
   3. Return result.
   4. Print 13! as an unsigned long long. */
/* Multiply 1 * 2 * ... * n. */
unsigned long long factorial(int n) {
    unsigned long long result = 1;
    for (int i = 2; i <= n; i++) {
        result *= i;
    }
    return result;
}

int main(void) {
    int n = 13;
    printf("%d! = %llu\n", n, factorial(n));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: factorial() multiplies result by every number from 2 up to n. main() prints
   13! as an unsigned long long, because factorials grow very fast. */
// END

/* Caption: Program to return the minimum, maximum and average of an array in a struct. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define a Stats struct with min, max and average.
   2. Write array_stats() that fills one Stats in a loop.
   3. Return the struct.
   4. Print st.min, st.max and st.average. */
typedef struct {
    int min;
    int max;
    double average;
} Stats;

/* Pack several results into one struct and return it. */
Stats array_stats(const int v[], int n) {
    Stats s = {v[0], v[0], 0.0};
    double total = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        if (v[i] < s.min) {
            s.min = v[i];
        }
        if (v[i] > s.max) {
            s.max = v[i];
        }
        total += v[i];
    }
    s.average = total / n;
    return s;
}

int main(void) {
    int marks[] = {12, 73, 8, 71, 30, 30};
    int n = sizeof(marks) / sizeof(marks[0]);
    Stats st = array_stats(marks, n);
    printf("Min %d, Max %d, Average %.2f\n", st.min, st.max, st.average);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: Stats groups three results. array_stats() fills one Stats while it loops
   over the 6 values and returns the whole struct, which is a clean way to return several
   results at once. main() reads them as st.min, st.max and st.average. */
// END

/* Caption: How do I return both the smallest and the largest value of an array through pointers in C? */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write min_max() with the array, its length and the pointers min and max.
   2. Start both at the first element.
   3. Update *min and *max while looping over the rest.
   4. Declare smallest and largest, pass their addresses and print them. */
/* One pass finds both results; they are stored through the pointers. */
void min_max(const int numbers[], int count, int *min, int *max) {
    *min = numbers[0];
    *max = numbers[0];
    for (int i = 1; i < count; i++) {
        if (numbers[i] < *min) {
            *min = numbers[i];
        }
        if (numbers[i] > *max) {
            *max = numbers[i];
        }
    }
}

int main(void) {
    int numbers[] = {52, 15, 64, 41, 89, 81, 47, 80, 43};
    int count = sizeof(numbers) / sizeof(numbers[0]);
    int smallest, largest;
    min_max(numbers, count, &smallest, &largest);
    printf("Min: %d, Max: %d\n", smallest, largest);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: A C function can return only one value, so min_max() returns void and
   writes its two results through the pointer parameters min and max. main() declares
   smallest and largest on one line and passes their addresses with &, then prints both
   results for the 9 values. */
// END

/* Caption: Reverse the elements of an array in place. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write reverse_array() for scores.
   2. Set left to the first index and right to the last.
   3. Swap scores[left] and scores[right], then move both inwards.
   4. Stop when left meets right and print the array. */
/* Swap the outer pair, then move both ends toward the middle. */
void reverse_array(int scores[], int n) {
    int left = 0;
    int right = n - 1;
    while (left < right) {
        int tmp = scores[left];
        scores[left] = scores[right];
        scores[right] = tmp;
        left++;
        right--;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    int scores[] = {89, 39, 2, 59};
    const int n = 4;
    reverse_array(scores, n);
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        printf("%d ", scores[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: reverse_array() swaps the first and last elements, then moves left forward
   and right backward until they meet, so the array is reversed in place without a second
   array. main() prints the reversed values. */
// END

/* Caption: Program to find the largest of four numbers with a function. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write max2() that returns the larger of two values.
   2. Write max_of_four() as max2(max2(a, b), max2(c, d)).
   3. Print the largest of the four values. */
/* Return the larger of two values. */
int max2(int a, int b) {
    return a > b ? a : b;
}

/* Reuse max2 to compare four values. */
int max_of_four(int a, int b, int c, int d) {
    return max2(max2(a, b), max2(c, d));
}

int main(void) {
    int a = 80, b = 4, c = 79, d = 87;
    printf("Largest: %d\n", max_of_four(a, b, c, d));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: max_of_four() takes four parameters and reuses the helper max2(), which
   returns the larger of two values: it compares a with b, c with d, and then the two
   winners. main() prints the largest of 80, 4, 79 and 87. */
// END

/* Caption: How do I decide if a number is odd or even in C? */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Read the number value.
   2. Check whether value % 2 is 0.
   3. Print even or odd. */
int main(void) {
    int value;
    printf("Enter a number: ");
    if (scanf("%d", &value) != 1) {
        printf("Invalid input\n");
        return 1;
    }
    /* Even numbers leave no remainder when divided by 2. */
    if (value % 2 == 0) {
        printf("%d is even\n", value);
    } else {
        printf("%d is odd\n", value);
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: The program reads value from the keyboard with scanf and stops with a
   message if the input is not valid. value % 2 is the remainder after dividing by 2: 0
   means even, anything else means odd, and the if-else prints which one it is. */
// END

/* Caption: Add two matrices element by element. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define ROWS as 2 and COLS as 4.
   2. Loop over every row r and column c.
   3. Store a[r][c] + b[r][c] in sum and print it. */
#define ROWS 2
#define COLS 4

int main(void) {
    int a[ROWS][COLS] = {{2, 5, 8, 6}, {5, 8, 6, 3}};
    int b[ROWS][COLS] = {{7, 8, 2, 8}, {3, 4, 6, 7}};
    int sum[ROWS][COLS];
    /* Each entry of the result is the sum of the matching entries. */
    for (int r = 0; r < ROWS; r++) {
        for (int c = 0; c < COLS; c++) {
            sum[r][c] = a[r][c] + b[r][c];
            printf("%3d", sum[r][c]);
        }
        printf("\n");
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: Both matrices are 2x4 two-dimensional arrays. Two nested loops visit every
   row r and column c, store a[r][c] + b[r][c] in sum and print each row. */
// END

/* Caption: How do I test if "network" reads the same backwards in C? */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <string.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write is_palindrome() for word.
   2. Compare the first and last characters, moving inwards.
   3. Return false at the first mismatch, otherwise true.
   4. Check network and print the result. */
/* Compare characters from the front and back, moving inwards. */
bool is_palindrome(const char *word) {
    int i = 0;
    int j = strlen(word) - 1;
    while (i < j) {
        if (word[i] != word[j]) {
            return false;
        }
        i++;
        j--;
    }
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    const char *word = "network";
    printf("%s %s a palindrome\n", word, is_palindrome(word) ? "is" : "is not");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: is_palindrome() compares the first and last characters and moves inwards;
   any mismatch means the word is not a palindrome. main() checks the word network and
   prints the result. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to generate the Fibonacci sequence. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write fib(n) that returns n when n < 2.
   2. Otherwise return fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2).
   3. Print fib(i) for i from 0 to 14. */
/* Each Fibonacci number is the sum of the two before it. */
long fib(int n) {
    if (n < 2) {
        return n;
    }
    return fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2);
}

int main(void) {
    for (int i = 0; i < 15; i++) {
        printf("%ld ", fib(i));
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: fib() returns n for 0 and 1 and otherwise adds the two previous Fibonacci
   numbers by calling itself twice, which is simple but slow for large n. main() prints the
   first 15 numbers. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to use Euclid's algorithm to compute the GCD. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write gcd() with Euclid's algorithm.
   2. Replace (a, b) by (b, a % b) until b is 0.
   3. Return a and print the GCD of 91 and 262. */
/* Euclid: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a % b) until b becomes zero. */
int gcd(int a, int b) {
    while (b != 0) {
        int r = a % b;
        a = b;
        b = r;
    }
    return a;
}

int main(void) {
    int x = 91, y = 262;
    printf("gcd(%d, %d) = %d\n", x, y, gcd(x, y));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: gcd() uses Euclid's algorithm: it keeps replacing (a, b) with (b, a % b)
   until b is 0. The last non-zero value is the greatest common divisor, and main() prints
   the GCD of 91 and 262. */
// END

/* Caption: How do I print all prime numbers up to 108 in C? */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write is_prime(n); numbers below 2 are not prime.
   2. Try every divisor d while d * d <= n.
   3. Return false if one divides n, otherwise true.
   4. Print every prime from 2 to 108. */
/* A prime has no divisor between 2 and its square root. */
bool is_prime(int n) {
    if (n < 2) {
        return false;
    }
    for (int d = 2; d * d <= n; d++) {
        if (n % d == 0) {
            return false;
        }
    }
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    for (int n = 2; n <= 108; n++) {
        if (is_prime(n)) {
            printf("%d ", n);
        }
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: is_prime() tries every divisor d from 2 while d * d <= n; if one divides n
   evenly, n is not prime. main() tests every number from 2 to 108 and prints the primes. */
// END

/* Caption: Decide if 2021 is a leap year. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write is_leap(year).
   2. A year divisible by 4 is a leap year, unless it is divisible by 100.
   3. Years divisible by 400 are leap years again.
   4. Check 2021 and print the result. */
/* Leap years divide by 4, except centuries, which must divide by 400. */
int is_leap(int year) {
    return (year % 4 == 0 && year % 100 != 0) || year % 400 == 0;
}

int main(void) {
    int year = 2021;
    if (is_leap(year)) {
        printf("%d is a leap year\n", year);
    } else {
        printf("%d is not a leap year\n", year);
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: is_leap() returns true for years divisible by 4, except century years,
   which must also be divisible by 400. main() checks 2021 and prints whether it is a leap
   year. */
// END

/* Caption: Convert 2 to binary. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write print_binary(n, bits).
   2. Go through the bits from the highest to the lowest.
   3. Print 1 when (n >> b) & 1 is set, otherwise 0.
   4. Print 2 in binary. */
/* Check each bit from the highest to the lowest. */
void print_binary(unsigned int n, int bits) {
    for (int b = bits - 1; b >= 0; b--) {
        putchar((n >> b) & 1 ? '1' : '0');
    }
    putchar('\n');
}

int main(void) {
    unsigned int number = 2;
    printf("%u in binary: ", number);
    print_binary(number, 16);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: print_binary() checks one bit at a time, from the highest to the lowest: (n
   >> b) & 1 is 1 when bit b is set, so it prints the character 1 or 0. main() prints 2 in
   binary. */
// END

/* Caption: Compute the mean of a list of numbers. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write average() that takes values and count.
   2. Add the values into the double result.
   3. Return result / count.
   4. Print the average with two decimals. */
/* Sum the values, then divide by how many there are. */
double average(const int values[], int count) {
    double result = 0.0;
    for (int i = 0; i < count; i++) {
        result += values[i];
    }
    return result / count;
}

int main(void) {
    int values[] = {92, 83, 47, 57};
    int count = 4;
    printf("The average is %.2f\n", average(values, count));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: average() adds the 4 values of values into the double result and divides by
   count, so the mean keeps its decimal part even when the values are whole numbers. main()
   prints it with two decimals. */
// END

/* Caption: Find the largest of 3 numbers. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Read a, b and c.
   2. Assume a is the largest.
   3. Compare it with the other two and keep the bigger value.
   4. Print the result. */
int main(void) {
    int a, b, c;
    printf("Enter 3 numbers: ");
    if (scanf("%d %d %d", &a, &b, &c) != 3) {
        printf("Invalid input\n");
        return 1;
    }
    int best = a;
    /* Compare with each of the others and keep the bigger one. */
    if (b > best) {
        best = b;
    }
    if (c > best) {
        best = c;
    }
    printf("The largest is %d\n", best);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: The program reads a, b and c from the keyboard with scanf and stops with a
   message if the input is not valid. It assumes a is the largest, compares it with the
   other two and keeps the bigger value in best, which it prints. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to search an array for its largest value. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write find_max() that takes values and n.
   2. Store values[0] in current.
   3. Loop over the other elements and keep the largest value in current.
   4. Return current and print it. */
/* Start with the first element and keep the largest value seen so far. */
long find_max(const long values[], int n) {
    long current = values[0];
    for (int idx = 1; idx < n; idx++) {
        if (values[idx] > current) {
            current = values[idx];
        }
    }
    return current;
}

int main(void) {
    long values[] = {47L, 59L, 99L, 41L};
    const int n = 4;
    printf("Largest: %ld\n", find_max(values, n));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: find_max() takes the first element as the largest value so far and stores
   it in current. The loop compares every other element with current using > and keeps the
   largest one. main() prints the largest of the 4 values. */
// END

/* Caption: Compute 5 to the power of 10 without pow(). */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write power(base, exp) with result = 1.
   2. Multiply result by base exp times.
   3. Print 5 to the power 10. */
/* Multiply the base by itself exp times. */
long long power(int base, int exp) {
    long long result = 1;
    for (int i = 0; i < exp; i++) {
        result *= base;
    }
    return result;
}

int main(void) {
    printf("5^10 = %lld\n", power(5, 10));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: power() starts result at 1 and multiplies it by base exp times. It uses
   long long because powers grow quickly. main() prints 5 to the power 10. */
// END

/* Caption: Compute the product of two square matrices. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define N as 3.
   2. For every i and j, add a[i][k] * b[k][j] over k into product[i][j].
   3. Print product row by row. */
#define N 3

int main(void) {
    int a[N][N] = {{6, 9, 6}, {8, 2, 6}, {9, 3, 3}};
    int b[N][N] = {{9, 7, 0}, {6, 5, 4}, {8, 8, 3}};
    int product[N][N] = {0};
    /* product[i][j] is row i of a times column j of b. */
    for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) {
        for (int j = 0; j < N; j++) {
            for (int k = 0; k < N; k++) {
                product[i][j] += a[i][k] * b[k][j];
            }
        }
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) {
        for (int j = 0; j < N; j++) {
            printf("%4d", product[i][j]);
        }
        printf("\n");
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: For each entry product[i][j] the innermost loop adds a[i][k] * b[k][j] over
   k, which is row i of a times column j of b. main() multiplies two 3x3 matrices and
   prints the product. */
// END

/* Caption: How do I implement a simple linked list with malloc and free in C? */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define ListNode with a value and a next pointer.
   2. Write push_front() that mallocs a node and links it in front of head.
   3. Write print_list() that follows next until NULL.
   4. Write free_list() that frees every node.
   5. Push 6 values, print the list and free it. */
typedef struct ListNode {
    int value;
    struct ListNode *next;
} ListNode;

/* Allocate a new node and put it in front of the current head. */
ListNode *push_front(ListNode *head, int value) {
    ListNode *node = malloc(sizeof(ListNode));
    if (node == NULL) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Out of memory\n");
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }
    node->value = value;
    node->next = head;
    return node;
}

void print_list(const ListNode *head) {
    for (const ListNode *cur = head; cur != NULL; cur = cur->next) {
        printf("%d -> ", cur->value);
    }
    printf("NULL\n");
}

/* Free every node; save next before freeing the current one. */
void free_list(ListNode *head) {
    while (head != NULL) {
        ListNode *next = head->next;
        free(head);
        head = next;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    ListNode *head = NULL;
    head = push_front(head, 41);
    head = push_front(head, 43);
    head = push_front(head, 84);
    head = push_front(head, 40);
    head = push_front(head, 24);
    head = push_front(head, 50);
    print_list(head);
    free_list(head);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: Each ListNode holds a value and a pointer to the next node. push_front()
   allocates a node with malloc, puts it in front of head and returns it; print_list()
   follows the next pointers until NULL; free_list() frees every node. main() pushes 6
   values, so they print in reverse order. */
// END

/* Caption: Check whether a number lies between two limits. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write in_range(x, low, high).
   2. Return true when x >= low and x <= high.
   3. Print whether 8 is inside 29 to 88. */
/* true when low <= x <= high */
bool in_range(int x, int low, int high) {
    return x >= low && x <= high;
}

int main(void) {
    int value = 8, low = 29, high = 88;
    printf("%d is %s the range %d to %d\n", value,
           in_range(value, low, high) ? "inside" : "outside", low, high);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: in_range() takes the value and both limits and returns true only when the
   value is at least low and at most high. main() declares value, low and high on one line
   and prints whether 8 is inside 29 to 88. */
// END

#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define Node with a value and a next pointer.
   2. Write push_front() that mallocs a node and links it in front of head.

/* Caption: Program to implement a stack with an array (push and pop). */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define a Stack with room for 8 items and a top counter.
   2. Write push() and pop(), returning false when the stack is full or empty.
   3. Push 5 values.
   4. Pop and print until the stack is empty. */
#define CAPACITY 8

typedef struct {
    int items[CAPACITY];
    int top;   /* number of items on the stack */
} Stack;

bool push(Stack *s, int value) {
    if (s->top == CAPACITY) {
        return false;   /* stack is full */
    }
    s->items[s->top++] = value;
    return true;
}

bool pop(Stack *s, int *value) {
    if (s->top == 0) {
        return false;   /* stack is empty */
    }
    *value = s->items[--s->top];
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    Stack s = {.top = 0};
    push(&s, 60);
    push(&s, 95);
    push(&s, 16);
    push(&s, 46);
    push(&s, 64);
    int value;
    /* Items come back out in reverse order (last in, first out). */
    while (pop(&s, &value)) {
        printf("%d ", value);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: The Stack keeps up to 8 items in an array, and top counts how many are
   stored. push() adds at the top and pop() removes from the top; both return false when
   they cannot. main() pushes 5 values and pops them all, so they come out in reverse order
   (last in, first out). */
// END

/* Caption: C program to create a singly linked list by inserting at the head. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define ListNode with a value and a next pointer.
   2. Write push_front() that mallocs a node and links it in front of head.

   4. Write free_list() that frees every node.

    int value;
    struct ListNode *next;

/* Allocate a new node and put it in front of the current head. */
ListNode *push_front(ListNode *head, int value) {
    ListNode *node = malloc(sizeof(ListNode));
    if (node == NULL) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Out of memory\n");
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }
    node->value = value;
    node->next = head;
    return node;
}

void print_list(const ListNode *head) {
    for (const ListNode *cur = head; cur != NULL; cur = cur->next) {
        printf("%d -> ", cur->value);
    }
    printf("NULL\n");
}

/* Free every node; save next before freeing the current one. */
void free_list(ListNode *head) {
    while (head != NULL) {
        ListNode *next = head->next;
        free(head);
        head = next;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    ListNode *head = NULL;
    head = push_front(head, 46);
    head = push_front(head, 84);
    head = push_front(head, 26);
    print_list(head);
    free_list(head);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: Each ListNode holds a value and a pointer to the next node. push_front()
   allocates a node with malloc, puts it in front of head and returns it; print_list()
   follows the next pointers until NULL; free_list() frees every node. main() pushes 3
   values, so they print in reverse order. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to find the largest of four numbers with a function. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write max2() that returns the larger of two values.
   2. Write max_of_four() as max2(max2(a, b), max2(c, d)).
   3. Print the largest of the four values. */
/* Return the larger of two values. */
int max2(int a, int b) {
    return a > b ? a : b;
}

/* Reuse max2 to compare four values. */
int max_of_four(int a, int b, int c, int d) {
    return max2(max2(a, b), max2(c, d));
}

int main(void) {
    int a = 90, b = 74, c = 53, d = 96;
    printf("Largest: %d\n", max_of_four(a, b, c, d));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: max_of_four() takes four parameters and reuses the helper max2(), which
   returns the larger of two values: it compares a with b, c with d, and then the two
   winners. main() prints the largest of 90, 74, 53 and 96. */
// END

/* Caption: Compute the LCM of two integers using the GCD. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write gcd() with Euclid's algorithm: replace (a, b) by (b, a % b) until b is 0.
   2. Write lcm() as a / gcd(a, b) * b.
   3. Print the LCM of 55 and 269. */
/* Euclid: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a % b) until b becomes zero. */
int gcd(int a, int b) {
    while (b != 0) {
        int r = a % b;
        a = b;
        b = r;
    }
    return a;
}

/* lcm(a, b) = a / gcd(a, b) * b (divide first to avoid overflow). */
long lcm(int a, int b) {
    return (long)a / gcd(a, b) * b;
}

int main(void) {
    printf("lcm(55, 269) = %ld\n", lcm(55, 269));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: gcd() uses Euclid's algorithm: it keeps replacing (a, b) with (b, a % b)
   until b is 0. lcm() divides a by the gcd before multiplying by b, which avoids overflow.
   main() prints the LCM of 55 and 269. */
// END

/* Caption: C program to compute the sum of the elements of an array. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write total_of() that takes the array scores and its length size.
   2. Start total at 0 and add every element in a for loop.
   3. Return total.
   4. In main(), fill scores with 5 values and print the sum. */
/* Walk through the array and accumulate each value. */
long total_of(const long scores[], int size) {
    long total = 0;
    for (int j = 0; j < size; j++) {
        total += scores[j];
    }
    return total;
}

int main(void) {

    int size = sizeof(scores) / sizeof(scores[0]);
    printf("Sum: %ld\n", total_of(scores, size));
    return 0;
}
