   1. Define a Rectangle struct with width and height.
   2. Write area() and perimeter().
   3. Make a 30 by 4 rectangle and print both results. */
typedef struct {
    int width;
    int height;
} Rectangle;

int area(Rectangle r) {
    return r.width * r.height;

    return 2 * (r.width + r.height);

    return 0;

   perimeter() returns 2 * (width + height). main() makes a 30 by 4 rectangle and prints
   both results. */
// END

/* Caption: Find a number in a sorted array with binary search. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Make sure the array is sorted.
   2. Set low to 0 and high to length - 1.
   3. While low <= high, compare the middle element mid with the key.
   4. Return the index if it matches; otherwise keep only the half that can hold the
      key.
   5. Return -1 if the range becomes empty, and print the index of 201. */
/* The array must be sorted. Each step halves the range that can still hold the key. */
int binary_search(const int readings[], int length, int key) {
    int low = 0;
    int high = length - 1;
    while (low <= high) {
        int mid = low + (high - low) / 2;
        if (readings[mid] == key) {
            return mid;
        } else if (readings[mid] < key) {
            low = mid + 1;   /* key is in the right half */
        } else {
            high = mid - 1;   /* key is in the left half */
        }
    }
    return -1;
}

int main(void) {
    int readings[] = {29, 52, 65, 138, 160, 192};
    const int length = 6;
    int index = binary_search(readings, length, 201);
    printf("Index of 201: %d\n", index);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: binary_search() needs a sorted array. It keeps the range from low to high,
   compares the middle element mid with the key and throws away the half that cannot
   contain it, so it needs only about log2(n) steps. main() looks for 201 and prints its
   index, or -1 if it is not there. */
// END

/* Caption: C program to implement a simple linked list with malloc and free. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define Item with a value and a next pointer.
   2. Write push_front() that mallocs a node and links it in front of head.
   3. Write print_list() that follows next until NULL.
   4. Write free_list() that frees every node.
   5. Push 4 values, print the list and free it. */
typedef struct Item {
    int value;
    struct Item *next;
} Item;

/* Allocate a new node and put it in front of the current head. */
Item *push_front(Item *head, int value) {
    Item *node = malloc(sizeof(Item));
    if (node == NULL) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Out of memory\n");
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }
    node->value = value;
    node->next = head;
    return node;
}

void print_list(const Item *head) {
    for (const Item *cur = head; cur != NULL; cur = cur->next) {
        printf("%d -> ", cur->value);
    }
    printf("NULL\n");
}

/* Free every node; save next before freeing the current one. */
void free_list(Item *head) {
    while (head != NULL) {
        Item *next = head->next;
        free(head);
        head = next;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    Item *head = NULL;
    head = push_front(head, 56);
    head = push_front(head, 18);
    head = push_front(head, 86);
    head = push_front(head, 59);
    print_list(head);
    free_list(head);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: Each Item holds a value and a pointer to the next node. push_front()
   allocates a node with malloc, puts it in front of head and returns it; print_list()
   follows the next pointers until NULL; free_list() frees every node. main() pushes 4
   values, so they print in reverse order. */
// END

/* Caption: C program to sort an array in ascending order using bubble sort. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write bubble_sort() for the int array numbers.
   2. Compare each pair of neighbours.
   3. Swap them when they are in the wrong order for ascending order.
   4. Repeat the passes until the array is sorted.
   5. Print the sorted values. */
/* Repeatedly swap neighbours that are in the wrong order. */
void bubble_sort(int numbers[], int len) {
    for (int i = 0; i < len - 1; i++) {
        for (int j = 0; j < len - 1 - i; j++) {
            if (numbers[j] > numbers[j + 1]) {
                int tmp = numbers[j];
                numbers[j] = numbers[j + 1];
                numbers[j + 1] = tmp;
            }
        }
    }
}

int main(void) {
    int numbers[] = {55, 98, 56, 7, 1, 68, 14, 91};
    int len = sizeof(numbers) / sizeof(numbers[0]);
    bubble_sort(numbers, len);
    for (int i = 0; i < len; i++) {
        printf("%d ", numbers[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: bubble_sort() walks through numbers again and again and swaps neighbours
   that are in the wrong order, so the largest values move to the end first. main() then
   prints the 8 values in ascending order. */
// END

/* Caption: Program to check whether a word is a palindrome. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <string.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write is_palindrome() for buffer.
   2. Compare the first and last characters, moving inwards.
   3. Return false at the first mismatch, otherwise true.
   4. Check network and print the result. */
/* Compare characters from the front and back, moving inwards. */
bool is_palindrome(const char *buffer) {
    int i = 0;
    int j = strlen(buffer) - 1;
    while (i < j) {
        if (buffer[i] != buffer[j]) {
            return false;
        }
        i++;
        j--;
    }
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    const char *buffer = "network";
    printf("%s %s a palindrome\n", buffer, is_palindrome(buffer) ? "is" : "is not");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: is_palindrome() compares the first and last characters and moves inwards;
   any mismatch means the word is not a palindrome. main() checks the word network and
   prints the result. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a function that returns the distance between two points given x1, y1, x2 and y2. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <math.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write distance(x1, y1, x2, y2).
   2. Compute dx and dy, then return sqrt(dx * dx + dy * dy).
   3. Print the distance between (-6, 6) and (7, 1). */
/* Pythagoras: the distance is sqrt(dx * dx + dy * dy). */
double distance(double x1, double y1, double x2, double y2) {
    double dx = x2 - x1, dy = y2 - y1;
    return sqrt(dx * dx + dy * dy);
}

int main(void) {
    printf("Distance: %.3f\n", distance(-6, 6, 7, 1));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: distance() takes the coordinates of both points as four parameters. It
   declares dx and dy on one line and uses Pythagoras with sqrt() from math.h. main()
   prints the distance between (-6, 6) and (7, 1). */
// END

/* Caption: C program to calculate the average of the values in an array. */

   1. Write mean() that takes samples and len.
   2. Add the values into the double sum.
   3. Return sum / len.
   4. Print the average with two decimals. */

   so the mean keeps its decimal part even when the values are whole numbers. main() prints
   it with two decimals. */

/* Caption: How do I implement a stack with an array (push and pop) in C? */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define a Stack with room for 8 items and a top counter.
   2. Write push() and pop(), returning false when the stack is full or empty.
   3. Push 5 values.
   4. Pop and print until the stack is empty. */
#define CAPACITY 8

typedef struct {
    int items[CAPACITY];
    int top;   /* number of items on the stack */
} Stack;

bool push(Stack *s, int value) {
    if (s->top == CAPACITY) {
        return false;   /* stack is full */
    }
    s->items[s->top++] = value;
    return true;
}

bool pop(Stack *s, int *value) {
    if (s->top == 0) {
        return false;   /* stack is empty */
    }
    *value = s->items[--s->top];
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    Stack s = {.top = 0};
    push(&s, 21);
    push(&s, 21);
    push(&s, 99);
    push(&s, 74);
    push(&s, 38);
    int value;
    /* Items come back out in reverse order (last in, first out). */
    while (pop(&s, &value)) {
        printf("%d ", value);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: The Stack keeps up to 8 items in an array, and top counts how many are
   stored. push() adds at the top and pop() removes from the top; both return false when
   they cannot. main() pushes 5 values and pops them all, so they come out in reverse order
   (last in, first out). */
// END

/* Caption: Return a sum and an average together using pointer parameters. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write sum_and_average() with the pointers sum and average.
   2. Add the values into *sum.
   3. Store *sum / n in *average.
   4. Declare total and mean, pass their addresses and print them. */
void sum_and_average(const double v[], int n, double *sum, double *average) {
    *sum = 0.0;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        *sum += v[i];
    }
    *average = *sum / n;
}

int main(void) {
    double readings[] = {3.3, 29.1, 61.9, 95.7, 76.4, 16.3, 36.3};
    int n = sizeof(readings) / sizeof(readings[0]);
    double total, mean;
    sum_and_average(readings, n, &total, &mean);
    printf("Sum: %.2f, Average: %.2f\n", total, mean);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: sum_and_average() takes the array, its length and two pointers. It adds up
   the 7 values through *sum and then stores *sum / n in *average. main() declares total
   and mean on one line and passes their addresses. */
// END

/* Return the sum of the first n elements. */

/* Caption: Write a C program to write a function that swaps two double values through pointers. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write swap() that takes pointers to two double values.
   2. Save *a in tmp, copy *b into *a, then tmp into *b.
   3. In main(), print a and b, call swap(&a, &b) and print them again. */
/* Pass addresses so the function can change the caller's variables. */
void swap(double *a, double *b) {
    double tmp = *a;
    *a = *b;
    *b = tmp;
}

int main(void) {
    double a = 14.1, b = 5.9;
    printf("Before: %.2f %.2f\n", a, b);
    swap(&a, &b);
    printf("After:  %.2f %.2f\n", a, b);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: swap() receives the addresses of a and b, so writing through the pointers
   *a and *b changes the caller's variables. tmp holds one value during the exchange.
   main() declares both variables on one line and prints them before and after the swap. */
// END

/* Caption: How do I find the minimum and maximum of an array with one function in C? */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write min_max() with the array, its length and the pointers min and max.
   2. Start both at the first element.
   3. Update *min and *max while looping over the rest.
   4. Declare smallest and largest, pass their addresses and print them. */
/* One pass finds both results; they are stored through the pointers. */
void min_max(const int readings[], int len, int *min, int *max) {
    *min = readings[0];
    *max = readings[0];
    for (int i = 1; i < len; i++) {
        if (readings[i] < *min) {
            *min = readings[i];
        }
        if (readings[i] > *max) {
            *max = readings[i];
        }
    }
}

int main(void) {
    int readings[] = {65, 66, 70, 49, 28, 29, 62, 96};
    int len = sizeof(readings) / sizeof(readings[0]);
    int smallest, largest;
    min_max(readings, len, &smallest, &largest);
    printf("Min: %d, Max: %d\n", smallest, largest);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: A C function can return only one value, so min_max() returns void and
   writes its two results through the pointer parameters min and max. main() declares
   smallest and largest on one line and passes their addresses with &, then prints both
   results for the 8 values. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to check whether a number is prime. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write is_prime(n); numbers below 2 are not prime.
   2. Try every divisor d while d * d <= n.
   3. Return false if one divides n, otherwise true.
   4. Check 395 and print the result. */
/* A prime has no divisor between 2 and its square root. */
bool is_prime(int n) {
    if (n < 2) {
        return false;
    }
    for (int d = 2; d * d <= n; d++) {
        if (n % d == 0) {
            return false;
        }
    }
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    int number = 395;
    printf("%d %s prime\n", number, is_prime(number) ? "is" : "is not");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: is_prime() tries every divisor d from 2 while d * d <= n; if one divides n
   evenly, n is not prime. main() checks 395 and prints whether it is prime. */
// END

/* Caption: Return a Duration struct built from a number of seconds. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define a Duration struct with hours, minutes and seconds.
   2. Write from_seconds() that fills it using / and %.
   3. Convert 64710 seconds and print the members. */
typedef struct {
    int hours;
    int minutes;
    int seconds;
} Duration;

Duration from_seconds(int total) {
    Duration d;
    d.hours = total / 3600;
    d.minutes = (total % 3600) / 60;
    d.seconds = total % 60;
    return d;
}

int main(void) {
    Duration d = from_seconds(64710);
    printf("%d h %d min %d s\n", d.hours, d.minutes, d.seconds);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: from_seconds() fills the three members of a Duration struct using / and %,
   then returns the struct. main() converts 64710 seconds and prints the members. */
// END

/* Caption: C program to multiply two fractions using a struct. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define a Fraction struct with num and den.
   2. Write multiply() that returns num = a.num * b.num and den = a.den * b.den.
   3. Print 8/7 times 1/8. */
typedef struct {
    int num;
    int den;
} Fraction;

/* Multiply the numerators and the denominators. */
Fraction multiply(Fraction a, Fraction b) {
    Fraction r = {a.num * b.num, a.den * b.den};
    return r;
}

int main(void) {
    Fraction x = {8, 7}, y = {1, 8};
    Fraction p = multiply(x, y);
    printf("%d/%d * %d/%d = %d/%d\n", x.num, x.den, y.num, y.den, p.num, p.den);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: Fraction stores a numerator and a denominator. multiply() takes two
   Fractions and returns a new one with num = a.num * b.num and den = a.den * b.den. main()
   multiplies 8/7 by 1/8 (without reducing the result). */
// END

/* Caption: Implement selection sort for an array of int values. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write selection_sort() for the int array data.
   2. For each position, find the largest remaining element.
   3. Swap it into that position.
   4. Print the sorted values. */
/* Select the right element for each position and swap it into place. */
void selection_sort(int data[], int count) {
    for (int i = 0; i < count - 1; i++) {
        int chosen = i;
        for (int j = i + 1; j < count; j++) {
            if (data[chosen] < data[j]) {
                chosen = j;
            }
        }
        int tmp = data[i];
        data[i] = data[chosen];
        data[chosen] = tmp;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    int data[] = {25, 35, 5, 66, 93, 96};
    int count = 6;
    selection_sort(data, count);
    for (int i = 0; i < count; i++) {
        printf("%d ", data[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: selection_sort() finds the largest remaining element for each position and
   swaps it into place. main() then prints the 6 values in descending order. */
// END

   2. Start result at 0 and add every element in a for loop.
   3. Return result.

double add_all(const double prices[], int len) {

   0, adds every element to it in a for loop and returns the total. main() fills prices
   with 4 double values and prints their sum. */

/* Caption: Write a program to test if "hello" reads the same backwards. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <string.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write is_palindrome() for line.
   2. Compare the first and last characters, moving inwards.
   3. Return false at the first mismatch, otherwise true.
   4. Check hello and print the result. */
/* Compare characters from the front and back, moving inwards. */
bool is_palindrome(const char *line) {
    int i = 0;
    int j = strlen(line) - 1;
    while (i < j) {
        if (line[i] != line[j]) {
            return false;
        }
        i++;
        j--;
    }
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    const char *line = "hello";
    printf("%s %s a palindrome\n", line, is_palindrome(line) ? "is" : "is not");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: is_palindrome() compares the first and last characters and moves inwards;
   any mismatch means the word is not a palindrome. main() checks the word hello and prints
   the result. */
// END

/* Caption: C program to write a function that tests if a value is inside a range. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write in_range(x, low, high).
   2. Return true when x >= low and x <= high.
   3. Print whether 99 is inside 44 to 64. */
/* true when low <= x <= high */
bool in_range(int x, int low, int high) {
    return x >= low && x <= high;
}

int main(void) {
    int value = 99, low = 44, high = 64;
    printf("%d is %s the range %d to %d\n", value,
           in_range(value, low, high) ? "inside" : "outside", low, high);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: in_range() takes the value and both limits and returns true only when the
   value is at least low and at most high. main() declares value, low and high on one line
   and prints whether 99 is inside 44 to 64. */
// END

/* Caption: Reverse the elements of an array in place. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write reverse_array() for samples.
   2. Set i to the first index and j to the last.
   3. Swap samples[i] and samples[j], then move both inwards.
   4. Stop when i meets j and print the array. */
/* Swap the outer pair, then move both ends toward the middle. */
void reverse_array(double samples[], int size) {
    int i = 0;
    int j = size - 1;
    while (i < j) {
        double tmp = samples[i];
        samples[i] = samples[j];
        samples[j] = tmp;
        i++;
        j--;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    double samples[] = {31.1, 51.3, 15.6, 61.6, 88.4};
    const int size = 5;
    reverse_array(samples, size);
    for (int i = 0; i < size; i++) {
        printf("%.2f ", samples[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: reverse_array() swaps the first and last elements, then moves i forward and
   j backward until they meet, so the array is reversed in place without a second array.
   main() prints the reversed values. */
// END

/* Caption: Save text to a file with fprintf and print it with fgets. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Open data.txt in write mode and check for NULL.
   2. Write 4 lines with fprintf and close the file.
   3. Open it again in read mode.
   4. Read and print each line with fgets, then close the file. */
int main(void) {
    FILE *file = fopen("data.txt", "w");
    if (file == NULL) {
        perror("fopen");
        return 1;
    }
    fprintf(file, "good comments explain why the code exists\n");
    fprintf(file, "strings end with a null character\n");
    fprintf(file, "loops repeat a block of code\n");
    fprintf(file, "structs group related data together\n");
    fclose(file);

    /* Reopen the file for reading and print it line by line. */
    file = fopen("data.txt", "r");
    if (file == NULL) {
        perror("fopen");
        return 1;
    }
    char line[128];
    while (fgets(line, sizeof(line), file) != NULL) {
        printf("%s", line);
    }
    fclose(file);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: fopen() in write mode creates data.txt, fprintf() writes 4 lines into it
   and fclose() saves it. The file is then opened again in read mode, and fgets() reads it
   back line by line into the buffer line, which is printed. Every fopen() result is
   checked for NULL. */
// END

/* Caption: Compute the sum of the digits of an integer. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Start result at 0.
   2. Add n % 10 to result, then divide n by 10.
   3. Repeat until n is 0.
   4. Apply it to 377631 and print the result. */
/* Take the last digit with % 10, then drop it with / 10. */
int sum_digits(int n) {
    int result = 0;
    while (n > 0) {
        result += n % 10;
        n /= 10;
    }
    return result;
}

int main(void) {
    int number = 377631;
    printf("sum of digits of %d: %d\n", number, sum_digits(number));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: sum_digits() adds the last digit (n % 10) to result and then removes it (n
   / 10) until no digits are left. main() applies it to 377631. */
// END

/* Caption: Divide two integers and get both the quotient and the remainder. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write divide(a, b, &quotient, &remainder) that returns a bool.
   2. Return false if b is 0.
   3. Store a / b and a % b through the pointers and return true.
   4. Divide 351 by 30 and print the results or the error. */
/* Returns false for division by zero; otherwise stores both results. */
bool divide(int a, int b, int *quotient, int *remainder) {
    if (b == 0) {
        return false;
    }
    *quotient = a / b;
    *remainder = a % b;
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    int a = 351, b = 30;
    int q, r;
    if (divide(a, b, &q, &r)) {
        printf("%d / %d = %d remainder %d\n", a, b, q, r);
    } else {
        printf("Cannot divide by zero\n");
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: divide() has four parameters: two inputs and two pointers for the results.
   Its bool return value reports success, while the quotient and remainder are written
   through the pointers. main() divides 351 by 30 and prints both results. */
// END

/* Caption: Program to raise a number to an integer power with a loop. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write power(base, exp) with result = 1.
   2. Multiply result by base exp times.
   3. Print 8 to the power 7. */
/* Multiply the base by itself exp times. */
long long power(int base, int exp) {
    long long result = 1;
    for (int i = 0; i < exp; i++) {
        result *= base;
    }
    return result;
}

int main(void) {
    printf("8^7 = %lld\n", power(8, 7));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: power() starts result at 1 and multiplies it by base exp times. It uses
   long long because powers grow quickly. main() prints 8 to the power 7. */
// END

/* Caption: Create a singly linked list by inserting at the head. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define ListNode with a value and a next pointer.
   2. Write push_front() that mallocs a node and links it in front of head.
   3. Write print_list() that follows next until NULL.
   4. Write free_list() that frees every node.
   5. Push 6 values, print the list and free it. */
typedef struct ListNode {
    int value;
    struct ListNode *next;
} ListNode;

/* Allocate a new node and put it in front of the current head. */
ListNode *push_front(ListNode *head, int value) {
    ListNode *node = malloc(sizeof(ListNode));
    if (node == NULL) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Out of memory\n");
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }
    node->value = value;
    node->next = head;
    return node;
}

void print_list(const ListNode *head) {
    for (const ListNode *cur = head; cur != NULL; cur = cur->next) {
        printf("%d -> ", cur->value);
    }
    printf("NULL\n");
}

/* Free every node; save next before freeing the current one. */
void free_list(ListNode *head) {
    while (head != NULL) {
        ListNode *next = head->next;
        free(head);
        head = next;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    ListNode *head = NULL;
    head = push_front(head, 55);
    head = push_front(head, 55);
    head = push_front(head, 97);
    head = push_front(head, 94);
    head = push_front(head, 3);
    head = push_front(head, 22);
    print_list(head);
    free_list(head);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: Each ListNode holds a value and a pointer to the next node. push_front()
   allocates a node with malloc, puts it in front of head and returns it; print_list()
   follows the next pointers until NULL; free_list() frees every node. main() pushes 6
   values, so they print in reverse order. */
// END

/* Caption: Compute the mean of a list of numbers. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write average() that takes samples and length.
   2. Add the values into the double sum.
   3. Return sum / length.
   4. Print the average with two decimals. */
/* The mean is the total divided by the count. */
double average(const int samples[], int length) {
    double sum = 0.0;
    for (int k = 0; k < length; k++) {
        sum += samples[k];
    }
    return sum / length;
}

int main(void) {
    int samples[] = {60, 41, 29};
    const int length = 3;
    printf("The average is %.2f\n", average(samples, length));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: average() adds the 3 values of samples into the double sum and divides by
   length, so the mean keeps its decimal part even when the values are whole numbers.
   main() prints it with two decimals. */
// END

   aeiouAEIOU and counts the matches. main() prints the number of vowels in the sentence. */

/* Caption: Use dynamic memory to store the first 10 evens. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Use malloc to get room for 10 ints and check for NULL.
   2. Fill table with evens.
   3. Print the values.
   4. Call free(table) at the end. */
int main(void) {
    int n = 10;
    /* Ask the heap for room for n ints; malloc returns NULL on failure. */
    int *table = malloc(n * sizeof(int));
    if (table == NULL) {
        fprintf(stderr, "malloc failed\n");
        return 1;
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        table[i] = 2 * i;
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        printf("%d ", table[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    free(table);   /* give the memory back */
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: malloc() reserves room for 10 ints on the heap and returns NULL if it
   fails, which the program checks. The first loop fills table with evens, the second
   prints them, and free() gives the memory back at the end. */
// END

    printf("\n");

   numbers by calling itself twice, which is simple but slow for large n. main() prints the
   first 25 numbers. */

/* Caption: C program to sort an array in ascending order using selection sort. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write selection_sort() for the int array ages.
   2. For each position, find the smallest remaining element.
   3. Swap it into that position.
   4. Print the sorted values. */
/* Select the right element for each position and swap it into place. */
void selection_sort(int ages[], int n) {
    for (int i = 0; i < n - 1; i++) {
        int chosen = i;
        for (int j = i + 1; j < n; j++) {
            if (ages[chosen] > ages[j]) {
                chosen = j;
            }
        }
        int tmp = ages[i];
        ages[i] = ages[chosen];
        ages[chosen] = tmp;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    int ages[] = {30, 86, 20, 79, 9, 21, 19, 41, 75, 1};
    const int n = 10;
    selection_sort(ages, n);
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        printf("%d ", ages[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: selection_sort() finds the smallest remaining element for each position and
   swaps it into place. main() then prints the 10 values in ascending order. */
// END

/* Caption: Write lines to a text file and read them back. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Open data.txt in write mode and check for NULL.
   2. Write 4 lines with fprintf and close the file.
   3. Open it again in read mode.
   4. Read and print each line with fgets, then close the file. */
int main(void) {
    FILE *file = fopen("data.txt", "w");
    if (file == NULL) {
        perror("fopen");
        return 1;
    }
    fprintf(file, "the quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog\n");
    fprintf(file, "loops repeat a block of code\n");
    fprintf(file, "strings end with a null character\n");
    fprintf(file, "good comments explain why the code exists\n");
    fclose(file);

    /* Reopen the file for reading and print it line by line. */
    file = fopen("data.txt", "r");
    if (file == NULL) {
        perror("fopen");
        return 1;
    }
    char line[128];
    while (fgets(line, sizeof(line), file) != NULL) {
        printf("%s", line);
    }
    fclose(file);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: fopen() in write mode creates data.txt, fprintf() writes 4 lines into it
   and fclose() saves it. The file is then opened again in read mode, and fgets() reads it
   back line by line into the buffer line, which is printed. Every fopen() result is
   checked for NULL. */

/* Caption: Program to reverse an array by swapping from both ends. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write reverse_array() for readings.
   2. Set start to the first index and end to the last.
   3. Swap readings[start] and readings[end], then move both inwards.
   4. Stop when start meets end and print the array. */
/* Swap the outer pair, then move both ends toward the middle. */
void reverse_array(long readings[], int n) {
    int start = 0;
    int end = n - 1;
    while (start < end) {
        long tmp = readings[start];
        readings[start] = readings[end];
        readings[end] = tmp;
        start++;
        end--;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    long readings[] = {25L, 66L, 77L, 80L, 3L, 50L, 69L, 61L, 99L};
    int n = sizeof(readings) / sizeof(readings[0]);
    reverse_array(readings, n);
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        printf("%ld ", readings[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: reverse_array() swaps the first and last elements, then moves start forward
   and end backward until they meet, so the array is reversed in place without a second
   array. main() prints the reversed values. */
// END

/* Caption: Raise a number to an integer power with a loop. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write power(base, exp) with result = 1.
   2. Multiply result by base exp times.
   3. Print 6 to the power 4. */
/* Multiply the base by itself exp times. */
long long power(int base, int exp) {
    long long result = 1;
    for (int i = 0; i < exp; i++) {
        result *= base;
    }
    return result;
}

int main(void) {
    printf("6^4 = %lld\n", power(6, 4));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: power() starts result at 1 and multiplies it by base exp times. It uses
   long long because powers grow quickly. main() prints 6 to the power 4. */
// END

/* Caption: C program to list the prime numbers below a limit. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write is_prime(n); numbers below 2 are not prime.
   2. Try every divisor d while d * d <= n.
   3. Return false if one divides n, otherwise true.
   4. Print every prime from 2 to 30. */
/* A prime has no divisor between 2 and its square root. */
bool is_prime(int n) {
    if (n < 2) {
        return false;
    }
    for (int d = 2; d * d <= n; d++) {
        if (n % d == 0) {
            return false;
        }
    }
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    for (int n = 2; n <= 30; n++) {
        if (is_prime(n)) {
            printf("%d ", n);
        }
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: is_prime() tries every divisor d from 2 while d * d <= n; if one divides n
   evenly, n is not prime. main() tests every number from 2 to 30 and prints the primes. */
// END

/* Caption: Sort an array in ascending order using bubble sort. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write bubble_sort() for the int array nums.
   2. Compare each pair of neighbours.
   3. Swap them when they are in the wrong order for ascending order.
   4. Repeat the passes until the array is sorted.
   5. Print the sorted values. */
/* Repeatedly swap neighbours that are in the wrong order. */
void bubble_sort(int nums[], int len) {
    for (int i = 0; i < len - 1; i++) {
        for (int j = 0; j < len - 1 - i; j++) {
            if (nums[j] > nums[j + 1]) {
                int tmp = nums[j];
                nums[j] = nums[j + 1];
                nums[j + 1] = tmp;
            }
        }
    }
}

int main(void) {
    int nums[] = {93, 87, 90, 13, 57};
    const int len = 5;
    bubble_sort(nums, len);
    for (int i = 0; i < len; i++) {
        printf("%d ", nums[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: bubble_sort() walks through nums again and again and swaps neighbours that
   are in the wrong order, so the largest values move to the end first. main() then prints
   the 5 values in ascending order. */
// END

/* Caption: Print an integer with its digits reversed. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Start result at 0.
   2. Multiply result by 10, add n % 10, then divide n by 10.
   3. Repeat until n is 0.
   4. Apply it to 637710 and print the result. */
/* Take the last digit with % 10, then drop it with / 10. */
int reverse_digits(int n) {
    int result = 0;
    while (n > 0) {
        result = result * 10 + n % 10;
        n /= 10;
    }
    return result;
}

int main(void) {
    int number = 637710;
    printf("reverse of digits of %d: %d\n", number, reverse_digits(number));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: reverse_digits() shifts result one place left (result * 10) and adds the
   last digit of n, which reverses the order. main() applies it to 637710. */
// END

/* Caption: Implement insertion sort for an array of int values. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write insertion_sort() for the int array values.
   2. Take each element in turn as current.
   3. Shift the smaller values of the sorted part one place right.
   4. Put current into the gap.
   5. Print the sorted values. */
/* Insert each element into the already sorted part on its left. */
void insertion_sort(int values[], int length) {
    for (int i = 1; i < length; i++) {
        int current = values[i];
        int j = i - 1;
        while (j >= 0 && values[j] < current) {
            values[j + 1] = values[j];   /* shift bigger values right */
            j--;
        }
        values[j + 1] = current;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    int values[] = {57, 18, 89, 5, 31, 73, 43, 84, 39};
    int length = sizeof(values) / sizeof(values[0]);
    insertion_sort(values, length);
    for (int i = 0; i < length; i++) {
        printf("%d ", values[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: insertion_sort() takes each element in turn and shifts the smaller values
   of the sorted part one place right until the element fits. main() then prints the 9
   values in descending order. */
// END

/* Caption: Program to build a fixed-size integer stack in C. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define a Stack with room for 10 items and a top counter.
   2. Write push() and pop(), returning false when the stack is full or empty.
   3. Push 3 values.
   4. Pop and print until the stack is empty. */
#define CAPACITY 10

typedef struct {
    int items[CAPACITY];
    int top;   /* number of items on the stack */
} Stack;

bool push(Stack *s, int value) {
    if (s->top == CAPACITY) {
        return false;   /* stack is full */
    }
    s->items[s->top++] = value;
    return true;
}

bool pop(Stack *s, int *value) {
    if (s->top == 0) {
        return false;   /* stack is empty */
    }
    *value = s->items[--s->top];
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    Stack s = {.top = 0};
    push(&s, 24);
    push(&s, 76);
    push(&s, 98);
    int value;
    /* Items come back out in reverse order (last in, first out). */
    while (pop(&s, &value)) {
        printf("%d ", value);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: The Stack keeps up to 10 items in an array, and top counts how many are
   stored. push() adds at the top and pop() removes from the top; both return false when
   they cannot. main() pushes 3 values and pops them all, so they come out in reverse order
   (last in, first out). */
// END

/* Caption: Find the greatest common divisor of two numbers. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write gcd() with Euclid's algorithm.
   2. Replace (a, b) by (b, a % b) until b is 0.
   3. Return a and print the GCD of 222 and 27. */
/* Euclid: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a % b) until b becomes zero. */
int gcd(int a, int b) {
    while (b != 0) {
        int r = a % b;
        a = b;
        b = r;
    }
    return a;
}

int main(void) {
    int x = 222, y = 27;

/* Caption: How do I count how many words are separated by spaces in a string in C? */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <ctype.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write count_words() with words = 0 and an in_word flag.
   2. A space ends a word; a non-space after a space starts a new word and adds one to
      words.
   3. Return words and print it. */
/* A new word starts when a non-space follows a space (or the start). */
int count_words(const char *text) {
    int words = 0;
    int in_word = 0;
    for (int i = 0; text[i] != '\0'; i++) {
        if (isspace((unsigned char)text[i])) {
            in_word = 0;
        } else if (!in_word) {
            in_word = 1;
            words++;
        }
    }
    return words;
}

int main(void) {
    const char *sentence = "a function can call itself recursively";
    printf("Words: %d\n", count_words(sentence));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: count_words() uses the flag in_word: a new word starts when a non-space
   character follows a space or the start of the text. main() prints the number of words in
   the sentence. */
// END

   4. Print total divided by the number of students. */

    int mark;
};

int main(void) {
    struct Student students[] = {
        {"Lena", 56},
        {"Jia", 44}
    };
    int count = sizeof(students) / sizeof(students[0]);
    double total = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < count; i++) {
        printf("%s: %d\n", students[i].name, students[i].mark);

/* Caption: Write a C program to implement insertion sort for an array of long values. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write insertion_sort() for the long array nums.
   2. Take each element in turn as current.
   3. Shift the larger values of the sorted part one place right.
   4. Put current into the gap.
   5. Print the sorted values. */
/* Insert each element into the already sorted part on its left. */
void insertion_sort(long nums[], int count) {
    for (int i = 1; i < count; i++) {
        long current = nums[i];
        int j = i - 1;
        while (j >= 0 && nums[j] > current) {
            nums[j + 1] = nums[j];   /* shift bigger values right */
            j--;
        }
        nums[j + 1] = current;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    long nums[] = {87L, 3L, 20L, 69L, 42L};
    const int count = 5;
    insertion_sort(nums, count);
    for (int i = 0; i < count; i++) {
        printf("%ld ", nums[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: insertion_sort() takes each element in turn and shifts the larger values of
   the sorted part one place right until the element fits. main() then prints the 5 values
   in ascending order. */
// END

/* Caption: C program to print the factorial of an integer. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write factorial(num) with result = 1.
   2. Multiply result by every number from 2 to num.
   3. Return result.
   4. Print 14! as an unsigned long long. */
/* Multiply 1 * 2 * ... * n. */
unsigned long long factorial(int num) {
    unsigned long long result = 1;
    for (int i = 2; i <= num; i++) {
        result *= i;
    }
    return result;
}

int main(void) {
    int num = 14;
    printf("%d! = %llu\n", num, factorial(num));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: factorial() multiplies result by every number from 2 up to num. main()
   prints 14! as an unsigned long long, because factorials grow very fast. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to compute the sum of the digits of an integer. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Start result at 0.
   2. Add n % 10 to result, then divide n by 10.
   3. Repeat until n is 0.
   4. Apply it to 804331 and print the result. */
/* Take the last digit with % 10, then drop it with / 10. */
int sum_digits(int n) {
    int result = 0;
    while (n > 0) {
        result += n % 10;
        n /= 10;
    }
    return result;
}

int main(void) {
    int number = 804331;
    printf("sum of digits of %d: %d\n", number, sum_digits(number));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: sum_digits() adds the last digit (n % 10) to result and then removes it (n
   / 10) until no digits are left. main() applies it to 804331. */
// END

/* Caption: How do I use Euclid's algorithm to compute the GCD in C? */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write gcd() with Euclid's algorithm.
   2. Replace (a, b) by (b, a % b) until b is 0.
   3. Return a and print the GCD of 276 and 155. */
/* Euclid: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a % b) until b becomes zero. */
int gcd(int a, int b) {
    while (b != 0) {
        int r = a % b;
        a = b;
        b = r;
    }
    return a;
}

int main(void) {
    int x = 276, y = 155;
    printf("gcd(%d, %d) = %d\n", x, y, gcd(x, y));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: gcd() uses Euclid's algorithm: it keeps replacing (a, b) with (b, a % b)
   until b is 0. The last non-zero value is the greatest common divisor, and main() prints
   the GCD of 276 and 155. */
// END

/* Caption: How do I check every element of an array to find a target value in C? */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write linear_search() with the array, its length and target.
   2. Compare each element with target.
   3. Return the index of the first match, or -1.
   4. In main(), search for 104 and print the result. */
/* Return the index of target, or -1 when it is not in the array. */
int linear_search(const int samples[], int count, int target) {
    for (int i = 0; i < count; i++) {
        if (samples[i] == target) {
            return i;
        }
    }
    return -1;
}

int main(void) {
    int samples[] = {26, 80, 68, 40, 65, 33, 68};
    const int count = 7;
    int target = 104;
    int pos = linear_search(samples, count, target);
    if (pos >= 0) {
        printf("Found %d at index %d\n", target, pos);
    } else {
        printf("%d is not in the array\n", target);
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: linear_search() checks the elements of samples one by one and returns the
   index of the first one equal to target, or -1 when it reaches the end without a match.
   main() searches for 104 and prints where it is, or that it is missing. */
// END

/* Caption: Return a Point struct from a function. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define a Point struct with x and y.
   2. Write midpoint() that returns a Point with the averages of x and y.
   3. Print mid.x and mid.y. */
typedef struct {
    double x;
    double y;
} Point;

/* A function can return a whole struct. */
Point midpoint(Point a, Point b) {
    Point m = {(a.x + b.x) / 2, (a.y + b.y) / 2};
    return m;
}

int main(void) {
    Point p = {-10, -11}, q = {13, 1};
    Point mid = midpoint(p, q);
    printf("Midpoint: (%.1f, %.1f)\n", mid.x, mid.y);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: midpoint() takes two Point structs and returns a new Point whose x and y
   are the averages of theirs. main() declares p and q on one line, (-10, -11) and (13, 1),
   and prints the midpoint using mid.x and mid.y. */
// END

/* Caption: Reverse a string in place. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <string.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write reverse_string() for buffer.
   2. Set i to the first index and j to the last.
   3. Swap the two characters and move i and j inwards until they meet.
   4. Reverse garden and print it. */
/* Swap characters from both ends until they meet in the middle. */
void reverse_string(char *buffer) {
    int i = 0;
    int j = strlen(buffer) - 1;
    while (i < j) {
        char tmp = buffer[i];
        buffer[i] = buffer[j];
        buffer[j] = tmp;
        i++;
        j--;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    char buffer[] = "garden";
    reverse_string(buffer);
    printf("%s\n", buffer);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: reverse_string() swaps characters from both ends of buffer, moving inwards
   until the two indexes meet. main() reverses the word garden in place and prints it. */
// END

/* Caption: C program to compute the length of a string without strlen. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write string_length() with a counter len = 0.
   2. Move through the string until the null character.
   3. Return len and print the length of stats. */
/* Count characters until the terminating '\0'. */
int string_length(const char *str) {
    int len = 0;
    while (str[len] != '\0') {
        len++;
    }
    return len;
}

int main(void) {
    const char *str = "stats";
    printf("Length of \"%s\" is %d\n", str, string_length(str));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: string_length() counts characters until it reaches the null character that
   ends every C string. main() prints the length of the word stats. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to test if "binary" reads the same backwards. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <string.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write is_palindrome() for buffer.
   2. Compare the first and last characters, moving inwards.
   3. Return false at the first mismatch, otherwise true.
   4. Check binary and print the result. */
/* Compare characters from the front and back, moving inwards. */
bool is_palindrome(const char *buffer) {
    int i = 0;
    int j = strlen(buffer) - 1;
    while (i < j) {
        if (buffer[i] != buffer[j]) {
            return false;
        }
        i++;
        j--;
    }
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    const char *buffer = "binary";
    printf("%s %s a palindrome\n", buffer, is_palindrome(buffer) ? "is" : "is not");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: is_palindrome() compares the first and last characters and moves inwards;
   any mismatch means the word is not a palindrome. main() checks the word binary and
   prints the result. */
// END

/* Caption: Program to generate the Fibonacci sequence. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Start with a = 0 and b = 1.
   2. Repeat 18 times and print a each time.
   3. Compute next = a + b, then set a = b and b = next. */
int main(void) {
    long a = 0, b = 1;
    /* Print a term, then slide the pair one step along the sequence. */
    for (int i = 0; i < 18; i++) {
        printf("%ld ", a);
        long next = a + b;
        a = b;
        b = next;
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: The loop keeps the last two numbers in a and b. Each round it prints a,
   then moves the pair forward: a becomes b and b becomes their sum. It prints the first 18
   Fibonacci numbers. */
// END

   3. Return count and print it. */

    /* Compare every character with the target. */

            count++;

}

    printf("'h' appears %d times\n", count_char(sentence, 'h'));

   and counts the matches. main() prints how many times h appears in the sentence. */

/* Caption: How do I find the minimum and maximum of an array with one function in C? */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write min_max() with the array, its length and the pointers min and max.
   2. Start both at the first element.
   3. Update *min and *max while looping over the rest.
   4. Declare smallest and largest, pass their addresses and print them. */
/* One pass finds both results; they are stored through the pointers. */
void min_max(const int numbers[], int length, int *min, int *max) {
    *min = numbers[0];
    *max = numbers[0];
    for (int i = 1; i < length; i++) {
        if (numbers[i] < *min) {
            *min = numbers[i];
        }
        if (numbers[i] > *max) {
            *max = numbers[i];
        }
    }
}

int main(void) {
    int numbers[] = {55, 93, 87, 65};
    const int length = 4;
    int smallest, largest;
    min_max(numbers, length, &smallest, &largest);
    printf("Min: %d, Max: %d\n", smallest, largest);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: A C function can return only one value, so min_max() returns void and
   writes its two results through the pointer parameters min and max. main() declares
   smallest and largest on one line and passes their addresses with &, then prints both
   results for the 4 values. */
// END

/* Caption: Convert a string to uppercase. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <ctype.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write to_upper() for buffer.
   2. Replace every character with toupper() until the null character.
   3. Print the sentence. */
/* toupper changes lowercase letters and leaves other characters alone. */
void to_upper(char *buffer) {
    for (int i = 0; buffer[i] != '\0'; i++) {
        buffer[i] = toupper((unsigned char)buffer[i]);
    }
}

int main(void) {
    char buffer[] = "the quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog";
    to_upper(buffer);
    printf("%s\n", buffer);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: to_upper() walks through buffer until the null character and replaces each
   character with toupper(), which only changes lowercase letters. main() prints the
   sentence in capitals. */
// END

/* Caption: Allocate an array with malloc and fill it with evens. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Use malloc to get room for 11 ints and check for NULL.
   2. Fill list with evens.
   3. Print the values.
   4. Call free(list) at the end. */
int main(void) {
    int n = 11;
    /* Ask the heap for room for n ints; malloc returns NULL on failure. */
    int *list = malloc(n * sizeof(int));
    if (list == NULL) {
        fprintf(stderr, "malloc failed\n");
        return 1;
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        list[i] = 2 * i;
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        printf("%d ", list[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    free(list);   /* give the memory back */
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: malloc() reserves room for 11 ints on the heap and returns NULL if it
   fails, which the program checks. The first loop fills list with evens, the second prints
   them, and free() gives the memory back at the end. */
// END

/* Caption: Implement a simple linked list with malloc and free. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define ListNode with a value and a next pointer.
   2. Write push_front() that mallocs a node and links it in front of head.
   3. Write print_list() that follows next until NULL.
   4. Write free_list() that frees every node.
   5. Push 6 values, print the list and free it. */
typedef struct ListNode {
    int value;
    struct ListNode *next;
} ListNode;

/* Allocate a new node and put it in front of the current head. */
ListNode *push_front(ListNode *head, int value) {
    ListNode *node = malloc(sizeof(ListNode));
    if (node == NULL) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Out of memory\n");
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }
    node->value = value;
    node->next = head;
    return node;
}

void print_list(const ListNode *head) {
    for (const ListNode *cur = head; cur != NULL; cur = cur->next) {
        printf("%d -> ", cur->value);
    }
    printf("NULL\n");
}

/* Free every node; save next before freeing the current one. */
void free_list(ListNode *head) {
    while (head != NULL) {
        ListNode *next = head->next;
        free(head);
        head = next;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    ListNode *head = NULL;
    head = push_front(head, 6);
    head = push_front(head, 40);
    head = push_front(head, 54);
    head = push_front(head, 37);
    head = push_front(head, 59);
    head = push_front(head, 41);
    print_list(head);
    free_list(head);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: Each ListNode holds a value and a pointer to the next node. push_front()
   allocates a node with malloc, puts it in front of head and returns it; print_list()
   follows the next pointers until NULL; free_list() frees every node. main() pushes 6
   values, so they print in reverse order. */
// END

/* Caption: Program to decide if 1964 is a leap year. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write is_leap(year).
   2. A year divisible by 4 is a leap year, unless it is divisible by 100.
   3. Years divisible by 400 are leap years again.
   4. Check 1964 and print the result. */
/* Leap years divide by 4, except centuries, which must divide by 400. */
int is_leap(int year) {
    return (year % 4 == 0 && year % 100 != 0) || year % 400 == 0;
}

int main(void) {
    int year = 1964;
    if (is_leap(year)) {
        printf("%d is a leap year\n", year);
    } else {
        printf("%d is not a leap year\n", year);
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: is_leap() returns true for years divisible by 4, except century years,
   which must also be divisible by 400. main() checks 1964 and prints whether it is a leap
   year. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to use selection sort to put numbers in ascending order. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write selection_sort() for the int array nums.
   2. For each position, find the smallest remaining element.
   3. Swap it into that position.
   4. Print the sorted values. */
/* Select the right element for each position and swap it into place. */
void selection_sort(int nums[], int n) {
    for (int i = 0; i < n - 1; i++) {
        int chosen = i;
        for (int j = i + 1; j < n; j++) {
            if (nums[chosen] > nums[j]) {
                chosen = j;
            }
        }
        int tmp = nums[i];
        nums[i] = nums[chosen];
        nums[chosen] = tmp;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    int nums[] = {95, 98, 47, 86, 32, 95, 75};
    const int n = 7;
    selection_sort(nums, n);
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        printf("%d ", nums[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: selection_sort() finds the smallest remaining element for each position and
   swaps it into place. main() then prints the 7 values in ascending order. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to swap two variables using pointers. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write swap() that takes pointers to two int values.
   2. Save *x in tmp, copy *y into *x, then tmp into *y.
   3. In main(), print x and y, call swap(&x, &y) and print them again. */
/* Pass addresses so the function can change the caller's variables. */
void swap(int *x, int *y) {
    int tmp = *x;
    *x = *y;
    *y = tmp;
}

int main(void) {
    int x = 8, y = 83;
    printf("Before: %d %d\n", x, y);
    swap(&x, &y);
    printf("After:  %d %d\n", x, y);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: swap() receives the addresses of x and y, so writing through the pointers
   *x and *y changes the caller's variables. tmp holds one value during the exchange.
   main() declares both variables on one line and prints them before and after the swap. */
// END

/* Caption: Raise a number to an integer power with a loop. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write power(base, exp) with result = 1.
   2. Multiply result by base exp times.
   3. Print 2 to the power 5. */
/* Multiply the base by itself exp times. */
long long power(int base, int exp) {
    long long result = 1;
    for (int i = 0; i < exp; i++) {
        result *= base;
    }
    return result;
}

int main(void) {
    printf("2^5 = %lld\n", power(2, 5));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: power() starts result at 1 and multiplies it by base exp times. It uses
   long long because powers grow quickly. main() prints 2 to the power 5. */
// END

/* Caption: How do I use insertion sort to put numbers in ascending order in C? */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write insertion_sort() for the int array data.
   2. Take each element in turn as current.
   3. Shift the larger values of the sorted part one place right.
   4. Put current into the gap.
   5. Print the sorted values. */
/* Insert each element into the already sorted part on its left. */
void insertion_sort(int data[], int len) {
    for (int i = 1; i < len; i++) {
        int current = data[i];
        int j = i - 1;
        while (j >= 0 && data[j] > current) {
            data[j + 1] = data[j];   /* shift bigger values right */
            j--;
        }
        data[j + 1] = current;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    int data[] = {47, 79, 24, 67, 78, 49};
    int len = 6;
    insertion_sort(data, len);
    for (int i = 0; i < len; i++) {
        printf("%d ", data[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: insertion_sort() takes each element in turn and shifts the larger values of
   the sorted part one place right until the element fits. main() then prints the 6 values
   in ascending order. */
// END

/* Caption: Print the factorial of an integer. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write factorial(num) that calls itself.
   2. Return 1 when num is 1 or less.
   3. Otherwise return num * factorial(num - 1).
   4. Print 6! as an unsigned long long. */
/* n! = n * (n - 1)!, and 0! = 1 stops the recursion. */
unsigned long long factorial(int num) {
    if (num <= 1) {
        return 1;
    }
    return num * factorial(num - 1);
}

int main(void) {
    int num = 6;
    printf("%d! = %llu\n", num, factorial(num));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: factorial() calls itself: n! is n * (n - 1)!, and the recursion stops when
   num is 1 or less. main() prints 6! as an unsigned long long, because factorials grow
   very fast. */
// END

/* Caption: Reverse the elements of an array in place. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write reverse_array() for numbers.
   2. Set start to the first index and end to the last.
   3. Swap numbers[start] and numbers[end], then move both inwards.
   4. Stop when start meets end and print the array. */
/* Swap the outer pair, then move both ends toward the middle. */
void reverse_array(int numbers[], int n) {
    int start = 0;
    int end = n - 1;
    while (start < end) {
        int tmp = numbers[start];
        numbers[start] = numbers[end];
        numbers[end] = tmp;
        start++;
        end--;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    int numbers[] = {51, 5, 75, 87};
    int n = 4;
    reverse_array(numbers, n);
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        printf("%d ", numbers[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: reverse_array() swaps the first and last elements, then moves start forward
   and end backward until they meet, so the array is reversed in place without a second
   array. main() prints the reversed values. */
// END

/* Caption: Find the least common multiple of two numbers. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write gcd() with Euclid's algorithm: replace (a, b) by (b, a % b) until b is 0.
   2. Write lcm() as a / gcd(a, b) * b.
   3. Print the LCM of 151 and 260. */
/* Euclid: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a % b) until b becomes zero. */
int gcd(int a, int b) {
    while (b != 0) {
        int r = a % b;
        a = b;
        b = r;
    }
    return a;
}

/* lcm(a, b) = a / gcd(a, b) * b (divide first to avoid overflow). */
long lcm(int a, int b) {
    return (long)a / gcd(a, b) * b;
}

int main(void) {
    printf("lcm(151, 260) = %ld\n", lcm(151, 260));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: gcd() uses Euclid's algorithm: it keeps replacing (a, b) with (b, a % b)
   until b is 0. lcm() divides a by the gcd before multiplying by b, which avoids overflow.
   main() prints the LCM of 151 and 260. */
// END

/* Caption: Find the index of a number using linear search. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write linear_search() with the array, its length and key.
   2. Compare each element with key.
   3. Return the index of the first match, or -1.
   4. In main(), search for 34 and print the result. */
/* Return the index of key, or -1 when it is not in the array. */
int linear_search(const int samples[], int size, int key) {
    for (int idx = 0; idx < size; idx++) {
        if (samples[idx] == key) {
            return idx;
        }
    }
    return -1;
}

int main(void) {
    int samples[] = {48, 80, 92, 34, 32, 13, 75, 96, 65};
    int size = 9;
    int key = 34;
    int pos = linear_search(samples, size, key);
    if (pos >= 0) {
        printf("Found %d at index %d\n", key, pos);
    } else {
        printf("%d is not in the array\n", key);
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: linear_search() checks the elements of samples one by one and returns the
   index of the first one equal to key, or -1 when it reaches the end without a match.
   main() searches for 34 and prints where it is, or that it is missing. */
// END

/* Caption: Return the largest element of an array of int values. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write find_max() that takes marks and n.
   2. Store marks[0] in m.
   3. Loop over the other elements and keep the largest value in m.
   4. Return m and print it. */
/* Start with the first element and keep the largest value seen so far. */
int find_max(const int marks[], int n) {
    int m = marks[0];
    for (int k = 1; k < n; k++) {
        if (marks[k] > m) {
            m = marks[k];
        }
    }
    return m;
}

int main(void) {
    int marks[] = {99, 22, 30, 59, 18, 43};
    int n = 6;
    printf("Largest: %d\n", find_max(marks, n));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: find_max() takes the first element as the largest value so far and stores
   it in m. The loop compares every other element with m using > and keeps the largest one.
   main() prints the largest of the 6 values. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to count how many odd numbers are in an array. */

   1. Write count_odd() that takes marks and count.

   3. Add one to tally for every odd number.
   4. Return tally and print it. */
/* A number is odd when the remainder after dividing by 2 is one. */
int count_odd(const int marks[], int count) {
    int tally = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < count; i++) {
        if (marks[i] % 2 != 0) {
            tally++;
        }
    }
    return tally;
}

int main(void) {
    int marks[] = {27, 82, 36, 21, 64, 64};
    const int count = 6;
    printf("Odd numbers: %d\n", count_odd(marks, count));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: count_odd() tests each element of marks with the % operator: a remainder of
   1 after dividing by 2 means the number is odd, so tally goes up by one. main() prints
   how many of the 6 values are odd. */
// END

/* Caption: Use a struct to return several results from one function. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define a Stats struct with min, max and average.
   2. Write array_stats() that fills one Stats in a loop.
   3. Return the struct.
   4. Print st.min, st.max and st.average. */
typedef struct {
    int min;
    int max;
    double average;
} Stats;

/* Pack several results into one struct and return it. */
Stats array_stats(const int v[], int n) {
    Stats s = {v[0], v[0], 0.0};
    double total = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        if (v[i] < s.min) {
            s.min = v[i];
        }
        if (v[i] > s.max) {
            s.max = v[i];
        }
        total += v[i];
    }
    s.average = total / n;
    return s;
}

int main(void) {
    int samples[] = {84, 3, 81, 95, 63};
    int n = sizeof(samples) / sizeof(samples[0]);
    Stats st = array_stats(samples, n);
    printf("Min %d, Max %d, Average %.2f\n", st.min, st.max, st.average);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: Stats groups three results. array_stats() fills one Stats while it loops
   over the 5 values and returns the whole struct, which is a clean way to return several
   results at once. main() reads them as st.min, st.max and st.average. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to change every letter in a sentence to a capital letter. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <ctype.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write to_upper() for text.
   2. Replace every character with toupper() until the null character.
   3. Print the sentence. */
/* toupper changes lowercase letters and leaves other characters alone. */
void to_upper(char *text) {
    for (int i = 0; text[i] != '\0'; i++) {
        text[i] = toupper((unsigned char)text[i]);
    }
}

int main(void) {
    char text[] = "learning c teaches how computers work";
    to_upper(text);
    printf("%s\n", text);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: to_upper() walks through text until the null character and replaces each
   character with toupper(), which only changes lowercase letters. main() prints the
   sentence in capitals. */
// END

/* Caption: Implement a simple linked list with malloc and free. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define ListNode with a value and a next pointer.
   2. Write push_front() that mallocs a node and links it in front of head.
   3. Write print_list() that follows next until NULL.
   4. Write free_list() that frees every node.
   5. Push 4 values, print the list and free it. */
typedef struct ListNode {
    int value;
    struct ListNode *next;
} ListNode;

/* Allocate a new node and put it in front of the current head. */
ListNode *push_front(ListNode *head, int value) {
    ListNode *node = malloc(sizeof(ListNode));
    if (node == NULL) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Out of memory\n");
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }
    node->value = value;
    node->next = head;
    return node;
}

void print_list(const ListNode *head) {
    for (const ListNode *cur = head; cur != NULL; cur = cur->next) {
        printf("%d -> ", cur->value);
    }
    printf("NULL\n");
}

/* Free every node; save next before freeing the current one. */
void free_list(ListNode *head) {
    while (head != NULL) {
        ListNode *next = head->next;
        free(head);
        head = next;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    ListNode *head = NULL;
    head = push_front(head, 85);
    head = push_front(head, 88);
    head = push_front(head, 13);
    head = push_front(head, 67);
    print_list(head);
    free_list(head);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: Each ListNode holds a value and a pointer to the next node. push_front()
   allocates a node with malloc, puts it in front of head and returns it; print_list()
   follows the next pointers until NULL; free_list() frees every node. main() pushes 4
   values, so they print in reverse order. */
// END

/* Check each bit from the highest to the lowest. */
void print_binary(unsigned int n, int bits) {

   >> b) & 1 is 1 when bit b is set, so it prints the character 1 or 0. main() prints 552
   in binary. */
// END

/* Caption: Calculate 11! using recursion. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write factorial(value) that calls itself.
   2. Return 1 when value is 1 or less.
   3. Otherwise return value * factorial(value - 1).
   4. Print 11! as an unsigned long long. */
/* n! = n * (n - 1)!, and 0! = 1 stops the recursion. */
unsigned long long factorial(int value) {
    if (value <= 1) {
        return 1;
    }
    return value * factorial(value - 1);
}

int main(void) {
    int value = 11;
    printf("%d! = %llu\n", value, factorial(value));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: factorial() calls itself: n! is n * (n - 1)!, and the recursion stops when
   value is 1 or less. main() prints 11! as an unsigned long long, because factorials grow
   very fast. */
// END

/* Caption: Write your own version of strcpy. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write copy_string(dest, src).
   2. Copy src into dest one character at a time.
   3. Stop after copying the null character.
   4. Copy planet into line and print it. */
/* Copy each character, including the final '\0'. */
void copy_string(char *dest, const char *src) {
    int i = 0;
    while ((dest[i] = src[i]) != '\0') {
        i++;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    char source[] = "planet";
    char line[100];
    copy_string(line, source);
    printf("Copied: %s\n", line);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: copy_string() copies src into dest one character at a time, including the
   final null character, which is what strcpy does. The array line must be big enough to
   hold the copy. main() copies the word planet and prints it. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to implement selection sort for an array of int values. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write selection_sort() for the int array items.
   2. For each position, find the smallest remaining element.
   3. Swap it into that position.
   4. Print the sorted values. */
/* Select the right element for each position and swap it into place. */
void selection_sort(int items[], int count) {
    for (int i = 0; i < count - 1; i++) {
        int chosen = i;
        for (int j = i + 1; j < count; j++) {
            if (items[chosen] > items[j]) {
                chosen = j;
            }
        }
        int tmp = items[i];
        items[i] = items[chosen];
        items[chosen] = tmp;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    int items[] = {59, 56, 20, 91, 24, 66, 16, 43};
    int count = sizeof(items) / sizeof(items[0]);
    selection_sort(items, count);
    for (int i = 0; i < count; i++) {
        printf("%d ", items[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: selection_sort() finds the smallest remaining element for each position and
   swaps it into place. main() then prints the 8 values in ascending order. */
// END

   how many of the 5 values are even. */

/* Caption: Add up the digits of a number. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Start result at 0.
   2. Add n % 10 to result, then divide n by 10.
   3. Repeat until n is 0.
   4. Apply it to 345369 and print the result. */
/* Take the last digit with % 10, then drop it with / 10. */
int sum_digits(int n) {
    int result = 0;
    while (n > 0) {
        result += n % 10;
        n /= 10;
    }

}

    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: sum_digits() adds the last digit (n % 10) to result and then removes it (n
   / 10) until no digits are left. main() applies it to 345369. */
// END

/* Caption: Implement a stack with an array (push and pop). */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define a Stack with room for 32 items and a top counter.
   2. Write push() and pop(), returning false when the stack is full or empty.
   3. Push 3 values.
   4. Pop and print until the stack is empty. */
#define CAPACITY 32

typedef struct {
    int items[CAPACITY];
    int top;   /* number of items on the stack */
} Stack;

bool push(Stack *s, int value) {
    if (s->top == CAPACITY) {
        return false;   /* stack is full */
    }
    s->items[s->top++] = value;
    return true;
}

bool pop(Stack *s, int *value) {
    if (s->top == 0) {
        return false;   /* stack is empty */
    }
    *value = s->items[--s->top];
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    Stack s = {.top = 0};
    push(&s, 62);
    push(&s, 24);
    push(&s, 3);
    int value;
    /* Items come back out in reverse order (last in, first out). */
    while (pop(&s, &value)) {
        printf("%d ", value);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: The Stack keeps up to 32 items in an array, and top counts how many are
   stored. push() adds at the top and pop() removes from the top; both return false when
   they cannot. main() pushes 3 values and pops them all, so they come out in reverse order
   (last in, first out). */
// END

/* Caption: How do I find the largest number in an array in C? */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write largest_value() that takes items and n.
   2. Store items[0] in current.
   3. Loop over the other elements and keep the largest value in current.
   4. Return current and print it. */
/* Start with the first element and keep the largest value seen so far. */
int largest_value(const int items[], int n) {
    int current = items[0];
    for (int i = 1; i < n; i++) {
        if (items[i] > current) {
            current = items[i];
        }
    }
    return current;
}

int main(void) {
    int items[] = {23, 71, 7, 87, 23};
    int n = sizeof(items) / sizeof(items[0]);
    printf("The largest value is %d\n", largest_value(items, n));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: largest_value() takes the first element as the largest value so far and
   stores it in current. The loop compares every other element with current using > and
   keeps the largest one. main() prints the largest of the 5 values. */
// END

/* Plan:

   2. Store PI * r * r and 2 * PI * r through them.
   3. Print both for a radius of 23.9. */
#define PI 3.14159265

void circle_measures(double radius, double *area, double *circumference) {
    *area = PI * radius * radius;
    *circumference = 2 * PI * radius;
}

    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: circle_measures() computes two results from one radius and stores them
   through the pointers area and circumference. main() declares both variables on one line,
   passes their addresses and prints the results for a radius of 23.9. */
// END

/* Caption: Check whether a number is prime. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write is_prime(n); numbers below 2 are not prime.
   2. Try every divisor d while d * d <= n.
   3. Return false if one divides n, otherwise true.
   4. Check 5 and print the result. */
/* A prime has no divisor between 2 and its square root. */
bool is_prime(int n) {
    if (n < 2) {
        return false;
    }
    for (int d = 2; d * d <= n; d++) {
        if (n % d == 0) {
            return false;
        }
    }
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    int number = 5;
    printf("%d %s prime\n", number, is_prime(number) ? "is" : "is not");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: is_prime() tries every divisor d from 2 while d * d <= n; if one divides n
   evenly, n is not prime. main() checks 5 and prints whether it is prime. */
// END

/* Caption: C program to compute the LCM of two integers using the GCD. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write gcd() with Euclid's algorithm: replace (a, b) by (b, a % b) until b is 0.
   2. Write lcm() as a / gcd(a, b) * b.
   3. Print the LCM of 81 and 67. */
/* Euclid: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a % b) until b becomes zero. */
int gcd(int a, int b) {
    while (b != 0) {
        int r = a % b;
        a = b;
        b = r;
    }
    return a;
}

/* lcm(a, b) = a / gcd(a, b) * b (divide first to avoid overflow). */
long lcm(int a, int b) {
    return (long)a / gcd(a, b) * b;
}

int main(void) {
    printf("lcm(81, 67) = %ld\n", lcm(81, 67));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: gcd() uses Euclid's algorithm: it keeps replacing (a, b) with (b, a % b)
   until b is 0. lcm() divides a by the gcd before multiplying by b, which avoids overflow.
   main() prints the LCM of 81 and 67. */
// END

/* Caption: Allocate an array with malloc and fill it with squares. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Use malloc to get room for 10 ints and check for NULL.
   2. Fill table with squares.
   3. Print the values.
   4. Call free(table) at the end. */
int main(void) {
    int n = 10;
    /* Ask the heap for room for n ints; malloc returns NULL on failure. */
    int *table = malloc(n * sizeof(int));
    if (table == NULL) {
        fprintf(stderr, "malloc failed\n");
        return 1;
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        table[i] = i * i;
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        printf("%d ", table[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    free(table);   /* give the memory back */
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: malloc() reserves room for 10 ints on the heap and returns NULL if it
   fails, which the program checks. The first loop fills table with squares, the second
   prints them, and free() gives the memory back at the end. */
// END

/* Caption: How do I use selection sort to put numbers in descending order in C? */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write selection_sort() for the int array marks.
   2. For each position, find the largest remaining element.
   3. Swap it into that position.
   4. Print the sorted values. */
/* Select the right element for each position and swap it into place. */
void selection_sort(int marks[], int length) {
    for (int i = 0; i < length - 1; i++) {
        int chosen = i;
        for (int j = i + 1; j < length; j++) {
            if (marks[chosen] < marks[j]) {
                chosen = j;
            }
        }
        int tmp = marks[i];
        marks[i] = marks[chosen];
        marks[chosen] = tmp;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    int marks[] = {66, 58, 26, 85, 64, 10, 96, 56, 11, 94};
    int length = 10;
    selection_sort(marks, length);
    for (int i = 0; i < length; i++) {
        printf("%d ", marks[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: selection_sort() finds the largest remaining element for each position and
   swaps it into place. main() then prints the 10 values in descending order. */
// END

/* Caption: Search an array for its largest value. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write max_of() that takes nums and n.
   2. Store nums[0] in best.
   3. Loop over the other elements and keep the largest value in best.
   4. Return best and print it. */
/* Start with the first element and keep the largest value seen so far. */
int max_of(const int nums[], int n) {
    int best = nums[0];
    for (int k = 1; k < n; k++) {
        if (nums[k] > best) {
            best = nums[k];
        }
    }
    return best;
}

    int n = sizeof(nums) / sizeof(nums[0]);
    printf("The largest value is %d\n", max_of(nums, n));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: max_of() takes the first element as the largest value so far and stores it
   in best. The loop compares every other element with best using > and keeps the largest
   one. main() prints the largest of the 5 values. */
// END

/* Caption: Print the factorial of an integer. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write factorial(value) that calls itself.
   2. Return 1 when value is 1 or less.
   3. Otherwise return value * factorial(value - 1).
   4. Print 6! as an unsigned long long. */
/* n! = n * (n - 1)!, and 0! = 1 stops the recursion. */
unsigned long long factorial(int value) {
    if (value <= 1) {
        return 1;
    }
    return value * factorial(value - 1);
}

int main(void) {
    int value = 6;
    printf("%d! = %llu\n", value, factorial(value));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: factorial() calls itself: n! is n * (n - 1)!, and the recursion stops when
   value is 1 or less. main() prints 6! as an unsigned long long, because factorials grow
   very fast. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to test if "integer" reads the same backwards. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <string.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write is_palindrome() for line.
   2. Compare the first and last characters, moving inwards.
   3. Return false at the first mismatch, otherwise true.
   4. Check integer and print the result. */
/* Compare characters from the front and back, moving inwards. */
bool is_palindrome(const char *line) {
    int i = 0;
    int j = strlen(line) - 1;
    while (i < j) {
        if (line[i] != line[j]) {
            return false;
        }
        i++;
        j--;
    }
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    const char *line = "integer";
    printf("%s %s a palindrome\n", line, is_palindrome(line) ? "is" : "is not");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: is_palindrome() compares the first and last characters and moves inwards;
   any mismatch means the word is not a palindrome. main() checks the word integer and
   prints the result. */
// END

/* Plan:

/* Add every element to a running total. */
int array_sum(const int items[], int n) {

    }

   0, adds every element to it in a while loop and returns the total. main() fills items
   with 6 int values and prints their sum. */
