/* Caption: Program to find the maximum of three numbers. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Read num1, num2 and num3.
   2. Assume num1 is the maximum.
   3. Compare it with the other two and keep the bigger value.
   4. Print the result. */
int main(void) {
    int num1, num2, num3;
    printf("Enter three numbers: ");
    if (scanf("%d %d %d", &num1, &num2, &num3) != 3) {
        printf("Invalid input\n");
        return 1;
    }
    int best = num1;
    /* Compare with each of the others and keep the bigger one. */
    if (num2 > best) {
        best = num2;
    }
    if (num3 > best) {
        best = num3;
    }
    printf("The maximum is %d\n", best);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: The program reads num1, num2 and num3 from the keyboard with scanf and
   stops with a message if the input is not valid. It assumes num1 is the maximum, compares
   it with the other two and keeps the bigger value in best, which it prints. */
// END

/* Caption: C program to divide two integers. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Set first and second.
   2. If second is 0, print an error and stop.
   3. Print first / second and the remainder first % second. */
int main(void) {
    int first = 66, second = 77;
    /* Dividing by zero is not allowed, so check first. */
    if (second == 0) {
        printf("Cannot divide by zero\n");
        return 1;
    }
    /* Integer division drops the fraction; % gives the remainder. */
    printf("Quotient: %d, remainder: %d\n", first / second, first % second);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: The program uses fixed values for first and second. It checks that second
   is not zero, then prints first / second, where integer division drops the fraction, and
   the remainder first % second. */
// END

/* Caption: C program to show the right way to declare several pointers on one line. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Declare x and y on one line.
   2. Declare the pointers px and py on one line, each with its own *.
   3. Add 14 to x through px and print the values. */
int main(void) {
    int x = 14, y = 36;
    /* Each pointer needs its own '*': in "int *p, q;" only p is a pointer. */
    int *px = &x, *py = &y;
    *px += 14;
    printf("x = %d, y = %d\n", x, y);
    printf("*px = %d, *py = %d\n", *px, *py);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: int *px = &x, *py = &y; declares two pointers in one statement; each name
   needs its own *. *px += 14 changes x through the pointer, so x becomes 28 while y stays
   36. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to find the bigger of two numbers. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Set num1 and num2.
   2. Pick the bigger of num1 and num2.
   3. Print it. */
int main(void) {
    int num1 = 5, num2 = 6;
    int best = (num1 > num2) ? num1 : num2;   /* the ?: operator picks one of two values */
    printf("The bigger is %d\n", best);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: The program uses fixed values for num1 and num2. The conditional operator
   (num1 > num2) ? num1 : num2 picks the bigger value, which is printed. */
// END

/* Caption: How do I split a number of seconds into hours, minutes and seconds with pointer parameters in C? */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write split_seconds() with the pointers hours, minutes and seconds.
   2. Store total / 3600, (total % 3600) / 60 and total % 60 through them.
   3. Convert 84231 seconds and print the parts. */
void split_seconds(int total, int *hours, int *minutes, int *seconds) {
    *hours = total / 3600;
    *minutes = (total % 3600) / 60;
    *seconds = total % 60;
}

int main(void) {
    int total = 84231;
    int h, m, s;
    split_seconds(total, &h, &m, &s);
    printf("%d seconds = %d h %d min %d s\n", total, h, m, s);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: split_seconds() fills three results through pointers: hours is total /
   3600, minutes is what is left divided by 60, and seconds is total % 60. main() declares
   h, m and s on one line and converts 84231 seconds. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to print the binary representation of an integer. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write print_binary(n, bits).
   2. Go through the bits from the highest to the lowest.
   3. Print 1 when (n >> b) & 1 is set, otherwise 0.
   4. Print 118 in binary. */
/* Check each bit from the highest to the lowest. */
void print_binary(unsigned int n, int bits) {
    for (int b = bits - 1; b >= 0; b--) {
        putchar((n >> b) & 1 ? '1' : '0');
    }
    putchar('\n');
}

int main(void) {
    unsigned int number = 118;
    printf("%u in binary: ", number);
    print_binary(number, 12);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: print_binary() checks one bit at a time, from the highest to the lowest: (n
   >> b) & 1 is 1 when bit b is set, so it prints the character 1 or 0. main() prints 118
   in binary. */
// END

/* Caption: Calculate the sum of the first n natural numbers. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Set n = 34.
   2. Compute n * (n + 1) / 2.
   3. Print the result. */
int main(void) {
    int n = 34;
    /* Gauss's formula: 1 + 2 + ... + n = n * (n + 1) / 2 */
    int sum = n * (n + 1) / 2;
    printf("Sum of 1 to %d = %d\n", n, sum);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: Instead of a loop it uses Gauss's formula n * (n + 1) / 2, which gives the
   sum of 1 to 34 in one step. */
// END

/* Caption: Reverse the elements of an array in place. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write reverse_array() for numbers.
   2. Set i to the first index and j to the last.
   3. Swap numbers[i] and numbers[j], then move both inwards.
   4. Stop when i meets j and print the array. */
/* Swap the outer pair, then move both ends toward the middle. */
void reverse_array(int numbers[], int length) {
    int i = 0;
    int j = length - 1;
    while (i < j) {
        int tmp = numbers[i];
        numbers[i] = numbers[j];
        numbers[j] = tmp;
        i++;
        j--;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    int numbers[] = {23, 74, 66, 43, 35, 21, 70, 60, 46};
    const int length = 9;
    reverse_array(numbers, length);
    for (int i = 0; i < length; i++) {
        printf("%d ", numbers[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: reverse_array() swaps the first and last elements, then moves i forward and
   j backward until they meet, so the array is reversed in place without a second array.
   main() prints the reversed values. */
// END

   4. Print the average with two decimals. */
/* The mean is the total divided by the count. */
double average(const int readings[], int count) {
    double total = 0.0;
    for (int k = 0; k < count; k++) {
        total += readings[k];
    }
    return total / count;
}

int main(void) {
    int readings[] = {61, 28, 76, 44, 12, 16};
    int count = sizeof(readings) / sizeof(readings[0]);
    printf("Mean = %.2f\n", average(readings, count));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: average() adds the 6 values of readings into the double total and divides
   by count, so the mean keeps its decimal part even when the values are whole numbers.
   main() prints it with two decimals. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a function that returns the distance between two points given x1, y1, x2 and y2. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <math.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write distance(x1, y1, x2, y2).
   2. Compute dx and dy, then return sqrt(dx * dx + dy * dy).
   3. Print the distance between (5, -8) and (-6, -2). */
/* Pythagoras: the distance is sqrt(dx * dx + dy * dy). */
double distance(double x1, double y1, double x2, double y2) {
    double dx = x2 - x1, dy = y2 - y1;
    return sqrt(dx * dx + dy * dy);
}

int main(void) {
    printf("Distance: %.3f\n", distance(5, -8, -6, -2));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: distance() takes the coordinates of both points as four parameters. It
   declares dx and dy on one line and uses Pythagoras with sqrt() from math.h. main()
   prints the distance between (5, -8) and (-6, -2). */
// END

/* Caption: How do I write a function that clamps a value between a minimum and a maximum in C? */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write clamp(value, low, high).
   2. Return low if the value is too small and high if it is too big.
   3. Otherwise return the value.
   4. Set low = 50 and high = 51 and print clamp() for 78, 4 and 83. */
/* Return value, but never less than low or more than high. */
int clamp(int value, int low, int high) {
    if (value < low) {
        return low;
    }
    if (value > high) {
        return high;
    }
    return value;
}

int main(void) {
    int low = 50, high = 51;
    printf("clamp(%d) = %d\n", 78, clamp(78, low, high));
    printf("clamp(%d) = %d\n", 4, clamp(4, low, high));
    printf("clamp(%d) = %d\n", 83, clamp(83, low, high));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: clamp() takes three parameters: the value and the two limits. It returns
   low when the value is too small, high when it is too big and the value itself otherwise.
   main() declares low = 50 and high = 51 on one line and clamps 78, 4 and 83. */
// END

/* Caption: C program to print the first 9 Fibonacci numbers. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write fib(n) that returns n when n < 2.
   2. Otherwise return fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2).
   3. Print fib(i) for i from 0 to 8. */
/* Each Fibonacci number is the sum of the two before it. */
long fib(int n) {
    if (n < 2) {
        return n;
    }
    return fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2);
}

int main(void) {
    for (int i = 0; i < 9; i++) {
        printf("%ld ", fib(i));
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: fib() returns n for 0 and 1 and otherwise adds the two previous Fibonacci
   numbers by calling itself twice, which is simple but slow for large n. main() prints the
   first 9 numbers. */
// END

/* Caption: Use binary search to locate a value in a sorted list. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Make sure the array is sorted.
   2. Set low to 0 and high to count - 1.
   3. While low <= high, compare the middle element mid with the key.
   4. Return the index if it matches; otherwise keep only the half that can hold the
      key.
   5. Return -1 if the range becomes empty, and print the index of 138. */
/* The array must be sorted. Each step halves the range that can still hold the key. */
int binary_search(const int numbers[], int count, int key) {
    int low = 0;
    int high = count - 1;
    while (low <= high) {
        int mid = low + (high - low) / 2;
        if (numbers[mid] == key) {
            return mid;
        } else if (numbers[mid] < key) {
            low = mid + 1;   /* key is in the right half */
        } else {
            high = mid - 1;   /* key is in the left half */
        }
    }
    return -1;
}

int main(void) {
    int numbers[] = {9, 59, 73, 78, 138, 161, 169, 173};
    const int count = 8;
    int index = binary_search(numbers, count, 138);
    printf("Index of 138: %d\n", index);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: binary_search() needs a sorted array. It keeps the range from low to high,
   compares the middle element mid with the key and throws away the half that cannot
   contain it, so it needs only about log2(n) steps. main() looks for 138 and prints its
   index, or -1 if it is not there. */
// END

/* Caption: Return the minimum, maximum and average of an array in a struct. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define a Stats struct with min, max and average.
   2. Write array_stats() that fills one Stats in a loop.
   3. Return the struct.
   4. Print st.min, st.max and st.average. */
typedef struct {
    int min;
    int max;
    double average;
} Stats;

/* Pack several results into one struct and return it. */
Stats array_stats(const int v[], int n) {
    Stats s = {v[0], v[0], 0.0};
    double total = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        if (v[i] < s.min) {
            s.min = v[i];
        }
        if (v[i] > s.max) {
            s.max = v[i];
        }
        total += v[i];
    }
    s.average = total / n;
    return s;
}

int main(void) {
    int readings[] = {13, 48, 59, 85, 22, 97, 93, 43};
    int n = sizeof(readings) / sizeof(readings[0]);
    Stats st = array_stats(readings, n);
    printf("Min %d, Max %d, Average %.2f\n", st.min, st.max, st.average);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: Stats groups three results. array_stats() fills one Stats while it loops
   over the 8 values and returns the whole struct, which is a clean way to return several
   results at once. main() reads them as st.min, st.max and st.average. */
// END

/* Caption: Compute the LCM of two integers using the GCD. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write gcd() with Euclid's algorithm: replace (a, b) by (b, a % b) until b is 0.
   2. Write lcm() as a / gcd(a, b) * b.
   3. Print the LCM of 206 and 20. */
/* Euclid: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a % b) until b becomes zero. */
int gcd(int a, int b) {
    while (b != 0) {
        int r = a % b;
        a = b;
        b = r;
    }
    return a;
}

/* lcm(a, b) = a / gcd(a, b) * b (divide first to avoid overflow). */
long lcm(int a, int b) {
    return (long)a / gcd(a, b) * b;
}

int main(void) {
    printf("lcm(206, 20) = %ld\n", lcm(206, 20));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: gcd() uses Euclid's algorithm: it keeps replacing (a, b) with (b, a % b)
   until b is 0. lcm() divides a by the gcd before multiplying by b, which avoids overflow.
   main() prints the LCM of 206 and 20. */
// END

/* Caption: Count how many odd numbers are in an array. */

/* Plan:
   1. Write count_odd() that takes ages and count.
   2. For each element, test ages[k] % 2 != 0.
   3. Add one to matches for every odd number.
   4. Return matches and print it. */
/* A number is odd when the remainder after dividing by 2 is one. */
int count_odd(const int ages[], int count) {
    int matches = 0;
    int k = 0;
    while (k < count) {
        if (ages[k] % 2 != 0) {
            matches++;
        }
        k++;
    }
    return matches;
}

    int count = sizeof(ages) / sizeof(ages[0]);

    return 0;
}

   1 after dividing by 2 means the number is odd, so matches goes up by one. main() prints
   how many of the 10 values are odd. */
// END

/* Caption: Search an array for its smallest value. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write smallest_value() that takes numbers and n.
   2. Store numbers[0] in smallest.
   3. Loop over the other elements and keep the smallest value in smallest.
   4. Return smallest and print it. */
/* Start with the first element and keep the smallest value seen so far. */
double smallest_value(const double numbers[], int n) {
    double smallest = numbers[0];
    for (int i = 1; i < n; i++) {
        if (numbers[i] < smallest) {
            smallest = numbers[i];

    }
    return smallest;
}

int main(void) {
    double numbers[] = {23.8, 27.7, 44.6, 56.1, 74.5, 27.3, 78.8, 18.1, 19.7, 65.6};
    int n = sizeof(numbers) / sizeof(numbers[0]);

    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: smallest_value() takes the first element as the smallest value so far and
   stores it in smallest. The loop compares every other element with smallest using < and
   keeps the smallest one. main() prints the smallest of the 10 values. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to build a FIFO queue using a ring buffer. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define a Queue with room for 16 items, a head and a count.
   2. Write enqueue() that stores at (head + count) % CAPACITY.
   3. Write dequeue() that takes the item at head and moves head on.
   4. Add 3 values, then remove and print them in order. */
#define CAPACITY 16

typedef struct {
    int items[CAPACITY];
    int head;
    int count;
} Queue;

bool enqueue(Queue *q, int value) {
    if (q->count == CAPACITY) {
        return false;
    }
    /* The tail wraps around to the start of the array. */
    q->items[(q->head + q->count) % CAPACITY] = value;
    q->count++;
    return true;
}

bool dequeue(Queue *q, int *value) {
    if (q->count == 0) {
        return false;
    }
    *value = q->items[q->head];
    q->head = (q->head + 1) % CAPACITY;
    q->count--;
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    Queue q = {.head = 0, .count = 0};
    enqueue(&q, 74);
    enqueue(&q, 97);
    enqueue(&q, 79);
    int value;
    /* Items come out in the order they went in (first in, first out). */
    while (dequeue(&q, &value)) {
        printf("%d ", value);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: The Queue stores up to 16 items in a ring buffer: head is the oldest item
   and % CAPACITY wraps positions back to the start of the array. enqueue() adds at the
   back and dequeue() removes from the front, so main() gets its 3 values back in the same
   order (first in, first out). */
// END

/* Caption: Use selection sort to put numbers in ascending order. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write selection_sort() for the int array numbers.
   2. For each position, find the smallest remaining element.
   3. Swap it into that position.
   4. Print the sorted values. */
/* Select the right element for each position and swap it into place. */
void selection_sort(int numbers[], int n) {
    for (int i = 0; i < n - 1; i++) {
        int chosen = i;
        for (int j = i + 1; j < n; j++) {
            if (numbers[chosen] > numbers[j]) {
                chosen = j;
            }
        }
        int tmp = numbers[i];
        numbers[i] = numbers[chosen];
        numbers[chosen] = tmp;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    int numbers[] = {18, 82, 78, 63, 76, 38, 53, 19, 71, 47};
    int n = sizeof(numbers) / sizeof(numbers[0]);
    selection_sort(numbers, n);
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        printf("%d ", numbers[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: selection_sort() finds the smallest remaining element for each position and
   swaps it into place. main() then prints the 10 values in ascending order. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to build a fixed-size integer stack in C. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define a Stack with room for 10 items and a top counter.
   2. Write push() and pop(), returning false when the stack is full or empty.
   3. Push 5 values.
   4. Pop and print until the stack is empty. */
#define CAPACITY 10

typedef struct {
    int items[CAPACITY];
    int top;   /* number of items on the stack */
} Stack;

bool push(Stack *s, int value) {
    if (s->top == CAPACITY) {
        return false;   /* stack is full */
    }
    s->items[s->top++] = value;
    return true;
}

bool pop(Stack *s, int *value) {
    if (s->top == 0) {
        return false;   /* stack is empty */
    }
    *value = s->items[--s->top];
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    Stack s = {.top = 0};
    push(&s, 77);
    push(&s, 54);
    push(&s, 28);
    push(&s, 9);
    push(&s, 21);
    int value;
    /* Items come back out in reverse order (last in, first out). */
    while (pop(&s, &value)) {
        printf("%d ", value);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: The Stack keeps up to 10 items in an array, and top counts how many are
   stored. push() adds at the top and pop() removes from the top; both return false when
   they cannot. main() pushes 5 values and pops them all, so they come out in reverse order
   (last in, first out). */
// END

/* Caption: Reverse the characters of a word. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <string.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write reverse_string() for str.
   2. Set i to the first index and j to the last.
   3. Swap the two characters and move i and j inwards until they meet.
   4. Reverse banana and print it. */
/* Swap characters from both ends until they meet in the middle. */
void reverse_string(char *str) {
    int i = 0;
    int j = strlen(str) - 1;
    while (i < j) {
        char tmp = str[i];
        str[i] = str[j];
        str[j] = tmp;
        i++;
        j--;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    char str[] = "banana";
    reverse_string(str);
    printf("%s\n", str);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: reverse_string() swaps characters from both ends of str, moving inwards
   until the two indexes meet. main() reverses the word banana in place and prints it. */
// END

/* Caption: Return the largest element of an array of long values. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write max_of() that takes data and length.
   2. Store data[0] in largest.
   3. Loop over the other elements and keep the largest value in largest.
   4. Return largest and print it. */
/* Start with the first element and keep the largest value seen so far. */
long max_of(const long data[], int length) {
    long largest = data[0];
    for (int i = 1; i < length; i++) {
        if (data[i] > largest) {
            largest = data[i];
        }
    }
    return largest;
}

int main(void) {

    int length = sizeof(data) / sizeof(data[0]);
    printf("The largest value is %ld\n", max_of(data, length));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: max_of() takes the first element as the largest value so far and stores it
   in largest. The loop compares every other element with largest using > and keeps the
   largest one. main() prints the largest of the 9 values. */
// END

/* Caption: Sort an array in ascending order using insertion sort. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write insertion_sort() for the int array items.
   2. Take each element in turn as current.
   3. Shift the larger values of the sorted part one place right.
   4. Put current into the gap.
   5. Print the sorted values. */
/* Insert each element into the already sorted part on its left. */
void insertion_sort(int items[], int n) {
    for (int i = 1; i < n; i++) {
        int current = items[i];
        int j = i - 1;
        while (j >= 0 && items[j] > current) {
            items[j + 1] = items[j];   /* shift bigger values right */
            j--;
        }
        items[j + 1] = current;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    int items[] = {55, 80, 8, 93, 11, 71, 29, 52, 54, 77};
    const int n = 10;
    insertion_sort(items, n);
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        printf("%d ", items[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: insertion_sort() takes each element in turn and shifts the larger values of
   the sorted part one place right until the element fits. main() then prints the 10 values
   in ascending order. */
// END

/* Caption: How do I pass three numbers to a function and return their mean in C? */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write average_of_three(a, b, c).
   2. Return (a + b + c) / 3.0.
   3. Declare a, b and c on one line and print the average. */
double average_of_three(double a, double b, double c) {

/* Caption: Compute the factorial of a number with a loop. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write factorial(n) with result = 1.
   2. Multiply result by every number from 2 to n.
   3. Return result.
   4. Print 14! as an unsigned long long. */
/* Multiply 1 * 2 * ... * n. */
unsigned long long factorial(int n) {
    unsigned long long result = 1;
    for (int i = 2; i <= n; i++) {
        result *= i;
    }
    return result;
}

int main(void) {
    int n = 14;
    printf("%d! = %llu\n", n, factorial(n));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: factorial() multiplies result by every number from 2 up to n. main() prints
   14! as an unsigned long long, because factorials grow very fast. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to decide if a number is odd or even. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Read the number num.
   2. Check whether num % 2 is 0.
   3. Print even or odd. */
int main(void) {
    int num;
    printf("Enter a number: ");
    if (scanf("%d", &num) != 1) {
        printf("Invalid input\n");
        return 1;
    }
    /* Even numbers leave no remainder when divided by 2. */
    if (num % 2 == 0) {
        printf("%d is even\n", num);
    } else {
        printf("%d is odd\n", num);
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: The program reads num from the keyboard with scanf and stops with a message
   if the input is not valid. num % 2 is the remainder after dividing by 2: 0 means even,
   anything else means odd, and the if-else prints which one it is. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to implement selection sort for an array of int values. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write selection_sort() for the int array numbers.
   2. For each position, find the smallest remaining element.
   3. Swap it into that position.
   4. Print the sorted values. */
/* Select the right element for each position and swap it into place. */
void selection_sort(int numbers[], int length) {
    for (int i = 0; i < length - 1; i++) {
        int chosen = i;
        for (int j = i + 1; j < length; j++) {
            if (numbers[chosen] > numbers[j]) {
                chosen = j;
            }
        }
        int tmp = numbers[i];
        numbers[i] = numbers[chosen];
        numbers[chosen] = tmp;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    int numbers[] = {82, 37, 65, 59, 83, 65, 95};
    int length = 7;
    selection_sort(numbers, length);
    for (int i = 0; i < length; i++) {
        printf("%d ", numbers[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: selection_sort() finds the smallest remaining element for each position and
   swaps it into place. main() then prints the 7 values in ascending order. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to print the first 12 Fibonacci numbers. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Start with a = 0 and b = 1.
   2. Repeat 12 times and print a each time.
   3. Compute next = a + b, then set a = b and b = next. */
int main(void) {
    long a = 0, b = 1;
    /* Print a term, then slide the pair one step along the sequence. */
    for (int i = 0; i < 12; i++) {
        printf("%ld ", a);
        long next = a + b;
        a = b;
        b = next;
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: The loop keeps the last two numbers in a and b. Each round it prints a,
   then moves the pair forward: a becomes b and b becomes their sum. It prints the first 12
   Fibonacci numbers. */
// END

/* Caption: Compute the factorial of a number recursively. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write factorial(x) that calls itself.
   2. Return 1 when x is 1 or less.
   3. Otherwise return x * factorial(x - 1).
   4. Print 11! as an unsigned long long. */
/* n! = n * (n - 1)!, and 0! = 1 stops the recursion. */
unsigned long long factorial(int x) {
    if (x <= 1) {
        return 1;
    }
    return x * factorial(x - 1);
}

int main(void) {
    int x = 11;
    printf("%d! = %llu\n", x, factorial(x));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: factorial() calls itself: n! is n * (n - 1)!, and the recursion stops when
   x is 1 or less. main() prints 11! as an unsigned long long, because factorials grow very
   fast. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to write a function that tests if a value is inside a range. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write in_range(x, low, high).
   2. Return true when x >= low and x <= high.
   3. Print whether 73 is inside 41 to 42. */
/* true when low <= x <= high */
bool in_range(int x, int low, int high) {
    return x >= low && x <= high;
}

int main(void) {
    int value = 73, low = 41, high = 42;
    printf("%d is %s the range %d to %d\n", value,
           in_range(value, low, high) ? "inside" : "outside", low, high);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: in_range() takes the value and both limits and returns true only when the
   value is at least low and at most high. main() declares value, low and high on one line
   and prints whether 73 is inside 41 to 42. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to count how many digits a number has. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Start result at 0.
   2. Divide n by 10 and add one to result.
   3. Repeat until n is 0.
   4. Apply it to 941192 and print the result. */
/* Take the last digit with % 10, then drop it with / 10. */
int count_digits(int n) {
    int result = 0;
    while (n > 0) {
        result++;
        n /= 10;
    }
    return result;
}

int main(void) {
    int number = 941192;
    printf("count of digits of %d: %d\n", number, count_digits(number));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: count_digits() removes the last digit (n / 10) and adds one to result each
   time, until n reaches 0. main() applies it to 941192. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to add up all the numbers from 1 to n. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Set n = 44.
   2. Compute n * (n + 1) / 2.
   3. Print the result. */
int main(void) {
    int n = 44;
    /* Gauss's formula: 1 + 2 + ... + n = n * (n + 1) / 2 */
    int sum = n * (n + 1) / 2;
    printf("Sum of 1 to %d = %d\n", n, sum);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: Instead of a loop it uses Gauss's formula n * (n + 1) / 2, which gives the
   sum of 1 to 44 in one step. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to allocate an array with malloc and fill it with multiples. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Use malloc to get room for 11 ints and check for NULL.
   2. Fill arr with multiples.
   3. Print the values.
   4. Call free(arr) at the end. */
int main(void) {
    int n = 11;
    /* Ask the heap for room for n ints; malloc returns NULL on failure. */
    int *arr = malloc(n * sizeof(int));
    if (arr == NULL) {
        fprintf(stderr, "malloc failed\n");
        return 1;
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        arr[i] = 8 * i;
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        printf("%d ", arr[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    free(arr);   /* give the memory back */
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: malloc() reserves room for 11 ints on the heap and returns NULL if it
   fails, which the program checks. The first loop fills arr with multiples, the second
   prints them, and free() gives the memory back at the end. */
// END

/* Caption: Print a Celsius to Fahrenheit conversion table. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write to_fahrenheit() with F = C * 9 / 5 + 32.
   2. Loop c from -20 to 60 in steps of 10.
   3. Print each Celsius value with its Fahrenheit value. */
/* F = C * 9 / 5 + 32 */
double to_fahrenheit(double celsius) {
    return celsius * 9.0 / 5.0 + 32.0;
}

int main(void) {
    printf("Celsius  Fahrenheit\n");
    for (int c = -20; c <= 60; c += 10) {
        printf("%7d  %10.1f\n", c, to_fahrenheit(c));
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: to_fahrenheit() applies F = C * 9 / 5 + 32. main() prints a table from -20
   to 60 degrees Celsius in steps of 10. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to reverse a string in place. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <string.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write reverse_string() for line.
   2. Set i to the first index and j to the last.
   3. Swap the two characters and move i and j inwards until they meet.
   4. Reverse binary and print it. */
/* Swap characters from both ends until they meet in the middle. */
void reverse_string(char *line) {
    int i = 0;
    int j = strlen(line) - 1;
    while (i < j) {
        char tmp = line[i];
        line[i] = line[j];
        line[j] = tmp;
        i++;
        j--;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    char line[] = "binary";
    reverse_string(line);
    printf("%s\n", line);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: reverse_string() swaps characters from both ends of line, moving inwards
   until the two indexes meet. main() reverses the word binary in place and prints it. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to compute the product of two square matrices. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define N as 2.
   2. For every i and j, add a[i][k] * b[k][j] over k into product[i][j].
   3. Print product row by row. */
#define N 2

int main(void) {
    int a[N][N] = {{0, 9}, {8, 4}};
    int b[N][N] = {{2, 0}, {8, 0}};
    int product[N][N] = {0};
    /* product[i][j] is row i of a times column j of b. */
    for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) {
        for (int j = 0; j < N; j++) {
            for (int k = 0; k < N; k++) {
                product[i][j] += a[i][k] * b[k][j];
            }
        }
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) {
        for (int j = 0; j < N; j++) {
            printf("%4d", product[i][j]);
        }
        printf("\n");
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: For each entry product[i][j] the innermost loop adds a[i][k] * b[k][j] over
   k, which is row i of a times column j of b. main() multiplies two 2x2 matrices and
   prints the product. */
// END

/* Explanation: The program reads a and b from the keyboard with scanf and stops with a

   is bigger, then prints best. */
// END

/* Caption: Write lines to a text file and read them back. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Open data.txt in write mode and check for NULL.
   2. Write 4 lines with fprintf and close the file.
   3. Open it again in read mode.
   4. Read and print each line with fgets, then close the file. */
int main(void) {
    FILE *file = fopen("data.txt", "w");
    if (file == NULL) {
        perror("fopen");
        return 1;
    }
    fprintf(file, "loops repeat a block of code\n");
    fprintf(file, "a function can call itself recursively\n");
    fprintf(file, "the compiler turns source code into machine code\n");
    fprintf(file, "c gives you direct control over memory\n");
    fclose(file);

    /* Reopen the file for reading and print it line by line. */
    file = fopen("data.txt", "r");
    if (file == NULL) {
        perror("fopen");
        return 1;
    }
    char line[128];
    while (fgets(line, sizeof(line), file) != NULL) {
        printf("%s", line);
    }
    fclose(file);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: fopen() in write mode creates data.txt, fprintf() writes 4 lines into it
   and fclose() saves it. The file is then opened again in read mode, and fgets() reads it
   back line by line into the buffer line, which is printed. Every fopen() result is
   checked for NULL. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to find a number in a sorted array with binary search. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Make sure the array is sorted.
   2. Set lo to 0 and hi to size - 1.
   3. While lo <= hi, compare the middle element mid with the key.
   4. Return the index if it matches; otherwise keep only the half that can hold the
      key.
   5. Return -1 if the range becomes empty, and print the index of 19. */
/* The array must be sorted. Each step halves the range that can still hold the key. */
int binary_search(const int nums[], int size, int key) {
    int lo = 0;
    int hi = size - 1;
    while (lo <= hi) {
        int mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;
        if (nums[mid] == key) {
            return mid;
        } else if (nums[mid] < key) {
            lo = mid + 1;   /* key is in the right half */
        } else {
            hi = mid - 1;   /* key is in the left half */
        }
    }
    return -1;
}

int main(void) {
    int nums[] = {14, 15, 19, 31, 33, 52, 66, 104, 150, 160};
    int size = 10;
    int index = binary_search(nums, size, 19);
    printf("Index of 19: %d\n", index);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: binary_search() needs a sorted array. It keeps the range from lo to hi,
   compares the middle element mid with the key and throws away the half that cannot
   contain it, so it needs only about log2(n) steps. main() looks for 19 and prints its
   index, or -1 if it is not there. */
// END

/* Caption: C program to evaluate the straight line y = m * x + c with a function. */

/* Explanation: line_y() takes the slope m, the position x and the offset c and returns m *

// END

/* Caption: Write a program to write a function that swaps two int values through pointers. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write swap() that takes pointers to two int values.
   2. Save *first in tmp, copy *second into *first, then tmp into *second.
   3. In main(), print first and second, call swap(&first, &second) and print them
      again. */
/* Pass addresses so the function can change the caller's variables. */
void swap(int *first, int *second) {
    int tmp = *first;
    *first = *second;
    *second = tmp;
}

int main(void) {
    int first = 32, second = 7;
    printf("Before: %d %d\n", first, second);
    swap(&first, &second);
    printf("After:  %d %d\n", first, second);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: swap() receives the addresses of first and second, so writing through the
   pointers *first and *second changes the caller's variables. tmp holds one value during
   the exchange. main() declares both variables on one line and prints them before and
   after the swap. */
// END

/* Caption: Program to print the factorial of an integer. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write factorial(x) with result = 1.
   2. Multiply result by every number from 2 to x.
   3. Return result.
   4. Print 11! as an unsigned long long. */
/* Multiply 1 * 2 * ... * n. */
unsigned long long factorial(int x) {
    unsigned long long result = 1;
    for (int i = 2; i <= x; i++) {
        result *= i;
    }
    return result;
}

int main(void) {
    int x = 11;
    printf("%d! = %llu\n", x, factorial(x));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: factorial() multiplies result by every number from 2 up to x. main() prints
   11! as an unsigned long long, because factorials grow very fast. */
// END

/* Caption: Return two values from a function using pointer parameters. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write circle_measures() with the pointers area and circumference.
   2. Store PI * r * r and 2 * PI * r through them.
   3. Print both for a radius of 29.2. */
#define PI 3.14159265

void circle_measures(double radius, double *area, double *circumference) {
    *area = PI * radius * radius;
    *circumference = 2 * PI * radius;
}

int main(void) {
    double radius = 29.2;
    double area, circumference;
    circle_measures(radius, &area, &circumference);
    printf("Area: %.2f, Circumference: %.2f\n", area, circumference);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: circle_measures() computes two results from one radius and stores them
   through the pointers area and circumference. main() declares both variables on one line,
   passes their addresses and prints the results for a radius of 29.2. */
// END

#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write linear_search() with the array, its length and key.
   2. Compare each element with key.
   3. Return the index of the first match, or -1.
   4. In main(), search for 97 and print the result. */
/* Return the index of key, or -1 when it is not in the array. */
int linear_search(const int marks[], int length, int key) {
    for (int i = 0; i < length; i++) {
        if (marks[i] == key) {
            return i;
        }
    }
    return -1;
}

int main(void) {
    int marks[] = {44, 66, 37, 61, 97, 97, 60, 44, 22, 30};
    const int length = 10;
    int key = 97;
    int pos = linear_search(marks, length, key);
    if (pos >= 0) {
        printf("Found %d at index %d\n", key, pos);
    } else {
        printf("%d is not in the array\n", key);
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: linear_search() checks the elements of marks one by one and returns the
   index of the first one equal to key, or -1 when it reaches the end without a match.
   main() searches for 97 and prints where it is, or that it is missing. */
// END

/* Caption: Add up the digits of a number. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Start result at 0.
   2. Add n % 10 to result, then divide n by 10.
   3. Repeat until n is 0.
   4. Apply it to 86913 and print the result. */
/* Take the last digit with % 10, then drop it with / 10. */
int sum_digits(int n) {
    int result = 0;
    while (n > 0) {
        result += n % 10;
        n /= 10;
    }
    return result;
}

int main(void) {
    int number = 86913;
    printf("sum of digits of %d: %d\n", number, sum_digits(number));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: sum_digits() adds the last digit (n % 10) to result and then removes it (n
   / 10) until no digits are left. main() applies it to 86913. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to find the total of all elements in an array using a loop. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write add_all() that takes the array readings and its length length.
   2. Start acc at 0 and add every element in a for loop.
   3. Return acc.
   4. In main(), fill readings with 4 values and print the sum. */
/* Walk through the array and accumulate each value. */
long add_all(const long readings[], int length) {
    long acc = 0;
    for (int idx = 0; idx < length; idx++) {
        acc += readings[idx];
    }
    return acc;
}

int main(void) {
    long readings[] = {49L, 97L, 60L, 73L};
    const int length = 4;
    printf("Total = %ld\n", add_all(readings, length));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: add_all() receives the array readings and its length length. It starts acc
   at 0, adds every element to it in a for loop and returns the total. main() fills
   readings with 4 long values and prints their sum. */
// END

/* Caption: Program to show the Fibonacci series using recursion. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write fib(n) that returns n when n < 2.
   2. Otherwise return fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2).
   3. Print fib(i) for i from 0 to 24. */
/* Each Fibonacci number is the sum of the two before it. */
long fib(int n) {
    if (n < 2) {
        return n;
    }
    return fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2);
}

int main(void) {
    for (int i = 0; i < 25; i++) {
        printf("%ld ", fib(i));
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: fib() returns n for 0 and 1 and otherwise adds the two previous Fibonacci
   numbers by calling itself twice, which is simple but slow for large n. main() prints the
   first 25 numbers. */
// END

/* Caption: Convert seconds into a struct with hours, minutes and seconds. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define a Duration struct with hours, minutes and seconds.
   2. Write from_seconds() that fills it using / and %.
   3. Convert 14535 seconds and print the members. */
typedef struct {
    int hours;
    int minutes;
    int seconds;
} Duration;

Duration from_seconds(int total) {
    Duration d;
    d.hours = total / 3600;
    d.minutes = (total % 3600) / 60;
    d.seconds = total % 60;
    return d;
}

int main(void) {

    printf("%d h %d min %d s\n", d.hours, d.minutes, d.seconds);
    return 0;
}

   then returns the struct. main() converts 14535 seconds and prints the members. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to compute 8 to the power of 4 without pow(). */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write power(base, exp) with result = 1.
   2. Multiply result by base exp times.
   3. Print 8 to the power 4. */
/* Multiply the base by itself exp times. */
long long power(int base, int exp) {
    long long result = 1;
    for (int i = 0; i < exp; i++) {
        result *= base;
    }
    return result;
}

int main(void) {
    printf("8^4 = %lld\n", power(8, 4));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: power() starts result at 1 and multiplies it by base exp times. It uses
   long long because powers grow quickly. main() prints 8 to the power 4. */
// END

#include <ctype.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write to_upper() for line.
   2. Replace every character with toupper() until the null character.
   3. Print the sentence. */
/* toupper changes lowercase letters and leaves other characters alone. */
void to_upper(char *line) {
    for (int i = 0; line[i] != '\0'; i++) {
        line[i] = toupper((unsigned char)line[i]);
    }
}

int main(void) {

    to_upper(line);
    printf("%s\n", line);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: to_upper() walks through line until the null character and replaces each
   character with toupper(), which only changes lowercase letters. main() prints the
   sentence in capitals. */
// END

/* Caption: Program to check whether a year is a leap year. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write is_leap(year).
   2. A year divisible by 4 is a leap year, unless it is divisible by 100.
   3. Years divisible by 400 are leap years again.
   4. Check 1890 and print the result. */
/* Leap years divide by 4, except centuries, which must divide by 400. */
int is_leap(int year) {
    return (year % 4 == 0 && year % 100 != 0) || year % 400 == 0;
}

int main(void) {
    int year = 1890;
    if (is_leap(year)) {
        printf("%d is a leap year\n", year);
    } else {
        printf("%d is not a leap year\n", year);
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: is_leap() returns true for years divisible by 4, except century years,
   which must also be divisible by 400. main() checks 1890 and prints whether it is a leap
   year. */
// END

/* Caption: Reverse the elements of an array in place. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write reverse_array() for nums.
   2. Set left to the first index and right to the last.
   3. Swap nums[left] and nums[right], then move both inwards.
   4. Stop when left meets right and print the array. */
/* Swap the outer pair, then move both ends toward the middle. */
void reverse_array(double nums[], int length) {
    int left = 0;
    int right = length - 1;
    while (left < right) {
        double tmp = nums[left];
        nums[left] = nums[right];
        nums[right] = tmp;
        left++;
        right--;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    double nums[] = {70.4, 93.5, 93.2, 42.5};
    const int length = 4;
    reverse_array(nums, length);
    for (int i = 0; i < length; i++) {
        printf("%.2f ", nums[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: reverse_array() swaps the first and last elements, then moves left forward
   and right backward until they meet, so the array is reversed in place without a second
   array. main() prints the reversed values. */
// END

/* Caption: How do I use dynamic memory to store the first 9 evens in C? */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Use malloc to get room for 9 ints and check for NULL.
   2. Fill arr with evens.
   3. Print the values.
   4. Call free(arr) at the end. */
int main(void) {
    int n = 9;
    /* Ask the heap for room for n ints; malloc returns NULL on failure. */
    int *arr = malloc(n * sizeof(int));
    if (arr == NULL) {
        fprintf(stderr, "malloc failed\n");
        return 1;
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        arr[i] = 2 * i;
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        printf("%d ", arr[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    free(arr);   /* give the memory back */
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: malloc() reserves room for 9 ints on the heap and returns NULL if it fails,
   which the program checks. The first loop fills arr with evens, the second prints them,
   and free() gives the memory back at the end. */
// END

/* Caption: Use Euclid's algorithm to compute the GCD. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write gcd() with Euclid's algorithm.
   2. Replace (a, b) by (b, a % b) until b is 0.
   3. Return a and print the GCD of 138 and 157. */
/* Euclid: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a % b) until b becomes zero. */
int gcd(int a, int b) {
    while (b != 0) {
        int r = a % b;
        a = b;
        b = r;
    }
    return a;
}

int main(void) {
    int x = 138, y = 157;
    printf("gcd(%d, %d) = %d\n", x, y, gcd(x, y));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: gcd() uses Euclid's algorithm: it keeps replacing (a, b) with (b, a % b)
   until b is 0. The last non-zero value is the greatest common divisor, and main() prints
   the GCD of 138 and 157. */
// END

/* Caption: Search an array for its largest value. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write find_max() that takes prices and size.
   2. Store prices[0] in current.
   3. Loop over the other elements and keep the largest value in current.
   4. Return current and print it. */
/* Start with the first element and keep the largest value seen so far. */
double find_max(const double prices[], int size) {
    double current = prices[0];
    for (int idx = 1; idx < size; idx++) {
        if (prices[idx] > current) {
            current = prices[idx];
        }
    }
    return current;
}

int main(void) {
    double prices[] = {69.9, 70.1, 93.8, 55.3, 29.5, 54.5, 45.0, 65.7};
    int size = sizeof(prices) / sizeof(prices[0]);
    printf("The largest value is %.2f\n", find_max(prices, size));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: find_max() takes the first element as the largest value so far and stores
   it in current. The loop compares every other element with current using > and keeps the
   largest one. main() prints the largest of the 8 values. */
// END

/* Caption: Copy one string into another by hand. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write copy_string(dest, src).
   2. Copy src into dest one character at a time.
   3. Stop after copying the null character.
   4. Copy bridge into word and print it. */
/* Copy each character, including the final '\0'. */
void copy_string(char *dest, const char *src) {
    int i = 0;
    while ((dest[i] = src[i]) != '\0') {
        i++;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    char source[] = "bridge";
    char word[32];
    copy_string(word, source);
    printf("Copied: %s\n", word);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: copy_string() copies src into dest one character at a time, including the
   final null character, which is what strcpy does. The array word must be big enough to
   hold the copy. main() copies the word bridge and prints it. */
// END

/* Caption: How do I find the arithmetic mean of 7 double values in C? */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write average() that takes nums and length.
   2. Add the values into the double total.
   3. Return total / length.
   4. Print the average with two decimals. */
/* The mean is the total divided by the count. */
double average(const double nums[], int length) {
    double total = 0.0;
    int k = 0;
    while (k < length) {
        total += nums[k];
        k++;
    }
    return total / length;
}

int main(void) {
    double nums[] = {86.4, 43.8, 14.6, 3.9, 75.4, 50.6, 58.3};
    int length = sizeof(nums) / sizeof(nums[0]);
    printf("Average: %.2f\n", average(nums, length));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: average() adds the 7 values of nums into the double total and divides by
   length, so the mean keeps its decimal part even when the values are whole numbers.
   main() prints it with two decimals. */
// END

/* Caption: Calculate 9! using recursion. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write factorial(x) that calls itself.
   2. Return 1 when x is 1 or less.
   3. Otherwise return x * factorial(x - 1).
   4. Print 9! as an unsigned long long. */
/* n! = n * (n - 1)!, and 0! = 1 stops the recursion. */
unsigned long long factorial(int x) {
    if (x <= 1) {
        return 1;
    }
    return x * factorial(x - 1);
}

int main(void) {
    int x = 9;
    printf("%d! = %llu\n", x, factorial(x));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: factorial() calls itself: n! is n * (n - 1)!, and the recursion stops when
   x is 1 or less. main() prints 9! as an unsigned long long, because factorials grow very
   fast. */
// END

/* Caption: Build a FIFO queue using a ring buffer. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define a Queue with room for 32 items, a head and a count.
   2. Write enqueue() that stores at (head + count) % CAPACITY.
   3. Write dequeue() that takes the item at head and moves head on.
   4. Add 3 values, then remove and print them in order. */
#define CAPACITY 32

typedef struct {
    int items[CAPACITY];
    int head;
    int count;
} Queue;

bool enqueue(Queue *q, int value) {
    if (q->count == CAPACITY) {
        return false;
    }
    /* The tail wraps around to the start of the array. */
    q->items[(q->head + q->count) % CAPACITY] = value;
    q->count++;
    return true;
}

bool dequeue(Queue *q, int *value) {
    if (q->count == 0) {
        return false;
    }
    *value = q->items[q->head];
    q->head = (q->head + 1) % CAPACITY;
    q->count--;
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    Queue q = {.head = 0, .count = 0};
    enqueue(&q, 72);
    enqueue(&q, 68);
    enqueue(&q, 68);
    int value;
    /* Items come out in the order they went in (first in, first out). */
    while (dequeue(&q, &value)) {
        printf("%d ", value);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: The Queue stores up to 32 items in a ring buffer: head is the oldest item
   and % CAPACITY wraps positions back to the start of the array. enqueue() adds at the
   back and dequeue() removes from the front, so main() gets its 3 values back in the same
   order (first in, first out). */
// END

/* Caption: Use binary search to locate a value in a sorted list. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Make sure the array is sorted.
   2. Set left to 0 and right to size - 1.
   3. While left <= right, compare the middle element middle with the key.
   4. Return the index if it matches; otherwise keep only the half that can hold the
      key.
   5. Return -1 if the range becomes empty, and print the index of 195. */
/* The array must be sorted. Each step halves the range that can still hold the key. */
int binary_search(const int marks[], int size, int key) {
    int left = 0;
    int right = size - 1;
    while (left <= right) {
        int middle = left + (right - left) / 2;
        if (marks[middle] == key) {
            return middle;
        } else if (marks[middle] < key) {
            left = middle + 1;   /* key is in the right half */
        } else {
            right = middle - 1;   /* key is in the left half */
        }
    }
    return -1;
}

int main(void) {
    int marks[] = {2, 20, 82, 109, 169, 180, 192, 195};
    const int size = 8;
    int index = binary_search(marks, size, 195);
    printf("Index of 195: %d\n", index);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: binary_search() needs a sorted array. It keeps the range from left to
   right, compares the middle element middle with the key and throws away the half that
   cannot contain it, so it needs only about log2(n) steps. main() looks for 195 and prints
   its index, or -1 if it is not there. */
// END

/* Caption: Check whether a word is a palindrome. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <string.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write is_palindrome() for line.
   2. Compare the first and last characters, moving inwards.
   3. Return false at the first mismatch, otherwise true.
   4. Check rotor and print the result. */
/* Compare characters from the front and back, moving inwards. */
bool is_palindrome(const char *line) {
    int i = 0;
    int j = strlen(line) - 1;
    while (i < j) {
        if (line[i] != line[j]) {
            return false;
        }
        i++;
        j--;
    }
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    const char *line = "rotor";
    printf("%s %s a palindrome\n", line, is_palindrome(line) ? "is" : "is not");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: is_palindrome() compares the first and last characters and moves inwards;
   any mismatch means the word is not a palindrome. main() checks the word rotor and prints
   the result. */
// END

#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Open notes.txt in write mode and check for NULL.
   2. Write 4 lines with fprintf and close the file.
   3. Open it again in read mode.
   4. Read and print each line with fgets, then close the file. */
int main(void) {
    FILE *file = fopen("notes.txt", "w");
    if (file == NULL) {
        perror("fopen");
        return 1;
    }
    fprintf(file, "learning c teaches how computers work\n");
    fprintf(file, "c gives you direct control over memory\n");
    fprintf(file, "arrays in c start at index zero\n");
    fprintf(file, "always free the memory you allocate\n");
    fclose(file);

    /* Reopen the file for reading and print it line by line. */
    file = fopen("notes.txt", "r");
    if (file == NULL) {
        perror("fopen");
        return 1;
    }
    char line[128];
    while (fgets(line, sizeof(line), file) != NULL) {
        printf("%s", line);
    }
    fclose(file);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: fopen() in write mode creates notes.txt, fprintf() writes 4 lines into it
   and fclose() saves it. The file is then opened again in read mode, and fgets() reads it
   back line by line into the buffer line, which is printed. Every fopen() result is
   checked for NULL. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to add two matrices element by element. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define ROWS as 4 and COLS as 4.
   2. Loop over every row r and column c.
   3. Store a[r][c] + b[r][c] in sum and print it. */
#define ROWS 4
#define COLS 4

int main(void) {
    int a[ROWS][COLS] = {{8, 8, 5, 5}, {0, 7, 7, 2}, {1, 3, 2, 2}, {1, 4, 0, 9}};
    int b[ROWS][COLS] = {{0, 4, 8, 4}, {3, 4, 0, 9}, {6, 6, 6, 6}, {9, 9, 1, 3}};
    int sum[ROWS][COLS];
    /* Each entry of the result is the sum of the matching entries. */
    for (int r = 0; r < ROWS; r++) {
        for (int c = 0; c < COLS; c++) {
            sum[r][c] = a[r][c] + b[r][c];
            printf("%3d", sum[r][c]);
        }
        printf("\n");
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: Both matrices are 4x4 two-dimensional arrays. Two nested loops visit every
   row r and column c, store a[r][c] + b[r][c] in sum and print each row. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to implement selection sort for an array of double values. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write selection_sort() for the double array numbers.
   2. For each position, find the smallest remaining element.
   3. Swap it into that position.
   4. Print the sorted values. */
/* Select the right element for each position and swap it into place. */
void selection_sort(double numbers[], int n) {
    for (int i = 0; i < n - 1; i++) {
        int chosen = i;
        for (int j = i + 1; j < n; j++) {
            if (numbers[chosen] > numbers[j]) {
                chosen = j;
            }
        }
        double tmp = numbers[i];
        numbers[i] = numbers[chosen];
        numbers[chosen] = tmp;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    double numbers[] = {65.6, 50.1, 77.1, 52.7, 63.5, 22.5, 50.4, 14.4, 33.9};
    const int n = 9;
    selection_sort(numbers, n);
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        printf("%.2f ", numbers[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: selection_sort() finds the smallest remaining element for each position and
   swaps it into place. main() then prints the 9 values in ascending order. */
// END

/* Caption: Compute the sum of the elements of an array. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write sum_values() that takes the array items and its length length.
   2. Start sum at 0 and add every element in a while loop.
   3. Return sum.
   4. In main(), fill items with 8 values and print the sum. */
/* Walk through the array and accumulate each value. */
double sum_values(const double items[], int length) {
    double sum = 0;
    int i = 0;
    while (i < length) {
        sum += items[i];
        i++;
    }
    return sum;
}

int main(void) {
    double items[] = {22.1, 79.0, 79.2, 58.9, 6.2, 53.0, 75.5, 49.5};
    int length = 8;
    printf("The sum is %.2f\n", sum_values(items, length));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: sum_values() receives the array items and its length length. It starts sum
   at 0, adds every element to it in a while loop and returns the total. main() fills items
   with 8 double values and prints their sum. */
// END

/* Plan:

   3. Add 10 to x through px and print the values. */
int main(void) {
    int x = 15, y = 29;
    /* Each pointer needs its own '*': in "int *p, q;" only p is a pointer. */
    int *px = &x, *py = &y;
    *px += 10;
    printf("x = %d, y = %d\n", x, y);
    printf("*px = %d, *py = %d\n", *px, *py);

   29. */

/* Caption: Reverse an array by swapping from both ends. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write reverse_array() for marks.
   2. Set start to the first index and end to the last.
   3. Swap marks[start] and marks[end], then move both inwards.
   4. Stop when start meets end and print the array. */
/* Swap the outer pair, then move both ends toward the middle. */
void reverse_array(int marks[], int count) {
    int start = 0;
    int end = count - 1;
    while (start < end) {
        int tmp = marks[start];
        marks[start] = marks[end];
        marks[end] = tmp;
        start++;
        end--;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    int marks[] = {34, 2, 5, 37, 69, 21, 25, 99};
    int count = sizeof(marks) / sizeof(marks[0]);
    reverse_array(marks, count);
    for (int i = 0; i < count; i++) {
        printf("%d ", marks[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: reverse_array() swaps the first and last elements, then moves start forward
   and end backward until they meet, so the array is reversed in place without a second
   array. main() prints the reversed values. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to calculate 15! using recursion. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write factorial(x) that calls itself.
   2. Return 1 when x is 1 or less.
   3. Otherwise return x * factorial(x - 1).
   4. Print 15! as an unsigned long long. */
/* n! = n * (n - 1)!, and 0! = 1 stops the recursion. */
unsigned long long factorial(int x) {
    if (x <= 1) {
        return 1;
    }
    return x * factorial(x - 1);
}

int main(void) {
    int x = 15;
    printf("%d! = %llu\n", x, factorial(x));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: factorial() calls itself: n! is n * (n - 1)!, and the recursion stops when
   x is 1 or less. main() prints 15! as an unsigned long long, because factorials grow very
   fast. */
// END

/* Caption: Compute the sum and the average of an array in one function. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write sum_and_average() with the pointers sum and average.
   2. Add the values into *sum.
   3. Store *sum / n in *average.
   4. Declare total and mean, pass their addresses and print them. */
void sum_and_average(const double v[], int n, double *sum, double *average) {
    *sum = 0.0;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        *sum += v[i];
    }
    *average = *sum / n;
}

int main(void) {
    double readings[] = {93.6, 92.6, 17.8};
    int n = sizeof(readings) / sizeof(readings[0]);
    double total, mean;
    sum_and_average(readings, n, &total, &mean);
    printf("Sum: %.2f, Average: %.2f\n", total, mean);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: sum_and_average() takes the array, its length and two pointers. It adds up
   the 3 values through *sum and then stores *sum / n in *average. main() declares total
   and mean on one line and passes their addresses. */
// END

/* Caption: Convert 703 to binary. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write print_binary(n, bits).
   2. Go through the bits from the highest to the lowest.
   3. Print 1 when (n >> b) & 1 is set, otherwise 0.
   4. Print 703 in binary. */
/* Check each bit from the highest to the lowest. */
void print_binary(unsigned int n, int bits) {
    for (int b = bits - 1; b >= 0; b--) {
        putchar((n >> b) & 1 ? '1' : '0');
    }
    putchar('\n');
}

int main(void) {
    unsigned int number = 703;
    printf("%u in binary: ", number);
    print_binary(number, 12);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: print_binary() checks one bit at a time, from the highest to the lowest: (n
   >> b) & 1 is 1 when bit b is set, so it prints the character 1 or 0. main() prints 703
   in binary. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to search an array for its smallest value. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write min_of() that takes data and n.
   2. Store data[0] in best.
   3. Loop over the other elements and keep the smallest value in best.
   4. Return best and print it. */
/* Start with the first element and keep the smallest value seen so far. */
long min_of(const long data[], int n) {
    long best = data[0];
    for (int i = 1; i < n; i++) {
        if (data[i] < best) {
            best = data[i];
        }
    }
    return best;
}

int main(void) {
    long data[] = {79L, 54L, 43L, 86L, 24L, 77L, 8L, 37L, 2L, 86L};
    int n = 10;
    printf("The smallest value is %ld\n", min_of(data, n));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: min_of() takes the first element as the smallest value so far and stores it
   in best. The loop compares every other element with best using < and keeps the smallest
   one. main() prints the smallest of the 10 values. */
// END

}
/* Explanation: count, total and i are declared together on one line without values, then
   assigned before they are used, because an uninitialised local variable holds garbage.
   The loop adds the squares of 1 to 10 to total. */
// END

   3. Return total.

/* Add every element to a running total. */
double array_sum(const double items[], int count) {
    double total = 0;

    const int count = 6;

   at 0, adds every element to it in a while loop and returns the total. main() fills items
   with 6 double values and prints their sum. */
// END

/* Caption: Program to build a fixed-size integer stack in C. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define a Stack with room for 8 items and a top counter.
   2. Write push() and pop(), returning false when the stack is full or empty.
   3. Push 6 values.
   4. Pop and print until the stack is empty. */
#define CAPACITY 8

typedef struct {
    int items[CAPACITY];
    int top;   /* number of items on the stack */
} Stack;

bool push(Stack *s, int value) {
    if (s->top == CAPACITY) {
        return false;   /* stack is full */
    }
    s->items[s->top++] = value;
    return true;
}

bool pop(Stack *s, int *value) {
    if (s->top == 0) {
        return false;   /* stack is empty */
    }
    *value = s->items[--s->top];
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    Stack s = {.top = 0};
    push(&s, 60);
    push(&s, 97);
    push(&s, 81);
    push(&s, 39);
    push(&s, 89);
    push(&s, 17);
    int value;
    /* Items come back out in reverse order (last in, first out). */
    while (pop(&s, &value)) {
        printf("%d ", value);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: The Stack keeps up to 8 items in an array, and top counts how many are
   stored. push() adds at the top and pop() removes from the top; both return false when
   they cannot. main() pushes 6 values and pops them all, so they come out in reverse order
   (last in, first out). */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to generate the Fibonacci sequence. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write fib(n) that returns n when n < 2.
   2. Otherwise return fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2).
   3. Print fib(i) for i from 0 to 21. */
/* Each Fibonacci number is the sum of the two before it. */
long fib(int n) {
    if (n < 2) {
        return n;
    }
    return fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2);
}

int main(void) {
    for (int i = 0; i < 22; i++) {
        printf("%ld ", fib(i));
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: fib() returns n for 0 and 1 and otherwise adds the two previous Fibonacci
   numbers by calling itself twice, which is simple but slow for large n. main() prints the
   first 22 numbers. */
// END

/* Caption: C program to copy one string into another by hand. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write copy_string(dest, src).
   2. Copy src into dest one character at a time.
   3. Stop after copying the null character.
   4. Copy orange into str and print it. */
/* Copy each character, including the final '\0'. */
void copy_string(char *dest, const char *src) {
    int i = 0;
    while ((dest[i] = src[i]) != '\0') {
        i++;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    char source[] = "orange";
    char str[64];
    copy_string(str, source);
    printf("Copied: %s\n", str);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: copy_string() copies src into dest one character at a time, including the
   final null character, which is what strcpy does. The array str must be big enough to
   hold the copy. main() copies the word orange and prints it. */
// END

/* Caption: Find the greatest common divisor of two numbers. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write gcd() with Euclid's algorithm.
   2. Replace (a, b) by (b, a % b) until b is 0.
   3. Return a and print the GCD of 77 and 110. */
/* Euclid: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a % b) until b becomes zero. */
int gcd(int a, int b) {
    while (b != 0) {
        int r = a % b;
        a = b;
        b = r;
    }
    return a;
}

int main(void) {
    int x = 77, y = 110;
    printf("gcd(%d, %d) = %d\n", x, y, gcd(x, y));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: gcd() uses Euclid's algorithm: it keeps replacing (a, b) with (b, a % b)
   until b is 0. The last non-zero value is the greatest common divisor, and main() prints
   the GCD of 77 and 110. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to find the index of a number using linear search. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write linear_search() with the array, its length and target.
   2. Compare each element with target.
   3. Return the index of the first match, or -1.
   4. In main(), search for 10 and print the result. */
/* Return the index of target, or -1 when it is not in the array. */
int linear_search(const int ages[], int length, int target) {
    for (int i = 0; i < length; i++) {
        if (ages[i] == target) {
            return i;
        }
    }
    return -1;
}

int main(void) {
    int ages[] = {72, 16, 28, 11, 10, 48};
    const int length = 6;
    int target = 10;
    int pos = linear_search(ages, length, target);
    if (pos >= 0) {
        printf("Found %d at index %d\n", target, pos);
    } else {
        printf("%d is not in the array\n", target);
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: linear_search() checks the elements of ages one by one and returns the
   index of the first one equal to target, or -1 when it reaches the end without a match.
   main() searches for 10 and prints where it is, or that it is missing. */
// END

/* Caption: How do I write a function that swaps two int values through pointers in C? */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write swap() that takes pointers to two int values.
   2. Save *x in tmp, copy *y into *x, then tmp into *y.
   3. In main(), print x and y, call swap(&x, &y) and print them again. */
/* Pass addresses so the function can change the caller's variables. */
void swap(int *x, int *y) {
    int tmp = *x;
    *x = *y;
    *y = tmp;
}

int main(void) {
    int x = 39, y = 74;
    printf("Before: %d %d\n", x, y);
    swap(&x, &y);
    printf("After:  %d %d\n", x, y);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: swap() receives the addresses of x and y, so writing through the pointers
   *x and *y changes the caller's variables. tmp holds one value during the exchange.
   main() declares both variables on one line and prints them before and after the swap. */
// END

   4. Copy deified into text and print it. */
/* Copy each character, including the final '\0'. */
void copy_string(char *dest, const char *src) {
    int i = 0;
    while ((dest[i] = src[i]) != '\0') {
        i++;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    char source[] = "deified";
    char text[100];
    copy_string(text, source);
    printf("Copied: %s\n", text);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: copy_string() copies src into dest one character at a time, including the
   final null character, which is what strcpy does. The array text must be big enough to
   hold the copy. main() copies the word deified and prints it. */
// END

/* Caption: Program to add up all the numbers in an array of double values. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write total_of() that takes the array readings and its length len.
   2. Start result at 0 and add every element in a while loop.
   3. Return result.
   4. In main(), fill readings with 5 values and print the sum. */
/* Return the sum of the first n elements. */
double total_of(const double readings[], int len) {
    double result = 0;
    int i = 0;
    while (i < len) {
        result += readings[i];
        i++;
    }
    return result;
}

int main(void) {
    double readings[] = {43.2, 64.3, 15.8, 72.0, 20.4};
    const int len = 5;
    printf("Sum: %.2f\n", total_of(readings, len));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: total_of() receives the array readings and its length len. It starts result
   at 0, adds every element to it in a while loop and returns the total. main() fills
   readings with 5 double values and prints their sum. */
// END

   2. Divide n by 10 and add one to result.
   3. Repeat until n is 0.
   4. Apply it to 600793 and print the result. */
/* Take the last digit with % 10, then drop it with / 10. */
int count_digits(int n) {
    int result = 0;

        result++;
        n /= 10;

/* Caption: Decide if 2029 is a leap year. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write is_leap(year).
   2. A year divisible by 4 is a leap year, unless it is divisible by 100.
   3. Years divisible by 400 are leap years again.
   4. Check 2029 and print the result. */
/* Leap years divide by 4, except centuries, which must divide by 400. */
int is_leap(int year) {
    return (year % 4 == 0 && year % 100 != 0) || year % 400 == 0;
}

int main(void) {
    int year = 2029;
    if (is_leap(year)) {
        printf("%d is a leap year\n", year);
    } else {
        printf("%d is not a leap year\n", year);
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: is_leap() returns true for years divisible by 4, except century years,
   which must also be divisible by 400. main() checks 2029 and prints whether it is a leap
   year. */
// END

/* Caption: Return two values from a function using pointer parameters. */

#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write divide(a, b, &quotient, &remainder) that returns a bool.
   2. Return false if b is 0.
   3. Store a / b and a % b through the pointers and return true.
   4. Divide 13 by 22 and print the results or the error. */
/* Returns false for division by zero; otherwise stores both results. */
bool divide(int a, int b, int *quotient, int *remainder) {
    if (b == 0) {
        return false;
    }
    *quotient = a / b;
    *remainder = a % b;
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    int a = 13, b = 22;
    int q, r;
    if (divide(a, b, &q, &r)) {
        printf("%d / %d = %d remainder %d\n", a, b, q, r);
    } else {
        printf("Cannot divide by zero\n");
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: divide() has four parameters: two inputs and two pointers for the results.
   Its bool return value reports success, while the quotient and remainder are written
   through the pointers. main() divides 13 by 22 and prints both results. */
// END

/* Caption: C program to find the minimum and maximum of an array with one function. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write min_max() with the array, its length and the pointers min and max.
   2. Start both at the first element.
   3. Update *min and *max while looping over the rest.
   4. Declare low and high, pass their addresses and print them. */
/* One pass finds both results; they are stored through the pointers. */
void min_max(const int numbers[], int size, int *min, int *max) {
    *min = numbers[0];
    *max = numbers[0];
    for (int i = 1; i < size; i++) {
        if (numbers[i] < *min) {
            *min = numbers[i];
        }
        if (numbers[i] > *max) {
            *max = numbers[i];
        }
    }
}

int main(void) {
    int numbers[] = {78, 1, 9, 11, 10};
    int size = sizeof(numbers) / sizeof(numbers[0]);
    int low, high;
    min_max(numbers, size, &low, &high);
    printf("Min: %d, Max: %d\n", low, high);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: A C function can return only one value, so min_max() returns void and
   writes its two results through the pointer parameters min and max. main() declares low
   and high on one line and passes their addresses with &, then prints both results for the
   5 values. */
// END
