/* Caption: Implement a circular queue with an array. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define a Queue with room for 16 items, a head and a count.
   2. Write enqueue() that stores at (head + count) % CAPACITY.
   3. Write dequeue() that takes the item at head and moves head on.
   4. Add 6 values, then remove and print them in order. */
#define CAPACITY 16

typedef struct {
    int items[CAPACITY];
    int head;
    int count;
} Queue;

bool enqueue(Queue *q, int value) {
    if (q->count == CAPACITY) {
        return false;
    }
    /* The tail wraps around to the start of the array. */
    q->items[(q->head + q->count) % CAPACITY] = value;
    q->count++;
    return true;
}

bool dequeue(Queue *q, int *value) {
    if (q->count == 0) {
        return false;
    }
    *value = q->items[q->head];
    q->head = (q->head + 1) % CAPACITY;
    q->count--;
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    Queue q = {.head = 0, .count = 0};
    enqueue(&q, 38);
    enqueue(&q, 49);
    enqueue(&q, 8);
    enqueue(&q, 55);
    enqueue(&q, 67);
    enqueue(&q, 31);
    int value;
    /* Items come out in the order they went in (first in, first out). */
    while (dequeue(&q, &value)) {
        printf("%d ", value);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: The Queue stores up to 16 items in a ring buffer: head is the oldest item
   and % CAPACITY wraps positions back to the start of the array. enqueue() adds at the
   back and dequeue() removes from the front, so main() gets its 6 values back in the same
   order (first in, first out). */
// END

/* Caption: How do I find the minimum and maximum of an array with one function in C? */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write min_max() with the array, its length and the pointers min and max.
   2. Start both at the first element.
   3. Update *min and *max while looping over the rest.
   4. Declare min and max, pass their addresses and print them. */
/* One pass finds both results; they are stored through the pointers. */
void min_max(const int nums[], int n, int *min, int *max) {
    *min = nums[0];
    *max = nums[0];
    for (int i = 1; i < n; i++) {
        if (nums[i] < *min) {
            *min = nums[i];
        }
        if (nums[i] > *max) {
            *max = nums[i];
        }
    }
}

int main(void) {
    int nums[] = {1, 66, 75, 66, 36, 86, 21, 69};
    int n = sizeof(nums) / sizeof(nums[0]);
    int min, max;
    min_max(nums, n, &min, &max);
    printf("Min: %d, Max: %d\n", min, max);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: A C function can return only one value, so min_max() returns void and
   writes its two results through the pointer parameters min and max. main() declares min
   and max on one line and passes their addresses with &, then prints both results for the
   8 values. */
// END

/* Caption: Program to compute the factorial of a number recursively. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write factorial(num) that calls itself.
   2. Return 1 when num is 1 or less.
   3. Otherwise return num * factorial(num - 1).
   4. Print 6! as an unsigned long long. */
/* n! = n * (n - 1)!, and 0! = 1 stops the recursion. */
unsigned long long factorial(int num) {
    if (num <= 1) {
        return 1;
    }
    return num * factorial(num - 1);
}

int main(void) {
    int num = 6;
    printf("%d! = %llu\n", num, factorial(num));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: factorial() calls itself: n! is n * (n - 1)!, and the recursion stops when
   num is 1 or less. main() prints 6! as an unsigned long long, because factorials grow
   very fast. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to compute the LCM of two integers using the GCD. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write gcd() with Euclid's algorithm: replace (a, b) by (b, a % b) until b is 0.
   2. Write lcm() as a / gcd(a, b) * b.
   3. Print the LCM of 214 and 190. */
/* Euclid: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a % b) until b becomes zero. */
int gcd(int a, int b) {
    while (b != 0) {
        int r = a % b;
        a = b;
        b = r;
    }
    return a;
}

/* lcm(a, b) = a / gcd(a, b) * b (divide first to avoid overflow). */
long lcm(int a, int b) {
    return (long)a / gcd(a, b) * b;
}

int main(void) {
    printf("lcm(214, 190) = %ld\n", lcm(214, 190));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: gcd() uses Euclid's algorithm: it keeps replacing (a, b) with (b, a % b)
   until b is 0. lcm() divides a by the gcd before multiplying by b, which avoids overflow.
   main() prints the LCM of 214 and 190. */
// END

/* Caption: Program to allocate an array with malloc and fill it with squares. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Use malloc to get room for 11 ints and check for NULL.
   2. Fill arr with squares.
   3. Print the values.
   4. Call free(arr) at the end. */
int main(void) {
    int n = 11;
    /* Ask the heap for room for n ints; malloc returns NULL on failure. */
    int *arr = malloc(n * sizeof(int));
    if (arr == NULL) {
        fprintf(stderr, "malloc failed\n");
        return 1;
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        arr[i] = i * i;
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        printf("%d ", arr[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    free(arr);   /* give the memory back */
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: malloc() reserves room for 11 ints on the heap and returns NULL if it
   fails, which the program checks. The first loop fills arr with squares, the second
   prints them, and free() gives the memory back at the end. */
// END

/* Caption: Write lines to a text file and read them back. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Open output.txt in write mode and check for NULL.
   2. Write 4 lines with fprintf and close the file.
   3. Open it again in read mode.
   4. Read and print each line with fgets, then close the file. */
int main(void) {
    FILE *file = fopen("output.txt", "w");
    if (file == NULL) {
        perror("fopen");
        return 1;
    }
    fprintf(file, "learning c teaches how computers work\n");
    fprintf(file, "always free the memory you allocate\n");
    fprintf(file, "c gives you direct control over memory\n");
    fprintf(file, "the quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog\n");
    fclose(file);

    /* Reopen the file for reading and print it line by line. */
    file = fopen("output.txt", "r");
    if (file == NULL) {
        perror("fopen");
        return 1;
    }
    char line[128];
    while (fgets(line, sizeof(line), file) != NULL) {
        printf("%s", line);
    }
    fclose(file);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: fopen() in write mode creates output.txt, fprintf() writes 4 lines into it
   and fclose() saves it. The file is then opened again in read mode, and fgets() reads it
   back line by line into the buffer line, which is printed. Every fopen() result is
   checked for NULL. */
// END

/* Caption: Program to search an array for its smallest value. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write find_min() that takes ages and count.
   2. Store ages[0] in smallest.
   3. Loop over the other elements and keep the smallest value in smallest.
   4. Return smallest and print it. */
/* Start with the first element and keep the smallest value seen so far. */
int find_min(const int ages[], int count) {
    int smallest = ages[0];
    for (int idx = 1; idx < count; idx++) {
        if (ages[idx] < smallest) {
            smallest = ages[idx];
        }
    }
    return smallest;
}

int main(void) {
    int ages[] = {81, 88, 85, 70};
    int count = 4;
    printf("Smallest: %d\n", find_min(ages, count));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: find_min() takes the first element as the smallest value so far and stores
   it in smallest. The loop compares every other element with smallest using < and keeps
   the smallest one. main() prints the smallest of the 4 values. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to count how many odd numbers are in an array. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write count_odd() that takes prices and length.
   2. For each element, test prices[j] % 2 != 0.
   3. Add one to matches for every odd number.
   4. Return matches and print it. */
/* A number is odd when the remainder after dividing by 2 is one. */
int count_odd(const int prices[], int length) {
    int matches = 0;
    for (int j = 0; j < length; j++) {
        if (prices[j] % 2 != 0) {
            matches++;
        }
    }
    return matches;
}

int main(void) {
    int prices[] = {12, 67, 87, 83, 6, 70, 60, 18, 4, 18, 44};
    int length = 11;
    printf("Count of odd values = %d\n", count_odd(prices, length));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: count_odd() tests each element of prices with the % operator: a remainder
   of 1 after dividing by 2 means the number is odd, so matches goes up by one. main()
   prints how many of the 11 values are odd. */
// END

/* Caption: Use selection sort to put numbers in ascending order. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write selection_sort() for the int array readings.
   2. For each position, find the smallest remaining element.
   3. Swap it into that position.
   4. Print the sorted values. */
/* Select the right element for each position and swap it into place. */
void selection_sort(int readings[], int len) {
    for (int i = 0; i < len - 1; i++) {
        int chosen = i;
        for (int j = i + 1; j < len; j++) {
            if (readings[chosen] > readings[j]) {
                chosen = j;
            }
        }
        int tmp = readings[i];
        readings[i] = readings[chosen];
        readings[chosen] = tmp;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    int readings[] = {15, 42, 10, 10, 98, 93, 53, 60};
    int len = sizeof(readings) / sizeof(readings[0]);
    selection_sort(readings, len);
    for (int i = 0; i < len; i++) {
        printf("%d ", readings[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: selection_sort() finds the smallest remaining element for each position and
   swaps it into place. main() then prints the 8 values in ascending order. */
// END

/* Caption: Evaluate the straight line y = m * x + c with a function. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write line_y(m, x, c) that returns m * x + c.
   2. Declare m and c on one line.
   3. Print y for every x from 0 to 5. */
/* A straight line: slope m, starting height c. */
double line_y(double m, double x, double c) {
    return m * x + c;
}

int main(void) {
    double m = 3.5, c = 2.1;
    for (int x = 0; x <= 5; x++) {
        printf("x = %d, y = %.1f\n", x, line_y(m, x, c));
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: line_y() takes the slope m, the position x and the offset c and returns m *
   x + c. main() declares m = 3.5 and c = 2.1 on one line and prints y for every x from 0
   to 5. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a function that swaps two long values through pointers. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write swap() that takes pointers to two long values.
   2. Save *a in tmp, copy *b into *a, then tmp into *b.
   3. In main(), print a and b, call swap(&a, &b) and print them again. */
/* Pass addresses so the function can change the caller's variables. */
void swap(long *a, long *b) {
    long tmp = *a;
    *a = *b;
    *b = tmp;
}

int main(void) {
    long a = 79L, b = 53L;
    printf("Before: %ld %ld\n", a, b);
    swap(&a, &b);
    printf("After:  %ld %ld\n", a, b);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: swap() receives the addresses of a and b, so writing through the pointers
   *a and *b changes the caller's variables. tmp holds one value during the exchange.
   main() declares both variables on one line and prints them before and after the swap. */
// END

/* Caption: Program to search an array for a value and print its position. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write linear_search() with the array, its length and key.
   2. Compare each element with key.
   3. Return the index of the first match, or -1.
   4. In main(), search for 52 and print the result. */
/* Return the index of key, or -1 when it is not in the array. */
int linear_search(const int values[], int n, int key) {
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        if (values[i] == key) {
            return i;
        }
    }
    return -1;
}

int main(void) {
    int values[] = {70, 40, 75, 87, 89, 10, 52, 20};
    int n = 8;
    int key = 52;
    int pos = linear_search(values, n, key);
    if (pos >= 0) {
        printf("Found %d at index %d\n", key, pos);
    } else {
        printf("%d is not in the array\n", key);
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: linear_search() checks the elements of values one by one and returns the
   index of the first one equal to key, or -1 when it reaches the end without a match.
   main() searches for 52 and prints where it is, or that it is missing. */
// END

/* Caption: Compute the LCM of two integers using the GCD. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write gcd() with Euclid's algorithm: replace (a, b) by (b, a % b) until b is 0.
   2. Write lcm() as a / gcd(a, b) * b.
   3. Print the LCM of 45 and 252. */
/* Euclid: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a % b) until b becomes zero. */
int gcd(int a, int b) {
    while (b != 0) {
        int r = a % b;
        a = b;
        b = r;
    }
    return a;
}

/* lcm(a, b) = a / gcd(a, b) * b (divide first to avoid overflow). */
long lcm(int a, int b) {
    return (long)a / gcd(a, b) * b;
}

int main(void) {
    printf("lcm(45, 252) = %ld\n", lcm(45, 252));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: gcd() uses Euclid's algorithm: it keeps replacing (a, b) with (b, a % b)
   until b is 0. lcm() divides a by the gcd before multiplying by b, which avoids overflow.
   main() prints the LCM of 45 and 252. */
// END

/* Caption: How do I save text to a file with fprintf and print it with fgets in C? */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Open notes.txt in write mode and check for NULL.
   2. Write 2 lines with fprintf and close the file.
   3. Open it again in read mode.
   4. Read and print each line with fgets, then close the file. */
int main(void) {
    FILE *file = fopen("notes.txt", "w");
    if (file == NULL) {
        perror("fopen");
        return 1;
    }
    fprintf(file, "every program starts in main\n");
    fprintf(file, "learning c teaches how computers work\n");
    fclose(file);

    /* Reopen the file for reading and print it line by line. */
    file = fopen("notes.txt", "r");
    if (file == NULL) {
        perror("fopen");
        return 1;
    }
    char line[128];
    while (fgets(line, sizeof(line), file) != NULL) {
        printf("%s", line);
    }
    fclose(file);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: fopen() in write mode creates notes.txt, fprintf() writes 2 lines into it
   and fclose() saves it. The file is then opened again in read mode, and fgets() reads it
   back line by line into the buffer line, which is printed. Every fopen() result is
   checked for NULL. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a function that tests if a value is inside a range. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write in_range(x, low, high).
   2. Return true when x >= low and x <= high.
   3. Print whether 101 is inside 25 to 50. */
/* true when low <= x <= high */
bool in_range(int x, int low, int high) {
    return x >= low && x <= high;

   and prints whether 101 is inside 25 to 50. */
// END

/* Caption: Program to count how many words are separated by spaces in a string. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <ctype.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write count_words() with words = 0 and an in_word flag.
   2. A space ends a word; a non-space after a space starts a new word and adds one to
      words.
   3. Return words and print it. */
/* A new word starts when a non-space follows a space (or the start). */
int count_words(const char *text) {
    int words = 0;
    int in_word = 0;
    for (int i = 0; text[i] != '\0'; i++) {
        if (isspace((unsigned char)text[i])) {
            in_word = 0;
        } else if (!in_word) {
            in_word = 1;
            words++;
        }
    }
    return words;
}

int main(void) {
    const char *sentence = "arrays in c start at index zero";
    printf("Words: %d\n", count_words(sentence));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: count_words() uses the flag in_word: a new word starts when a non-space
   character follows a space or the start of the text. main() prints the number of words in
   the sentence. */
// END

/* Caption: Create a singly linked list by inserting at the head. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define Item with a value and a next pointer.
   2. Write push_front() that mallocs a node and links it in front of head.
   3. Write print_list() that follows next until NULL.
   4. Write free_list() that frees every node.
   5. Push 3 values, print the list and free it. */
typedef struct Item {
    int value;
    struct Item *next;
} Item;

/* Allocate a new node and put it in front of the current head. */
Item *push_front(Item *head, int value) {
    Item *node = malloc(sizeof(Item));
    if (node == NULL) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Out of memory\n");
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }
    node->value = value;
    node->next = head;
    return node;
}

void print_list(const Item *head) {
    for (const Item *cur = head; cur != NULL; cur = cur->next) {
        printf("%d -> ", cur->value);
    }
    printf("NULL\n");
}

/* Free every node; save next before freeing the current one. */
void free_list(Item *head) {
    while (head != NULL) {
        Item *next = head->next;
        free(head);
        head = next;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    Item *head = NULL;
    head = push_front(head, 26);
    head = push_front(head, 51);
    head = push_front(head, 19);
    print_list(head);
    free_list(head);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: Each Item holds a value and a pointer to the next node. push_front()
   allocates a node with malloc, puts it in front of head and returns it; print_list()
   follows the next pointers until NULL; free_list() frees every node. main() pushes 3
   values, so they print in reverse order. */
// END

/* Caption: Copy one string into another by hand. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write copy_string(dest, src).
   2. Copy src into dest one character at a time.
   3. Stop after copying the null character.
   4. Copy library into str and print it. */
/* Copy each character, including the final '\0'. */
void copy_string(char *dest, const char *src) {
    int i = 0;
    while ((dest[i] = src[i]) != '\0') {
        i++;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    char source[] = "library";
    char str[64];
    copy_string(str, source);
    printf("Copied: %s\n", str);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: copy_string() copies src into dest one character at a time, including the
   final null character, which is what strcpy does. The array str must be big enough to
   hold the copy. main() copies the word library and prints it. */
// END

/* Caption: C program to write a function that returns a Fraction struct. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define a Fraction struct with num and den.
   2. Write multiply() that returns num = a.num * b.num and den = a.den * b.den.
   3. Print 9/5 times 1/6. */
typedef struct {
    int num;
    int den;
} Fraction;

/* Multiply the numerators and the denominators. */
Fraction multiply(Fraction a, Fraction b) {
    Fraction r = {a.num * b.num, a.den * b.den};
    return r;
}

int main(void) {
    Fraction x = {9, 5}, y = {1, 6};
    Fraction p = multiply(x, y);
    printf("%d/%d * %d/%d = %d/%d\n", x.num, x.den, y.num, y.den, p.num, p.den);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: Fraction stores a numerator and a denominator. multiply() takes two
   Fractions and returns a new one with num = a.num * b.num and den = a.den * b.den. main()
   multiplies 9/5 by 1/6 (without reducing the result). */
// END

/* Caption: Program to show the Fibonacci series with a loop. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Start with first = 0 and second = 1.
   2. Repeat 19 times and print first each time.
   3. Compute next = first + second, then set first = second and second = next. */
int main(void) {
    long first = 0, second = 1;
    /* Print a term, then slide the pair one step along the sequence. */
    for (int i = 0; i < 19; i++) {
        printf("%ld ", first);
        long next = first + second;
        first = second;
        second = next;
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: The loop keeps the last two numbers in first and second. Each round it
   prints first, then moves the pair forward: first becomes second and second becomes their
   sum. It prints the first 19 Fibonacci numbers. */
// END

/* Caption: Count how many odd numbers are in an array. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write count_odd() that takes data and count.
   2. For each element, test data[i] % 2 != 0.
   3. Add one to tally for every odd number.
   4. Return tally and print it. */
/* A number is odd when the remainder after dividing by 2 is one. */
int count_odd(const int data[], int count) {
    int tally = 0;
    int i = 0;
    while (i < count) {
        if (data[i] % 2 != 0) {
            tally++;
        }
        i++;
    }
    return tally;
}

int main(void) {
    int data[] = {46, 66, 29, 41, 71};
    const int count = 5;
    printf("Odd numbers: %d\n", count_odd(data, count));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: count_odd() tests each element of data with the % operator: a remainder of
   1 after dividing by 2 means the number is odd, so tally goes up by one. main() prints
   how many of the 5 values are odd. */
// END

/* Caption: Program to use binary search to locate a value in a sorted list. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Make sure the array is sorted.
   2. Set left to 0 and right to length - 1.
   3. While left <= right, compare the middle element middle with the key.
   4. Return the index if it matches; otherwise keep only the half that can hold the
      key.
   5. Return -1 if the range becomes empty, and print the index of 110. */
/* The array must be sorted. Each step halves the range that can still hold the key. */
int binary_search(const int prices[], int length, int key) {
    int left = 0;
    int right = length - 1;
    while (left <= right) {
        int middle = left + (right - left) / 2;
        if (prices[middle] == key) {
            return middle;
        } else if (prices[middle] < key) {
            left = middle + 1;   /* key is in the right half */
        } else {
            right = middle - 1;   /* key is in the left half */
        }
    }
    return -1;
}

int main(void) {
    int prices[] = {43, 53, 74, 110, 138, 146, 155, 185, 192};
    int length = sizeof(prices) / sizeof(prices[0]);
    int index = binary_search(prices, length, 110);
    printf("Index of 110: %d\n", index);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: binary_search() needs a sorted array. It keeps the range from left to
   right, compares the middle element middle with the key and throws away the half that
   cannot contain it, so it needs only about log2(n) steps. main() looks for 110 and prints
   its index, or -1 if it is not there. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to implement a stack with an array (push and pop). */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define a Stack with room for 10 items and a top counter.
   2. Write push() and pop(), returning false when the stack is full or empty.
   3. Push 6 values.
   4. Pop and print until the stack is empty. */
#define CAPACITY 10

typedef struct {
    int items[CAPACITY];
    int top;   /* number of items on the stack */
} Stack;

bool push(Stack *s, int value) {
    if (s->top == CAPACITY) {
        return false;   /* stack is full */
    }
    s->items[s->top++] = value;
    return true;
}

bool pop(Stack *s, int *value) {
    if (s->top == 0) {
        return false;   /* stack is empty */
    }
    *value = s->items[--s->top];
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    Stack s = {.top = 0};
    push(&s, 4);
    push(&s, 68);
    push(&s, 64);
    push(&s, 93);
    push(&s, 76);
    push(&s, 22);
    int value;
    /* Items come back out in reverse order (last in, first out). */
    while (pop(&s, &value)) {
        printf("%d ", value);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: The Stack keeps up to 10 items in an array, and top counts how many are
   stored. push() adds at the top and pop() removes from the top; both return false when
   they cannot. main() pushes 6 values and pops them all, so they come out in reverse order
   (last in, first out). */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to build a fixed-size integer stack in C. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define a Stack with room for 32 items and a top counter.
   2. Write push() and pop(), returning false when the stack is full or empty.
   3. Push 6 values.
   4. Pop and print until the stack is empty. */
#define CAPACITY 32

typedef struct {
    int items[CAPACITY];
    int top;   /* number of items on the stack */
} Stack;

bool push(Stack *s, int value) {
    if (s->top == CAPACITY) {
        return false;   /* stack is full */
    }
    s->items[s->top++] = value;
    return true;
}

bool pop(Stack *s, int *value) {
    if (s->top == 0) {
        return false;   /* stack is empty */
    }
    *value = s->items[--s->top];
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    Stack s = {.top = 0};
    push(&s, 16);
    push(&s, 63);
    push(&s, 48);
    push(&s, 71);
    push(&s, 17);
    push(&s, 82);
    int value;
    /* Items come back out in reverse order (last in, first out). */
    while (pop(&s, &value)) {
        printf("%d ", value);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: The Stack keeps up to 32 items in an array, and top counts how many are
   stored. push() adds at the top and pop() removes from the top; both return false when
   they cannot. main() pushes 6 values and pops them all, so they come out in reverse order
   (last in, first out). */
// END

/* Caption: How do I implement bubble sort for an array of int values in C? */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write bubble_sort() for the int array marks.
   2. Compare each pair of neighbours.
   3. Swap them when they are in the wrong order for descending order.
   4. Repeat the passes until the array is sorted.
   5. Print the sorted values. */
/* Repeatedly swap neighbours that are in the wrong order. */
void bubble_sort(int marks[], int size) {
    for (int i = 0; i < size - 1; i++) {
        for (int j = 0; j < size - 1 - i; j++) {
            if (marks[j] < marks[j + 1]) {
                int tmp = marks[j];
                marks[j] = marks[j + 1];
                marks[j + 1] = tmp;
            }
        }
    }
}

int main(void) {
    int marks[] = {39, 58, 12, 59, 81, 85, 82};
    int size = 7;
    bubble_sort(marks, size);
    for (int i = 0; i < size; i++) {
        printf("%d ", marks[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: bubble_sort() walks through marks again and again and swaps neighbours that
   are in the wrong order, so the smallest values move to the end first. main() then prints
   the 7 values in descending order. */
// END

/* Caption: Add up the digits of a number. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Start result at 0.
   2. Add n % 10 to result, then divide n by 10.
   3. Repeat until n is 0.
   4. Apply it to 130945 and print the result. */
/* Take the last digit with % 10, then drop it with / 10. */
int sum_digits(int n) {
    int result = 0;
    while (n > 0) {
        result += n % 10;
        n /= 10;
    }
    return result;
}

int main(void) {
    int number = 130945;
    printf("sum of digits of %d: %d\n", number, sum_digits(number));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: sum_digits() adds the last digit (n % 10) to result and then removes it (n
   / 10) until no digits are left. main() applies it to 130945. */
// END

/* Caption: Count the even values in a list of integers. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write count_even() that takes nums and size.
   2. For each element, test nums[idx] % 2 == 0.
   3. Add one to tally for every even number.
   4. Return tally and print it. */
/* A number is even when the remainder after dividing by 2 is zero. */
int count_even(const int nums[], int size) {
    int tally = 0;
    int idx = 0;
    while (idx < size) {
        if (nums[idx] % 2 == 0) {
            tally++;
        }
        idx++;
    }
    return tally;
}

int main(void) {
    int nums[] = {95, 69, 12, 94, 53};
    int size = sizeof(nums) / sizeof(nums[0]);
    printf("Count of even values = %d\n", count_even(nums, size));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: count_even() tests each element of nums with the % operator: a remainder of
   0 after dividing by 2 means the number is even, so tally goes up by one. main() prints
   how many of the 5 values are even. */
// END

/* Caption: How do I reverse the elements of an array in place in C? */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write reverse_array() for ages.
   2. Set start to the first index and end to the last.
   3. Swap ages[start] and ages[end], then move both inwards.
   4. Stop when start meets end and print the array. */
/* Swap the outer pair, then move both ends toward the middle. */
void reverse_array(int ages[], int count) {
    int start = 0;
    int end = count - 1;
    while (start < end) {
        int tmp = ages[start];
        ages[start] = ages[end];
        ages[end] = tmp;
        start++;
        end--;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    int ages[] = {56, 68, 67, 26, 95, 1, 30, 53};
    int count = sizeof(ages) / sizeof(ages[0]);
    reverse_array(ages, count);
    for (int i = 0; i < count; i++) {
        printf("%d ", ages[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: reverse_array() swaps the first and last elements, then moves start forward
   and end backward until they meet, so the array is reversed in place without a second
   array. main() prints the reversed values. */
// END

/* Caption: Test if "banana" reads the same backwards. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <string.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write is_palindrome() for line.
   2. Compare the first and last characters, moving inwards.
   3. Return false at the first mismatch, otherwise true.
   4. Check banana and print the result. */
/* Compare characters from the front and back, moving inwards. */
bool is_palindrome(const char *line) {
    int i = 0;
    int j = strlen(line) - 1;
    while (i < j) {
        if (line[i] != line[j]) {
            return false;
        }
        i++;
        j--;
    }
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    const char *line = "banana";
    printf("%s %s a palindrome\n", line, is_palindrome(line) ? "is" : "is not");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: is_palindrome() compares the first and last characters and moves inwards;
   any mismatch means the word is not a palindrome. main() checks the word banana and
   prints the result. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to use bubble sort to put numbers in ascending order. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write bubble_sort() for the int array prices.
   2. Compare each pair of neighbours.
   3. Swap them when they are in the wrong order for ascending order.
   4. Repeat the passes until the array is sorted.
   5. Print the sorted values. */
/* Repeatedly swap neighbours that are in the wrong order. */
void bubble_sort(int prices[], int count) {
    for (int i = 0; i < count - 1; i++) {
        for (int j = 0; j < count - 1 - i; j++) {
            if (prices[j] > prices[j + 1]) {
                int tmp = prices[j];
                prices[j] = prices[j + 1];
                prices[j + 1] = tmp;
            }
        }
    }
}

int main(void) {
    int prices[] = {75, 14, 51, 31, 65};
    int count = sizeof(prices) / sizeof(prices[0]);
    bubble_sort(prices, count);
    for (int i = 0; i < count; i++) {
        printf("%d ", prices[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: bubble_sort() walks through prices again and again and swaps neighbours
   that are in the wrong order, so the largest values move to the end first. main() then
   prints the 5 values in ascending order. */
// END

/* Caption: Use Euclid's algorithm to compute the GCD. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write gcd() with Euclid's algorithm.
   2. Replace (a, b) by (b, a % b) until b is 0.
   3. Return a and print the GCD of 26 and 33. */
/* Euclid: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a % b) until b becomes zero. */
int gcd(int a, int b) {
    while (b != 0) {
        int r = a % b;
        a = b;
        b = r;
    }
    return a;
}

int main(void) {
    int x = 26, y = 33;
    printf("gcd(%d, %d) = %d\n", x, y, gcd(x, y));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: gcd() uses Euclid's algorithm: it keeps replacing (a, b) with (b, a % b)
   until b is 0. The last non-zero value is the greatest common divisor, and main() prints
   the GCD of 26 and 33. */
// END

/* Caption: C program to calculate 5! using recursion. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write factorial(x) that calls itself.
   2. Return 1 when x is 1 or less.
   3. Otherwise return x * factorial(x - 1).
   4. Print 5! as an unsigned long long. */
/* n! = n * (n - 1)!, and 0! = 1 stops the recursion. */
unsigned long long factorial(int x) {
    if (x <= 1) {
        return 1;
    }
    return x * factorial(x - 1);
}

int main(void) {
    int x = 5;
    printf("%d! = %llu\n", x, factorial(x));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: factorial() calls itself: n! is n * (n - 1)!, and the recursion stops when
   x is 1 or less. main() prints 5! as an unsigned long long, because factorials grow very
   fast. */
// END

/* Caption: Search an array for a value and print its position. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write linear_search() with the array, its length and target.
   2. Compare each element with target.
   3. Return the index of the first match, or -1.
   4. In main(), search for 65 and print the result. */
/* Return the index of target, or -1 when it is not in the array. */
int linear_search(const int nums[], int n, int target) {
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        if (nums[i] == target) {
            return i;
        }
    }
    return -1;
}

int main(void) {
    int nums[] = {49, 65, 14, 58, 64, 47};
    int n = sizeof(nums) / sizeof(nums[0]);
    int target = 65;
    int pos = linear_search(nums, n, target);
    if (pos >= 0) {
        printf("Found %d at index %d\n", target, pos);
    } else {
        printf("%d is not in the array\n", target);
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: linear_search() checks the elements of nums one by one and returns the
   index of the first one equal to target, or -1 when it reaches the end without a match.
   main() searches for 65 and prints where it is, or that it is missing. */
// END

/* Caption: How do I write a function with four parameters that returns the maximum in C? */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write max2() that returns the larger of two values.
   2. Write max_of_four() as max2(max2(a, b), max2(c, d)).
   3. Print the largest of the four values. */
/* Return the larger of two values. */
int max2(int a, int b) {
    return a > b ? a : b;
}

/* Reuse max2 to compare four values. */
int max_of_four(int a, int b, int c, int d) {
    return max2(max2(a, b), max2(c, d));
}

int main(void) {
    int a = 85, b = 75, c = 47, d = 29;
    printf("Largest: %d\n", max_of_four(a, b, c, d));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: max_of_four() takes four parameters and reuses the helper max2(), which
   returns the larger of two values: it compares a with b, c with d, and then the two
   winners. main() prints the largest of 85, 75, 47 and 29. */
// END

/* Caption: Program to swap two variables using pointers. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write swap() that takes pointers to two int values.
   2. Save *a in tmp, copy *b into *a, then tmp into *b.
   3. In main(), print a and b, call swap(&a, &b) and print them again. */
/* Pass addresses so the function can change the caller's variables. */
void swap(int *a, int *b) {
    int tmp = *a;
    *a = *b;
    *b = tmp;
}

int main(void) {
    int a = 51, b = 4;
    printf("Before: %d %d\n", a, b);
    swap(&a, &b);
    printf("After:  %d %d\n", a, b);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: swap() receives the addresses of a and b, so writing through the pointers
   *a and *b changes the caller's variables. tmp holds one value during the exchange.
   main() declares both variables on one line and prints them before and after the swap. */
// END

/* Caption: Check whether a year is a leap year. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write is_leap(year).
   2. A year divisible by 4 is a leap year, unless it is divisible by 100.
   3. Years divisible by 400 are leap years again.
   4. Check 1996 and print the result. */
/* Leap years divide by 4, except centuries, which must divide by 400. */
int is_leap(int year) {
    return (year % 4 == 0 && year % 100 != 0) || year % 400 == 0;
}

int main(void) {
    int year = 1996;
    if (is_leap(year)) {
        printf("%d is a leap year\n", year);
    } else {
        printf("%d is not a leap year\n", year);
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: is_leap() returns true for years divisible by 4, except century years,
   which must also be divisible by 400. main() checks 1996 and prints whether it is a leap
   year. */
// END

/* Caption: How do I search a sorted array by halving the search range each step in C? */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Make sure the array is sorted.
   2. Set left to 0 and right to len - 1.
   3. While left <= right, compare the middle element middle with the key.
   4. Return the index if it matches; otherwise keep only the half that can hold the
      key.
   5. Return -1 if the range becomes empty, and print the index of 88. */
/* The array must be sorted. Each step halves the range that can still hold the key. */
int binary_search(const int scores[], int len, int key) {
    int left = 0;
    int right = len - 1;
    while (left <= right) {
        int middle = left + (right - left) / 2;
        if (scores[middle] == key) {
            return middle;
        } else if (scores[middle] < key) {
            left = middle + 1;   /* key is in the right half */
        } else {
            right = middle - 1;   /* key is in the left half */
        }
    }
    return -1;
}

int main(void) {
    int scores[] = {6, 17, 29, 44, 84, 88, 95, 160, 174};
    int len = sizeof(scores) / sizeof(scores[0]);
    int index = binary_search(scores, len, 88);
    printf("Index of 88: %d\n", index);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: binary_search() needs a sorted array. It keeps the range from left to
   right, compares the middle element middle with the key and throws away the half that
   cannot contain it, so it needs only about log2(n) steps. main() looks for 88 and prints
   its index, or -1 if it is not there. */
// END

/* Caption: Return the minimum, maximum and average of an array in a struct. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define a Stats struct with min, max and average.
   2. Write array_stats() that fills one Stats in a loop.
   3. Return the struct.
   4. Print st.min, st.max and st.average. */
typedef struct {
    int min;
    int max;
    double average;
} Stats;

/* Pack several results into one struct and return it. */
Stats array_stats(const int v[], int n) {
    Stats s = {v[0], v[0], 0.0};
    double total = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        if (v[i] < s.min) {
            s.min = v[i];
        }
        if (v[i] > s.max) {
            s.max = v[i];
        }
        total += v[i];
    }
    s.average = total / n;
    return s;
}

int main(void) {
    int items[] = {96, 86, 92, 70, 80, 26, 60, 10, 3};
    int n = sizeof(items) / sizeof(items[0]);
    Stats st = array_stats(items, n);
    printf("Min %d, Max %d, Average %.2f\n", st.min, st.max, st.average);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: Stats groups three results. array_stats() fills one Stats while it loops
   over the 9 values and returns the whole struct, which is a clean way to return several
   results at once. main() reads them as st.min, st.max and st.average. */
// END

/* Caption: Sort an array in ascending order using insertion sort. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write insertion_sort() for the double array items.
   2. Take each element in turn as current.
   3. Shift the larger values of the sorted part one place right.
   4. Put current into the gap.
   5. Print the sorted values. */
/* Insert each element into the already sorted part on its left. */
void insertion_sort(double items[], int size) {
    for (int i = 1; i < size; i++) {
        double current = items[i];
        int j = i - 1;
        while (j >= 0 && items[j] > current) {
            items[j + 1] = items[j];   /* shift bigger values right */
            j--;
        }
        items[j + 1] = current;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    double items[] = {37.8, 41.9, 2.4, 87.7, 40.3, 18.2, 43.8, 67.9};
    int size = sizeof(items) / sizeof(items[0]);
    insertion_sort(items, size);
    for (int i = 0; i < size; i++) {
        printf("%.2f ", items[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: insertion_sort() takes each element in turn and shifts the larger values of
   the sorted part one place right until the element fits. main() then prints the 8 values
   in ascending order. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to generate the Fibonacci sequence. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write fib(n) that returns n when n < 2.
   2. Otherwise return fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2).
   3. Print fib(i) for i from 0 to 11. */
/* Each Fibonacci number is the sum of the two before it. */
long fib(int n) {
    if (n < 2) {
        return n;
    }
    return fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2);
}

int main(void) {
    for (int i = 0; i < 12; i++) {
        printf("%ld ", fib(i));
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: fib() returns n for 0 and 1 and otherwise adds the two previous Fibonacci
   numbers by calling itself twice, which is simple but slow for large n. main() prints the
   first 12 numbers. */
// END

/* Caption: Program to implement selection sort for an array of int values. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write selection_sort() for the int array numbers.
   2. For each position, find the largest remaining element.
   3. Swap it into that position.
   4. Print the sorted values. */
/* Select the right element for each position and swap it into place. */
void selection_sort(int numbers[], int size) {
    for (int i = 0; i < size - 1; i++) {
        int chosen = i;
        for (int j = i + 1; j < size; j++) {
            if (numbers[chosen] < numbers[j]) {
                chosen = j;
            }
        }
        int tmp = numbers[i];
        numbers[i] = numbers[chosen];
        numbers[chosen] = tmp;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    int numbers[] = {25, 45, 79, 92, 13, 57};
    int size = 6;
    selection_sort(numbers, size);
    for (int i = 0; i < size; i++) {
        printf("%d ", numbers[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: selection_sort() finds the largest remaining element for each position and
   swaps it into place. main() then prints the 6 values in descending order. */
// END

/* Caption: Build a linked list, print it, and free it. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define ListNode with a value and a next pointer.
   2. Write push_front() that mallocs a node and links it in front of head.
   3. Write print_list() that follows next until NULL.
   4. Write free_list() that frees every node.
   5. Push 3 values, print the list and free it. */
typedef struct ListNode {
    int value;
    struct ListNode *next;
} ListNode;

/* Allocate a new node and put it in front of the current head. */
ListNode *push_front(ListNode *head, int value) {
    ListNode *node = malloc(sizeof(ListNode));
    if (node == NULL) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Out of memory\n");
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }
    node->value = value;
    node->next = head;
    return node;
}

void print_list(const ListNode *head) {
    for (const ListNode *cur = head; cur != NULL; cur = cur->next) {
        printf("%d -> ", cur->value);
    }
    printf("NULL\n");
}

/* Free every node; save next before freeing the current one. */
void free_list(ListNode *head) {
    while (head != NULL) {
        ListNode *next = head->next;
        free(head);
        head = next;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    ListNode *head = NULL;
    head = push_front(head, 42);
    head = push_front(head, 30);
    head = push_front(head, 50);
    print_list(head);
    free_list(head);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: Each ListNode holds a value and a pointer to the next node. push_front()
   allocates a node with malloc, puts it in front of head and returns it; print_list()
   follows the next pointers until NULL; free_list() frees every node. main() pushes 3
   values, so they print in reverse order. */
// END

/* A prime has no divisor between 2 and its square root. */

/* Caption: Transpose a matrix. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define ROWS as 3 and COLS as 4.
   2. Copy m[r][c] into t[c][r] for every element.
   3. Print t row by row. */
#define ROWS 3
#define COLS 4

int main(void) {
    int m[ROWS][COLS] = {{3, 1, 2, 6}, {1, 0, 1, 7}, {7, 5, 1, 0}};
    int t[COLS][ROWS];
    /* Element (r, c) moves to (c, r). */
    for (int r = 0; r < ROWS; r++) {
        for (int c = 0; c < COLS; c++) {
            t[c][r] = m[r][c];
        }
    }
    for (int r = 0; r < COLS; r++) {
        for (int c = 0; c < ROWS; c++) {
            printf("%3d", t[r][c]);
        }
        printf("\n");
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: The nested loops copy m[r][c] into t[c][r], so the 3x4 matrix becomes 4x3.
   A second pair of loops prints the result. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to generate the Fibonacci sequence. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Start with a = 0 and b = 1.
   2. Repeat 17 times and print a each time.
   3. Compute next = a + b, then set a = b and b = next. */
int main(void) {
    long a = 0, b = 1;
    /* Print a term, then slide the pair one step along the sequence. */
    for (int i = 0; i < 17; i++) {
        printf("%ld ", a);
        long next = a + b;
        a = b;
        b = next;
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: The loop keeps the last two numbers in a and b. Each round it prints a,
   then moves the pair forward: a becomes b and b becomes their sum. It prints the first 17
   Fibonacci numbers. */
// END

/* Caption: Build a fixed-size integer stack in C. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define a Stack with room for 32 items and a top counter.
   2. Write push() and pop(), returning false when the stack is full or empty.
   3. Push 4 values.
   4. Pop and print until the stack is empty. */
#define CAPACITY 32

typedef struct {
    int items[CAPACITY];
    int top;   /* number of items on the stack */
} Stack;

bool push(Stack *s, int value) {
    if (s->top == CAPACITY) {
        return false;   /* stack is full */
    }
    s->items[s->top++] = value;
    return true;
}

bool pop(Stack *s, int *value) {
    if (s->top == 0) {
        return false;   /* stack is empty */
    }
    *value = s->items[--s->top];
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    Stack s = {.top = 0};
    push(&s, 93);
    push(&s, 75);
    push(&s, 81);
    push(&s, 59);
    int value;
    /* Items come back out in reverse order (last in, first out). */
    while (pop(&s, &value)) {
        printf("%d ", value);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: The Stack keeps up to 32 items in an array, and top counts how many are
   stored. push() adds at the top and pop() removes from the top; both return false when
   they cannot. main() pushes 4 values and pops them all, so they come out in reverse order
   (last in, first out). */
// END

/* Caption: Find the minimum and maximum of an array with one function. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write min_max() with the array, its length and the pointers min and max.
   2. Start both at the first element.
   3. Update *min and *max while looping over the rest.
   4. Declare low and high, pass their addresses and print them. */
/* One pass finds both results; they are stored through the pointers. */
void min_max(const int samples[], int n, int *min, int *max) {
    *min = samples[0];
    *max = samples[0];
    for (int i = 1; i < n; i++) {
        if (samples[i] < *min) {
            *min = samples[i];
        }
        if (samples[i] > *max) {
            *max = samples[i];
        }
    }
}

int main(void) {
    int samples[] = {21, 4, 37, 5, 14};
    int n = sizeof(samples) / sizeof(samples[0]);
    int low, high;
    min_max(samples, n, &low, &high);
    printf("Min: %d, Max: %d\n", low, high);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: A C function can return only one value, so min_max() returns void and
   writes its two results through the pointer parameters min and max. main() declares low
   and high on one line and passes their addresses with &, then prints both results for the
   5 values. */
// END

/* Caption: Search an array for its smallest value. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write smallest_value() that takes marks and count.
   2. Store marks[0] in smallest.
   3. Loop over the other elements and keep the smallest value in smallest.
   4. Return smallest and print it. */
/* Start with the first element and keep the smallest value seen so far. */
int smallest_value(const int marks[], int count) {
    int smallest = marks[0];
    for (int i = 1; i < count; i++) {
        if (marks[i] < smallest) {
            smallest = marks[i];
        }
    }
    return smallest;
}

int main(void) {
    int marks[] = {88, 95, 29, 75, 99, 54, 83, 67, 47, 35};
    int count = 10;
    printf("The smallest value is %d\n", smallest_value(marks, count));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: smallest_value() takes the first element as the smallest value so far and
   stores it in smallest. The loop compares every other element with smallest using < and
   keeps the smallest one. main() prints the smallest of the 10 values. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to write a function that swaps two long values through pointers. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write swap() that takes pointers to two long values.
   2. Save *x in tmp, copy *y into *x, then tmp into *y.
   3. In main(), print x and y, call swap(&x, &y) and print them again. */
/* Pass addresses so the function can change the caller's variables. */
void swap(long *x, long *y) {
    long tmp = *x;
    *x = *y;
    *y = tmp;
}

int main(void) {
    long x = 9L, y = 20L;
    printf("Before: %ld %ld\n", x, y);
    swap(&x, &y);
    printf("After:  %ld %ld\n", x, y);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: swap() receives the addresses of x and y, so writing through the pointers
   *x and *y changes the caller's variables. tmp holds one value during the exchange.
   main() declares both variables on one line and prints them before and after the swap. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to reverse the characters of a word. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <string.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write reverse_string() for str.
   2. Set i to the first index and j to the last.
   3. Swap the two characters and move i and j inwards until they meet.
   4. Reverse window and print it. */
/* Swap characters from both ends until they meet in the middle. */
void reverse_string(char *str) {
    int i = 0;
    int j = strlen(str) - 1;
    while (i < j) {
        char tmp = str[i];
        str[i] = str[j];
        str[j] = tmp;
        i++;
        j--;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    char str[] = "window";
    reverse_string(str);
    printf("%s\n", str);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: reverse_string() swaps characters from both ends of str, moving inwards
   until the two indexes meet. main() reverses the word window in place and prints it. */
// END

/* Caption: Search an array for a value and print its position. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write linear_search() with the array, its length and key.
   2. Compare each element with key.
   3. Return the index of the first match, or -1.
   4. In main(), search for 173 and print the result. */
/* Return the index of key, or -1 when it is not in the array. */
int linear_search(const int ages[], int n, int key) {
    for (int idx = 0; idx < n; idx++) {
        if (ages[idx] == key) {
            return idx;
        }
    }
    return -1;
}

int main(void) {
    int ages[] = {66, 47, 21, 29, 73, 35, 1, 79};
    int n = sizeof(ages) / sizeof(ages[0]);
    int key = 173;
    int pos = linear_search(ages, n, key);
    if (pos >= 0) {
        printf("Found %d at index %d\n", key, pos);
    } else {
        printf("%d is not in the array\n", key);
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: linear_search() checks the elements of ages one by one and returns the
   index of the first one equal to key, or -1 when it reaches the end without a match.
   main() searches for 173 and prints where it is, or that it is missing. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to search a sorted array by halving the search range each step. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Make sure the array is sorted.
   2. Set low to 0 and high to length - 1.
   3. While low <= high, compare the middle element mid with the key.
   4. Return the index if it matches; otherwise keep only the half that can hold the
      key.
   5. Return -1 if the range becomes empty, and print the index of 117. */
/* The array must be sorted. Each step halves the range that can still hold the key. */
int binary_search(const int readings[], int length, int key) {
    int low = 0;
    int high = length - 1;
    while (low <= high) {
        int mid = low + (high - low) / 2;
        if (readings[mid] == key) {
            return mid;
        } else if (readings[mid] < key) {
            low = mid + 1;   /* key is in the right half */
        } else {
            high = mid - 1;   /* key is in the left half */
        }
    }
    return -1;
}

int main(void) {
    int readings[] = {17, 19, 22, 108, 117, 133, 135, 144, 187, 196};
    int length = 10;
    int index = binary_search(readings, length, 117);
    printf("Index of 117: %d\n", index);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: binary_search() needs a sorted array. It keeps the range from low to high,
   compares the middle element mid with the key and throws away the half that cannot
   contain it, so it needs only about log2(n) steps. main() looks for 117 and prints its
   index, or -1 if it is not there. */
// END

/* Caption: Return a Point struct from a function. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define a Point struct with x and y.
   2. Write midpoint() that returns a Point with the averages of x and y.
   3. Print mid.x and mid.y. */
typedef struct {
    double x;
    double y;
} Point;

/* A function can return a whole struct. */
Point midpoint(Point a, Point b) {
    Point m = {(a.x + b.x) / 2, (a.y + b.y) / 2};
    return m;
}

int main(void) {
    Point p = {13, 6}, q = {-12, 16};
    Point mid = midpoint(p, q);
    printf("Midpoint: (%.1f, %.1f)\n", mid.x, mid.y);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: midpoint() takes two Point structs and returns a new Point whose x and y
   are the averages of theirs. main() declares p and q on one line, (13, 6) and (-12, 16),
   and prints the midpoint using mid.x and mid.y. */
// END

/* Caption: Print the factorial of an integer. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write factorial(value) with result = 1.
   2. Multiply result by every number from 2 to value.
   3. Return result.
   4. Print 14! as an unsigned long long. */
/* Multiply 1 * 2 * ... * n. */
unsigned long long factorial(int value) {
    unsigned long long result = 1;
    for (int i = 2; i <= value; i++) {
        result *= i;
    }
    return result;
}

int main(void) {
    int value = 14;
    printf("%d! = %llu\n", value, factorial(value));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: factorial() multiplies result by every number from 2 up to value. main()
   prints 14! as an unsigned long long, because factorials grow very fast. */
// END

/* Caption: Program to use insertion sort to put numbers in descending order. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write insertion_sort() for the double array marks.
   2. Take each element in turn as current.
   3. Shift the smaller values of the sorted part one place right.
   4. Put current into the gap.
   5. Print the sorted values. */
/* Insert each element into the already sorted part on its left. */
void insertion_sort(double marks[], int length) {
    for (int i = 1; i < length; i++) {
        double current = marks[i];
        int j = i - 1;
        while (j >= 0 && marks[j] < current) {
            marks[j + 1] = marks[j];   /* shift bigger values right */
            j--;
        }
        marks[j + 1] = current;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    double marks[] = {48.3, 93.2, 11.0, 68.6, 35.7, 30.8};
    int length = 6;
    insertion_sort(marks, length);
    for (int i = 0; i < length; i++) {
        printf("%.2f ", marks[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: insertion_sort() takes each element in turn and shifts the smaller values
   of the sorted part one place right until the element fits. main() then prints the 6
   values in descending order. */
// END

/* Caption: How do I find a number in a sorted array with binary search in C? */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Make sure the array is sorted.
   2. Set left to 0 and right to length - 1.
   3. While left <= right, compare the middle element middle with the key.
   4. Return the index if it matches; otherwise keep only the half that can hold the
      key.
   5. Return -1 if the range becomes empty, and print the index of 196. */
/* The array must be sorted. Each step halves the range that can still hold the key. */
int binary_search(const int numbers[], int length, int key) {
    int left = 0;
    int right = length - 1;
    while (left <= right) {
        int middle = left + (right - left) / 2;
        if (numbers[middle] == key) {
            return middle;
        } else if (numbers[middle] < key) {
            left = middle + 1;   /* key is in the right half */
        } else {
            right = middle - 1;   /* key is in the left half */
        }
    }
    return -1;
}

int main(void) {
    int numbers[] = {2, 14, 23, 27, 62, 70, 99, 135, 170, 172, 196};
    const int length = 11;
    int index = binary_search(numbers, length, 196);
    printf("Index of 196: %d\n", index);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: binary_search() needs a sorted array. It keeps the range from left to
   right, compares the middle element middle with the key and throws away the half that
   cannot contain it, so it needs only about log2(n) steps. main() looks for 196 and prints
   its index, or -1 if it is not there. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to convert 50 to binary. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write print_binary(n, bits).
   2. Go through the bits from the highest to the lowest.
   3. Print 1 when (n >> b) & 1 is set, otherwise 0.
   4. Print 50 in binary. */
/* Check each bit from the highest to the lowest. */
void print_binary(unsigned int n, int bits) {
    for (int b = bits - 1; b >= 0; b--) {
        putchar((n >> b) & 1 ? '1' : '0');
    }
    putchar('\n');
}

int main(void) {
    unsigned int number = 50;
    printf("%u in binary: ", number);
    print_binary(number, 10);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: print_binary() checks one bit at a time, from the highest to the lowest: (n
   >> b) & 1 is 1 when bit b is set, so it prints the character 1 or 0. main() prints 50 in
   binary. */
// END

/* Caption: How do I count the odd values in a list of integers in C? */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write count_odd() that takes marks and len.
   2. For each element, test marks[i] % 2 != 0.
   3. Add one to found for every odd number.
   4. Return found and print it. */
/* A number is odd when the remainder after dividing by 2 is one. */
int count_odd(const int marks[], int len) {
    int found = 0;
    int i = 0;
    while (i < len) {
        if (marks[i] % 2 != 0) {
            found++;
        }
        i++;
    }
    return found;
}

int main(void) {
    int marks[] = {14, 90, 9, 44, 13, 61};
    const int len = 6;
    printf("Odd numbers: %d\n", count_odd(marks, len));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: count_odd() tests each element of marks with the % operator: a remainder of
   1 after dividing by 2 means the number is odd, so found goes up by one. main() prints
   how many of the 6 values are odd. */
// END

/* Caption: Allocate an array with malloc and fill it with cubes. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Use malloc to get room for 8 ints and check for NULL.
   2. Fill table with cubes.
   3. Print the values.
   4. Call free(table) at the end. */
int main(void) {
    int n = 8;
    /* Ask the heap for room for n ints; malloc returns NULL on failure. */
    int *table = malloc(n * sizeof(int));
    if (table == NULL) {
        fprintf(stderr, "malloc failed\n");
        return 1;
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        table[i] = i * i * i;
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        printf("%d ", table[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    free(table);   /* give the memory back */
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: malloc() reserves room for 8 ints on the heap and returns NULL if it fails,
   which the program checks. The first loop fills table with cubes, the second prints them,
   and free() gives the memory back at the end. */
// END

/* Caption: Swap two variables using pointers. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write swap() that takes pointers to two long values.
   2. Save *x in tmp, copy *y into *x, then tmp into *y.
   3. In main(), print x and y, call swap(&x, &y) and print them again. */
/* Pass addresses so the function can change the caller's variables. */
void swap(long *x, long *y) {
    long tmp = *x;
    *x = *y;
    *y = tmp;
}

int main(void) {
    long x = 54L, y = 55L;
    printf("Before: %ld %ld\n", x, y);
    swap(&x, &y);
    printf("After:  %ld %ld\n", x, y);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: swap() receives the addresses of x and y, so writing through the pointers
   *x and *y changes the caller's variables. tmp holds one value during the exchange.
   main() declares both variables on one line and prints them before and after the swap. */
// END

/* Caption: Check whether a year is a leap year. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write is_leap(year).
   2. A year divisible by 4 is a leap year, unless it is divisible by 100.
   3. Years divisible by 400 are leap years again.
   4. Check 1900 and print the result. */
/* Leap years divide by 4, except centuries, which must divide by 400. */
int is_leap(int year) {
    return (year % 4 == 0 && year % 100 != 0) || year % 400 == 0;
}

int main(void) {
    int year = 1900;
    if (is_leap(year)) {
        printf("%d is a leap year\n", year);
    } else {
        printf("%d is not a leap year\n", year);
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: is_leap() returns true for years divisible by 4, except century years,
   which must also be divisible by 400. main() checks 1900 and prints whether it is a leap
   year. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to use Euclid's algorithm to compute the GCD. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write gcd() with Euclid's algorithm.
   2. Replace (a, b) by (b, a % b) until b is 0.
   3. Return a and print the GCD of 47 and 119. */
/* Euclid: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a % b) until b becomes zero. */
int gcd(int a, int b) {
    while (b != 0) {
        int r = a % b;
        a = b;
        b = r;
    }
    return a;
}

int main(void) {
    int x = 47, y = 119;
    printf("gcd(%d, %d) = %d\n", x, y, gcd(x, y));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: gcd() uses Euclid's algorithm: it keeps replacing (a, b) with (b, a % b)
   until b is 0. The last non-zero value is the greatest common divisor, and main() prints
   the GCD of 47 and 119. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to sort an array in ascending order using insertion sort. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write insertion_sort() for the long array data.
   2. Take each element in turn as current.
   3. Shift the larger values of the sorted part one place right.
   4. Put current into the gap.
   5. Print the sorted values. */
/* Insert each element into the already sorted part on its left. */
void insertion_sort(long data[], int length) {
    for (int i = 1; i < length; i++) {
        long current = data[i];
        int j = i - 1;
        while (j >= 0 && data[j] > current) {
            data[j + 1] = data[j];   /* shift bigger values right */
            j--;
        }
        data[j + 1] = current;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    long data[] = {75L, 49L, 87L, 95L, 56L, 20L, 45L};
    int length = 7;
    insertion_sort(data, length);
    for (int i = 0; i < length; i++) {
        printf("%ld ", data[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: insertion_sort() takes each element in turn and shifts the larger values of
   the sorted part one place right until the element fits. main() then prints the 7 values
   in ascending order. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to build a fixed-size integer stack in C. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define a Stack with room for 32 items and a top counter.
   2. Write push() and pop(), returning false when the stack is full or empty.
   3. Push 3 values.
   4. Pop and print until the stack is empty. */
#define CAPACITY 32

typedef struct {
    int items[CAPACITY];
    int top;   /* number of items on the stack */
} Stack;

bool push(Stack *s, int value) {
    if (s->top == CAPACITY) {
        return false;   /* stack is full */
    }
    s->items[s->top++] = value;
    return true;
}

bool pop(Stack *s, int *value) {
    if (s->top == 0) {
        return false;   /* stack is empty */
    }
    *value = s->items[--s->top];
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    Stack s = {.top = 0};
    push(&s, 9);
    push(&s, 56);
    push(&s, 8);
    int value;
    /* Items come back out in reverse order (last in, first out). */
    while (pop(&s, &value)) {
        printf("%d ", value);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: The Stack keeps up to 32 items in an array, and top counts how many are
   stored. push() adds at the top and pop() removes from the top; both return false when
   they cannot. main() pushes 3 values and pops them all, so they come out in reverse order
   (last in, first out). */
// END

/* Caption: Use binary search to locate a value in a sorted list. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Make sure the array is sorted.
   2. Set left to 0 and right to count - 1.
   3. While left <= right, compare the middle element middle with the key.
   4. Return the index if it matches; otherwise keep only the half that can hold the
      key.
   5. Return -1 if the range becomes empty, and print the index of 201. */
/* The array must be sorted. Each step halves the range that can still hold the key. */
int binary_search(const int scores[], int count, int key) {
    int left = 0;
    int right = count - 1;
    while (left <= right) {
        int middle = left + (right - left) / 2;
        if (scores[middle] == key) {
            return middle;
        } else if (scores[middle] < key) {
            left = middle + 1;   /* key is in the right half */
        } else {
            right = middle - 1;   /* key is in the left half */
        }
    }
    return -1;
}

int main(void) {
    int scores[] = {23, 26, 45, 51, 90, 92, 125, 127, 131, 154, 178};
    int count = sizeof(scores) / sizeof(scores[0]);
    int index = binary_search(scores, count, 201);
    printf("Index of 201: %d\n", index);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: binary_search() needs a sorted array. It keeps the range from left to
   right, compares the middle element middle with the key and throws away the half that
   cannot contain it, so it needs only about log2(n) steps. main() looks for 201 and prints
   its index, or -1 if it is not there. */
// END

/* Caption: How do I print an integer with its digits reversed in C? */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Start result at 0.
   2. Multiply result by 10, add n % 10, then divide n by 10.
   3. Repeat until n is 0.
   4. Apply it to 748280 and print the result. */
/* Take the last digit with % 10, then drop it with / 10. */
int reverse_digits(int n) {
    int result = 0;
    while (n > 0) {
        result = result * 10 + n % 10;
        n /= 10;
    }
    return result;
}

int main(void) {
    int number = 748280;
    printf("reverse of digits of %d: %d\n", number, reverse_digits(number));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: reverse_digits() shifts result one place left (result * 10) and adds the
   last digit of n, which reverses the order. main() applies it to 748280. */
// END

/* Caption: Reverse an array by swapping from both ends. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write reverse_array() for prices.
   2. Set left to the first index and right to the last.
   3. Swap prices[left] and prices[right], then move both inwards.
   4. Stop when left meets right and print the array. */
/* Swap the outer pair, then move both ends toward the middle. */
void reverse_array(int prices[], int size) {
    int left = 0;
    int right = size - 1;
    while (left < right) {
        int tmp = prices[left];
        prices[left] = prices[right];
        prices[right] = tmp;
        left++;
        right--;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    int prices[] = {64, 87, 92, 18, 37, 99, 90, 55, 40};
    const int size = 9;
    reverse_array(prices, size);
    for (int i = 0; i < size; i++) {
        printf("%d ", prices[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: reverse_array() swaps the first and last elements, then moves left forward
   and right backward until they meet, so the array is reversed in place without a second
   array. main() prints the reversed values. */
// END

/* Caption: Show the Fibonacci series with a loop. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Start with a = 0 and b = 1.
   2. Repeat 16 times and print a each time.
   3. Compute next = a + b, then set a = b and b = next. */
int main(void) {
    long a = 0, b = 1;
    /* Print a term, then slide the pair one step along the sequence. */
    for (int i = 0; i < 16; i++) {
        printf("%ld ", a);
        long next = a + b;
        a = b;
        b = next;
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: The loop keeps the last two numbers in a and b. Each round it prints a,
   then moves the pair forward: a becomes b and b becomes their sum. It prints the first 16
   Fibonacci numbers. */
// END

/* Caption: Find the minimum and maximum of an array with one function. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write min_max() with the array, its length and the pointers min and max.
   2. Start both at the first element.
   3. Update *min and *max while looping over the rest.
   4. Declare lowest and highest, pass their addresses and print them. */
/* One pass finds both results; they are stored through the pointers. */
void min_max(const int prices[], int count, int *min, int *max) {
    *min = prices[0];
    *max = prices[0];
    for (int i = 1; i < count; i++) {
        if (prices[i] < *min) {
            *min = prices[i];
        }
        if (prices[i] > *max) {
            *max = prices[i];
        }
    }
}

int main(void) {
    int prices[] = {1, 97, 96, 20, 1};
    int count = sizeof(prices) / sizeof(prices[0]);
    int lowest, highest;
    min_max(prices, count, &lowest, &highest);
    printf("Min: %d, Max: %d\n", lowest, highest);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: A C function can return only one value, so min_max() returns void and
   writes its two results through the pointer parameters min and max. main() declares
   lowest and highest on one line and passes their addresses with &, then prints both
   results for the 5 values. */
// END

/* Caption: C program to compute 5 to the power of 10 without pow(). */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write power(base, exp) with result = 1.
   2. Multiply result by base exp times.
   3. Print 5 to the power 10. */
/* Multiply the base by itself exp times. */
long long power(int base, int exp) {
    long long result = 1;
    for (int i = 0; i < exp; i++) {
        result *= base;
    }
    return result;
}

int main(void) {
    printf("5^10 = %lld\n", power(5, 10));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: power() starts result at 1 and multiplies it by base exp times. It uses
   long long because powers grow quickly. main() prints 5 to the power 10. */
// END

/* Caption: Program to build a FIFO queue using a ring buffer. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define a Queue with room for 8 items, a head and a count.
   2. Write enqueue() that stores at (head + count) % CAPACITY.
   3. Write dequeue() that takes the item at head and moves head on.
   4. Add 4 values, then remove and print them in order. */
#define CAPACITY 8

typedef struct {
    int items[CAPACITY];
    int head;
    int count;
} Queue;

bool enqueue(Queue *q, int value) {
    if (q->count == CAPACITY) {
        return false;
    }
    /* The tail wraps around to the start of the array. */
    q->items[(q->head + q->count) % CAPACITY] = value;
    q->count++;
    return true;
}

bool dequeue(Queue *q, int *value) {
    if (q->count == 0) {
        return false;
    }
    *value = q->items[q->head];
    q->head = (q->head + 1) % CAPACITY;
    q->count--;
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    Queue q = {.head = 0, .count = 0};
    enqueue(&q, 67);
    enqueue(&q, 45);
    enqueue(&q, 28);
    enqueue(&q, 60);
    int value;
    /* Items come out in the order they went in (first in, first out). */
    while (dequeue(&q, &value)) {
        printf("%d ", value);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: The Queue stores up to 8 items in a ring buffer: head is the oldest item
   and % CAPACITY wraps positions back to the start of the array. enqueue() adds at the
   back and dequeue() removes from the front, so main() gets its 4 values back in the same
   order (first in, first out). */
// END

   3. Add 11 to x through px and print the values. */

    int *px = &x, *py = &y;
    *px += 11;

    printf("*px = %d, *py = %d\n", *px, *py);

   2. */
// END

/* Caption: C program to find a number in a sorted array with binary search. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Make sure the array is sorted.
   2. Set lo to 0 and hi to size - 1.
   3. While lo <= hi, compare the middle element mid with the key.
   4. Return the index if it matches; otherwise keep only the half that can hold the
      key.
   5. Return -1 if the range becomes empty, and print the index of 50. */
/* The array must be sorted. Each step halves the range that can still hold the key. */
int binary_search(const int marks[], int size, int key) {
    int lo = 0;
    int hi = size - 1;
    while (lo <= hi) {
        int mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;
        if (marks[mid] == key) {
            return mid;
        } else if (marks[mid] < key) {
            lo = mid + 1;   /* key is in the right half */
        } else {
            hi = mid - 1;   /* key is in the left half */
        }
    }
    return -1;
}

int main(void) {
    int marks[] = {42, 50, 53, 58, 94, 124, 171, 173, 192, 193};
    const int size = 10;
    int index = binary_search(marks, size, 50);
    printf("Index of 50: %d\n", index);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: binary_search() needs a sorted array. It keeps the range from lo to hi,
   compares the middle element mid with the key and throws away the half that cannot
   contain it, so it needs only about log2(n) steps. main() looks for 50 and prints its
   index, or -1 if it is not there. */
// END

/* Caption: Reverse the digits of a number. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Start result at 0.
   2. Multiply result by 10, add n % 10, then divide n by 10.
   3. Repeat until n is 0.
   4. Apply it to 302942 and print the result. */
/* Take the last digit with % 10, then drop it with / 10. */
int reverse_digits(int n) {
    int result = 0;
    while (n > 0) {
        result = result * 10 + n % 10;
        n /= 10;
    }
    return result;
}

int main(void) {
    int number = 302942;
    printf("reverse of digits of %d: %d\n", number, reverse_digits(number));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: reverse_digits() shifts result one place left (result * 10) and adds the
   last digit of n, which reverses the order. main() applies it to 302942. */
// END
