/* Caption: Use dynamic memory to store the first 15 evens. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Use malloc to get room for 15 ints and check for NULL.
   2. Fill table with evens.
   3. Print the values.
   4. Call free(table) at the end. */
int main(void) {
    int n = 15;
    /* Ask the heap for room for n ints; malloc returns NULL on failure. */
    int *table = malloc(n * sizeof(int));
    if (table == NULL) {
        fprintf(stderr, "malloc failed\n");
        return 1;
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        table[i] = 2 * i;
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        printf("%d ", table[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    free(table);   /* give the memory back */
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: malloc() reserves room for 15 ints on the heap and returns NULL if it
   fails, which the program checks. The first loop fills table with evens, the second
   prints them, and free() gives the memory back at the end. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to build a linked list, print it, and free it. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define Node with a value and a next pointer.
   2. Write push_front() that mallocs a node and links it in front of head.
   3. Write print_list() that follows next until NULL.
   4. Write free_list() that frees every node.
   5. Push 6 values, print the list and free it. */
typedef struct Node {
    int value;
    struct Node *next;
} Node;

/* Allocate a new node and put it in front of the current head. */
Node *push_front(Node *head, int value) {
    Node *node = malloc(sizeof(Node));
    if (node == NULL) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Out of memory\n");
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }
    node->value = value;
    node->next = head;
    return node;
}

void print_list(const Node *head) {
    for (const Node *cur = head; cur != NULL; cur = cur->next) {
        printf("%d -> ", cur->value);
    }
    printf("NULL\n");
}

/* Free every node; save next before freeing the current one. */
void free_list(Node *head) {
    while (head != NULL) {
        Node *next = head->next;
        free(head);
        head = next;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    Node *head = NULL;
    head = push_front(head, 7);
    head = push_front(head, 26);
    head = push_front(head, 54);
    head = push_front(head, 84);
    head = push_front(head, 58);
    head = push_front(head, 73);
    print_list(head);
    free_list(head);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: Each Node holds a value and a pointer to the next node. push_front()
   allocates a node with malloc, puts it in front of head and returns it; print_list()
   follows the next pointers until NULL; free_list() frees every node. main() pushes 6
   values, so they print in reverse order. */
// END

/* Caption: How do I use bubble sort to put numbers in ascending order in C? */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write bubble_sort() for the double array values.
   2. Compare each pair of neighbours.
   3. Swap them when they are in the wrong order for ascending order.
   4. Repeat the passes until the array is sorted.
   5. Print the sorted values. */
/* Repeatedly swap neighbours that are in the wrong order. */
void bubble_sort(double values[], int len) {
    for (int i = 0; i < len - 1; i++) {
        for (int j = 0; j < len - 1 - i; j++) {
            if (values[j] > values[j + 1]) {
                double tmp = values[j];
                values[j] = values[j + 1];
                values[j + 1] = tmp;
            }
        }
    }
}

int main(void) {
    double values[] = {94.5, 43.8, 50.0, 70.0, 32.6};
    const int len = 5;
    bubble_sort(values, len);
    for (int i = 0; i < len; i++) {
        printf("%.2f ", values[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: bubble_sort() walks through values again and again and swaps neighbours
   that are in the wrong order, so the largest values move to the end first. main() then
   prints the 5 values in ascending order. */
// END

/* Caption: How do I reverse the characters of a word in C? */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <string.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write reverse_string() for text.
   2. Set i to the first index and j to the last.
   3. Swap the two characters and move i and j inwards until they meet.
   4. Reverse madam and print it. */
/* Swap characters from both ends until they meet in the middle. */
void reverse_string(char *text) {
    int i = 0;
    int j = strlen(text) - 1;
    while (i < j) {
        char tmp = text[i];
        text[i] = text[j];
        text[j] = tmp;
        i++;
        j--;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    char text[] = "madam";
    reverse_string(text);
    printf("%s\n", text);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: reverse_string() swaps characters from both ends of text, moving inwards
   until the two indexes meet. main() reverses the word madam in place and prints it. */
// END

/* Caption: Program to save text to a file with fprintf and print it with fgets. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Open data.txt in write mode and check for NULL.
   2. Write 3 lines with fprintf and close the file.
   3. Open it again in read mode.
   4. Read and print each line with fgets, then close the file. */
int main(void) {
    FILE *file = fopen("data.txt", "w");
    if (file == NULL) {
        perror("fopen");
        return 1;
    }
    fprintf(file, "strings end with a null character\n");
    fprintf(file, "loops repeat a block of code\n");
    fprintf(file, "c gives you direct control over memory\n");
    fclose(file);

    /* Reopen the file for reading and print it line by line. */
    file = fopen("data.txt", "r");
    if (file == NULL) {
        perror("fopen");
        return 1;
    }
    char line[128];
    while (fgets(line, sizeof(line), file) != NULL) {
        printf("%s", line);
    }
    fclose(file);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: fopen() in write mode creates data.txt, fprintf() writes 3 lines into it
   and fclose() saves it. The file is then opened again in read mode, and fgets() reads it
   back line by line into the buffer line, which is printed. Every fopen() result is
   checked for NULL. */
// END

/* Caption: Swap two variables using pointers. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write swap() that takes pointers to two long values.
   2. Save *x in tmp, copy *y into *x, then tmp into *y.
   3. In main(), print x and y, call swap(&x, &y) and print them again. */
/* Pass addresses so the function can change the caller's variables. */
void swap(long *x, long *y) {
    long tmp = *x;
    *x = *y;
    *y = tmp;
}

int main(void) {
    long x = 36L, y = 58L;
    printf("Before: %ld %ld\n", x, y);
    swap(&x, &y);
    printf("After:  %ld %ld\n", x, y);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: swap() receives the addresses of x and y, so writing through the pointers
   *x and *y changes the caller's variables. tmp holds one value during the exchange.
   main() declares both variables on one line and prints them before and after the swap. */
// END

/* Caption: Return the minimum, maximum and average of an array in a struct. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define a Stats struct with min, max and average.
   2. Write array_stats() that fills one Stats in a loop.
   3. Return the struct.
   4. Print st.min, st.max and st.average. */
typedef struct {
    int min;
    int max;
    double average;
} Stats;

/* Pack several results into one struct and return it. */
Stats array_stats(const int v[], int n) {
    Stats s = {v[0], v[0], 0.0};
    double total = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        if (v[i] < s.min) {
            s.min = v[i];
        }
        if (v[i] > s.max) {
            s.max = v[i];
        }
        total += v[i];
    }
    s.average = total / n;
    return s;
}

int main(void) {
    int readings[] = {45, 54, 42, 65, 88};
    int n = sizeof(readings) / sizeof(readings[0]);
    Stats st = array_stats(readings, n);
    printf("Min %d, Max %d, Average %.2f\n", st.min, st.max, st.average);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: Stats groups three results. array_stats() fills one Stats while it loops
   over the 5 values and returns the whole struct, which is a clean way to return several
   results at once. main() reads them as st.min, st.max and st.average. */
// END

/* Plan:
   1. Write string_length() with a counter len = 0.
   2. Move through the string until the null character.
   3. Return len and print the length of rocket. */
/* Count characters until the terminating '\0'. */
int string_length(const char *word) {

   ends every C string. main() prints the length of the word rocket. */

/* Caption: Write a C program to multiply two 2x2 matrices. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define N as 2.
   2. For every i and j, add a[i][k] * b[k][j] over k into product[i][j].
   3. Print product row by row. */
#define N 2

int main(void) {
    int a[N][N] = {{3, 7}, {2, 0}};
    int b[N][N] = {{2, 2}, {9, 5}};
    int product[N][N] = {0};
    /* product[i][j] is row i of a times column j of b. */
    for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) {
        for (int j = 0; j < N; j++) {
            for (int k = 0; k < N; k++) {
                product[i][j] += a[i][k] * b[k][j];
            }
        }
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) {
        for (int j = 0; j < N; j++) {
            printf("%4d", product[i][j]);
        }
        printf("\n");
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: For each entry product[i][j] the innermost loop adds a[i][k] * b[k][j] over
   k, which is row i of a times column j of b. main() multiplies two 2x2 matrices and
   prints the product. */
// END

/* Caption: Compute 2 to the power of 9 without pow(). */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write power(base, exp) with result = 1.
   2. Multiply result by base exp times.
   3. Print 2 to the power 9. */
/* Multiply the base by itself exp times. */
long long power(int base, int exp) {
    long long result = 1;
    for (int i = 0; i < exp; i++) {
        result *= base;
    }
    return result;
}

int main(void) {
    printf("2^9 = %lld\n", power(2, 9));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: power() starts result at 1 and multiplies it by base exp times. It uses
   long long because powers grow quickly. main() prints 2 to the power 9. */
// END

/* Caption: How do I find the maximum of two numbers in C? */

/* Plan:
   1. Read a and b.
   2. Pick the bigger of a and b.
   3. Print it. */
int main(void) {
    int a, b;
    printf("Enter two numbers: ");
    if (scanf("%d %d", &a, &b) != 2) {
        printf("Invalid input\n");
        return 1;
    }
    int best = b;
    if (a > b) {
        best = a;
    }
    printf("The maximum is %d\n", best);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: The program reads a and b from the keyboard with scanf and stops with a
   message if the input is not valid. It starts with best = b and replaces it with a when a
   is bigger, then prints best. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to decide if 1907 is a leap year. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write is_leap(year).
   2. A year divisible by 4 is a leap year, unless it is divisible by 100.
   3. Years divisible by 400 are leap years again.
   4. Check 1907 and print the result. */
/* Leap years divide by 4, except centuries, which must divide by 400. */
int is_leap(int year) {
    return (year % 4 == 0 && year % 100 != 0) || year % 400 == 0;
}

int main(void) {
    int year = 1907;
    if (is_leap(year)) {
        printf("%d is a leap year\n", year);
    } else {
        printf("%d is not a leap year\n", year);
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: is_leap() returns true for years divisible by 4, except century years,
   which must also be divisible by 400. main() checks 1907 and prints whether it is a leap
   year. */
// END

/* Caption: Reverse the digits of a number. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Start result at 0.
   2. Multiply result by 10, add n % 10, then divide n by 10.
   3. Repeat until n is 0.
   4. Apply it to 466494 and print the result. */
/* Take the last digit with % 10, then drop it with / 10. */
int reverse_digits(int n) {
    int result = 0;
    while (n > 0) {
        result = result * 10 + n % 10;
        n /= 10;
    }
    return result;
}

int main(void) {
    int number = 466494;
    printf("reverse of digits of %d: %d\n", number, reverse_digits(number));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: reverse_digits() shifts result one place left (result * 10) and adds the
   last digit of n, which reverses the order. main() applies it to 466494. */
// END

/* Caption: C program to write a function that returns the distance between two points given x1, y1, x2 and y2. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <math.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write distance(x1, y1, x2, y2).
   2. Compute dx and dy, then return sqrt(dx * dx + dy * dy).
   3. Print the distance between (-2, -5) and (-6, 5). */
/* Pythagoras: the distance is sqrt(dx * dx + dy * dy). */
double distance(double x1, double y1, double x2, double y2) {
    double dx = x2 - x1, dy = y2 - y1;
    return sqrt(dx * dx + dy * dy);
}

int main(void) {
    printf("Distance: %.3f\n", distance(-2, -5, -6, 5));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: distance() takes the coordinates of both points as four parameters. It
   declares dx and dy on one line and uses Pythagoras with sqrt() from math.h. main()
   prints the distance between (-2, -5) and (-6, 5). */
// END

/* Caption: Count the even values in a list of integers. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write count_even() that takes samples and count.
   2. For each element, test samples[i] % 2 == 0.
   3. Add one to found for every even number.
   4. Return found and print it. */
/* A number is even when the remainder after dividing by 2 is zero. */
int count_even(const int samples[], int count) {
    int found = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < count; i++) {
        if (samples[i] % 2 == 0) {
            found++;
        }
    }
    return found;
}

int main(void) {
    int samples[] = {14, 86, 94, 67, 26, 92, 32};
    int count = 7;
    printf("Even numbers: %d\n", count_even(samples, count));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: count_even() tests each element of samples with the % operator: a remainder
   of 0 after dividing by 2 means the number is even, so found goes up by one. main()
   prints how many of the 7 values are even. */
// END

/* Caption: C program to print the binary representation of an integer. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write print_binary(n, bits).
   2. Go through the bits from the highest to the lowest.
   3. Print 1 when (n >> b) & 1 is set, otherwise 0.
   4. Print 197 in binary. */
/* Check each bit from the highest to the lowest. */
void print_binary(unsigned int n, int bits) {
    for (int b = bits - 1; b >= 0; b--) {
        putchar((n >> b) & 1 ? '1' : '0');
    }
    putchar('\n');
}

int main(void) {
    unsigned int number = 197;
    printf("%u in binary: ", number);
    print_binary(number, 8);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: print_binary() checks one bit at a time, from the highest to the lowest: (n
   >> b) & 1 is 1 when bit b is set, so it prints the character 1 or 0. main() prints 197
   in binary. */
// END

/* Caption: How do I search an array for a value and print its position in C? */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write linear_search() with the array, its length and needle.

/* Caption: Print all prime numbers up to 33. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write is_prime(n); numbers below 2 are not prime.
   2. Try every divisor d while d * d <= n.
   3. Return false if one divides n, otherwise true.
   4. Print every prime from 2 to 33. */
/* A prime has no divisor between 2 and its square root. */
bool is_prime(int n) {
    if (n < 2) {
        return false;
    }
    for (int d = 2; d * d <= n; d++) {
        if (n % d == 0) {
            return false;
        }
    }
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    for (int n = 2; n <= 33; n++) {
        if (is_prime(n)) {
            printf("%d ", n);
        }
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: is_prime() tries every divisor d from 2 while d * d <= n; if one divides n
   evenly, n is not prime. main() tests every number from 2 to 33 and prints the primes. */
// END

/* Caption: Return a circle's area and circumference through pointers. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write circle_measures() with the pointers area and circumference.
   2. Store PI * r * r and 2 * PI * r through them.
   3. Print both for a radius of 11.4. */
#define PI 3.14159265

void circle_measures(double radius, double *area, double *circumference) {
    *area = PI * radius * radius;
    *circumference = 2 * PI * radius;
}

int main(void) {
    double radius = 11.4;
    double area, circumference;
    circle_measures(radius, &area, &circumference);
    printf("Area: %.2f, Circumference: %.2f\n", area, circumference);
    return 0;
}

   through the pointers area and circumference. main() declares both variables on one line,
   passes their addresses and prints the results for a radius of 11.4. */
// END

/* Caption: Return the minimum, maximum and average of an array in a struct. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define a Stats struct with min, max and average.
   2. Write array_stats() that fills one Stats in a loop.
   3. Return the struct.
   4. Print st.min, st.max and st.average. */
typedef struct {
    int min;
    int max;
    double average;
} Stats;

/* Pack several results into one struct and return it. */
Stats array_stats(const int v[], int n) {
    Stats s = {v[0], v[0], 0.0};
    double total = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        if (v[i] < s.min) {
            s.min = v[i];
        }
        if (v[i] > s.max) {
            s.max = v[i];
        }
        total += v[i];
    }
    s.average = total / n;
    return s;
}

int main(void) {
    int prices[] = {53, 16, 41, 91, 43};
    int n = sizeof(prices) / sizeof(prices[0]);
    Stats st = array_stats(prices, n);
    printf("Min %d, Max %d, Average %.2f\n", st.min, st.max, st.average);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: Stats groups three results. array_stats() fills one Stats while it loops
   over the 5 values and returns the whole struct, which is a clean way to return several
   results at once. main() reads them as st.min, st.max and st.average. */
// END

/* Caption: C program to show the Fibonacci series with a loop. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Start with prev = 0 and curr = 1.
   2. Repeat 21 times and print prev each time.
   3. Compute next = prev + curr, then set prev = curr and curr = next. */
int main(void) {
    long prev = 0, curr = 1;
    /* Print a term, then slide the pair one step along the sequence. */
    for (int i = 0; i < 21; i++) {
        printf("%ld ", prev);
        long next = prev + curr;
        prev = curr;
        curr = next;
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: The loop keeps the last two numbers in prev and curr. Each round it prints
   prev, then moves the pair forward: prev becomes curr and curr becomes their sum. It
   prints the first 21 Fibonacci numbers. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to use binary search to locate a value in a sorted list. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Make sure the array is sorted.
   2. Set lo to 0 and hi to size - 1.
   3. While lo <= hi, compare the middle element mid with the key.
   4. Return the index if it matches; otherwise keep only the half that can hold the
      key.
   5. Return -1 if the range becomes empty, and print the index of 9. */
/* The array must be sorted. Each step halves the range that can still hold the key. */
int binary_search(const int ages[], int size, int key) {
    int lo = 0;
    int hi = size - 1;
    while (lo <= hi) {
        int mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;
        if (ages[mid] == key) {
            return mid;
        } else if (ages[mid] < key) {
            lo = mid + 1;   /* key is in the right half */
        } else {
            hi = mid - 1;   /* key is in the left half */
        }
    }
    return -1;
}

int main(void) {
    int ages[] = {9, 14, 41, 55, 59, 64, 101, 133, 153, 178, 192, 193};
    int size = 12;
    int index = binary_search(ages, size, 9);
    printf("Index of 9: %d\n", index);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: binary_search() needs a sorted array. It keeps the range from lo to hi,
   compares the middle element mid with the key and throws away the half that cannot
   contain it, so it needs only about log2(n) steps. main() looks for 9 and prints its
   index, or -1 if it is not there. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to find the largest number in an array. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write find_max() that takes items and size.
   2. Store items[0] in best.
   3. Loop over the other elements and keep the largest value in best.
   4. Return best and print it. */
/* Start with the first element and keep the largest value seen so far. */
double find_max(const double items[], int size) {
    double best = items[0];
    for (int k = 1; k < size; k++) {
        if (items[k] > best) {
            best = items[k];
        }
    }
    return best;
}

int main(void) {
    double items[] = {41.0, 33.3, 96.7, 5.4, 61.4, 34.3, 42.2, 9.3};
    int size = sizeof(items) / sizeof(items[0]);
    printf("Largest: %.2f\n", find_max(items, size));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: find_max() takes the first element as the largest value so far and stores
   it in best. The loop compares every other element with best using > and keeps the
   largest one. main() prints the largest of the 8 values. */
// END

/* Caption: Program to find a number in a sorted array with binary search. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Make sure the array is sorted.
   2. Set low to 0 and high to size - 1.
   3. While low <= high, compare the middle element mid with the key.
   4. Return the index if it matches; otherwise keep only the half that can hold the
      key.
   5. Return -1 if the range becomes empty, and print the index of 82. */
/* The array must be sorted. Each step halves the range that can still hold the key. */
int binary_search(const int readings[], int size, int key) {
    int low = 0;
    int high = size - 1;
    while (low <= high) {
        int mid = low + (high - low) / 2;
        if (readings[mid] == key) {
            return mid;

            low = mid + 1;   /* key is in the right half */
        } else {
            high = mid - 1;   /* key is in the left half */
        }
    }
    return -1;
}

int main(void) {
    int readings[] = {16, 29, 38, 73, 82, 100, 148};
    const int size = 7;
    int index = binary_search(readings, size, 82);
    printf("Index of 82: %d\n", index);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: binary_search() needs a sorted array. It keeps the range from low to high,
   compares the middle element mid with the key and throws away the half that cannot
   contain it, so it needs only about log2(n) steps. main() looks for 82 and prints its
   index, or -1 if it is not there. */
// END

/* Caption: Find the arithmetic mean of 8 int values. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write array_average() that takes data and size.
   2. Add the values into the double acc.
   3. Return acc / size.
   4. Print the average with two decimals. */
/* Sum the values, then divide by how many there are. */
double array_average(const int data[], int size) {
    double acc = 0.0;
    int i = 0;
    while (i < size) {
        acc += data[i];
        i++;
    }
    return acc / size;
}

int main(void) {
    int data[] = {91, 22, 30, 17, 93, 91, 74, 49};
    const int size = 8;
    printf("Average: %.2f\n", array_average(data, size));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: array_average() adds the 8 values of data into the double acc and divides
   by size, so the mean keeps its decimal part even when the values are whole numbers.
   main() prints it with two decimals. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to reverse the digits of a number. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Start result at 0.
   2. Multiply result by 10, add n % 10, then divide n by 10.
   3. Repeat until n is 0.
   4. Apply it to 576942 and print the result. */
/* Take the last digit with % 10, then drop it with / 10. */
int reverse_digits(int n) {
    int result = 0;
    while (n > 0) {
        result = result * 10 + n % 10;
        n /= 10;
    }
    return result;
}

int main(void) {
    int number = 576942;
    printf("reverse of digits of %d: %d\n", number, reverse_digits(number));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: reverse_digits() shifts result one place left (result * 10) and adds the
   last digit of n, which reverses the order. main() applies it to 576942. */
// END

/* Caption: Show the right way to declare several pointers on one line. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Declare x and y on one line.
   2. Declare the pointers px and py on one line, each with its own *.
   3. Add 19 to x through px and print the values. */
int main(void) {
    int x = 5, y = 8;
    /* Each pointer needs its own '*': in "int *p, q;" only p is a pointer. */
    int *px = &x, *py = &y;
    *px += 19;
    printf("x = %d, y = %d\n", x, y);
    printf("*px = %d, *py = %d\n", *px, *py);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: int *px = &x, *py = &y; declares two pointers in one statement; each name
   needs its own *. *px += 19 changes x through the pointer, so x becomes 24 while y stays
   8. */
// END

/* Caption: Compute the factorial of a number with a loop. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write factorial(x) with result = 1.
   2. Multiply result by every number from 2 to x.
   3. Return result.
   4. Print 15! as an unsigned long long. */
/* Multiply 1 * 2 * ... * n. */
unsigned long long factorial(int x) {
    unsigned long long result = 1;
    for (int i = 2; i <= x; i++) {
        result *= i;
    }
    return result;
}

int main(void) {
    int x = 15;
    printf("%d! = %llu\n", x, factorial(x));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: factorial() multiplies result by every number from 2 up to x. main() prints
   15! as an unsigned long long, because factorials grow very fast. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to compute the mean of a list of numbers. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write array_average() that takes marks and size.
   2. Add the values into the double result.
   3. Return result / size.
   4. Print the average with two decimals. */
/* The mean is the total divided by the count. */
double array_average(const int marks[], int size) {
    double result = 0.0;
    for (int j = 0; j < size; j++) {
        result += marks[j];
    }
    return result / size;
}

int main(void) {
    int marks[] = {40, 49, 65, 52, 18, 38, 59, 47, 51};
    int size = 9;
    printf("The average is %.2f\n", array_average(marks, size));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: array_average() adds the 9 values of marks into the double result and
   divides by size, so the mean keeps its decimal part even when the values are whole
   numbers. main() prints it with two decimals. */
// END

/* Caption: Return a sum and an average together using pointer parameters. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write sum_and_average() with the pointers sum and average.
   2. Add the values into *sum.
   3. Store *sum / n in *average.
   4. Declare total and mean, pass their addresses and print them. */
void sum_and_average(const double v[], int n, double *sum, double *average) {
    *sum = 0.0;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        *sum += v[i];
    }
    *average = *sum / n;
}

int main(void) {
    double numbers[] = {29.2, 68.1, 76.3, 23.8, 28.5};
    int n = sizeof(numbers) / sizeof(numbers[0]);
    double total, mean;
    sum_and_average(numbers, n, &total, &mean);
    printf("Sum: %.2f, Average: %.2f\n", total, mean);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: sum_and_average() takes the array, its length and two pointers. It adds up
   the 5 values through *sum and then stores *sum / n in *average. main() declares total
   and mean on one line and passes their addresses. */
// END

/* Caption: Check whether a word is a palindrome. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <string.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write is_palindrome() for str.
   2. Compare the first and last characters, moving inwards.
   3. Return false at the first mismatch, otherwise true.
   4. Check matrix and print the result. */
/* Compare characters from the front and back, moving inwards. */
bool is_palindrome(const char *str) {
    int i = 0;
    int j = strlen(str) - 1;
    while (i < j) {
        if (str[i] != str[j]) {
            return false;
        }
        i++;
        j--;
    }
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    const char *str = "matrix";
    printf("%s %s a palindrome\n", str, is_palindrome(str) ? "is" : "is not");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: is_palindrome() compares the first and last characters and moves inwards;
   any mismatch means the word is not a palindrome. main() checks the word matrix and
   prints the result. */
// END

/* Caption: Sort an array in ascending order using insertion sort. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write insertion_sort() for the int array samples.
   2. Take each element in turn as current.
   3. Shift the larger values of the sorted part one place right.
   4. Put current into the gap.
   5. Print the sorted values. */
/* Insert each element into the already sorted part on its left. */
void insertion_sort(int samples[], int length) {
    for (int i = 1; i < length; i++) {
        int current = samples[i];
        int j = i - 1;
        while (j >= 0 && samples[j] > current) {
            samples[j + 1] = samples[j];   /* shift bigger values right */
            j--;
        }
        samples[j + 1] = current;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    int samples[] = {92, 82, 32, 66, 9, 69, 65, 25, 66};
    int length = sizeof(samples) / sizeof(samples[0]);
    insertion_sort(samples, length);
    for (int i = 0; i < length; i++) {
        printf("%d ", samples[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: insertion_sort() takes each element in turn and shifts the larger values of
   the sorted part one place right until the element fits. main() then prints the 9 values
   in ascending order. */
// END

/* Caption: Find the maximum of three numbers. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Read a, b and c.
   2. Assume a is the maximum.
   3. Compare it with the other two and keep the bigger value.
   4. Print the result. */
int main(void) {
    double a, b, c;
    printf("Enter three numbers: ");
    if (scanf("%lf %lf %lf", &a, &b, &c) != 3) {
        printf("Invalid input\n");
        return 1;
    }
    double best = a;
    /* Compare with each of the others and keep the bigger one. */
    if (b > best) {
        best = b;
    }
    if (c > best) {
        best = c;
    }
    printf("The maximum is %.2f\n", best);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: The program reads a, b and c from the keyboard with scanf and stops with a
   message if the input is not valid. It assumes a is the maximum, compares it with the
   other two and keeps the bigger value in best, which it prints. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to implement insertion sort for an array of double values. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write insertion_sort() for the double array scores.
   2. Take each element in turn as current.
   3. Shift the smaller values of the sorted part one place right.
   4. Put current into the gap.
   5. Print the sorted values. */
/* Insert each element into the already sorted part on its left. */
void insertion_sort(double scores[], int n) {
    for (int i = 1; i < n; i++) {
        double current = scores[i];
        int j = i - 1;
        while (j >= 0 && scores[j] < current) {
            scores[j + 1] = scores[j];   /* shift bigger values right */
            j--;
        }
        scores[j + 1] = current;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    double scores[] = {59.4, 68.2, 90.1, 84.4, 56.1, 43.2};
    int n = sizeof(scores) / sizeof(scores[0]);
    insertion_sort(scores, n);
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        printf("%.2f ", scores[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: insertion_sort() takes each element in turn and shifts the smaller values
   of the sorted part one place right until the element fits. main() then prints the 6
   values in descending order. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to search an array for its smallest value. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write find_min() that takes nums and length.
   2. Store nums[0] in m.
   3. Loop over the other elements and keep the smallest value in m.
   4. Return m and print it. */
/* Start with the first element and keep the smallest value seen so far. */
long find_min(const long nums[], int length) {
    long m = nums[0];
    for (int j = 1; j < length; j++) {
        if (nums[j] < m) {
            m = nums[j];
        }
    }
    return m;
}

int main(void) {
    long nums[] = {83L, 15L, 33L, 71L};
    int length = 4;
    printf("The smallest value is %ld\n", find_min(nums, length));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: find_min() takes the first element as the smallest value so far and stores
   it in m. The loop compares every other element with m using < and keeps the smallest
   one. main() prints the smallest of the 4 values. */
// END

/* Plan:
   1. Write string_length() with a counter len = 0.
   2. Move through the string until the null character.
   3. Return len and print the length of noon. */
/* Count characters until the terminating '\0'. */
int string_length(const char *word) {
    int len = 0;
    while (word[len] != '\0') {
        len++;
    }
    return len;
}

/* Caption: Use bubble sort to put numbers in ascending order. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write bubble_sort() for the long array readings.
   2. Compare each pair of neighbours.
   3. Swap them when they are in the wrong order for ascending order.
   4. Repeat the passes until the array is sorted.
   5. Print the sorted values. */
/* Repeatedly swap neighbours that are in the wrong order. */
void bubble_sort(long readings[], int count) {
    for (int i = 0; i < count - 1; i++) {
        for (int j = 0; j < count - 1 - i; j++) {
            if (readings[j] > readings[j + 1]) {
                long tmp = readings[j];
                readings[j] = readings[j + 1];
                readings[j + 1] = tmp;
            }
        }
    }
}

int main(void) {
    long readings[] = {30L, 77L, 88L, 21L, 71L};
    const int count = 5;
    bubble_sort(readings, count);
    for (int i = 0; i < count; i++) {
        printf("%ld ", readings[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: bubble_sort() walks through readings again and again and swaps neighbours
   that are in the wrong order, so the largest values move to the end first. main() then
   prints the 5 values in ascending order. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to use binary search to locate a value in a sorted list. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Make sure the array is sorted.
   2. Set left to 0 and right to count - 1.
   3. While left <= right, compare the middle element middle with the key.
   4. Return the index if it matches; otherwise keep only the half that can hold the
      key.
   5. Return -1 if the range becomes empty, and print the index of 143. */
/* The array must be sorted. Each step halves the range that can still hold the key. */
int binary_search(const int values[], int count, int key) {
    int left = 0;
    int right = count - 1;
    while (left <= right) {
        int middle = left + (right - left) / 2;
        if (values[middle] == key) {
            return middle;
        } else if (values[middle] < key) {
            left = middle + 1;   /* key is in the right half */
        } else {
            right = middle - 1;   /* key is in the left half */
        }
    }
    return -1;
}

int main(void) {
    int values[] = {37, 43, 67, 93, 143, 154, 158};
    int count = 7;
    int index = binary_search(values, count, 143);
    printf("Index of 143: %d\n", index);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: binary_search() needs a sorted array. It keeps the range from left to
   right, compares the middle element middle with the key and throws away the half that
   cannot contain it, so it needs only about log2(n) steps. main() looks for 143 and prints
   its index, or -1 if it is not there. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to find the index of a number using linear search. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write linear_search() with the array, its length and key.
   2. Compare each element with key.
   3. Return the index of the first match, or -1.
   4. In main(), search for 97 and print the result. */
/* Return the index of key, or -1 when it is not in the array. */
int linear_search(const int values[], int length, int key) {
    for (int k = 0; k < length; k++) {
        if (values[k] == key) {
            return k;
        }
    }
    return -1;
}

int main(void) {
    int values[] = {21, 19, 97, 54, 39, 83};
    int length = sizeof(values) / sizeof(values[0]);
    int key = 97;
    int pos = linear_search(values, length, key);
    if (pos >= 0) {
        printf("Found %d at index %d\n", key, pos);
    } else {
        printf("%d is not in the array\n", key);
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: linear_search() checks the elements of values one by one and returns the
   index of the first one equal to key, or -1 when it reaches the end without a match.
   main() searches for 97 and prints where it is, or that it is missing. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to transpose a matrix. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define ROWS as 3 and COLS as 3.
   2. Copy m[r][c] into t[c][r] for every element.
   3. Print t row by row. */
#define ROWS 3
#define COLS 3

int main(void) {
    int m[ROWS][COLS] = {{6, 1, 5}, {8, 7, 1}, {2, 1, 3}};
    int t[COLS][ROWS];
    /* Element (r, c) moves to (c, r). */
    for (int r = 0; r < ROWS; r++) {
        for (int c = 0; c < COLS; c++) {
            t[c][r] = m[r][c];
        }
    }
    for (int r = 0; r < COLS; r++) {
        for (int c = 0; c < ROWS; c++) {
            printf("%3d", t[r][c]);
        }
        printf("\n");
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: The nested loops copy m[r][c] into t[c][r], so the 3x3 matrix becomes 3x3.
   A second pair of loops prints the result. */
// END

/* Caption: Create a singly linked list by inserting at the head. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define ListNode with a value and a next pointer.
   2. Write push_front() that mallocs a node and links it in front of head.
   3. Write print_list() that follows next until NULL.
   4. Write free_list() that frees every node.
   5. Push 5 values, print the list and free it. */
typedef struct ListNode {
    int value;
    struct ListNode *next;
} ListNode;

/* Allocate a new node and put it in front of the current head. */
ListNode *push_front(ListNode *head, int value) {
    ListNode *node = malloc(sizeof(ListNode));
    if (node == NULL) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Out of memory\n");
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }
    node->value = value;
    node->next = head;
    return node;
}

void print_list(const ListNode *head) {
    for (const ListNode *cur = head; cur != NULL; cur = cur->next) {
        printf("%d -> ", cur->value);
    }
    printf("NULL\n");
}

/* Free every node; save next before freeing the current one. */
void free_list(ListNode *head) {
    while (head != NULL) {
        ListNode *next = head->next;
        free(head);
        head = next;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    ListNode *head = NULL;
    head = push_front(head, 90);
    head = push_front(head, 62);
    head = push_front(head, 55);
    head = push_front(head, 2);
    head = push_front(head, 61);
    print_list(head);
    free_list(head);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: Each ListNode holds a value and a pointer to the next node. push_front()
   allocates a node with malloc, puts it in front of head and returns it; print_list()
   follows the next pointers until NULL; free_list() frees every node. main() pushes 5
   values, so they print in reverse order. */
// END

/* Caption: Compute the sum of the elements of an array. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write total_of() that takes the array values and its length len.
   2. Start total at 0 and add every element in a for loop.
   3. Return total.
   4. In main(), fill values with 5 values and print the sum. */
/* Walk through the array and accumulate each value. */
int total_of(const int values[], int len) {
    int total = 0;
    for (int k = 0; k < len; k++) {
        total += values[k];
    }
    return total;
}

int main(void) {
    int values[] = {70, 48, 29, 26, 45};
    int len = sizeof(values) / sizeof(values[0]);
    printf("Sum: %d\n", total_of(values, len));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: total_of() receives the array values and its length len. It starts total at
   0, adds every element to it in a for loop and returns the total. main() fills values
   with 5 int values and prints their sum. */
// END

/* Caption: Check whether a year is a leap year. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write is_leap(year).
   2. A year divisible by 4 is a leap year, unless it is divisible by 100.
   3. Years divisible by 400 are leap years again.
   4. Check 2021 and print the result. */
/* Leap years divide by 4, except centuries, which must divide by 400. */
int is_leap(int year) {
    return (year % 4 == 0 && year % 100 != 0) || year % 400 == 0;
}

int main(void) {
    int year = 2021;
    if (is_leap(year)) {
        printf("%d is a leap year\n", year);
    } else {
        printf("%d is not a leap year\n", year);
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: is_leap() returns true for years divisible by 4, except century years,
   which must also be divisible by 400. main() checks 2021 and prints whether it is a leap
   year. */
// END

/* Caption: Generate the Fibonacci sequence. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Start with prev = 0 and curr = 1.
   2. Repeat 15 times and print prev each time.
   3. Compute next = prev + curr, then set prev = curr and curr = next. */
int main(void) {
    long prev = 0, curr = 1;
    /* Print a term, then slide the pair one step along the sequence. */
    for (int i = 0; i < 15; i++) {
        printf("%ld ", prev);
        long next = prev + curr;
        prev = curr;
        curr = next;
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: The loop keeps the last two numbers in prev and curr. Each round it prints
   prev, then moves the pair forward: prev becomes curr and curr becomes their sum. It
   prints the first 15 Fibonacci numbers. */
// END

/* Caption: Find the largest of four numbers with a function. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write max2() that returns the larger of two values.
   2. Write max_of_four() as max2(max2(a, b), max2(c, d)).
   3. Print the largest of the four values. */
/* Return the larger of two values. */
int max2(int a, int b) {
    return a > b ? a : b;
}

/* Reuse max2 to compare four values. */
int max_of_four(int a, int b, int c, int d) {
    return max2(max2(a, b), max2(c, d));
}

int main(void) {
    int a = 39, b = 15, c = 60, d = 49;
    printf("Largest: %d\n", max_of_four(a, b, c, d));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: max_of_four() takes four parameters and reuses the helper max2(), which
   returns the larger of two values: it compares a with b, c with d, and then the two
   winners. main() prints the largest of 39, 15, 60 and 49. */
// END

/* Caption: Reverse the elements of an array in place. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write reverse_array() for items.
   2. Set i to the first index and j to the last.
   3. Swap items[i] and items[j], then move both inwards.
   4. Stop when i meets j and print the array. */
/* Swap the outer pair, then move both ends toward the middle. */
void reverse_array(long items[], int length) {
    int i = 0;
    int j = length - 1;
    while (i < j) {
        long tmp = items[i];
        items[i] = items[j];
        items[j] = tmp;
        i++;
        j--;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    long items[] = {21L, 79L, 62L, 31L, 15L, 80L};
    const int length = 6;
    reverse_array(items, length);
    for (int i = 0; i < length; i++) {
        printf("%ld ", items[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: reverse_array() swaps the first and last elements, then moves i forward and
   j backward until they meet, so the array is reversed in place without a second array.
   main() prints the reversed values. */
// END

/* Caption: C program to find the greatest common divisor of two numbers. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write gcd() with Euclid's algorithm.
   2. Replace (a, b) by (b, a % b) until b is 0.
   3. Return a and print the GCD of 248 and 8. */
/* Euclid: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a % b) until b becomes zero. */
int gcd(int a, int b) {
    while (b != 0) {
        int r = a % b;
        a = b;
        b = r;
    }
    return a;
}

int main(void) {
    int x = 248, y = 8;
    printf("gcd(%d, %d) = %d\n", x, y, gcd(x, y));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: gcd() uses Euclid's algorithm: it keeps replacing (a, b) with (b, a % b)
   until b is 0. The last non-zero value is the greatest common divisor, and main() prints
   the GCD of 248 and 8. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a function that tests if a value is inside a range. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write in_range(x, low, high).
   2. Return true when x >= low and x <= high.
   3. Print whether 2 is inside 48 to 65. */
/* true when low <= x <= high */
bool in_range(int x, int low, int high) {
    return x >= low && x <= high;
}

int main(void) {
    int value = 2, low = 48, high = 65;
    printf("%d is %s the range %d to %d\n", value,
           in_range(value, low, high) ? "inside" : "outside", low, high);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: in_range() takes the value and both limits and returns true only when the
   value is at least low and at most high. main() declares value, low and high on one line
   and prints whether 2 is inside 48 to 65. */
// END

/* Caption: How do I write lines to a text file and read them back in C? */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Open log.txt in write mode and check for NULL.
   2. Write 4 lines with fprintf and close the file.
   3. Open it again in read mode.
   4. Read and print each line with fgets, then close the file. */
int main(void) {
    FILE *file = fopen("log.txt", "w");
    if (file == NULL) {
        perror("fopen");
        return 1;
    }
    fprintf(file, "strings end with a null character\n");
    fprintf(file, "c gives you direct control over memory\n");
    fprintf(file, "pointers store the address of another variable\n");
    fprintf(file, "every program starts in main\n");
    fclose(file);

    /* Reopen the file for reading and print it line by line. */
    file = fopen("log.txt", "r");
    if (file == NULL) {
        perror("fopen");
        return 1;
    }
    char line[128];
    while (fgets(line, sizeof(line), file) != NULL) {
        printf("%s", line);
    }
    fclose(file);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: fopen() in write mode creates log.txt, fprintf() writes 4 lines into it and
   fclose() saves it. The file is then opened again in read mode, and fgets() reads it back
   line by line into the buffer line, which is printed. Every fopen() result is checked for
   NULL. */
// END

/* Caption: Count the odd values in a list of integers. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write count_odd() that takes prices and count.
   2. For each element, test prices[k] % 2 != 0.
   3. Add one to found for every odd number.
   4. Return found and print it. */
/* A number is odd when the remainder after dividing by 2 is one. */
int count_odd(const int prices[], int count) {
    int found = 0;
    for (int k = 0; k < count; k++) {
        if (prices[k] % 2 != 0) {
            found++;
        }
    }
    return found;
}

int main(void) {
    int prices[] = {93, 1, 74, 30, 70, 87, 64};
    int count = sizeof(prices) / sizeof(prices[0]);
    printf("Odd numbers: %d\n", count_odd(prices, count));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: count_odd() tests each element of prices with the % operator: a remainder
   of 1 after dividing by 2 means the number is odd, so found goes up by one. main() prints
   how many of the 7 values are odd. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a function that swaps two int values through pointers. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write swap() that takes pointers to two int values.
   2. Save *x in tmp, copy *y into *x, then tmp into *y.
   3. In main(), print x and y, call swap(&x, &y) and print them again. */
/* Pass addresses so the function can change the caller's variables. */
void swap(int *x, int *y) {
    int tmp = *x;
    *x = *y;
    *y = tmp;
}

int main(void) {
    int x = 53, y = 36;
    printf("Before: %d %d\n", x, y);
    swap(&x, &y);
    printf("After:  %d %d\n", x, y);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: swap() receives the addresses of x and y, so writing through the pointers
   *x and *y changes the caller's variables. tmp holds one value during the exchange.
   main() declares both variables on one line and prints them before and after the swap. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to print the factorial of an integer. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write factorial(value) with result = 1.
   2. Multiply result by every number from 2 to value.
   3. Return result.
   4. Print 10! as an unsigned long long. */
/* Multiply 1 * 2 * ... * n. */
unsigned long long factorial(int value) {
    unsigned long long result = 1;
    for (int i = 2; i <= value; i++) {
        result *= i;
    }
    return result;
}

int main(void) {
    int value = 10;
    printf("%d! = %llu\n", value, factorial(value));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: factorial() multiplies result by every number from 2 up to value. main()
   prints 10! as an unsigned long long, because factorials grow very fast. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to use insertion sort to put numbers in ascending order. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write insertion_sort() for the int array scores.
   2. Take each element in turn as current.
   3. Shift the larger values of the sorted part one place right.
   4. Put current into the gap.
   5. Print the sorted values. */
/* Insert each element into the already sorted part on its left. */
void insertion_sort(int scores[], int count) {
    for (int i = 1; i < count; i++) {
        int current = scores[i];
        int j = i - 1;
        while (j >= 0 && scores[j] > current) {
            scores[j + 1] = scores[j];   /* shift bigger values right */
            j--;
        }
        scores[j + 1] = current;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    int scores[] = {28, 77, 98, 89, 14, 94, 40};
    int count = sizeof(scores) / sizeof(scores[0]);
    insertion_sort(scores, count);
    for (int i = 0; i < count; i++) {
        printf("%d ", scores[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: insertion_sort() takes each element in turn and shifts the larger values of
   the sorted part one place right until the element fits. main() then prints the 7 values
   in ascending order. */
// END

#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write power(base, exp) with result = 1.
   2. Multiply result by base exp times.
   3. Print 2 to the power 3. */
/* Multiply the base by itself exp times. */
long long power(int base, int exp) {
    long long result = 1;
    for (int i = 0; i < exp; i++) {
        result *= base;
    }
    return result;
}

int main(void) {
    printf("2^3 = %lld\n", power(2, 3));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: power() starts result at 1 and multiplies it by base exp times. It uses
   long long because powers grow quickly. main() prints 2 to the power 3. */
// END

/* Caption: Print the binary representation of an integer. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write print_binary(n, bits).
   2. Go through the bits from the highest to the lowest.
   3. Print 1 when (n >> b) & 1 is set, otherwise 0.
   4. Print 1022 in binary. */
/* Check each bit from the highest to the lowest. */
void print_binary(unsigned int n, int bits) {
    for (int b = bits - 1; b >= 0; b--) {
        putchar((n >> b) & 1 ? '1' : '0');
    }
    putchar('\n');
}

int main(void) {
    unsigned int number = 1022;
    printf("%u in binary: ", number);
    print_binary(number, 12);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: print_binary() checks one bit at a time, from the highest to the lowest: (n
   >> b) & 1 is 1 when bit b is set, so it prints the character 1 or 0. main() prints 1022
   in binary. */
// END

    int width;
    int height;

    return 0;

   perimeter() returns 2 * (width + height). main() makes a 5 by 19 rectangle and prints
   both results. */

/* Caption: Write a C program to write a function with four parameters that returns the maximum. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write max2() that returns the larger of two values.
   2. Write max_of_four() as max2(max2(a, b), max2(c, d)).
   3. Print the largest of the four values. */
/* Return the larger of two values. */
int max2(int a, int b) {
    return a > b ? a : b;
}

/* Reuse max2 to compare four values. */
int max_of_four(int a, int b, int c, int d) {
    return max2(max2(a, b), max2(c, d));
}

int main(void) {
    int a = 60, b = 70, c = 13, d = 97;
    printf("Largest: %d\n", max_of_four(a, b, c, d));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: max_of_four() takes four parameters and reuses the helper max2(), which
   returns the larger of two values: it compares a with b, c with d, and then the two
   winners. main() prints the largest of 60, 70, 13 and 97. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to return the smallest element of an array of int values. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write min_of() that takes readings and n.
   2. Store readings[0] in current.
   3. Loop over the other elements and keep the smallest value in current.
   4. Return current and print it. */
/* Start with the first element and keep the smallest value seen so far. */
int min_of(const int readings[], int n) {
    int current = readings[0];
    for (int idx = 1; idx < n; idx++) {
        if (readings[idx] < current) {
            current = readings[idx];
        }
    }
    return current;
}

int main(void) {
    int readings[] = {43, 37, 59, 71, 87, 19, 60, 15, 27};
    const int n = 9;
    printf("The smallest value is %d\n", min_of(readings, n));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: min_of() takes the first element as the smallest value so far and stores it
   in current. The loop compares every other element with current using < and keeps the
   smallest one. main() prints the smallest of the 9 values. */
// END

/* Caption: Count how many digits a number has. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Start result at 0.
   2. Divide n by 10 and add one to result.
   3. Repeat until n is 0.
   4. Apply it to 796137 and print the result. */
/* Take the last digit with % 10, then drop it with / 10. */
int count_digits(int n) {
    int result = 0;
    while (n > 0) {
        result++;
        n /= 10;
    }
    return result;
}

int main(void) {
    int number = 796137;
    printf("count of digits of %d: %d\n", number, count_digits(number));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: count_digits() removes the last digit (n / 10) and adds one to result each
   time, until n reaches 0. main() applies it to 796137. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to return two values from a function using pointer parameters. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write min_max() with the array, its length and the pointers min and max.
   2. Start both at the first element.
   3. Update *min and *max while looping over the rest.
   4. Declare min and max, pass their addresses and print them. */
/* One pass finds both results; they are stored through the pointers. */
void min_max(const int ages[], int count, int *min, int *max) {
    *min = ages[0];
    *max = ages[0];
    for (int i = 1; i < count; i++) {
        if (ages[i] < *min) {
            *min = ages[i];
        }
        if (ages[i] > *max) {
            *max = ages[i];
        }
    }
}

int main(void) {
    int ages[] = {64, 98, 33, 19, 9, 19};
    int count = 6;
    int min, max;
    min_max(ages, count, &min, &max);
    printf("Min: %d, Max: %d\n", min, max);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: A C function can return only one value, so min_max() returns void and
   writes its two results through the pointer parameters min and max. main() declares min
   and max on one line and passes their addresses with &, then prints both results for the
   6 values. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to return the minimum, maximum and average of an array in a struct. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define a Stats struct with min, max and average.
   2. Write array_stats() that fills one Stats in a loop.
   3. Return the struct.
   4. Print st.min, st.max and st.average. */
typedef struct {
    int min;
    int max;
    double average;
} Stats;

/* Pack several results into one struct and return it. */
Stats array_stats(const int v[], int n) {
    Stats s = {v[0], v[0], 0.0};
    double total = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        if (v[i] < s.min) {
            s.min = v[i];
        }
        if (v[i] > s.max) {
            s.max = v[i];
        }
        total += v[i];
    }
    s.average = total / n;
    return s;
}

int main(void) {
    int samples[] = {74, 98, 98, 94, 51, 27, 2, 21};
    int n = sizeof(samples) / sizeof(samples[0]);
    Stats st = array_stats(samples, n);
    printf("Min %d, Max %d, Average %.2f\n", st.min, st.max, st.average);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: Stats groups three results. array_stats() fills one Stats while it loops
   over the 8 values and returns the whole struct, which is a clean way to return several
   results at once. main() reads them as st.min, st.max and st.average. */
// END

/* Caption: Create a singly linked list by inserting at the head. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define Item with a value and a next pointer.
   2. Write push_front() that mallocs a node and links it in front of head.
   3. Write print_list() that follows next until NULL.
   4. Write free_list() that frees every node.
   5. Push 5 values, print the list and free it. */
typedef struct Item {
    int value;
    struct Item *next;
} Item;

/* Allocate a new node and put it in front of the current head. */
Item *push_front(Item *head, int value) {
    Item *node = malloc(sizeof(Item));
    if (node == NULL) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Out of memory\n");
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }
    node->value = value;
    node->next = head;
    return node;
}

void print_list(const Item *head) {
    for (const Item *cur = head; cur != NULL; cur = cur->next) {
        printf("%d -> ", cur->value);
    }
    printf("NULL\n");
}

/* Free every node; save next before freeing the current one. */
void free_list(Item *head) {
    while (head != NULL) {
        Item *next = head->next;
        free(head);
        head = next;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    Item *head = NULL;
    head = push_front(head, 53);
    head = push_front(head, 70);
    head = push_front(head, 46);
    head = push_front(head, 7);
    head = push_front(head, 29);
    print_list(head);
    free_list(head);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: Each Item holds a value and a pointer to the next node. push_front()
   allocates a node with malloc, puts it in front of head and returns it; print_list()
   follows the next pointers until NULL; free_list() frees every node. main() pushes 5
   values, so they print in reverse order. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to save text to a file with fprintf and print it with fgets. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Open data.txt in write mode and check for NULL.
   2. Write 2 lines with fprintf and close the file.
   3. Open it again in read mode.
   4. Read and print each line with fgets, then close the file. */
int main(void) {
    FILE *file = fopen("data.txt", "w");
    if (file == NULL) {
        perror("fopen");
        return 1;
    }
    fprintf(file, "always free the memory you allocate\n");
    fprintf(file, "arrays in c start at index zero\n");
    fclose(file);

    /* Reopen the file for reading and print it line by line. */
    file = fopen("data.txt", "r");
    if (file == NULL) {
        perror("fopen");
        return 1;
    }
    char line[128];
    while (fgets(line, sizeof(line), file) != NULL) {
        printf("%s", line);
    }
    fclose(file);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: fopen() in write mode creates data.txt, fprintf() writes 2 lines into it
   and fclose() saves it. The file is then opened again in read mode, and fgets() reads it
   back line by line into the buffer line, which is printed. Every fopen() result is
   checked for NULL. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a function that swaps two int values through pointers. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write swap() that takes pointers to two int values.
   2. Save *a in tmp, copy *b into *a, then tmp into *b.
   3. In main(), print a and b, call swap(&a, &b) and print them again. */
/* Pass addresses so the function can change the caller's variables. */
void swap(int *a, int *b) {
    int tmp = *a;
    *a = *b;
    *b = tmp;
}

int main(void) {
    int a = 31, b = 6;
    printf("Before: %d %d\n", a, b);
    swap(&a, &b);
    printf("After:  %d %d\n", a, b);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: swap() receives the addresses of a and b, so writing through the pointers
   *a and *b changes the caller's variables. tmp holds one value during the exchange.
   main() declares both variables on one line and prints them before and after the swap. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to sort an array in ascending order using bubble sort. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write bubble_sort() for the int array nums.
   2. Compare each pair of neighbours.
   3. Swap them when they are in the wrong order for ascending order.
   4. Repeat the passes until the array is sorted.
   5. Print the sorted values. */
/* Repeatedly swap neighbours that are in the wrong order. */
void bubble_sort(int nums[], int len) {
    for (int i = 0; i < len - 1; i++) {
        for (int j = 0; j < len - 1 - i; j++) {
            if (nums[j] > nums[j + 1]) {
                int tmp = nums[j];
                nums[j] = nums[j + 1];
                nums[j + 1] = tmp;
            }
        }
    }
}

int main(void) {
    int nums[] = {18, 92, 85, 23, 83, 80, 14, 42};
    int len = 8;
    bubble_sort(nums, len);
    for (int i = 0; i < len; i++) {
        printf("%d ", nums[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: bubble_sort() walks through nums again and again and swaps neighbours that
   are in the wrong order, so the largest values move to the end first. main() then prints
   the 8 values in ascending order. */
// END

/* Caption: C program to reverse an array by swapping from both ends. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write reverse_array() for scores.
   2. Set left to the first index and right to the last.
   3. Swap scores[left] and scores[right], then move both inwards.
   4. Stop when left meets right and print the array. */
/* Swap the outer pair, then move both ends toward the middle. */
void reverse_array(int scores[], int n) {
    int left = 0;
    int right = n - 1;
    while (left < right) {
        int tmp = scores[left];
        scores[left] = scores[right];
        scores[right] = tmp;
        left++;
        right--;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    int scores[] = {72, 12, 82, 86, 38, 22, 18};
    int n = sizeof(scores) / sizeof(scores[0]);
    reverse_array(scores, n);
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        printf("%d ", scores[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: reverse_array() swaps the first and last elements, then moves left forward
   and right backward until they meet, so the array is reversed in place without a second
   array. main() prints the reversed values. */

/* Caption: Implement a circular queue with an array. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define a Queue with room for 32 items, a head and a count.
   2. Write enqueue() that stores at (head + count) % CAPACITY.
   3. Write dequeue() that takes the item at head and moves head on.
   4. Add 3 values, then remove and print them in order. */
#define CAPACITY 32

typedef struct {
    int items[CAPACITY];
    int head;
    int count;
} Queue;

bool enqueue(Queue *q, int value) {
    if (q->count == CAPACITY) {
        return false;
    }
    /* The tail wraps around to the start of the array. */
    q->items[(q->head + q->count) % CAPACITY] = value;
    q->count++;
    return true;
}

bool dequeue(Queue *q, int *value) {
    if (q->count == 0) {
        return false;
    }
    *value = q->items[q->head];
    q->head = (q->head + 1) % CAPACITY;
    q->count--;
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    Queue q = {.head = 0, .count = 0};
    enqueue(&q, 90);
    enqueue(&q, 87);
    enqueue(&q, 80);
    int value;
    /* Items come out in the order they went in (first in, first out). */
    while (dequeue(&q, &value)) {
        printf("%d ", value);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: The Queue stores up to 32 items in a ring buffer: head is the oldest item
   and % CAPACITY wraps positions back to the start of the array. enqueue() adds at the
   back and dequeue() removes from the front, so main() gets its 3 values back in the same
   order (first in, first out). */
// END

/* Caption: How do I save text to a file with fprintf and print it with fgets in C? */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Open log.txt in write mode and check for NULL.
   2. Write 4 lines with fprintf and close the file.
   3. Open it again in read mode.
   4. Read and print each line with fgets, then close the file. */
int main(void) {
    FILE *file = fopen("log.txt", "w");
    if (file == NULL) {
        perror("fopen");
        return 1;
    }
    fprintf(file, "keep functions short and focused\n");
    fprintf(file, "a function can call itself recursively\n");
    fprintf(file, "always free the memory you allocate\n");
    fprintf(file, "the compiler turns source code into machine code\n");
    fclose(file);

    /* Reopen the file for reading and print it line by line. */
    file = fopen("log.txt", "r");
    if (file == NULL) {
        perror("fopen");
        return 1;
    }
    char line[128];
    while (fgets(line, sizeof(line), file) != NULL) {
        printf("%s", line);
    }
    fclose(file);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: fopen() in write mode creates log.txt, fprintf() writes 4 lines into it and
   fclose() saves it. The file is then opened again in read mode, and fgets() reads it back
   line by line into the buffer line, which is printed. Every fopen() result is checked for
   NULL. */
// END

/* Caption: How do I list the prime numbers below a limit in C? */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write is_prime(n); numbers below 2 are not prime.
   2. Try every divisor d while d * d <= n.
   3. Return false if one divides n, otherwise true.
   4. Print every prime from 2 to 76. */
/* A prime has no divisor between 2 and its square root. */
bool is_prime(int n) {
    if (n < 2) {
        return false;
    }
    for (int d = 2; d * d <= n; d++) {
        if (n % d == 0) {
            return false;
        }
    }
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    for (int n = 2; n <= 76; n++) {
        if (is_prime(n)) {
            printf("%d ", n);
        }
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: is_prime() tries every divisor d from 2 while d * d <= n; if one divides n
   evenly, n is not prime. main() tests every number from 2 to 76 and prints the primes. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a function that swaps two double values through pointers. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write swap() that takes pointers to two double values.
   2. Save *first in tmp, copy *second into *first, then tmp into *second.
   3. In main(), print first and second, call swap(&first, &second) and print them
      again. */
/* Pass addresses so the function can change the caller's variables. */
void swap(double *first, double *second) {
    double tmp = *first;
    *first = *second;
    *second = tmp;
}

int main(void) {
    double first = 44.8, second = 60.3;
    printf("Before: %.2f %.2f\n", first, second);
    swap(&first, &second);
    printf("After:  %.2f %.2f\n", first, second);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: swap() receives the addresses of first and second, so writing through the
   pointers *first and *second changes the caller's variables. tmp holds one value during
   the exchange. main() declares both variables on one line and prints them before and
   after the swap. */
// END

   4. Print total divided by the number of students. */

    int mark;

   prints how many of the 8 values are odd. */

/* Caption: Program to decide if 2012 is a leap year. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write is_leap(year).
   2. A year divisible by 4 is a leap year, unless it is divisible by 100.
   3. Years divisible by 400 are leap years again.
   4. Check 2012 and print the result. */
/* Leap years divide by 4, except centuries, which must divide by 400. */
int is_leap(int year) {
    return (year % 4 == 0 && year % 100 != 0) || year % 400 == 0;
}

int main(void) {
    int year = 2012;
    if (is_leap(year)) {
        printf("%d is a leap year\n", year);
    } else {
        printf("%d is not a leap year\n", year);
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: is_leap() returns true for years divisible by 4, except century years,
   which must also be divisible by 400. main() checks 2012 and prints whether it is a leap
   year. */
// END

/* Caption: Sort an array in ascending order using selection sort. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write selection_sort() for the int array prices.
   2. For each position, find the smallest remaining element.
   3. Swap it into that position.
   4. Print the sorted values. */
/* Select the right element for each position and swap it into place. */
void selection_sort(int prices[], int count) {
    for (int i = 0; i < count - 1; i++) {
        int chosen = i;
        for (int j = i + 1; j < count; j++) {
            if (prices[chosen] > prices[j]) {
                chosen = j;
            }
        }
        int tmp = prices[i];
        prices[i] = prices[chosen];
        prices[chosen] = tmp;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    int prices[] = {99, 92, 71, 86, 47, 34, 63, 13, 32};
    int count = sizeof(prices) / sizeof(prices[0]);
    selection_sort(prices, count);
    for (int i = 0; i < count; i++) {
        printf("%d ", prices[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: selection_sort() finds the smallest remaining element for each position and
   swaps it into place. main() then prints the 9 values in ascending order. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to build a FIFO queue using a ring buffer. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define a Queue with room for 16 items, a head and a count.
   2. Write enqueue() that stores at (head + count) % CAPACITY.
   3. Write dequeue() that takes the item at head and moves head on.
   4. Add 3 values, then remove and print them in order. */
#define CAPACITY 16

typedef struct {
    int items[CAPACITY];
    int head;
    int count;
} Queue;

bool enqueue(Queue *q, int value) {
    if (q->count == CAPACITY) {
        return false;
    }
    /* The tail wraps around to the start of the array. */
    q->items[(q->head + q->count) % CAPACITY] = value;
    q->count++;
    return true;
}

bool dequeue(Queue *q, int *value) {
    if (q->count == 0) {
        return false;
    }
    *value = q->items[q->head];
    q->head = (q->head + 1) % CAPACITY;
    q->count--;
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    Queue q = {.head = 0, .count = 0};
    enqueue(&q, 95);
    enqueue(&q, 72);
    enqueue(&q, 14);
    int value;
    /* Items come out in the order they went in (first in, first out). */
    while (dequeue(&q, &value)) {
        printf("%d ", value);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: The Queue stores up to 16 items in a ring buffer: head is the oldest item
   and % CAPACITY wraps positions back to the start of the array. enqueue() adds at the
   back and dequeue() removes from the front, so main() gets its 3 values back in the same
   order (first in, first out). */
// END

/* Caption: Find the greatest common divisor of two numbers. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write gcd() with Euclid's algorithm.
   2. Replace (a, b) by (b, a % b) until b is 0.
   3. Return a and print the GCD of 290 and 36. */
/* Euclid: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a % b) until b becomes zero. */
int gcd(int a, int b) {
    while (b != 0) {
        int r = a % b;
        a = b;
        b = r;
    }
    return a;
}

int main(void) {
    int x = 290, y = 36;
    printf("gcd(%d, %d) = %d\n", x, y, gcd(x, y));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: gcd() uses Euclid's algorithm: it keeps replacing (a, b) with (b, a % b)
   until b is 0. The last non-zero value is the greatest common divisor, and main() prints
   the GCD of 290 and 36. */
// END

/* Caption: Return two values from a function using pointer parameters. */

   1. Write min_max() with the array, its length and the pointers min and max.
   2. Start both at the first element.
   3. Update *min and *max while looping over the rest.
   4. Declare low and high, pass their addresses and print them. */
/* One pass finds both results; they are stored through the pointers. */
void min_max(const int values[], int length, int *min, int *max) {
    *min = values[0];
    *max = values[0];
    for (int i = 1; i < length; i++) {
        if (values[i] < *min) {
            *min = values[i];
        }
        if (values[i] > *max) {
            *max = values[i];
        }
    }
}

    printf("Min: %d, Max: %d\n", low, high);
    return 0;
}

   writes its two results through the pointer parameters min and max. main() declares low

/* One pass finds both results; they are stored through the pointers. */

    *min = data[0];
    *max = data[0];
    for (int i = 1; i < size; i++) {

            *max = data[i];
        }
    }
}

int main(void) {
    int data[] = {40, 45, 43, 70};
    int size = sizeof(data) / sizeof(data[0]);
    int lowest, highest;
    min_max(data, size, &lowest, &highest);
    printf("Min: %d, Max: %d\n", lowest, highest);

}

/* Caption: Search an array for its largest value. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write largest_value() that takes data and count.
   2. Store data[0] in largest.
   3. Loop over the other elements and keep the largest value in largest.
   4. Return largest and print it. */
/* Start with the first element and keep the largest value seen so far. */
int largest_value(const int data[], int count) {
    int largest = data[0];
    for (int idx = 1; idx < count; idx++) {
        if (data[idx] > largest) {
            largest = data[idx];
        }
    }
    return largest;
}

int main(void) {
    int data[] = {35, 72, 30, 50, 13, 3, 64, 82, 24};
    int count = 9;
    printf("Largest: %d\n", largest_value(data, count));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: largest_value() takes the first element as the largest value so far and
   stores it in largest. The loop compares every other element with largest using > and
   keeps the largest one. main() prints the largest of the 9 values. */
// END

/* Plan:

   2. Store total / 3600, (total % 3600) / 60 and total % 60 through them.
   3. Convert 67395 seconds and print the parts. */
void split_seconds(int total, int *hours, int *minutes, int *seconds) {
    *hours = total / 3600;
    *minutes = (total % 3600) / 60;
    *seconds = total % 60;
}

int main(void) {
    int total = 67395;
    int h, m, s;
    split_seconds(total, &h, &m, &s);
    printf("%d seconds = %d h %d min %d s\n", total, h, m, s);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: split_seconds() fills three results through pointers: hours is total /
   3600, minutes is what is left divided by 60, and seconds is total % 60. main() declares
   h, m and s on one line and converts 67395 seconds. */
// END

/* Plan:
   1. Write min_of() that takes values and len.
   2. Store values[0] in m.
   3. Loop over the other elements and keep the smallest value in m.
   4. Return m and print it. */
/* Start with the first element and keep the smallest value seen so far. */
int min_of(const int values[], int len) {
    int m = values[0];
    for (int idx = 1; idx < len; idx++) {
        if (values[idx] < m) {
            m = values[idx];
        }
    }
    return m;
}

int main(void) {
    int values[] = {86, 30, 49, 16};
    int len = 4;
    printf("The smallest value is %d\n", min_of(values, len));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: min_of() takes the first element as the smallest value so far and stores it
   in m. The loop compares every other element with m using < and keeps the smallest one.
   main() prints the smallest of the 4 values. */
// END

/* Caption: C program to use insertion sort to put numbers in ascending order. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write insertion_sort() for the int array items.
   2. Take each element in turn as current.
   3. Shift the larger values of the sorted part one place right.
   4. Put current into the gap.
   5. Print the sorted values. */
/* Insert each element into the already sorted part on its left. */
void insertion_sort(int items[], int size) {
    for (int i = 1; i < size; i++) {
        int current = items[i];
        int j = i - 1;
        while (j >= 0 && items[j] > current) {
            items[j + 1] = items[j];   /* shift bigger values right */
            j--;
        }
        items[j + 1] = current;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    int items[] = {69, 61, 88, 22, 99, 95, 97};
    int size = sizeof(items) / sizeof(items[0]);
    insertion_sort(items, size);
    for (int i = 0; i < size; i++) {
        printf("%d ", items[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: insertion_sort() takes each element in turn and shifts the larger values of
   the sorted part one place right until the element fits. main() then prints the 7 values
   in ascending order. */
// END

/* Caption: How do I print an integer with its digits reversed in C? */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Start result at 0.
   2. Multiply result by 10, add n % 10, then divide n by 10.
   3. Repeat until n is 0.
   4. Apply it to 947160 and print the result. */
/* Take the last digit with % 10, then drop it with / 10. */
int reverse_digits(int n) {
    int result = 0;
    while (n > 0) {
        result = result * 10 + n % 10;
        n /= 10;
    }
    return result;
}

int main(void) {
    int number = 947160;
    printf("reverse of digits of %d: %d\n", number, reverse_digits(number));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: reverse_digits() shifts result one place left (result * 10) and adds the
   last digit of n, which reverses the order. main() applies it to 947160. */
// END

/* Caption: Print the binary representation of an integer. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write print_binary(n, bits).
   2. Go through the bits from the highest to the lowest.
   3. Print 1 when (n >> b) & 1 is set, otherwise 0.
   4. Print 775 in binary. */
/* Check each bit from the highest to the lowest. */
void print_binary(unsigned int n, int bits) {
    for (int b = bits - 1; b >= 0; b--) {
        putchar((n >> b) & 1 ? '1' : '0');
    }
    putchar('\n');
}

int main(void) {
    unsigned int number = 775;
    printf("%u in binary: ", number);
    print_binary(number, 10);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: print_binary() checks one bit at a time, from the highest to the lowest: (n
   >> b) & 1 is 1 when bit b is set, so it prints the character 1 or 0. main() prints 775
   in binary. */
// END

/* Leap years divide by 4, except centuries, which must divide by 400. */

}

int main(void) {
