/* Caption: How do I implement bubble sort for an array of int values in C? */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write bubble_sort() for the int array numbers.
   2. Compare each pair of neighbours.
   3. Swap them when they are in the wrong order for ascending order.
   4. Repeat the passes until the array is sorted.
   5. Print the sorted values. */
/* Repeatedly swap neighbours that are in the wrong order. */
void bubble_sort(int numbers[], int n) {
    for (int i = 0; i < n - 1; i++) {
        for (int j = 0; j < n - 1 - i; j++) {
            if (numbers[j] > numbers[j + 1]) {
                int tmp = numbers[j];
                numbers[j] = numbers[j + 1];
                numbers[j + 1] = tmp;
            }
        }
    }
}

int main(void) {
    int numbers[] = {54, 9, 78, 86, 41, 6, 58};
    const int n = 7;
    bubble_sort(numbers, n);
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        printf("%d ", numbers[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: bubble_sort() walks through numbers again and again and swaps neighbours
   that are in the wrong order, so the largest values move to the end first. main() then
   prints the 7 values in ascending order. */
// END

/* Caption: Create a singly linked list by inserting at the head. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define ListNode with a value and a next pointer.
   2. Write push_front() that mallocs a node and links it in front of head.
   3. Write print_list() that follows next until NULL.
   4. Write free_list() that frees every node.
   5. Push 3 values, print the list and free it. */
typedef struct ListNode {
    int value;
    struct ListNode *next;
} ListNode;

/* Allocate a new node and put it in front of the current head. */
ListNode *push_front(ListNode *head, int value) {
    ListNode *node = malloc(sizeof(ListNode));
    if (node == NULL) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Out of memory\n");
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }
    node->value = value;
    node->next = head;
    return node;
}

void print_list(const ListNode *head) {
    for (const ListNode *cur = head; cur != NULL; cur = cur->next) {
        printf("%d -> ", cur->value);
    }
    printf("NULL\n");
}

/* Free every node; save next before freeing the current one. */
void free_list(ListNode *head) {
    while (head != NULL) {
        ListNode *next = head->next;
        free(head);
        head = next;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    ListNode *head = NULL;
    head = push_front(head, 48);
    head = push_front(head, 4);
    head = push_front(head, 32);
    print_list(head);
    free_list(head);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: Each ListNode holds a value and a pointer to the next node. push_front()
   allocates a node with malloc, puts it in front of head and returns it; print_list()
   follows the next pointers until NULL; free_list() frees every node. main() pushes 3
   values, so they print in reverse order. */
// END

/* Caption: C program to compute the product of two square matrices. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define N as 3.
   2. For every i and j, add a[i][k] * b[k][j] over k into product[i][j].
   3. Print product row by row. */
#define N 3

int main(void) {
    int a[N][N] = {{6, 1, 7}, {1, 7, 0}, {4, 5, 4}};
    int b[N][N] = {{9, 2, 3}, {3, 9, 6}, {0, 3, 3}};
    int product[N][N] = {0};
    /* product[i][j] is row i of a times column j of b. */
    for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) {
        for (int j = 0; j < N; j++) {
            for (int k = 0; k < N; k++) {
                product[i][j] += a[i][k] * b[k][j];
            }
        }
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) {
        for (int j = 0; j < N; j++) {
            printf("%4d", product[i][j]);
        }
        printf("\n");
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: For each entry product[i][j] the innermost loop adds a[i][k] * b[k][j] over
   k, which is row i of a times column j of b. main() multiplies two 3x3 matrices and
   prints the product. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to use selection sort to put numbers in ascending order. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write selection_sort() for the long array prices.
   2. For each position, find the smallest remaining element.
   3. Swap it into that position.
   4. Print the sorted values. */
/* Select the right element for each position and swap it into place. */
void selection_sort(long prices[], int size) {
    for (int i = 0; i < size - 1; i++) {
        int chosen = i;
        for (int j = i + 1; j < size; j++) {
            if (prices[chosen] > prices[j]) {
                chosen = j;
            }
        }
        long tmp = prices[i];
        prices[i] = prices[chosen];
        prices[chosen] = tmp;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    long prices[] = {33L, 52L, 37L, 94L, 58L, 32L, 81L, 59L};
    int size = 8;
    selection_sort(prices, size);
    for (int i = 0; i < size; i++) {
        printf("%ld ", prices[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: selection_sort() finds the smallest remaining element for each position and
   swaps it into place. main() then prints the 8 values in ascending order. */
// END

/* Caption: Check every element of an array to find a target value. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write linear_search() with the array, its length and key.
   2. Compare each element with key.
   3. Return the index of the first match, or -1.
   4. In main(), search for 16 and print the result. */
/* Return the index of key, or -1 when it is not in the array. */
int linear_search(const int values[], int len, int key) {
    for (int idx = 0; idx < len; idx++) {
        if (values[idx] == key) {
            return idx;
        }
    }
    return -1;
}

int main(void) {
    int values[] = {92, 67, 55, 7, 16, 24, 92, 74, 93, 78};
    const int len = 10;
    int key = 16;
    int pos = linear_search(values, len, key);
    if (pos >= 0) {
        printf("Found %d at index %d\n", key, pos);
    } else {
        printf("%d is not in the array\n", key);
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: linear_search() checks the elements of values one by one and returns the
   index of the first one equal to key, or -1 when it reaches the end without a match.
   main() searches for 16 and prints where it is, or that it is missing. */
// END

/* Caption: Return the largest element of an array of double values. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write find_max() that takes items and n.
   2. Store items[0] in current.
   3. Loop over the other elements and keep the largest value in current.
   4. Return current and print it. */
/* Start with the first element and keep the largest value seen so far. */
double find_max(const double items[], int n) {
    double current = items[0];
    for (int k = 1; k < n; k++) {
        if (items[k] > current) {
            current = items[k];
        }
    }
    return current;
}

int main(void) {
    double items[] = {38.6, 6.7, 5.3, 59.2, 96.1, 75.2};
    int n = sizeof(items) / sizeof(items[0]);
    printf("The largest value is %.2f\n", find_max(items, n));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: find_max() takes the first element as the largest value so far and stores
   it in current. The loop compares every other element with current using > and keeps the
   largest one. main() prints the largest of the 6 values. */
// END

/* Caption: How do I use dynamic memory to store the first 14 cubes in C? */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Use malloc to get room for 14 ints and check for NULL.
   2. Fill buffer with cubes.
   3. Print the values.
   4. Call free(buffer) at the end. */
int main(void) {
    int n = 14;
    /* Ask the heap for room for n ints; malloc returns NULL on failure. */
    int *buffer = malloc(n * sizeof(int));
    if (buffer == NULL) {
        fprintf(stderr, "malloc failed\n");
        return 1;
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        buffer[i] = i * i * i;
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        printf("%d ", buffer[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    free(buffer);   /* give the memory back */
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: malloc() reserves room for 14 ints on the heap and returns NULL if it
   fails, which the program checks. The first loop fills buffer with cubes, the second
   prints them, and free() gives the memory back at the end. */
// END

/* Caption: Count the occurrences of a character in a sentence. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write count_char() with count = 0.
   2. Compare each character with the target t.
   3. Return count and print it. */
int count_char(const char *text, char target) {
    int count = 0;
    /* Compare every character with the target. */
    for (int i = 0; text[i] != '\0'; i++) {
        if (text[i] == target) {
            count++;
        }
    }
    return count;
}

int main(void) {
    const char *sentence = "c gives you direct control over memory";
    printf("'t' appears %d times\n", count_char(sentence, 't'));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: count_char() compares every character of the text with the target character
   and counts the matches. main() prints how many times t appears in the sentence. */
// END

/* Caption: Show the Fibonacci series with a loop. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Start with first = 0 and second = 1.
   2. Repeat 25 times and print first each time.
   3. Compute next = first + second, then set first = second and second = next. */
int main(void) {
    long first = 0, second = 1;
    /* Print a term, then slide the pair one step along the sequence. */
    for (int i = 0; i < 25; i++) {
        printf("%ld ", first);
        long next = first + second;
        first = second;
        second = next;
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: The loop keeps the last two numbers in first and second. Each round it
   prints first, then moves the pair forward: first becomes second and second becomes their
   sum. It prints the first 25 Fibonacci numbers. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to reverse the elements of an array in place. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write reverse_array() for scores.
   2. Set i to the first index and j to the last.
   3. Swap scores[i] and scores[j], then move both inwards.
   4. Stop when i meets j and print the array. */
/* Swap the outer pair, then move both ends toward the middle. */
void reverse_array(long scores[], int size) {
    int i = 0;
    int j = size - 1;
    while (i < j) {
        long tmp = scores[i];
        scores[i] = scores[j];
        scores[j] = tmp;
        i++;
        j--;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    long scores[] = {95L, 23L, 44L, 47L, 70L, 77L, 25L};
    const int size = 7;
    reverse_array(scores, size);
    for (int i = 0; i < size; i++) {
        printf("%ld ", scores[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: reverse_array() swaps the first and last elements, then moves i forward and
   j backward until they meet, so the array is reversed in place without a second array.
   main() prints the reversed values. */
// END

/* Caption: Create a singly linked list by inserting at the head. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define ListNode with a value and a next pointer.
   2. Write push_front() that mallocs a node and links it in front of head.
   3. Write print_list() that follows next until NULL.
   4. Write free_list() that frees every node.
   5. Push 4 values, print the list and free it. */
typedef struct ListNode {
    int value;
    struct ListNode *next;
} ListNode;

/* Allocate a new node and put it in front of the current head. */
ListNode *push_front(ListNode *head, int value) {
    ListNode *node = malloc(sizeof(ListNode));
    if (node == NULL) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Out of memory\n");
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }
    node->value = value;
    node->next = head;
    return node;
}

void print_list(const ListNode *head) {
    for (const ListNode *cur = head; cur != NULL; cur = cur->next) {
        printf("%d -> ", cur->value);
    }
    printf("NULL\n");
}

/* Free every node; save next before freeing the current one. */
void free_list(ListNode *head) {
    while (head != NULL) {
        ListNode *next = head->next;
        free(head);
        head = next;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    ListNode *head = NULL;
    head = push_front(head, 65);
    head = push_front(head, 83);
    head = push_front(head, 75);
    head = push_front(head, 2);
    print_list(head);
    free_list(head);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: Each ListNode holds a value and a pointer to the next node. push_front()
   allocates a node with malloc, puts it in front of head and returns it; print_list()
   follows the next pointers until NULL; free_list() frees every node. main() pushes 4
   values, so they print in reverse order. */
// END

/* Caption: Search an array for its smallest value. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write min_of() that takes readings and length.
   2. Store readings[0] in smallest.
   3. Loop over the other elements and keep the smallest value in smallest.
   4. Return smallest and print it. */
/* Start with the first element and keep the smallest value seen so far. */
double min_of(const double readings[], int length) {
    double smallest = readings[0];
    for (int j = 1; j < length; j++) {
        if (readings[j] < smallest) {
            smallest = readings[j];
        }
    }
    return smallest;
}

int main(void) {
    double readings[] = {22.7, 89.1, 90.6, 82.6};
    int length = 4;
    printf("Smallest: %.2f\n", min_of(readings, length));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: min_of() takes the first element as the smallest value so far and stores it
   in smallest. The loop compares every other element with smallest using < and keeps the
   smallest one. main() prints the smallest of the 4 values. */
// END

/* Caption: Program to search an array for a value and print its position. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write linear_search() with the array, its length and key.
   2. Compare each element with key.
   3. Return the index of the first match, or -1.
   4. In main(), search for 50 and print the result. */
/* Return the index of key, or -1 when it is not in the array. */
int linear_search(const int data[], int count, int key) {
    for (int i = 0; i < count; i++) {
        if (data[i] == key) {
            return i;
        }
    }
    return -1;
}

int main(void) {
    int data[] = {87, 77, 25, 50, 91, 68, 48, 62};
    const int count = 8;
    int key = 50;
    int pos = linear_search(data, count, key);
    if (pos >= 0) {
        printf("Found %d at index %d\n", key, pos);
    } else {
        printf("%d is not in the array\n", key);
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: linear_search() checks the elements of data one by one and returns the
   index of the first one equal to key, or -1 when it reaches the end without a match.
   main() searches for 50 and prints where it is, or that it is missing. */

/* Caption: How do I implement a stack with an array (push and pop) in C? */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define a Stack with room for 32 items and a top counter.
   2. Write push() and pop(), returning false when the stack is full or empty.
   3. Push 5 values.
   4. Pop and print until the stack is empty. */
#define CAPACITY 32

typedef struct {
    int items[CAPACITY];
    int top;   /* number of items on the stack */
} Stack;

bool push(Stack *s, int value) {
    if (s->top == CAPACITY) {
        return false;   /* stack is full */
    }
    s->items[s->top++] = value;
    return true;
}

bool pop(Stack *s, int *value) {
    if (s->top == 0) {
        return false;   /* stack is empty */
    }
    *value = s->items[--s->top];
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    Stack s = {.top = 0};
    push(&s, 91);
    push(&s, 58);
    push(&s, 60);
    push(&s, 68);
    push(&s, 38);
    int value;
    /* Items come back out in reverse order (last in, first out). */
    while (pop(&s, &value)) {
        printf("%d ", value);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: The Stack keeps up to 32 items in an array, and top counts how many are
   stored. push() adds at the top and pop() removes from the top; both return false when
   they cannot. main() pushes 5 values and pops them all, so they come out in reverse order
   (last in, first out). */
// END

/* Caption: Program to find a number in a sorted array with binary search. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Make sure the array is sorted.
   2. Set left to 0 and right to len - 1.
   3. While left <= right, compare the middle element middle with the key.
   4. Return the index if it matches; otherwise keep only the half that can hold the
      key.
   5. Return -1 if the range becomes empty, and print the index of 77. */
/* The array must be sorted. Each step halves the range that can still hold the key. */
int binary_search(const int data[], int len, int key) {
    int left = 0;
    int right = len - 1;
    while (left <= right) {
        int middle = left + (right - left) / 2;
        if (data[middle] == key) {
            return middle;
        } else if (data[middle] < key) {
            left = middle + 1;   /* key is in the right half */
        } else {
            right = middle - 1;   /* key is in the left half */
        }
    }
    return -1;
}

int main(void) {
    int data[] = {4, 47, 51, 59, 64, 73, 77, 109, 151, 154};
    int len = sizeof(data) / sizeof(data[0]);
    int index = binary_search(data, len, 77);
    printf("Index of 77: %d\n", index);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: binary_search() needs a sorted array. It keeps the range from left to
   right, compares the middle element middle with the key and throws away the half that
   cannot contain it, so it needs only about log2(n) steps. main() looks for 77 and prints
   its index, or -1 if it is not there. */
// END

/* A function can return a whole struct. */

int main(void) {

/* Caption: Write a program to compute the product of two square matrices. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define N as 2.
   2. For every i and j, add a[i][k] * b[k][j] over k into product[i][j].
   3. Print product row by row. */
#define N 2

int main(void) {
    int a[N][N] = {{8, 6}, {8, 8}};
    int b[N][N] = {{7, 7}, {6, 8}};
    int product[N][N] = {0};
    /* product[i][j] is row i of a times column j of b. */
    for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) {
        for (int j = 0; j < N; j++) {
            for (int k = 0; k < N; k++) {
                product[i][j] += a[i][k] * b[k][j];
            }
        }
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) {
        for (int j = 0; j < N; j++) {
            printf("%4d", product[i][j]);
        }
        printf("\n");
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: For each entry product[i][j] the innermost loop adds a[i][k] * b[k][j] over
   k, which is row i of a times column j of b. main() multiplies two 2x2 matrices and
   prints the product. */
// END

/* Caption: Program to implement a circular queue with an array. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define a Queue with room for 8 items, a head and a count.
   2. Write enqueue() that stores at (head + count) % CAPACITY.
   3. Write dequeue() that takes the item at head and moves head on.
   4. Add 4 values, then remove and print them in order. */
#define CAPACITY 8

typedef struct {
    int items[CAPACITY];
    int head;
    int count;
} Queue;

bool enqueue(Queue *q, int value) {
    if (q->count == CAPACITY) {
        return false;
    }
    /* The tail wraps around to the start of the array. */
    q->items[(q->head + q->count) % CAPACITY] = value;
    q->count++;
    return true;
}

bool dequeue(Queue *q, int *value) {
    if (q->count == 0) {
        return false;
    }
    *value = q->items[q->head];
    q->head = (q->head + 1) % CAPACITY;
    q->count--;
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    Queue q = {.head = 0, .count = 0};
    enqueue(&q, 82);
    enqueue(&q, 18);
    enqueue(&q, 1);
    enqueue(&q, 52);
    int value;
    /* Items come out in the order they went in (first in, first out). */
    while (dequeue(&q, &value)) {
        printf("%d ", value);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: The Queue stores up to 8 items in a ring buffer: head is the oldest item
   and % CAPACITY wraps positions back to the start of the array. enqueue() adds at the
   back and dequeue() removes from the front, so main() gets its 4 values back in the same
   order (first in, first out). */
// END

/* Caption: Print the binary representation of an integer. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write print_binary(n, bits).
   2. Go through the bits from the highest to the lowest.
   3. Print 1 when (n >> b) & 1 is set, otherwise 0.
   4. Print 329 in binary. */
/* Check each bit from the highest to the lowest. */
void print_binary(unsigned int n, int bits) {
    for (int b = bits - 1; b >= 0; b--) {
        putchar((n >> b) & 1 ? '1' : '0');
    }
    putchar('\n');
}

int main(void) {
    unsigned int number = 329;
    printf("%u in binary: ", number);
    print_binary(number, 8);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: print_binary() checks one bit at a time, from the highest to the lowest: (n
   >> b) & 1 is 1 when bit b is set, so it prints the character 1 or 0. main() prints 329
   in binary. */
// END

   3. Add one to matches for every even number.

}

    int size = sizeof(marks) / sizeof(marks[0]);
    printf("Count of even values = %d\n", count_even(marks, size));
    return 0;
}

   of 0 after dividing by 2 means the number is even, so matches goes up by one. main()
   prints how many of the 6 values are even. */

/* Caption: Show the Fibonacci series with a loop. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Start with prev = 0 and curr = 1.
   2. Repeat 9 times and print prev each time.
   3. Compute next = prev + curr, then set prev = curr and curr = next. */
int main(void) {
    long prev = 0, curr = 1;
    /* Print a term, then slide the pair one step along the sequence. */
    for (int i = 0; i < 9; i++) {
        printf("%ld ", prev);
        long next = prev + curr;
        prev = curr;
        curr = next;
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: The loop keeps the last two numbers in prev and curr. Each round it prints
   prev, then moves the pair forward: prev becomes curr and curr becomes their sum. It
   prints the first 9 Fibonacci numbers. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to implement a stack with an array (push and pop). */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define a Stack with room for 32 items and a top counter.
   2. Write push() and pop(), returning false when the stack is full or empty.
   3. Push 3 values.
   4. Pop and print until the stack is empty. */
#define CAPACITY 32

typedef struct {
    int items[CAPACITY];
    int top;   /* number of items on the stack */
} Stack;

bool push(Stack *s, int value) {
    if (s->top == CAPACITY) {
        return false;   /* stack is full */
    }
    s->items[s->top++] = value;
    return true;
}

bool pop(Stack *s, int *value) {
    if (s->top == 0) {
        return false;   /* stack is empty */
    }
    *value = s->items[--s->top];
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    Stack s = {.top = 0};
    push(&s, 61);
    push(&s, 61);
    push(&s, 20);
    int value;
    /* Items come back out in reverse order (last in, first out). */
    while (pop(&s, &value)) {
        printf("%d ", value);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: The Stack keeps up to 32 items in an array, and top counts how many are
   stored. push() adds at the top and pop() removes from the top; both return false when
   they cannot. main() pushes 3 values and pops them all, so they come out in reverse order
   (last in, first out). */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to calculate 8! using recursion. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write factorial(value) that calls itself.
   2. Return 1 when value is 1 or less.
   3. Otherwise return value * factorial(value - 1).
   4. Print 8! as an unsigned long long. */
/* n! = n * (n - 1)!, and 0! = 1 stops the recursion. */
unsigned long long factorial(int value) {
    if (value <= 1) {
        return 1;
    }
    return value * factorial(value - 1);
}

int main(void) {
    int value = 8;
    printf("%d! = %llu\n", value, factorial(value));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: factorial() calls itself: n! is n * (n - 1)!, and the recursion stops when
   value is 1 or less. main() prints 8! as an unsigned long long, because factorials grow
   very fast. */
// END

/* Caption: Return two values from a function using pointer parameters. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write min_max() with the array, its length and the pointers min and max.
   2. Start both at the first element.
   3. Update *min and *max while looping over the rest.
   4. Declare low and high, pass their addresses and print them. */
/* One pass finds both results; they are stored through the pointers. */
void min_max(const int samples[], int count, int *min, int *max) {
    *min = samples[0];
    *max = samples[0];
    for (int i = 1; i < count; i++) {
        if (samples[i] < *min) {
            *min = samples[i];
        }
        if (samples[i] > *max) {
            *max = samples[i];
        }
    }
}

int main(void) {
    int samples[] = {3, 86, 44, 39, 79, 93, 37, 18, 72};
    int count = sizeof(samples) / sizeof(samples[0]);
    int low, high;
    min_max(samples, count, &low, &high);
    printf("Min: %d, Max: %d\n", low, high);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: A C function can return only one value, so min_max() returns void and
   writes its two results through the pointer parameters min and max. main() declares low
   and high on one line and passes their addresses with &, then prints both results for the
   9 values. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a function with four parameters that returns the maximum. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write max2() that returns the larger of two values.
   2. Write max_of_four() as max2(max2(a, b), max2(c, d)).
   3. Print the largest of the four values. */
/* Return the larger of two values. */
int max2(int a, int b) {
    return a > b ? a : b;
}

/* Reuse max2 to compare four values. */
int max_of_four(int a, int b, int c, int d) {
    return max2(max2(a, b), max2(c, d));
}

int main(void) {
    int a = 52, b = 23, c = 74, d = 78;
    printf("Largest: %d\n", max_of_four(a, b, c, d));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: max_of_four() takes four parameters and reuses the helper max2(), which
   returns the larger of two values: it compares a with b, c with d, and then the two
   winners. main() prints the largest of 52, 23, 74 and 78. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to compute the sum of the digits of an integer. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Start result at 0.
   2. Add n % 10 to result, then divide n by 10.
   3. Repeat until n is 0.
   4. Apply it to 719016 and print the result. */
/* Take the last digit with % 10, then drop it with / 10. */
int sum_digits(int n) {
    int result = 0;
    while (n > 0) {
        result += n % 10;
        n /= 10;
    }
    return result;
}

int main(void) {
    int number = 719016;
    printf("sum of digits of %d: %d\n", number, sum_digits(number));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: sum_digits() adds the last digit (n % 10) to result and then removes it (n
   / 10) until no digits are left. main() applies it to 719016. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a function that swaps two int values through pointers. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write swap() that takes pointers to two int values.
   2. Save *first in tmp, copy *second into *first, then tmp into *second.
   3. In main(), print first and second, call swap(&first, &second) and print them
      again. */
/* Pass addresses so the function can change the caller's variables. */
void swap(int *first, int *second) {
    int tmp = *first;
    *first = *second;
    *second = tmp;
}

int main(void) {
    int first = 23, second = 24;
    printf("Before: %d %d\n", first, second);
    swap(&first, &second);
    printf("After:  %d %d\n", first, second);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: swap() receives the addresses of first and second, so writing through the
   pointers *first and *second changes the caller's variables. tmp holds one value during
   the exchange. main() declares both variables on one line and prints them before and
   after the swap. */
// END

/* Caption: Compute the distance between two points using a struct. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <math.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define a Point struct with x and y.
   2. Write distance() using sqrt(dx * dx + dy * dy).
   3. Print the distance between p and q. */
typedef struct {
    double x;
    double y;
} Point;

/* Pythagoras: sqrt(dx * dx + dy * dy). */
double distance(Point a, Point b) {
    double dx = b.x - a.x;
    double dy = b.y - a.y;
    return sqrt(dx * dx + dy * dy);
}

int main(void) {
    Point p = {3, 5};
    Point q = {-5, 10};
    printf("Distance: %.3f\n", distance(p, q));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: Point is a typedef struct with x and y. distance() uses Pythagoras, sqrt(dx
   * dx + dy * dy), to measure the gap between the two points, and main() prints it. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to create a singly linked list by inserting at the head. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define Node with a value and a next pointer.
   2. Write push_front() that mallocs a node and links it in front of head.
   3. Write print_list() that follows next until NULL.
   4. Write free_list() that frees every node.
   5. Push 3 values, print the list and free it. */
typedef struct Node {
    int value;
    struct Node *next;
} Node;

/* Allocate a new node and put it in front of the current head. */
Node *push_front(Node *head, int value) {
    Node *node = malloc(sizeof(Node));
    if (node == NULL) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Out of memory\n");
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }
    node->value = value;
    node->next = head;
    return node;
}

void print_list(const Node *head) {
    for (const Node *cur = head; cur != NULL; cur = cur->next) {
        printf("%d -> ", cur->value);
    }
    printf("NULL\n");
}

/* Free every node; save next before freeing the current one. */
void free_list(Node *head) {
    while (head != NULL) {
        Node *next = head->next;
        free(head);
        head = next;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    Node *head = NULL;
    head = push_front(head, 45);
    head = push_front(head, 90);
    head = push_front(head, 57);
    print_list(head);
    free_list(head);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: Each Node holds a value and a pointer to the next node. push_front()
   allocates a node with malloc, puts it in front of head and returns it; print_list()
   follows the next pointers until NULL; free_list() frees every node. main() pushes 3
   values, so they print in reverse order. */
// END

/* Caption: Check whether a number is prime. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write is_prime(n); numbers below 2 are not prime.
   2. Try every divisor d while d * d <= n.
   3. Return false if one divides n, otherwise true.
   4. Check 77 and print the result. */
/* A prime has no divisor between 2 and its square root. */
bool is_prime(int n) {
    if (n < 2) {
        return false;
    }
    for (int d = 2; d * d <= n; d++) {
        if (n % d == 0) {
            return false;
        }
    }
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    int number = 77;
    printf("%d %s prime\n", number, is_prime(number) ? "is" : "is not");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: is_prime() tries every divisor d from 2 while d * d <= n; if one divides n
   evenly, n is not prime. main() checks 77 and prints whether it is prime. */
// END

/* Caption: Build a fixed-size integer stack in C. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define a Stack with room for 32 items and a top counter.
   2. Write push() and pop(), returning false when the stack is full or empty.
   3. Push 4 values.
   4. Pop and print until the stack is empty. */
#define CAPACITY 32

typedef struct {
    int items[CAPACITY];
    int top;   /* number of items on the stack */
} Stack;

bool push(Stack *s, int value) {
    if (s->top == CAPACITY) {
        return false;   /* stack is full */
    }
    s->items[s->top++] = value;
    return true;
}

bool pop(Stack *s, int *value) {
    if (s->top == 0) {
        return false;   /* stack is empty */
    }
    *value = s->items[--s->top];
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    Stack s = {.top = 0};
    push(&s, 96);
    push(&s, 16);
    push(&s, 17);
    push(&s, 13);
    int value;
    /* Items come back out in reverse order (last in, first out). */
    while (pop(&s, &value)) {
        printf("%d ", value);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: The Stack keeps up to 32 items in an array, and top counts how many are
   stored. push() adds at the top and pop() removes from the top; both return false when
   they cannot. main() pushes 4 values and pops them all, so they come out in reverse order
   (last in, first out). */
// END

/* Caption: C program to calculate the sum of the first n natural numbers. */

/* Caption: Write a function that swaps two int values through pointers. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write swap() that takes pointers to two int values.
   2. Save *first in tmp, copy *second into *first, then tmp into *second.
   3. In main(), print first and second, call swap(&first, &second) and print them
      again. */
/* Pass addresses so the function can change the caller's variables. */
void swap(int *first, int *second) {
    int tmp = *first;
    *first = *second;
    *second = tmp;
}

int main(void) {
    int first = 18, second = 8;
    printf("Before: %d %d\n", first, second);
    swap(&first, &second);
    printf("After:  %d %d\n", first, second);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: swap() receives the addresses of first and second, so writing through the
   pointers *first and *second changes the caller's variables. tmp holds one value during
   the exchange. main() declares both variables on one line and prints them before and
   after the swap. */
// END

/* Caption: Decide if 1898 is a leap year. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write is_leap(year).
   2. A year divisible by 4 is a leap year, unless it is divisible by 100.
   3. Years divisible by 400 are leap years again.
   4. Check 1898 and print the result. */
/* Leap years divide by 4, except centuries, which must divide by 400. */
int is_leap(int year) {
    return (year % 4 == 0 && year % 100 != 0) || year % 400 == 0;
}

int main(void) {
    int year = 1898;
    if (is_leap(year)) {
        printf("%d is a leap year\n", year);
    } else {
        printf("%d is not a leap year\n", year);
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: is_leap() returns true for years divisible by 4, except century years,
   which must also be divisible by 400. main() checks 1898 and prints whether it is a leap
   year. */
// END

/* Caption: Implement a stack with an array (push and pop). */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define a Stack with room for 32 items and a top counter.
   2. Write push() and pop(), returning false when the stack is full or empty.
   3. Push 5 values.
   4. Pop and print until the stack is empty. */
#define CAPACITY 32

typedef struct {
    int items[CAPACITY];
    int top;   /* number of items on the stack */
} Stack;

bool push(Stack *s, int value) {
    if (s->top == CAPACITY) {
        return false;   /* stack is full */
    }
    s->items[s->top++] = value;
    return true;
}

bool pop(Stack *s, int *value) {
    if (s->top == 0) {
        return false;   /* stack is empty */
    }
    *value = s->items[--s->top];
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    Stack s = {.top = 0};
    push(&s, 89);
    push(&s, 2);
    push(&s, 94);
    push(&s, 1);
    push(&s, 57);
    int value;
    /* Items come back out in reverse order (last in, first out). */
    while (pop(&s, &value)) {
        printf("%d ", value);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: The Stack keeps up to 32 items in an array, and top counts how many are
   stored. push() adds at the top and pop() removes from the top; both return false when
   they cannot. main() pushes 5 values and pops them all, so they come out in reverse order
   (last in, first out). */
// END

/* Caption: Compute the mean of a list of numbers. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write array_average() that takes nums and size.
   2. Add the values into the double sum.
   3. Return sum / size.
   4. Print the average with two decimals. */
/* Sum the values, then divide by how many there are. */
double array_average(const int nums[], int size) {
    double sum = 0.0;
    for (int i = 0; i < size; i++) {
        sum += nums[i];
    }
    return sum / size;
}

int main(void) {
    int nums[] = {37, 53, 81, 85, 18, 42, 74};
    int size = 7;
    printf("Mean = %.2f\n", array_average(nums, size));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: array_average() adds the 7 values of nums into the double sum and divides
   by size, so the mean keeps its decimal part even when the values are whole numbers.
   main() prints it with two decimals. */
// END

/* Caption: Implement insertion sort for an array of double values. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write insertion_sort() for the double array items.
   2. Take each element in turn as current.
   3. Shift the smaller values of the sorted part one place right.
   4. Put current into the gap.
   5. Print the sorted values. */
/* Insert each element into the already sorted part on its left. */
void insertion_sort(double items[], int len) {
    for (int i = 1; i < len; i++) {
        double current = items[i];
        int j = i - 1;
        while (j >= 0 && items[j] < current) {
            items[j + 1] = items[j];   /* shift bigger values right */
            j--;
        }
        items[j + 1] = current;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    double items[] = {2.5, 98.9, 20.4, 45.9, 77.9, 63.4};
    int len = 6;
    insertion_sort(items, len);
    for (int i = 0; i < len; i++) {
        printf("%.2f ", items[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: insertion_sort() takes each element in turn and shifts the smaller values
   of the sorted part one place right until the element fits. main() then prints the 6
   values in descending order. */
// END

/* Caption: How do I create a singly linked list by inserting at the head in C? */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define Item with a value and a next pointer.
   2. Write push_front() that mallocs a node and links it in front of head.
   3. Write print_list() that follows next until NULL.
   4. Write free_list() that frees every node.
   5. Push 5 values, print the list and free it. */
typedef struct Item {
    int value;
    struct Item *next;
} Item;

/* Allocate a new node and put it in front of the current head. */
Item *push_front(Item *head, int value) {
    Item *node = malloc(sizeof(Item));
    if (node == NULL) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Out of memory\n");
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }
    node->value = value;
    node->next = head;
    return node;
}

void print_list(const Item *head) {
    for (const Item *cur = head; cur != NULL; cur = cur->next) {
        printf("%d -> ", cur->value);
    }
    printf("NULL\n");
}

/* Free every node; save next before freeing the current one. */
void free_list(Item *head) {
    while (head != NULL) {
        Item *next = head->next;
        free(head);
        head = next;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    Item *head = NULL;
    head = push_front(head, 50);
    head = push_front(head, 83);
    head = push_front(head, 33);
    head = push_front(head, 40);
    head = push_front(head, 2);
    print_list(head);
    free_list(head);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: Each Item holds a value and a pointer to the next node. push_front()
   allocates a node with malloc, puts it in front of head and returns it; print_list()
   follows the next pointers until NULL; free_list() frees every node. main() pushes 5
   values, so they print in reverse order. */
// END

/* Caption: Program to generate the Fibonacci sequence. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Start with a = 0 and b = 1.
   2. Repeat 17 times and print a each time.
   3. Compute next = a + b, then set a = b and b = next. */
int main(void) {
    long a = 0, b = 1;
    /* Print a term, then slide the pair one step along the sequence. */
    for (int i = 0; i < 17; i++) {
        printf("%ld ", a);
        long next = a + b;
        a = b;
        b = next;
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: The loop keeps the last two numbers in a and b. Each round it prints a,
   then moves the pair forward: a becomes b and b becomes their sum. It prints the first 17
   Fibonacci numbers. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to write a function with four parameters that returns the maximum. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write max2() that returns the larger of two values.
   2. Write max_of_four() as max2(max2(a, b), max2(c, d)).
   3. Print the largest of the four values. */
/* Return the larger of two values. */
int max2(int a, int b) {
    return a > b ? a : b;
}

/* Reuse max2 to compare four values. */
int max_of_four(int a, int b, int c, int d) {
    return max2(max2(a, b), max2(c, d));
}

int main(void) {
    int a = 40, b = 69, c = 45, d = 62;
    printf("Largest: %d\n", max_of_four(a, b, c, d));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: max_of_four() takes four parameters and reuses the helper max2(), which
   returns the larger of two values: it compares a with b, c with d, and then the two
   winners. main() prints the largest of 40, 69, 45 and 62. */
// END

/* Caption: Compute the distance between two points with a four-parameter function. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <math.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write distance(x1, y1, x2, y2).
   2. Compute dx and dy, then return sqrt(dx * dx + dy * dy).
   3. Print the distance between (-5, 5) and (5, 4). */
/* Pythagoras: the distance is sqrt(dx * dx + dy * dy). */
double distance(double x1, double y1, double x2, double y2) {
    double dx = x2 - x1, dy = y2 - y1;
    return sqrt(dx * dx + dy * dy);
}

int main(void) {
    printf("Distance: %.3f\n", distance(-5, 5, 5, 4));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: distance() takes the coordinates of both points as four parameters. It
   declares dx and dy on one line and uses Pythagoras with sqrt() from math.h. main()
   prints the distance between (-5, 5) and (5, 4). */
// END

/* Caption: C program to search an array for its largest value. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write find_max() that takes items and n.
   2. Store items[0] in largest.
   3. Loop over the other elements and keep the largest value in largest.
   4. Return largest and print it. */
/* Start with the first element and keep the largest value seen so far. */
int find_max(const int items[], int n) {
    int largest = items[0];
    for (int idx = 1; idx < n; idx++) {
        if (items[idx] > largest) {
            largest = items[idx];
        }
    }
    return largest;
}

int main(void) {
    int items[] = {41, 54, 84, 79, 58, 57, 15, 20, 31, 44};
    const int n = 10;
    printf("Largest: %d\n", find_max(items, n));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: find_max() takes the first element as the largest value so far and stores
   it in largest. The loop compares every other element with largest using > and keeps the
   largest one. main() prints the largest of the 10 values. */
// END

/* Explanation: The program uses fixed values for x and y. The conditional operator (x > y)
   ? x : y picks the bigger value, which is printed. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to find the largest number in an array. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write find_max() that takes ages and count.
   2. Store ages[0] in m.
   3. Loop over the other elements and keep the largest value in m.
   4. Return m and print it. */
/* Start with the first element and keep the largest value seen so far. */
double find_max(const double ages[], int count) {
    double m = ages[0];
    for (int i = 1; i < count; i++) {
        if (ages[i] > m) {
            m = ages[i];
        }
    }
    return m;
}

int main(void) {
    double ages[] = {66.2, 68.1, 26.4, 84.0};
    int count = sizeof(ages) / sizeof(ages[0]);
    printf("Largest: %.2f\n", find_max(ages, count));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: find_max() takes the first element as the largest value so far and stores
   it in m. The loop compares every other element with m using > and keeps the largest one.
   main() prints the largest of the 4 values. */
// END

/* Caption: Sort an array in ascending order using selection sort. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write selection_sort() for the int array ages.
   2. For each position, find the smallest remaining element.
   3. Swap it into that position.
   4. Print the sorted values. */
/* Select the right element for each position and swap it into place. */
void selection_sort(int ages[], int length) {
    for (int i = 0; i < length - 1; i++) {
        int chosen = i;
        for (int j = i + 1; j < length; j++) {
            if (ages[chosen] > ages[j]) {
                chosen = j;
            }
        }
        int tmp = ages[i];
        ages[i] = ages[chosen];
        ages[chosen] = tmp;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    int ages[] = {79, 96, 61, 42, 30};
    int length = sizeof(ages) / sizeof(ages[0]);
    selection_sort(ages, length);
    for (int i = 0; i < length; i++) {
        printf("%d ", ages[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: selection_sort() finds the smallest remaining element for each position and
   swaps it into place. main() then prints the 5 values in ascending order. */
// END

/* Caption: How do I save text to a file with fprintf and print it with fgets in C? */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Open output.txt in write mode and check for NULL.
   2. Write 2 lines with fprintf and close the file.
   3. Open it again in read mode.
   4. Read and print each line with fgets, then close the file. */
int main(void) {
    FILE *file = fopen("output.txt", "w");
    if (file == NULL) {
        perror("fopen");
        return 1;
    }
    fprintf(file, "pointers store the address of another variable\n");
    fprintf(file, "keep functions short and focused\n");
    fclose(file);

    /* Reopen the file for reading and print it line by line. */
    file = fopen("output.txt", "r");
    if (file == NULL) {
        perror("fopen");
        return 1;
    }
    char line[128];
    while (fgets(line, sizeof(line), file) != NULL) {
        printf("%s", line);
    }
    fclose(file);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: fopen() in write mode creates output.txt, fprintf() writes 2 lines into it
   and fclose() saves it. The file is then opened again in read mode, and fgets() reads it
   back line by line into the buffer line, which is printed. Every fopen() result is
   checked for NULL. */
// END

/* Caption: Use a struct to return several results from one function. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define a Stats struct with min, max and average.
   2. Write array_stats() that fills one Stats in a loop.
   3. Return the struct.
   4. Print st.min, st.max and st.average. */
typedef struct {
    int min;
    int max;
    double average;
} Stats;

/* Pack several results into one struct and return it. */
Stats array_stats(const int v[], int n) {
    Stats s = {v[0], v[0], 0.0};
    double total = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        if (v[i] < s.min) {
            s.min = v[i];
        }
        if (v[i] > s.max) {
            s.max = v[i];
        }
        total += v[i];
    }
    s.average = total / n;
    return s;
}

int main(void) {
    int items[] = {61, 92, 23, 11, 3, 91, 17, 38};
    int n = sizeof(items) / sizeof(items[0]);
    Stats st = array_stats(items, n);
    printf("Min %d, Max %d, Average %.2f\n", st.min, st.max, st.average);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: Stats groups three results. array_stats() fills one Stats while it loops
   over the 8 values and returns the whole struct, which is a clean way to return several
   results at once. main() reads them as st.min, st.max and st.average. */
// END

/* Caption: Reverse a string in place. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <string.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write reverse_string() for word.
   2. Set i to the first index and j to the last.
   3. Swap the two characters and move i and j inwards until they meet.
   4. Reverse program and print it. */
/* Swap characters from both ends until they meet in the middle. */
void reverse_string(char *word) {
    int i = 0;
    int j = strlen(word) - 1;
    while (i < j) {
        char tmp = word[i];
        word[i] = word[j];
        word[j] = tmp;
        i++;
        j--;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    char word[] = "program";
    reverse_string(word);
    printf("%s\n", word);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: reverse_string() swaps characters from both ends of word, moving inwards
   until the two indexes meet. main() reverses the word program in place and prints it. */
// END

/* Caption: Add up all the numbers in an array of double values. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write add_all() that takes the array prices and its length count.
   2. Start acc at 0 and add every element in a while loop.
   3. Return acc.
   4. In main(), fill prices with 4 values and print the sum. */
/* Return the sum of the first n elements. */
double add_all(const double prices[], int count) {
    double acc = 0;
    int k = 0;
    while (k < count) {
        acc += prices[k];
        k++;
    }
    return acc;
}

int main(void) {
    double prices[] = {34.1, 41.5, 59.4, 78.0};
    int count = 4;
    printf("Sum: %.2f\n", add_all(prices, count));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: add_all() receives the array prices and its length count. It starts acc at
   0, adds every element to it in a while loop and returns the total. main() fills prices
   with 4 double values and prints their sum. */
// END

/* Caption: Program to find the smallest number in an array. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write min_of() that takes values and size.
   2. Store values[0] in best.
   3. Loop over the other elements and keep the smallest value in best.
   4. Return best and print it. */
/* Start with the first element and keep the smallest value seen so far. */
int min_of(const int values[], int size) {
    int best = values[0];
    for (int i = 1; i < size; i++) {
        if (values[i] < best) {
            best = values[i];
        }
    }
    return best;
}

int main(void) {
    int values[] = {85, 60, 93, 44, 37, 58, 65, 12};
    const int size = 8;
    printf("The smallest value is %d\n", min_of(values, size));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: min_of() takes the first element as the smallest value so far and stores it
   in best. The loop compares every other element with best using < and keeps the smallest
   one. main() prints the smallest of the 8 values. */
// END

/* Caption: Check every element of an array to find a target value. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write linear_search() with the array, its length and needle.
   2. Compare each element with needle.
   3. Return the index of the first match, or -1.
   4. In main(), search for 1 and print the result. */
/* Return the index of needle, or -1 when it is not in the array. */
int linear_search(const int marks[], int size, int needle) {
    for (int i = 0; i < size; i++) {
        if (marks[i] == needle) {
            return i;
        }
    }
    return -1;
}

int main(void) {
    int marks[] = {31, 1, 7, 45, 60, 80, 67, 51, 52};
    const int size = 9;
    int needle = 1;
    int pos = linear_search(marks, size, needle);
    if (pos >= 0) {
        printf("Found %d at index %d\n", needle, pos);
    } else {
        printf("%d is not in the array\n", needle);
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: linear_search() checks the elements of marks one by one and returns the
   index of the first one equal to needle, or -1 when it reaches the end without a match.
   main() searches for 1 and prints where it is, or that it is missing. */
// END

/* Caption: Return a Point struct from a function. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define a Point struct with x and y.
   2. Write midpoint() that returns a Point with the averages of x and y.
   3. Print mid.x and mid.y. */
typedef struct {
    double x;
    double y;
} Point;

/* A function can return a whole struct. */
Point midpoint(Point a, Point b) {
    Point m = {(a.x + b.x) / 2, (a.y + b.y) / 2};
    return m;
}

int main(void) {
    Point p = {-16, -20}, q = {8, 18};
    Point mid = midpoint(p, q);
    printf("Midpoint: (%.1f, %.1f)\n", mid.x, mid.y);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: midpoint() takes two Point structs and returns a new Point whose x and y
   are the averages of theirs. main() declares p and q on one line, (-16, -20) and (8, 18),
   and prints the midpoint using mid.x and mid.y. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to find the least common multiple of two numbers. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write gcd() with Euclid's algorithm: replace (a, b) by (b, a % b) until b is 0.
   2. Write lcm() as a / gcd(a, b) * b.
   3. Print the LCM of 33 and 213. */
/* Euclid: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a % b) until b becomes zero. */
int gcd(int a, int b) {
    while (b != 0) {
        int r = a % b;
        a = b;
        b = r;
    }
    return a;
}

/* lcm(a, b) = a / gcd(a, b) * b (divide first to avoid overflow). */
long lcm(int a, int b) {
    return (long)a / gcd(a, b) * b;
}

int main(void) {
    printf("lcm(33, 213) = %ld\n", lcm(33, 213));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: gcd() uses Euclid's algorithm: it keeps replacing (a, b) with (b, a % b)
   until b is 0. lcm() divides a by the gcd before multiplying by b, which avoids overflow.
   main() prints the LCM of 33 and 213. */
// END

/* Caption: How do I find the arithmetic mean of 9 int values in C? */

/* Plan:
   1. Write array_average() that takes scores and count.
   2. Add the values into the double result.
   3. Return result / count.
   4. Print the average with two decimals. */
/* The mean is the total divided by the count. */
double array_average(const int scores[], int count) {
    double result = 0.0;
    int idx = 0;

        result += scores[idx];
        idx++;
    }
    return result / count;
}

int main(void) {

    int count = 9;
    printf("Average: %.2f\n", array_average(scores, count));

}
/* Explanation: array_average() adds the 9 values of scores into the double result and
   divides by count, so the mean keeps its decimal part even when the values are whole
   numbers. main() prints it with two decimals. */
// END

/* Caption: Swap two variables using pointers. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write swap() that takes pointers to two int values.
   2. Save *a in tmp, copy *b into *a, then tmp into *b.
   3. In main(), print a and b, call swap(&a, &b) and print them again. */
/* Pass addresses so the function can change the caller's variables. */
void swap(int *a, int *b) {
    int tmp = *a;
    *a = *b;
    *b = tmp;
}

int main(void) {
    int a = 14, b = 30;
    printf("Before: %d %d\n", a, b);
    swap(&a, &b);
    printf("After:  %d %d\n", a, b);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: swap() receives the addresses of a and b, so writing through the pointers
   *a and *b changes the caller's variables. tmp holds one value during the exchange.
   main() declares both variables on one line and prints them before and after the swap. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to reverse an array by swapping from both ends. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write reverse_array() for data.
   2. Set start to the first index and end to the last.
   3. Swap data[start] and data[end], then move both inwards.
   4. Stop when start meets end and print the array. */
/* Swap the outer pair, then move both ends toward the middle. */
void reverse_array(int data[], int count) {
    int start = 0;
    int end = count - 1;
    while (start < end) {
        int tmp = data[start];
        data[start] = data[end];
        data[end] = tmp;
        start++;
        end--;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    int data[] = {25, 33, 27, 52, 59, 43};
    int count = sizeof(data) / sizeof(data[0]);
    reverse_array(data, count);
    for (int i = 0; i < count; i++) {
        printf("%d ", data[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: reverse_array() swaps the first and last elements, then moves start forward
   and end backward until they meet, so the array is reversed in place without a second
   array. main() prints the reversed values. */
// END

/* Count characters until the terminating '\0'. */
int string_length(const char *text) {

    }
    return len;
}

int main(void) {

    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: string_length() counts characters until it reaches the null character that
   ends every C string. main() prints the length of the word refer. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to reverse the digits of a number. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Start result at 0.
   2. Multiply result by 10, add n % 10, then divide n by 10.
   3. Repeat until n is 0.
   4. Apply it to 93990 and print the result. */
/* Take the last digit with % 10, then drop it with / 10. */
int reverse_digits(int n) {
    int result = 0;
    while (n > 0) {
        result = result * 10 + n % 10;
        n /= 10;
    }
    return result;
}

int main(void) {
    int number = 93990;
    printf("reverse of digits of %d: %d\n", number, reverse_digits(number));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: reverse_digits() shifts result one place left (result * 10) and adds the
   last digit of n, which reverses the order. main() applies it to 93990. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to create a singly linked list by inserting at the head. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define Node with a value and a next pointer.
   2. Write push_front() that mallocs a node and links it in front of head.
   3. Write print_list() that follows next until NULL.
   4. Write free_list() that frees every node.
   5. Push 6 values, print the list and free it. */
typedef struct Node {
    int value;
    struct Node *next;
} Node;

/* Allocate a new node and put it in front of the current head. */
Node *push_front(Node *head, int value) {
    Node *node = malloc(sizeof(Node));
    if (node == NULL) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Out of memory\n");
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }
    node->value = value;
    node->next = head;
    return node;
}

void print_list(const Node *head) {
    for (const Node *cur = head; cur != NULL; cur = cur->next) {
        printf("%d -> ", cur->value);
    }
    printf("NULL\n");
}

/* Free every node; save next before freeing the current one. */
void free_list(Node *head) {
    while (head != NULL) {
        Node *next = head->next;
        free(head);
        head = next;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    Node *head = NULL;
    head = push_front(head, 42);
    head = push_front(head, 57);
    head = push_front(head, 49);
    head = push_front(head, 17);
    head = push_front(head, 35);
    head = push_front(head, 10);
    print_list(head);
    free_list(head);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: Each Node holds a value and a pointer to the next node. push_front()
   allocates a node with malloc, puts it in front of head and returns it; print_list()
   follows the next pointers until NULL; free_list() frees every node. main() pushes 6
   values, so they print in reverse order. */
// END

/* Caption: Search an array for its smallest value. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write find_min() that takes items and size.
   2. Store items[0] in best.
   3. Loop over the other elements and keep the smallest value in best.
   4. Return best and print it. */
/* Start with the first element and keep the smallest value seen so far. */
int find_min(const int items[], int size) {
    int best = items[0];
    for (int idx = 1; idx < size; idx++) {
        if (items[idx] < best) {
            best = items[idx];
        }
    }
    return best;
}

int main(void) {
    int items[] = {3, 66, 83, 91, 78, 65};
    int size = sizeof(items) / sizeof(items[0]);
    printf("The smallest value is %d\n", find_min(items, size));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: find_min() takes the first element as the smallest value so far and stores
   it in best. The loop compares every other element with best using < and keeps the
   smallest one. main() prints the smallest of the 6 values. */
// END

/* Caption: Compute the factorial of a number recursively. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write factorial(n) that calls itself.
   2. Return 1 when n is 1 or less.
   3. Otherwise return n * factorial(n - 1).
   4. Print 10! as an unsigned long long. */
/* n! = n * (n - 1)!, and 0! = 1 stops the recursion. */
unsigned long long factorial(int n) {
    if (n <= 1) {
        return 1;
    }
    return n * factorial(n - 1);
}

int main(void) {
    int n = 10;
    printf("%d! = %llu\n", n, factorial(n));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: factorial() calls itself: n! is n * (n - 1)!, and the recursion stops when
   n is 1 or less. main() prints 10! as an unsigned long long, because factorials grow very
   fast. */
// END

/* Caption: C program to count how many odd numbers are in an array. */
#include <stdio.h>

   1. Write count_odd() that takes readings and count.

   3. Add one to found for every odd number.

/* A number is odd when the remainder after dividing by 2 is one. */

    for (int i = 0; i < count; i++) {

    }
    return found;
}

    const int count = 11;
    printf("Count of odd values = %d\n", count_odd(readings, count));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: count_odd() tests each element of readings with the % operator: a remainder
   of 1 after dividing by 2 means the number is odd, so found goes up by one. main() prints
   how many of the 11 values are odd. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to test if "silver" reads the same backwards. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <string.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write is_palindrome() for str.
   2. Compare the first and last characters, moving inwards.
   3. Return false at the first mismatch, otherwise true.
   4. Check silver and print the result. */
/* Compare characters from the front and back, moving inwards. */
bool is_palindrome(const char *str) {
    int i = 0;
    int j = strlen(str) - 1;
    while (i < j) {
        if (str[i] != str[j]) {
            return false;
        }
        i++;
        j--;
    }
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    const char *str = "silver";
    printf("%s %s a palindrome\n", str, is_palindrome(str) ? "is" : "is not");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: is_palindrome() compares the first and last characters and moves inwards;
   any mismatch means the word is not a palindrome. main() checks the word silver and
   prints the result. */
// END

/* Compare characters from the front and back, moving inwards. */

/* Caption: Find a number in a sorted array with binary search. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Make sure the array is sorted.
   2. Set low to 0 and high to size - 1.
   3. While low <= high, compare the middle element mid with the key.
   4. Return the index if it matches; otherwise keep only the half that can hold the
      key.
   5. Return -1 if the range becomes empty, and print the index of 152. */
/* The array must be sorted. Each step halves the range that can still hold the key. */
int binary_search(const int samples[], int size, int key) {
    int low = 0;
    int high = size - 1;
    while (low <= high) {
        int mid = low + (high - low) / 2;
        if (samples[mid] == key) {
            return mid;
        } else if (samples[mid] < key) {
            low = mid + 1;   /* key is in the right half */
        } else {
            high = mid - 1;   /* key is in the left half */
        }
    }
    return -1;
}

int main(void) {
    int samples[] = {22, 28, 33, 37, 97, 129, 130, 152, 156, 189, 195};
    int size = sizeof(samples) / sizeof(samples[0]);
    int index = binary_search(samples, size, 152);
    printf("Index of 152: %d\n", index);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: binary_search() needs a sorted array. It keeps the range from low to high,
   compares the middle element mid with the key and throws away the half that cannot
   contain it, so it needs only about log2(n) steps. main() looks for 152 and prints its
   index, or -1 if it is not there. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to use a struct to hold names and marks, then print the average mark. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define struct Student with a name and a mark.
   2. Store 3 students in an array.
   3. Print each student and add the marks to total.
   4. Print total divided by the number of students. */
/* A struct groups a student's name and mark together. */
struct Student {
    char name[20];
    int mark;
};

int main(void) {
    struct Student students[] = {
        {"Noor", 69},
        {"Fatima", 45},
        {"Gabe", 50}
    };
    int count = sizeof(students) / sizeof(students[0]);
    double total = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < count; i++) {
        printf("%s: %d\n", students[i].name, students[i].mark);
        total += students[i].mark;
    }
    printf("Average mark: %.1f\n", total / count);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: struct Student groups a name and a mark. main() stores 3 students in an
   array of structs, prints each one, adds the marks to total and prints the average. */
// END

/* Caption: Raise a number to an integer power with a loop. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write power(base, exp) with result = 1.
   2. Multiply result by base exp times.
   3. Print 4 to the power 12. */
/* Multiply the base by itself exp times. */
long long power(int base, int exp) {
    long long result = 1;
    for (int i = 0; i < exp; i++) {
        result *= base;
    }
    return result;
}

int main(void) {
    printf("4^12 = %lld\n", power(4, 12));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: power() starts result at 1 and multiplies it by base exp times. It uses
   long long because powers grow quickly. main() prints 4 to the power 12. */
// END

/* Caption: C program to swap two variables using pointers. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write swap() that takes pointers to two int values.
   2. Save *a in tmp, copy *b into *a, then tmp into *b.
   3. In main(), print a and b, call swap(&a, &b) and print them again. */
/* Pass addresses so the function can change the caller's variables. */
void swap(int *a, int *b) {
    int tmp = *a;
    *a = *b;
    *b = tmp;
}

int main(void) {
    int a = 25, b = 37;
    printf("Before: %d %d\n", a, b);
    swap(&a, &b);
    printf("After:  %d %d\n", a, b);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: swap() receives the addresses of a and b, so writing through the pointers
   *a and *b changes the caller's variables. tmp holds one value during the exchange.
   main() declares both variables on one line and prints them before and after the swap. */
// END

/* Caption: C program to compute the sum of the elements of an array. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write total_of() that takes the array numbers and its length n.
   2. Start acc at 0 and add every element in a for loop.
   3. Return acc.
   4. In main(), fill numbers with 9 values and print the sum. */
/* Walk through the array and accumulate each value. */
int total_of(const int numbers[], int n) {
    int acc = 0;
    for (int idx = 0; idx < n; idx++) {
        acc += numbers[idx];
    }
    return acc;
}

int main(void) {
    int numbers[] = {39, 80, 82, 72, 11, 11, 64, 55, 4};
    int n = 9;
    printf("Sum: %d\n", total_of(numbers, n));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: total_of() receives the array numbers and its length n. It starts acc at 0,
   adds every element to it in a for loop and returns the total. main() fills numbers with
   9 int values and prints their sum. */
// END

/* Caption: How do I compute the sum of the digits of an integer in C? */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Start result at 0.
   2. Add n % 10 to result, then divide n by 10.
   3. Repeat until n is 0.
   4. Apply it to 790269 and print the result. */
/* Take the last digit with % 10, then drop it with / 10. */
int sum_digits(int n) {
    int result = 0;
    while (n > 0) {
        result += n % 10;
        n /= 10;
    }
    return result;
}

int main(void) {
    int number = 790269;
    printf("sum of digits of %d: %d\n", number, sum_digits(number));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: sum_digits() adds the last digit (n % 10) to result and then removes it (n
   / 10) until no digits are left. main() applies it to 790269. */
// END

/* Caption: Raise a number to an integer power with a loop. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write power(base, exp) with result = 1.
   2. Multiply result by base exp times.
   3. Print 2 to the power 11. */
/* Multiply the base by itself exp times. */
long long power(int base, int exp) {
    long long result = 1;
    for (int i = 0; i < exp; i++) {
        result *= base;
    }
    return result;
}

int main(void) {
    printf("2^11 = %lld\n", power(2, 11));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: power() starts result at 1 and multiplies it by base exp times. It uses
   long long because powers grow quickly. main() prints 2 to the power 11. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to save text to a file with fprintf and print it with fgets. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Open output.txt in write mode and check for NULL.
   2. Write 4 lines with fprintf and close the file.
   3. Open it again in read mode.
   4. Read and print each line with fgets, then close the file. */
int main(void) {
    FILE *file = fopen("output.txt", "w");
    if (file == NULL) {
        perror("fopen");
        return 1;
    }
    fprintf(file, "structs group related data together\n");
    fprintf(file, "a function can call itself recursively\n");
    fprintf(file, "good comments explain why the code exists\n");
    fprintf(file, "the quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog\n");
    fclose(file);

    /* Reopen the file for reading and print it line by line. */
    file = fopen("output.txt", "r");
    if (file == NULL) {
        perror("fopen");
        return 1;
    }
    char line[128];
    while (fgets(line, sizeof(line), file) != NULL) {
        printf("%s", line);
    }
    fclose(file);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: fopen() in write mode creates output.txt, fprintf() writes 4 lines into it
   and fclose() saves it. The file is then opened again in read mode, and fgets() reads it
   back line by line into the buffer line, which is printed. Every fopen() result is
   checked for NULL. */
// END

/* Caption: C program to print the binary representation of an integer. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write print_binary(n, bits).
   2. Go through the bits from the highest to the lowest.
   3. Print 1 when (n >> b) & 1 is set, otherwise 0.
   4. Print 651 in binary. */
/* Check each bit from the highest to the lowest. */
void print_binary(unsigned int n, int bits) {
    for (int b = bits - 1; b >= 0; b--) {
        putchar((n >> b) & 1 ? '1' : '0');
    }
    putchar('\n');
}

int main(void) {
    unsigned int number = 651;
    printf("%u in binary: ", number);
    print_binary(number, 8);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: print_binary() checks one bit at a time, from the highest to the lowest: (n
   >> b) & 1 is 1 when bit b is set, so it prints the character 1 or 0. main() prints 651
   in binary. */
// END

/* Caption: How do I implement a stack with an array (push and pop) in C? */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define a Stack with room for 32 items and a top counter.
   2. Write push() and pop(), returning false when the stack is full or empty.
   3. Push 6 values.
   4. Pop and print until the stack is empty. */
#define CAPACITY 32

typedef struct {
    int items[CAPACITY];
    int top;   /* number of items on the stack */
} Stack;

bool push(Stack *s, int value) {
    if (s->top == CAPACITY) {
        return false;   /* stack is full */
    }
    s->items[s->top++] = value;
    return true;
}

bool pop(Stack *s, int *value) {
    if (s->top == 0) {
        return false;   /* stack is empty */
    }
    *value = s->items[--s->top];
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    Stack s = {.top = 0};
    push(&s, 85);
    push(&s, 54);
    push(&s, 23);
    push(&s, 32);
    push(&s, 27);
    push(&s, 60);
    int value;
    /* Items come back out in reverse order (last in, first out). */
    while (pop(&s, &value)) {
        printf("%d ", value);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: The Stack keeps up to 32 items in an array, and top counts how many are
   stored. push() adds at the top and pop() removes from the top; both return false when
   they cannot. main() pushes 6 values and pops them all, so they come out in reverse order
   (last in, first out). */
// END

/* Caption: Program to check whether a number is prime. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write is_prime(n); numbers below 2 are not prime.
   2. Try every divisor d while d * d <= n.
   3. Return false if one divides n, otherwise true.
   4. Check 23 and print the result. */
/* A prime has no divisor between 2 and its square root. */
bool is_prime(int n) {
    if (n < 2) {
        return false;
    }
    for (int d = 2; d * d <= n; d++) {
        if (n % d == 0) {
            return false;
        }
    }
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    int number = 23;
    printf("%d %s prime\n", number, is_prime(number) ? "is" : "is not");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: is_prime() tries every divisor d from 2 while d * d <= n; if one divides n
   evenly, n is not prime. main() checks 23 and prints whether it is prime. */
// END

/* Caption: Find the least common multiple of two numbers. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write gcd() with Euclid's algorithm: replace (a, b) by (b, a % b) until b is 0.
   2. Write lcm() as a / gcd(a, b) * b.
   3. Print the LCM of 22 and 108. */
/* Euclid: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a % b) until b becomes zero. */
int gcd(int a, int b) {
    while (b != 0) {
        int r = a % b;
        a = b;
        b = r;
    }
    return a;
}

/* lcm(a, b) = a / gcd(a, b) * b (divide first to avoid overflow). */
long lcm(int a, int b) {
    return (long)a / gcd(a, b) * b;
}

int main(void) {
    printf("lcm(22, 108) = %ld\n", lcm(22, 108));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: gcd() uses Euclid's algorithm: it keeps replacing (a, b) with (b, a % b)
   until b is 0. lcm() divides a by the gcd before multiplying by b, which avoids overflow.
   main() prints the LCM of 22 and 108. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to create a singly linked list by inserting at the head. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define Item with a value and a next pointer.
   2. Write push_front() that mallocs a node and links it in front of head.
   3. Write print_list() that follows next until NULL.
   4. Write free_list() that frees every node.
   5. Push 4 values, print the list and free it. */
typedef struct Item {
    int value;
    struct Item *next;
} Item;

/* Allocate a new node and put it in front of the current head. */
Item *push_front(Item *head, int value) {
    Item *node = malloc(sizeof(Item));
    if (node == NULL) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Out of memory\n");
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }
    node->value = value;
    node->next = head;
    return node;
}

void print_list(const Item *head) {
    for (const Item *cur = head; cur != NULL; cur = cur->next) {
        printf("%d -> ", cur->value);
    }
    printf("NULL\n");
}

/* Free every node; save next before freeing the current one. */
void free_list(Item *head) {
    while (head != NULL) {
        Item *next = head->next;
        free(head);
        head = next;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    Item *head = NULL;
    head = push_front(head, 82);
    head = push_front(head, 15);
    head = push_front(head, 24);
    head = push_front(head, 36);
    print_list(head);
    free_list(head);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: Each Item holds a value and a pointer to the next node. push_front()
   allocates a node with malloc, puts it in front of head and returns it; print_list()
   follows the next pointers until NULL; free_list() frees every node. main() pushes 4
   values, so they print in reverse order. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a function that returns a Fraction struct. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define a Fraction struct with num and den.
   2. Write multiply() that returns num = a.num * b.num and den = a.den * b.den.
   3. Print 1/7 times 1/2. */
typedef struct {
    int num;
    int den;
} Fraction;

/* Multiply the numerators and the denominators. */
Fraction multiply(Fraction a, Fraction b) {
    Fraction r = {a.num * b.num, a.den * b.den};
    return r;
}

int main(void) {
    Fraction x = {1, 7}, y = {1, 2};
    Fraction p = multiply(x, y);
    printf("%d/%d * %d/%d = %d/%d\n", x.num, x.den, y.num, y.den, p.num, p.den);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: Fraction stores a numerator and a denominator. multiply() takes two
   Fractions and returns a new one with num = a.num * b.num and den = a.den * b.den. main()
   multiplies 1/7 by 1/2 (without reducing the result). */
// END
