/* Caption: Find the arithmetic mean of 4 double values. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write compute_mean() that takes marks and len.
   2. Add the values into the double acc.
   3. Return acc / len.
   4. Print the average with two decimals. */
/* The mean is the total divided by the count. */
double compute_mean(const double marks[], int len) {
    double acc = 0.0;
    int j = 0;
    while (j < len) {
        acc += marks[j];
        j++;
    }
    return acc / len;
}

int main(void) {
    double marks[] = {21.7, 25.0, 29.0, 88.2};
    int len = sizeof(marks) / sizeof(marks[0]);
    printf("Mean = %.2f\n", compute_mean(marks, len));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: compute_mean() adds the 4 values of marks into the double acc and divides
   by len, so the mean keeps its decimal part even when the values are whole numbers.
   main() prints it with two decimals. */
// END

/* Caption: C program to calculate 6! using iteration. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write factorial(x) with result = 1.
   2. Multiply result by every number from 2 to x.
   3. Return result.
   4. Print 6! as an unsigned long long. */
/* Multiply 1 * 2 * ... * n. */
unsigned long long factorial(int x) {
    unsigned long long result = 1;
    for (int i = 2; i <= x; i++) {
        result *= i;
    }
    return result;
}

int main(void) {
    int x = 6;
    printf("%d! = %llu\n", x, factorial(x));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: factorial() multiplies result by every number from 2 up to x. main() prints
   6! as an unsigned long long, because factorials grow very fast. */
// END

/* Caption: Implement selection sort for an array of int values. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write selection_sort() for the int array ages.
   2. For each position, find the smallest remaining element.
   3. Swap it into that position.
   4. Print the sorted values. */
/* Select the right element for each position and swap it into place. */
void selection_sort(int ages[], int len) {
    for (int i = 0; i < len - 1; i++) {
        int chosen = i;
        for (int j = i + 1; j < len; j++) {
            if (ages[chosen] > ages[j]) {
                chosen = j;
            }
        }
        int tmp = ages[i];
        ages[i] = ages[chosen];
        ages[chosen] = tmp;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    int ages[] = {57, 88, 69, 7, 42, 72, 31, 77, 84};
    int len = 9;
    selection_sort(ages, len);
    for (int i = 0; i < len; i++) {
        printf("%d ", ages[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: selection_sort() finds the smallest remaining element for each position and
   swaps it into place. main() then prints the 9 values in ascending order. */
// END

/* Caption: Reverse the elements of an array in place. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write reverse_array() for ages.
   2. Set left to the first index and right to the last.
   3. Swap ages[left] and ages[right], then move both inwards.
   4. Stop when left meets right and print the array. */
/* Swap the outer pair, then move both ends toward the middle. */
void reverse_array(int ages[], int count) {
    int left = 0;
    int right = count - 1;
    while (left < right) {
        int tmp = ages[left];
        ages[left] = ages[right];
        ages[right] = tmp;
        left++;
        right--;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    int ages[] = {82, 43, 92, 66};
    int count = 4;
    reverse_array(ages, count);
    for (int i = 0; i < count; i++) {
        printf("%d ", ages[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: reverse_array() swaps the first and last elements, then moves left forward
   and right backward until they meet, so the array is reversed in place without a second
   array. main() prints the reversed values. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to write a function that returns a Fraction struct. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define a Fraction struct with num and den.
   2. Write multiply() that returns num = a.num * b.num and den = a.den * b.den.
   3. Print 6/8 times 4/6. */
typedef struct {
    int num;
    int den;
} Fraction;

/* Multiply the numerators and the denominators. */
Fraction multiply(Fraction a, Fraction b) {
    Fraction r = {a.num * b.num, a.den * b.den};
    return r;
}

    Fraction x = {6, 8}, y = {4, 6};
    Fraction p = multiply(x, y);
    printf("%d/%d * %d/%d = %d/%d\n", x.num, x.den, y.num, y.den, p.num, p.den);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: Fraction stores a numerator and a denominator. multiply() takes two
   Fractions and returns a new one with num = a.num * b.num and den = a.den * b.den. main()
   multiplies 6/8 by 4/6 (without reducing the result). */
// END

/* Caption: Convert 202 to binary. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write print_binary(n, bits).
   2. Go through the bits from the highest to the lowest.
   3. Print 1 when (n >> b) & 1 is set, otherwise 0.
   4. Print 202 in binary. */
/* Check each bit from the highest to the lowest. */
void print_binary(unsigned int n, int bits) {
    for (int b = bits - 1; b >= 0; b--) {
        putchar((n >> b) & 1 ? '1' : '0');
    }
    putchar('\n');
}

int main(void) {
    unsigned int number = 202;
    printf("%u in binary: ", number);
    print_binary(number, 10);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: print_binary() checks one bit at a time, from the highest to the lowest: (n
   >> b) & 1 is 1 when bit b is set, so it prints the character 1 or 0. main() prints 202
   in binary. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to decide if 2046 is a leap year. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write is_leap(year).
   2. A year divisible by 4 is a leap year, unless it is divisible by 100.
   3. Years divisible by 400 are leap years again.
   4. Check 2046 and print the result. */
/* Leap years divide by 4, except centuries, which must divide by 400. */
int is_leap(int year) {
    return (year % 4 == 0 && year % 100 != 0) || year % 400 == 0;
}

int main(void) {
    int year = 2046;
    if (is_leap(year)) {
        printf("%d is a leap year\n", year);
    } else {
        printf("%d is not a leap year\n", year);
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: is_leap() returns true for years divisible by 4, except century years,
   which must also be divisible by 400. main() checks 2046 and prints whether it is a leap
   year. */
// END

/* Caption: Compute the LCM of two integers using the GCD. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write gcd() with Euclid's algorithm: replace (a, b) by (b, a % b) until b is 0.
   2. Write lcm() as a / gcd(a, b) * b.
   3. Print the LCM of 184 and 194. */
/* Euclid: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a % b) until b becomes zero. */
int gcd(int a, int b) {
    while (b != 0) {
        int r = a % b;
        a = b;
        b = r;
    }
    return a;
}

/* lcm(a, b) = a / gcd(a, b) * b (divide first to avoid overflow). */
long lcm(int a, int b) {
    return (long)a / gcd(a, b) * b;
}

int main(void) {
    printf("lcm(184, 194) = %ld\n", lcm(184, 194));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: gcd() uses Euclid's algorithm: it keeps replacing (a, b) with (b, a % b)
   until b is 0. lcm() divides a by the gcd before multiplying by b, which avoids overflow.
   main() prints the LCM of 184 and 194. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to find a number in a sorted array with binary search. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Make sure the array is sorted.
   2. Set low to 0 and high to n - 1.
   3. While low <= high, compare the middle element mid with the key.
   4. Return the index if it matches; otherwise keep only the half that can hold the
      key.
   5. Return -1 if the range becomes empty, and print the index of 88. */
/* The array must be sorted. Each step halves the range that can still hold the key. */
int binary_search(const int prices[], int n, int key) {
    int low = 0;
    int high = n - 1;
    while (low <= high) {
        int mid = low + (high - low) / 2;
        if (prices[mid] == key) {
            return mid;
        } else if (prices[mid] < key) {
            low = mid + 1;   /* key is in the right half */
        } else {
            high = mid - 1;   /* key is in the left half */
        }
    }
    return -1;
}

int main(void) {
    int prices[] = {24, 48, 56, 59, 61, 67, 81, 83, 88, 108, 110, 183};
    const int n = 12;
    int index = binary_search(prices, n, 88);
    printf("Index of 88: %d\n", index);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: binary_search() needs a sorted array. It keeps the range from low to high,
   compares the middle element mid with the key and throws away the half that cannot
   contain it, so it needs only about log2(n) steps. main() looks for 88 and prints its
   index, or -1 if it is not there. */
// END

/* Caption: Calculate the area and perimeter of a rectangle struct. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define a Rectangle struct with width and height.
   2. Write area() and perimeter().
   3. Make a 17 by 24 rectangle and print both results. */
typedef struct {
    int width;
    int height;
} Rectangle;

int area(Rectangle r) {
    return r.width * r.height;
}

int perimeter(Rectangle r) {
    return 2 * (r.width + r.height);
}

int main(void) {
    Rectangle box = {17, 24};
    printf("Area: %d, Perimeter: %d\n", area(box), perimeter(box));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: Rectangle stores a width and a height. area() returns width * height and
   perimeter() returns 2 * (width + height). main() makes a 17 by 24 rectangle and prints
   both results. */
// END

/* Caption: Use binary search to locate a value in a sorted list. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Make sure the array is sorted.
   2. Set lo to 0 and hi to length - 1.
   3. While lo <= hi, compare the middle element mid with the key.
   4. Return the index if it matches; otherwise keep only the half that can hold the
      key.
   5. Return -1 if the range becomes empty, and print the index of 161. */
/* The array must be sorted. Each step halves the range that can still hold the key. */
int binary_search(const int values[], int length, int key) {
    int lo = 0;
    int hi = length - 1;
    while (lo <= hi) {
        int mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;
        if (values[mid] == key) {
            return mid;
        } else if (values[mid] < key) {
            lo = mid + 1;   /* key is in the right half */
        } else {
            hi = mid - 1;   /* key is in the left half */
        }
    }
    return -1;
}

int main(void) {
    int values[] = {22, 72, 81, 95, 101, 126, 154, 161, 165};
    int length = sizeof(values) / sizeof(values[0]);
    int index = binary_search(values, length, 161);
    printf("Index of 161: %d\n", index);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: binary_search() needs a sorted array. It keeps the range from lo to hi,
   compares the middle element mid with the key and throws away the half that cannot
   contain it, so it needs only about log2(n) steps. main() looks for 161 and prints its
   index, or -1 if it is not there. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to compute the sum of the elements of an array. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write sum_array() that takes the array prices and its length size.
   2. Start sum at 0 and add every element in a while loop.
   3. Return sum.
   4. In main(), fill prices with 9 values and print the sum. */
/* Return the sum of the first n elements. */
double sum_array(const double prices[], int size) {
    double sum = 0;
    int i = 0;
    while (i < size) {
        sum += prices[i];
        i++;
    }
    return sum;
}

int main(void) {
    double prices[] = {49.9, 82.8, 64.1, 19.1, 80.5, 1.9, 13.9, 2.0, 48.5};
    int size = sizeof(prices) / sizeof(prices[0]);
    printf("Sum: %.2f\n", sum_array(prices, size));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: sum_array() receives the array prices and its length size. It starts sum at
   0, adds every element to it in a while loop and returns the total. main() fills prices
   with 9 double values and prints their sum. */
// END

/* Caption: Implement a circular queue with an array. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define a Queue with room for 32 items, a head and a count.
   2. Write enqueue() that stores at (head + count) % CAPACITY.
   3. Write dequeue() that takes the item at head and moves head on.
   4. Add 3 values, then remove and print them in order. */
#define CAPACITY 32

typedef struct {
    int items[CAPACITY];
    int head;
    int count;
} Queue;

bool enqueue(Queue *q, int value) {
    if (q->count == CAPACITY) {
        return false;
    }
    /* The tail wraps around to the start of the array. */
    q->items[(q->head + q->count) % CAPACITY] = value;
    q->count++;
    return true;
}

bool dequeue(Queue *q, int *value) {
    if (q->count == 0) {
        return false;
    }
    *value = q->items[q->head];
    q->head = (q->head + 1) % CAPACITY;
    q->count--;
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    Queue q = {.head = 0, .count = 0};
    enqueue(&q, 32);
    enqueue(&q, 35);
    enqueue(&q, 38);
    int value;
    /* Items come out in the order they went in (first in, first out). */
    while (dequeue(&q, &value)) {
        printf("%d ", value);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: The Queue stores up to 32 items in a ring buffer: head is the oldest item
   and % CAPACITY wraps positions back to the start of the array. enqueue() adds at the
   back and dequeue() removes from the front, so main() gets its 3 values back in the same
   order (first in, first out). */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to compute the sum of the elements of an array. */

/* Plan:

   2. Start acc at 0 and add every element in a for loop.
   3. Return acc.
   4. In main(), fill values with 4 values and print the sum. */
/* Walk through the array and accumulate each value. */
int sum_values(const int values[], int len) {

}

   0, adds every element to it in a for loop and returns the total. main() fills values
   with 4 int values and prints their sum. */
// END

   in binary. */

/* Caption: How do I compute 4 to the power of 4 without pow() in C? */

/* Plan:

   2. Multiply result by base exp times.
   3. Print 4 to the power 4. */
/* Multiply the base by itself exp times. */
long long power(int base, int exp) {
    long long result = 1;
    for (int i = 0; i < exp; i++) {
        result *= base;
    }
    return result;

    return 0;

   long long because powers grow quickly. main() prints 4 to the power 4. */

/* Caption: Use insertion sort to put numbers in ascending order. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write insertion_sort() for the long array marks.
   2. Take each element in turn as current.
   3. Shift the larger values of the sorted part one place right.
   4. Put current into the gap.
   5. Print the sorted values. */
/* Insert each element into the already sorted part on its left. */
void insertion_sort(long marks[], int size) {
    for (int i = 1; i < size; i++) {
        long current = marks[i];
        int j = i - 1;
        while (j >= 0 && marks[j] > current) {
            marks[j + 1] = marks[j];   /* shift bigger values right */
            j--;
        }
        marks[j + 1] = current;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    long marks[] = {78L, 58L, 44L, 34L, 41L, 25L, 8L, 1L};
    int size = sizeof(marks) / sizeof(marks[0]);
    insertion_sort(marks, size);
    for (int i = 0; i < size; i++) {
        printf("%ld ", marks[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: insertion_sort() takes each element in turn and shifts the larger values of
   the sorted part one place right until the element fits. main() then prints the 8 values
   in ascending order. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to return the minimum, maximum and average of an array in a struct. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define a Stats struct with min, max and average.
   2. Write array_stats() that fills one Stats in a loop.
   3. Return the struct.
   4. Print st.min, st.max and st.average. */
typedef struct {
    int min;
    int max;
    double average;
} Stats;

/* Pack several results into one struct and return it. */
Stats array_stats(const int v[], int n) {
    Stats s = {v[0], v[0], 0.0};
    double total = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        if (v[i] < s.min) {
            s.min = v[i];
        }
        if (v[i] > s.max) {
            s.max = v[i];
        }
        total += v[i];
    }
    s.average = total / n;
    return s;
}

int main(void) {
    int prices[] = {96, 82, 98, 83, 22, 46, 50};
    int n = sizeof(prices) / sizeof(prices[0]);
    Stats st = array_stats(prices, n);
    printf("Min %d, Max %d, Average %.2f\n", st.min, st.max, st.average);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: Stats groups three results. array_stats() fills one Stats while it loops
   over the 7 values and returns the whole struct, which is a clean way to return several
   results at once. main() reads them as st.min, st.max and st.average. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a function that returns the midpoint of two points as a struct. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define a Point struct with x and y.
   2. Write midpoint() that returns a Point with the averages of x and y.
   3. Print mid.x and mid.y. */
typedef struct {
    double x;
    double y;
} Point;

/* A function can return a whole struct. */
Point midpoint(Point a, Point b) {
    Point m = {(a.x + b.x) / 2, (a.y + b.y) / 2};
    return m;
}

int main(void) {
    Point p = {-6, 18}, q = {-18, 2};
    Point mid = midpoint(p, q);
    printf("Midpoint: (%.1f, %.1f)\n", mid.x, mid.y);
    return 0;
}

   are the averages of theirs. main() declares p and q on one line, (-6, 18) and (-18, 2),
   and prints the midpoint using mid.x and mid.y. */
// END

/* Caption: How do I return both the smallest and the largest value of an array through pointers in C? */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write min_max() with the array, its length and the pointers min and max.
   2. Start both at the first element.
   3. Update *min and *max while looping over the rest.
   4. Declare low and high, pass their addresses and print them. */
/* One pass finds both results; they are stored through the pointers. */
void min_max(const int marks[], int n, int *min, int *max) {
    *min = marks[0];
    *max = marks[0];
    for (int i = 1; i < n; i++) {
        if (marks[i] < *min) {
            *min = marks[i];
        }
        if (marks[i] > *max) {
            *max = marks[i];
        }
    }
}

int main(void) {
    int marks[] = {84, 76, 71, 56};
    int n = 4;
    int low, high;
    min_max(marks, n, &low, &high);
    printf("Min: %d, Max: %d\n", low, high);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: A C function can return only one value, so min_max() returns void and
   writes its two results through the pointer parameters min and max. main() declares low
   and high on one line and passes their addresses with &, then prints both results for the
   4 values. */
// END

/* Caption: Find a number in a sorted array with binary search. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Make sure the array is sorted.
   2. Set left to 0 and right to n - 1.
   3. While left <= right, compare the middle element middle with the key.
   4. Return the index if it matches; otherwise keep only the half that can hold the
      key.
   5. Return -1 if the range becomes empty, and print the index of 201. */
/* The array must be sorted. Each step halves the range that can still hold the key. */
int binary_search(const int marks[], int n, int key) {
    int left = 0;
    int right = n - 1;
    while (left <= right) {
        int middle = left + (right - left) / 2;
        if (marks[middle] == key) {
            return middle;
        } else if (marks[middle] < key) {
            left = middle + 1;   /* key is in the right half */
        } else {
            right = middle - 1;   /* key is in the left half */
        }
    }
    return -1;
}

int main(void) {
    int marks[] = {11, 13, 41, 78, 79, 87, 119, 135, 143, 187};
    const int n = 10;
    int index = binary_search(marks, n, 201);
    printf("Index of 201: %d\n", index);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: binary_search() needs a sorted array. It keeps the range from left to
   right, compares the middle element middle with the key and throws away the half that
   cannot contain it, so it needs only about log2(n) steps. main() looks for 201 and prints
   its index, or -1 if it is not there. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to write your own version of strcpy. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write copy_string(dest, src).
   2. Copy src into dest one character at a time.
   3. Stop after copying the null character.
   4. Copy rotor into text and print it. */
/* Copy each character, including the final '\0'. */
void copy_string(char *dest, const char *src) {
    int i = 0;
    while ((dest[i] = src[i]) != '\0') {
        i++;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    char source[] = "rotor";
    char text[100];
    copy_string(text, source);
    printf("Copied: %s\n", text);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: copy_string() copies src into dest one character at a time, including the
   final null character, which is what strcpy does. The array text must be big enough to
   hold the copy. main() copies the word rotor and prints it. */
// END

/* Caption: C program to show the Fibonacci series with a loop. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Start with prev = 0 and curr = 1.
   2. Repeat 22 times and print prev each time.
   3. Compute next = prev + curr, then set prev = curr and curr = next. */
int main(void) {
    long prev = 0, curr = 1;
    /* Print a term, then slide the pair one step along the sequence. */
    for (int i = 0; i < 22; i++) {
        printf("%ld ", prev);
        long next = prev + curr;
        prev = curr;
        curr = next;
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: The loop keeps the last two numbers in prev and curr. Each round it prints
   prev, then moves the pair forward: prev becomes curr and curr becomes their sum. It
   prints the first 22 Fibonacci numbers. */
// END

/* Caption: C program to find the greatest common divisor of two numbers. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write gcd() with Euclid's algorithm.
   2. Replace (a, b) by (b, a % b) until b is 0.
   3. Return a and print the GCD of 157 and 32. */
/* Euclid: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a % b) until b becomes zero. */
int gcd(int a, int b) {
    while (b != 0) {
        int r = a % b;
        a = b;
        b = r;
    }
    return a;
}

int main(void) {
    int x = 157, y = 32;
    printf("gcd(%d, %d) = %d\n", x, y, gcd(x, y));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: gcd() uses Euclid's algorithm: it keeps replacing (a, b) with (b, a % b)
   until b is 0. The last non-zero value is the greatest common divisor, and main() prints
   the GCD of 157 and 32. */
// END

/* Caption: How do I multiply two fractions using a struct in C? */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define a Fraction struct with num and den.
   2. Write multiply() that returns num = a.num * b.num and den = a.den * b.den.
   3. Print 6/6 times 3/6. */
typedef struct {
    int num;
    int den;
} Fraction;

/* Multiply the numerators and the denominators. */
Fraction multiply(Fraction a, Fraction b) {
    Fraction r = {a.num * b.num, a.den * b.den};
    return r;
}

int main(void) {
    Fraction x = {6, 6}, y = {3, 6};
    Fraction p = multiply(x, y);
    printf("%d/%d * %d/%d = %d/%d\n", x.num, x.den, y.num, y.den, p.num, p.den);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: Fraction stores a numerator and a denominator. multiply() takes two
   Fractions and returns a new one with num = a.num * b.num and den = a.den * b.den. main()
   multiplies 6/6 by 3/6 (without reducing the result). */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to compute the mean of a list of numbers. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write array_average() that takes samples and count.
   2. Add the values into the double result.
   3. Return result / count.
   4. Print the average with two decimals. */
/* Sum the values, then divide by how many there are. */
double array_average(const int samples[], int count) {
    double result = 0.0;
    int k = 0;
    while (k < count) {
        result += samples[k];
        k++;
    }
    return result / count;
}

int main(void) {
    int samples[] = {54, 62, 44, 1, 5, 96, 67};
    int count = 7;
    printf("Average: %.2f\n", array_average(samples, count));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: array_average() adds the 7 values of samples into the double result and
   divides by count, so the mean keeps its decimal part even when the values are whole
   numbers. main() prints it with two decimals. */
// END

/* Caption: List the prime numbers below a limit. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write is_prime(n); numbers below 2 are not prime.
   2. Try every divisor d while d * d <= n.
   3. Return false if one divides n, otherwise true.
   4. Print every prime from 2 to 64. */
/* A prime has no divisor between 2 and its square root. */
bool is_prime(int n) {
    if (n < 2) {
        return false;
    }
    for (int d = 2; d * d <= n; d++) {
        if (n % d == 0) {
            return false;
        }
    }
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    for (int n = 2; n <= 64; n++) {
        if (is_prime(n)) {
            printf("%d ", n);
        }
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: is_prime() tries every divisor d from 2 while d * d <= n; if one divides n
   evenly, n is not prime. main() tests every number from 2 to 64 and prints the primes. */
// END

/* Caption: Program to copy one string into another by hand. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write copy_string(dest, src).
   2. Copy src into dest one character at a time.
   3. Stop after copying the null character.
   4. Copy program into buffer and print it. */
/* Copy each character, including the final '\0'. */
void copy_string(char *dest, const char *src) {
    int i = 0;
    while ((dest[i] = src[i]) != '\0') {
        i++;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    char source[] = "program";
    char buffer[64];
    copy_string(buffer, source);
    printf("Copied: %s\n", buffer);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: copy_string() copies src into dest one character at a time, including the
   final null character, which is what strcpy does. The array buffer must be big enough to
   hold the copy. main() copies the word program and prints it. */
// END

/* Caption: Print the binary representation of an integer. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write print_binary(n, bits).
   2. Go through the bits from the highest to the lowest.
   3. Print 1 when (n >> b) & 1 is set, otherwise 0.
   4. Print 734 in binary. */
/* Check each bit from the highest to the lowest. */
void print_binary(unsigned int n, int bits) {
    for (int b = bits - 1; b >= 0; b--) {
        putchar((n >> b) & 1 ? '1' : '0');
    }
    putchar('\n');
}

int main(void) {
    unsigned int number = 734;
    printf("%u in binary: ", number);
    print_binary(number, 10);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: print_binary() checks one bit at a time, from the highest to the lowest: (n
   >> b) & 1 is 1 when bit b is set, so it prints the character 1 or 0. main() prints 734
   in binary. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to count how many words are separated by spaces in a string. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <ctype.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write count_words() with words = 0 and an in_word flag.
   2. A space ends a word; a non-space after a space starts a new word and adds one to
      words.
   3. Return words and print it. */
/* A new word starts when a non-space follows a space (or the start). */
int count_words(const char *text) {
    int words = 0;
    int in_word = 0;
    for (int i = 0; text[i] != '\0'; i++) {
        if (isspace((unsigned char)text[i])) {
            in_word = 0;
        } else if (!in_word) {
            in_word = 1;
            words++;
        }
    }
    return words;
}

int main(void) {
    const char *sentence = "keep functions short and focused";
    printf("Words: %d\n", count_words(sentence));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: count_words() uses the flag in_word: a new word starts when a non-space
   character follows a space or the start of the text. main() prints the number of words in
   the sentence. */
// END

/* Caption: Program to use binary search to locate a value in a sorted list. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Make sure the array is sorted.
   2. Set low to 0 and high to count - 1.
   3. While low <= high, compare the middle element mid with the key.
   4. Return the index if it matches; otherwise keep only the half that can hold the
      key.
   5. Return -1 if the range becomes empty, and print the index of 65. */
/* The array must be sorted. Each step halves the range that can still hold the key. */
int binary_search(const int data[], int count, int key) {
    int low = 0;
    int high = count - 1;
    while (low <= high) {
        int mid = low + (high - low) / 2;
        if (data[mid] == key) {
            return mid;
        } else if (data[mid] < key) {
            low = mid + 1;   /* key is in the right half */
        } else {
            high = mid - 1;   /* key is in the left half */
        }
    }
    return -1;
}

int main(void) {
    int data[] = {5, 19, 23, 65, 70, 81, 85, 108, 113, 114, 195};
    int count = sizeof(data) / sizeof(data[0]);
    int index = binary_search(data, count, 65);
    printf("Index of 65: %d\n", index);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: binary_search() needs a sorted array. It keeps the range from low to high,
   compares the middle element mid with the key and throws away the half that cannot
   contain it, so it needs only about log2(n) steps. main() looks for 65 and prints its
   index, or -1 if it is not there. */
// END

/* Caption: Check every element of an array to find a target value. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write linear_search() with the array, its length and key.
   2. Compare each element with key.
   3. Return the index of the first match, or -1.
   4. In main(), search for 73 and print the result. */
/* Return the index of key, or -1 when it is not in the array. */
int linear_search(const int samples[], int length, int key) {
    for (int i = 0; i < length; i++) {
        if (samples[i] == key) {
            return i;
        }
    }
    return -1;
}

int main(void) {
    int samples[] = {7, 47, 40, 9, 23, 96, 73, 6};
    int length = sizeof(samples) / sizeof(samples[0]);
    int key = 73;
    int pos = linear_search(samples, length, key);
    if (pos >= 0) {
        printf("Found %d at index %d\n", key, pos);
    } else {
        printf("%d is not in the array\n", key);
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: linear_search() checks the elements of samples one by one and returns the
   index of the first one equal to key, or -1 when it reaches the end without a match.
   main() searches for 73 and prints where it is, or that it is missing. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to compute the factorial of a number recursively. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write factorial(value) that calls itself.
   2. Return 1 when value is 1 or less.
   3. Otherwise return value * factorial(value - 1).
   4. Print 3! as an unsigned long long. */
/* n! = n * (n - 1)!, and 0! = 1 stops the recursion. */
unsigned long long factorial(int value) {
    if (value <= 1) {
        return 1;
    }
    return value * factorial(value - 1);
}

int main(void) {
    int value = 3;
    printf("%d! = %llu\n", value, factorial(value));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: factorial() calls itself: n! is n * (n - 1)!, and the recursion stops when
   value is 1 or less. main() prints 3! as an unsigned long long, because factorials grow
   very fast. */
// END

/* Caption: Find the largest of four numbers with a function. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write max2() that returns the larger of two values.
   2. Write max_of_four() as max2(max2(a, b), max2(c, d)).
   3. Print the largest of the four values. */
/* Return the larger of two values. */
int max2(int a, int b) {
    return a > b ? a : b;
}

/* Reuse max2 to compare four values. */
int max_of_four(int a, int b, int c, int d) {
    return max2(max2(a, b), max2(c, d));
}

int main(void) {
    int a = 15, b = 75, c = 26, d = 43;
    printf("Largest: %d\n", max_of_four(a, b, c, d));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: max_of_four() takes four parameters and reuses the helper max2(), which
   returns the larger of two values: it compares a with b, c with d, and then the two
   winners. main() prints the largest of 15, 75, 26 and 43. */
// END

/* Caption: Show the Fibonacci series using recursion. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write fib(n) that returns n when n < 2.
   2. Otherwise return fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2).
   3. Print fib(i) for i from 0 to 9. */
/* Each Fibonacci number is the sum of the two before it. */
long fib(int n) {
    if (n < 2) {
        return n;
    }
    return fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2);
}

int main(void) {
    for (int i = 0; i < 10; i++) {
        printf("%ld ", fib(i));
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: fib() returns n for 0 and 1 and otherwise adds the two previous Fibonacci
   numbers by calling itself twice, which is simple but slow for large n. main() prints the
   first 10 numbers. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to write a function that swaps two int values through pointers. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write swap() that takes pointers to two int values.
   2. Save *a in tmp, copy *b into *a, then tmp into *b.
   3. In main(), print a and b, call swap(&a, &b) and print them again. */
/* Pass addresses so the function can change the caller's variables. */
void swap(int *a, int *b) {
    int tmp = *a;
    *a = *b;
    *b = tmp;
}

int main(void) {
    int a = 96, b = 93;
    printf("Before: %d %d\n", a, b);
    swap(&a, &b);
    printf("After:  %d %d\n", a, b);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: swap() receives the addresses of a and b, so writing through the pointers
   *a and *b changes the caller's variables. tmp holds one value during the exchange.
   main() declares both variables on one line and prints them before and after the swap. */
// END

/* Caption: Reverse a string in place. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <string.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write reverse_string() for text.
   2. Set i to the first index and j to the last.
   3. Swap the two characters and move i and j inwards until they meet.
   4. Reverse memory and print it. */
/* Swap characters from both ends until they meet in the middle. */
void reverse_string(char *text) {
    int i = 0;
    int j = strlen(text) - 1;
    while (i < j) {
        char tmp = text[i];
        text[i] = text[j];
        text[j] = tmp;
        i++;
        j--;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    char text[] = "memory";
    reverse_string(text);
    printf("%s\n", text);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: reverse_string() swaps characters from both ends of text, moving inwards
   until the two indexes meet. main() reverses the word memory in place and prints it. */
// END

/* Caption: Define a Point struct and measure the distance between two points. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <math.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define a Point struct with x and y.
   2. Write distance() using sqrt(dx * dx + dy * dy).
   3. Print the distance between p and q. */
typedef struct {
    double x;
    double y;
} Point;

/* Pythagoras: sqrt(dx * dx + dy * dy). */
double distance(Point a, Point b) {
    double dx = b.x - a.x;
    double dy = b.y - a.y;
    return sqrt(dx * dx + dy * dy);
}

int main(void) {
    Point p = {1, 9};
    Point q = {8, 2};
    printf("Distance: %.3f\n", distance(p, q));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: Point is a typedef struct with x and y. distance() uses Pythagoras, sqrt(dx
   * dx + dy * dy), to measure the gap between the two points, and main() prints it. */
// END

/* Caption: Sum a long array with a helper function. */

   1. Write add_all() that takes the array marks and its length length.
   2. Start result at 0 and add every element in a for loop.
   3. Return result.
   4. In main(), fill marks with 9 values and print the sum. */
/* Add every element to a running total. */
long add_all(const long marks[], int length) {
    long result = 0;
    for (int j = 0; j < length; j++) {

    return result;
}

int main(void) {

    const int length = 9;
    printf("Sum: %ld\n", add_all(marks, length));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: add_all() receives the array marks and its length length. It starts result
   at 0, adds every element to it in a for loop and returns the total. main() fills marks
   with 9 long values and prints their sum. */
// END

/* Caption: Use insertion sort to put numbers in descending order. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write insertion_sort() for the double array items.
   2. Take each element in turn as current.
   3. Shift the smaller values of the sorted part one place right.
   4. Put current into the gap.
   5. Print the sorted values. */
/* Insert each element into the already sorted part on its left. */
void insertion_sort(double items[], int n) {
    for (int i = 1; i < n; i++) {
        double current = items[i];
        int j = i - 1;
        while (j >= 0 && items[j] < current) {
            items[j + 1] = items[j];   /* shift bigger values right */
            j--;
        }
        items[j + 1] = current;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    double items[] = {15.5, 34.8, 59.7, 89.6, 73.1, 61.2, 44.3};
    const int n = 7;
    insertion_sort(items, n);
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        printf("%.2f ", items[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: insertion_sort() takes each element in turn and shifts the smaller values
   of the sorted part one place right until the element fits. main() then prints the 7
   values in descending order. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to check whether a word is a palindrome. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <string.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write is_palindrome() for text.
   2. Compare the first and last characters, moving inwards.
   3. Return false at the first mismatch, otherwise true.
   4. Check stats and print the result. */
/* Compare characters from the front and back, moving inwards. */
bool is_palindrome(const char *text) {
    int i = 0;
    int j = strlen(text) - 1;
    while (i < j) {
        if (text[i] != text[j]) {
            return false;
        }
        i++;
        j--;
    }
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    const char *text = "stats";
    printf("%s %s a palindrome\n", text, is_palindrome(text) ? "is" : "is not");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: is_palindrome() compares the first and last characters and moves inwards;
   any mismatch means the word is not a palindrome. main() checks the word stats and prints
   the result. */
// END

/* Caption: How do I raise a number to an integer power with a loop in C? */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write power(base, exp) with result = 1.
   2. Multiply result by base exp times.
   3. Print 8 to the power 7. */
/* Multiply the base by itself exp times. */
long long power(int base, int exp) {
    long long result = 1;
    for (int i = 0; i < exp; i++) {
        result *= base;
    }
    return result;
}

int main(void) {
    printf("8^7 = %lld\n", power(8, 7));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: power() starts result at 1 and multiplies it by base exp times. It uses
   long long because powers grow quickly. main() prints 8 to the power 7. */
// END

/* Caption: Return the smallest element of an array of double values. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write smallest_value() that takes readings and length.
   2. Store readings[0] in smallest.
   3. Loop over the other elements and keep the smallest value in smallest.
   4. Return smallest and print it. */
/* Start with the first element and keep the smallest value seen so far. */
double smallest_value(const double readings[], int length) {
    double smallest = readings[0];
    for (int idx = 1; idx < length; idx++) {
        if (readings[idx] < smallest) {
            smallest = readings[idx];
        }
    }
    return smallest;
}

int main(void) {
    double readings[] = {22.1, 66.4, 72.8, 81.8, 12.3, 73.0};
    int length = sizeof(readings) / sizeof(readings[0]);
    printf("Smallest: %.2f\n", smallest_value(readings, length));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: smallest_value() takes the first element as the smallest value so far and
   stores it in smallest. The loop compares every other element with smallest using < and
   keeps the smallest one. main() prints the smallest of the 6 values. */
// END

/* Caption: How do I build a fixed-size integer stack in C in C? */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define a Stack with room for 32 items and a top counter.
   2. Write push() and pop(), returning false when the stack is full or empty.
   3. Push 5 values.
   4. Pop and print until the stack is empty. */
#define CAPACITY 32

typedef struct {
    int items[CAPACITY];
    int top;   /* number of items on the stack */
} Stack;

bool push(Stack *s, int value) {
    if (s->top == CAPACITY) {
        return false;   /* stack is full */
    }
    s->items[s->top++] = value;
    return true;
}

bool pop(Stack *s, int *value) {
    if (s->top == 0) {
        return false;   /* stack is empty */
    }
    *value = s->items[--s->top];
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    Stack s = {.top = 0};
    push(&s, 86);
    push(&s, 45);
    push(&s, 87);
    push(&s, 40);
    push(&s, 45);
    int value;
    /* Items come back out in reverse order (last in, first out). */
    while (pop(&s, &value)) {
        printf("%d ", value);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: The Stack keeps up to 32 items in an array, and top counts how many are
   stored. push() adds at the top and pop() removes from the top; both return false when
   they cannot. main() pushes 5 values and pops them all, so they come out in reverse order
   (last in, first out). */
// END

    int *px = &x, *py = &y;
    *px += 17;
    printf("x = %d, y = %d\n", x, y);
    printf("*px = %d, *py = %d\n", *px, *py);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: int *px = &x, *py = &y; declares two pointers in one statement; each name
   needs its own *. *px += 17 changes x through the pointer, so x becomes 25 while y stays
   21. */
// END

/* Caption: Print an integer with its digits reversed. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Start result at 0.
   2. Multiply result by 10, add n % 10, then divide n by 10.
   3. Repeat until n is 0.
   4. Apply it to 549631 and print the result. */
/* Take the last digit with % 10, then drop it with / 10. */
int reverse_digits(int n) {
    int result = 0;
    while (n > 0) {
        result = result * 10 + n % 10;
        n /= 10;
    }
    return result;
}

int main(void) {
    int number = 549631;
    printf("reverse of digits of %d: %d\n", number, reverse_digits(number));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: reverse_digits() shifts result one place left (result * 10) and adds the
   last digit of n, which reverses the order. main() applies it to 549631. */
// END

/* Caption: How do I list the prime numbers below a limit in C? */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write is_prime(n); numbers below 2 are not prime.
   2. Try every divisor d while d * d <= n.
   3. Return false if one divides n, otherwise true.
   4. Print every prime from 2 to 53. */
/* A prime has no divisor between 2 and its square root. */
bool is_prime(int n) {
    if (n < 2) {
        return false;
    }
    for (int d = 2; d * d <= n; d++) {
        if (n % d == 0) {
            return false;
        }
    }
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    for (int n = 2; n <= 53; n++) {
        if (is_prime(n)) {
            printf("%d ", n);
        }
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: is_prime() tries every divisor d from 2 while d * d <= n; if one divides n
   evenly, n is not prime. main() tests every number from 2 to 53 and prints the primes. */
// END

/* Caption: How do I show the right way to declare several pointers on one line in C? */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Declare x and y on one line.
   2. Declare the pointers px and py on one line, each with its own *.
   3. Add 9 to x through px and print the values. */
int main(void) {
    int x = 6, y = 37;
    /* Each pointer needs its own '*': in "int *p, q;" only p is a pointer. */
    int *px = &x, *py = &y;
    *px += 9;
    printf("x = %d, y = %d\n", x, y);
    printf("*px = %d, *py = %d\n", *px, *py);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: int *px = &x, *py = &y; declares two pointers in one statement; each name
   needs its own *. *px += 9 changes x through the pointer, so x becomes 15 while y stays
   37. */
// END

/* Caption: Find the arithmetic mean of 4 long values. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write mean() that takes samples and size.
   2. Add the values into the double total.
   3. Return total / size.
   4. Print the average with two decimals. */
/* Sum the values, then divide by how many there are. */
double mean(const long samples[], int size) {
    double total = 0.0;
    int j = 0;
    while (j < size) {
        total += samples[j];
        j++;
    }
    return total / size;
}

int main(void) {
    long samples[] = {86L, 2L, 89L, 60L};
    int size = sizeof(samples) / sizeof(samples[0]);
    printf("The average is %.2f\n", mean(samples, size));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: mean() adds the 4 values of samples into the double total and divides by
   size, so the mean keeps its decimal part even when the values are whole numbers. main()
   prints it with two decimals. */
// END

/* Caption: Allocate an array with malloc and fill it with cubes. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Use malloc to get room for 6 ints and check for NULL.
   2. Fill list with cubes.
   3. Print the values.
   4. Call free(list) at the end. */
int main(void) {
    int n = 6;
    /* Ask the heap for room for n ints; malloc returns NULL on failure. */
    int *list = malloc(n * sizeof(int));
    if (list == NULL) {
        fprintf(stderr, "malloc failed\n");
        return 1;
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        list[i] = i * i * i;
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        printf("%d ", list[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    free(list);   /* give the memory back */
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: malloc() reserves room for 6 ints on the heap and returns NULL if it fails,
   which the program checks. The first loop fills list with cubes, the second prints them,
   and free() gives the memory back at the end. */
// END

/* Caption: Find the least common multiple of two numbers. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write gcd() with Euclid's algorithm: replace (a, b) by (b, a % b) until b is 0.
   2. Write lcm() as a / gcd(a, b) * b.
   3. Print the LCM of 83 and 13. */
/* Euclid: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a % b) until b becomes zero. */
int gcd(int a, int b) {
    while (b != 0) {
        int r = a % b;
        a = b;
        b = r;
    }
    return a;
}

/* lcm(a, b) = a / gcd(a, b) * b (divide first to avoid overflow). */
long lcm(int a, int b) {
    return (long)a / gcd(a, b) * b;
}

int main(void) {
    printf("lcm(83, 13) = %ld\n", lcm(83, 13));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: gcd() uses Euclid's algorithm: it keeps replacing (a, b) with (b, a % b)
   until b is 0. lcm() divides a by the gcd before multiplying by b, which avoids overflow.
   main() prints the LCM of 83 and 13. */
// END

/* Euclid: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a % b) until b becomes zero. */

        int r = a % b;

/* Caption: How do I find the index of a number using linear search in C? */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write linear_search() with the array, its length and wanted.
   2. Compare each element with wanted.
   3. Return the index of the first match, or -1.
   4. In main(), search for 21 and print the result. */
/* Return the index of wanted, or -1 when it is not in the array. */
int linear_search(const int prices[], int len, int wanted) {
    for (int i = 0; i < len; i++) {
        if (prices[i] == wanted) {
            return i;
        }
    }
    return -1;
}

int main(void) {
    int prices[] = {66, 21, 21, 50, 39, 98, 3};
    const int len = 7;
    int wanted = 21;
    int pos = linear_search(prices, len, wanted);
    if (pos >= 0) {
        printf("Found %d at index %d\n", wanted, pos);
    } else {
        printf("%d is not in the array\n", wanted);
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: linear_search() checks the elements of prices one by one and returns the
   index of the first one equal to wanted, or -1 when it reaches the end without a match.
   main() searches for 21 and prints where it is, or that it is missing. */
// END

/* Caption: Raise a number to an integer power with a loop. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write power(base, exp) with result = 1.
   2. Multiply result by base exp times.
   3. Print 4 to the power 2. */
/* Multiply the base by itself exp times. */
long long power(int base, int exp) {
    long long result = 1;
    for (int i = 0; i < exp; i++) {
        result *= base;
    }
    return result;
}

int main(void) {
    printf("4^2 = %lld\n", power(4, 2));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: power() starts result at 1 and multiplies it by base exp times. It uses
   long long because powers grow quickly. main() prints 4 to the power 2. */
// END

/* Caption: Compute the sum of the elements of an array. */

/* Plan:
   1. Write sum_array() that takes the array scores and its length len.
   2. Start sum at 0 and add every element in a for loop.
   3. Return sum.
   4. In main(), fill scores with 4 values and print the sum. */
/* Add every element to a running total. */
double sum_array(const double scores[], int len) {
    double sum = 0;
    for (int idx = 0; idx < len; idx++) {
        sum += scores[idx];

    return sum;

    printf("Total = %.2f\n", sum_array(scores, len));
    return 0;
}

   0, adds every element to it in a for loop and returns the total. main() fills scores
   with 4 double values and prints their sum. */
// END

#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write string_length() with a counter len = 0.
   2. Move through the string until the null character.
   3. Return len and print the length of pointer. */
/* Count characters until the terminating '\0'. */
int string_length(const char *line) {
    int len = 0;
    while (line[len] != '\0') {
        len++;

    return len;

    printf("Length of \"%s\" is %d\n", line, string_length(line));
    return 0;

   ends every C string. main() prints the length of the word pointer. */

/* Caption: Write a C program to compute the factorial of a number with a loop. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write factorial(num) with result = 1.
   2. Multiply result by every number from 2 to num.
   3. Return result.
   4. Print 15! as an unsigned long long. */
/* Multiply 1 * 2 * ... * n. */
unsigned long long factorial(int num) {
    unsigned long long result = 1;
    for (int i = 2; i <= num; i++) {
        result *= i;
    }
    return result;
}

int main(void) {
    int num = 15;
    printf("%d! = %llu\n", num, factorial(num));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: factorial() multiplies result by every number from 2 up to num. main()
   prints 15! as an unsigned long long, because factorials grow very fast. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to decide if 2034 is a leap year. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write is_leap(year).
   2. A year divisible by 4 is a leap year, unless it is divisible by 100.
   3. Years divisible by 400 are leap years again.
   4. Check 2034 and print the result. */
/* Leap years divide by 4, except centuries, which must divide by 400. */
int is_leap(int year) {
    return (year % 4 == 0 && year % 100 != 0) || year % 400 == 0;
}

int main(void) {
    int year = 2034;
    if (is_leap(year)) {
        printf("%d is a leap year\n", year);
    } else {
        printf("%d is not a leap year\n", year);
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: is_leap() returns true for years divisible by 4, except century years,
   which must also be divisible by 400. main() checks 2034 and prints whether it is a leap
   year. */
// END

/* Plan:
   1. Start i at 17.
   2. Print i and subtract one until i reaches 1. */
int main(void) {
    /* Start high and subtract one each time round the loop. */
    for (int i = 17; i >= 1; i--) {
        printf("%d ", i);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: The for loop starts at 17 and subtracts one each round (i--) until it
   reaches 1. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to use dynamic memory to store the first 13 multiples. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Use malloc to get room for 13 ints and check for NULL.
   2. Fill list with multiples.
   3. Print the values.
   4. Call free(list) at the end. */
int main(void) {
    int n = 13;
    /* Ask the heap for room for n ints; malloc returns NULL on failure. */
    int *list = malloc(n * sizeof(int));
    if (list == NULL) {
        fprintf(stderr, "malloc failed\n");
        return 1;
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        list[i] = 9 * i;
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        printf("%d ", list[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    free(list);   /* give the memory back */
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: malloc() reserves room for 13 ints on the heap and returns NULL if it
   fails, which the program checks. The first loop fills list with multiples, the second
   prints them, and free() gives the memory back at the end. */
// END

/* Caption: Convert a string to uppercase. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <ctype.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write to_upper() for word.
   2. Replace every character with toupper() until the null character.
   3. Print the sentence. */
/* toupper changes lowercase letters and leaves other characters alone. */
void to_upper(char *word) {
    for (int i = 0; word[i] != '\0'; i++) {
        word[i] = toupper((unsigned char)word[i]);
    }
}

int main(void) {
    char word[] = "every program starts in main";
    to_upper(word);
    printf("%s\n", word);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: to_upper() walks through word until the null character and replaces each
   character with toupper(), which only changes lowercase letters. main() prints the
   sentence in capitals. */
// END

/* Caption: Program to sum a int array with a helper function. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write add_all() that takes the array items and its length n.
   2. Start result at 0 and add every element in a while loop.
   3. Return result.
   4. In main(), fill items with 9 values and print the sum. */
/* Return the sum of the first n elements. */
int add_all(const int items[], int n) {
    int result = 0;
    int i = 0;
    while (i < n) {
        result += items[i];
        i++;
    }
    return result;
}

int main(void) {

    int n = 9;
    printf("Sum: %d\n", add_all(items, n));

}
/* Explanation: add_all() receives the array items and its length n. It starts result at 0,
   adds every element to it in a while loop and returns the total. main() fills items with
   9 int values and prints their sum. */
// END

/* Caption: Implement insertion sort for an array of int values. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write insertion_sort() for the int array items.
   2. Take each element in turn as current.
   3. Shift the smaller values of the sorted part one place right.
   4. Put current into the gap.
   5. Print the sorted values. */
/* Insert each element into the already sorted part on its left. */
void insertion_sort(int items[], int n) {
    for (int i = 1; i < n; i++) {
        int current = items[i];
        int j = i - 1;
        while (j >= 0 && items[j] < current) {
            items[j + 1] = items[j];   /* shift bigger values right */
            j--;
        }
        items[j + 1] = current;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    int items[] = {57, 78, 43, 44, 1, 19, 81, 83, 82, 13};
    int n = sizeof(items) / sizeof(items[0]);
    insertion_sort(items, n);
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        printf("%d ", items[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: insertion_sort() takes each element in turn and shifts the smaller values
   of the sorted part one place right until the element fits. main() then prints the 10
   values in descending order. */
// END

/* Caption: Show the right way to declare several pointers on one line. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Declare x and y on one line.
   2. Declare the pointers px and py on one line, each with its own *.
   3. Add 12 to x through px and print the values. */
int main(void) {
    int x = 21, y = 38;
    /* Each pointer needs its own '*': in "int *p, q;" only p is a pointer. */
    int *px = &x, *py = &y;
    *px += 12;
    printf("x = %d, y = %d\n", x, y);
    printf("*px = %d, *py = %d\n", *px, *py);
    return 0;
}

   needs its own *. *px += 12 changes x through the pointer, so x becomes 33 while y stays
   38. */

/* Caption: Write a program to compute the factorial of a number with a loop. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write factorial(n) with result = 1.
   2. Multiply result by every number from 2 to n.
   3. Return result.
   4. Print 13! as an unsigned long long. */
/* Multiply 1 * 2 * ... * n. */
unsigned long long factorial(int n) {
    unsigned long long result = 1;
    for (int i = 2; i <= n; i++) {
        result *= i;
    }
    return result;
}

int main(void) {
    int n = 13;
    printf("%d! = %llu\n", n, factorial(n));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: factorial() multiplies result by every number from 2 up to n. main() prints
   13! as an unsigned long long, because factorials grow very fast. */
// END

/* Caption: How do I check whether a year is a leap year in C? */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write is_leap(year).
   2. A year divisible by 4 is a leap year, unless it is divisible by 100.
   3. Years divisible by 400 are leap years again.
   4. Check 2053 and print the result. */
/* Leap years divide by 4, except centuries, which must divide by 400. */
int is_leap(int year) {
    return (year % 4 == 0 && year % 100 != 0) || year % 400 == 0;
}

int main(void) {
    int year = 2053;
    if (is_leap(year)) {
        printf("%d is a leap year\n", year);
    } else {
        printf("%d is not a leap year\n", year);
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: is_leap() returns true for years divisible by 4, except century years,
   which must also be divisible by 400. main() checks 2053 and prints whether it is a leap
   year. */
// END

/* Caption: How do I implement a simple linked list with malloc and free in C? */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define ListNode with a value and a next pointer.
   2. Write push_front() that mallocs a node and links it in front of head.
   3. Write print_list() that follows next until NULL.
   4. Write free_list() that frees every node.
   5. Push 3 values, print the list and free it. */
typedef struct ListNode {
    int value;
    struct ListNode *next;
} ListNode;

/* Allocate a new node and put it in front of the current head. */
ListNode *push_front(ListNode *head, int value) {
    ListNode *node = malloc(sizeof(ListNode));
    if (node == NULL) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Out of memory\n");
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }
    node->value = value;
    node->next = head;
    return node;
}

void print_list(const ListNode *head) {
    for (const ListNode *cur = head; cur != NULL; cur = cur->next) {
        printf("%d -> ", cur->value);
    }
    printf("NULL\n");
}

/* Free every node; save next before freeing the current one. */
void free_list(ListNode *head) {
    while (head != NULL) {
        ListNode *next = head->next;
        free(head);
        head = next;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    ListNode *head = NULL;
    head = push_front(head, 65);
    head = push_front(head, 27);
    head = push_front(head, 21);
    print_list(head);
    free_list(head);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: Each ListNode holds a value and a pointer to the next node. push_front()
   allocates a node with malloc, puts it in front of head and returns it; print_list()
   follows the next pointers until NULL; free_list() frees every node. main() pushes 3
   values, so they print in reverse order. */
// END

/* Caption: Compute the area and circumference of a circle with one function. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write circle_measures() with the pointers area and circumference.
   2. Store PI * r * r and 2 * PI * r through them.
   3. Print both for a radius of 24.4. */
#define PI 3.14159265

void circle_measures(double radius, double *area, double *circumference) {
    *area = PI * radius * radius;
    *circumference = 2 * PI * radius;
}

int main(void) {
    double radius = 24.4;
    double area, circumference;
    circle_measures(radius, &area, &circumference);
    printf("Area: %.2f, Circumference: %.2f\n", area, circumference);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: circle_measures() computes two results from one radius and stores them
   through the pointers area and circumference. main() declares both variables on one line,
   passes their addresses and prints the results for a radius of 24.4. */
// END

/* Caption: List the prime numbers below a limit. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write is_prime(n); numbers below 2 are not prime.
   2. Try every divisor d while d * d <= n.
   3. Return false if one divides n, otherwise true.
   4. Print every prime from 2 to 111. */
/* A prime has no divisor between 2 and its square root. */
bool is_prime(int n) {
    if (n < 2) {
        return false;
    }
    for (int d = 2; d * d <= n; d++) {
        if (n % d == 0) {
            return false;
        }
    }
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    for (int n = 2; n <= 111; n++) {
        if (is_prime(n)) {
            printf("%d ", n);
        }
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: is_prime() tries every divisor d from 2 while d * d <= n; if one divides n
   evenly, n is not prime. main() tests every number from 2 to 111 and prints the primes. */
// END

/* Caption: How do I return a Duration struct built from a number of seconds in C? */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define a Duration struct with hours, minutes and seconds.
   2. Write from_seconds() that fills it using / and %.
   3. Convert 32919 seconds and print the members. */

    int hours;
    int minutes;
    int seconds;
} Duration;

Duration from_seconds(int total) {
    Duration d;
    d.hours = total / 3600;
    d.minutes = (total % 3600) / 60;
    d.seconds = total % 60;
    return d;

    return 0;

   then returns the struct. main() converts 32919 seconds and prints the members. */

/* Caption: Program to write a function that returns the distance between two points given x1, y1, x2 and y2. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <math.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write distance(x1, y1, x2, y2).
   2. Compute dx and dy, then return sqrt(dx * dx + dy * dy).
   3. Print the distance between (6, 7) and (0, 6). */
/* Pythagoras: the distance is sqrt(dx * dx + dy * dy). */
double distance(double x1, double y1, double x2, double y2) {
    double dx = x2 - x1, dy = y2 - y1;
    return sqrt(dx * dx + dy * dy);
}

int main(void) {
    printf("Distance: %.3f\n", distance(6, 7, 0, 6));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: distance() takes the coordinates of both points as four parameters. It
   declares dx and dy on one line and uses Pythagoras with sqrt() from math.h. main()
   prints the distance between (6, 7) and (0, 6). */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to compute the factorial of a number with a loop. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write factorial(num) with result = 1.
   2. Multiply result by every number from 2 to num.
   3. Return result.
   4. Print 12! as an unsigned long long. */
/* Multiply 1 * 2 * ... * n. */
unsigned long long factorial(int num) {
    unsigned long long result = 1;
    for (int i = 2; i <= num; i++) {
        result *= i;
    }
    return result;
}

int main(void) {
    int num = 12;
    printf("%d! = %llu\n", num, factorial(num));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: factorial() multiplies result by every number from 2 up to num. main()
   prints 12! as an unsigned long long, because factorials grow very fast. */
// END

/* Caption: How do I swap two variables using pointers in C? */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write swap() that takes pointers to two long values.
   2. Save *x in tmp, copy *y into *x, then tmp into *y.
   3. In main(), print x and y, call swap(&x, &y) and print them again. */
/* Pass addresses so the function can change the caller's variables. */
void swap(long *x, long *y) {
    long tmp = *x;
    *x = *y;
    *y = tmp;
}

int main(void) {
    long x = 99L, y = 2L;
    printf("Before: %ld %ld\n", x, y);
    swap(&x, &y);
    printf("After:  %ld %ld\n", x, y);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: swap() receives the addresses of x and y, so writing through the pointers
   *x and *y changes the caller's variables. tmp holds one value during the exchange.
   main() declares both variables on one line and prints them before and after the swap. */
// END

/* Caption: Count the characters in a string. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write string_length() with a counter len = 0.
   2. Move through the string until the null character.
   3. Return len and print the length of racecar. */
/* Count characters until the terminating '\0'. */
int string_length(const char *word) {
    int len = 0;
    while (word[len] != '\0') {
        len++;
    }
    return len;
}

    const char *word = "racecar";
    printf("Length of \"%s\" is %d\n", word, string_length(word));
    return 0;

   ends every C string. main() prints the length of the word racecar. */

/* Caption: Allocate an array with malloc and fill it with cubes. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Use malloc to get room for 5 ints and check for NULL.
   2. Fill list with cubes.
   3. Print the values.
   4. Call free(list) at the end. */
int main(void) {
    int n = 5;
    /* Ask the heap for room for n ints; malloc returns NULL on failure. */
    int *list = malloc(n * sizeof(int));
    if (list == NULL) {
        fprintf(stderr, "malloc failed\n");
        return 1;
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        list[i] = i * i * i;
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        printf("%d ", list[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    free(list);   /* give the memory back */
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: malloc() reserves room for 5 ints on the heap and returns NULL if it fails,
   which the program checks. The first loop fills list with cubes, the second prints them,
   and free() gives the memory back at the end. */
// END

/* Caption: Divide two integers and get both the quotient and the remainder. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write divide(a, b, &quotient, &remainder) that returns a bool.
   2. Return false if b is 0.
   3. Store a / b and a % b through the pointers and return true.
   4. Divide 312 by 17 and print the results or the error. */
/* Returns false for division by zero; otherwise stores both results. */
bool divide(int a, int b, int *quotient, int *remainder) {
    if (b == 0) {
        return false;
    }
    *quotient = a / b;
    *remainder = a % b;
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    int a = 312, b = 17;
    int q, r;
    if (divide(a, b, &q, &r)) {
        printf("%d / %d = %d remainder %d\n", a, b, q, r);
    } else {
        printf("Cannot divide by zero\n");
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: divide() has four parameters: two inputs and two pointers for the results.
   Its bool return value reports success, while the quotient and remainder are written
   through the pointers. main() divides 312 by 17 and prints both results. */
// END

/* Caption: Reverse the elements of an array in place. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write reverse_array() for readings.
   2. Set start to the first index and end to the last.
   3. Swap readings[start] and readings[end], then move both inwards.
   4. Stop when start meets end and print the array. */
/* Swap the outer pair, then move both ends toward the middle. */
void reverse_array(int readings[], int len) {
    int start = 0;
    int end = len - 1;
    while (start < end) {
        int tmp = readings[start];
        readings[start] = readings[end];
        readings[end] = tmp;
        start++;
        end--;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    int readings[] = {88, 59, 17, 31, 48};
    int len = sizeof(readings) / sizeof(readings[0]);
    reverse_array(readings, len);
    for (int i = 0; i < len; i++) {
        printf("%d ", readings[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: reverse_array() swaps the first and last elements, then moves start forward
   and end backward until they meet, so the array is reversed in place without a second
   array. main() prints the reversed values. */
// END

/* Caption: How do I raise a number to an integer power with a loop in C? */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write power(base, exp) with result = 1.
   2. Multiply result by base exp times.
   3. Print 3 to the power 8. */
/* Multiply the base by itself exp times. */
long long power(int base, int exp) {
    long long result = 1;
    for (int i = 0; i < exp; i++) {
        result *= base;
    }
    return result;
}

int main(void) {
    printf("3^8 = %lld\n", power(3, 8));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: power() starts result at 1 and multiplies it by base exp times. It uses
   long long because powers grow quickly. main() prints 3 to the power 8. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to limit a number to a range with a three-parameter function. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write clamp(value, low, high).
   2. Return low if the value is too small and high if it is too big.
   3. Otherwise return the value.
   4. Set low = 32 and high = 82 and print clamp() for 36, 90 and 83. */
/* Return value, but never less than low or more than high. */
int clamp(int value, int low, int high) {
    if (value < low) {
        return low;
    }
    if (value > high) {
        return high;
    }
    return value;
}

int main(void) {
    int low = 32, high = 82;
    printf("clamp(%d) = %d\n", 36, clamp(36, low, high));
    printf("clamp(%d) = %d\n", 90, clamp(90, low, high));
    printf("clamp(%d) = %d\n", 83, clamp(83, low, high));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: clamp() takes three parameters: the value and the two limits. It returns
   low when the value is too small, high when it is too big and the value itself otherwise.
   main() declares low = 32 and high = 82 on one line and clamps 36, 90 and 83. */
// END

/* Caption: Count how many odd numbers are in an array. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write count_odd() that takes samples and length.
   2. For each element, test samples[k] % 2 != 0.
   3. Add one to found for every odd number.
   4. Return found and print it. */
/* A number is odd when the remainder after dividing by 2 is one. */
int count_odd(const int samples[], int length) {
    int found = 0;
    for (int k = 0; k < length; k++) {
        if (samples[k] % 2 != 0) {
            found++;
        }
    }
    return found;
}

int main(void) {
    int samples[] = {58, 35, 58, 80, 62, 95, 82, 73, 39};
    int length = 9;
    printf("Odd numbers: %d\n", count_odd(samples, length));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: count_odd() tests each element of samples with the % operator: a remainder
   of 1 after dividing by 2 means the number is odd, so found goes up by one. main() prints
   how many of the 9 values are odd. */
// END

/* Caption: Return the smallest element of an array of double values. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write find_min() that takes items and n.
   2. Store items[0] in m.
   3. Loop over the other elements and keep the smallest value in m.
   4. Return m and print it. */
/* Start with the first element and keep the smallest value seen so far. */
double find_min(const double items[], int n) {
    double m = items[0];
    for (int k = 1; k < n; k++) {
        if (items[k] < m) {
            m = items[k];
        }
    }
    return m;
}

int main(void) {
    double items[] = {94.4, 54.8, 17.8, 88.1, 43.9};
    int n = 5;
    printf("The smallest value is %.2f\n", find_min(items, n));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: find_min() takes the first element as the smallest value so far and stores
   it in m. The loop compares every other element with m using < and keeps the smallest
   one. main() prints the smallest of the 5 values. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to print the factorial of an integer. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write factorial(value) with result = 1.
   2. Multiply result by every number from 2 to value.
   3. Return result.
   4. Print 15! as an unsigned long long. */
/* Multiply 1 * 2 * ... * n. */
unsigned long long factorial(int value) {
    unsigned long long result = 1;
    for (int i = 2; i <= value; i++) {
        result *= i;
    }
    return result;
}

int main(void) {
    int value = 15;
    printf("%d! = %llu\n", value, factorial(value));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: factorial() multiplies result by every number from 2 up to value. main()
   prints 15! as an unsigned long long, because factorials grow very fast. */
// END

/* Caption: Return a Duration struct built from a number of seconds. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define a Duration struct with hours, minutes and seconds.
   2. Write from_seconds() that fills it using / and %.
   3. Convert 37739 seconds and print the members. */
typedef struct {
    int hours;
    int minutes;
    int seconds;
} Duration;

Duration from_seconds(int total) {
    Duration d;
    d.hours = total / 3600;
    d.minutes = (total % 3600) / 60;
    d.seconds = total % 60;
    return d;
}

int main(void) {
    Duration d = from_seconds(37739);
    printf("%d h %d min %d s\n", d.hours, d.minutes, d.seconds);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: from_seconds() fills the three members of a Duration struct using / and %,
   then returns the struct. main() converts 37739 seconds and prints the members. */
// END

/* Caption: C program to create a singly linked list by inserting at the head. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define ListNode with a value and a next pointer.
   2. Write push_front() that mallocs a node and links it in front of head.
   3. Write print_list() that follows next until NULL.
   4. Write free_list() that frees every node.
   5. Push 3 values, print the list and free it. */
typedef struct ListNode {
    int value;
    struct ListNode *next;
} ListNode;

/* Allocate a new node and put it in front of the current head. */
ListNode *push_front(ListNode *head, int value) {
    ListNode *node = malloc(sizeof(ListNode));
    if (node == NULL) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Out of memory\n");
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }
    node->value = value;
    node->next = head;
    return node;
}

void print_list(const ListNode *head) {
    for (const ListNode *cur = head; cur != NULL; cur = cur->next) {
        printf("%d -> ", cur->value);
    }
    printf("NULL\n");
}

/* Free every node; save next before freeing the current one. */
void free_list(ListNode *head) {
    while (head != NULL) {
        ListNode *next = head->next;
        free(head);
        head = next;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    ListNode *head = NULL;
    head = push_front(head, 74);
    head = push_front(head, 57);
    head = push_front(head, 47);
    print_list(head);
    free_list(head);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: Each ListNode holds a value and a pointer to the next node. push_front()
   allocates a node with malloc, puts it in front of head and returns it; print_list()
   follows the next pointers until NULL; free_list() frees every node. main() pushes 3
   values, so they print in reverse order. */
// END

/* Caption: Implement selection sort for an array of int values. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write selection_sort() for the int array scores.
   2. For each position, find the smallest remaining element.
   3. Swap it into that position.
   4. Print the sorted values. */
/* Select the right element for each position and swap it into place. */
void selection_sort(int scores[], int length) {
    for (int i = 0; i < length - 1; i++) {
        int chosen = i;
        for (int j = i + 1; j < length; j++) {
            if (scores[chosen] > scores[j]) {
                chosen = j;
            }
        }
        int tmp = scores[i];
        scores[i] = scores[chosen];
        scores[chosen] = tmp;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    int scores[] = {56, 53, 59, 98, 23, 38, 82, 97};
    const int length = 8;
    selection_sort(scores, length);
    for (int i = 0; i < length; i++) {
        printf("%d ", scores[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: selection_sort() finds the smallest remaining element for each position and
   swaps it into place. main() then prints the 8 values in ascending order. */
// END

/* Caption: Allocate an array with malloc and fill it with cubes. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Use malloc to get room for 12 ints and check for NULL.
   2. Fill arr with cubes.
   3. Print the values.
   4. Call free(arr) at the end. */
int main(void) {
    int n = 12;
    /* Ask the heap for room for n ints; malloc returns NULL on failure. */
    int *arr = malloc(n * sizeof(int));
    if (arr == NULL) {
        fprintf(stderr, "malloc failed\n");
        return 1;
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        arr[i] = i * i * i;
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        printf("%d ", arr[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    free(arr);   /* give the memory back */
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: malloc() reserves room for 12 ints on the heap and returns NULL if it
   fails, which the program checks. The first loop fills arr with cubes, the second prints
   them, and free() gives the memory back at the end. */
// END
