/* Caption: Write a program to implement a circular queue with an array. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define a Queue with room for 10 items, a head and a count.
   2. Write enqueue() that stores at (head + count) % CAPACITY.
   3. Write dequeue() that takes the item at head and moves head on.
   4. Add 3 values, then remove and print them in order. */
#define CAPACITY 10

typedef struct {
    int items[CAPACITY];
    int head;
    int count;
} Queue;

bool enqueue(Queue *q, int value) {
    if (q->count == CAPACITY) {
        return false;
    }
    /* The tail wraps around to the start of the array. */
    q->items[(q->head + q->count) % CAPACITY] = value;
    q->count++;
    return true;
}

bool dequeue(Queue *q, int *value) {
    if (q->count == 0) {
        return false;
    }
    *value = q->items[q->head];
    q->head = (q->head + 1) % CAPACITY;
    q->count--;
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    Queue q = {.head = 0, .count = 0};
    enqueue(&q, 48);
    enqueue(&q, 46);
    enqueue(&q, 1);
    int value;
    /* Items come out in the order they went in (first in, first out). */
    while (dequeue(&q, &value)) {
        printf("%d ", value);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: The Queue stores up to 10 items in a ring buffer: head is the oldest item
   and % CAPACITY wraps positions back to the start of the array. enqueue() adds at the
   back and dequeue() removes from the front, so main() gets its 3 values back in the same
   order (first in, first out). */
// END

/* Caption: Implement insertion sort for an array of double values. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write insertion_sort() for the double array marks.
   2. Take each element in turn as current.
   3. Shift the larger values of the sorted part one place right.
   4. Put current into the gap.
   5. Print the sorted values. */
/* Insert each element into the already sorted part on its left. */
void insertion_sort(double marks[], int length) {
    for (int i = 1; i < length; i++) {
        double current = marks[i];
        int j = i - 1;
        while (j >= 0 && marks[j] > current) {
            marks[j + 1] = marks[j];   /* shift bigger values right */
            j--;
        }
        marks[j + 1] = current;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    double marks[] = {25.5, 15.0, 31.2, 39.2, 7.2, 19.5};
    int length = sizeof(marks) / sizeof(marks[0]);
    insertion_sort(marks, length);
    for (int i = 0; i < length; i++) {
        printf("%.2f ", marks[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: insertion_sort() takes each element in turn and shifts the larger values of
   the sorted part one place right until the element fits. main() then prints the 6 values
   in ascending order. */
// END

/* Caption: How do I compute 6 to the power of 5 without pow() in C? */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write power(base, exp) with result = 1.
   2. Multiply result by base exp times.
   3. Print 6 to the power 5. */
/* Multiply the base by itself exp times. */
long long power(int base, int exp) {
    long long result = 1;
    for (int i = 0; i < exp; i++) {
        result *= base;
    }
    return result;
}

int main(void) {
    printf("6^5 = %lld\n", power(6, 5));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: power() starts result at 1 and multiplies it by base exp times. It uses
   long long because powers grow quickly. main() prints 6 to the power 5. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to compute the product of two square matrices. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define N as 3.
   2. For every i and j, add a[i][k] * b[k][j] over k into product[i][j].
   3. Print product row by row. */
#define N 3

int main(void) {
    int a[N][N] = {{2, 8, 8}, {4, 8, 5}, {0, 9, 0}};
    int b[N][N] = {{8, 0, 8}, {5, 3, 9}, {4, 3, 7}};
    int product[N][N] = {0};
    /* product[i][j] is row i of a times column j of b. */
    for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) {
        for (int j = 0; j < N; j++) {
            for (int k = 0; k < N; k++) {
                product[i][j] += a[i][k] * b[k][j];
            }
        }
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) {
        for (int j = 0; j < N; j++) {
            printf("%4d", product[i][j]);
        }
        printf("\n");
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: For each entry product[i][j] the innermost loop adds a[i][k] * b[k][j] over
   k, which is row i of a times column j of b. main() multiplies two 3x3 matrices and
   prints the product. */
// END

/* Caption: Build a linked list, print it, and free it. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define Item with a value and a next pointer.
   2. Write push_front() that mallocs a node and links it in front of head.
   3. Write print_list() that follows next until NULL.
   4. Write free_list() that frees every node.
   5. Push 4 values, print the list and free it. */
typedef struct Item {
    int value;
    struct Item *next;
} Item;

/* Allocate a new node and put it in front of the current head. */
Item *push_front(Item *head, int value) {
    Item *node = malloc(sizeof(Item));
    if (node == NULL) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Out of memory\n");
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }
    node->value = value;
    node->next = head;
    return node;
}

void print_list(const Item *head) {
    for (const Item *cur = head; cur != NULL; cur = cur->next) {
        printf("%d -> ", cur->value);
    }
    printf("NULL\n");
}

/* Free every node; save next before freeing the current one. */
void free_list(Item *head) {
    while (head != NULL) {
        Item *next = head->next;
        free(head);
        head = next;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    Item *head = NULL;
    head = push_front(head, 23);
    head = push_front(head, 48);
    head = push_front(head, 43);
    head = push_front(head, 70);
    print_list(head);
    free_list(head);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: Each Item holds a value and a pointer to the next node. push_front()
   allocates a node with malloc, puts it in front of head and returns it; print_list()
   follows the next pointers until NULL; free_list() frees every node. main() pushes 4
   values, so they print in reverse order. */
// END

/* Caption: C program to count how many times 't' appears in a string. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write count_char() with count = 0.
   2. Compare each character with the target t.
   3. Return count and print it. */
int count_char(const char *text, char target) {
    int count = 0;
    /* Compare every character with the target. */
    for (int i = 0; text[i] != '\0'; i++) {
        if (text[i] == target) {
            count++;
        }
    }
    return count;
}

int main(void) {
    const char *sentence = "good comments explain why the code exists";
    printf("'t' appears %d times\n", count_char(sentence, 't'));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: count_char() compares every character of the text with the target character
   and counts the matches. main() prints how many times t appears in the sentence. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to find the number of digits in an integer. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Start result at 0.
   2. Divide n by 10 and add one to result.
   3. Repeat until n is 0.
   4. Apply it to 577750 and print the result. */
/* Take the last digit with % 10, then drop it with / 10. */
int count_digits(int n) {
    int result = 0;
    while (n > 0) {
        result++;
        n /= 10;
    }
    return result;
}

int main(void) {
    int number = 577750;
    printf("count of digits of %d: %d\n", number, count_digits(number));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: count_digits() removes the last digit (n / 10) and adds one to result each
   time, until n reaches 0. main() applies it to 577750. */
// END

/* Caption: Search an array for its smallest value. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write smallest_value() that takes items and length.
   2. Store items[0] in smallest.
   3. Loop over the other elements and keep the smallest value in smallest.
   4. Return smallest and print it. */
/* Start with the first element and keep the smallest value seen so far. */
double smallest_value(const double items[], int length) {
    double smallest = items[0];
    for (int idx = 1; idx < length; idx++) {
        if (items[idx] < smallest) {
            smallest = items[idx];
        }
    }
    return smallest;
}

int main(void) {
    double items[] = {89.0, 93.0, 76.5, 85.9, 28.3, 10.2};
    const int length = 6;
    printf("The smallest value is %.2f\n", smallest_value(items, length));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: smallest_value() takes the first element as the smallest value so far and
   stores it in smallest. The loop compares every other element with smallest using < and
   keeps the smallest one. main() prints the smallest of the 6 values. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to reverse the elements of an array in place. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write reverse_array() for marks.
   2. Set i to the first index and j to the last.
   3. Swap marks[i] and marks[j], then move both inwards.
   4. Stop when i meets j and print the array. */
/* Swap the outer pair, then move both ends toward the middle. */
void reverse_array(long marks[], int len) {
    int i = 0;
    int j = len - 1;
    while (i < j) {
        long tmp = marks[i];
        marks[i] = marks[j];
        marks[j] = tmp;
        i++;
        j--;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    long marks[] = {19L, 24L, 88L, 6L, 3L};
    const int len = 5;
    reverse_array(marks, len);
    for (int i = 0; i < len; i++) {
        printf("%ld ", marks[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: reverse_array() swaps the first and last elements, then moves i forward and
   j backward until they meet, so the array is reversed in place without a second array.
   main() prints the reversed values. */
// END

/* Caption: Split a number of seconds into hours, minutes and seconds with pointer parameters. */

   1. Write split_seconds() with the pointers hours, minutes and seconds.
   2. Store total / 3600, (total % 3600) / 60 and total % 60 through them.

void split_seconds(int total, int *hours, int *minutes, int *seconds) {

    return 0;
}

   3600, minutes is what is left divided by 60, and seconds is total % 60. main() declares
   h, m and s on one line and converts 80868 seconds. */
// END

/* Caption: Find the total of all elements in an array using a loop. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write total_of() that takes the array prices and its length length.
   2. Start acc at 0 and add every element in a for loop.
   3. Return acc.
   4. In main(), fill prices with 8 values and print the sum. */
/* Return the sum of the first n elements. */
double total_of(const double prices[], int length) {
    double acc = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < length; i++) {
        acc += prices[i];
    }
    return acc;
}

int main(void) {
    double prices[] = {69.9, 28.0, 60.4, 82.8, 31.8, 53.1, 96.8, 50.2};
    int length = sizeof(prices) / sizeof(prices[0]);
    printf("Sum: %.2f\n", total_of(prices, length));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: total_of() receives the array prices and its length length. It starts acc
   at 0, adds every element to it in a for loop and returns the total. main() fills prices
   with 8 double values and prints their sum. */
// END

/* Caption: C program to compute the mean of a list of numbers. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write average() that takes items and count.
   2. Add the values into the double sum.
   3. Return sum / count.
   4. Print the average with two decimals. */
/* The mean is the total divided by the count. */
double average(const int items[], int count) {
    double sum = 0.0;
    for (int j = 0; j < count; j++) {
        sum += items[j];
    }
    return sum / count;
}

int main(void) {
    int items[] = {74, 71, 19};
    const int count = 3;
    printf("Mean = %.2f\n", average(items, count));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: average() adds the 3 values of items into the double sum and divides by
   count, so the mean keeps its decimal part even when the values are whole numbers. main()
   prints it with two decimals. */
// END

/* Caption: C program to return both the smallest and the largest value of an array through pointers. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write min_max() with the array, its length and the pointers min and max.
   2. Start both at the first element.
   3. Update *min and *max while looping over the rest.
   4. Declare min and max, pass their addresses and print them. */
/* One pass finds both results; they are stored through the pointers. */
void min_max(const int ages[], int count, int *min, int *max) {
    *min = ages[0];
    *max = ages[0];
    for (int i = 1; i < count; i++) {
        if (ages[i] < *min) {
            *min = ages[i];
        }
        if (ages[i] > *max) {
            *max = ages[i];
        }
    }
}

int main(void) {
    int ages[] = {71, 1, 29, 71, 53};
    int count = 5;
    int min, max;
    min_max(ages, count, &min, &max);
    printf("Min: %d, Max: %d\n", min, max);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: A C function can return only one value, so min_max() returns void and
   writes its two results through the pointer parameters min and max. main() declares min
   and max on one line and passes their addresses with &, then prints both results for the
   5 values. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to compare 3 numbers and print the biggest. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Read num1, num2 and num3.
   2. Assume num1 is the biggest.
   3. Compare it with the other two and keep the bigger value.
   4. Print the result. */
int main(void) {
    int num1, num2, num3;
    printf("Enter 3 numbers: ");
    if (scanf("%d %d %d", &num1, &num2, &num3) != 3) {
        printf("Invalid input\n");
        return 1;
    }
    int best = num1;
    /* Compare with each of the others and keep the bigger one. */
    if (num2 > best) {
        best = num2;
    }
    if (num3 > best) {
        best = num3;
    }
    printf("The biggest is %d\n", best);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: The program reads num1, num2 and num3 from the keyboard with scanf and
   stops with a message if the input is not valid. It assumes num1 is the biggest, compares
   it with the other two and keeps the bigger value in best, which it prints. */

/* Caption: Check whether a year is a leap year. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write is_leap(year).
   2. A year divisible by 4 is a leap year, unless it is divisible by 100.
   3. Years divisible by 400 are leap years again.
   4. Check 1959 and print the result. */
/* Leap years divide by 4, except centuries, which must divide by 400. */
int is_leap(int year) {
    return (year % 4 == 0 && year % 100 != 0) || year % 400 == 0;
}

int main(void) {
    int year = 1959;
    if (is_leap(year)) {
        printf("%d is a leap year\n", year);
    } else {
        printf("%d is not a leap year\n", year);
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: is_leap() returns true for years divisible by 4, except century years,
   which must also be divisible by 400. main() checks 1959 and prints whether it is a leap
   year. */
// END

/* Caption: How do I find the index of a number using linear search in C? */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write linear_search() with the array, its length and key.
   2. Compare each element with key.
   3. Return the index of the first match, or -1.
   4. In main(), search for 1 and print the result. */
/* Return the index of key, or -1 when it is not in the array. */
int linear_search(const int data[], int n, int key) {
    for (int idx = 0; idx < n; idx++) {
        if (data[idx] == key) {
            return idx;
        }
    }
    return -1;
}

int main(void) {
    int data[] = {51, 1, 63, 54, 85, 66, 17};
    int n = sizeof(data) / sizeof(data[0]);
    int key = 1;
    int pos = linear_search(data, n, key);
    if (pos >= 0) {
        printf("Found %d at index %d\n", key, pos);
    } else {
        printf("%d is not in the array\n", key);
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: linear_search() checks the elements of data one by one and returns the
   index of the first one equal to key, or -1 when it reaches the end without a match.
   main() searches for 1 and prints where it is, or that it is missing. */
// END

/* Caption: Program to implement a circular queue with an array. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define a Queue with room for 10 items, a head and a count.
   2. Write enqueue() that stores at (head + count) % CAPACITY.
   3. Write dequeue() that takes the item at head and moves head on.
   4. Add 3 values, then remove and print them in order. */
#define CAPACITY 10

typedef struct {
    int items[CAPACITY];
    int head;
    int count;
} Queue;

bool enqueue(Queue *q, int value) {
    if (q->count == CAPACITY) {
        return false;
    }
    /* The tail wraps around to the start of the array. */
    q->items[(q->head + q->count) % CAPACITY] = value;
    q->count++;
    return true;
}

bool dequeue(Queue *q, int *value) {
    if (q->count == 0) {
        return false;
    }
    *value = q->items[q->head];
    q->head = (q->head + 1) % CAPACITY;
    q->count--;
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    Queue q = {.head = 0, .count = 0};
    enqueue(&q, 59);
    enqueue(&q, 76);
    enqueue(&q, 53);
    int value;
    /* Items come out in the order they went in (first in, first out). */
    while (dequeue(&q, &value)) {
        printf("%d ", value);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: The Queue stores up to 10 items in a ring buffer: head is the oldest item
   and % CAPACITY wraps positions back to the start of the array. enqueue() adds at the
   back and dequeue() removes from the front, so main() gets its 3 values back in the same
   order (first in, first out). */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to implement a simple linked list with malloc and free. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define Node with a value and a next pointer.
   2. Write push_front() that mallocs a node and links it in front of head.
   3. Write print_list() that follows next until NULL.
   4. Write free_list() that frees every node.
   5. Push 4 values, print the list and free it. */
typedef struct Node {
    int value;
    struct Node *next;
} Node;

/* Allocate a new node and put it in front of the current head. */
Node *push_front(Node *head, int value) {
    Node *node = malloc(sizeof(Node));
    if (node == NULL) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Out of memory\n");
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }
    node->value = value;
    node->next = head;
    return node;
}

void print_list(const Node *head) {
    for (const Node *cur = head; cur != NULL; cur = cur->next) {
        printf("%d -> ", cur->value);
    }
    printf("NULL\n");
}

/* Free every node; save next before freeing the current one. */
void free_list(Node *head) {
    while (head != NULL) {
        Node *next = head->next;
        free(head);
        head = next;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    Node *head = NULL;
    head = push_front(head, 76);
    head = push_front(head, 64);
    head = push_front(head, 67);
    head = push_front(head, 58);
    print_list(head);
    free_list(head);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: Each Node holds a value and a pointer to the next node. push_front()
   allocates a node with malloc, puts it in front of head and returns it; print_list()
   follows the next pointers until NULL; free_list() frees every node. main() pushes 4
   values, so they print in reverse order. */
// END

/* Caption: Transpose a matrix. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define ROWS as 4 and COLS as 3.
   2. Copy m[r][c] into t[c][r] for every element.
   3. Print t row by row. */
#define ROWS 4
#define COLS 3

int main(void) {
    int m[ROWS][COLS] = {{9, 3, 9}, {8, 8, 8}, {1, 6, 4}, {0, 6, 7}};
    int t[COLS][ROWS];
    /* Element (r, c) moves to (c, r). */
    for (int r = 0; r < ROWS; r++) {
        for (int c = 0; c < COLS; c++) {
            t[c][r] = m[r][c];
        }
    }
    for (int r = 0; r < COLS; r++) {
        for (int c = 0; c < ROWS; c++) {
            printf("%3d", t[r][c]);
        }
        printf("\n");
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: The nested loops copy m[r][c] into t[c][r], so the 4x3 matrix becomes 3x4.
   A second pair of loops prints the result. */
// END

/* Caption: Reverse an array by swapping from both ends. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write reverse_array() for items.
   2. Set left to the first index and right to the last.
   3. Swap items[left] and items[right], then move both inwards.
   4. Stop when left meets right and print the array. */
/* Swap the outer pair, then move both ends toward the middle. */
void reverse_array(int items[], int count) {
    int left = 0;
    int right = count - 1;
    while (left < right) {
        int tmp = items[left];
        items[left] = items[right];
        items[right] = tmp;
        left++;
        right--;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    int items[] = {9, 8, 5, 83, 48, 55, 50, 91, 65};
    int count = 9;
    reverse_array(items, count);
    for (int i = 0; i < count; i++) {
        printf("%d ", items[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: reverse_array() swaps the first and last elements, then moves left forward
   and right backward until they meet, so the array is reversed in place without a second
   array. main() prints the reversed values. */
// END

/* Caption: C program to swap two variables using pointers. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write swap() that takes pointers to two long values.
   2. Save *a in tmp, copy *b into *a, then tmp into *b.
   3. In main(), print a and b, call swap(&a, &b) and print them again. */
/* Pass addresses so the function can change the caller's variables. */
void swap(long *a, long *b) {
    long tmp = *a;
    *a = *b;
    *b = tmp;
}

int main(void) {
    long a = 51L, b = 56L;
    printf("Before: %ld %ld\n", a, b);
    swap(&a, &b);
    printf("After:  %ld %ld\n", a, b);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: swap() receives the addresses of a and b, so writing through the pointers
   *a and *b changes the caller's variables. tmp holds one value during the exchange.
   main() declares both variables on one line and prints them before and after the swap. */
// END

}

/* Explanation: count_char() compares every character of the text with the target character
   and counts the matches. main() prints how many times o appears in the sentence. */

/* Caption: Program to reverse the digits of a number. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Start result at 0.
   2. Multiply result by 10, add n % 10, then divide n by 10.
   3. Repeat until n is 0.
   4. Apply it to 923015 and print the result. */
/* Take the last digit with % 10, then drop it with / 10. */
int reverse_digits(int n) {
    int result = 0;
    while (n > 0) {
        result = result * 10 + n % 10;
        n /= 10;
    }
    return result;
}

int main(void) {
    int number = 923015;
    printf("reverse of digits of %d: %d\n", number, reverse_digits(number));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: reverse_digits() shifts result one place left (result * 10) and adds the
   last digit of n, which reverses the order. main() applies it to 923015. */
// END

/* Caption: Sort an array in descending order using bubble sort. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write bubble_sort() for the int array data.
   2. Compare each pair of neighbours.
   3. Swap them when they are in the wrong order for descending order.
   4. Repeat the passes until the array is sorted.
   5. Print the sorted values. */
/* Repeatedly swap neighbours that are in the wrong order. */
void bubble_sort(int data[], int n) {
    for (int i = 0; i < n - 1; i++) {
        for (int j = 0; j < n - 1 - i; j++) {
            if (data[j] < data[j + 1]) {
                int tmp = data[j];
                data[j] = data[j + 1];
                data[j + 1] = tmp;
            }
        }
    }
}

int main(void) {
    int data[] = {91, 3, 43, 17, 17, 9, 54, 58, 95, 45};
    int n = sizeof(data) / sizeof(data[0]);
    bubble_sort(data, n);
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        printf("%d ", data[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: bubble_sort() walks through data again and again and swaps neighbours that
   are in the wrong order, so the smallest values move to the end first. main() then prints
   the 10 values in descending order. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to compute the LCM of two integers using the GCD. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write gcd() with Euclid's algorithm: replace (a, b) by (b, a % b) until b is 0.
   2. Write lcm() as a / gcd(a, b) * b.
   3. Print the LCM of 9 and 63. */
/* Euclid: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a % b) until b becomes zero. */
int gcd(int a, int b) {
    while (b != 0) {
        int r = a % b;
        a = b;
        b = r;
    }
    return a;
}

/* lcm(a, b) = a / gcd(a, b) * b (divide first to avoid overflow). */
long lcm(int a, int b) {
    return (long)a / gcd(a, b) * b;
}

int main(void) {
    printf("lcm(9, 63) = %ld\n", lcm(9, 63));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: gcd() uses Euclid's algorithm: it keeps replacing (a, b) with (b, a % b)
   until b is 0. lcm() divides a by the gcd before multiplying by b, which avoids overflow.
   main() prints the LCM of 9 and 63. */
// END

/* Caption: Sort an array in ascending order using insertion sort. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write insertion_sort() for the long array items.
   2. Take each element in turn as current.
   3. Shift the larger values of the sorted part one place right.
   4. Put current into the gap.
   5. Print the sorted values. */
/* Insert each element into the already sorted part on its left. */
void insertion_sort(long items[], int n) {
    for (int i = 1; i < n; i++) {
        long current = items[i];
        int j = i - 1;
        while (j >= 0 && items[j] > current) {
            items[j + 1] = items[j];   /* shift bigger values right */
            j--;
        }
        items[j + 1] = current;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    long items[] = {70L, 59L, 32L, 81L, 61L, 6L};
    int n = sizeof(items) / sizeof(items[0]);
    insertion_sort(items, n);
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        printf("%ld ", items[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: insertion_sort() takes each element in turn and shifts the larger values of
   the sorted part one place right until the element fits. main() then prints the 6 values
   in ascending order. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to check whether a word is a palindrome. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <string.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write is_palindrome() for line.
   2. Compare the first and last characters, moving inwards.
   3. Return false at the first mismatch, otherwise true.
   4. Check window and print the result. */
/* Compare characters from the front and back, moving inwards. */
bool is_palindrome(const char *line) {
    int i = 0;
    int j = strlen(line) - 1;
    while (i < j) {
        if (line[i] != line[j]) {
            return false;
        }
        i++;
        j--;
    }
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    const char *line = "window";
    printf("%s %s a palindrome\n", line, is_palindrome(line) ? "is" : "is not");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: is_palindrome() compares the first and last characters and moves inwards;
   any mismatch means the word is not a palindrome. main() checks the word window and
   prints the result. */
// END

/* Caption: Keep a value inside the limits low and high. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write clamp(value, low, high).
   2. Return low if the value is too small and high if it is too big.
   3. Otherwise return the value.
   4. Set low = 16 and high = 65 and print clamp() for 106, 15 and 97. */
/* Return value, but never less than low or more than high. */
int clamp(int value, int low, int high) {
    if (value < low) {
        return low;
    }
    if (value > high) {
        return high;
    }
    return value;
}

int main(void) {
    int low = 16, high = 65;
    printf("clamp(%d) = %d\n", 106, clamp(106, low, high));
    printf("clamp(%d) = %d\n", 15, clamp(15, low, high));
    printf("clamp(%d) = %d\n", 97, clamp(97, low, high));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: clamp() takes three parameters: the value and the two limits. It returns
   low when the value is too small, high when it is too big and the value itself otherwise.
   main() declares low = 16 and high = 65 on one line and clamps 106, 15 and 97. */
// END

/* Caption: Generate the Fibonacci sequence. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Start with prev = 0 and curr = 1.
   2. Repeat 24 times and print prev each time.
   3. Compute next = prev + curr, then set prev = curr and curr = next. */
int main(void) {
    long prev = 0, curr = 1;
    /* Print a term, then slide the pair one step along the sequence. */
    for (int i = 0; i < 24; i++) {
        printf("%ld ", prev);
        long next = prev + curr;
        prev = curr;
        curr = next;
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: The loop keeps the last two numbers in prev and curr. Each round it prints
   prev, then moves the pair forward: prev becomes curr and curr becomes their sum. It
   prints the first 24 Fibonacci numbers. */
// END

/* Caption: Count the odd values in a list of integers. */

   1. Write count_odd() that takes samples and len.

   3. Add one to tally for every odd number.
   4. Return tally and print it. */
/* A number is odd when the remainder after dividing by 2 is one. */
int count_odd(const int samples[], int len) {
    int tally = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < len; i++) {
        if (samples[i] % 2 != 0) {
            tally++;
        }
    }
    return tally;
}

int main(void) {
    int samples[] = {47, 7, 11, 92, 64, 2, 21};
    int len = sizeof(samples) / sizeof(samples[0]);
    printf("Odd numbers: %d\n", count_odd(samples, len));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: count_odd() tests each element of samples with the % operator: a remainder
   of 1 after dividing by 2 means the number is odd, so tally goes up by one. main() prints
   how many of the 7 values are odd. */
// END

/* Caption: Copy one string into another by hand. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write copy_string(dest, src).
   2. Copy src into dest one character at a time.
   3. Stop after copying the null character.
   4. Copy pointer into buffer and print it. */
/* Copy each character, including the final '\0'. */
void copy_string(char *dest, const char *src) {
    int i = 0;
    while ((dest[i] = src[i]) != '\0') {
        i++;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    char source[] = "pointer";
    char buffer[64];
    copy_string(buffer, source);
    printf("Copied: %s\n", buffer);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: copy_string() copies src into dest one character at a time, including the
   final null character, which is what strcpy does. The array buffer must be big enough to
   hold the copy. main() copies the word pointer and prints it. */
// END

        perror("fopen");
        return 1;

    char line[128];

        printf("%s", line);
    }
    fclose(file);

/* Caption: Subtract 2 numbers. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Read a and b.
   2. Store a - b in result.
   3. Print the calculation. */
int main(void) {
    int a, b;
    printf("Enter 2 numbers: ");
    if (scanf("%d %d", &a, &b) != 2) {
        printf("Invalid input\n");
        return 1;
    }
    int result = a - b;   /* the difference */
    printf("%d - %d = %d\n", a, b, result);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: The program reads a and b from the keyboard with scanf and stops with a
   message if the input is not valid. It stores a - b in result and prints the whole
   calculation. */
// END

/* Caption: How do I keep a value inside the limits low and high in C? */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write clamp(value, low, high).
   2. Return low if the value is too small and high if it is too big.
   3. Otherwise return the value.
   4. Set low = 12 and high = 92 and print clamp() for -18, -20 and 81. */
/* Return value, but never less than low or more than high. */
int clamp(int value, int low, int high) {
    if (value < low) {
        return low;
    }
    if (value > high) {
        return high;
    }
    return value;
}

int main(void) {
    int low = 12, high = 92;
    printf("clamp(%d) = %d\n", -18, clamp(-18, low, high));
    printf("clamp(%d) = %d\n", -20, clamp(-20, low, high));
    printf("clamp(%d) = %d\n", 81, clamp(81, low, high));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: clamp() takes three parameters: the value and the two limits. It returns
   low when the value is too small, high when it is too big and the value itself otherwise.
   main() declares low = 12 and high = 92 on one line and clamps -18, -20 and 81. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to swap two variables using pointers. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write swap() that takes pointers to two int values.
   2. Save *a in tmp, copy *b into *a, then tmp into *b.
   3. In main(), print a and b, call swap(&a, &b) and print them again. */
/* Pass addresses so the function can change the caller's variables. */
void swap(int *a, int *b) {
    int tmp = *a;
    *a = *b;
    *b = tmp;
}

int main(void) {
    int a = 90, b = 25;
    printf("Before: %d %d\n", a, b);
    swap(&a, &b);
    printf("After:  %d %d\n", a, b);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: swap() receives the addresses of a and b, so writing through the pointers
   *a and *b changes the caller's variables. tmp holds one value during the exchange.
   main() declares both variables on one line and prints them before and after the swap. */
// END

/* Caption: Implement bubble sort for an array of double values. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write bubble_sort() for the double array readings.
   2. Compare each pair of neighbours.
   3. Swap them when they are in the wrong order for ascending order.
   4. Repeat the passes until the array is sorted.
   5. Print the sorted values. */
/* Repeatedly swap neighbours that are in the wrong order. */
void bubble_sort(double readings[], int len) {
    for (int i = 0; i < len - 1; i++) {
        for (int j = 0; j < len - 1 - i; j++) {
            if (readings[j] > readings[j + 1]) {
                double tmp = readings[j];
                readings[j] = readings[j + 1];
                readings[j + 1] = tmp;
            }
        }
    }
}

int main(void) {
    double readings[] = {55.1, 27.1, 75.3, 16.5, 82.8, 97.0, 1.7};
    const int len = 7;
    bubble_sort(readings, len);
    for (int i = 0; i < len; i++) {
        printf("%.2f ", readings[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: bubble_sort() walks through readings again and again and swaps neighbours
   that are in the wrong order, so the largest values move to the end first. main() then
   prints the 7 values in ascending order. */
// END

/* Caption: Reverse the digits of a number. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Start result at 0.
   2. Multiply result by 10, add n % 10, then divide n by 10.
   3. Repeat until n is 0.
   4. Apply it to 47846 and print the result. */
/* Take the last digit with % 10, then drop it with / 10. */
int reverse_digits(int n) {
    int result = 0;
    while (n > 0) {
        result = result * 10 + n % 10;
        n /= 10;
    }
    return result;
}

int main(void) {
    int number = 47846;
    printf("reverse of digits of %d: %d\n", number, reverse_digits(number));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: reverse_digits() shifts result one place left (result * 10) and adds the
   last digit of n, which reverses the order. main() applies it to 47846. */
// END

/* Caption: Program to add two 4x3 matrices. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define ROWS as 4 and COLS as 3.
   2. Loop over every row r and column c.
   3. Store a[r][c] + b[r][c] in sum and print it. */
#define ROWS 4
#define COLS 3

int main(void) {
    int a[ROWS][COLS] = {{7, 3, 4}, {2, 0, 9}, {2, 6, 3}, {5, 8, 0}};
    int b[ROWS][COLS] = {{9, 7, 3}, {2, 5, 2}, {2, 4, 3}, {2, 6, 4}};
    int sum[ROWS][COLS];
    /* Each entry of the result is the sum of the matching entries. */
    for (int r = 0; r < ROWS; r++) {
        for (int c = 0; c < COLS; c++) {
            sum[r][c] = a[r][c] + b[r][c];
            printf("%3d", sum[r][c]);
        }
        printf("\n");
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: Both matrices are 4x3 two-dimensional arrays. Two nested loops visit every
   row r and column c, store a[r][c] + b[r][c] in sum and print each row. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to show the Fibonacci series with a loop. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Start with first = 0 and second = 1.
   2. Repeat 20 times and print first each time.
   3. Compute next = first + second, then set first = second and second = next. */
int main(void) {
    long first = 0, second = 1;
    /* Print a term, then slide the pair one step along the sequence. */
    for (int i = 0; i < 20; i++) {
        printf("%ld ", first);
        long next = first + second;
        first = second;
        second = next;
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: The loop keeps the last two numbers in first and second. Each round it
   prints first, then moves the pair forward: first becomes second and second becomes their
   sum. It prints the first 20 Fibonacci numbers. */
// END

/* Caption: How do I find the least common multiple of two numbers in C? */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write gcd() with Euclid's algorithm: replace (a, b) by (b, a % b) until b is 0.
   2. Write lcm() as a / gcd(a, b) * b.
   3. Print the LCM of 102 and 178. */
/* Euclid: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a % b) until b becomes zero. */
int gcd(int a, int b) {
    while (b != 0) {
        int r = a % b;
        a = b;
        b = r;
    }
    return a;
}

/* lcm(a, b) = a / gcd(a, b) * b (divide first to avoid overflow). */
long lcm(int a, int b) {
    return (long)a / gcd(a, b) * b;
}

int main(void) {
    printf("lcm(102, 178) = %ld\n", lcm(102, 178));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: gcd() uses Euclid's algorithm: it keeps replacing (a, b) with (b, a % b)
   until b is 0. lcm() divides a by the gcd before multiplying by b, which avoids overflow.
   main() prints the LCM of 102 and 178. */
// END

/* Caption: Define a Point struct and measure the distance between two points. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <math.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define a Point struct with x and y.
   2. Write distance() using sqrt(dx * dx + dy * dy).
   3. Print the distance between p and q. */
typedef struct {
    double x;
    double y;
} Point;

/* Pythagoras: sqrt(dx * dx + dy * dy). */
double distance(Point a, Point b) {
    double dx = b.x - a.x;
    double dy = b.y - a.y;
    return sqrt(dx * dx + dy * dy);
}

int main(void) {
    Point p = {-10, 4};
    Point q = {-1, -3};
    printf("Distance: %.3f\n", distance(p, q));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: Point is a typedef struct with x and y. distance() uses Pythagoras, sqrt(dx
   * dx + dy * dy), to measure the gap between the two points, and main() prints it. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to search a sorted array by halving the search range each step. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Make sure the array is sorted.
   2. Set lo to 0 and hi to len - 1.
   3. While lo <= hi, compare the middle element mid with the key.
   4. Return the index if it matches; otherwise keep only the half that can hold the
      key.
   5. Return -1 if the range becomes empty, and print the index of 201. */
/* The array must be sorted. Each step halves the range that can still hold the key. */
int binary_search(const int readings[], int len, int key) {
    int lo = 0;
    int hi = len - 1;
    while (lo <= hi) {
        int mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;
        if (readings[mid] == key) {
            return mid;
        } else if (readings[mid] < key) {
            lo = mid + 1;   /* key is in the right half */
        } else {
            hi = mid - 1;   /* key is in the left half */
        }
    }
    return -1;
}

int main(void) {
    int readings[] = {20, 30, 51, 62, 149, 168};
    int len = sizeof(readings) / sizeof(readings[0]);
    int index = binary_search(readings, len, 201);
    printf("Index of 201: %d\n", index);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: binary_search() needs a sorted array. It keeps the range from lo to hi,
   compares the middle element mid with the key and throws away the half that cannot
   contain it, so it needs only about log2(n) steps. main() looks for 201 and prints its
   index, or -1 if it is not there. */
// END

/* Caption: Count how many odd numbers are in an array. */

   1. Write count_odd() that takes marks and len.

   3. Add one to count for every odd number.
   4. Return count and print it. */
/* A number is odd when the remainder after dividing by 2 is one. */

   1 after dividing by 2 means the number is odd, so count goes up by one. main() prints
   how many of the 7 values are odd. */
// END

/* Caption: Program to build a FIFO queue using a ring buffer. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define a Queue with room for 32 items, a head and a count.
   2. Write enqueue() that stores at (head + count) % CAPACITY.
   3. Write dequeue() that takes the item at head and moves head on.
   4. Add 4 values, then remove and print them in order. */
#define CAPACITY 32

typedef struct {
    int items[CAPACITY];
    int head;
    int count;
} Queue;

bool enqueue(Queue *q, int value) {
    if (q->count == CAPACITY) {
        return false;
    }
    /* The tail wraps around to the start of the array. */
    q->items[(q->head + q->count) % CAPACITY] = value;
    q->count++;
    return true;
}

bool dequeue(Queue *q, int *value) {
    if (q->count == 0) {
        return false;
    }
    *value = q->items[q->head];
    q->head = (q->head + 1) % CAPACITY;
    q->count--;
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    Queue q = {.head = 0, .count = 0};
    enqueue(&q, 76);
    enqueue(&q, 49);
    enqueue(&q, 91);
    enqueue(&q, 47);
    int value;
    /* Items come out in the order they went in (first in, first out). */
    while (dequeue(&q, &value)) {
        printf("%d ", value);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: The Queue stores up to 32 items in a ring buffer: head is the oldest item
   and % CAPACITY wraps positions back to the start of the array. enqueue() adds at the
   back and dequeue() removes from the front, so main() gets its 4 values back in the same
   order (first in, first out). */
// END

/* Caption: C program to count the even values in a list of integers. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write count_even() that takes scores and len.
   2. For each element, test scores[i] % 2 == 0.
   3. Add one to matches for every even number.
   4. Return matches and print it. */
/* A number is even when the remainder after dividing by 2 is zero. */
int count_even(const int scores[], int len) {
    int matches = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < len; i++) {
        if (scores[i] % 2 == 0) {
            matches++;
        }
    }
    return matches;
}

int main(void) {
    int scores[] = {71, 31, 11, 55, 90, 89, 56, 23};
    int len = 8;
    printf("Count of even values = %d\n", count_even(scores, len));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: count_even() tests each element of scores with the % operator: a remainder
   of 0 after dividing by 2 means the number is even, so matches goes up by one. main()
   prints how many of the 8 values are even. */
// END

/* Caption: Divide two integers and get both the quotient and the remainder. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:

   2. Return false if b is 0.
   3. Store a / b and a % b through the pointers and return true.
   4. Divide 468 by 12 and print the results or the error. */
/* Returns false for division by zero; otherwise stores both results. */
bool divide(int a, int b, int *quotient, int *remainder) {
    if (b == 0) {
        return false;
    }
    *quotient = a / b;
    *remainder = a % b;
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    int a = 468, b = 12;
    int q, r;
    if (divide(a, b, &q, &r)) {
        printf("%d / %d = %d remainder %d\n", a, b, q, r);
    } else {
        printf("Cannot divide by zero\n");
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: divide() has four parameters: two inputs and two pointers for the results.
   Its bool return value reports success, while the quotient and remainder are written
   through the pointers. main() divides 468 by 12 and prints both results. */
// END

/* Caption: C program to compute the LCM of two integers using the GCD. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write gcd() with Euclid's algorithm: replace (a, b) by (b, a % b) until b is 0.
   2. Write lcm() as a / gcd(a, b) * b.
   3. Print the LCM of 249 and 30. */
/* Euclid: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a % b) until b becomes zero. */
int gcd(int a, int b) {
    while (b != 0) {
        int r = a % b;
        a = b;
        b = r;
    }
    return a;
}

/* lcm(a, b) = a / gcd(a, b) * b (divide first to avoid overflow). */
long lcm(int a, int b) {
    return (long)a / gcd(a, b) * b;
}

int main(void) {
    printf("lcm(249, 30) = %ld\n", lcm(249, 30));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: gcd() uses Euclid's algorithm: it keeps replacing (a, b) with (b, a % b)
   until b is 0. lcm() divides a by the gcd before multiplying by b, which avoids overflow.
   main() prints the LCM of 249 and 30. */
// END

/* Caption: How do I print the binary representation of an integer in C? */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write print_binary(n, bits).
   2. Go through the bits from the highest to the lowest.
   3. Print 1 when (n >> b) & 1 is set, otherwise 0.
   4. Print 872 in binary. */
/* Check each bit from the highest to the lowest. */
void print_binary(unsigned int n, int bits) {
    for (int b = bits - 1; b >= 0; b--) {
        putchar((n >> b) & 1 ? '1' : '0');
    }
    putchar('\n');
}

int main(void) {
    unsigned int number = 872;
    printf("%u in binary: ", number);
    print_binary(number, 12);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: print_binary() checks one bit at a time, from the highest to the lowest: (n
   >> b) & 1 is 1 when bit b is set, so it prints the character 1 or 0. main() prints 872
   in binary. */
// END

/* Caption: Return a Duration struct built from a number of seconds. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define a Duration struct with hours, minutes and seconds.
   2. Write from_seconds() that fills it using / and %.
   3. Convert 30346 seconds and print the members. */
typedef struct {
    int hours;
    int minutes;
    int seconds;
} Duration;

Duration from_seconds(int total) {
    Duration d;
    d.hours = total / 3600;
    d.minutes = (total % 3600) / 60;
    d.seconds = total % 60;
    return d;
}

int main(void) {
    Duration d = from_seconds(30346);
    printf("%d h %d min %d s\n", d.hours, d.minutes, d.seconds);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: from_seconds() fills the three members of a Duration struct using / and %,
   then returns the struct. main() converts 30346 seconds and prints the members. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to calculate the average of the values in an array. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write average() that takes numbers and length.
   2. Add the values into the double acc.
   3. Return acc / length.
   4. Print the average with two decimals. */
/* The mean is the total divided by the count. */
double average(const int numbers[], int length) {
    double acc = 0.0;
    for (int k = 0; k < length; k++) {
        acc += numbers[k];
    }
    return acc / length;
}

int main(void) {
    int numbers[] = {79, 30, 14};
    int length = sizeof(numbers) / sizeof(numbers[0]);
    printf("The average is %.2f\n", average(numbers, length));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: average() adds the 3 values of numbers into the double acc and divides by
   length, so the mean keeps its decimal part even when the values are whole numbers.
   main() prints it with two decimals. */
// END

/* Caption: Compute the distance between two points with a four-parameter function. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <math.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write distance(x1, y1, x2, y2).
   2. Compute dx and dy, then return sqrt(dx * dx + dy * dy).
   3. Print the distance between (5, 2) and (2, 3). */
/* Pythagoras: the distance is sqrt(dx * dx + dy * dy). */
double distance(double x1, double y1, double x2, double y2) {
    double dx = x2 - x1, dy = y2 - y1;
    return sqrt(dx * dx + dy * dy);
}

int main(void) {
    printf("Distance: %.3f\n", distance(5, 2, 2, 3));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: distance() takes the coordinates of both points as four parameters. It
   declares dx and dy on one line and uses Pythagoras with sqrt() from math.h. main()
   prints the distance between (5, 2) and (2, 3). */
// END

/* Caption: Build a fixed-size integer stack in C. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define a Stack with room for 16 items and a top counter.
   2. Write push() and pop(), returning false when the stack is full or empty.
   3. Push 4 values.
   4. Pop and print until the stack is empty. */
#define CAPACITY 16

typedef struct {
    int items[CAPACITY];
    int top;   /* number of items on the stack */
} Stack;

bool push(Stack *s, int value) {
    if (s->top == CAPACITY) {
        return false;   /* stack is full */
    }
    s->items[s->top++] = value;
    return true;
}

bool pop(Stack *s, int *value) {
    if (s->top == 0) {
        return false;   /* stack is empty */
    }
    *value = s->items[--s->top];
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    Stack s = {.top = 0};
    push(&s, 79);
    push(&s, 57);
    push(&s, 2);
    push(&s, 22);
    int value;
    /* Items come back out in reverse order (last in, first out). */
    while (pop(&s, &value)) {
        printf("%d ", value);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: The Stack keeps up to 16 items in an array, and top counts how many are
   stored. push() adds at the top and pop() removes from the top; both return false when
   they cannot. main() pushes 4 values and pops them all, so they come out in reverse order
   (last in, first out). */
// END

/* Caption: Turn the rows of a 2x2 matrix into columns. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define ROWS as 2 and COLS as 2.
   2. Copy m[r][c] into t[c][r] for every element.
   3. Print t row by row. */
#define ROWS 2
#define COLS 2

int main(void) {
    int m[ROWS][COLS] = {{0, 4}, {1, 3}};
    int t[COLS][ROWS];
    /* Element (r, c) moves to (c, r). */
    for (int r = 0; r < ROWS; r++) {
        for (int c = 0; c < COLS; c++) {
            t[c][r] = m[r][c];
        }
    }
    for (int r = 0; r < COLS; r++) {
        for (int c = 0; c < ROWS; c++) {
            printf("%3d", t[r][c]);
        }
        printf("\n");
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: The nested loops copy m[r][c] into t[c][r], so the 2x2 matrix becomes 2x2.
   A second pair of loops prints the result. */
// END

   2. Replace every character with toupper() until the null character.
   3. Print the sentence. */

void to_upper(char *word) {

}

int main(void) {

    to_upper(word);
    printf("%s\n", word);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: to_upper() walks through word until the null character and replaces each
   character with toupper(), which only changes lowercase letters. main() prints the
   sentence in capitals. */
// END

/* Caption: Use bubble sort to put numbers in descending order. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write bubble_sort() for the double array numbers.
   2. Compare each pair of neighbours.
   3. Swap them when they are in the wrong order for descending order.
   4. Repeat the passes until the array is sorted.
   5. Print the sorted values. */
/* Repeatedly swap neighbours that are in the wrong order. */
void bubble_sort(double numbers[], int n) {
    for (int i = 0; i < n - 1; i++) {
        for (int j = 0; j < n - 1 - i; j++) {
            if (numbers[j] < numbers[j + 1]) {
                double tmp = numbers[j];
                numbers[j] = numbers[j + 1];
                numbers[j + 1] = tmp;
            }
        }
    }
}

int main(void) {
    double numbers[] = {72.9, 45.0, 53.5, 22.5, 59.3, 89.1, 57.3, 76.8};
    int n = sizeof(numbers) / sizeof(numbers[0]);
    bubble_sort(numbers, n);
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        printf("%.2f ", numbers[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: bubble_sort() walks through numbers again and again and swaps neighbours
   that are in the wrong order, so the smallest values move to the end first. main() then
   prints the 8 values in descending order. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to implement insertion sort for an array of double values. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write insertion_sort() for the double array scores.
   2. Take each element in turn as current.
   3. Shift the larger values of the sorted part one place right.
   4. Put current into the gap.
   5. Print the sorted values. */
/* Insert each element into the already sorted part on its left. */
void insertion_sort(double scores[], int size) {
    for (int i = 1; i < size; i++) {
        double current = scores[i];
        int j = i - 1;
        while (j >= 0 && scores[j] > current) {
            scores[j + 1] = scores[j];   /* shift bigger values right */
            j--;
        }
        scores[j + 1] = current;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    double scores[] = {54.5, 90.3, 13.9, 2.6, 83.6, 43.8};
    int size = 6;
    insertion_sort(scores, size);
    for (int i = 0; i < size; i++) {
        printf("%.2f ", scores[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: insertion_sort() takes each element in turn and shifts the larger values of
   the sorted part one place right until the element fits. main() then prints the 6 values
   in ascending order. */
// END

/* Caption: Count the even values in a list of integers. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write count_even() that takes ages and n.
   2. For each element, test ages[i] % 2 == 0.
   3. Add one to count for every even number.
   4. Return count and print it. */
/* A number is even when the remainder after dividing by 2 is zero. */
int count_even(const int ages[], int n) {
    int count = 0;
    int i = 0;
    while (i < n) {
        if (ages[i] % 2 == 0) {
            count++;
        }
        i++;
    }
    return count;
}

int main(void) {
    int ages[] = {52, 97, 76, 45, 18};
    int n = 5;
    printf("Count of even values = %d\n", count_even(ages, n));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: count_even() tests each element of ages with the % operator: a remainder of
   0 after dividing by 2 means the number is even, so count goes up by one. main() prints
   how many of the 5 values are even. */
// END

/* Caption: Use binary search to locate a value in a sorted list. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Make sure the array is sorted.
   2. Set low to 0 and high to count - 1.
   3. While low <= high, compare the middle element mid with the key.
   4. Return the index if it matches; otherwise keep only the half that can hold the
      key.
   5. Return -1 if the range becomes empty, and print the index of 42. */
/* The array must be sorted. Each step halves the range that can still hold the key. */
int binary_search(const int nums[], int count, int key) {
    int low = 0;
    int high = count - 1;
    while (low <= high) {
        int mid = low + (high - low) / 2;
        if (nums[mid] == key) {
            return mid;
        } else if (nums[mid] < key) {
            low = mid + 1;   /* key is in the right half */
        } else {
            high = mid - 1;   /* key is in the left half */
        }
    }
    return -1;
}

int main(void) {
    int nums[] = {38, 42, 47, 83, 145, 149, 165, 171, 175, 177, 192};
    int count = 11;
    int index = binary_search(nums, count, 42);
    printf("Index of 42: %d\n", index);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: binary_search() needs a sorted array. It keeps the range from low to high,
   compares the middle element mid with the key and throws away the half that cannot
   contain it, so it needs only about log2(n) steps. main() looks for 42 and prints its
   index, or -1 if it is not there. */
// END

/* Caption: How do I swap two variables using pointers in C? */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write swap() that takes pointers to two int values.
   2. Save *x in tmp, copy *y into *x, then tmp into *y.
   3. In main(), print x and y, call swap(&x, &y) and print them again. */
/* Pass addresses so the function can change the caller's variables. */
void swap(int *x, int *y) {
    int tmp = *x;
    *x = *y;
    *y = tmp;
}

int main(void) {
    int x = 90, y = 67;
    printf("Before: %d %d\n", x, y);
    swap(&x, &y);
    printf("After:  %d %d\n", x, y);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: swap() receives the addresses of x and y, so writing through the pointers
   *x and *y changes the caller's variables. tmp holds one value during the exchange.
   main() declares both variables on one line and prints them before and after the swap. */

/* Caption: Write a C program to write lines to a text file and read them back. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Open notes.txt in write mode and check for NULL.
   2. Write 3 lines with fprintf and close the file.
   3. Open it again in read mode.
   4. Read and print each line with fgets, then close the file. */
int main(void) {
    FILE *file = fopen("notes.txt", "w");
    if (file == NULL) {
        perror("fopen");
        return 1;
    }
    fprintf(file, "the compiler turns source code into machine code\n");
    fprintf(file, "c gives you direct control over memory\n");
    fprintf(file, "loops repeat a block of code\n");
    fclose(file);

    /* Reopen the file for reading and print it line by line. */
    file = fopen("notes.txt", "r");
    if (file == NULL) {
        perror("fopen");
        return 1;
    }
    char line[128];
    while (fgets(line, sizeof(line), file) != NULL) {
        printf("%s", line);
    }
    fclose(file);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: fopen() in write mode creates notes.txt, fprintf() writes 3 lines into it
   and fclose() saves it. The file is then opened again in read mode, and fgets() reads it
   back line by line into the buffer line, which is printed. Every fopen() result is
   checked for NULL. */
// END

/* Caption: Program to convert 438 to binary. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write print_binary(n, bits).
   2. Go through the bits from the highest to the lowest.
   3. Print 1 when (n >> b) & 1 is set, otherwise 0.
   4. Print 438 in binary. */
/* Check each bit from the highest to the lowest. */
void print_binary(unsigned int n, int bits) {
    for (int b = bits - 1; b >= 0; b--) {
        putchar((n >> b) & 1 ? '1' : '0');
    }
    putchar('\n');
}

int main(void) {
    unsigned int number = 438;
    printf("%u in binary: ", number);
    print_binary(number, 10);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: print_binary() checks one bit at a time, from the highest to the lowest: (n
   >> b) & 1 is 1 when bit b is set, so it prints the character 1 or 0. main() prints 438
   in binary. */
// END

/* Caption: C program to compute 9 to the power of 9 without pow(). */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write power(base, exp) with result = 1.
   2. Multiply result by base exp times.
   3. Print 9 to the power 9. */
/* Multiply the base by itself exp times. */
long long power(int base, int exp) {
    long long result = 1;
    for (int i = 0; i < exp; i++) {
        result *= base;
    }
    return result;
}

int main(void) {
    printf("9^9 = %lld\n", power(9, 9));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: power() starts result at 1 and multiplies it by base exp times. It uses
   long long because powers grow quickly. main() prints 9 to the power 9. */
// END

/* Plan:
   1. Write factorial(n) with result = 1.
   2. Multiply result by every number from 2 to n.
   3. Return result.
   4. Print 4! as an unsigned long long. */
/* Multiply 1 * 2 * ... * n. */
unsigned long long factorial(int n) {
    unsigned long long result = 1;
    for (int i = 2; i <= n; i++) {
        result *= i;
    }
    return result;
}

int main(void) {

    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: factorial() multiplies result by every number from 2 up to n. main() prints
   4! as an unsigned long long, because factorials grow very fast. */

/* Caption: Count how many digits a number has. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Start result at 0.
   2. Divide n by 10 and add one to result.
   3. Repeat until n is 0.
   4. Apply it to 658208 and print the result. */
/* Take the last digit with % 10, then drop it with / 10. */
int count_digits(int n) {
    int result = 0;
    while (n > 0) {
        result++;
        n /= 10;
    }
    return result;
}

int main(void) {
    int number = 658208;
    printf("count of digits of %d: %d\n", number, count_digits(number));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: count_digits() removes the last digit (n / 10) and adds one to result each
   time, until n reaches 0. main() applies it to 658208. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to allocate an array with malloc and fill it with evens. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Use malloc to get room for 5 ints and check for NULL.
   2. Fill buffer with evens.
   3. Print the values.
   4. Call free(buffer) at the end. */
int main(void) {
    int n = 5;
    /* Ask the heap for room for n ints; malloc returns NULL on failure. */
    int *buffer = malloc(n * sizeof(int));
    if (buffer == NULL) {
        fprintf(stderr, "malloc failed\n");
        return 1;
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        buffer[i] = 2 * i;
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        printf("%d ", buffer[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    free(buffer);   /* give the memory back */
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: malloc() reserves room for 5 ints on the heap and returns NULL if it fails,
   which the program checks. The first loop fills buffer with evens, the second prints
   them, and free() gives the memory back at the end. */
// END

/* Caption: Program to convert a string to uppercase. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <ctype.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write to_upper() for buffer.
   2. Replace every character with toupper() until the null character.
   3. Print the sentence. */
/* toupper changes lowercase letters and leaves other characters alone. */
void to_upper(char *buffer) {
    for (int i = 0; buffer[i] != '\0'; i++) {
        buffer[i] = toupper((unsigned char)buffer[i]);
    }
}

int main(void) {
    char buffer[] = "the quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog";
    to_upper(buffer);
    printf("%s\n", buffer);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: to_upper() walks through buffer until the null character and replaces each
   character with toupper(), which only changes lowercase letters. main() prints the
   sentence in capitals. */
// END

/* Caption: Sort an array in ascending order using selection sort. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write selection_sort() for the int array data.
   2. For each position, find the smallest remaining element.
   3. Swap it into that position.
   4. Print the sorted values. */
/* Select the right element for each position and swap it into place. */
void selection_sort(int data[], int n) {
    for (int i = 0; i < n - 1; i++) {
        int chosen = i;
        for (int j = i + 1; j < n; j++) {
            if (data[chosen] > data[j]) {
                chosen = j;
            }
        }
        int tmp = data[i];
        data[i] = data[chosen];
        data[chosen] = tmp;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    int data[] = {81, 2, 92, 89, 33, 79, 21, 15, 68, 41};
    int n = 10;
    selection_sort(data, n);
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        printf("%d ", data[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: selection_sort() finds the smallest remaining element for each position and
   swaps it into place. main() then prints the 10 values in ascending order. */
// END

/* Caption: How do I split a number of seconds into hours, minutes and seconds with pointer parameters in C? */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write split_seconds() with the pointers hours, minutes and seconds.
   2. Store total / 3600, (total % 3600) / 60 and total % 60 through them.
   3. Convert 1800 seconds and print the parts. */
void split_seconds(int total, int *hours, int *minutes, int *seconds) {
    *hours = total / 3600;
    *minutes = (total % 3600) / 60;
    *seconds = total % 60;
}

int main(void) {
    int total = 1800;
    int h, m, s;
    split_seconds(total, &h, &m, &s);
    printf("%d seconds = %d h %d min %d s\n", total, h, m, s);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: split_seconds() fills three results through pointers: hours is total /
   3600, minutes is what is left divided by 60, and seconds is total % 60. main() declares
   h, m and s on one line and converts 1800 seconds. */
// END

/* Caption: Compute the distance between two points with a four-parameter function. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <math.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write distance(x1, y1, x2, y2).
   2. Compute dx and dy, then return sqrt(dx * dx + dy * dy).
   3. Print the distance between (-2, -4) and (2, 4). */
/* Pythagoras: the distance is sqrt(dx * dx + dy * dy). */
double distance(double x1, double y1, double x2, double y2) {
    double dx = x2 - x1, dy = y2 - y1;
    return sqrt(dx * dx + dy * dy);
}

int main(void) {
    printf("Distance: %.3f\n", distance(-2, -4, 2, 4));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: distance() takes the coordinates of both points as four parameters. It
   declares dx and dy on one line and uses Pythagoras with sqrt() from math.h. main()
   prints the distance between (-2, -4) and (2, 4). */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to return two values from a function using pointer parameters. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write min_max() with the array, its length and the pointers min and max.
   2. Start both at the first element.
   3. Update *min and *max while looping over the rest.
   4. Declare min and max, pass their addresses and print them. */
/* One pass finds both results; they are stored through the pointers. */
void min_max(const int nums[], int count, int *min, int *max) {
    *min = nums[0];
    *max = nums[0];
    for (int i = 1; i < count; i++) {
        if (nums[i] < *min) {
            *min = nums[i];
        }
        if (nums[i] > *max) {
            *max = nums[i];
        }
    }
}

int main(void) {
    int nums[] = {62, 65, 43, 83, 1, 99};
    int count = sizeof(nums) / sizeof(nums[0]);
    int min, max;
    min_max(nums, count, &min, &max);
    printf("Min: %d, Max: %d\n", min, max);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: A C function can return only one value, so min_max() returns void and
   writes its two results through the pointer parameters min and max. main() declares min
   and max on one line and passes their addresses with &, then prints both results for the
   6 values. */
// END

/* Caption: Find the smallest number in an array. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write find_min() that takes values and n.
   2. Store values[0] in best.
   3. Loop over the other elements and keep the smallest value in best.
   4. Return best and print it. */
/* Start with the first element and keep the smallest value seen so far. */
long find_min(const long values[], int n) {
    long best = values[0];
    for (int idx = 1; idx < n; idx++) {
        if (values[idx] < best) {
            best = values[idx];
        }
    }
    return best;
}

int main(void) {
    long values[] = {79L, 79L, 73L, 27L, 16L, 30L, 62L, 31L};
    int n = 8;
    printf("The smallest value is %ld\n", find_min(values, n));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: find_min() takes the first element as the smallest value so far and stores
   it in best. The loop compares every other element with best using < and keeps the
   smallest one. main() prints the smallest of the 8 values. */
// END

/* Caption: Implement insertion sort for an array of long values. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write insertion_sort() for the long array values.
   2. Take each element in turn as current.
   3. Shift the larger values of the sorted part one place right.
   4. Put current into the gap.
   5. Print the sorted values. */
/* Insert each element into the already sorted part on its left. */
void insertion_sort(long values[], int count) {
    for (int i = 1; i < count; i++) {
        long current = values[i];
        int j = i - 1;
        while (j >= 0 && values[j] > current) {
            values[j + 1] = values[j];   /* shift bigger values right */
            j--;
        }
        values[j + 1] = current;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    long values[] = {81L, 95L, 1L, 73L, 80L, 35L, 86L, 74L, 87L};
    int count = 9;
    insertion_sort(values, count);
    for (int i = 0; i < count; i++) {
        printf("%ld ", values[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: insertion_sort() takes each element in turn and shifts the larger values of
   the sorted part one place right until the element fits. main() then prints the 9 values
   in ascending order. */
// END

/* Caption: Build a linked list, print it, and free it. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define Node with a value and a next pointer.
   2. Write push_front() that mallocs a node and links it in front of head.
   3. Write print_list() that follows next until NULL.
   4. Write free_list() that frees every node.
   5. Push 3 values, print the list and free it. */
typedef struct Node {
    int value;
    struct Node *next;
} Node;

/* Allocate a new node and put it in front of the current head. */
Node *push_front(Node *head, int value) {
    Node *node = malloc(sizeof(Node));
    if (node == NULL) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Out of memory\n");
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }
    node->value = value;
    node->next = head;
    return node;
}

void print_list(const Node *head) {
    for (const Node *cur = head; cur != NULL; cur = cur->next) {
        printf("%d -> ", cur->value);
    }
    printf("NULL\n");
}

/* Free every node; save next before freeing the current one. */
void free_list(Node *head) {
    while (head != NULL) {
        Node *next = head->next;
        free(head);
        head = next;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    Node *head = NULL;
    head = push_front(head, 45);
    head = push_front(head, 93);
    head = push_front(head, 65);
    print_list(head);
    free_list(head);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: Each Node holds a value and a pointer to the next node. push_front()
   allocates a node with malloc, puts it in front of head and returns it; print_list()
   follows the next pointers until NULL; free_list() frees every node. main() pushes 3
   values, so they print in reverse order. */
// END

/* Caption: Reverse the digits of a number. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Start result at 0.
   2. Multiply result by 10, add n % 10, then divide n by 10.
   3. Repeat until n is 0.
   4. Apply it to 730567 and print the result. */
/* Take the last digit with % 10, then drop it with / 10. */
int reverse_digits(int n) {
    int result = 0;
    while (n > 0) {
        result = result * 10 + n % 10;
        n /= 10;
    }
    return result;
}

int main(void) {
    int number = 730567;
    printf("reverse of digits of %d: %d\n", number, reverse_digits(number));
    return 0;

   last digit of n, which reverses the order. main() applies it to 730567. */
// END

/* Caption: Search a sorted array by halving the search range each step. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Make sure the array is sorted.
   2. Set low to 0 and high to len - 1.
   3. While low <= high, compare the middle element mid with the key.
   4. Return the index if it matches; otherwise keep only the half that can hold the
      key.
   5. Return -1 if the range becomes empty, and print the index of 21. */
/* The array must be sorted. Each step halves the range that can still hold the key. */
int binary_search(const int readings[], int len, int key) {
    int low = 0;
    int high = len - 1;
    while (low <= high) {
        int mid = low + (high - low) / 2;
        if (readings[mid] == key) {
            return mid;
        } else if (readings[mid] < key) {
            low = mid + 1;   /* key is in the right half */
        } else {
            high = mid - 1;   /* key is in the left half */
        }
    }
    return -1;
}

int main(void) {
    int readings[] = {21, 94, 102, 108, 123, 144, 168, 176, 192};
    int len = 9;
    int index = binary_search(readings, len, 21);
    printf("Index of 21: %d\n", index);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: binary_search() needs a sorted array. It keeps the range from low to high,
   compares the middle element mid with the key and throws away the half that cannot
   contain it, so it needs only about log2(n) steps. main() looks for 21 and prints its
   index, or -1 if it is not there. */
// END

/* Caption: Print the binary representation of an integer. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write print_binary(n, bits).
   2. Go through the bits from the highest to the lowest.
   3. Print 1 when (n >> b) & 1 is set, otherwise 0.
   4. Print 481 in binary. */
/* Check each bit from the highest to the lowest. */
void print_binary(unsigned int n, int bits) {
    for (int b = bits - 1; b >= 0; b--) {
        putchar((n >> b) & 1 ? '1' : '0');
    }
    putchar('\n');
}

int main(void) {
    unsigned int number = 481;
    printf("%u in binary: ", number);
    print_binary(number, 16);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: print_binary() checks one bit at a time, from the highest to the lowest: (n
   >> b) & 1 is 1 when bit b is set, so it prints the character 1 or 0. main() prints 481
   in binary. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to compute 2 to the power of 11 without pow(). */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write power(base, exp) with result = 1.
   2. Multiply result by base exp times.
   3. Print 2 to the power 11. */
/* Multiply the base by itself exp times. */
long long power(int base, int exp) {
    long long result = 1;
    for (int i = 0; i < exp; i++) {
        result *= base;
    }
    return result;
}

    printf("2^11 = %lld\n", power(2, 11));
    return 0;

   long long because powers grow quickly. main() prints 2 to the power 11. */

/* Caption: Print all prime numbers up to 92. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write is_prime(n); numbers below 2 are not prime.
   2. Try every divisor d while d * d <= n.
   3. Return false if one divides n, otherwise true.
   4. Print every prime from 2 to 92. */
/* A prime has no divisor between 2 and its square root. */
bool is_prime(int n) {
    if (n < 2) {
        return false;
    }
    for (int d = 2; d * d <= n; d++) {
        if (n % d == 0) {
            return false;
        }
    }
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    for (int n = 2; n <= 92; n++) {
        if (is_prime(n)) {
            printf("%d ", n);
        }
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: is_prime() tries every divisor d from 2 while d * d <= n; if one divides n
   evenly, n is not prime. main() tests every number from 2 to 92 and prints the primes. */
// END

   2. Go through the bits from the highest to the lowest.
   3. Print 1 when (n >> b) & 1 is set, otherwise 0.
   4. Print 361 in binary. */
/* Check each bit from the highest to the lowest. */
void print_binary(unsigned int n, int bits) {

/* Caption: Return the minimum, maximum and average of an array in a struct. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define a Stats struct with min, max and average.
   2. Write array_stats() that fills one Stats in a loop.
   3. Return the struct.
   4. Print st.min, st.max and st.average. */
typedef struct {
    int min;
    int max;
    double average;
} Stats;

/* Pack several results into one struct and return it. */
Stats array_stats(const int v[], int n) {
    Stats s = {v[0], v[0], 0.0};
    double total = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        if (v[i] < s.min) {
            s.min = v[i];
        }
        if (v[i] > s.max) {
            s.max = v[i];
        }
        total += v[i];
    }
    s.average = total / n;
    return s;
}

int main(void) {
    int samples[] = {88, 80, 90, 79, 14};
    int n = sizeof(samples) / sizeof(samples[0]);
    Stats st = array_stats(samples, n);
    printf("Min %d, Max %d, Average %.2f\n", st.min, st.max, st.average);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: Stats groups three results. array_stats() fills one Stats while it loops
   over the 5 values and returns the whole struct, which is a clean way to return several
   results at once. main() reads them as st.min, st.max and st.average. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to implement bubble sort for an array of int values. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write bubble_sort() for the int array data.
   2. Compare each pair of neighbours.
   3. Swap them when they are in the wrong order for descending order.
   4. Repeat the passes until the array is sorted.
   5. Print the sorted values. */
/* Repeatedly swap neighbours that are in the wrong order. */
void bubble_sort(int data[], int len) {
    for (int i = 0; i < len - 1; i++) {
        for (int j = 0; j < len - 1 - i; j++) {
            if (data[j] < data[j + 1]) {
                int tmp = data[j];
                data[j] = data[j + 1];
                data[j + 1] = tmp;
            }
        }
    }
}

int main(void) {
    int data[] = {57, 92, 44, 58, 27, 77};
    int len = 6;
    bubble_sort(data, len);
    for (int i = 0; i < len; i++) {
        printf("%d ", data[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: bubble_sort() walks through data again and again and swaps neighbours that
   are in the wrong order, so the smallest values move to the end first. main() then prints
   the 6 values in descending order. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to decide if 1947 is a leap year. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write is_leap(year).
   2. A year divisible by 4 is a leap year, unless it is divisible by 100.
   3. Years divisible by 400 are leap years again.
   4. Check 1947 and print the result. */
/* Leap years divide by 4, except centuries, which must divide by 400. */
int is_leap(int year) {
    return (year % 4 == 0 && year % 100 != 0) || year % 400 == 0;
}

int main(void) {
    int year = 1947;
    if (is_leap(year)) {
        printf("%d is a leap year\n", year);
    } else {
        printf("%d is not a leap year\n", year);
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: is_leap() returns true for years divisible by 4, except century years,
   which must also be divisible by 400. main() checks 1947 and prints whether it is a leap
   year. */
// END

   4. In main(), search for 155 and print the result. */
/* Return the index of needle, or -1 when it is not in the array. */
int linear_search(const int scores[], int length, int needle) {
    for (int i = 0; i < length; i++) {
        if (scores[i] == needle) {
            return i;

    }
    return -1;
}

    if (pos >= 0) {
        printf("Found %d at index %d\n", needle, pos);
    } else {
        printf("%d is not in the array\n", needle);
    }
    return 0;
}

   index of the first one equal to needle, or -1 when it reaches the end without a match.
   main() searches for 155 and prints where it is, or that it is missing. */
