/* Caption: Print all prime numbers up to 44. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write is_prime(n); numbers below 2 are not prime.
   2. Try every divisor d while d * d <= n.
   3. Return false if one divides n, otherwise true.
   4. Print every prime from 2 to 44. */
/* A prime has no divisor between 2 and its square root. */
bool is_prime(int n) {
    if (n < 2) {
        return false;
    }
    for (int d = 2; d * d <= n; d++) {
        if (n % d == 0) {
            return false;
        }
    }
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    for (int n = 2; n <= 44; n++) {
        if (is_prime(n)) {
            printf("%d ", n);
        }
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: is_prime() tries every divisor d from 2 while d * d <= n; if one divides n
   evenly, n is not prime. main() tests every number from 2 to 44 and prints the primes. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to keep a value inside the limits low and high. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write clamp(value, low, high).
   2. Return low if the value is too small and high if it is too big.
   3. Otherwise return the value.
   4. Set low = 2 and high = 46 and print clamp() for 15, 6 and 112. */
/* Return value, but never less than low or more than high. */
int clamp(int value, int low, int high) {
    if (value < low) {
        return low;
    }
    if (value > high) {
        return high;
    }
    return value;
}

int main(void) {
    int low = 2, high = 46;
    printf("clamp(%d) = %d\n", 15, clamp(15, low, high));
    printf("clamp(%d) = %d\n", 6, clamp(6, low, high));
    printf("clamp(%d) = %d\n", 112, clamp(112, low, high));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: clamp() takes three parameters: the value and the two limits. It returns
   low when the value is too small, high when it is too big and the value itself otherwise.
   main() declares low = 2 and high = 46 on one line and clamps 15, 6 and 112. */
// END

/* Caption: Program to use Euclid's algorithm to compute the GCD. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write gcd() with Euclid's algorithm.
   2. Replace (a, b) by (b, a % b) until b is 0.
   3. Return a and print the GCD of 286 and 113. */
/* Euclid: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a % b) until b becomes zero. */
int gcd(int a, int b) {
    while (b != 0) {
        int r = a % b;
        a = b;
        b = r;
    }
    return a;
}

int main(void) {
    int x = 286, y = 113;
    printf("gcd(%d, %d) = %d\n", x, y, gcd(x, y));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: gcd() uses Euclid's algorithm: it keeps replacing (a, b) with (b, a % b)
   until b is 0. The last non-zero value is the greatest common divisor, and main() prints
   the GCD of 286 and 113. */
// END

/* Caption: Check every element of an array to find a target value. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write linear_search() with the array, its length and wanted.
   2. Compare each element with wanted.
   3. Return the index of the first match, or -1.
   4. In main(), search for 195 and print the result. */
/* Return the index of wanted, or -1 when it is not in the array. */
int linear_search(const int prices[], int len, int wanted) {
    for (int i = 0; i < len; i++) {
        if (prices[i] == wanted) {
            return i;
        }
    }
    return -1;
}

    if (pos >= 0) {
        printf("Found %d at index %d\n", wanted, pos);
    } else {
        printf("%d is not in the array\n", wanted);
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: linear_search() checks the elements of prices one by one and returns the
   index of the first one equal to wanted, or -1 when it reaches the end without a match.
   main() searches for 195 and prints where it is, or that it is missing. */

   3. Add one to found for every odd number.

/* A number is odd when the remainder after dividing by 2 is one. */

    int found = 0;

}

    const int size = 9;

   1 after dividing by 2 means the number is odd, so found goes up by one. main() prints
   how many of the 9 values are odd. */
// END

/* Caption: Program to return a sum and an average together using pointer parameters. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write sum_and_average() with the pointers sum and average.
   2. Add the values into *sum.
   3. Store *sum / n in *average.
   4. Declare total and mean, pass their addresses and print them. */
void sum_and_average(const double v[], int n, double *sum, double *average) {
    *sum = 0.0;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        *sum += v[i];
    }
    *average = *sum / n;
}

int main(void) {
    double ages[] = {94.6, 80.7, 41.9};
    int n = sizeof(ages) / sizeof(ages[0]);
    double total, mean;
    sum_and_average(ages, n, &total, &mean);
    printf("Sum: %.2f, Average: %.2f\n", total, mean);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: sum_and_average() takes the array, its length and two pointers. It adds up
   the 3 values through *sum and then stores *sum / n in *average. main() declares total
   and mean on one line and passes their addresses. */
// END

/* Caption: Create a singly linked list by inserting at the head. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define ListNode with a value and a next pointer.
   2. Write push_front() that mallocs a node and links it in front of head.
   3. Write print_list() that follows next until NULL.
   4. Write free_list() that frees every node.
   5. Push 5 values, print the list and free it. */
typedef struct ListNode {
    int value;
    struct ListNode *next;
} ListNode;

/* Allocate a new node and put it in front of the current head. */
ListNode *push_front(ListNode *head, int value) {
    ListNode *node = malloc(sizeof(ListNode));
    if (node == NULL) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Out of memory\n");
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }
    node->value = value;
    node->next = head;
    return node;
}

void print_list(const ListNode *head) {
    for (const ListNode *cur = head; cur != NULL; cur = cur->next) {
        printf("%d -> ", cur->value);
    }
    printf("NULL\n");
}

/* Free every node; save next before freeing the current one. */
void free_list(ListNode *head) {
    while (head != NULL) {
        ListNode *next = head->next;
        free(head);
        head = next;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    ListNode *head = NULL;
    head = push_front(head, 39);
    head = push_front(head, 16);
    head = push_front(head, 75);
    head = push_front(head, 85);
    head = push_front(head, 4);
    print_list(head);
    free_list(head);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: Each ListNode holds a value and a pointer to the next node. push_front()
   allocates a node with malloc, puts it in front of head and returns it; print_list()
   follows the next pointers until NULL; free_list() frees every node. main() pushes 5
   values, so they print in reverse order. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to compute the sum of the digits of an integer. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Start result at 0.
   2. Add n % 10 to result, then divide n by 10.
   3. Repeat until n is 0.
   4. Apply it to 481138 and print the result. */
/* Take the last digit with % 10, then drop it with / 10. */
int sum_digits(int n) {
    int result = 0;
    while (n > 0) {
        result += n % 10;
        n /= 10;
    }
    return result;
}

int main(void) {
    int number = 481138;
    printf("sum of digits of %d: %d\n", number, sum_digits(number));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: sum_digits() adds the last digit (n % 10) to result and then removes it (n
   / 10) until no digits are left. main() applies it to 481138. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to reverse the elements of an array in place. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write reverse_array() for readings.
   2. Set i to the first index and j to the last.
   3. Swap readings[i] and readings[j], then move both inwards.
   4. Stop when i meets j and print the array. */
/* Swap the outer pair, then move both ends toward the middle. */
void reverse_array(int readings[], int size) {
    int i = 0;
    int j = size - 1;
    while (i < j) {
        int tmp = readings[i];
        readings[i] = readings[j];
        readings[j] = tmp;
        i++;
        j--;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    int readings[] = {48, 4, 39, 5, 97};
    int size = 5;
    reverse_array(readings, size);
    for (int i = 0; i < size; i++) {
        printf("%d ", readings[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: reverse_array() swaps the first and last elements, then moves i forward and
   j backward until they meet, so the array is reversed in place without a second array.
   main() prints the reversed values. */
// END

/* Caption: C program to count how many vowels a string contains. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <string.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write count_vowels() with count = 0.
   2. For each character, check whether strchr finds it in aeiouAEIOU.
   3. Return count and print it. */
/* strchr finds the letter in the list of vowels, or returns NULL. */
int count_vowels(const char *text) {
    int count = 0;
    for (int i = 0; text[i] != '\0'; i++) {
        if (strchr("aeiouAEIOU", text[i]) != NULL) {
            count++;
        }
    }
    return count;
}

int main(void) {
    const char *sentence = "the compiler turns source code into machine code";
    printf("Vowels: %d\n", count_vowels(sentence));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: count_vowels() uses strchr to test whether each character is one of
   aeiouAEIOU and counts the matches. main() prints the number of vowels in the sentence. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to search a sorted array by halving the search range each step. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Make sure the array is sorted.
   2. Set left to 0 and right to size - 1.
   3. While left <= right, compare the middle element middle with the key.
   4. Return the index if it matches; otherwise keep only the half that can hold the
      key.
   5. Return -1 if the range becomes empty, and print the index of 201. */
/* The array must be sorted. Each step halves the range that can still hold the key. */
int binary_search(const int scores[], int size, int key) {
    int left = 0;
    int right = size - 1;
    while (left <= right) {
        int middle = left + (right - left) / 2;
        if (scores[middle] == key) {
            return middle;
        } else if (scores[middle] < key) {
            left = middle + 1;   /* key is in the right half */
        } else {
            right = middle - 1;   /* key is in the left half */
        }
    }
    return -1;
}

int main(void) {
    int scores[] = {12, 24, 58, 92, 95, 110, 111};
    int size = 7;
    int index = binary_search(scores, size, 201);
    printf("Index of 201: %d\n", index);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: binary_search() needs a sorted array. It keeps the range from left to
   right, compares the middle element middle with the key and throws away the half that
   cannot contain it, so it needs only about log2(n) steps. main() looks for 201 and prints
   its index, or -1 if it is not there. */
// END

/* Caption: Turn the rows of a 4x3 matrix into columns. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define ROWS as 4 and COLS as 3.
   2. Copy m[r][c] into t[c][r] for every element.
   3. Print t row by row. */
#define ROWS 4
#define COLS 3

int main(void) {
    int m[ROWS][COLS] = {{3, 7, 5}, {6, 1, 3}, {7, 7, 3}, {1, 0, 0}};
    int t[COLS][ROWS];
    /* Element (r, c) moves to (c, r). */
    for (int r = 0; r < ROWS; r++) {
        for (int c = 0; c < COLS; c++) {
            t[c][r] = m[r][c];
        }
    }
    for (int r = 0; r < COLS; r++) {
        for (int c = 0; c < ROWS; c++) {
            printf("%3d", t[r][c]);
        }
        printf("\n");
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: The nested loops copy m[r][c] into t[c][r], so the 4x3 matrix becomes 3x4.
   A second pair of loops prints the result. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a function that returns the distance between two points given x1, y1, x2 and y2. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <math.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write distance(x1, y1, x2, y2).
   2. Compute dx and dy, then return sqrt(dx * dx + dy * dy).
   3. Print the distance between (-8, 2) and (-5, 3). */
/* Pythagoras: the distance is sqrt(dx * dx + dy * dy). */
double distance(double x1, double y1, double x2, double y2) {
    double dx = x2 - x1, dy = y2 - y1;
    return sqrt(dx * dx + dy * dy);
}

int main(void) {
    printf("Distance: %.3f\n", distance(-8, 2, -5, 3));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: distance() takes the coordinates of both points as four parameters. It
   declares dx and dy on one line and uses Pythagoras with sqrt() from math.h. main()
   prints the distance between (-8, 2) and (-5, 3). */
// END

/* Caption: C program to check whether a word is a palindrome. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <string.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write is_palindrome() for buffer.
   2. Compare the first and last characters, moving inwards.
   3. Return false at the first mismatch, otherwise true.
   4. Check rotor and print the result. */
/* Compare characters from the front and back, moving inwards. */
bool is_palindrome(const char *buffer) {
    int i = 0;
    int j = strlen(buffer) - 1;
    while (i < j) {
        if (buffer[i] != buffer[j]) {
            return false;
        }
        i++;
        j--;
    }
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    const char *buffer = "rotor";
    printf("%s %s a palindrome\n", buffer, is_palindrome(buffer) ? "is" : "is not");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: is_palindrome() compares the first and last characters and moves inwards;
   any mismatch means the word is not a palindrome. main() checks the word rotor and prints
   the result. */
// END

/* Caption: Create a singly linked list by inserting at the head. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define Item with a value and a next pointer.
   2. Write push_front() that mallocs a node and links it in front of head.
   3. Write print_list() that follows next until NULL.
   4. Write free_list() that frees every node.
   5. Push 6 values, print the list and free it. */
typedef struct Item {
    int value;
    struct Item *next;
} Item;

/* Allocate a new node and put it in front of the current head. */
Item *push_front(Item *head, int value) {
    Item *node = malloc(sizeof(Item));
    if (node == NULL) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Out of memory\n");
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }
    node->value = value;
    node->next = head;
    return node;
}

void print_list(const Item *head) {
    for (const Item *cur = head; cur != NULL; cur = cur->next) {
        printf("%d -> ", cur->value);
    }
    printf("NULL\n");
}

/* Free every node; save next before freeing the current one. */
void free_list(Item *head) {
    while (head != NULL) {
        Item *next = head->next;
        free(head);
        head = next;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    Item *head = NULL;
    head = push_front(head, 60);
    head = push_front(head, 12);
    head = push_front(head, 5);
    head = push_front(head, 66);
    head = push_front(head, 89);
    head = push_front(head, 83);
    print_list(head);
    free_list(head);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: Each Item holds a value and a pointer to the next node. push_front()
   allocates a node with malloc, puts it in front of head and returns it; print_list()
   follows the next pointers until NULL; free_list() frees every node. main() pushes 6
   values, so they print in reverse order. */
// END

/* Caption: Sum a long array with a helper function. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write total_of() that takes the array items and its length length.
   2. Start total at 0 and add every element in a for loop.
   3. Return total.
   4. In main(), fill items with 9 values and print the sum. */
/* Walk through the array and accumulate each value. */
long total_of(const long items[], int length) {
    long total = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < length; i++) {
        total += items[i];
    }
    return total;
}

    int length = sizeof(items) / sizeof(items[0]);
    printf("Sum: %ld\n", total_of(items, length));
    return 0;
}

   at 0, adds every element to it in a for loop and returns the total. main() fills items
   with 9 long values and prints their sum. */
// END

/* Caption: Compute the sum of the digits of an integer. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Start result at 0.
   2. Add n % 10 to result, then divide n by 10.
   3. Repeat until n is 0.
   4. Apply it to 843715 and print the result. */
/* Take the last digit with % 10, then drop it with / 10. */
int sum_digits(int n) {
    int result = 0;
    while (n > 0) {
        result += n % 10;
        n /= 10;
    }
    return result;
}

int main(void) {
    int number = 843715;
    printf("sum of digits of %d: %d\n", number, sum_digits(number));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: sum_digits() adds the last digit (n % 10) to result and then removes it (n
   / 10) until no digits are left. main() applies it to 843715. */
// END

/* Caption: C program to allocate an array with malloc and fill it with multiples. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Use malloc to get room for 15 ints and check for NULL.
   2. Fill arr with multiples.
   3. Print the values.
   4. Call free(arr) at the end. */
int main(void) {
    int n = 15;
    /* Ask the heap for room for n ints; malloc returns NULL on failure. */
    int *arr = malloc(n * sizeof(int));
    if (arr == NULL) {
        fprintf(stderr, "malloc failed\n");
        return 1;
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        arr[i] = 7 * i;
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        printf("%d ", arr[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    free(arr);   /* give the memory back */
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: malloc() reserves room for 15 ints on the heap and returns NULL if it
   fails, which the program checks. The first loop fills arr with multiples, the second
   prints them, and free() gives the memory back at the end. */
// END

/* Caption: Calculate 12! using iteration. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write factorial(n) with result = 1.
   2. Multiply result by every number from 2 to n.
   3. Return result.
   4. Print 12! as an unsigned long long. */
/* Multiply 1 * 2 * ... * n. */
unsigned long long factorial(int n) {
    unsigned long long result = 1;
    for (int i = 2; i <= n; i++) {
        result *= i;
    }
    return result;
}

int main(void) {
    int n = 12;
    printf("%d! = %llu\n", n, factorial(n));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: factorial() multiplies result by every number from 2 up to n. main() prints
   12! as an unsigned long long, because factorials grow very fast. */
// END

/* Caption: C program to find a number in a sorted array with binary search. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Make sure the array is sorted.
   2. Set low to 0 and high to len - 1.
   3. While low <= high, compare the middle element mid with the key.
   4. Return the index if it matches; otherwise keep only the half that can hold the
      key.
   5. Return -1 if the range becomes empty, and print the index of 68. */
/* The array must be sorted. Each step halves the range that can still hold the key. */
int binary_search(const int samples[], int len, int key) {
    int low = 0;
    int high = len - 1;
    while (low <= high) {
        int mid = low + (high - low) / 2;
        if (samples[mid] == key) {
            return mid;
        } else if (samples[mid] < key) {
            low = mid + 1;   /* key is in the right half */
        } else {
            high = mid - 1;   /* key is in the left half */
        }
    }
    return -1;
}

int main(void) {
    int samples[] = {22, 54, 68, 100, 113, 168};
    const int len = 6;
    int index = binary_search(samples, len, 68);
    printf("Index of 68: %d\n", index);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: binary_search() needs a sorted array. It keeps the range from low to high,
   compares the middle element mid with the key and throws away the half that cannot
   contain it, so it needs only about log2(n) steps. main() looks for 68 and prints its
   index, or -1 if it is not there. */
// END

/* Caption: Swap two variables using pointers. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write swap() that takes pointers to two double values.
   2. Save *a in tmp, copy *b into *a, then tmp into *b.
   3. In main(), print a and b, call swap(&a, &b) and print them again. */
/* Pass addresses so the function can change the caller's variables. */
void swap(double *a, double *b) {
    double tmp = *a;
    *a = *b;
    *b = tmp;
}

int main(void) {
    double a = 70.9, b = 48.4;
    printf("Before: %.2f %.2f\n", a, b);
    swap(&a, &b);
    printf("After:  %.2f %.2f\n", a, b);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: swap() receives the addresses of a and b, so writing through the pointers
   *a and *b changes the caller's variables. tmp holds one value during the exchange.
   main() declares both variables on one line and prints them before and after the swap. */
// END

/* Caption: Return the smallest element of an array of int values. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write find_min() that takes readings and n.
   2. Store readings[0] in m.
   3. Loop over the other elements and keep the smallest value in m.
   4. Return m and print it. */
/* Start with the first element and keep the smallest value seen so far. */
int find_min(const int readings[], int n) {
    int m = readings[0];
    for (int idx = 1; idx < n; idx++) {
        if (readings[idx] < m) {
            m = readings[idx];
        }
    }
    return m;
}

int main(void) {
    int readings[] = {18, 73, 85, 80, 35, 94, 6, 2};
    int n = 8;
    printf("The smallest value is %d\n", find_min(readings, n));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: find_min() takes the first element as the smallest value so far and stores
   it in m. The loop compares every other element with m using < and keeps the smallest
   one. main() prints the smallest of the 8 values. */
// END

   h, m and s on one line and converts 34155 seconds. */
// END

/* Plan:

/* Caption: C program to list the prime numbers below a limit. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write is_prime(n); numbers below 2 are not prime.
   2. Try every divisor d while d * d <= n.
   3. Return false if one divides n, otherwise true.
   4. Print every prime from 2 to 36. */
/* A prime has no divisor between 2 and its square root. */
bool is_prime(int n) {
    if (n < 2) {
        return false;
    }
    for (int d = 2; d * d <= n; d++) {
        if (n % d == 0) {
            return false;
        }
    }
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    for (int n = 2; n <= 36; n++) {
        if (is_prime(n)) {
            printf("%d ", n);
        }
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: is_prime() tries every divisor d from 2 while d * d <= n; if one divides n
   evenly, n is not prime. main() tests every number from 2 to 36 and prints the primes. */
// END

/* Caption: Program to compute the sum and the average of an array in one function. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write sum_and_average() with the pointers sum and average.
   2. Add the values into *sum.
   3. Store *sum / n in *average.
   4. Declare total and mean, pass their addresses and print them. */
void sum_and_average(const double v[], int n, double *sum, double *average) {
    *sum = 0.0;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        *sum += v[i];
    }
    *average = *sum / n;
}

int main(void) {
    double nums[] = {11.9, 1.2, 31.1, 72.3, 79.6, 14.0, 82.6, 4.1};
    int n = sizeof(nums) / sizeof(nums[0]);
    double total, mean;
    sum_and_average(nums, n, &total, &mean);
    printf("Sum: %.2f, Average: %.2f\n", total, mean);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: sum_and_average() takes the array, its length and two pointers. It adds up
   the 8 values through *sum and then stores *sum / n in *average. main() declares total
   and mean on one line and passes their addresses. */
// END

/* Caption: C program to implement a stack with an array (push and pop). */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define a Stack with room for 16 items and a top counter.
   2. Write push() and pop(), returning false when the stack is full or empty.
   3. Push 5 values.
   4. Pop and print until the stack is empty. */
#define CAPACITY 16

typedef struct {
    int items[CAPACITY];
    int top;   /* number of items on the stack */
} Stack;

bool push(Stack *s, int value) {
    if (s->top == CAPACITY) {
        return false;   /* stack is full */
    }
    s->items[s->top++] = value;
    return true;
}

bool pop(Stack *s, int *value) {
    if (s->top == 0) {
        return false;   /* stack is empty */
    }
    *value = s->items[--s->top];
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    Stack s = {.top = 0};
    push(&s, 84);
    push(&s, 59);
    push(&s, 78);
    push(&s, 9);
    push(&s, 38);
    int value;
    /* Items come back out in reverse order (last in, first out). */
    while (pop(&s, &value)) {
        printf("%d ", value);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: The Stack keeps up to 16 items in an array, and top counts how many are
   stored. push() adds at the top and pop() removes from the top; both return false when
   they cannot. main() pushes 5 values and pops them all, so they come out in reverse order
   (last in, first out). */
// END

/* Caption: Save text to a file with fprintf and print it with fgets. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Open data.txt in write mode and check for NULL.
   2. Write 2 lines with fprintf and close the file.
   3. Open it again in read mode.
   4. Read and print each line with fgets, then close the file. */
int main(void) {
    FILE *file = fopen("data.txt", "w");
    if (file == NULL) {
        perror("fopen");
        return 1;
    }
    fprintf(file, "c gives you direct control over memory\n");
    fprintf(file, "always free the memory you allocate\n");
    fclose(file);

    /* Reopen the file for reading and print it line by line. */
    file = fopen("data.txt", "r");
    if (file == NULL) {
        perror("fopen");
        return 1;
    }
    char line[128];
    while (fgets(line, sizeof(line), file) != NULL) {
        printf("%s", line);
    }
    fclose(file);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: fopen() in write mode creates data.txt, fprintf() writes 2 lines into it
   and fclose() saves it. The file is then opened again in read mode, and fgets() reads it
   back line by line into the buffer line, which is printed. Every fopen() result is
   checked for NULL. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to implement bubble sort for an array of long values. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write bubble_sort() for the long array scores.
   2. Compare each pair of neighbours.
   3. Swap them when they are in the wrong order for ascending order.
   4. Repeat the passes until the array is sorted.
   5. Print the sorted values. */
/* Repeatedly swap neighbours that are in the wrong order. */
void bubble_sort(long scores[], int count) {
    for (int i = 0; i < count - 1; i++) {
        for (int j = 0; j < count - 1 - i; j++) {
            if (scores[j] > scores[j + 1]) {
                long tmp = scores[j];
                scores[j] = scores[j + 1];
                scores[j + 1] = tmp;
            }
        }
    }
}

int main(void) {
    long scores[] = {61L, 67L, 9L, 97L, 4L, 92L, 53L, 45L, 45L, 83L};
    int count = 10;
    bubble_sort(scores, count);
    for (int i = 0; i < count; i++) {
        printf("%ld ", scores[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: bubble_sort() walks through scores again and again and swaps neighbours
   that are in the wrong order, so the largest values move to the end first. main() then
   prints the 10 values in ascending order. */
// END

/* Caption: C program to check every element of an array to find a target value. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write linear_search() with the array, its length and needle.
   2. Compare each element with needle.
   3. Return the index of the first match, or -1.
   4. In main(), search for 59 and print the result. */
/* Return the index of needle, or -1 when it is not in the array. */
int linear_search(const int scores[], int len, int needle) {
    for (int idx = 0; idx < len; idx++) {
        if (scores[idx] == needle) {
            return idx;
        }
    }
    return -1;
}

int main(void) {
    int scores[] = {8, 40, 59, 27, 46, 26, 59, 43};
    const int len = 8;
    int needle = 59;
    int pos = linear_search(scores, len, needle);
    if (pos >= 0) {
        printf("Found %d at index %d\n", needle, pos);
    } else {
        printf("%d is not in the array\n", needle);
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: linear_search() checks the elements of scores one by one and returns the
   index of the first one equal to needle, or -1 when it reaches the end without a match.
   main() searches for 59 and prints where it is, or that it is missing. */
// END

   2. Write area() and perimeter().
   3. Make a 1 by 18 rectangle and print both results. */

    int width;
    int height;
} Rectangle;

int area(Rectangle r) {
    return r.width * r.height;

int perimeter(Rectangle r) {
    return 2 * (r.width + r.height);

    return 0;

   perimeter() returns 2 * (width + height). main() makes a 1 by 18 rectangle and prints
   both results. */

/* Caption: Print an integer with its digits reversed. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Start result at 0.
   2. Multiply result by 10, add n % 10, then divide n by 10.
   3. Repeat until n is 0.
   4. Apply it to 83840 and print the result. */
/* Take the last digit with % 10, then drop it with / 10. */
int reverse_digits(int n) {
    int result = 0;
    while (n > 0) {
        result = result * 10 + n % 10;
        n /= 10;
    }
    return result;
}

int main(void) {
    int number = 83840;
    printf("reverse of digits of %d: %d\n", number, reverse_digits(number));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: reverse_digits() shifts result one place left (result * 10) and adds the
   last digit of n, which reverses the order. main() applies it to 83840. */
// END

/* Caption: Limit a number to a range with a three-parameter function. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write clamp(value, low, high).
   2. Return low if the value is too small and high if it is too big.
   3. Otherwise return the value.
   4. Set low = 4 and high = 45 and print clamp() for 36, 4 and 89. */
/* Return value, but never less than low or more than high. */
int clamp(int value, int low, int high) {
    if (value < low) {
        return low;
    }
    if (value > high) {
        return high;
    }
    return value;
}

int main(void) {
    int low = 4, high = 45;
    printf("clamp(%d) = %d\n", 36, clamp(36, low, high));
    printf("clamp(%d) = %d\n", 4, clamp(4, low, high));
    printf("clamp(%d) = %d\n", 89, clamp(89, low, high));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: clamp() takes three parameters: the value and the two limits. It returns
   low when the value is too small, high when it is too big and the value itself otherwise.
   main() declares low = 4 and high = 45 on one line and clamps 36, 4 and 89. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to change every letter in a sentence to a capital letter. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <ctype.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write to_upper() for buffer.
   2. Replace every character with toupper() until the null character.
   3. Print the sentence. */
/* toupper changes lowercase letters and leaves other characters alone. */
void to_upper(char *buffer) {
    for (int i = 0; buffer[i] != '\0'; i++) {
        buffer[i] = toupper((unsigned char)buffer[i]);
    }
}

int main(void) {
    char buffer[] = "strings end with a null character";
    to_upper(buffer);
    printf("%s\n", buffer);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: to_upper() walks through buffer until the null character and replaces each
   character with toupper(), which only changes lowercase letters. main() prints the
   sentence in capitals. */

/* Caption: Write a program to return two values from a function using pointer parameters. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write min_max() with the array, its length and the pointers min and max.
   2. Start both at the first element.
   3. Update *min and *max while looping over the rest.
   4. Declare min and max, pass their addresses and print them. */
/* One pass finds both results; they are stored through the pointers. */
void min_max(const int readings[], int size, int *min, int *max) {
    *min = readings[0];
    *max = readings[0];
    for (int i = 1; i < size; i++) {
        if (readings[i] < *min) {
            *min = readings[i];
        }
        if (readings[i] > *max) {
            *max = readings[i];
        }
    }
}

int main(void) {
    int readings[] = {52, 93, 53, 10};
    int size = 4;
    int min, max;
    min_max(readings, size, &min, &max);
    printf("Min: %d, Max: %d\n", min, max);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: A C function can return only one value, so min_max() returns void and
   writes its two results through the pointer parameters min and max. main() declares min
   and max on one line and passes their addresses with &, then prints both results for the
   4 values. */
// END

/* Caption: Compute the distance between two points using a struct. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <math.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define a Point struct with x and y.
   2. Write distance() using sqrt(dx * dx + dy * dy).
   3. Print the distance between p and q. */
typedef struct {
    double x;
    double y;
} Point;

/* Pythagoras: sqrt(dx * dx + dy * dy). */
double distance(Point a, Point b) {
    double dx = b.x - a.x;
    double dy = b.y - a.y;
    return sqrt(dx * dx + dy * dy);
}

int main(void) {
    Point p = {8, -4};
    Point q = {7, -2};
    printf("Distance: %.3f\n", distance(p, q));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: Point is a typedef struct with x and y. distance() uses Pythagoras, sqrt(dx
   * dx + dy * dy), to measure the gap between the two points, and main() prints it. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to compute 9 to the power of 5 without pow(). */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write power(base, exp) with result = 1.
   2. Multiply result by base exp times.
   3. Print 9 to the power 5. */
/* Multiply the base by itself exp times. */
long long power(int base, int exp) {
    long long result = 1;
    for (int i = 0; i < exp; i++) {
        result *= base;
    }
    return result;
}

int main(void) {
    printf("9^5 = %lld\n", power(9, 5));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: power() starts result at 1 and multiplies it by base exp times. It uses
   long long because powers grow quickly. main() prints 9 to the power 5. */
// END

/* Caption: Write lines to a text file and read them back. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Open output.txt in write mode and check for NULL.
   2. Write 4 lines with fprintf and close the file.
   3. Open it again in read mode.
   4. Read and print each line with fgets, then close the file. */
int main(void) {
    FILE *file = fopen("output.txt", "w");
    if (file == NULL) {
        perror("fopen");
        return 1;
    }
    fprintf(file, "the compiler turns source code into machine code\n");
    fprintf(file, "good comments explain why the code exists\n");
    fprintf(file, "strings end with a null character\n");
    fprintf(file, "learning c teaches how computers work\n");
    fclose(file);

    /* Reopen the file for reading and print it line by line. */
    file = fopen("output.txt", "r");
    if (file == NULL) {
        perror("fopen");
        return 1;
    }
    char line[128];
    while (fgets(line, sizeof(line), file) != NULL) {
        printf("%s", line);
    }
    fclose(file);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: fopen() in write mode creates output.txt, fprintf() writes 4 lines into it
   and fclose() saves it. The file is then opened again in read mode, and fgets() reads it

/* Caption: Write a C program to count the words in a sentence. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <ctype.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write count_words() with words = 0 and an in_word flag.
   2. A space ends a word; a non-space after a space starts a new word and adds one to
      words.
   3. Return words and print it. */
/* A new word starts when a non-space follows a space (or the start). */
int count_words(const char *text) {
    int words = 0;
    int in_word = 0;
    for (int i = 0; text[i] != '\0'; i++) {
        if (isspace((unsigned char)text[i])) {
            in_word = 0;
        } else if (!in_word) {
            in_word = 1;
            words++;
        }
    }
    return words;
}

int main(void) {
    const char *sentence = "every program starts in main";
    printf("Words: %d\n", count_words(sentence));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: count_words() uses the flag in_word: a new word starts when a non-space
   character follows a space or the start of the text. main() prints the number of words in
   the sentence. */
// END

/* Explanation: int *px = &x, *py = &y; declares two pointers in one statement; each name
   needs its own *. *px += 3 changes x through the pointer, so x becomes 45 while y stays
   44. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to calculate the average of the values in an array. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write array_average() that takes marks and count.
   2. Add the values into the double result.
   3. Return result / count.
   4. Print the average with two decimals. */
/* The mean is the total divided by the count. */
double array_average(const int marks[], int count) {
    double result = 0.0;
    int j = 0;
    while (j < count) {
        result += marks[j];
        j++;
    }
    return result / count;
}

int main(void) {
    int marks[] = {25, 18, 38, 47, 11, 14, 15, 51, 26};
    int count = 9;
    printf("Average: %.2f\n", array_average(marks, count));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: array_average() adds the 9 values of marks into the double result and
   divides by count, so the mean keeps its decimal part even when the values are whole
   numbers. main() prints it with two decimals. */
// END

/* Return the index of wanted, or -1 when it is not in the array. */

        printf("%d is not in the array\n", wanted);
    }
    return 0;
}

   index of the first one equal to wanted, or -1 when it reaches the end without a match.
   main() searches for 179 and prints where it is, or that it is missing. */

/* Caption: Write a C program to use Euclid's algorithm to compute the GCD. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write gcd() with Euclid's algorithm.
   2. Replace (a, b) by (b, a % b) until b is 0.
   3. Return a and print the GCD of 271 and 178. */
/* Euclid: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a % b) until b becomes zero. */
int gcd(int a, int b) {
    while (b != 0) {
        int r = a % b;
        a = b;
        b = r;
    }
    return a;
}

int main(void) {
    int x = 271, y = 178;
    printf("gcd(%d, %d) = %d\n", x, y, gcd(x, y));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: gcd() uses Euclid's algorithm: it keeps replacing (a, b) with (b, a % b)
   until b is 0. The last non-zero value is the greatest common divisor, and main() prints
   the GCD of 271 and 178. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to print all prime numbers up to 73. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write is_prime(n); numbers below 2 are not prime.
   2. Try every divisor d while d * d <= n.
   3. Return false if one divides n, otherwise true.
   4. Print every prime from 2 to 73. */
/* A prime has no divisor between 2 and its square root. */
bool is_prime(int n) {
    if (n < 2) {
        return false;
    }
    for (int d = 2; d * d <= n; d++) {
        if (n % d == 0) {
            return false;
        }
    }
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    for (int n = 2; n <= 73; n++) {
        if (is_prime(n)) {
            printf("%d ", n);
        }
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: is_prime() tries every divisor d from 2 while d * d <= n; if one divides n
   evenly, n is not prime. main() tests every number from 2 to 73 and prints the primes. */
// END

/* Caption: Implement selection sort for an array of int values. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write selection_sort() for the int array scores.
   2. For each position, find the smallest remaining element.
   3. Swap it into that position.
   4. Print the sorted values. */
/* Select the right element for each position and swap it into place. */
void selection_sort(int scores[], int length) {
    for (int i = 0; i < length - 1; i++) {
        int chosen = i;
        for (int j = i + 1; j < length; j++) {
            if (scores[chosen] > scores[j]) {
                chosen = j;
            }
        }
        int tmp = scores[i];
        scores[i] = scores[chosen];
        scores[chosen] = tmp;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    int scores[] = {82, 31, 77, 6, 92, 25};
    const int length = 6;
    selection_sort(scores, length);
    for (int i = 0; i < length; i++) {
        printf("%d ", scores[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: selection_sort() finds the smallest remaining element for each position and
   swaps it into place. main() then prints the 6 values in ascending order. */
// END

double to_fahrenheit(double celsius) {

   to 60 degrees Celsius in steps of 10. */
// END

/* Caption: Search a sorted array by halving the search range each step. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Make sure the array is sorted.
   2. Set left to 0 and right to length - 1.
   3. While left <= right, compare the middle element middle with the key.
   4. Return the index if it matches; otherwise keep only the half that can hold the
      key.
   5. Return -1 if the range becomes empty, and print the index of 70. */
/* The array must be sorted. Each step halves the range that can still hold the key. */
int binary_search(const int samples[], int length, int key) {
    int left = 0;
    int right = length - 1;
    while (left <= right) {
        int middle = left + (right - left) / 2;
        if (samples[middle] == key) {
            return middle;
        } else if (samples[middle] < key) {
            left = middle + 1;   /* key is in the right half */
        } else {
            right = middle - 1;   /* key is in the left half */
        }
    }
    return -1;
}

int main(void) {
    int samples[] = {7, 12, 65, 70, 108, 122, 132, 139, 145, 190};
    int length = 10;
    int index = binary_search(samples, length, 70);
    printf("Index of 70: %d\n", index);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: binary_search() needs a sorted array. It keeps the range from left to
   right, compares the middle element middle with the key and throws away the half that
   cannot contain it, so it needs only about log2(n) steps. main() looks for 70 and prints
   its index, or -1 if it is not there. */
// END

/* Caption: C program to return a sum and an average together using pointer parameters. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write sum_and_average() with the pointers sum and average.
   2. Add the values into *sum.
   3. Store *sum / n in *average.
   4. Declare total and mean, pass their addresses and print them. */
void sum_and_average(const double v[], int n, double *sum, double *average) {
    *sum = 0.0;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        *sum += v[i];
    }
    *average = *sum / n;
}

int main(void) {
    double scores[] = {85.3, 38.6, 45.7};
    int n = sizeof(scores) / sizeof(scores[0]);
    double total, mean;
    sum_and_average(scores, n, &total, &mean);
    printf("Sum: %.2f, Average: %.2f\n", total, mean);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: sum_and_average() takes the array, its length and two pointers. It adds up
   the 3 values through *sum and then stores *sum / n in *average. main() declares total
   and mean on one line and passes their addresses. */
// END

/* Caption: Decide if 2073 is a leap year. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write is_leap(year).
   2. A year divisible by 4 is a leap year, unless it is divisible by 100.
   3. Years divisible by 400 are leap years again.
   4. Check 2073 and print the result. */
/* Leap years divide by 4, except centuries, which must divide by 400. */
int is_leap(int year) {
    return (year % 4 == 0 && year % 100 != 0) || year % 400 == 0;
}

int main(void) {
    int year = 2073;
    if (is_leap(year)) {
        printf("%d is a leap year\n", year);
    } else {
        printf("%d is not a leap year\n", year);
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: is_leap() returns true for years divisible by 4, except century years,
   which must also be divisible by 400. main() checks 2073 and prints whether it is a leap
   year. */
// END

/* Caption: C program to add two matrices element by element. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define ROWS as 2 and COLS as 2.
   2. Loop over every row r and column c.
   3. Store a[r][c] + b[r][c] in sum and print it. */
#define ROWS 2
#define COLS 2

int main(void) {
    int a[ROWS][COLS] = {{9, 8}, {6, 2}};
    int b[ROWS][COLS] = {{3, 2}, {7, 3}};
    int sum[ROWS][COLS];
    /* Each entry of the result is the sum of the matching entries. */
    for (int r = 0; r < ROWS; r++) {
        for (int c = 0; c < COLS; c++) {
            sum[r][c] = a[r][c] + b[r][c];
            printf("%3d", sum[r][c]);
        }
        printf("\n");
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: Both matrices are 2x2 two-dimensional arrays. Two nested loops visit every
   row r and column c, store a[r][c] + b[r][c] in sum and print each row. */
// END

/* Caption: Program to write a function that returns the quotient and remainder through pointers. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write divide(a, b, &quotient, &remainder) that returns a bool.
   2. Return false if b is 0.
   3. Store a / b and a % b through the pointers and return true.
   4. Divide 469 by 20 and print the results or the error. */
/* Returns false for division by zero; otherwise stores both results. */
bool divide(int a, int b, int *quotient, int *remainder) {
    if (b == 0) {
        return false;
    }
    *quotient = a / b;
    *remainder = a % b;
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    int a = 469, b = 20;
    int q, r;
    if (divide(a, b, &q, &r)) {
        printf("%d / %d = %d remainder %d\n", a, b, q, r);
    } else {
        printf("Cannot divide by zero\n");
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: divide() has four parameters: two inputs and two pointers for the results.
   Its bool return value reports success, while the quotient and remainder are written
   through the pointers. main() divides 469 by 20 and prints both results. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to store a name, age and height in variables and print them. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Caption: Write a program to find the number of digits in an integer. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Start result at 0.
   2. Divide n by 10 and add one to result.
   3. Repeat until n is 0.
   4. Apply it to 44299 and print the result. */
/* Take the last digit with % 10, then drop it with / 10. */
int count_digits(int n) {
    int result = 0;
    while (n > 0) {
        result++;
        n /= 10;
    }
    return result;
}

int main(void) {
    int number = 44299;
    printf("count of digits of %d: %d\n", number, count_digits(number));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: count_digits() removes the last digit (n / 10) and adds one to result each
   time, until n reaches 0. main() applies it to 44299. */
// END

/* Caption: Check whether a year is a leap year. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write is_leap(year).
   2. A year divisible by 4 is a leap year, unless it is divisible by 100.
   3. Years divisible by 400 are leap years again.
   4. Check 2087 and print the result. */
/* Leap years divide by 4, except centuries, which must divide by 400. */
int is_leap(int year) {
    return (year % 4 == 0 && year % 100 != 0) || year % 400 == 0;
}

int main(void) {
    int year = 2087;
    if (is_leap(year)) {
        printf("%d is a leap year\n", year);
    } else {
        printf("%d is not a leap year\n", year);
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: is_leap() returns true for years divisible by 4, except century years,
   which must also be divisible by 400. main() checks 2087 and prints whether it is a leap
   year. */
// END

/* Caption: C program to use selection sort to put numbers in ascending order. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write selection_sort() for the int array readings.
   2. For each position, find the smallest remaining element.
   3. Swap it into that position.
   4. Print the sorted values. */
/* Select the right element for each position and swap it into place. */
void selection_sort(int readings[], int size) {
    for (int i = 0; i < size - 1; i++) {
        int chosen = i;
        for (int j = i + 1; j < size; j++) {
            if (readings[chosen] > readings[j]) {
                chosen = j;
            }
        }
        int tmp = readings[i];
        readings[i] = readings[chosen];
        readings[chosen] = tmp;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    int readings[] = {94, 91, 97, 30, 46, 74, 87, 72, 56};
    const int size = 9;
    selection_sort(readings, size);
    for (int i = 0; i < size; i++) {
        printf("%d ", readings[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: selection_sort() finds the smallest remaining element for each position and
   swaps it into place. main() then prints the 9 values in ascending order. */
// END

/* Caption: How do I check whether a number lies between two limits in C? */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write in_range(x, low, high).
   2. Return true when x >= low and x <= high.
   3. Print whether 110 is inside 1 to 83. */
/* true when low <= x <= high */
bool in_range(int x, int low, int high) {
    return x >= low && x <= high;
}

int main(void) {
    int value = 110, low = 1, high = 83;
    printf("%d is %s the range %d to %d\n", value,
           in_range(value, low, high) ? "inside" : "outside", low, high);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: in_range() takes the value and both limits and returns true only when the
   value is at least low and at most high. main() declares value, low and high on one line
   and prints whether 110 is inside 1 to 83. */
// END

/* Caption: Find the arithmetic mean of 8 int values. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write array_average() that takes readings and n.
   2. Add the values into the double acc.
   3. Return acc / n.
   4. Print the average with two decimals. */
/* The mean is the total divided by the count. */
double array_average(const int readings[], int n) {
    double acc = 0.0;
    int j = 0;
    while (j < n) {
        acc += readings[j];
        j++;

    return acc / n;
}

    int n = sizeof(readings) / sizeof(readings[0]);
    printf("Mean = %.2f\n", array_average(readings, n));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: array_average() adds the 8 values of readings into the double acc and
   divides by n, so the mean keeps its decimal part even when the values are whole numbers.
   main() prints it with two decimals. */
// END

/* Caption: Allocate an array with malloc and fill it with multiples. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Use malloc to get room for 8 ints and check for NULL.
   2. Fill table with multiples.
   3. Print the values.
   4. Call free(table) at the end. */
int main(void) {
    int n = 8;
    /* Ask the heap for room for n ints; malloc returns NULL on failure. */
    int *table = malloc(n * sizeof(int));
    if (table == NULL) {
        fprintf(stderr, "malloc failed\n");
        return 1;
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        table[i] = 3 * i;
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        printf("%d ", table[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    free(table);   /* give the memory back */
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: malloc() reserves room for 8 ints on the heap and returns NULL if it fails,
   which the program checks. The first loop fills table with multiples, the second prints
   them, and free() gives the memory back at the end. */
// END

/* Caption: Limit a number to a range with a three-parameter function. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write clamp(value, low, high).
   2. Return low if the value is too small and high if it is too big.
   3. Otherwise return the value.
   4. Set low = 19 and high = 95 and print clamp() for 104, 120 and 69. */
/* Return value, but never less than low or more than high. */
int clamp(int value, int low, int high) {
    if (value < low) {
        return low;
    }
    if (value > high) {
        return high;
    }
    return value;
}

int main(void) {
    int low = 19, high = 95;
    printf("clamp(%d) = %d\n", 104, clamp(104, low, high));
    printf("clamp(%d) = %d\n", 120, clamp(120, low, high));
    printf("clamp(%d) = %d\n", 69, clamp(69, low, high));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: clamp() takes three parameters: the value and the two limits. It returns
   low when the value is too small, high when it is too big and the value itself otherwise.
   main() declares low = 19 and high = 95 on one line and clamps 104, 120 and 69. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to count the even values in a list of integers. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write count_even() that takes numbers and len.
   2. For each element, test numbers[i] % 2 == 0.
   3. Add one to count for every even number.
   4. Return count and print it. */
/* A number is even when the remainder after dividing by 2 is zero. */
int count_even(const int numbers[], int len) {
    int count = 0;
    int i = 0;
    while (i < len) {
        if (numbers[i] % 2 == 0) {
            count++;
        }
        i++;
    }
    return count;
}

int main(void) {
    int numbers[] = {35, 26, 14, 63, 58, 84, 88, 79, 28, 9, 83};
    int len = 11;
    printf("Count of even values = %d\n", count_even(numbers, len));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: count_even() tests each element of numbers with the % operator: a remainder
   of 0 after dividing by 2 means the number is even, so count goes up by one. main()
   prints how many of the 11 values are even. */
// END

/* Caption: How do I find the index of a number using linear search in C? */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write linear_search() with the array, its length and wanted.
   2. Compare each element with wanted.
   3. Return the index of the first match, or -1.
   4. In main(), search for 166 and print the result. */
/* Return the index of wanted, or -1 when it is not in the array. */
int linear_search(const int ages[], int length, int wanted) {
    for (int idx = 0; idx < length; idx++) {
        if (ages[idx] == wanted) {
            return idx;
        }
    }
    return -1;
}

int main(void) {
    int ages[] = {50, 11, 50, 43, 36, 78};
    int length = sizeof(ages) / sizeof(ages[0]);
    int wanted = 166;
    int pos = linear_search(ages, length, wanted);
    if (pos >= 0) {
        printf("Found %d at index %d\n", wanted, pos);
    } else {
        printf("%d is not in the array\n", wanted);
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: linear_search() checks the elements of ages one by one and returns the
   index of the first one equal to wanted, or -1 when it reaches the end without a match.
   main() searches for 166 and prints where it is, or that it is missing. */
// END

/* Caption: Reverse the digits of a number. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Start result at 0.
   2. Multiply result by 10, add n % 10, then divide n by 10.
   3. Repeat until n is 0.
   4. Apply it to 38753 and print the result. */
/* Take the last digit with % 10, then drop it with / 10. */
int reverse_digits(int n) {
    int result = 0;
    while (n > 0) {
        result = result * 10 + n % 10;
        n /= 10;
    }
    return result;
}

int main(void) {
    int number = 38753;
    printf("reverse of digits of %d: %d\n", number, reverse_digits(number));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: reverse_digits() shifts result one place left (result * 10) and adds the
   last digit of n, which reverses the order. main() applies it to 38753. */
// END

/* Caption: Reverse an array by swapping from both ends. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write reverse_array() for items.
   2. Set start to the first index and end to the last.
   3. Swap items[start] and items[end], then move both inwards.
   4. Stop when start meets end and print the array. */
/* Swap the outer pair, then move both ends toward the middle. */
void reverse_array(int items[], int length) {
    int start = 0;
    int end = length - 1;
    while (start < end) {
        int tmp = items[start];
        items[start] = items[end];
        items[end] = tmp;
        start++;
        end--;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    int items[] = {94, 28, 84, 77, 52, 43};
    int length = 6;
    reverse_array(items, length);
    for (int i = 0; i < length; i++) {
        printf("%d ", items[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: reverse_array() swaps the first and last elements, then moves start forward
   and end backward until they meet, so the array is reversed in place without a second
   array. main() prints the reversed values. */
// END

   main() prints it with two decimals. */

/* Caption: Implement a circular queue with an array. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define a Queue with room for 8 items, a head and a count.
   2. Write enqueue() that stores at (head + count) % CAPACITY.
   3. Write dequeue() that takes the item at head and moves head on.
   4. Add 6 values, then remove and print them in order. */
#define CAPACITY 8

typedef struct {
    int items[CAPACITY];
    int head;
    int count;
} Queue;

bool enqueue(Queue *q, int value) {
    if (q->count == CAPACITY) {
        return false;
    }
    /* The tail wraps around to the start of the array. */
    q->items[(q->head + q->count) % CAPACITY] = value;
    q->count++;
    return true;
}

bool dequeue(Queue *q, int *value) {
    if (q->count == 0) {
        return false;
    }
    *value = q->items[q->head];
    q->head = (q->head + 1) % CAPACITY;
    q->count--;
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    Queue q = {.head = 0, .count = 0};
    enqueue(&q, 39);
    enqueue(&q, 67);
    enqueue(&q, 61);
    enqueue(&q, 89);
    enqueue(&q, 18);
    enqueue(&q, 63);
    int value;
    /* Items come out in the order they went in (first in, first out). */
    while (dequeue(&q, &value)) {
        printf("%d ", value);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: The Queue stores up to 8 items in a ring buffer: head is the oldest item
   and % CAPACITY wraps positions back to the start of the array. enqueue() adds at the
   back and dequeue() removes from the front, so main() gets its 6 values back in the same
   order (first in, first out). */
// END

/* Caption: Use insertion sort to put numbers in ascending order. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write insertion_sort() for the int array marks.
   2. Take each element in turn as current.
   3. Shift the larger values of the sorted part one place right.
   4. Put current into the gap.
   5. Print the sorted values. */
/* Insert each element into the already sorted part on its left. */
void insertion_sort(int marks[], int n) {
    for (int i = 1; i < n; i++) {
        int current = marks[i];
        int j = i - 1;
        while (j >= 0 && marks[j] > current) {
            marks[j + 1] = marks[j];   /* shift bigger values right */
            j--;
        }
        marks[j + 1] = current;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    int marks[] = {75, 75, 38, 3, 93, 53};
    int n = sizeof(marks) / sizeof(marks[0]);
    insertion_sort(marks, n);
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        printf("%d ", marks[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: insertion_sort() takes each element in turn and shifts the larger values of
   the sorted part one place right until the element fits. main() then prints the 6 values
   in ascending order. */
// END

/* Caption: Divide two integers and get both the quotient and the remainder. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write divide(a, b, &quotient, &remainder) that returns a bool.
   2. Return false if b is 0.
   3. Store a / b and a % b through the pointers and return true.
   4. Divide 495 by 3 and print the results or the error. */
/* Returns false for division by zero; otherwise stores both results. */
bool divide(int a, int b, int *quotient, int *remainder) {
    if (b == 0) {
        return false;
    }
    *quotient = a / b;
    *remainder = a % b;
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    int a = 495, b = 3;
    int q, r;
    if (divide(a, b, &q, &r)) {
        printf("%d / %d = %d remainder %d\n", a, b, q, r);
    } else {
        printf("Cannot divide by zero\n");
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: divide() has four parameters: two inputs and two pointers for the results.
   Its bool return value reports success, while the quotient and remainder are written
   through the pointers. main() divides 495 by 3 and prints both results. */
// END

/* Caption: Use Euclid's algorithm to compute the GCD. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write gcd() with Euclid's algorithm.
   2. Replace (a, b) by (b, a % b) until b is 0.
   3. Return a and print the GCD of 206 and 55. */
/* Euclid: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a % b) until b becomes zero. */
int gcd(int a, int b) {
    while (b != 0) {
        int r = a % b;
        a = b;
        b = r;
    }
    return a;
}

int main(void) {
    int x = 206, y = 55;
    printf("gcd(%d, %d) = %d\n", x, y, gcd(x, y));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: gcd() uses Euclid's algorithm: it keeps replacing (a, b) with (b, a % b)
   until b is 0. The last non-zero value is the greatest common divisor, and main() prints
   the GCD of 206 and 55. */
// END

/* Plan:
   1. Set a and b.
   2. Pick the bigger of a and b.
   3. Print it. */

/* Caption: Copy one string into another by hand. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write copy_string(dest, src).
   2. Copy src into dest one character at a time.
   3. Stop after copying the null character.
   4. Copy planet into str and print it. */
/* Copy each character, including the final '\0'. */
void copy_string(char *dest, const char *src) {
    int i = 0;
    while ((dest[i] = src[i]) != '\0') {
        i++;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    char source[] = "planet";
    char str[100];
    copy_string(str, source);
    printf("Copied: %s\n", str);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: copy_string() copies src into dest one character at a time, including the
   final null character, which is what strcpy does. The array str must be big enough to
   hold the copy. main() copies the word planet and prints it. */
// END

/* Caption: Count the characters in a string. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write string_length() with a counter len = 0.
   2. Move through the string until the null character.
   3. Return len and print the length of stats. */
/* Count characters until the terminating '\0'. */
int string_length(const char *word) {
    int len = 0;
    while (word[len] != '\0') {
        len++;
    }
    return len;
}

int main(void) {
    const char *word = "stats";
    printf("Length of \"%s\" is %d\n", word, string_length(word));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: string_length() counts characters until it reaches the null character that
   ends every C string. main() prints the length of the word stats. */
// END

/* Caption: Check every element of an array to find a target value. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write linear_search() with the array, its length and wanted.
   2. Compare each element with wanted.
   3. Return the index of the first match, or -1.
   4. In main(), search for 1 and print the result. */
/* Return the index of wanted, or -1 when it is not in the array. */
int linear_search(const int nums[], int size, int wanted) {
    for (int k = 0; k < size; k++) {
        if (nums[k] == wanted) {
            return k;
        }
    }
    return -1;
}

int main(void) {
    int nums[] = {53, 57, 56, 83, 1, 47, 21};
    const int size = 7;
    int wanted = 1;
    int pos = linear_search(nums, size, wanted);
    if (pos >= 0) {
        printf("Found %d at index %d\n", wanted, pos);
    } else {
        printf("%d is not in the array\n", wanted);
    }
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: linear_search() checks the elements of nums one by one and returns the
   index of the first one equal to wanted, or -1 when it reaches the end without a match.
   main() searches for 1 and prints where it is, or that it is missing. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to use binary search to locate a value in a sorted list. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Make sure the array is sorted.
   2. Set low to 0 and high to n - 1.
   3. While low <= high, compare the middle element mid with the key.
   4. Return the index if it matches; otherwise keep only the half that can hold the
      key.
   5. Return -1 if the range becomes empty, and print the index of 40. */
/* The array must be sorted. Each step halves the range that can still hold the key. */
int binary_search(const int marks[], int n, int key) {
    int low = 0;
    int high = n - 1;
    while (low <= high) {
        int mid = low + (high - low) / 2;
        if (marks[mid] == key) {
            return mid;
        } else if (marks[mid] < key) {
            low = mid + 1;   /* key is in the right half */
        } else {
            high = mid - 1;   /* key is in the left half */
        }
    }
    return -1;
}

int main(void) {
    int marks[] = {15, 40, 53, 64, 101, 113, 114, 131, 170};
    const int n = 9;
    int index = binary_search(marks, n, 40);
    printf("Index of 40: %d\n", index);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: binary_search() needs a sorted array. It keeps the range from low to high,
   compares the middle element mid with the key and throws away the half that cannot
   contain it, so it needs only about log2(n) steps. main() looks for 40 and prints its
   index, or -1 if it is not there. */
// END

/* Caption: C program to convert 696 to binary. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write print_binary(n, bits).
   2. Go through the bits from the highest to the lowest.
   3. Print 1 when (n >> b) & 1 is set, otherwise 0.
   4. Print 696 in binary. */
/* Check each bit from the highest to the lowest. */
void print_binary(unsigned int n, int bits) {
    for (int b = bits - 1; b >= 0; b--) {
        putchar((n >> b) & 1 ? '1' : '0');
    }
    putchar('\n');
}

int main(void) {
    unsigned int number = 696;
    printf("%u in binary: ", number);
    print_binary(number, 8);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: print_binary() checks one bit at a time, from the highest to the lowest: (n
   >> b) & 1 is 1 when bit b is set, so it prints the character 1 or 0. main() prints 696
   in binary. */
// END

/* Caption: C program to declare variables first and give them values later. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Declare count, total and i on one line without values.
   2. Set count = 11 and total = 0.
   3. Add the squares of 1 to count to total and print it. */
int main(void) {
    int count, total, i;   /* declared now, given values below */
    count = 11;
    total = 0;
    for (i = 1; i <= count; i++) {
        total += i * i;
    }
    printf("Sum of the first %d squares: %d\n", count, total);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: count, total and i are declared together on one line without values, then
   assigned before they are used, because an uninitialised local variable holds garbage.
   The loop adds the squares of 1 to 11 to total. */
// END

/* Caption: Implement a stack with an array (push and pop). */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdbool.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define a Stack with room for 10 items and a top counter.
   2. Write push() and pop(), returning false when the stack is full or empty.
   3. Push 4 values.
   4. Pop and print until the stack is empty. */
#define CAPACITY 10

typedef struct {
    int items[CAPACITY];
    int top;   /* number of items on the stack */
} Stack;

bool push(Stack *s, int value) {
    if (s->top == CAPACITY) {
        return false;   /* stack is full */
    }
    s->items[s->top++] = value;
    return true;
}

bool pop(Stack *s, int *value) {
    if (s->top == 0) {
        return false;   /* stack is empty */
    }
    *value = s->items[--s->top];
    return true;
}

int main(void) {
    Stack s = {.top = 0};
    push(&s, 5);
    push(&s, 90);
    push(&s, 82);
    push(&s, 6);
    int value;
    /* Items come back out in reverse order (last in, first out). */
    while (pop(&s, &value)) {
        printf("%d ", value);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: The Stack keeps up to 10 items in an array, and top counts how many are
   stored. push() adds at the top and pop() removes from the top; both return false when
   they cannot. main() pushes 4 values and pops them all, so they come out in reverse order
   (last in, first out). */
// END

/* Caption: Write a program to implement bubble sort for an array of long values. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write bubble_sort() for the long array marks.
   2. Compare each pair of neighbours.
   3. Swap them when they are in the wrong order for ascending order.
   4. Repeat the passes until the array is sorted.
   5. Print the sorted values. */
/* Repeatedly swap neighbours that are in the wrong order. */
void bubble_sort(long marks[], int len) {
    for (int i = 0; i < len - 1; i++) {
        for (int j = 0; j < len - 1 - i; j++) {
            if (marks[j] > marks[j + 1]) {
                long tmp = marks[j];
                marks[j] = marks[j + 1];
                marks[j + 1] = tmp;
            }
        }
    }
}

int main(void) {
    long marks[] = {64L, 40L, 88L, 4L, 33L, 82L};
    int len = 6;
    bubble_sort(marks, len);
    for (int i = 0; i < len; i++) {
        printf("%ld ", marks[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: bubble_sort() walks through marks again and again and swaps neighbours that
   are in the wrong order, so the largest values move to the end first. main() then prints
   the 6 values in ascending order. */
// END

}
/* Explanation: circle_measures() computes two results from one radius and stores them
   through the pointers area and circumference. main() declares both variables on one line,
   passes their addresses and prints the results for a radius of 8.8. */
// END

/* Caption: C program to save text to a file with fprintf and print it with fgets. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Open data.txt in write mode and check for NULL.
   2. Write 3 lines with fprintf and close the file.
   3. Open it again in read mode.
   4. Read and print each line with fgets, then close the file. */
int main(void) {
    FILE *file = fopen("data.txt", "w");
    if (file == NULL) {
        perror("fopen");
        return 1;
    }
    fprintf(file, "every program starts in main\n");
    fprintf(file, "a function can call itself recursively\n");
    fprintf(file, "the quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog\n");
    fclose(file);

    /* Reopen the file for reading and print it line by line. */
    file = fopen("data.txt", "r");
    if (file == NULL) {
        perror("fopen");
        return 1;
    }
    char line[128];
    while (fgets(line, sizeof(line), file) != NULL) {
        printf("%s", line);
    }
    fclose(file);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: fopen() in write mode creates data.txt, fprintf() writes 3 lines into it
   and fclose() saves it. The file is then opened again in read mode, and fgets() reads it
   back line by line into the buffer line, which is printed. Every fopen() result is
   checked for NULL. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to create a singly linked list by inserting at the head. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Define Item with a value and a next pointer.
   2. Write push_front() that mallocs a node and links it in front of head.
   3. Write print_list() that follows next until NULL.
   4. Write free_list() that frees every node.
   5. Push 5 values, print the list and free it. */
typedef struct Item {
    int value;
    struct Item *next;
} Item;

/* Allocate a new node and put it in front of the current head. */
Item *push_front(Item *head, int value) {
    Item *node = malloc(sizeof(Item));
    if (node == NULL) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Out of memory\n");
        exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
    }
    node->value = value;
    node->next = head;
    return node;
}

void print_list(const Item *head) {
    for (const Item *cur = head; cur != NULL; cur = cur->next) {
        printf("%d -> ", cur->value);
    }
    printf("NULL\n");
}

/* Free every node; save next before freeing the current one. */
void free_list(Item *head) {
    while (head != NULL) {
        Item *next = head->next;
        free(head);
        head = next;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    Item *head = NULL;
    head = push_front(head, 66);
    head = push_front(head, 76);
    head = push_front(head, 68);
    head = push_front(head, 73);
    head = push_front(head, 33);
    print_list(head);
    free_list(head);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: Each Item holds a value and a pointer to the next node. push_front()
   allocates a node with malloc, puts it in front of head and returns it; print_list()
   follows the next pointers until NULL; free_list() frees every node. main() pushes 5
   values, so they print in reverse order. */
// END

/* Caption: Count how many digits a number has. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Start result at 0.
   2. Divide n by 10 and add one to result.
   3. Repeat until n is 0.
   4. Apply it to 611872 and print the result. */
/* Take the last digit with % 10, then drop it with / 10. */
int count_digits(int n) {
    int result = 0;
    while (n > 0) {
        result++;
        n /= 10;
    }
    return result;
}

int main(void) {
    int number = 611872;
    printf("count of digits of %d: %d\n", number, count_digits(number));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: count_digits() removes the last digit (n / 10) and adds one to result each
   time, until n reaches 0. main() applies it to 611872. */
// END

/* Caption: Count how many odd numbers are in an array. */
#include <stdio.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Write count_odd() that takes scores and length.
   2. For each element, test scores[idx] % 2 != 0.
   3. Add one to matches for every odd number.
   4. Return matches and print it. */
/* A number is odd when the remainder after dividing by 2 is one. */
int count_odd(const int scores[], int length) {
    int matches = 0;
    int idx = 0;
    while (idx < length) {
        if (scores[idx] % 2 != 0) {
            matches++;
        }
        idx++;
    }
    return matches;
}

int main(void) {
    int scores[] = {82, 2, 6, 45, 91};
    int length = 5;
    printf("Odd numbers: %d\n", count_odd(scores, length));
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: count_odd() tests each element of scores with the % operator: a remainder
   of 1 after dividing by 2 means the number is odd, so matches goes up by one. main()
   prints how many of the 5 values are odd. */
// END

/* Caption: Write a C program to use dynamic memory to store the first 11 multiples. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

/* Plan:
   1. Use malloc to get room for 11 ints and check for NULL.
   2. Fill arr with multiples.
   3. Print the values.
   4. Call free(arr) at the end. */
int main(void) {
    int n = 11;
    /* Ask the heap for room for n ints; malloc returns NULL on failure. */
    int *arr = malloc(n * sizeof(int));
    if (arr == NULL) {
        fprintf(stderr, "malloc failed\n");
        return 1;
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        arr[i] = 4 * i;
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        printf("%d ", arr[i]);
    }
    printf("\n");
    free(arr);   /* give the memory back */
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: malloc() reserves room for 11 ints on the heap and returns NULL if it
   fails, which the program checks. The first loop fills arr with multiples, the second
   prints them, and free() gives the memory back at the end. */
// END

/* Caption: Program to change every letter in a sentence to a capital letter. */

/* Plan:

   2. Replace every character with toupper() until the null character.
   3. Print the sentence. */
/* toupper changes lowercase letters and leaves other characters alone. */
void to_upper(char *text) {
    for (int i = 0; text[i] != '\0'; i++) {

    }
}

int main(void) {

    to_upper(text);
    printf("%s\n", text);
    return 0;
}
/* Explanation: to_upper() walks through text until the null character and replaces each
   character with toupper(), which only changes lowercase letters. main() prints the
   sentence in capitals. */
// END
